title: 14.24.12 Concentrating smooth test potentials
text: The next proposition produces smooth test potentials whose Monge–Ampère density dominates a fixed multiple of a prescribed function $g$, with a constant independent of $\sup _ Xg$ and of the derivatives of $g$. This uniformity allows the test densities to concentrate near a set of measure zero. Proposition 14.24.13 . 7F590FD94846 For every $B_0>\| 1\| _{L^2(\omega ^ n)}$ there is $\varepsilon =\varepsilon (X,\omega ,B_0)>0$ such that every smooth function $g\geq 1$ with $\| g\| _{L^2(\omega ^ n)}\leq B_0$ admits a smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function $q$ satisfying 6928CCD52E25 14.24.14 \begin{equation}  \omega _ q^ n\geq \varepsilon g \omega ^ n. \end{equation} Proof. Choose finitely many coordinate balls $B_ j=\{ |z_ j|<R_ j\} $, with closures in their charts, such that the concentric smaller balls $\{ |z_ j|<r_ j\} $ cover $X$. On $B_ j$, let $\psi _ j$ solve the Dirichlet problem 768EAB7723D9 14.24.15 \begin{equation}  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ j)^ n=g\omega ^ n,\qquad \psi _ j|_{\partial B_ j}=0. \end{equation} The density of $g\omega ^ n$ with respect to coordinate volume is smooth and strictly positive. The classical smooth Dirichlet theorem therefore applies, since $C_ j(|z_ j|^2-R_ j^2)$ is a smooth strict subsolution with zero boundary values for sufficiently large $C_ j>0$. Thus $\psi _ j$ is smooth and strictly plurisubharmonic on $\overline B_ j$, and the maximum principle gives $\psi _ j\leq 0$. We need a lower bound for $\psi _ j$ independent of $\sup _ Xg$. Write the coordinate equation as $\det (\partial _ a\bar\partial _ b\psi _ j)=D_ j$, and put $M_ j=-\min _{B_ j}\psi _ j$. Let $x_ j$ be a minimum point. For each real slope $p$ with $|p|<M_ j/(2R_ j)$, the function $\psi _ j-p\cdot (x-x_ j)$ attains its minimum at an interior point, because its value at $x_ j$ is $-M_ j$, while its boundary values are larger than $-M_ j$. At such a contact point the real Hessian $S$ of $\psi _ j$ is nonnegative, and the gradient of $\psi _ j$ maps the contact set onto the ball of these slopes. The area formula and the matrix inequality \[  \det _{\mathbb R}S\leq 4^ n\bigl (\det _{\mathbb C}(\partial _ a\bar\partial _ b\psi _ j)\bigr )^2=4^ nD_ j^2  \] therefore give $M_ j\leq C(n,R_ j)\| D_ j\| _{L^2(B_ j)}^{1/n}$. To prove the matrix inequality, let $J$ be the standard complex structure on the real coordinate space and average $S$ with $J^\mathsf TSJ$. Concavity of $\log \det $, and the fact that the eigenvalues of this $J$-invariant average occur in pairs, give the displayed factor; singular matrices are handled by approximation. Since the ratio of $\omega ^ n$ to coordinate volume is fixed and bounded, $\| D_ j\| _2$ is controlled by $B_0$. Consequently 7044361ECDC0 14.24.16 \begin{equation}  -M_0\leq \psi _ j\leq 0\quad \text{on every }B_ j, \end{equation} where $M_0$ depends only on $X,\omega ,B_0$ and the chosen finite cover. Next we glue the local solutions. Put $\beta _ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z_ j|^2$. Choose $a_ j>0$ such that $a_ j\beta _ j\leq \omega /2$ on $B_ j$, and let $t_ j=(R_ j^2+r_ j^2)/2$. Fix $\tau >0$ so small that $\tau M_0<a_ j(R_ j^2-r_ j^2)/4$ for every $j$. The smooth function \[  s_ j=\tau \psi _ j+a_ j(t_ j-|z_ j|^2)  \] is bounded below by a fixed positive constant on the smaller ball, negative on a collar of $\partial B_ j$, and satisfies $\omega _{s_ j}\geq \omega /2+\tau \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ j$. Choose a smooth convex function $\phi _ j:\mathbb R\to \mathbb R$ approximating $s\mapsto \max (s,0)$, equal to zero below a small negative threshold and to $s$ above the corresponding positive threshold, with $0\leq \phi _ j'\leq 1$ and $\phi _ j''\geq 0$; the thresholds are chosen smaller in absolute value than both margins of $s_ j$. Set $Q_ j=\phi _ j(s_ j)$ on $B_ j$ and extend it by zero. This extension is smooth, and \[  \omega _{Q_ j}=\phi _ j'(s_ j)\omega _{s_ j}+\bigl (1-\phi _ j'(s_ j)\bigr )\omega +\phi _ j''(s_ j)\, \mathrm{d} s_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s_ j\geq \omega /2.  \] On the smaller ball, $Q_ j=s_ j$ and $\omega _{Q_ j}\geq \tau \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ j$. If $N$ is the number of balls, put $q=N^{-1}\sum _ jQ_ j$. Then $\omega _ q=N^{-1}\sum _ j\omega _{Q_ j}\geq \omega /2$ everywhere. Each point belongs to at least one smaller ball $\{ |z_ j|<r_ j\} $, so positivity of the other summands and ( 14.24.15 ) give \[  \omega _ q^ n\geq (\tau /N)^ n(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ j)^ n=(\tau /N)^ n g \omega ^ n.  \] Thus ( 14.24.14 ) holds with $\varepsilon =(\tau /N)^ n$, independent of $\sup g$ and of all derivatives of $g$. $\square$ of theorem 14.24.1 . By corollary 14.19.29 , $u,v$ are continuous. In dimension one, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=0$, so the maximum principle makes $w$ constant. Assume $n\geq 2$. Suppose that $w=u-v$ is nonconstant. Let $a=\min _ Xw$, $K=\{ w=a\} $, and $\mu =F\omega ^ n$. By lemma 14.24.11 , $\mu (K)=0$. Choose $B_0>\| 1\| _{L^2(\omega ^ n)}$ and let $\varepsilon >0$ be the constant from proposition 14.24.13 . Since $\mu (K)=0$, the compact set $K_0=K\cap \{ F\geq \varepsilon /2\} $ has zero $\omega ^ n$-volume. Fix $A>1$ with $\varepsilon A>\max _ XF$. By outer regularity of the smooth volume measure, choose an open neighborhood $O$ of $K_0$ so small that \[  \int _ X\omega ^ n+(A^2-1)\int _ O\omega ^ n<B_0^2.  \] Take a smooth $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ equal to one near $K_0$ and supported in $O$, and set $g=1+(A-1)\chi $. If $K_0=\varnothing $, take $\chi =0$. Then $g\geq 1$, $g=A$ on $K_0$, and $\| g\| _{L^2(\omega ^ n)}<B_0$. By proposition 14.24.13 , there is a smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic $q$ with $\omega _ q^ n=G\omega ^ n\geq \varepsilon g\omega ^ n$. On $K_0$ we have $G\geq \varepsilon A>F$; on $K\setminus K_0$ we have $F<\varepsilon /2<\varepsilon \leq G$. Thus $G>F$ throughout the compact set $K$. By compactness and continuity, we can choose $0<\kappa <1$ such that $F<\kappa G$ on $K$; put $W=\{ F<\kappa G\} $. The complement of this open neighborhood of $K$ is compact, and $w-a$ has a strictly positive minimum there if it is nonempty. Hence some $\eta >0$ satisfies $\{ w<a+\eta \} \subset W$. Proposition 14.24.2 asserts that $\mu (\{ w<a+\eta \} \cap \{ F>\kappa G\} )>0$. By the preceding inclusion, however, this set is empty. This contradiction shows that $w$ is constant. If $\sup _ Xu=\sup _ Xv$, the constant is zero. $\square$ For a bounded measurable density, a positive lower bound gives the same conclusion. In this case coercivity holds on all of $X$, and the concentrating test potential can dominate the essential upper bound of the density on a whole neighborhood of the extremal set. Corollary 14.24.17 . 527FB17149BB If $0<c_0\leq F\leq C_0<\infty $ almost everywhere and bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions satisfy $\omega _ u^ n=\omega _ v^ n=F\omega ^ n$, then $u-v$ is constant. Proof. The functions $u,v$ are continuous by corollary 14.19.29 , and in dimension one the assertion follows from $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u-v)=0$ and the maximum principle. Let $n\geq 2$, suppose that $w=u-v$ is nonconstant, and put $K=\{ w=\min _ Xw\} $. The proof of lemma 14.24.11 applies with $U=X$, since proposition 14.24.5 gives the pushforward identity and local coercivity on every chart. Thus $K$ has zero volume. Fix $B_0>\| 1\| _{L^2(\omega ^ n)}$ and the corresponding $\varepsilon $ in proposition 14.24.13 . Choose $A>1$ with $\varepsilon A>C_0$, and a smooth cutoff function $\chi $, equal to one on a neighborhood $W$ of $K$ and supported in an open set of volume so small that $g=1+(A-1)\chi $ satisfies $\| g\| _2<B_0$. The resulting test potential $q$ has density $G\geq \varepsilon g$. Choose $\kappa <1$ with $C_0<\kappa \varepsilon A$. Then $F<\kappa G$ almost everywhere on $W$. By continuity of $w$, a sufficiently thin set $\{ w<\min _ Xw+\eta \} $ lies inside $W$, which contradicts proposition 14.24.2 . Hence $w$ is constant. $\square$

title: 14.25 Comparison and invariant mass
text: The preceding argument controls the extremal level sets of $u-v$ through connectedness of the set where the density is positive. When the background satisfies the Guan–Li condition below, invariance of the total mass gives the ordinary comparison principle instead. An auxiliary solution whose density is larger on a strict sublevel set of $u-v$ then forces this set to have zero mass for the common Monge–Ampère measure, and the domination principle proves uniqueness. Set $V=\int _ X\omega ^ n$. The Guan–Li condition 0B3AF72C81CB 14.25.1 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0,\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^2)=0  \end{equation} is equivalent to invariance of the total mass $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)$ by lemma 11.1.3 , theorem 11.1.7 . In dimension one it holds automatically, for degree reasons. Theorem 14.25.2 . 27DED19DBC11 Assume ( 14.25.1 ), let $p>1$, and let $f\geq 0$ belong to $L^ p(X,\omega ^ n)$ with positive integral. Then there is exactly one pair $(c,u)$, with $c>0$, $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty (X)$ and $\sup _ Xu=0$, satisfying \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=c f\, \omega ^ n.  \] Moreover \[  c=\frac{\int _ X\omega ^ n}{\int f\, \omega ^ n},  \] and $u$ is continuous. Thus two bounded solutions with the same $L^ p$ density differ by a constant, without any positive lower bound on $f$. We first show that the ordinary comparison principle is equivalent to invariance of the mass. Theorem 14.25.3 . FE27B72E2DB5 Condition ( 14.25.1 ) holds if and only if every pair of bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $a,b$ satisfies A25B3D75AF64 14.25.4 \begin{equation}  \int _{\{ a<b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (b) \leq \int _{\{ a<b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (a). \end{equation} For the converse implication, it suffices to require this inequality for smooth potentials. Proof. Under ( 14.25.1 ), theorem 11.1.7 gives $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\omega (a)=V$ for every bounded potential $a$; for $n=1$ this is Stokes' theorem. Set $q=\max (a,b)$. On $\{ a<b\} $, plurifine locality gives $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (q)=\mathrm{MA}_\omega (b)$. On $\{ a\geq b\} $, one has $a=q$, and $a\leq q$ everywhere, so bounded ordered contact (lemma 5.28.3 ) gives \[  \mathbf1_{\{ a\geq b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (a) \leq \mathbf1_{\{ a\geq b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (q).  \] The total masses of $a$, $b$ and $q$ all equal $V$. Hence \[  \int _{\{ a<b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (b)=V-\int _{\{ a\geq b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (q) \leq V-\int _{\{ a\geq b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (a)=\int _{\{ a<b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (a),  \] which is ( 14.25.4 ). Conversely, comparison for smooth potentials implies that all smooth potentials have the same mass: given a smooth pair $a,b$, add to $b$ a constant so large that $\{ a<b\} =X$, apply ( 14.25.4 ), and then interchange the roles of $a$ and $b$. Comparison with the zero potential shows that the common mass is $V$. By theorem 11.1.7 , lemma 11.1.3 , this implies ( 14.25.1 ) when $n\geq 2$; for $n=1$ that condition holds for degree reasons. $\square$ For the uniqueness argument we need, in addition to comparison, auxiliary solutions and the mixed inequality ( 5.28.9 ). The auxiliary solutions come from continuous existence: if $G\geq 0$ lies in $L^ p(X,\omega ^ n)$ and $\int _ XG\omega ^ n=V$, theorem 14.19.2 gives a continuous solution of $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (\rho )=cG\omega ^ n$ with a constant $c>0$, and since all bounded potentials have mass $V$, this constant equals one. Thus A548048D0134 14.25.5 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (\rho )=G\omega ^ n \end{equation} has a continuous solution $\rho $ for every such $G$, in particular for the density with an indicator factor used below. of 14.25.2 . We use the domination principle in the form of the case $c=0$ of theorem 14.19.10 : if $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (a)(\{ a<b\} )=0$ for bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $a,b$, then $a\geq b$. We first prove that two bounded solutions $u,v$ of $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=\mathrm{MA}_\omega (v)=\mu =F\omega ^ n$, with $F\in L^ p$, $p>1$, differ by a constant. The mass identity gives $\mu (X)=V$. If $u-v$ is nonconstant, add a constant to $u$ so that $u-v$ has supremum $s>0$ and infimum $-s$. Since $\{ v<u\} $ and $\{ u<v\} $ are disjoint, after interchanging $u$ and $v$ if necessary, the set $S=\{ v<u\} $ satisfies $\mu (S)\leq V/2$. Define \[  b_0=\frac{V-2\mu (S)}V\geq 0, \qquad G=2F\mathbf1_ S+b_0.  \] This nonnegative $L^ p$ function has total integral $V$, so we can choose a continuous solution $\rho $ of ( 14.25.5 ). Take $C_0$ with $\rho -C_0\leq u$, and set \[  q_\delta =(1-\delta )u+\delta (\rho -C_0),\qquad E_\delta =\{ v<q_\delta \} \subset S, \qquad 0<\delta <1.  \] Since $G\geq 2F$ on $S$, the mixed inequality ( 5.28.9 ) gives, on $S$, 0024EEF19B40 14.25.6 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (q_\delta )\geq \bigl ((1-\delta )+\delta 2^{1/n}\bigr )^ n\mu =:A_\delta \mu , \qquad A_\delta >1. \end{equation} Ordinary comparison ( 14.25.4 ), applied to the pair $v,q_\delta $, yields \[  A_\delta \mu (E_\delta ) \leq \int _{E_\delta }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (q_\delta ) \leq \int _{E_\delta }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (v)=\mu (E_\delta ).  \] Thus $\mu (E_\delta )=0$, that is, $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (v)(\{ v<q_\delta \} )=0$. Bounded domination gives $v\geq q_\delta $ everywhere, and letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ gives $v\geq u$, which contradicts $\sup _ X(u-v)=s>0$. Therefore $u-v$ is constant. The argument never divides by $F$, so $F$ may vanish on an open set. Finally, for the density $f$ in the theorem, put $I=\int _ Xf\omega ^ n>0$ and $c=V/I$. By ( 14.25.5 ) with $G=cf$, there is a continuous solution, which we normalize by subtracting its supremum. Any other bounded solution, with constant $c'$, satisfies $V=c'I$ by mass invariance, hence $c'=c$; the uniqueness just proved and the common normalization then identify the potentials. In particular, every bounded solution with this $L^ p$ density is continuous, although continuity was not assumed. $\square$ Remark 14.25.7 . EFB13673C92A 14.25.3 is an equivalence between a differential condition, the comparison principle and mass invariance. It is not an equivalence between the Guan–Li condition and uniqueness: the other criteria in this chapter apply without that condition on the background. On the other hand, imposing the Guan–Li condition on an auxiliary metric rather than on $\omega $ does not give ( 14.25.4 ) for $\mathrm{MA}_\omega $.

text: Theorem 14.25.3 . FE27B72E2DB5 Condition ( 14.25.1 ) holds if and only if every pair of bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $a,b$ satisfies A25B3D75AF64 14.25.4 \begin{equation}  \int _{\{ a<b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (b) \leq \int _{\{ a<b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (a). \end{equation} For the converse implication, it suffices to require this inequality for smooth potentials. On $\{ a<b\} $, plurifine locality gives $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (q)=\mathrm{MA}_\omega (b)$. On $\{ a\geq b\} $, one has $a=q$, and $a\leq q$ everywhere, so bounded ordered contact (lemma 5.28.3 ) gives \[  \mathbf1_{\{ a\geq b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (a) \leq \mathbf1_{\{ a\geq b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (q).  \] The total masses of $a$, $b$ and $q$ all equal $V$. Hence \[  \int _{\{ a<b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (b)=V-\int _{\{ a\geq b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (q) \leq V-\int _{\{ a\geq b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (a)=\int _{\{ a<b\} }\mathrm{MA}_\omega (a),  \] which is ( 14.25.4 ). Conversely, comparison for smooth potentials implies that all smooth potentials have the same mass: given a smooth pair $a,b$, add to $b$ a constant so large that $\{ a<b\} =X$, apply ( 14.25.4 ), and then interchange the roles of $a$ and $b$. Comparison with the zero potential shows that the common mass is $V$. By theorem 11.1.7 , lemma 11.1.3 , this implies ( 14.25.1 ) when $n\geq 2$; for $n=1$ that condition holds for degree reasons. $\square$

section: 14.26 Smooth nonuniqueness for a degenerate density
text: The first example places the freedom in the potential inside an open region where the density vanishes. Three independent semipositive forms of rank one reduce equality of the Monge–Ampère measures to equality of products of three scalar coefficients. We construct two semipositive forms with the same cube, and then add the same exact correction to both to obtain a strictly positive background. In this section and the following ones, $X=\mathbb P(\mathbb C^2\oplus \mathbb C^2)=\mathbb P^3$, with block homogeneous coordinates $[A:B]$, where $A,B\in \mathbb C^2$, and $\omega _ X$ is its Fubini–Study form. Here $A$ and $B$ denote coordinates, not the forms of ( 14.20.1 ); the two solution forms will be written $A_0$ and $B_0$. Theorem 14.26.1 . 050594389138 On $X=\mathbb P^3$ there exist a smooth Hermitian form $\omega $ with $\mathrm{d}\omega \ne 0$, a smooth nonnegative nonzero function $f$, and distinct smooth functions $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ such that \[  \sup _ Xu=\sup _ Xv=0,\qquad (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3=f\omega _ X^3=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^3.  \] The density vanishes on a nonempty open set, and both potentials have minimal singularities.

title: Theorem 14.26.1
section: 14.26 Smooth nonuniqueness for a degenerate density
text: Theorem 14.26.1 . 050594389138 On $X=\mathbb P^3$ there exist a smooth Hermitian form $\omega $ with $\mathrm{d}\omega \ne 0$, a smooth nonnegative nonzero function $f$, and distinct smooth functions $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ such that \[  \sup _ Xu=\sup _ Xv=0,\qquad (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3=f\omega _ X^3=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^3.  \] The density vanishes on a nonempty open set, and both potentials have minimal singularities. of theorem 14.26.1 . Set $\widetilde u=-w/2-\rho $ and $\widetilde v=w/2-\rho $. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=2H$, the construction gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u=A_0\geq 0,\qquad \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v=B_0\geq 0.  \] Subtracting their respective suprema gives $u,v$. Their Hessians are unchanged, and $v-u=w+\text{constant}$ is nonconstant. The function $f=A_0^3/\omega _ X^3=B_0^3/\omega _ X^3$ is smooth, nonnegative and nonzero, and it vanishes on the nonempty open band $|r|<1$. Both potentials are smooth, hence bounded, so they have minimal singularities: for a Hermitian background, the envelope $V_\omega $ of section 5.40 is zero. $\square$

title: 14.26.2 Three rank-one directions
section: 14.26 Smooth nonuniqueness for a degenerate density
text: On $U=\{ A\ne 0,B\ne 0\} $ put \[  r=\log \frac{|A|^2}{|B|^2},\qquad P=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |A|^2,\quad Q=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |B|^2,\quad R=\mathrm{d}r\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}r.  \] The logarithms are computed in a local homogeneous lift, but their Hessians do not depend on the lift. The forms $P,Q$ are pullbacks of Fubini–Study forms from the two projective lines $\mathbb P(\mathbb C^2)$. All three forms are semipositive of rank one, and 6970E9123EB5 14.26.3 \begin{equation}  P^2=Q^2=R^2=0,\qquad P\wedge Q\wedge R>0. \end{equation} Indeed, in local coordinates $A=(1,a)$ and $B=\tau (1,b)$, $P$ and $Q$ are positive multiples of $\mathrm{i}\, \mathrm{d}a\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar a$ and $\mathrm{i}\, \mathrm{d}b\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar b$, while \[  \partial r=\frac{\bar a\, \mathrm{d}a}{1+|a|^2} -\frac{\mathrm{d}\tau }{\tau } -\frac{\bar b\, \mathrm{d}b}{1+|b|^2}.  \] Its $\mathrm{d}\tau $ component is nonzero, so the three rank-one forms correspond to independent directions. In particular, for nonnegative $x,y,z$, 71DFC7D0861C 14.26.4 \begin{equation}  (xP+yQ+zR)^3=6xyz\, P\wedge Q\wedge R, \end{equation} and the form is positive exactly when all three coefficients are positive. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r=P-Q$, the chain rule gives, for a smooth function $G:\mathbb R\to \mathbb R$, 1C52D8C53893 14.26.5 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G(r)=G'(r)(P-Q)+G''(r)R. \end{equation} Let $\sigma (r)=\mathrm{e}^ r/(1+\mathrm{e}^ r)$. Since $\log (|A|^2+|B|^2)=\log |B|^2+\log (1+\mathrm{e}^ r)$, we have DE71ED12948B 14.26.6 \begin{equation}  \omega _ X=\sigma (r)P+\sigma (-r)Q+\sigma '(r)R. \end{equation} A function of $r$ that is constant near each end of $\mathbb R$ extends smoothly across $X\setminus U$. A form $xP+yQ+zR$ whose coefficients equal those of ( 14.26.6 ) for $|r|\geq 2$ extends smoothly by $\omega _ X$ across $X\setminus U$.

title: 14.26.7 The scalar coefficients
section: 14.26 Smooth nonuniqueness for a degenerate density
text: On the central interval $-1\leq r\leq 1$, the coefficients will make a different rank-one factor vanish in each of the two solution forms. Outside a larger interval they coincide with the Fubini–Study coefficients, so the resulting forms extend across the omitted projective lines. Primes denote derivatives with respect to $r$. Choose an even smooth function $\beta $ supported in $[-1,1]$, strictly positive on $(-1,1)$, with $\beta '>0$ on $(-1,0)$, and normalized by $\int _{-1}^1\beta =2$; for instance, a positive multiple of $\exp (-1/(1-r^2))$ on $(-1,1)$, extended by zero. Define \[  F(r)=-1+\int _{-1}^ r\beta (t)\, \mathrm{d}t\quad (-1<r<1), \qquad F=-1\  (r\leq -1),\quad F=1\  (r\geq 1),  \] and put $p=\beta /2$, $q=\beta '/2$. Then $F$ is smooth and odd, $p$ is even, and $q$ is odd, positive on $(-1,0)$ and negative on $(0,1)$. Both $p$ and $q$ vanish to infinite order at the endpoints. Take smooth $a\geq 0$ with $a=1$ on $(-\infty ,-2/3]$ and $a=0$ on $[-1/3,\infty )$, and put $b(r)=a(-r)$. Choose an even nonnegative $\chi \in C_ c^\infty ((-1/3,1/3))$ with $\chi (0)>0$. On $[-1,1]$ set \[  z_0=(q^2+\chi ^2)^{1/2}.  \] It is smooth: the expression under the square root is positive in the interior, and near each endpoint $z_0=|q|$, where $q$ has a fixed sign. It is positive in the interior and vanishes to infinite order at the endpoints. Also, 6C8664C40E89 14.26.8 \begin{equation}  z_0\geq |q|,\qquad a(z_0-q)=0,\qquad b(z_0+q)=0. \end{equation} The first cancellation holds because $\chi =0$ on the support of $a$ and $q\geq 0$ there; the second follows by reflection. On $(-\infty ,-1]$ choose smooth functions $\ell ,s$ such that $0\leq \ell \leq 1$, $\ell =0$ on $(-\infty ,-2]$, $\ell =1$ on $[-3/2,-1]$, while $s>0$ for $r<-1$, $s=1$ on $(-\infty ,-3/2]$, and $s$ vanishes to infinite order at $-1$. Such functions are easily obtained from smooth cutoff functions and a function like $\exp (-1/(r+1)^2)$. Define \[  \begin{aligned}  x& =(1-\ell )\sigma +\ell ,&  y& =(1-\ell )\sigma (-r)+\ell s,&  z& =(1-\ell )\sigma '+\ell s & & (r\leq -1),\\  x& =p+a,&  y& =p+b,&  z& =z_0 & & (-1\leq r\leq 1), \end{aligned}  \] and for $r\geq 1$ use $x(r)=y(-r)$, $y(r)=x(-r)$, $z(r)=z(-r)$. The definitions join smoothly: at $-1$ both definitions give the values $(1,0,0)$, and their differences vanish to infinite order there, since $a=1$ and $b=0$ near $-1$. The central definitions are symmetric under reflection, so the same holds at $1$. We have \[  x,y,z>0\quad \hbox{for }r\ne \pm 1,\qquad (x,y,z)(-1)=(1,0,0),\quad (x,y,z)(1)=(0,1,0).  \] For $|r|\geq 2$ their values are $(\sigma (r),\sigma (-r),\sigma '(r))$.

title: 14.26.9 Two forms with the same cube
search_title: Two forms with the same cube
section: 14.26 Smooth nonuniqueness for a degenerate density
text: The cancellation identities now turn the scalar coefficients into two semipositive forms with the same cube. Their average is strictly positive except at the two ends of the central interval. By the extensions described above, the form and the function \[  \omega _0=x(r)P+y(r)Q+z(r)R,\qquad w=F(r)  \] are smooth on $X$. The form is semipositive, and positive except on the hypersurfaces $M_- =\{ r=-1\} $ and $M_+=\{ r=1\} $. Put \[  H=\tfrac 12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=p(P-Q)+qR,\qquad A_0=\omega _0-H,\quad B_0=\omega _0+H.  \] For $|r|\geq 1$ we have $H=0$. On $|r|<1$, \[  A_0=aP+(2p+b)Q+(z_0-q)R,\qquad B_0=(2p+a)P+bQ+(z_0+q)R.  \] All coefficients are nonnegative, and by ( 14.26.4 ) and ( 14.26.8 ), $A_0^3=B_0^3=0$ on this band. Outside it both cubes equal $\omega _0^3$. Thus $A_0,B_0$ are smooth semipositive forms on $X$ with equal cubes. This common top-degree form vanishes on the closed band $|r|\leq 1$ and is positive on its complement, including near $X\setminus U$.

title: 14.26.10 Restoring strict positivity of the background
search_title: Restoring strict positivity of the background
section: 14.26 Smooth nonuniqueness for a degenerate density
text: The forms $A_0,B_0$ already have the required common measure. We obtain a Hermitian background by adding an exact correction $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ to their average $\omega _0$ and subtracting $\rho $ from both potentials. The correction must restore positivity at $M_\pm $ while preserving it in the transition regions. Take $\kappa \in C_ c^\infty ((-2,2))$, equal to one on $[-3/2,3/2]$. For a parameter $\varepsilon >0$ to be chosen, set \[  \rho (r)=\varepsilon (r^2-1)\kappa (r),\qquad \omega =\omega _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho .  \] By ( 14.26.5 ), its coefficients on $U$ are $x+\rho '$, $y-\rho '$ and $z+\rho ''$. On $[-3/2,3/2]$ one has $\rho '=2\varepsilon r$ and $\rho ''=2\varepsilon $, so the last coefficient is positive there. For $r\geq 0$, $x+2\varepsilon r$ is positive, including at $r=0$ since $x(0)=p(0)>0$. On $[-3/2,0]$, the function $x$ has a positive minimum $m$, so $x+2\varepsilon r\geq m-3\varepsilon >0$ for small $\varepsilon $. Reflection gives the corresponding estimate for $y-2\varepsilon r$. On the compact region $3/2\leq |r|\leq 2$, all three original coefficients have a positive minimum and the perturbations are $O(\varepsilon )$. For $|r|\geq 2$ and near $X\setminus U$, the form is exactly $\omega _ X$. Hence $\omega $ is strictly positive on $X$ for sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$. The form $\omega $ is not closed. Indeed, since $\mathrm{d}R=-\mathrm{d}r\wedge (P-Q)$, 0711E4CCA0FE 14.26.11 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{d}\omega =\mathrm{d}\omega _0 =\mathrm{d}r\wedge \bigl ((x'-z)P+(y'+z)Q\bigr ). \end{equation} At $r=0$, $x'=y'=0$ and $z=\chi (0)>0$. Hence $\mathrm{d}\omega =z\, \mathrm{d}r\wedge (Q-P)\ne 0$ there. The nonzero $\mathrm{d}\tau $ component used in ( 14.26.3 ) also shows that $\mathrm{d}r\wedge P$ and $\mathrm{d}r\wedge Q$ are linearly independent. of theorem 14.26.1 . Set $\widetilde u=-w/2-\rho $ and $\widetilde v=w/2-\rho $. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=2H$, the construction gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u=A_0\geq 0,\qquad \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v=B_0\geq 0.  \] Subtracting their respective suprema gives $u,v$. Their Hessians are unchanged, and $v-u=w+\text{constant}$ is nonconstant. The function $f=A_0^3/\omega _ X^3=B_0^3/\omega _ X^3$ is smooth, nonnegative and nonzero, and it vanishes on the nonempty open band $|r|<1$. Both potentials are smooth, hence bounded, so they have minimal singularities: for a Hermitian background, the envelope $V_\omega $ of section 5.40 is zero. $\square$ Every Hermitian background on $\mathbb P^3$ has the bounded mass property of definition 13.14.14 : since the Fubini–Study form is closed, Stokes' theorem for bounded potentials shows that all its bounded potentials have the same mass, and proposition 13.14.15 shows that the property does not depend on the metric. This applies to all the backgrounds on $\mathbb P^3$ constructed below. The linearized equation also explains why the maximum principle argument fails. The form \[  T=A_0^2+A_0\wedge B_0+B_0^2  \] satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge T=B_0^3-A_0^3=0$, but $T=0$ on $M_\pm $, where $A_0=B_0=\omega _0$ has rank one. Thus the linear equation for $w$ is not elliptic everywhere, even though both potentials and their common density are smooth.

title: 14.26.12 A continuum of radial solutions
section: 14.26 Smooth nonuniqueness for a degenerate density
text: The open band where the density vanishes allows more solutions than the two smooth ones constructed above. Writing a further potential as $G(r)-\rho $, with $G$ a function of one real variable, reduces the equation on the band to choosing the slope $G'$ so that one of the three coefficients vanishes. Switching the vanishing coefficient at two suitable levels produces a continuum of $C^{1,1}$ solutions for the same background $\omega $ and density $f$. Recall that $q=p'$ and $z_0\geq |q|$. The strict inequality $z_0>|p'|$ near zero, where $\chi >0$, gives 381112F03D1E 14.26.13 \begin{equation}  \int _0^1z_0(r)\, \mathrm{d}r>\int _0^1|p'(r)|\, \mathrm{d}r=p(0). \end{equation} Proposition 14.26.14 . 3A73F825D91B For the smooth background $\omega $ and the smooth density $f$ of theorem 14.26.1 , the equation \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=f\omega _ X^3  \] has uncountably many distinct $C^{1,1}$ solutions normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$. If the cutoff $\kappa $ defining $\rho $ is chosen even, one of them, constructed explicitly, is invariant under the block exchange $\iota [A:B]=[B:A]$. Proof. Consider pairs $-1<I<0<J<1$ satisfying D2FC90D7554B 14.26.15 \begin{equation}  \int _ I^ J z_0(r)\, \mathrm{d}r=p(I)+p(J). \end{equation} We first show that such pairs exist, with $I$ ranging over an interval. Define \[  K(I,J)=\int _ I^ Jz_0(r)\, \mathrm{d}r-p(I)-p(J).  \] We have $K(0,0)=-2p(0)<0$ and $K(0,1)>0$ by ( 14.26.13 ). By continuity, there is $\epsilon >0$ such that $K(I,0)<0<K(I,1)$ for every $I\in [-\epsilon ,0]$. For $0<J<1$, \[  \partial _ JK(I,J)=z_0(J)-p'(J)>0.  \] The intermediate value theorem therefore gives a unique $J=J(I)\in (0,1)$ satisfying ( 14.26.15 ) for every $I\in [-\epsilon ,0)$; we may assume $\epsilon <1$. For any pair satisfying ( 14.26.15 ), define the slope on $[-1,1]$ by \[  h_{I,J}(r)= \begin{cases}  p(r),& -1\leq r\leq I,\\  p(I)-\displaystyle \int _ I^ r z_0(s)\, \mathrm{d}s,& I\leq r\leq J,\\  -p(r),& J\leq r\leq 1, \end{cases}  \] and extend it by zero outside that interval. The balance identity makes it continuous at $J$, and continuity at $I$ is immediate. Each piece has bounded derivative, so $h_{I,J}$ is Lipschitz on $\mathbb R$; it vanishes to infinite order at $\pm 1$. Let $G_{I,J}$ be a primitive of $h_{I,J}$. It is $C^{1,1}$ and constant near each end of the real line. Consequently $G_{I,J}(r)$ extends to a $C^{1,1}$ function on $X$ that is smooth near $X\setminus U$. On the middle interval $[I,J]$ the slope lies between $-p$ and $p$. Indeed, \[  (h_{I,J}-p)'=-z_0-p'\leq 0, \qquad (h_{I,J}+p)'=-z_0+p'\leq 0.  \] The first difference vanishes at $I$, and the second vanishes at $J$. Since both are nonincreasing, $h_{I,J}\leq p$ and $h_{I,J}\geq -p$ on $[I,J]$. Put $\widetilde u_{I,J}=G_{I,J}(r)-\rho $. By ( 14.26.5 ), almost everywhere on $U$, 2EC8417EFF1E 14.26.16 \begin{equation}  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u_{I,J} =\omega _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_{I,J}(r) =(x+h_{I,J})P+(y-h_{I,J})Q+(z+h_{I,J}')R. \end{equation} On $I<r<J$, the first two coefficients are nonnegative because $x=p+a$, $y=p+b$ and $-p\leq h_{I,J}\leq p$, and the third is zero. On $-1<r<I$, we have $h_{I,J}=p$ and $b=0$, since $I<0$; so the second coefficient is zero, and the others are nonnegative because $z_0+p'\geq 0$. On $J<r<1$, we have $h_{I,J}=-p$ and $a=0$; so the first coefficient is zero, and the others are nonnegative because $z_0-p'\geq 0$. Outside the band, $h_{I,J}=h_{I,J}'=0$, so the form equals $\omega _0$. Formula ( 14.26.16 ) has no additional term supported on the hypersurfaces $r=I$ and $r=J$: the function $G_{I,J}$ is $C^{1,1}$, so its first derivative is continuous at both transition points, and its distributional Hessian is its bounded almost-everywhere Hessian. The preceding coefficient inequalities therefore prove $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u_{I,J}\geq 0$ as a current. By proposition 5.28.5 , its Monge–Ampère measure is the pointwise cube of ( 14.26.16 ), computed almost everywhere. By the rank-one identities ( 14.26.3 ) and ( 14.26.4 ), this cube is zero almost everywhere on the band, since one coefficient vanishes there, and it equals $\omega _0^3$ off the band. These are exactly the values of $f\omega _ X^3$ in the preceding construction. Thus $\widetilde u_{I,J}$ solves the equation, and subtracting its supremum gives a normalized solution $u_{I,J}$. Different values of $I\in [-\epsilon ,0)$ give different normalized solutions. If $I_1<I_2<0$ and $I_1<r<I_2$, then the slope belonging to $I_2$ is $p(r)$, whereas \[  p(r)-h_{I_1,J(I_1)}(r) =\int _{I_1}^ r(p'(s)+z_0(s))\, \mathrm{d}s>0,  \] because $p'>0$ on $(-1,0)$. The two primitives therefore do not differ by a constant. Since the interval $[-\epsilon ,0)$ is uncountable, this proves the first assertion. None of these slopes equals $p$ or $-p$ on all of $(-1,1)$, so the constructed solutions are also distinct from the two smooth solutions of theorem 14.26.1 . Finally, the function \[  L(t)=\int _0^ t z_0(r)\, \mathrm{d}r-p(t),\qquad 0\leq t\leq 1,  \] is negative at zero, positive at one, and strictly increasing on $(0,1)$. Its unique zero $t_*$ gives a symmetric pair $I=-t_*$, $J=t_*$ satisfying ( 14.26.15 ). Since $z_0$ and $p$ are even, $h_{I,J}$ is odd: on the middle interval it equals $-\int _0^ r z_0(s)\, \mathrm{d}s$. Choose its primitive even. Since $\iota $ changes $r$ into $-r$, if $\rho $ is even, the potential $G_{I,J}(r)-\rho $ and its normalization are fixed by $\iota $. This proves the last assertion. $\square$ For these symmetric data, the normalized solutions of the equations with a positive exponent converge, as the exponent tends to zero, to the symmetric solution just constructed; see theorem 15.20.4 .

Indeed, \[  (h_{I,J}-p)'=-z_0-p'\leq 0, \qquad (h_{I,J}+p)'=-z_0+p'\leq 0.  \] The first difference vanishes at $I$, and the second vanishes at $J$. Since both are nonincreasing, $h_{I,J}\leq p$ and $h_{I,J}\geq -p$ on $[I,J]$. Put $\widetilde u_{I,J}=G_{I,J}(r)-\rho $. By ( 14.26.5 ), almost everywhere on $U$, 2EC8417EFF1E 14.26.16 \begin{equation}  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u_{I,J} =\omega _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_{I,J}(r) =(x+h_{I,J})P+(y-h_{I,J})Q+(z+h_{I,J}')R. \end{equation} On $I<r<J$, the first two coefficients are nonnegative because $x=p+a$, $y=p+b$ and $-p\leq h_{I,J}\leq p$, and the third is zero. On $-1<r<I$, we have $h_{I,J}=p$ and $b=0$, since $I<0$; so the second coefficient is zero, and the others are nonnegative because $z_0+p'\geq 0$. On $J<r<1$, we have $h_{I,J}=-p$ and $a=0$; so the first coefficient is zero, and the others are nonnegative because $z_0-p'\geq 0$. Outside the band, $h_{I,J}=h_{I,J}'=0$, so the form equals $\omega _0$. Formula ( 14.26.16 ) has no additional term supported on the hypersurfaces $r=I$ and $r=J$: the function $G_{I,J}$ is $C^{1,1}$, so its first derivative is continuous at both transition points, and its distributional Hessian is its bounded almost-everywhere Hessian. The preceding coefficient inequalities therefore prove $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u_{I,J}\geq 0$ as a current. By proposition 5.28.5 , its Monge–Ampère measure is the pointwise cube of ( 14.26.16 ), computed almost everywhere. By the rank-one identities ( 14.26.3 ) and ( 14.26.4 ), this cube is zero almost everywhere on the band, since one coefficient vanishes there, and it equals $\omega _0^3$ off the band. These are exactly the values of $f\omega _ X^3$ in the preceding construction. Thus $\widetilde u_{I,J}$ solves the equation, and subtracting its supremum gives a normalized solution $u_{I,J}$. Different values of $I\in [-\epsilon ,0)$ give different normalized solutions. If $I_1<I_2<0$ and $I_1<r<I_2$, then the slope belonging to $I_2$ is $p(r)$, whereas \[  p(r)-h_{I_1,J(I_1)}(r) =\int _{I_1}^ r(p'(s)+z_0(s))\, \mathrm{d}s>0,  \] because $p'>0$ on $(-1,0)$. The two primitives therefore do not differ by a constant. Since the interval $[-\epsilon ,0)$ is uncountable, this proves the first assertion. None of these slopes equals $p$ or $-p$ on all of $(-1,1)$, so the constructed solutions are also distinct from the two smooth solutions of theorem 14.26.1 . Finally, the function \[  L(t)=\int _0^ t z_0(r)\, \mathrm{d}r-p(t),\qquad 0\leq t\leq 1,  \] is negative at zero, positive at one, and strictly increasing on $(0,1)$. Its unique zero $t_*$ gives a symmetric pair $I=-t_*$, $J=t_*$ satisfying ( 14.26.15 ). Since $z_0$ and $p$ are even, $h_{I,J}$ is odd: on the middle interval it equals $-\int _0^ r z_0(s)\, \mathrm{d}s$. Choose its primitive even. Since $\iota $ changes $r$ into $-r$, if $\rho $ is even, the potential $G_{I,J}(r)-\rho $ and its normalization are fixed by $\iota $. This proves the last assertion. $\square$

text: We now keep the Hermitian background of theorem 14.26.1 , but change the density so that it is positive off $M_-\cup M_+$, where $M_\pm =\{ r=\pm 1\} $. For potentials of the form $G(r)-\rho $, the equation on the middle band becomes a first-order ordinary differential equation for the slope $G'$. Barriers keep its solutions between the admissible slopes, and infinite-order vanishing at the endpoints then makes their extensions by zero smooth. Theorem 14.27.1 . E16A6F31A061 There are a smooth nonclosed Hermitian form $\omega $ on $\mathbb P^3$ and a smooth nonnegative density $g$, positive off two disjoint smooth real hypersurfaces, such that the equation \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=g\omega _ X^3  \] has uncountably many distinct smooth solutions normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$. The background $\omega $ has bounded mass. Thus a zero set with empty interior, even one of measure zero, does not ensure uniqueness of smooth normalized solutions. We use the coefficients of 14.26.7 , with the explicit choice \[  p(r)=C\exp \! \left(-\frac1{1-r^2}\right),\qquad -1<r<1, \qquad \int _{-1}^1p(r)\, \mathrm{d}r=1,  \] extended by zero, where the integral condition determines $C>0$; then $q=p'$. Fix $0<s<1$, and set \[  k_ s(r)=(x(r)+sp(r))(y(r)-sp(r))(z(r)+sq(r)).  \] For $|r|>1$ this is $xyz$. If $G'=sp$, then the potential $G(r)-\rho $ has $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(G(r)-\rho )=\omega _0+sH$. This form is strictly positive for $-1<r<1$, since \[  x+sp=a+(1+s)p>0,\quad y-sp=b+(1-s)p>0,\quad z_0+sq\geq (1-s)z_0>0.  \] It is also strictly positive outside the closed band, and at $r=\pm 1$ it equals the rank-one form $\omega _0$. Consequently 42198F5D282A 14.27.2 \begin{equation}  g\omega _ X^3=(\omega _0+sH)^3 \end{equation} defines a smooth density $g$ that is positive exactly off $M_-\cup M_+$. These hypersurfaces have measure zero and empty interior. On the band $|r|<1$, a potential $G(r)-\rho $ with slope $h=G'$ solves the equation exactly when $(x+h)(y-h)(z+h')=k_ s$, which is the differential equation ( 14.27.4 ) below. Lemma 14.27.3 . C96C68E6BB33 There exists $\eta _0>0$ such that for every $0<\eta <\eta _0$ the initial-value problem FE5D8F02666F 14.27.4 \begin{equation}  h'=\frac{k_ s(r)}{(x(r)+h)(y(r)-h)}-z(r), \qquad h(0)=sp(0)-\eta , \end{equation} has a smooth solution on $(-1,1)$ with $-x<h<y$ and $h<sp$. Moreover, on some fixed endpoint neighborhoods there are constants $0<c_ L<s<t<1$, independent of $\eta $, such that \[  c_ Lp<h<sp\quad \hbox{near }-1, \qquad -tp<h<sp\quad \hbox{near }1.  \] Proof. The function $h_ s=sp$ solves ( 14.27.4 ) and lies strictly between $-x$ and $y$ throughout $(-1,1)$. Write $F_ s(r,h)$ for the right-hand side of the equation, which is smooth on the open domain $-x(r)<h<y(r)$. Near $-1$ the coefficients are exactly \[  x=1+p,\qquad y=p,\qquad z=q>0.  \] For a constant $c\in (-1,1)$, the product of coefficients for the trial slope $cp$ is \[  k_ c=(1-c^2)\bigl (1+(1+c)p\bigr )pq.  \] Fix $c_ L\in (0,s)$. At $p=0$, the factor preceding $pq$ for $c=c_ L$ exceeds that for $c=s$ by $s^2-c_ L^2>0$. Thus, on a sufficiently small fixed neighborhood of the left endpoint, $k_{c_ L}>k_ s$ and FCE58E25CF39 14.27.5 \begin{equation}  F_ s(r,c_ Lp)-(c_ Lp)'= \frac{k_ s-k_{c_ L}}{(x+c_ Lp)(y-c_ Lp)}<0. \end{equation} Thus $c_ Lp$ is a lower barrier when the equation is solved backward, that is, toward $-1$. Near $1$ the exact coefficients are \[  x=p,\qquad y=1+p,\qquad z=-q>0,  \] and the trial slope $cp$ has product of coefficients \[  k_ c=(1-c^2)\bigl (1+(1-c)p\bigr )p(-q).  \] Fix $s<t<1$. At $p=0$, the factor for $c=s$ exceeds that for $c=-t$ by $t^2-s^2>0$. On a sufficiently small fixed neighborhood of the right endpoint, therefore, $k_ s>k_{-t}$, so DDB2BCDB3552 14.27.6 \begin{equation}  F_ s(r,-tp)-(-tp)'= \frac{k_ s-k_{-t}}{(x-tp)(y+tp)}>0. \end{equation} Thus $-tp$ is a lower barrier when the equation is solved forward, toward $1$. Choose $r_ L<0<r_ R$ in these respective neighborhoods. The graph of $h_ s$ over $[r_ L,r_ R]$ is a compact subset of the domain of $F_ s$. Existence and continuous dependence on initial values for smooth ordinary differential equations therefore give $\eta _0>0$ such that, for every $0<\eta <\eta _0$, the solution with initial value $sp(0)-\eta $ exists on $[r_ L,r_ R]$, stays in the domain, and satisfies \[  h(r_ L)>c_ Lp(r_ L),\qquad h(r_ R)>-tp(r_ R).  \] By local uniqueness, two solutions of the equation cannot cross. Since $h(0)<h_ s(0)$, we have $h<h_ s$ wherever $h$ exists. Follow the solution backwards from $r_ L$; it cannot cross $c_ Lp$. Indeed, at a first crossing point the difference $h-c_ Lp$ would vanish and be positive immediately to its right, so its derivative there would be nonnegative, whereas ( 14.27.5 ) shows that this derivative is strictly negative. Thus $c_ Lp<h<sp$ on the part of the interval of existence to the left of $r_ L$. Likewise, ( 14.27.6 ) prevents a first downward crossing of $-tp$ to the right of $r_ R$, giving $-tp<h<sp$ there. These bounds also show that the maximal interval of existence is all of $(-1,1)$. Indeed, near a possible endpoint inside $(-1,1)$, the factors $x+h$ and $y-h$ stay bounded away from zero, so the graph of $h$ stays in a compact subset of the domain of $F_ s$, and the continuation theorem for ordinary differential equations extends the solution beyond that endpoint. Hence the solution exists on $(-1,1)$ and satisfies the claimed bounds. $\square$ Lemma 14.27.7 . 31CA87ECD1DF Every solution furnished by lemma 14.27.3 , extended by zero outside $(-1,1)$, is smooth on $\mathbb R$ and vanishes to infinite order at $\pm 1$. Proof. Let $h$ be one of the solutions in lemma 14.27.3 . On either endpoint neighborhood put $\xi =h/p$; since $p>0$ on $(-1,1)$, this quotient is smooth there, and the trapping bounds place $\xi $ in a fixed compact subinterval of $(-1,1)$. Define the rational functions \[  R_ L(p,\xi )= \frac{(1-s^2)(1+(1+s)p)}{(1+(1+\xi )p)(1-\xi )}-1,  \] \[  R_ R(p,\xi )=1- \frac{(1-s^2)(1+(1-s)p)}{(1+\xi )(1+(1-\xi )p)}.  \] The explicit formulas for the coefficients near the endpoints give \[  h'=q\, R_ L(p,\xi )\quad \hbox{on the left},\qquad h'=q\, R_ R(p,\xi )\quad \hbox{on the right}.  \] Both rational functions are smooth, with all derivatives bounded, on a neighborhood of the relevant set of pairs $(p,\xi )$ with $p\geq 0$ small and $\xi $ in the compact interval above. Writing $R_{L/R}$ for the function corresponding to the endpoint under consideration, we obtain from $h'=p'\xi +p\xi '$ and $q=p'$ 5C8FF3274F30 14.27.8 \begin{equation}  \xi '=\frac{p'}p\bigl (R_{L/R}(p,\xi )-\xi \bigr ). \end{equation} For the chosen bump, \[  \frac{p'}p=-\frac{2r}{(1-r^2)^2}.  \] This rational function and each of its derivatives grow at most like a power of the inverse distance to the endpoint. Moreover, each derivative of $p$ is $p$ times a rational function with the same property. An induction using ( 14.27.8 ) shows that every derivative $\xi ^{(j)}$ grows at most polynomially in the inverse distance to the endpoint. The case $j=0$ is the trapping bound on $\xi $. For the induction step, differentiate the right-hand side of ( 14.27.8 ), including its term $-\xi $, $j$ times. Every resulting term is a product of a derivative of $p'/p$, a bounded partial derivative of $R_{L/R}$, and derivatives of $p$ and of $\xi $ of order at most $j$. All of these factors have polynomial bounds, by the induction hypothesis for the derivatives of $\xi $ and since every derivative of $p$ is bounded. This gives the bound for $\xi ^{(j+1)}$. Leibniz' rule for $h=p\xi $ now gives, for each $j$, constants $C_ j,N_ j$ such that \[  |h^{(j)}(r)|\leq C_ j p(r)(1-|r|)^{-N_ j}  \] near the endpoints. The right-hand side tends to zero at the endpoints, because $p$ decays exponentially in the inverse distance to the endpoint. Thus all derivatives of $h$ tend to zero at $\pm 1$. Extend each derivative by zero outside $(-1,1)$. By the mean value theorem, the difference quotient of $h^{(j)}$ at an endpoint tends to the limit of $h^{(j+1)}$, which is zero. Hence these extensions are the successive derivatives of the extension of $h$, which is therefore smooth and vanishes to infinite order at $\pm 1$. $\square$ of theorem 14.27.1 . Let $\eta _0$ be as in lemma 14.27.3 , and for $0<\eta <\eta _0$ denote by $h_\eta $ the solution with initial value $sp(0)-\eta $. Extend $h_\eta $ by zero, which gives a smooth function by the preceding lemma, and take a primitive $G_\eta $. It is constant near each end of the real line, so $G_\eta (r)$ extends smoothly to all of $\mathbb P^3$, including the two omitted projective lines. Set \[  \widetilde u_\eta =G_\eta (r)-\rho .  \] On the open band, \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u_\eta =(x+h_\eta )P+(y-h_\eta )Q+(z+h_\eta ')R.  \] The coefficients of $P$ and $Q$ are strictly positive by lemma 14.27.3 , while the equation gives \[  z+h_\eta '=\frac{k_ s}{(x+h_\eta )(y-h_\eta )}>0.  \] Outside the band the form is $\omega _0$, and on the two boundary hypersurfaces it is also the rank-one form $\omega _0$, since $h_\eta $ vanishes to infinite order there. It is therefore semipositive on $X$, and by ( 14.26.4 ) its cube equals $6k_ sP\wedge Q\wedge R=(\omega _0+sH)^3$ on the band and $\omega _0^3=(\omega _0+sH)^3$ elsewhere. Thus its cube is everywhere the measure $g\omega _ X^3$ of ( 14.27.2 ). Finally, normalize by subtracting $\sup _ X\widetilde u_\eta $. Distinct values of $\eta $ give different slopes at $r=0$, so the corresponding potentials do not differ by a constant, and their normalized versions are distinct. This gives an uncountable family. The background is that of theorem 14.26.1 , so it has bounded mass. $\square$ The density vanishes to infinite order on the two hypersurfaces. Their complement has three components, and on each of the two outer components, two different solutions differ by a constant, with different constants on the two components. The differential equation on the middle component joins these constants smoothly across the degenerate hypersurfaces. This is why ellipticity at every point of the positive-density set does not give a maximum principle argument across its boundary.

title: 14.28 Quadratic density zeros
text: Infinite-order vanishing of the density is not needed for smooth nonuniqueness. We change the coefficients of $\omega _0$ so that its coefficient of $R$ stays positive and one of its coefficients of $P$ and $Q$ vanishes quadratically at each of the two hypersurfaces $M_\pm $. The resulting singular differential equation forces the slopes of differences of solutions to decay like $\exp (-A/d)$, where $d$ is the distance to the hypersurface and $A>0$. The slopes therefore extend smoothly by zero, even though the density vanishes only to finite order. Theorem 14.28.1 . 9C11A9E88B60 On $\mathbb P^3$ there exist a smooth nonclosed Hermitian form $\omega $ and a smooth nonnegative density $g$ such that: The zero set of $g$ consists of two disjoint smooth real hypersurfaces. Near either hypersurface, $g$ is the square of a smooth defining function times a smooth strictly positive function. The equation $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3=g\omega _ X^3$ has uncountably many distinct smooth $\omega $-plurisubharmonic solutions normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$. The background $\omega $ has bounded mass. We keep the rank-one forms $P,Q,R$ and the function $r$ of 14.26.2 , and use new scalar coefficients. Choose a smooth function $a$ valued in $[0,1]$, equal to one for $r\leq -2/3$ and zero for $r\geq -1/3$, and put $b(r)=a(-r)$. Choose a smooth even cutoff $\chi $ valued in $[0,1]$, zero for $|r|\leq 5/4$ and one for $|r|\geq 3/2$. Set $p(r)=(1-r^2)^2$ and ACD0920D4D78 14.28.2 \begin{equation}  \begin{split}  x& =(1-\chi )(p+a)+\chi \sigma ,\\  y& =(1-\chi )(p+b)+\chi (1-\sigma ),\\  z& =1-\chi +\chi \sigma ',\qquad \omega _0=xP+yQ+zR. \end{split} \end{equation} Since these coefficients coincide with those of ( 14.26.6 ) for $|r|\geq 3/2$, the form $\omega _0$ extends by $\omega _ X$ across the two omitted projective lines. The coefficient $z$ is strictly positive, and $x,y$ are strictly positive except that $y(-1)=0$ and $x(1)=0$. Thus $\omega _0$ is positive off $M_\pm =\{ r=\pm 1\} $ and has rank two there. Choose a smooth cutoff $\kappa \in C_ c^\infty ((-2,2))$ equal to one on $[-3/2,3/2]$. For a parameter $\varepsilon >0$ to be chosen, define the correction \[  \rho =\varepsilon (r^2-1)\kappa (r),\qquad \omega =\omega _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho .  \] For sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$, the form $\omega $ is strictly positive. Indeed, on $[-3/2,3/2]$ its coefficients are $x+2\varepsilon r$, $y-2\varepsilon r$ and $z+2\varepsilon $. The first is positive for $r\geq 0$, and on $[-3/2,0]$ the function $x$ has a positive minimum, so it remains positive for small $\varepsilon $. Reflection gives the positivity of the second coefficient, and that of the third is immediate. On $3/2\leq |r|\leq 2$, the form $\omega _0$ is strictly positive on a compact set and the correction is $O(\varepsilon )$. Near the projective ends there is no correction. The form $\omega $ is not closed: at $r=0$, $x'=y'=0$ and $z=1$, so by ( 14.26.11 ) \[  \mathrm{d}\omega =\mathrm{d}r\wedge \bigl ((x'-z)P+(y'+z)Q\bigr )\ne 0.  \] Define the density $g$ by \[  g\omega _ X^3=\omega _0^3.  \] It is smooth and positive exactly off $M_-\cup M_+$. By ( 14.26.6 ) and ( 14.26.4 ), $g=xyz/(\sigma (r)(1-\sigma (r))\sigma '(r))$. Near either hypersurface, $xyz=(1+p)p$, and hence \[  g(r)=\frac{(1+p(r))(1-r^2)^2}{\sigma (r)(1-\sigma (r))\sigma '(r)}.  \] The denominator is smooth and strictly positive at $\pm 1$, and $1-r^2$ is a defining function for $M_\pm $ near these hypersurfaces. This proves the asserted quadratic vanishing. The potential $-\rho $ is one smooth solution. Lemma 14.28.3 . 624B2CF7FBA2 For every sufficiently small $\eta >0$, the equation 3D1CCE4952BA 14.28.4 \begin{equation}  h'=\frac{xyz}{(x+h)(y-h)}-z,\qquad h(0)=-\eta \end{equation} has a smooth solution on $(-1,1)$ with $-x<h<y$ and $h<0$. There are a constant $0<c<1$ and fixed neighborhoods of both endpoints, independent of $\eta $, on which \[  -cp<h<0.  \] Every such solution, extended by zero, is a smooth function on $\mathbb R$ that vanishes to infinite order at $\pm 1$. Proof. The right-hand side $F(r,h)$ is smooth on $-x<h<y$, and $h=0$ is a solution. Near $-1$, $(x,y,z)=(1+p,p,1)$; near $1$, $(x,y,z)=(p,1+p,1)$. Fix $0<c<1$. For the trial function $-cp$, near the left endpoint \[  F(r,-cp)+cp' =\frac{1+p}{(1+(1-c)p)(1+c)}-1+cp' \longrightarrow -\frac{c}{1+c}<0,  \] whereas near the right endpoint \[  F(r,-cp)+cp' =\frac{1+p}{(1-c)(1+(1+c)p)}-1+cp' \longrightarrow \frac{c}{1-c}>0.  \] as $r\to \pm 1$, since $p,p'\to 0$ at both endpoints. The strict inequalities therefore hold on fixed neighborhoods of the endpoints, and $-cp$ is a lower barrier for the equation solved backwards near $-1$ and forwards near $1$. Choose a compact interval $[r_ L,r_ R]\ni 0$ with endpoints in those neighborhoods. Continuous dependence on initial values, around the solution $h=0$, gives $\eta _0>0$ such that for every $0<\eta <\eta _0$ the solution exists on $[r_ L,r_ R]$, stays in the domain of $F$, and lies above $-cp$ at $r_ L$ and $r_ R$. By uniqueness of solutions, it cannot meet the solution zero, so $h<0$. The barrier argument used in the proof of lemma 14.27.3 then gives $-cp<h<0$ near both ends. On each compact subinterval of $(-1,1)$ the trapped graph stays at a positive distance from the boundary of the domain of $F$; hence, by the continuation theorem, the solution exists on all of $(-1,1)$. The equation factors as 86148D5BD1E9 14.28.5 \begin{equation}  h'=h\, L(r,h),\qquad L(r,h)=\frac{z(x-y+h)}{(x+h)(y-h)}. \end{equation} Since $h<0$, we have $(\log (-h))'=L(r,h)$. Near the left endpoint, the trapping bounds and the explicit coefficients imply \[  L(r,h)=\frac{1+h}{(1+p+h)(p-h)}\geq \frac{C_1}{p}  \] after shrinking that neighborhood, with $C_1>0$. Near the right endpoint they give \[  L(r,h)=\frac{-1+h}{(p+h)(1+p-h)}\leq -\frac{C_2}{p}, \qquad C_2>0.  \] Indeed, on the left, $1+h\geq 1-cp\geq 1/2$ and the denominator is at most $(1+p)(1+c)p$; on the right, the numerator is at most $-1$, and the denominator is at most $p(1+(1+c)p)$. Since $p$ is comparable to the square of the distance $d=1-|r|$ to the endpoint, integrating these inequalities backwards on the left and forwards on the right gives, for some $A>0$, 94F5CC68CD22 14.28.6 \begin{equation}  |h(r)|\leq C \mathrm{e}^{-A/d} \end{equation} near either endpoint. The constants may depend on the solution; uniformity in $\eta $ is not needed for the smooth extension. It remains to control all derivatives. On the trapped graph, all partial derivatives in $(r,h)$ of the rational function $L$ grow at most polynomially in $d^{-1}$. Indeed, near an endpoint $x,y$ are polynomials in $r$, $z=1$, $h$ is bounded, and of the two factors in the denominator, one is bounded below by a positive constant and the other by $(1-c)p$. Repeated differentiation of the quotient therefore only introduces finite powers of $p^{-1}$. Inductively, for every $j\geq 0$ there are constants $C_ j,N_ j$ with \[  |h^{(j)}(r)|\leq C_ j \mathrm{e}^{-A/d}d^{-N_ j}.  \] The case $j=0$ is ( 14.28.6 ). Differentiate $h'=hL(r,h(r))$ $j$ times. Every resulting term is the product of a derivative of the factor $h$, of order at most $j$, and a derivative of the composite function $L(r,h(r))$. The latter involves only partial derivatives of $L$ and derivatives of $h$ of order at most $j$, which are polynomially bounded by the induction hypothesis, while the first factor has the exponential bound. This proves the case $j+1$. All derivatives of $h$ therefore tend to zero at $\pm 1$. Extending them by zero and applying the mean value theorem to the difference quotients at the endpoints, as in lemma 14.27.7 , shows that the extension of $h$ by zero is smooth and vanishes to infinite order at $\pm 1$. $\square$ of theorem 14.28.1 . Let $\eta _0>0$ be such that lemma 14.28.3 applies for $0<\eta <\eta _0$, and let $h_\eta $ denote the solution with $h_\eta (0)=-\eta $. Take a primitive $G_\eta $ of its extension by zero. Since $G_\eta $ is constant near each end of the real line, $G_\eta (r)$ defines a smooth function on $X$. The potential $u_\eta =G_\eta (r)-\rho $ satisfies \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\eta =(x+h_\eta )P+(y-h_\eta )Q+(z+h_\eta ')R.  \] Inside the band, the first two coefficients are positive by the lemma, and the equation gives \[  z+h_\eta '=\frac{xyz}{(x+h_\eta )(y-h_\eta )}>0.  \] Outside the band the form is $\omega _0$, and on the two boundary hypersurfaces it is also the rank-two form $\omega _0$, since $h_\eta $ vanishes to infinite order there. Thus it is semipositive on $X$, and by ( 14.26.4 ) its cube is $6xyzP\wedge Q\wedge R=\omega _0^3=g\omega _ X^3$. Different initial values give potentials that do not differ by constants, so after normalization by the supremum we obtain an uncountable family. Bounded mass follows from proposition 13.14.15 , as for theorem 14.26.1 . $\square$ At each of the hypersurfaces $M_\pm $, the difference of two of these solutions agrees to infinite order with a constant, because its derivative is a difference of slopes that vanish to infinite order there. The constants at the two hypersurfaces need not agree. Thus the singular differential equation produces differences that are flat at $M_\pm $, even though the density has only quadratic zeros.

title: 14.29 A real analytic density
text: A globally real analytic density can occur in an equation with a smooth nonclosed Hermitian background and distinct smooth normalized solutions. We prescribe it as a polynomial in a real analytic function on projective space. Two symmetric radial perturbations give the required determinant on the middle band; patching the coefficients while preserving their product extends the construction across the projective ends. The two hypersurfaces where the density vanishes quadratically separate regions with different extremal values of the difference of the solutions. Theorem 14.29.1 . DD001DBBE659 On $X=\mathbb P^3$, with block homogeneous coordinates $[A:B]$ and Fubini–Study form $\omega _ X$, put \[  t=\frac{|A|^2}{|A|^2+|B|^2},\qquad a=\frac1{1+\mathrm{e}},\qquad b=\frac{\mathrm{e}}{1+\mathrm{e}},\qquad f_*(t)=(t-a)^2(t-b)^2.  \] There exist a smooth nonclosed Hermitian form $\omega $ and distinct smooth $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $u,v$, normalized by $\sup _ Xu=\sup _ Xv=0$, with B358F4101DED 14.29.2 \begin{equation}  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^3=f_*(t)\omega _ X^3. \end{equation} Both solution forms are positive away from the two connected real analytic hypersurfaces $\{ t=a\} $, $\{ t=b\} $, and have complex rank two on them. The density is real analytic on $X$, and it vanishes exactly to second order in the direction transverse to these hypersurfaces. For every $n\geq 4$ the same assertions hold on $\mathbb {P}^3\times \mathbb {P}^{n-3}$, with the pulled-back density and the product Fubini–Study volume, and with rank $n-1$ on the two product hypersurfaces. Proof. We use the forms $P,Q,R$ and the function $r$ of 14.26.2 . By ( 14.26.4 ), the construction reduces to finding scalar coefficients with a prescribed product. By ( 14.26.6 ), 07B68FE9B8BC 14.29.3 \begin{equation}  \omega _ X^3=6(\sigma ')^2P\wedge Q\wedge R, \qquad \sigma '=\sigma (r)\sigma (-r)>0. \end{equation} $\square$

title: 14.29.4 Prescribing the determinant
text: On $U$, one has $t=\sigma (r)$. We first construct two triples of coefficients, positive on the middle band, with product $f_*(\sigma )(\sigma ')^2$. At each endpoint of the band, exactly one of the coefficients of $P$ and $Q$ will vanish. Put $d_*(r)=f_*(\sigma (r))(\sigma '(r))^2$. Since $a=\sigma (-1)$, $b=\sigma (1)$, define the positive smooth divided differences \[  k_-(r)=\int _0^1\sigma '(-1+s(r+1))\, \mathrm{d}s,\qquad k_+(r)=\int _0^1\sigma '(1+s(r-1))\, \mathrm{d}s,  \] and $H_*(r)=k_-(r)k_+(r)\sigma '(r)>0$. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives 3FD3DD269BA8 14.29.5 \begin{equation}  \sigma (r)-a=(r+1)k_-(r),\quad \sigma (r)-b=(r-1)k_+(r),\quad d_*=(1-r^2)^2H_*^2. \end{equation} These formulas show that $H_*$ is smooth and positive also at the endpoints, without any division by a vanishing function. The symmetry $\sigma (-r)=1-\sigma (r)$ makes $d_*$, and hence $H_*$, even. Choose the function \[  p(r)= \begin{cases} \mathrm{e}^{-1/(1-r^2)},& |r|<1,\\ 0,& |r|\geq 1, \end{cases} \qquad q=p'.  \] All its derivatives vanish at $r=\pm 1$: each derivative is a finite sum of polynomials in $r$ times powers of $(1-r^2)^{-1}$, multiplied by the exponential, and the exponential factor dominates every such power. On $|r|<1$, $q=-2rp/(1-r^2)^2$. Define 14762A8A84D0 14.29.6 \begin{align}  z_ b& =\sqrt{q^2+2H_*^2},\qquad S_* =\sqrt{r^2+4p^2+2z_ b(1-r^2)^2},\\  x_ b& =(S_*-r)/2,\qquad y_ b=(S_*+r)/2.\tag{14.29.7} \end{align} Both radicands are strictly positive everywhere, so these formulas define smooth functions on $\mathbb R$, including at the endpoints. They satisfy E916650EE31A 14.29.8 \begin{equation}  z_ b>|q|,\qquad x_ b-y_ b=-r,\qquad x_ by_ b=p^2+\frac{z_ b}2(1-r^2)^2. \end{equation} The coefficients $x_ b,y_ b$ are nonnegative, positive away from the endpoints, with values $(1,0)$ at $-1$ and $(0,1)$ at $1$. On the open band, \[  S_*^2-(2p+|r|)^2=2(1-r^2)^2(z_ b-|q|)>0,  \] so $x_ b>p$, $y_ b>p$. Consequently both triples 025CE4264442 14.29.9 \begin{equation}  (x_ b-p,y_ b+p,z_ b-q),\qquad (x_ b+p,y_ b-p,z_ b+q) \end{equation} are strictly positive there. We now verify that the two triples have the same product. Set $D_*=x_ by_ b-p^2$, $E_*=p(x_ b-y_ b)=-rp$. Equations ( 14.29.8 ) and the formula for $q$ give \[  D_*=(z_ b/2)(1-r^2)^2,\qquad qD_*=z_ bE_*.  \] The two products in ( 14.29.9 ) therefore equal 17DDFD1D68B2 14.29.10 \begin{equation}  (D_*+E_*)(z_ b-q)=(D_*-E_*)(z_ b+q) =\frac{D_*}{z_ b}(z_ b^2-q^2)=d_*. \end{equation} For $|r|\geq 1$, $p=q=0$ and the same identity reads $x_ by_ bz_ b=d_*$. Thus both triples have exactly the prescribed product, and at the endpoints exactly one of their entries vanishes.

title: 14.29.11 Extension over the projective ends
text: The coefficients just constructed have the right product but need not extend across the projective ends. Away from the zero levels of $f_*(t)$, we interpolate the coefficients of $P$ and $Q$ to those of $f_*(t)^{1/3}\omega _ X$, and determine the coefficient of $R$ by the prescribed product. Choose a smooth even cutoff $0\leq \eta \leq 1$, equal to one on $|r|\leq 3/2$ and zero on $|r|\geq 2$. On $|r|<3/2$ set $(x,y,z)=(x_ b,y_ b,z_ b)$. On $|r|>5/4$, where $f_*(\sigma (r))>0$, put \begin{align*}  \kappa & =f_*(\sigma (r))^{1/3},\\  x& =\eta x_ b+(1-\eta )\kappa \sigma (r),\\  y& =\eta y_ b+(1-\eta )\kappa \sigma (-r),\qquad z=d_*/(xy). \end{align*} These coefficients are smooth and positive on the outer region. On the overlap $5/4<|r|<3/2$, we have $\eta =1$, $p=q=0$ and $x_ by_ bz_ b=d_*$, so the two definitions agree. For $|r|\geq 2$ they equal $\kappa (\sigma (r),\sigma (-r),\sigma '(r))$. Thus \[  \omega _0=xP+yQ+zR  \] extends smoothly across both omitted projective lines, being equal near them to $f_*(t)^{1/3}\omega _ X$, which is smooth and positive there since $f_*(0)=f_*(1)=a^2b^2>0$. On $X$, the form $\omega _0$ is semipositive, positive away from $r=\pm 1$, and of rank two on these levels. The function \[  F(r)=2\int _0^ r p(s)\, \mathrm{d}s  \] is constant on each of the intervals $(-\infty ,-1]$ and $[1,\infty )$, and so $F(r)$ extends to a smooth nonconstant function on $X$. By ( 14.26.5 ), half of its complex Hessian is $H_0=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F/2=p(P-Q)+qR$. By ( 14.29.10 ) and ( 14.29.3 ), the forms $A_0=\omega _0-H_0$, $B_0=\omega _0+H_0$ satisfy \[  A_0^3=B_0^3=f_*(t)\omega _ X^3  \] on $U$, and hence on $X$. Their ranks and positivity were determined above, after ( 14.29.9 ). The construction is symmetric: $x(-r)=y(r)$, and $z$ is even.

title: 14.29.12 A positive equation background
text: As in the first example, an exact correction makes the average form strictly positive without changing the two solution forms. Here the coefficient of $R$ is already positive, and the correction restores the missing coefficient of $P$ or $Q$ at each endpoint. Let $\varepsilon >0$ be a parameter, restricted below. Let $h(r)=(r^2-1)\eta (r)$, extend it by zero on the tails, and set $\rho =\varepsilon h$. The coefficients of $\omega =\omega _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ are 1FC5DA40EAF0 14.29.13 \begin{equation}  (x+\varepsilon h',\  y-\varepsilon h',\  z+\varepsilon h''). \end{equation} On $|r|\leq 3/2$, we have $h'=2r$ and $h''=2$. For $0\leq r\leq 3/2$, $x+2\varepsilon r>0$, since the only zero of $x$ there is at $r=1$, where the correction is positive. On $[-3/2,0]$, $x$ has a positive minimum $m_0$, so positivity holds if $3\varepsilon <m_0$. Reflection proves positivity of the second coefficient, and the third is $z+2\varepsilon >0$. On the compact transition region $3/2\leq |r|\leq 2$, all original coefficients have a common positive lower bound $m_1$. If $M_1$ bounds $|h'|+|h''|$, taking also $\varepsilon <m_1/(M_1+1)$ preserves their positivity there. For $|r|\geq 2$, the background equals $f_*(t)^{1/3}\omega _ X>0$. Hence $\omega $ is strictly positive on $X$. The correction is exact, so $\mathrm{d}\omega =\mathrm{d}\omega _0$. At $r=0$, where $x=x_ b$ and $y=y_ b$, evenness of $S_*$ gives $x'(0)=-1/2$ and $y'(0)=1/2$. Hence ( 14.26.11 ) gives \[  \mathrm{d}\omega _0=(z_ b(0)+1/2)\, \mathrm{d}r\wedge (Q-P)\ne 0.  \] Indeed, if $\mathrm{d}r\wedge (Q-P)=0$, wedging with $P$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}r$ would contradict $P\wedge Q\wedge R>0$. Thus the Hermitian background $\omega $ is not closed. Now put $\widetilde u=-F/2-\rho $ and $\widetilde v=F/2-\rho $. Then $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u=A_0$, $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v=B_0$. Subtracting their respective suprema gives $u,v$ with $\sup _ Xu=\sup _ Xv=0$, and ( 14.29.2 ) holds. Their difference is nonconstant because $F$ is nonconstant.

title: 14.29.14 Zeros and higher dimensions
text: It remains to examine the regularity of the density and the geometry of its zero levels. Taking a product with projective space then preserves the equality of the Monge–Ampère measures and gives examples in every higher dimension. The function $t$ is real analytic in every affine chart of $X$, being a quotient of real polynomials with positive denominator. Hence $f_*(t)$ is real analytic on $X$. Its two zero levels are regular hypersurfaces because $t=\sigma (r)$, $\sigma '>0$, and $\mathrm{d}r\ne 0$. Each level is connected, since it is the quotient of the product of two three-spheres of fixed nonzero radii by the diagonal action of the circle. Each level is compact and has zero volume. The divided differences in ( 14.29.5 ) show near the two levels that E3CA723897C6 14.29.15 \begin{equation}  f_*(\sigma (r))=(r+1)^2g_-(r),\qquad f_*(\sigma (r))=(r-1)^2g_+(r), \end{equation} respectively, with smooth strictly positive functions $g_\pm $. For $n\geq 4$, let $\theta $ be the Fubini–Study form on $Y=\mathbb {P}^{n-3}$, let $\pi _1:X\times Y\to X$ and $\pi _2:X\times Y\to Y$ be the projections, and set, on $X\times Y$, \[  \omega _ n=\pi _1^*\omega +\pi _2^*\theta ,\qquad \Omega _ n=\pi _1^*\omega _ X+\pi _2^*\theta ,\qquad u_ n=\pi _1^*u,\quad v_ n=\pi _1^*v.  \] In the expansion of an $n$-fold product, only the terms with exactly three factors pulled back from $X$ survive. Consequently \[  (\omega _ n+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n)^ n =\binom n3\pi _1^*(A_0^3)\wedge \pi _2^*(\theta ^{n-3}) =f_*(\pi _1^*t)\Omega _ n^ n,  \] and the same holds for $v_ n$. On the two product levels, the solution forms have rank $2+(n-3)=n-1$. Restriction to a slice $X\times \{ y\} $ recovers $\mathrm{d}\omega \ne 0$, so $\omega _ n$ is not closed. Normalization, distinctness and real analyticity are preserved by pullback. Write $\operatorname {Vol}$ for the volume with respect to $\omega _ X^3$, or $\Omega _ n^ n$ in dimension $n$. The quadratic zeros complete the proof of the sharpness assertion in 14.21.13 . In finitely many tubular charts around the zero levels, the density is bounded above and below by positive multiples of the square of a real transverse coordinate, and the volume form has a bounded positive density with respect to coordinate volume. Away from these charts, the density is bounded below by a positive constant. Thus, for $s>0$ and $\alpha >0$, C72BCF7334A2 14.29.16 \begin{equation}  \operatorname {Vol}\{ f_*\leq s\} \asymp \sqrt s\quad (s\downarrow 0), \qquad f_*^{-\alpha }\in L^1\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \alpha <\tfrac 12. \end{equation} Thus, for every $0<\alpha <1/2$ and every dimension $n\geq 3$, there are smooth examples of nonuniqueness whose density $f$ satisfies $f^{-\alpha }\in L^1$; this condition is weaker than the hypothesis $f^{-1/2}\in L^1$ of 14.21.13 . Remark 14.29.17 . DF533F76B4CE For this example, the positive-density set $\{ f_*(t)>0\} $ has three components: the middle band and the two outer regions. The two solution forms have the same missing direction on each zero level, so $E_{\rm unif}=\{ f_*(t)>0\} $. The maximum and the minimum of the difference of the two potentials are attained on the two outer components, whose closures are disjoint, in accordance with 14.21.3 . Although the closure of the middle component meets both outer closures, the extremal values do not propagate through the middle component.
