title: 8.1 Complex Hessian equations
text: Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n$, let $\omega $ be a smooth positive Hermitian form, and fix $2\leq m<n$. The complex Hessian operator $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m}$ replaces the determinant by an intermediate symmetric polynomial. Its admissible cone allows negative eigenvalues, so the product calculus for plurisubharmonic potentials from section 5.21 no longer applies directly. For a continuous admissible weak solution with smooth positive density depending on the potential, the difficulty is to obtain derivative estimates before smoothness is known. Proper exponential equations associate smooth solutions to its smooth admissible approximations. The complex-Hessian estimate is independent of derivatives of the prescribed approximation, so it survives passage to the limit. Uniform convergence defines the continuous mixed products, while obstacle envelopes give the domination principle that identifies the limit with the original solution. A concave uniformly elliptic extension then supplies classical interior regularity. The determinant case is treated in theorem 14.19.32 ; the argument here concerns the intermediate Hessian degrees. Uniform stability also constructs solutions for strictly increasing exponents, by contraction between constant barriers. Bounded admissible potentials require decreasing approximation. The recursion first gives currents with measure coefficients below degree $m$; local Hessian capacities control multiplication by their discontinuous potentials. Quasicontinuity and weighted convergence make the products symmetric and allow all approximation indices to tend to their limits together. At degree $m$, the positive product after wedging with $\omega ^{n-m}$ is a Radon measure. These weighted limits pass locality and the maximum inequality to bounded potentials. Truncation above the infimum then proves that the Hessian measure of each potential is nonzero on an arbitrary Hermitian background. In global comparison, the maximum inequality leaves a signed total-mass difference. The complex Hessians of the background powers determine when this difference vanishes for every bounded admissible list. On small sublevel sets, a modified comparison estimate absorbs the torsion error on arbitrary Hermitian backgrounds. It yields strict domination, bounded stability for proper equations and smoothness for their solutions with smooth data between constant barriers.

title: 8.2 The admissible cone
text: For $\lambda \in \mathbb R^ n$, let $S_ j(\lambda )$ be the elementary symmetric polynomial of degree $j$, put $\sigma _ j=S_ j/\binom nj$ and $\sigma _0=1$, and set \[  \Gamma _ m=\{ \lambda :S_ j(\lambda )>0,\  1\leq j\leq m\} .  \] A real $(1,1)$-form belongs to $\Gamma _ m(\omega )$ if its eigenvalues relative to $\omega $ belong to $\Gamma _ m$. Write $C_{n,m}$ for the corresponding closed cone of Hermitian matrices. The algebraic assertions below also apply when $m=n$. We use the classical Gårding facts: the closed spectral cone is convex, contains the nonnegative matrices, and is preserved by adding them; adding a positive matrix puts a closed-cone matrix in its interior. The normalized root $F=\sigma _ m^{1/m}$ is concave and increasing there. Polarized products of $k$ forms in $\Gamma _ k(\omega )$ with $\omega ^{n-k}$ are positive, and Maclaurin's inequalities give $\sigma _ j^{1/j}\geq \sigma _ k^{1/k}$ for $j\leq k$. These algebraic facts will serve as inputs to the analytic arguments. A continuous real function $v$ on $X$ is admissible if C5A4D9AE83ED 8.2.1 \begin{equation}  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)\wedge \gamma _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \gamma _{m-1} \wedge \omega ^{n-m}\geq 0 \end{equation} in distributions for every smooth collection $\gamma _1,\ldots ,\gamma _{m-1}\in \Gamma _ m(\omega )$. For smooth $v$ this is equivalent to the pointwise closed-cone condition; strict admissibility means membership in the open cone. Maxima and convex combinations preserve continuous admissibility. To check the maximum property, fix one smooth positive linear test in ( 8.2.1 ). Locally a smooth solution of its inhomogeneous linear equation reduces the assertion to the maximum property for subsolutions of a smooth elliptic operator. For a bounded upper semicontinuous function $v$, admissibility means that every local $C^2$ upper test $q$ at $x$ satisfies B372916B922F 8.2.2 \begin{equation}  \omega (x)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q(x)\in \overline{\Gamma _ m(\omega (x))}. \end{equation} For continuous $v$, this agrees with ( 8.2.1 ): Gårding duality reduces both conditions to subsolution inequalities for smooth strictly elliptic linear operators. We use their classical viscosity–distributional equivalence, with the usual subharmonic representative in the bounded class. The first estimate controls a scalar shift of the cone. It will give lower bounds for every coefficient of the linearized Hessian operator. Lemma 8.2.3 . F86594126C69 For $\lambda \in \Gamma _ m$, put \[  e_ m=\frac{\sigma _ m(\lambda )}{m\sigma _{m-1}(\lambda )}.  \] Then $\lambda -t\mathbf1\in \Gamma _ m$ for $0\leq t<e_ m$. If $m\geq 2$, the conclusion also holds for $t=e_ m$. For $m=1$, the endpoint lies on the boundary. Proof. The polynomial \[  P(x)=\sigma _ m(\lambda +x\mathbf1) =\sum _{j=0}^ m\binom mj\sigma _ j(\lambda )x^{m-j}  \] is a positive multiple of the $(n-m)$th derivative of $\prod _ i(x+\lambda _ i)$. Hence all its roots are real, by Rolle's theorem. Its coefficients are positive, so all its roots are strictly negative. Write $P(x)=\prod _{i=1}^ m(x+r_ i)$ with $r_ i>0$. Logarithmic differentiation at zero gives \[  \sum _{i=1}^ m r_ i^{-1} =\frac{m\sigma _{m-1}(\lambda )}{\sigma _ m(\lambda )} =e_ m^{-1}.  \] Thus $\min _ i r_ i\geq e_ m$, with strict inequality if $m\geq 2$. For $x> -\min _ i r_ i$, every derivative of $P$ is positive: differentiating its product expansion produces sums of products of positive factors. Since \[  P^{(m-j)}(x)=\frac{m!}{j!}\sigma _ j(\lambda +x\mathbf1), \qquad 1\leq j\leq m,  \] all the required symmetric polynomials are positive at $x=-t$. When $m=1$, the sole root is $-e_1$. $\square$ Lemma 8.2.4 . 94C4E018DD25 If $\alpha ,\gamma \in \Gamma _ m(\omega )$, then \[  \frac{\alpha ^{m-1}\wedge \gamma \wedge \omega ^{n-m}}{\omega ^ n} \frac{\alpha \wedge \omega ^{n-1}}{\omega ^ n} \geq \frac1{m!} \frac{\alpha ^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m}}{\omega ^ n} \frac{\gamma \wedge \omega ^{n-1}}{\omega ^ n}.  \] The assertion extends to $\gamma \in \overline{\Gamma _ m(\omega )}$ by continuity. Proof. Write $\sigma _ k=\alpha ^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-k}/\omega ^ n$, and $M_ k=\alpha ^{k-1}\wedge \gamma \wedge \omega ^{n-k}/\omega ^ n$. For $1\leq k<m$, the cone shift with index $k+1$ and Gårding positivity give \[  M_{k+1}\geq tM_ k \quad \left(0\leq t<\frac{\sigma _{k+1}}{(k+1)\sigma _ k}\right).  \] Let $t$ increase to the displayed endpoint. Iterating, starting with $M_1=\gamma \wedge \omega ^{n-1}/\omega ^ n$, yields \[  M_ m\geq \frac{\sigma _ m}{m!\sigma _1}M_1.  \] All denominators are positive. Approximating a form in the closed cone by $\gamma +\delta \omega $, $\delta \downarrow 0$, gives the last assertion. $\square$ At a diagonal Hermitian matrix $\Lambda $ in the open cone, order its eigenvalues as $\lambda _1\geq \cdots \geq \lambda _ n$ and write \[  f=F(\Lambda ),\quad F_ i=\partial _{\lambda _ i}F,\quad S=\operatorname {tr}\Lambda ,\quad \mathcal F=\sum _ iF_ i, \quad Q=\sum _ iF_ i\lambda _ i^2.  \] The next inequalities use these derivatives of the normalized root, rather than derivatives of the polynomial $S_ m$. Lemma 8.2.5 . 7710D01DF6F5 If $M$ belongs to the closed Hermitian $m$-cone, then \[  W:=\sum _ iF_ iM_{i\bar i}\geq \frac{f}{m!S}\operatorname {tr}M, \qquad F_ i\geq \frac{f}{m!S},\qquad |M_{1\bar1}|\leq \operatorname {tr}M.  \] No simultaneous diagonalization of $M$ and $\Lambda $ is required. Proof. In the wedge notation of the mixed-trace estimate, differentiation gives $DF_\Lambda (M)=fM_ m/\sigma _ m$. The estimate $M_ m\geq \sigma _ m M_1/(m!\sigma _1)$, with $M_1=\operatorname {tr}M/n$ and $\sigma _1=S/n$, proves the first inequality. The positive semidefinite rank-one coordinate projections belong to the closed $m$-cone; taking $M$ to be each projection proves the second inequality. The closed $m$-cone is contained in the closed $2$-cone. Its eigenvalues $\mu $ satisfy \[  \operatorname {tr}M\geq 0,\qquad \sum _ i\mu _ i^2=(\operatorname {tr}M)^2-2S_2(\mu ) \leq (\operatorname {tr}M)^2.  \] Thus the operator norm of $M$ is at most its trace, which proves the last inequality. The wedge pairing computes the derivative in the diagonal frame of $\Lambda $, regardless of the eigenvectors of $M$. $\square$ Lemma 8.2.6 . 473C52E484B0 If $0<f_0\leq f\leq f_1$, then \[  Q:=\sum _ iF_ i\lambda _ i^2 \geq \frac{f_0}{m}S-\frac{n-m}{m}f_1^2, \qquad \mathcal F\geq 1.  \] Proof. The derivative of the normalized root is $F_ i=fS_{m-1}(\lambda |i)/(mS_ m)$. The splitting identity gives \[  Q=\frac fm S-\frac{(m+1)f}{mS_ m}S_{m+1}.  \] For $m=n$, set $S_{n+1}=0$. If $S_{m+1}\leq 0$, the second term is nonnegative. Otherwise $\lambda \in \Gamma _{m+1}$ and Maclaurin gives $S_{m+1}\leq \binom n{m+1}f^{m+1}$. Since $S_ m=\binom nm f^ m$, the subtracted term is at most $(n-m)f^2/m$. This proves the first assertion. Summing the derivatives gives $\mathcal F=f\sigma _{m-1}/\sigma _ m\geq 1$, again by Maclaurin. $\square$ When $m<n$, admissible forms need not be semipositive. Positivity of a mixed Hessian measure therefore does not directly bound every coefficient of its factors. For degrees below $m$, deleted-coordinate positivity supplies the required absolute bound: if $S_{j;I}$ means $S_ j$ with the coordinates indexed by $I$ omitted, then $S_{j;I}(\lambda )>0$ for $j+|I|\leq m$, by polarized Gårding positivity. Lemma 8.2.7 . B0643A9A1173 If $0\leq r<m$, $\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ r\in \Gamma _ m(\omega )$, and $\Xi $ is a smooth complementary form, then \[  |\alpha _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \alpha _ r\wedge \Xi | \leq C_{n,m,\Xi }(\alpha _1+\cdots +\alpha _ r)^ r\wedge \omega ^{n-r}.  \] For $r=0$ the right-hand side means $C_{n,m,\Xi }\omega ^ n$. Proof. First take a single form $\alpha $, diagonal in an $\omega $-unitary frame, with ordered eigenvalues $\lambda \in \Gamma _ m$. For $1\leq r<m$, repeated splitting and deleted-coordinate positivity give $S_ r(\lambda )\geq \lambda _1\cdots \lambda _ r$. The sum of the last $n-r$ eigenvalues is positive, so each negative eigenvalue has modulus at most $(n-r)\lambda _{r+1}$. Thus every product of $r$ distinct eigenvalues has modulus at most \[  (n-r)^ r\lambda _1\cdots \lambda _ r\leq (n-r)^ r S_ r(\lambda ).  \] Indeed, replace its negative factors by this bound and its positive factors by the corresponding largest eigenvalues. In the diagonal frame only complementary diagonal coefficients of $\Xi $ contribute to $\alpha ^ r\wedge \Xi $. This proves $|\alpha ^ r\wedge \Xi |\leq C_{n,m,\Xi }\alpha ^ r\wedge \omega ^{n-r}$. Apply this bound to the polynomial $(\alpha _1+t_2\alpha _2+\cdots +t_ r\alpha _ r)^ r\wedge \Xi $, with $0\leq t_ i\leq 1$. Its absolute value is bounded by the stated right-hand side, by polarized positivity and monotonicity on the cone. A fixed invertible interpolation matrix on this finite-dimensional polynomial space bounds each coefficient by its supremum on the cube. The coefficient of $t_2\cdots t_ r$ is a fixed positive multiple of $\alpha _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \alpha _ r\wedge \Xi $. This proves the mixed bound. The closed-cone case follows by adding $\varepsilon \omega $ to each form and taking the limit. $\square$ The next coefficient bound also controls a torsion form whose diagonal coefficients can have either sign. It compares each two-coordinate coefficient with the positive coefficients of the associated gradient pairing. Lemma 8.2.8 . 8673FC834527 If $\lambda \in \overline{\Gamma _ m}$, $1\leq q\leq \min \{ m-1,n-2\} $, and $i\ne j$, then, with $N=n-2$ and \[  c_{N,q}=\frac{q(N-q)}{(q+1)(N-q+1)}<1,  \] one has \[  |S_{q;ij}(\lambda )|^2 \leq \frac{S_{q;i}(\lambda )S_{q;j}(\lambda )}{1-c_{N,q}}.  \] This includes $q=N$, when $c_{N,N}=0$. Proof. First prove the unnormalized Newton inequality for an arbitrary real list $\mu $ of length $N$. For $1\leq q<N$, put $R(x)=\prod _{a=1}^ N(x+\mu _ a)$ and $G=R^{(N-q-1)}$. Repeated Rolle's theorem makes $G$ a real-rooted polynomial of degree $d=q+1$. Away from its roots $r_ a$, logarithmic differentiation and Cauchy–Schwarz give \[  G'^2-GG''=G^2\sum _{a=1}^ d\frac1{(x-r_ a)^2} \geq \frac1dG^2\left(\sum _{a=1}^ d\frac1{x-r_ a}\right)^2 =\frac1dG'^2.  \] Continuity extends this polynomial inequality to every real $x$. At zero, \[  G=(N-q-1)!S_{q+1}(\mu ),\quad G'=(N-q)!S_ q(\mu ),\quad G''=(N-q+1)!S_{q-1}(\mu ).  \] Consequently $S_{q-1}(\mu )S_{q+1}(\mu )\leq c_{N,q}S_ q(\mu )^2$. No sign restriction on $\mu $ or on these coefficients was used. For $q=N$, its left side is zero and the same assertion holds with $c_{N,N}=0$. Apply this to the list with $i,j$ deleted. Put $A=S_{q-1;ij}$, $B=S_{q;ij}$, $C=S_{q+1;ij}$ and $D_ i=S_{q;i}$, $D_ j=S_{q;j}$. Deleted-coordinate positivity gives $A,D_ i,D_ j\geq 0$: the required degrees are $q+1\leq m$. Splitting in the two omitted coordinates gives the exact identity \[  D_ iD_ j=A S_{q+1}(\lambda )+B^2-AC.  \] Since $S_{q+1}(\lambda )\geq 0$ and $AC\leq c_{N,q}B^2$, this is at least $(1-c_{N,q})B^2$. There is no division by $A$ or $D_ i$; all degenerate endpoints are therefore included. Equivalently one may first add $\epsilon \mathbf1$ and pass to the closed cone. $\square$ A smooth maximum preserves the cone condition and can be chosen monotone in its smoothing scale as well as in its two arguments. Lemma 8.2.9 . 365519F85C5A If smooth uniformly bounded admissible $u_ j\downarrow u$ and $v_ j\downarrow v$ are given, there are smooth uniformly bounded admissible $w_ j\downarrow \max \{ u,v\} $. For any chosen $\epsilon _ j>0$ decreasing to zero, they can be chosen to satisfy $w_ j=u_ j$ on $\{ u_ j-v_ j>\epsilon _ j\} $ and $w_ j=v_ j$ on $\{ v_ j-u_ j>\epsilon _ j\} $. For smooth functions $f,g$ on an open subset of $X$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g\in \overline{\Gamma _ m(\omega )}$, the regularized maximum $M_\epsilon (f,g)$ constructed below satisfies the same unshifted cone condition. Proof. Choose a nonnegative even smooth probability density $\zeta $ supported in $[-1,1]$, and set \[  r_\epsilon (t)=\int |t-\epsilon s|\zeta (s)\, \mathrm ds, \qquad M_\epsilon (x,y)=\tfrac 12(x+y+r_\epsilon (x-y)).  \] The function $r_\epsilon $ is smooth and convex, $|r_\epsilon '|\leq 1$, and $r_\epsilon (t)=|t|$ for $|t|\geq \epsilon $. Jensen's inequality and the triangle inequality give \[  \max \{ x,y\} \leq M_\epsilon (x,y) \leq \max \{ x,y\} +\epsilon /2.  \] Its partial derivatives in $x,y$ are nonnegative. For fixed $t$, $r_\epsilon (t)$ is an even convex function of $\epsilon $, since $\zeta $ is even. It is therefore nondecreasing for $\epsilon \geq 0$. Consequently $w_ j=M_{\epsilon _ j}(u_ j,v_ j)$ decreases pointwise to $\max \{ u,v\} $ and has the asserted equalities and bounds. Put $h_ j=u_ j-v_ j$ and $a_ j=(1+r_{\epsilon _ j}'(h_ j))/2$. The chain rule gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j =a_ j(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)+(1-a_ j)(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j) +\tfrac 12r_{\epsilon _ j}''(h_ j) \mathrm dh_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}h_ j.  \] Here $0\leq a_ j\leq 1$, and the last form is semipositive. Convexity of the cone and its stability under semipositive addition prove admissibility. For smooth local functions satisfying the unshifted cone condition, omit $\omega $ from this chain rule; the same argument proves preservation of that condition. The pointwise maximum is itself admissible: an upper test for it at a point is an upper test for a potential attaining the maximum there. Its canonical representative is thus the indicated pointwise maximum. $\square$ Lemma 8.2.10 . A1FFEE061CF5 If bounded admissible $u,v$ satisfy $u\leq v$ almost everywhere with respect to $\omega ^ n$, then $u\leq v$ everywhere. Proof. By 8.2.9 , $w=\max \{ u,v\} $ is bounded admissible with its indicated canonical representative. Since $w=v$ almost everywhere, they represent the same distribution. The canonical subharmonic representative used in ( 8.2.2 ) is determined by that distribution. Thus $w=v$ pointwise, which is the assertion. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.2.3
text: Lemma 8.2.3 . F86594126C69 For $\lambda \in \Gamma _ m$, put \[  e_ m=\frac{\sigma _ m(\lambda )}{m\sigma _{m-1}(\lambda )}.  \] Then $\lambda -t\mathbf1\in \Gamma _ m$ for $0\leq t<e_ m$. If $m\geq 2$, the conclusion also holds for $t=e_ m$. For $m=1$, the endpoint lies on the boundary. Proof. The polynomial \[  P(x)=\sigma _ m(\lambda +x\mathbf1) =\sum _{j=0}^ m\binom mj\sigma _ j(\lambda )x^{m-j}  \] is a positive multiple of the $(n-m)$th derivative of $\prod _ i(x+\lambda _ i)$. Hence all its roots are real, by Rolle's theorem. Its coefficients are positive, so all its roots are strictly negative. Write $P(x)=\prod _{i=1}^ m(x+r_ i)$ with $r_ i>0$. Logarithmic differentiation at zero gives \[  \sum _{i=1}^ m r_ i^{-1} =\frac{m\sigma _{m-1}(\lambda )}{\sigma _ m(\lambda )} =e_ m^{-1}.  \] Thus $\min _ i r_ i\geq e_ m$, with strict inequality if $m\geq 2$. For $x> -\min _ i r_ i$, every derivative of $P$ is positive: differentiating its product expansion produces sums of products of positive factors. Since \[  P^{(m-j)}(x)=\frac{m!}{j!}\sigma _ j(\lambda +x\mathbf1), \qquad 1\leq j\leq m,  \] all the required symmetric polynomials are positive at $x=-t$. When $m=1$, the sole root is $-e_1$. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.2.4
text: Lemma 8.2.4 . 94C4E018DD25 If $\alpha ,\gamma \in \Gamma _ m(\omega )$, then \[  \frac{\alpha ^{m-1}\wedge \gamma \wedge \omega ^{n-m}}{\omega ^ n} \frac{\alpha \wedge \omega ^{n-1}}{\omega ^ n} \geq \frac1{m!} \frac{\alpha ^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m}}{\omega ^ n} \frac{\gamma \wedge \omega ^{n-1}}{\omega ^ n}.  \] The assertion extends to $\gamma \in \overline{\Gamma _ m(\omega )}$ by continuity. Proof. Write $\sigma _ k=\alpha ^ k\wedge \omega ^{n-k}/\omega ^ n$, and $M_ k=\alpha ^{k-1}\wedge \gamma \wedge \omega ^{n-k}/\omega ^ n$. For $1\leq k<m$, the cone shift with index $k+1$ and Gårding positivity give \[  M_{k+1}\geq tM_ k \quad \left(0\leq t<\frac{\sigma _{k+1}}{(k+1)\sigma _ k}\right).  \] Let $t$ increase to the displayed endpoint. Iterating, starting with $M_1=\gamma \wedge \omega ^{n-1}/\omega ^ n$, yields \[  M_ m\geq \frac{\sigma _ m}{m!\sigma _1}M_1.  \] All denominators are positive. Approximating a form in the closed cone by $\gamma +\delta \omega $, $\delta \downarrow 0$, gives the last assertion. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.2.5
text: Lemma 8.2.5 . 7710D01DF6F5 If $M$ belongs to the closed Hermitian $m$-cone, then \[  W:=\sum _ iF_ iM_{i\bar i}\geq \frac{f}{m!S}\operatorname {tr}M, \qquad F_ i\geq \frac{f}{m!S},\qquad |M_{1\bar1}|\leq \operatorname {tr}M.  \] No simultaneous diagonalization of $M$ and $\Lambda $ is required. Proof. In the wedge notation of the mixed-trace estimate, differentiation gives $DF_\Lambda (M)=fM_ m/\sigma _ m$. The estimate $M_ m\geq \sigma _ m M_1/(m!\sigma _1)$, with $M_1=\operatorname {tr}M/n$ and $\sigma _1=S/n$, proves the first inequality. The positive semidefinite rank-one coordinate projections belong to the closed $m$-cone; taking $M$ to be each projection proves the second inequality. The closed $m$-cone is contained in the closed $2$-cone. Its eigenvalues $\mu $ satisfy \[  \operatorname {tr}M\geq 0,\qquad \sum _ i\mu _ i^2=(\operatorname {tr}M)^2-2S_2(\mu ) \leq (\operatorname {tr}M)^2.  \] Thus the operator norm of $M$ is at most its trace, which proves the last inequality. The wedge pairing computes the derivative in the diagonal frame of $\Lambda $, regardless of the eigenvectors of $M$. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.2.6
text: Lemma 8.2.6 . 473C52E484B0 If $0<f_0\leq f\leq f_1$, then \[  Q:=\sum _ iF_ i\lambda _ i^2 \geq \frac{f_0}{m}S-\frac{n-m}{m}f_1^2, \qquad \mathcal F\geq 1.  \] Proof. The derivative of the normalized root is $F_ i=fS_{m-1}(\lambda |i)/(mS_ m)$. The splitting identity gives \[  Q=\frac fm S-\frac{(m+1)f}{mS_ m}S_{m+1}.  \] For $m=n$, set $S_{n+1}=0$. If $S_{m+1}\leq 0$, the second term is nonnegative. Otherwise $\lambda \in \Gamma _{m+1}$ and Maclaurin gives $S_{m+1}\leq \binom n{m+1}f^{m+1}$. Since $S_ m=\binom nm f^ m$, the subtracted term is at most $(n-m)f^2/m$. This proves the first assertion. Summing the derivatives gives $\mathcal F=f\sigma _{m-1}/\sigma _ m\geq 1$, again by Maclaurin. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.2.7
text: Lemma 8.2.7 . B0643A9A1173 If $0\leq r<m$, $\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ r\in \Gamma _ m(\omega )$, and $\Xi $ is a smooth complementary form, then \[  |\alpha _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \alpha _ r\wedge \Xi | \leq C_{n,m,\Xi }(\alpha _1+\cdots +\alpha _ r)^ r\wedge \omega ^{n-r}.  \] For $r=0$ the right-hand side means $C_{n,m,\Xi }\omega ^ n$. Proof. First take a single form $\alpha $, diagonal in an $\omega $-unitary frame, with ordered eigenvalues $\lambda \in \Gamma _ m$. For $1\leq r<m$, repeated splitting and deleted-coordinate positivity give $S_ r(\lambda )\geq \lambda _1\cdots \lambda _ r$. The sum of the last $n-r$ eigenvalues is positive, so each negative eigenvalue has modulus at most $(n-r)\lambda _{r+1}$. Thus every product of $r$ distinct eigenvalues has modulus at most \[  (n-r)^ r\lambda _1\cdots \lambda _ r\leq (n-r)^ r S_ r(\lambda ).  \] Indeed, replace its negative factors by this bound and its positive factors by the corresponding largest eigenvalues. In the diagonal frame only complementary diagonal coefficients of $\Xi $ contribute to $\alpha ^ r\wedge \Xi $. This proves $|\alpha ^ r\wedge \Xi |\leq C_{n,m,\Xi }\alpha ^ r\wedge \omega ^{n-r}$. Apply this bound to the polynomial $(\alpha _1+t_2\alpha _2+\cdots +t_ r\alpha _ r)^ r\wedge \Xi $, with $0\leq t_ i\leq 1$. Its absolute value is bounded by the stated right-hand side, by polarized positivity and monotonicity on the cone. A fixed invertible interpolation matrix on this finite-dimensional polynomial space bounds each coefficient by its supremum on the cube. The coefficient of $t_2\cdots t_ r$ is a fixed positive multiple of $\alpha _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \alpha _ r\wedge \Xi $. This proves the mixed bound. The closed-cone case follows by adding $\varepsilon \omega $ to each form and taking the limit. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.2.8
text: Lemma 8.2.8 . 8673FC834527 If $\lambda \in \overline{\Gamma _ m}$, $1\leq q\leq \min \{ m-1,n-2\} $, and $i\ne j$, then, with $N=n-2$ and \[  c_{N,q}=\frac{q(N-q)}{(q+1)(N-q+1)}<1,  \] one has \[  |S_{q;ij}(\lambda )|^2 \leq \frac{S_{q;i}(\lambda )S_{q;j}(\lambda )}{1-c_{N,q}}.  \] This includes $q=N$, when $c_{N,N}=0$. Proof. First prove the unnormalized Newton inequality for an arbitrary real list $\mu $ of length $N$. For $1\leq q<N$, put $R(x)=\prod _{a=1}^ N(x+\mu _ a)$ and $G=R^{(N-q-1)}$. Repeated Rolle's theorem makes $G$ a real-rooted polynomial of degree $d=q+1$. Away from its roots $r_ a$, logarithmic differentiation and Cauchy–Schwarz give \[  G'^2-GG''=G^2\sum _{a=1}^ d\frac1{(x-r_ a)^2} \geq \frac1dG^2\left(\sum _{a=1}^ d\frac1{x-r_ a}\right)^2 =\frac1dG'^2.  \] Continuity extends this polynomial inequality to every real $x$. At zero, \[  G=(N-q-1)!S_{q+1}(\mu ),\quad G'=(N-q)!S_ q(\mu ),\quad G''=(N-q+1)!S_{q-1}(\mu ).  \] Consequently $S_{q-1}(\mu )S_{q+1}(\mu )\leq c_{N,q}S_ q(\mu )^2$. No sign restriction on $\mu $ or on these coefficients was used. For $q=N$, its left side is zero and the same assertion holds with $c_{N,N}=0$. Apply this to the list with $i,j$ deleted. Put $A=S_{q-1;ij}$, $B=S_{q;ij}$, $C=S_{q+1;ij}$ and $D_ i=S_{q;i}$, $D_ j=S_{q;j}$. Deleted-coordinate positivity gives $A,D_ i,D_ j\geq 0$: the required degrees are $q+1\leq m$. Splitting in the two omitted coordinates gives the exact identity \[  D_ iD_ j=A S_{q+1}(\lambda )+B^2-AC.  \] Since $S_{q+1}(\lambda )\geq 0$ and $AC\leq c_{N,q}B^2$, this is at least $(1-c_{N,q})B^2$. There is no division by $A$ or $D_ i$; all degenerate endpoints are therefore included. Equivalently one may first add $\epsilon \mathbf1$ and pass to the closed cone. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.2.9
text: Lemma 8.2.9 . 365519F85C5A If smooth uniformly bounded admissible $u_ j\downarrow u$ and $v_ j\downarrow v$ are given, there are smooth uniformly bounded admissible $w_ j\downarrow \max \{ u,v\} $. For any chosen $\epsilon _ j>0$ decreasing to zero, they can be chosen to satisfy $w_ j=u_ j$ on $\{ u_ j-v_ j>\epsilon _ j\} $ and $w_ j=v_ j$ on $\{ v_ j-u_ j>\epsilon _ j\} $. For smooth functions $f,g$ on an open subset of $X$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f,\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g\in \overline{\Gamma _ m(\omega )}$, the regularized maximum $M_\epsilon (f,g)$ constructed below satisfies the same unshifted cone condition. Proof. Choose a nonnegative even smooth probability density $\zeta $ supported in $[-1,1]$, and set \[  r_\epsilon (t)=\int |t-\epsilon s|\zeta (s)\, \mathrm ds, \qquad M_\epsilon (x,y)=\tfrac 12(x+y+r_\epsilon (x-y)).  \] The function $r_\epsilon $ is smooth and convex, $|r_\epsilon '|\leq 1$, and $r_\epsilon (t)=|t|$ for $|t|\geq \epsilon $. Jensen's inequality and the triangle inequality give \[  \max \{ x,y\} \leq M_\epsilon (x,y) \leq \max \{ x,y\} +\epsilon /2.  \] Its partial derivatives in $x,y$ are nonnegative. For fixed $t$, $r_\epsilon (t)$ is an even convex function of $\epsilon $, since $\zeta $ is even. It is therefore nondecreasing for $\epsilon \geq 0$. Consequently $w_ j=M_{\epsilon _ j}(u_ j,v_ j)$ decreases pointwise to $\max \{ u,v\} $ and has the asserted equalities and bounds. Put $h_ j=u_ j-v_ j$ and $a_ j=(1+r_{\epsilon _ j}'(h_ j))/2$. The chain rule gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j =a_ j(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)+(1-a_ j)(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j) +\tfrac 12r_{\epsilon _ j}''(h_ j) \mathrm dh_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}h_ j.  \] Here $0\leq a_ j\leq 1$, and the last form is semipositive. Convexity of the cone and its stability under semipositive addition prove admissibility. For smooth local functions satisfying the unshifted cone condition, omit $\omega $ from this chain rule; the same argument proves preservation of that condition. The pointwise maximum is itself admissible: an upper test for it at a point is an upper test for a potential attaining the maximum there. Its canonical representative is thus the indicated pointwise maximum. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.2.10
text: Lemma 8.2.10 . A1FFEE061CF5 If bounded admissible $u,v$ satisfy $u\leq v$ almost everywhere with respect to $\omega ^ n$, then $u\leq v$ everywhere. Proof. By 8.2.9 , $w=\max \{ u,v\} $ is bounded admissible with its indicated canonical representative. Since $w=v$ almost everywhere, they represent the same distribution. The canonical subharmonic representative used in ( 8.2.2 ) is determined by that distribution. Thus $w=v$ pointwise, which is the assertion. $\square$

title: 8.3 Liouville and gradient estimates
text: The gradient estimate comes from rescaling a sequence at points of large gradient. The background then disappears, leaving a maximal function for a constant Euclidean cone. We first establish the Liouville theorem that rules out such a nonconstant limit. For this Euclidean argument allow $1\leq m\leq n$. Write $H(v)=(v_{i\bar j})$. A continuous real function $v$ on a Euclidean domain is admissible for $C_{n,m}$ if \[  \operatorname {tr}(QH(v))\geq 0 \quad \text{in distributions for every }Q\in C_{n,m}^*,  \] where $C_{n,m}^*=\{ Q:\operatorname {tr}(QA)\geq 0\text{ for all }A\in C_{n,m}\} $. For smooth functions this says $H(v)\in C_{n,m}$. Call $v$ maximal if every smooth lower test has Hessian outside the interior of $C_{n,m}$ at the contact point. Admissibility implies subharmonicity and is preserved by nonnegative convolution. The cone polynomial $S_ m$ increases under nonnegative matrix addition in the interior. Lemma 8.3.1 . 89F810E43B3E Local uniform limits of admissible maximal functions are admissible and maximal. Suppose $v$ is admissible and maximal on a bounded open set $D$, and $h$ is smooth and admissible there. If both are continuous on $\overline D$ and $h\leq v$ on $\partial D$, then $h\leq v$ on $D$. Proof. The distributional inequalities pass to local uniform limits. If a lower test $h$ for the limit at $z_0$ has Hessian in the interior, subtract $\delta |z-z_0|^2$, for sufficiently small $\delta >0$, to make the contact strict while retaining interior admissibility near $z_0$. Interior minimum points for the approximants then tend to $z_0$. Adding the minimum value produces lower tests for them with Hessian in the interior, contradicting their maximality. For comparison choose $R$ with $\overline D\subset \{ |z|\leq R\} $. If $h>v$ somewhere, the function $h_\delta =h+\delta (|z|^2-R^2)$ still exceeds $v$ somewhere for small $\delta >0$ and is at most $v$ on the boundary. The negative minimum of $v-h_\delta $ is attained inside $D$. Since $H(h_\delta )=H(h)+\delta I$ belongs to the interior, adding the minimum value gives a forbidden lower test. This argument requires no regularity of the boundary. $\square$ Theorem 8.3.2 . 96D01E7C4F0F Every bounded globally Lipschitz admissible function on $\mathbb C^ n$ that is maximal for $C_{n,m}$ is constant. Proof. For $m=1$, the distributional subharmonicity and the lower-test condition say that the function is a viscosity solution of the Laplace equation. The elementary equivalence with harmonicity and bounded harmonic Liouville give the conclusion. For $m=n$, admissibility is distributional plurisubharmonicity. The continuous representative is plurisubharmonic, and bounded plurisubharmonic Liouville applies. For a fixed $m\geq 2$, we therefore argue by induction on $n\geq m$. The reduction in dimension is particularly simple for this cone. For a Hermitian $(n-1)$-by-$(n-1)$ matrix $A$ and $m<n$, \[  S_ j(A\oplus 0)=S_ j(A),\qquad 1\leq j\leq m.  \] Consequently $A\oplus 0$ belongs to $C_{n,m}$, respectively its interior, exactly when $A$ belongs to $C_{n-1,m}$, respectively its interior. For the closed cones, the nonnegative inequalities characterize the closure: the expansion of $S_ j(\lambda +\delta \mathbf1)$ has nonnegative coefficients and a strictly positive $\delta ^ j$ term. If an admissible function is independent of $z_ n$, convolving it and using the block identity shows that the function in the remaining variables is admissible. Extending its lower tests independently of $z_ n$ shows that maximality also passes to dimension $n-1$. Suppose $v$ is nonconstant. Normalize $\inf v=0$, $\sup v=1$, and let $L$ be its Lipschitz constant. Choose a smooth radial nonnegative probability kernel $\eta $, supported in the closed unit ball and positive in its interior. Put \[  [f]_ r(x)=\int f(x+y)\eta _ r(y)\, \mathrm dy, \qquad \eta _ r(y)=r^{-2n}\eta (y/r),\qquad v_\epsilon =[v]_\epsilon .  \] Both $v$ and $v^2$ are subharmonic: for the second assertion use $\Delta (v_\epsilon ^2)=2v_\epsilon \Delta v_\epsilon +2|\nabla v_\epsilon |^2\geq 0$ and pass to the uniform limit. Their radial averages increase with $r$, by monotonicity of spherical means. For either $f=v$ or $f=v^2$, \[  |[f]_ r(x)-[f]_ r(y)| \leq \| f\| _\infty \| \eta _ r(\cdot -x)-\eta _ r(\cdot -y)\| _{L^1} \leq C\frac{|x-y|}{r}.  \] Thus the limiting average is independent of its center. The submean inequality makes it at least $f(x)$ for every $x$, and the upper bound is $\sup f=1$. Hence \[  [v]_ r(x)\longrightarrow 1,\qquad [v^2]_ r(x)\longrightarrow 1.  \] First suppose there are a fixed $\rho >0$, numbers $\epsilon _ k\downarrow 0$, $r_ k\to \infty $, points $x_ k$, and unit complex directions $\xi _ k$, such that \[  [v^2]_{r_ k}(x_ k)+[v]_\rho (x_ k)-2v(x_ k)\geq \frac43, \qquad \int _{B(x_ k,r_ k)}|\partial _{\xi _ k}v_{\epsilon _ k}|^2\, \mathrm dy\longrightarrow 0.  \] Translate and rotate to make $x_ k$ the origin and $\xi _ k$ the last complex direction. Compactness of uniformly bounded Lipschitz functions and the preceding lemma give a locally uniform limit $a$ that is admissible and maximal. The transformed mollifications have the same limit. Their last derivatives tend to zero in $L^2$ on every fixed ball, so $\partial _{z_ n}a=0$ in distributions. Since $a$ is real and continuous, it is independent of $z_ n$. The induction hypothesis gives $a=c\in [0,1]$. In the displayed gap inequality the first average is at most one, while the fixed-radius average and the value at the origin tend to $c$. This would give $4/3\leq 1-c\leq 1$, a contradiction. If this case does not occur, then for every fixed $\rho >0$ there is $C_\rho \geq 1$ such that \[  \int _{B(x,r)}|\partial _\xi v_\epsilon |^2\, \mathrm dy\geq C_\rho ^{-1}  \] for every unit complex direction $\xi $, whenever $0<\epsilon <C_\rho ^{-1}$, $r>C_\rho $ and $[v^2]_ r(x)+[v]_\rho (x)-2v(x)\geq 4/3$. Indeed, failure for every integer choice $C_\rho =k$ produces the sequences excluded above. The dependence on the fixed radius $\rho $ is retained. Translate so that $v(0)<1/12$. Choose $\rho $ with $[v]_\rho (0)>3/4$, then $r>C_\rho $ with $[v^2]_ r(0)>3/4$. The open set \[  D=\{ x:2v(x)<[v^2]_ r(x)+[v]_\rho (x)-4/3\}   \] contains the origin. On this set, $[v^2]_ r-c|z|^2$ is smooth and admissible for some fixed $c>0$. To prove this, decompose \[  H([v_\epsilon ^2]_ r) = [2v_\epsilon H(v_\epsilon )]_ r +[2(\partial _ i v_\epsilon \overline{\partial _ jv_\epsilon })_{ij}]_ r =A_\epsilon +B_\epsilon .  \] The matrix $A_\epsilon $ belongs to $C_{n,m}$ by convexity and $v_\epsilon \geq 0$. For every complex direction the unweighted energy on $B(x,r)$ is at least $C_\rho ^{-1}$. Since $|\nabla v_\epsilon |\leq L$, a sufficiently thin boundary annulus carries at most half that amount, uniformly in $x,\epsilon ,\xi $. On the remaining smaller closed ball $\eta _ r$ has a positive minimum. Therefore $B_\epsilon \geq c_0I$ on $D$, with $c_0>0$ independent of small $\epsilon $. Choose $0<c\leq c_0$. Then $A_\epsilon +B_\epsilon -cI\in C_{n,m}$. Uniform convergence of $v_\epsilon ^2$ and convolution at the fixed radius give convergence of every derivative to those of $[v^2]_ r$, proving the assertion. The smooth function \[  h=\tfrac 12\bigl ([v^2]_ r-c|z|^2+[v]_\rho -4/3\bigr )  \] is admissible on $D$. The set $D'=\{ v<h\} $ contains the origin, is bounded, and lies in $D$. Continuity gives $v=h$ on its boundary. The comparison lemma gives $h\leq v$ on $D'$, a contradiction. This completes the induction. $\square$ A trace bound now suffices to bound the gradient. The following statement permits a smooth background different from the metric. Proposition 8.3.3 . B863BB49A505 Fix a compact complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n$, a smooth Hermitian form $\omega $, a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $, an integer $2\leq m\leq n$, and constants $M,A,B>0$. There is a uniform bound for $\sup _ X|\partial u|_\omega $ over all smooth real $u$ such that $\theta _ u=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\in \Gamma _ m(\omega )$ and \[  |u|\leq M,\qquad \frac{\theta _ u^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m}}{\omega ^ n}\leq B, \qquad \operatorname {tr}_\omega \theta _ u \leq A\bigl (1+\sup _ X|\partial u|_\omega ^2\bigr ).  \] The bound requires no derivatives of the Hessian density. Proof. In local holomorphic coordinates write $\omega =\mathrm i g_{i\bar j}\, \mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$ and $\theta _ u=\mathrm i(b_{i\bar j}+\kappa u_{i\bar j})\, \mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$, where the fixed constant $\kappa >0$ accounts for the convention for $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$. For eigenvalues $\lambda \in \Gamma _ m$, $m\geq 2$, one has \[  \sum _ i\lambda _ i^2 =\left(\sum _ i\lambda _ i\right)^2-2S_2(\lambda ) <\left(\sum _ i\lambda _ i\right)^2.  \] Thus the assumed trace estimate bounds every eigenvalue in absolute value by $A(1+\sup |\partial u|^2)$. Suppose contrary to the claim that a sequence $u_ j$ has maxima $R_ j=\sup |\partial u_ j|_\omega \to \infty $, attained at $x_ j$. Pass to $x_ j\to x_\infty $ and work in a fixed chart, changing coordinates linearly so that $g(x_\infty )=I$. If $y_ j$ is the coordinate of $x_ j$, set \begin{align*}  v_ j(z)& =u_ j(y_ j+z/R_ j),\qquad g_ j(z)=g(y_ j+z/R_ j),\\  E_ j(z)& =R_ j^{-2}b(y_ j+z/R_ j)+\kappa H(v_ j)(z). \end{align*} These are defined on balls with radii tending to infinity. On each fixed ball $g_ j\to I$, the smooth background term tends to zero, and $E_ j$ is uniformly bounded by the eigenvalue estimate. In particular $H(v_ j)$ and its Euclidean trace are uniformly bounded. Interior estimates for the fixed Euclidean Laplacian give local uniform $W^{2,q}$ bounds for every finite $q$. A diagonal subsequence converges in $C^1$ on compact subsets to a bounded globally Lipschitz $v$, with $|\partial v(0)|=1$. The Hermitian matrices $g_ j^{-1/2}E_ jg_ j^{-1/2}$ belong to the interior of $C_{n,m}$ and differ from $\kappa H(v_ j)$ by a term tending uniformly to zero on fixed balls. Pairing with any fixed matrix in the dual cone and passing in distributions proves that $v$ is admissible. Its equation is \[  \frac{S_ m(g_ j^{-1/2}E_ jg_ j^{-1/2})}{\binom nm} =R_ j^{-2m}\frac{\theta _{u_ j}^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m}}{\omega ^ n} (y_ j+z/R_ j)\leq BR_ j^{-2m}.  \] We show maximality by lower tests, rather than by an unproved convergence assertion for variable-background Hessian measures. If a smooth lower test $\psi $ at $z_0$ had $H(\psi )(z_0)$ in the interior, choose a small $\delta >0$ so that $H(\psi )-\delta I$ remains there near $z_0$. Strictifying the contact by subtracting $\delta |z-z_0|^2$ gives interior minimum points $z_ j\to z_0$ for $v_ j$ minus this test. At those points \[  E_ j\geq R_ j^{-2}b+\kappa (H(\psi )-\delta I).  \] The matrix on the right, measured with $g_ j$, is uniformly inside the cone. Monotonicity of $S_ m$ under nonnegative addition gives a fixed positive lower bound for the left side of the preceding equation. This contradicts $BR_ j^{-2m}\to 0$. Hence $v$ is maximal. The Liouville theorem makes it constant, contradicting $|\partial v(0)|=1$. $\square$ On a fixed rescaled ball the metric varies by order $R_ j^{-1}$, whereas the background form enters with factor $R_ j^{-2}$. Thus this argument uses fixed smooth backgrounds and an upper bound for the Hessian density, without derivatives of that density.

The induction hypothesis gives $a=c\in [0,1]$. In the displayed gap inequality the first average is at most one, while the fixed-radius average and the value at the origin tend to $c$. This would give $4/3\leq 1-c\leq 1$, a contradiction. If this case does not occur, then for every fixed $\rho >0$ there is $C_\rho \geq 1$ such that \[  \int _{B(x,r)}|\partial _\xi v_\epsilon |^2\, \mathrm dy\geq C_\rho ^{-1}  \] for every unit complex direction $\xi $, whenever $0<\epsilon <C_\rho ^{-1}$, $r>C_\rho $ and $[v^2]_ r(x)+[v]_\rho (x)-2v(x)\geq 4/3$. Indeed, failure for every integer choice $C_\rho =k$ produces the sequences excluded above. The dependence on the fixed radius $\rho $ is retained. Translate so that $v(0)<1/12$. Choose $\rho $ with $[v]_\rho (0)>3/4$, then $r>C_\rho $ with $[v^2]_ r(0)>3/4$. The open set \[  D=\{ x:2v(x)<[v^2]_ r(x)+[v]_\rho (x)-4/3\}   \] contains the origin. On this set, $[v^2]_ r-c|z|^2$ is smooth and admissible for some fixed $c>0$. To prove this, decompose \[  H([v_\epsilon ^2]_ r) = [2v_\epsilon H(v_\epsilon )]_ r +[2(\partial _ i v_\epsilon \overline{\partial _ jv_\epsilon })_{ij}]_ r =A_\epsilon +B_\epsilon .  \] The matrix $A_\epsilon $ belongs to $C_{n,m}$ by convexity and $v_\epsilon \geq 0$. For every complex direction the unweighted energy on $B(x,r)$ is at least $C_\rho ^{-1}$. Since $|\nabla v_\epsilon |\leq L$, a sufficiently thin boundary annulus carries at most half that amount, uniformly in $x,\epsilon ,\xi $. On the remaining smaller closed ball $\eta _ r$ has a positive minimum. Therefore $B_\epsilon \geq c_0I$ on $D$, with $c_0>0$ independent of small $\epsilon $. Choose $0<c\leq c_0$. Then $A_\epsilon +B_\epsilon -cI\in C_{n,m}$. Uniform convergence of $v_\epsilon ^2$ and convolution at the fixed radius give convergence of every derivative to those of $[v^2]_ r$, proving the assertion. The smooth function \[  h=\tfrac 12\bigl ([v^2]_ r-c|z|^2+[v]_\rho -4/3\bigr )  \] is admissible on $D$. The set $D'=\{ v<h\} $ contains the origin, is bounded, and lies in $D$. Continuity gives $v=h$ on its boundary. The comparison lemma gives $h\leq v$ on $D'$, a contradiction. This completes the induction. $\square$

title: Proposition 8.3.3
text: Proposition 8.3.3 . B863BB49A505 Fix a compact complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n$, a smooth Hermitian form $\omega $, a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $, an integer $2\leq m\leq n$, and constants $M,A,B>0$. There is a uniform bound for $\sup _ X|\partial u|_\omega $ over all smooth real $u$ such that $\theta _ u=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\in \Gamma _ m(\omega )$ and \[  |u|\leq M,\qquad \frac{\theta _ u^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m}}{\omega ^ n}\leq B, \qquad \operatorname {tr}_\omega \theta _ u \leq A\bigl (1+\sup _ X|\partial u|_\omega ^2\bigr ).  \] The bound requires no derivatives of the Hessian density. Proof. In local holomorphic coordinates write $\omega =\mathrm i g_{i\bar j}\, \mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$ and $\theta _ u=\mathrm i(b_{i\bar j}+\kappa u_{i\bar j})\, \mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$, where the fixed constant $\kappa >0$ accounts for the convention for $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$. For eigenvalues $\lambda \in \Gamma _ m$, $m\geq 2$, one has \[  \sum _ i\lambda _ i^2 =\left(\sum _ i\lambda _ i\right)^2-2S_2(\lambda ) <\left(\sum _ i\lambda _ i\right)^2.  \] Thus the assumed trace estimate bounds every eigenvalue in absolute value by $A(1+\sup |\partial u|^2)$. Suppose contrary to the claim that a sequence $u_ j$ has maxima $R_ j=\sup |\partial u_ j|_\omega \to \infty $, attained at $x_ j$. Pass to $x_ j\to x_\infty $ and work in a fixed chart, changing coordinates linearly so that $g(x_\infty )=I$. If $y_ j$ is the coordinate of $x_ j$, set \begin{align*}  v_ j(z)& =u_ j(y_ j+z/R_ j),\qquad g_ j(z)=g(y_ j+z/R_ j),\\  E_ j(z)& =R_ j^{-2}b(y_ j+z/R_ j)+\kappa H(v_ j)(z). \end{align*} These are defined on balls with radii tending to infinity. On each fixed ball $g_ j\to I$, the smooth background term tends to zero, and $E_ j$ is uniformly bounded by the eigenvalue estimate. In particular $H(v_ j)$ and its Euclidean trace are uniformly bounded. Interior estimates for the fixed Euclidean Laplacian give local uniform $W^{2,q}$ bounds for every finite $q$. A diagonal subsequence converges in $C^1$ on compact subsets to a bounded globally Lipschitz $v$, with $|\partial v(0)|=1$. The Hermitian matrices $g_ j^{-1/2}E_ jg_ j^{-1/2}$ belong to the interior of $C_{n,m}$ and differ from $\kappa H(v_ j)$ by a term tending uniformly to zero on fixed balls. Pairing with any fixed matrix in the dual cone and passing in distributions proves that $v$ is admissible. Its equation is \[  \frac{S_ m(g_ j^{-1/2}E_ jg_ j^{-1/2})}{\binom nm} =R_ j^{-2m}\frac{\theta _{u_ j}^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m}}{\omega ^ n} (y_ j+z/R_ j)\leq BR_ j^{-2m}.  \] We show maximality by lower tests, rather than by an unproved convergence assertion for variable-background Hessian measures. If a smooth lower test $\psi $ at $z_0$ had $H(\psi )(z_0)$ in the interior, choose a small $\delta >0$ so that $H(\psi )-\delta I$ remains there near $z_0$. Strictifying the contact by subtracting $\delta |z-z_0|^2$ gives interior minimum points $z_ j\to z_0$ for $v_ j$ minus this test. At those points \[  E_ j\geq R_ j^{-2}b+\kappa (H(\psi )-\delta I).  \] The matrix on the right, measured with $g_ j$, is uniformly inside the cone. Monotonicity of $S_ m$ under nonnegative addition gives a fixed positive lower bound for the left side of the preceding equation. This contradicts $BR_ j^{-2m}\to 0$. Hence $v$ is maximal. The Liouville theorem makes it constant, contradicting $|\partial v(0)|=1$. $\square$

The positive semidefinite tensor $B$, diagonal in this frame with entries $0, eta ,\ldots , eta $, satisfies $
abla B=0$ at the point and $|

Differentiating the normalized eigenvector equation gives \[  \widetilde\lambda _{;k}=H_{1 ar1;k},\qquad \widetilde\lambda _{;k ar k}\geq H_{1 ar1;k ar k} +\sum _{p>1} rac{|H_{p ar1;k}|^2+|H_{1 ar p;k}|^2}{\lambda _1-\lambda _ p+ eta }-C eta .  \] The denominators are at most $(n+1)\lambda _1$. There is $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$, depending only on $M,B,h,\omega ,n,m$, with the following property. For every smooth real $\varphi $ with $\| \varphi \| _\infty \leq B$, there is $C<\infty $, depending also on its $C^2$ norm, such that if smooth real $u,v$ satisfy  egin{gather*}  W\in \Gamma _ m,\qquad I+v_{i ar j}\in \overline{\Gamma _ m},\  \| u\| _\infty \leq M,\qquad \| v-\varphi \| _\infty \leq \varepsilon ,\  F(W)=\exp  igl ((u+h(x,v))/m igr ), \end{gather*} then \[  \operatorname {tr}_\omega (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u) \leq C igl (1+\sup _ X|\partial u|_ g^2 igr ).  \] The cone condition on $v$ is understood in a unitary frame. The tolerance $\varepsilon $ uses no derivatives of $\varphi $; the constant $C$ uses no derivatives of $v$. Proof. For $\varepsilon \leq 1$ the density has fixed bounds $0<f_0\leq f\leq f_1$. Its first derivative is \[  f_ k= rac fm(u_ k+h_ k(x,v)+h_ t(x,v)v_ k).  \] The nonnegative $u_ k$ contribution can be dropped from the gradient lemma. At a point with $\lambda _1>1$, differentiating once more gives \[  f_{1 ar1}\geq -C(1+|\partial v|^2+|1+v_{1 ar1}|).  \] Here $u_{1 ar1}=\lambda _1-1>0$, the square from differentiating the exponential is nonnegative, and all derivatives of $h$ are bounded on the fixed interval. Set  egin{align*}  \Phi (s)& =-	frac 12\log (1-s/(2K)),\qquad \Psi (u)=-2Au+(A	au /2)u^2,\  \chi (t)& =-	frac 1{12}\log (2\varepsilon -t),\qquad 	au =(M+1)^{-1}. \end{align*} Then $(4K)^{-1}\leq \Phi '\leq (2K)^{-1}$, $\Phi ''=2(\Phi ')^2$, $-3A\leq \Psi '\leq -A$, $\Psi ''=A	au $, and $q=\chi '$ lies between $1/(36\varepsilon )$ and $1/(12\varepsilon )$, with $\chi ''=12q^2$. Take a maximum of $G=\log \lambda _1+\Phi (s)+\Psi (u)+\chi (v-\varphi )$ and use the smooth lower support from the eigenvalue lemma. At this point put \[  a_ i=v_ i,\quad b_ i=\varphi _ i,\quad P_ v=I+v_{i ar j},\quad W_ v=\sum _ iF_ i(P_ v)_{i ar i},\quad x_ i=\Phi 's_ i,\quad y_ i=\Psi 'u_ i.  \] The first derivative condition and the torsion identity give \[  H_{1 ar1;i}/\lambda _1=-x_ i-y_ i-q(a_ i-b_ i),\qquad Z_ i=-x_ i-y_ i-qa_ i+e_ i,\quad e_ i=qb_ i+(1-\lambda _1^{-1})T^1_{i1}.  \] Thus $|e_ i|\leq E_0$, with $E_0$ independent of $A$ and of derivatives of $v$. If either eigenvalue threshold fails, the required bound follows directly. Otherwise, with fixed $C_ H,C_ G,C_0$ independent of $A$, the second derivative condition gives  egin{align*}  0\geq {}& N-\sum _ iF_ i|Z_ i|^2+2\sum _ iF_ i|x_ i|^2 +	frac 34\Psi ''\sum _ iF_ i|u_ i|^2+ rac{Q}{32K} +\Psi '(f-\mathcal F)-C_0\mathcal F\ & +q(W_ v-\mathcal F)- rac{C_ H}{\lambda _1}|(P_ v)_{1 ar1}| - rac{C_ G}S\sum _ i|a_ i|^2 +\sum _ iF_ i igl (12q^2|a_ i-b_ i|^2-q|a_ i| igr ). \end{align*} The fixed $qL\varphi $ term is included in $C_0$. Choose $\varepsilon $ so the lower bound for $q$ meets all thresholds of the derivative-absorption lemma. These thresholds depend on $M,B,h$ and the metric, and not on derivatives of $\varphi $. This choice precedes that of $A$. First suppose $\lambda _ n<-\delta \lambda _1$. Concavity gives $N\geq 0$, and \[  -|Z_ i|^2+2|x_ i|^2 \geq -6|y_ i|^2-6q^2|a_ i|^2-6E_0^2.  \] The derivative-absorption lemma applies after decreasing the right side further by $(3q^2+2q)|a_ i|^2$. Drop its nonnegative reserves and $\Psi ''$ term. Since $\Psi 'f\geq -3Af_1$, this gives \[  0\geq  rac{Q}{32K}-(54A^2+C_*)K\mathcal F-3Af_1,  \] where $C_*$ is fixed independently of $A,\delta $. Now suppose $\lambda _ n\geq -\delta \lambda _1$, and let $I=\{ i:F_ i>\delta ^{-1}F_1\} $. For $i\in I$, $\lambda _ i<\lambda _1$ and \[   rac{F_ i-F_1}{\lambda _1-\lambda _ i} \geq  rac{(1-\delta )F_ i}{(1+\delta )\lambda _1} \geq  rac{(1-2\delta )F_ i}{\lambda _1}.  \] The spectral formula for $D^2F$, including its nonpositive diagonal part, therefore gives $N\geq (1-2\delta )\sum _{i\in I}F_ i|Z_ i|^2$. This uses the original eigenvalues; repeated eigenvalues do not occur in $I$. Using $x_ i=-Z_ i-y_ i-qa_ i+e_ i$ and $|z+w|^2\geq \delta |z|^2-\delta |w|^2/(1-\delta )$, one obtains  egin{align*}  N-\sum _{i\in I}F_ i|Z_ i|^2+2\sum _{i\in I}F_ i|x_ i|^2 & \geq - rac{4\delta (\Psi ')^2}{1-\delta }\sum _{i\in I}F_ i|u_ i|^2\ & \quad -r q^2\sum _{i\in I}F_ i|a_ i|^2-rE_0^2\mathcal F, \qquad r= rac{8\delta }{1-\delta }. \end{align*} Choose $\delta \leq \min \{ 1/17,	au /(72A+	au )\} $. Then the first coefficient is at most $\Psi ''/2$, and $r\leq 1/2$. On the complementary indices the preceding elementary bound gives \[  -\sum _{i
otin I}F_ i|Z_ i|^2+2\sum _{i
otin I}F_ i|x_ i|^2 \geq - rac{54A^2+6nE_0^2}{\delta }KF_1 -6q^2\sum _{i
otin I}F_ i|a_ i|^2.  \] Apply the derivative-absorption lemma, with penalty $r$ on $I$ and zero outside it; adding the unused negative $(9q^2+2q)|a_ i|^2$ on $I$, and $(3q^2+2q)|a_ i|^2$ off $I$, only decreases its input. The constants in its fixed-comparison error and the high-index $rE_0^2$ error are bounded independently of $A,\delta $. Enlarge $C_*$ to include them. We obtain \[  0\geq  rac{Q}{32K}- rac{54A^2+6nE_0^2}{\delta }KF_1 +(A-C_*)\mathcal F-3Af_1.  \] Take $A\geq \max \{ 1,C_*+1\} $, then fix the displayed $\delta $ and the threshold $L_0(A)$. Both case inequalities now satisfy the hypotheses of the conditional eigenvalue proposition, with fixed data. Hence $\lambda _1\leq CK$ at the maximum point. Finally $\Phi ,\Psi ,\chi $ have oscillations bounded independently of $K$ and of derivatives of $v$. Comparing $G$ at any other point with its maximum gives the same bound for $\lambda _1$ everywhere. Since $S\leq n\lambda _1$, this proves the trace estimate. $\square$ Corollary 8.4.7 . BEA27E46DAEE Under the hypotheses of the proposition, one has \[  \sup _ X|\partial u|_ g+\sup _ X|\partial  ar\partial u|_ g\leq C,  \] with a constant depending on the same fixed data and no derivatives of $v$. Proof. The Hessian density is $F(W)^ m\leq f_1^ m$. Apply the trace-to-gradient blowup proposition to the fixed background $	heta =\omega $ and the preceding trace estimate. It gives the uniform gradient bound. The trace is then uniformly bounded, and the $\Gamma _2$ identity bounds the absolute value of every eigenvalue of $W$ by its trace. Subtracting the identity matrix gives the complex-Hessian bound. $\square$ The bound controls the complex Hessian. An estimate for all entries of the real Hessian is not needed: the Euclidean Laplacian supplies finite $L^ p$ estimates for those derivatives.

text: Lemma 8.4.1 . B276B9DFAC29 For $\epsilon >0$, let $\chi (t)=-(1/12)\log (2\epsilon -t)$ on $|t|\leq \epsilon $. Suppose $q=\chi '(t)\geq 8$. For any $a,b\in \mathbb C$, \[  \chi ''(t)|a-b|^2-(9q^2+2q)|a|^2-q|a| \geq q^2|a|^2-1-84q^2|b|^2.  \] In particular, let $v,\widetilde\varphi $ be smooth real functions with $|v-\widetilde\varphi |\leq \epsilon $, and take derivatives in an $\omega $-unitary frame. For a positive diagonal linearized operator with coefficients $B_ p$, setting $t=v-\widetilde\varphi $, $a=v_ p$, $b=\widetilde\varphi _ p$ and summing gives an error bounded by $(1+84q^2\sup |\partial \widetilde\varphi |_\omega ^2)\sum _ pB_ p$. The condition $q\geq 8$ holds throughout this interval if $\epsilon \leq 1/288$. Proof. Young's inequality gives $|a-b|^2\geq (7/8)|a|^2-7|b|^2$. Since $\chi ''=12q^2$, the coefficient of $|a|^2$ after subtracting $9q^2$ is $3q^2/2$. Moreover, $2q\leq q^2/4$ and $q|a|\leq q^2|a|^2/4+1$. The remaining coefficient is at least $q^2$, and the error involving $b$ is $84q^2|b|^2$. Finally $q\geq 1/(36\epsilon )$, which proves the last assertion. The weighted version follows by summing the scalar inequality with positive coefficients. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.4.2
section: 8.4 A trace estimate with a prescribed potential
text: Lemma 8.4.2 . 61C6DAF48B41 Suppose $f\geq f_0>0$, $C_ H,C_ G\geq 0$, and $q$ satisfies \[  q\geq 8,\qquad q\geq \frac{2nm!C_ H}{f_0},\qquad q^2\geq \frac{4m!C_ G}{f_0}.  \] For $0\leq r\leq 1/2$, $a,b\in \mathbb C^ n$ and $M\in C_{n,m}$, put $W_ M=\sum _ iF_ iM_{i\bar i}$ and \begin{align*}  E={}& q(W_ M-\mathcal F)-\frac{C_ H}{\lambda _1}|M_{1\bar1}| -\frac{C_ G}{S}\sum _ i|a_ i|^2\\ & +\sum _ iF_ i\bigl (12q^2|a_ i-b_ i|^2 -(9q^2+2q+rq^2)|a_ i|^2-q|a_ i|\bigr ). \end{align*} Then \[  E\geq \frac q2W_ M+\frac{q^2}{4}\sum _ iF_ i|a_ i|^2 -(q+1+84q^2\max _ i|b_ i|^2)\mathcal F.  \] Proof. 8.4.1 gives \[  12q^2|a_ i-b_ i|^2-(9q^2+2q)|a_ i|^2-q|a_ i| \geq q^2|a_ i|^2-1-84q^2|b_ i|^2.  \] Subtracting $rq^2|a_ i|^2$ leaves at least $q^2|a_ i|^2/2$. Since $S\leq n\lambda _1$, 8.2.5 and the hypothesis on $q$ imply \[  \frac{C_ H}{\lambda _1}|M_{1\bar1}| \leq \frac{nC_ H}{S}\operatorname {tr}M\leq \frac q2 W_ M.  \] The lower bound for each $F_ i$ similarly gives \[  \frac{C_ G}{S}\sum _ i|a_ i|^2 \leq \frac{q^2}{4}\sum _ iF_ i|a_ i|^2.  \] Combining these inequalities yields the assertion. The error depends on the fixed comparison vector $b$ and is not discarded. $\square$

title: Proposition 8.4.3
section: 8.4 A trace estimate with a prescribed potential
text: Proposition 8.4.3 . FDAFFF47B8A3 Fix $a>0$, $b,d,e\geq 0$ and $0<\delta <1$. Let $K\geq 1$ and $0<f_0\leq f\leq f_1$. Suppose the following inequality holds according to the sign of $\lambda _ n+\delta \lambda _1$: If $\lambda _ n<-\delta \lambda _1$, then $0\geq aQ/K-bK\mathcal F-d\lambda _1\mathcal F-e$. If $\lambda _ n\geq -\delta \lambda _1$, then $0\geq aQ/K-bKF_1-e$. Then $S\leq CK$ and $\lambda _1\leq CK$, with $C$ depending only on the fixed displayed data and $n,m$. Proof. In the first case, symmetry and concavity of $F$ imply $F_ n\geq F_ i$ for every $i$, so $Q\geq \delta ^2\lambda _1^2\mathcal F/n$. To see the derivative ordering, apply monotonicity of the gradient of a concave function to $\lambda $ and the vector obtained by exchanging its $i$th and $n$th coordinates. Divide the assumed inequality by $K\mathcal F$, use $\mathcal F\geq 1$, and set $t=\lambda _1/K$. It yields $a\delta ^2t^2/n\leq b+dt+e$, which bounds $t$. Since $S\leq n\lambda _1$, the trace bound follows. In the second case, either $\lambda _1^2\leq 2bK^2/a$, which gives the same trace bound directly, or $aQ/(2K)\geq bKF_1$. The assumed inequality then gives $Q\leq 2eK/a$. 8.2.6 bounds $S$ by a multiple of $K$. Finally the $\Gamma _2$ identity gives $\lambda _1\leq (\sum _ i\lambda _ i^2)^{1/2}<S$. $\square$

Lemma 8.4.4 . C357698AC1AF At a point with $\lambda _1>1$, the largest eigenvalue has a smooth local lower support $\widetilde\lambda $, equal to $\lambda _1$ at the point, for which \[  L\log \widetilde\lambda \geq  rac{f_{1 ar1}}{\lambda _1}+N -\sum _ iF_ i|Z_ i|^2-C\mathcal F - rac{C}{\lambda _1^2}\sum _ iF_ i|H_{1 ar1;i}|,  \] where \[  N=- rac{D^2F_ W(
abla _1W,
abla _{ ar1}W)}{\lambda _1}, \qquad Z_ i= rac{H_{i ar1;1}}{\lambda _1}.  \] Here $C$ depends only on the fixed metric. Derivatives of $F$ are evaluated at $W$. Proof. Choose a smooth unitary frame parallel for the Chern connection at the point and diagonalizing $H$ there. The positive semidefinite tensor $B$, diagonal in this frame with entries $0, eta ,\ldots , eta $, satisfies $
abla B=0$ at the point and $|
abla ^2B|\leq C eta $. For $0< eta <1$, the largest eigenvalue of $W-B$ is simple, lies below that of $W$, and agrees with it at the point. This gives the required smooth support. Only its largest eigenvalue is perturbed; the equation still uses $F(W)$. Differentiating the normalized eigenvector equation gives \[  \widetilde\lambda _{;k}=H_{1 ar1;k},\qquad \widetilde\lambda _{;k ar k}\geq H_{1 ar1;k ar k} +\sum _{p>1} rac{|H_{p ar1;k}|^2+|H_{1 ar p;k}|^2}{\lambda _1-\lambda _ p+ eta }-C eta .  \] The denominators are at most $(n+1)\lambda _1$. Let $U=\partial  ar\partial u$, and take $T^ p_{ki}=\Gamma ^ p_{ki}-\Gamma ^ p_{ik}$. The first commutations are \[  U_{i ar j;k}=U_{k ar j;i}-T^ p_{ki}U_{p ar j},\qquad U_{i ar j; ar k}=U_{i ar k; ar j} -\overline{T^ p_{kj}}U_{i ar p}.  \] Apply the first identity, commute one mixed pair of covariant derivatives, and apply the conjugate identity. The result has the form \[  U_{1 ar1;k ar k}=U_{k ar k;1 ar1} -2\operatorname {Re}\sum _ p U_{k ar p;1}\overline{T^ p_{k1}}+E_ k, \qquad |E_ k|\leq C|U|.  \] Indeed the mixed commutator contracts curvature with $U$, differentiating the first torsion coefficient contracts $
abla T$ with $U$, and the second use of the first identities produces contractions of two torsion coefficients with $U$. Thus all the omitted terms satisfy the displayed bound. Since $g$ is parallel, the same derivative relations apply to $H$ apart from the explicit $g$ terms in the first commutation. At the diagonal point $|U|\leq C\lambda _1$. For $p>1$, rewrite $U_{k ar p;1}=U_{1 ar p;k}+T^ j_{k1}U_{j ar p}$. Young's inequality absorbs its third derivative into the positive eigenvalue square, at the cost of $C\lambda _1$. Consequently \[  \widetilde\lambda _{;k ar k}\geq H_{k ar k;1 ar1} -2\operatorname {Re}(H_{k ar1;1}\overline{T^1_{k1}})-C\lambda _1.  \] Differentiate $F(W)=f$ twice and sum this inequality with weights $F_ k$. Write $D_ k=H_{1 ar1;k}$ and $t_ k=T^1_{k1}$. The first commutation, using $U_{1 ar1}=\lambda _1-1$, gives \[  D_ k=\lambda _1Z_ k-(\lambda _1-1)t_ k.  \] The negative logarithmic square and the remaining torsion term therefore satisfy \[  - rac{|D_ k|^2}{\lambda _1^2}-2\operatorname {Re}(Z_ k ar t_ k) \geq -|Z_ k|^2-C-C\lambda _1^{-2}|D_ k|.  \] For example, expanding the left side leaves $-|Z_ k|^2-2\lambda _1^{-1}\operatorname {Re}(Z_ k ar t_ k)-(1-\lambda _1^{-1})^2|t_ k|^2$, and $\lambda _1|Z_ k|\leq |D_ k|+C\lambda _1$. This proves the claim, uniformly for small $ eta $. $\square$

text: Lemma 8.4.5 . 174BDA603BF2 Put $s=|\partial u|_ g^2$ and $K=1+\sup _ Xs$. For every $\eta >0$ one has \[  Ls\geq \sum _{i,k}F_ i(|u_{ki}|^2+|u_{k\bar i}|^2) +2\operatorname {Re}\sum _ k f_ k u_{\bar k}-\eta Q-C_\eta K\mathcal F.  \] The constant depends only on the metric and $\eta $. Proof. Differentiate the squared norm using metric compatibility. Its quadratic part is the displayed sum. Commuting the remaining third derivatives gives \[  u_{ki\bar i}=u_{i\bar i;k}-T^ p_{ik}u_{p\bar i} +R^ p_{i\bar i k}u_ p, \qquad u_{\bar k i\bar i}=u_{i\bar i;\bar k} -\overline{T^ p_{ik}}u_{i\bar p}.  \] The first differentiated equation is $\sum _ iF_ i u_{i\bar i;k}=f_ k$, because the background $g$ is parallel. At the diagonal point the torsion errors are bounded by $C\sqrt K\sum _ iF_ i(|\lambda _ i|+1)$, and the curvature errors by $CK\mathcal F$. Use \[  C\sqrt K F_ i|\lambda _ i| \leq \eta ' F_ i\lambda _ i^2+C_{\eta '}KF_ i  \] with a sufficiently small $\eta '$ for the finite sum. This gives the asserted bound. $\square$

Proposition 8.4.6 . 23966DC8CDBF Fix $M,B\geq 1$ and a smooth real $h(x,t)$ on a neighborhood of $X	imes [-B-1,B+1]$. There is $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$, depending only on $M,B,h,\omega ,n,m$, with the following property. For every smooth real $\varphi $ with $\| \varphi \| _\infty \leq B$, there is $C<\infty $, depending also on its $C^2$ norm, such that if smooth real $u,v$ satisfy  egin{gather*}  W\in \Gamma _ m,\qquad I+v_{i ar j}\in \overline{\Gamma _ m},\  \| u\| _\infty \leq M,\qquad \| v-\varphi \| _\infty \leq \varepsilon ,\  F(W)=\exp  igl ((u+h(x,v))/m igr ), \end{gather*} then \[  \operatorname {tr}_\omega (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u) \leq C igl (1+\sup _ X|\partial u|_ g^2 igr ).  \] The cone condition on $v$ is understood in a unitary frame. The tolerance $\varepsilon $ uses no derivatives of $\varphi $; the constant $C$ uses no derivatives of $v$. Proof. For $\varepsilon \leq 1$ the density has fixed bounds $0<f_0\leq f\leq f_1$. Its first derivative is \[  f_ k= rac fm(u_ k+h_ k(x,v)+h_ t(x,v)v_ k).  \] The nonnegative $u_ k$ contribution can be dropped from the gradient lemma. At a point with $\lambda _1>1$, differentiating once more gives \[  f_{1 ar1}\geq -C(1+|\partial v|^2+|1+v_{1 ar1}|).  \] Here $u_{1 ar1}=\lambda _1-1>0$, the square from differentiating the exponential is nonnegative, and all derivatives of $h$ are bounded on the fixed interval. Set  egin{align*}  \Phi (s)& =-	frac 12\log (1-s/(2K)),\qquad \Psi (u)=-2Au+(A	au /2)u^2,\  \chi (t)& =-	frac 1{12}\log (2\varepsilon -t),\qquad 	au =(M+1)^{-1}. \end{align*} Then $(4K)^{-1}\leq \Phi '\leq (2K)^{-1}$, $\Phi ''=2(\Phi ')^2$, $-3A\leq \Psi '\leq -A$, $\Psi ''=A	au $, and $q=\chi '$ lies between $1/(36\varepsilon )$ and $1/(12\varepsilon )$, with $\chi ''=12q^2$. Take a maximum of $G=\log \lambda _1+\Phi (s)+\Psi (u)+\chi (v-\varphi )$ and use the smooth lower support from the eigenvalue lemma. At this point put \[  a_ i=v_ i,\quad b_ i=\varphi _ i,\quad P_ v=I+v_{i ar j},\quad W_ v=\sum _ iF_ i(P_ v)_{i ar i},\quad x_ i=\Phi 's_ i,\quad y_ i=\Psi 'u_ i.  \] The first derivative condition and the torsion identity give \[  H_{1 ar1;i}/\lambda _1=-x_ i-y_ i-q(a_ i-b_ i),\qquad Z_ i=-x_ i-y_ i-qa_ i+e_ i,\quad e_ i=qb_ i+(1-\lambda _1^{-1})T^1_{i1}.  \] Thus $|e_ i|\leq E_0$, with $E_0$ independent of $A$ and of derivatives of $v$. We make the initial maximum inequality explicit. The gradient lemma and the identity $u_{i ar j}=(\lambda _ i-1)\delta _{ij}$ give, after multiplication by $\Phi '$, \[  \Phi 'Ls\geq  rac1{8K}\sum _{i,k}F_ i(|u_{ki}|^2+|u_{k ar i}|^2) + rac{3}{64K}Q-C\mathcal F - rac{C_ G'}S\sum _ i|a_ i|^2.  \] To justify the constants, retain half of the positive quadratic term, use $(\lambda _ i-1)^2\geq \lambda _ i^2/2-1$, and choose the torsion parameter to cost at most $Q/(128K)$. The remaining density-gradient error is $C|a|/\sqrt K$. Young's inequality bounds it by $C_ G'|a|^2/S+cS/K$; choose $C_ G'$ large enough that the quadratic coercivity lemma absorbs $cS/K$ by $Q/(128K)$, with a fixed constant error. This leaves $3Q/(64K)$. The linear $H_{1 ar1;i}$ error in the eigenvalue lemma is estimated using the first derivative condition. Its $x_ i$ term costs at most half of the retained quadratic sum and $C\mathcal F$. Its $y_ i$ term costs at most $\Psi ''\sum _ iF_ i|u_ i|^2/4+\mathcal F$ whenever $\lambda _1\geq L_0(A)$, where $L_0(A)$ is fixed independently of $K,v$. Its $qa_ i$ term costs at most $q\sum _ iF_ i|a_ i|$ when $\lambda _1$ exceeds a fixed metric constant; its $qb_ i$ term costs $C\mathcal F$. If either eigenvalue threshold fails, the required bound follows directly. Otherwise, with fixed $C_ H,C_ G,C_0$ independent of $A$, the second derivative condition gives  egin{align*}  0\geq {}& N-\sum _ iF_ i|Z_ i|^2+2\sum _ iF_ i|x_ i|^2 +	frac 34\Psi ''\sum _ iF_ i|u_ i|^2+ rac{Q}{32K} +\Psi '(f-\mathcal F)-C_0\mathcal F\ & +q(W_ v-\mathcal F)- rac{C_ H}{\lambda _1}|(P_ v)_{1 ar1}| - rac{C_ G}S\sum _ i|a_ i|^2 +\sum _ iF_ i igl (12q^2|a_ i-b_ i|^2-q|a_ i| igr ). \end{align*} The fixed $qL\varphi $ term is included in $C_0$. Choose $\varepsilon $ so the lower bound for $q$ meets all thresholds of the derivative-absorption lemma. These thresholds depend on $M,B,h$ and the metric, and not on derivatives of $\varphi $. This choice precedes that of $A$. First suppose $\lambda _ n<-\delta \lambda _1$. Concavity gives $N\geq 0$, and \[  -|Z_ i|^2+2|x_ i|^2 \geq -6|y_ i|^2-6q^2|a_ i|^2-6E_0^2.  \] The derivative-absorption lemma applies after decreasing the right side further by $(3q^2+2q)|a_ i|^2$. Drop its nonnegative reserves and $\Psi ''$ term. Since $\Psi 'f\geq -3Af_1$, this gives \[  0\geq  rac{Q}{32K}-(54A^2+C_*)K\mathcal F-3Af_1,  \] where $C_*$ is fixed independently of $A,\delta $. Now suppose $\lambda _ n\geq -\delta \lambda _1$, and let $I=\{ i:F_ i>\delta ^{-1}F_1\} $. For $i\in I$, $\lambda _ i<\lambda _1$ and \[   rac{F_ i-F_1}{\lambda _1-\lambda _ i} \geq  rac{(1-\delta )F_ i}{(1+\delta )\lambda _1} \geq  rac{(1-2\delta )F_ i}{\lambda _1}.  \] The spectral formula for $D^2F$, including its nonpositive diagonal part, therefore gives $N\geq (1-2\delta )\sum _{i\in I}F_ i|Z_ i|^2$. This uses the original eigenvalues; repeated eigenvalues do not occur in $I$. Using $x_ i=-Z_ i-y_ i-qa_ i+e_ i$ and $|z+w|^2\geq \delta |z|^2-\delta |w|^2/(1-\delta )$, one obtains  egin{align*}  N-\sum _{i\in I}F_ i|Z_ i|^2+2\sum _{i\in I}F_ i|x_ i|^2 & \geq - rac{4\delta (\Psi ')^2}{1-\delta }\sum _{i\in I}F_ i|u_ i|^2\ & \quad -r q^2\sum _{i\in I}F_ i|a_ i|^2-rE_0^2\mathcal F, \qquad r= rac{8\delta }{1-\delta }. \end{align*} Choose $\delta \leq \min \{ 1/17,	au /(72A+	au )\} $. Then the first coefficient is at most $\Psi ''/2$, and $r\leq 1/2$. On the complementary indices the preceding elementary bound gives \[  -\sum _{i
otin I}F_ i|Z_ i|^2+2\sum _{i
otin I}F_ i|x_ i|^2 \geq - rac{54A^2+6nE_0^2}{\delta }KF_1 -6q^2\sum _{i
otin I}F_ i|a_ i|^2.  \] Apply the derivative-absorption lemma, with penalty $r$ on $I$ and zero outside it; adding the unused negative $(9q^2+2q)|a_ i|^2$ on $I$, and $(3q^2+2q)|a_ i|^2$ off $I$, only decreases its input. The constants in its fixed-comparison error and the high-index $rE_0^2$ error are bounded independently of $A,\delta $. Enlarge $C_*$ to include them. We obtain \[  0\geq  rac{Q}{32K}- rac{54A^2+6nE_0^2}{\delta }KF_1 +(A-C_*)\mathcal F-3Af_1.  \] Take $A\geq \max \{ 1,C_*+1\} $, then fix the displayed $\delta $ and the threshold $L_0(A)$. Both case inequalities now satisfy the hypotheses of the conditional eigenvalue proposition, with fixed data. Hence $\lambda _1\leq CK$ at the maximum point. Finally $\Phi ,\Psi ,\chi $ have oscillations bounded independently of $K$ and of derivatives of $v$. Comparing $G$ at any other point with its maximum gives the same bound for $\lambda _1$ everywhere. Since $S\leq n\lambda _1$, this proves the trace estimate. $\square$
