text: Corollary 8.4.7 . BEA27E46DAEE Under the hypotheses of the proposition, one has \[  \sup _ X|\partial u|_ g+\sup _ X|\partial \bar\partial u|_ g\leq C,  \] with a constant depending on the same fixed data and no derivatives of $v$. Proof. The Hessian density is $F(W)^ m\leq f_1^ m$. Apply the trace-to-gradient blowup proposition to the fixed background $\theta =\omega $ and the preceding trace estimate. It gives the uniform gradient bound. The trace is then uniformly bounded, and the $\Gamma _2$ identity bounds the absolute value of every eigenvalue of $W$ by its trace. Subtracting the identity matrix gives the complex-Hessian bound. $\square$

title: 8.5 Bounded complex Hessians and elliptic extensions
search_title: Bounded complex Hessians and elliptic extensions
section: 8.5 Bounded complex Hessians and elliptic extensions
text: Uniform complex-Hessian bounds give enough compactness both to pass the nonlinear products to a limit and to make the Hessian root uniformly elliptic. In coordinates use the metric matrix $g$ of the preceding section and write $H(u)=(u_{i\bar j})$. Coefficient products with bounded measurable factors will be identified with currents by convolution. Lemma 8.5.1 . 89771FD1FD15 Suppose $u_ j$ is smooth, \[  \sup _ j\bigl (\| u_ j\| _\infty +\| \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\| _{L^\infty }\bigr )<\infty , \qquad u_ j\longrightarrow u\quad \hbox{uniformly on }X.  \] Then $u\in W^{2,p}(X)$ for every $1<p<\infty $, its distributional complex Hessian has bounded coefficients, and $u_ j\to u$ in $C^{1,\alpha }(X)$ for every $0<\alpha <1$. The same hypotheses give uniform $W^{2,p}$ bounds for the sequence. Proof. On a coordinate ball the Euclidean Laplacian is $\Delta u_ j=4\sum _ i (u_ j)_{i\bar i}$, so it is uniformly bounded. The interior Laplace estimate on two nested balls gives \[  \| u_ j\| _{W^{2,p}(B')}\leq C_ p \bigl (\| \Delta u_ j\| _{L^ p(B)}+\| u_ j\| _{L^ p(B)}\bigr ).  \] A finite cover gives the global bound. Weak $W^{2,p}$ limits coincide with the uniform limit. The bounded complex Hessians have weak-star limits in $L^\infty $; testing against compactly supported smooth functions identifies them with $H(u)$. Choose $p$ with $1-2n/p>\alpha $. The compact Sobolev embedding into $C^{1,\alpha }$ gives convergence of subsequences. Every such limit is $u$, hence the whole sequence converges. This estimates the full real Hessian in every finite $L^ p$ space, without asserting that it is bounded. $\square$ Lemma 8.5.2 . 1881F6670EF4 For $1\leq a\leq k\leq n$, suppose $u_ j^ a$ and $u^ a$ satisfy the preceding lemma. Let $\theta _ a$ be fixed smooth real $(1,1)$-forms. Then \[  \bigwedge _{a=1}^ k(\theta _ a+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j^ a) \longrightarrow \bigwedge _{a=1}^ k(\theta _ a+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u^ a) \quad \hbox{as currents}.  \] The current on the right is the product of the almost-everywhere coefficients. No closedness or positivity of the $\theta _ a$ is required. For each compactly supported smooth complementary test form $\eta $, the difference of its pairings is bounded by $C_\eta \max _ a\| u_ j^ a-u^ a\| _\infty $. Proof. Set $D_ j^ a=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j^ a$ and $D^ a=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u^ a$. On a smaller coordinate ball, convolution gives smooth $u_\epsilon ^ a$ whose complex Hessians are uniformly bounded and converge to $H(u^ a)$ in every finite $L^ p$ space. Their coefficient products consequently converge in finite $L^ p$ spaces. In particular the products of the $D^ a$ are closed currents, since their smooth approximants are closed. Expand the smooth background factors and telescope each remaining product. Every difference has the form \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ j^ a-u^ a)\wedge T_ j,  \] where $T_ j$ is a product of $D_ j^ b$ and $D^ b$ with $b\ne a$. It has uniformly bounded coefficients and is closed. Local convolution, followed by strong convergence of its finite coefficient products, justifies integration by parts: \[  \left\langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ j^ a-u^ a)\wedge T_ j,\xi \right\rangle =\int (u_ j^ a-u^ a)\, T_ j\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\xi .  \] Here $\xi $ includes the chosen smooth background factors and the test form, so their derivatives are retained. The right-hand side has the asserted uniform bound. A finite partition of unity proves the claim on $X$. This argument also proves that the coefficient product is the distributional limit; it does not identify a separately defined bounded Hessian operator for all nonsmooth admissible functions. $\square$ Lemma 8.5.3 . BAC60298D0F2 For $f_0>0$ and $L>0$, assume the set \[  K=\{ A\in C_{n,m}:\operatorname {tr}A\leq L, \  \sigma _ m(A)\geq f_0^ m\}   \] is nonempty. It is a compact subset of the interior, and there are $\vartheta ,\Theta >0$, depending only on $n,m,f_0,L$, such that \[  \vartheta I\leq DF_ A\leq \Theta I\qquad (A\in K).  \] The function on all Hermitian matrices defined by \[  \widehat F(B)=\inf _{A\in K} \bigl (F(A)+\operatorname {tr}(DF_ A(B-A))\bigr )  \] is concave, agrees with $F$ on $K$, and satisfies, for $P\geq 0$, \[  \vartheta \operatorname {tr}P\leq \widehat F(B+P)-\widehat F(B) \leq \Theta \operatorname {tr}P.  \] Proof. In the closed $2$-cone, \[  \sum _ i\lambda _ i^2=(\operatorname {tr}A)^2-2S_2(A) \leq L^2.  \] Thus $K$ is bounded and closed. Maclaurin gives $\sigma _ j(A)\geq \sigma _ m(A)^{j/m}\geq f_0^ j$ for $j\leq m$, so every matrix in $K$ is in the interior. In a unitary eigenframe, \[  F_ i=\frac{F^{1-m}S_{m-1}(\lambda |i)}{m\binom nm}, \qquad \frac{f_0}{m!L}\leq F_ i\leq \frac{L^{m-1}}{n f_0^{m-1}}.  \] The lower bound is 8.2.5 ; the upper bound uses $|\lambda _ i|\leq L$ in the polynomial numerator and its positivity. These bounds give possible values of $\vartheta $ and $\Theta $. Concavity places each tangent plane above $F$ on the cone; the plane at $B$ gives equality when $B\in K$. An infimum of affine functions is concave. Each plane increases under $P\geq 0$ by a number between the two displayed trace bounds; taking infima preserves these bounds. The same estimates give global Lipschitz continuity of $\widehat F$. $\square$ To interpret this as a real elliptic operator, let $\mathcal C(R)$ be the complex Hessian of the real quadratic function $q(x)=\frac12 x^{\mathsf T}Rx$, where $x\in \mathbb R^{2n}$. For $R\geq 0$, one has $\mathcal C(R)\geq 0$ and $\operatorname {tr}\mathcal C(R)=\operatorname {tr}R/4$. If $\mu I\leq g(x)\leq MI$, then \[  \mathcal G(x,R)=\widehat F \bigl (I+g(x)^{-1/2}\mathcal C(R)g(x)^{-1/2}\bigr )  \] is uniformly elliptic on real symmetric matrices, with constants $\vartheta /(4M)$ and $\Theta /(4\mu )$. Its dependence on $x$ satisfies on compact coordinate balls \[  |\mathcal G(x,R)-\mathcal G(y,R)| \leq C|x-y|(1+\| R\| ).  \] These follow respectively from the trace bound and the smooth dependence of the positive matrix square root of the fixed metric. We use the classical interior Evans–Krylov–Caffarelli estimate for a concave operator on all real symmetric matrices with fixed positive ellipticity constants and coefficient oscillation bounded by $C|x-y|^\gamma (1+\| R\| )$, where $\gamma >0$. A Hölder right-hand side then gives an interior $C^{2,\beta }$ estimate, for some $\beta >0$. This estimate applies also to continuous viscosity solutions. The real extension just constructed satisfies these conditions. Once its solution is $C^{2,\beta }$ and the attained complex Hessians remain in a compact subset of the open cone, the original smooth Hessian operator and Schauder estimates give the higher derivatives. We next identify the limit of the proper auxiliary equations that will be used for regularity. Proposition 8.5.4 . 6FBA7BB8AC94 Suppose $v_ j\to \varphi $ uniformly on $X$, $h(x,t)$ is smooth on a fixed bounded interval containing their values, and smooth admissible $u_ j$ satisfy \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m} =e^{u_ j+h(x,v_ j)}\omega ^ n.  \] Assume $u_ j\to u$ uniformly and the complex Hessians of $u_ j$ are uniformly bounded. Then $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is admissible almost everywhere and its coefficient product satisfies \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m} =e^{u+h(x,\varphi )}\omega ^ n.  \] On every coordinate ball $u$ also solves the corresponding uniformly elliptic concave extension in the viscosity sense. Proof. The first lemma gives $u\in W^{2,p}$ for every finite $p$ and a bounded complex Hessian. The matrices $A_ j=I+g^{-1/2}H(u_ j)g^{-1/2}$ converge weakly in $L^2$ to the analogous matrix $A$ for $u$. Mazur's lemma gives convex combinations of tails converging strongly in $L^2$, hence almost everywhere along a subsequence. The pointwise closed cone is convex, so $A\in C_{n,m}$ almost everywhere. The product lemma passes the equation to the limit as currents, since its right-hand side converges uniformly. Equality of the bounded densities then gives the equation almost everywhere. The right-hand sides are bounded above and away from zero. The complex Hessian bound gives a uniform upper bound $L$ for $\operatorname {tr}A_ j$. Choose $f_0>0$ below all their normalized roots. Thus every $A_ j$, and almost every $A$, belongs to the compact set $K$ of the preceding lemma. Every $u_ j$ is a classical solution of \[  \mathcal G(x,D^2u_ j)=r_ j(x),\qquad r_ j(x)=e^{(u_ j+h(x,v_ j))/m}.  \] For completeness, if a smooth test $q$ touches $u$ from above at an interior point $x_0$, add a small positive quartic term to make the local contact strict. Local maximum points of $u_ j-q$ tend to $x_0$. At these points $D^2u_ j\leq D^2q$, and ellipticity gives $\mathcal G(x,D^2q)\geq r_ j(x)$. Pass to the limit, then remove the quartic term. A test from below gives the reverse inequality. The extension is defined on every real Hessian, so no admissibility of a lower test has been assumed. This proves the viscosity statement. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.5.1
section: 8.5 Bounded complex Hessians and elliptic extensions
text: Lemma 8.5.1 . 89771FD1FD15 Suppose $u_ j$ is smooth, \[  \sup _ j\bigl (\| u_ j\| _\infty +\| \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\| _{L^\infty }\bigr )<\infty , \qquad u_ j\longrightarrow u\quad \hbox{uniformly on }X.  \] Then $u\in W^{2,p}(X)$ for every $1<p<\infty $, its distributional complex Hessian has bounded coefficients, and $u_ j\to u$ in $C^{1,\alpha }(X)$ for every $0<\alpha <1$. The same hypotheses give uniform $W^{2,p}$ bounds for the sequence. Proof. On a coordinate ball the Euclidean Laplacian is $\Delta u_ j=4\sum _ i (u_ j)_{i\bar i}$, so it is uniformly bounded. The interior Laplace estimate on two nested balls gives \[  \| u_ j\| _{W^{2,p}(B')}\leq C_ p \bigl (\| \Delta u_ j\| _{L^ p(B)}+\| u_ j\| _{L^ p(B)}\bigr ).  \] A finite cover gives the global bound. Weak $W^{2,p}$ limits coincide with the uniform limit. The bounded complex Hessians have weak-star limits in $L^\infty $; testing against compactly supported smooth functions identifies them with $H(u)$. Choose $p$ with $1-2n/p>\alpha $. The compact Sobolev embedding into $C^{1,\alpha }$ gives convergence of subsequences. Every such limit is $u$, hence the whole sequence converges. This estimates the full real Hessian in every finite $L^ p$ space, without asserting that it is bounded. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.5.2
section: 8.5 Bounded complex Hessians and elliptic extensions
text: Lemma 8.5.2 . 1881F6670EF4 For $1\leq a\leq k\leq n$, suppose $u_ j^ a$ and $u^ a$ satisfy the preceding lemma. Let $\theta _ a$ be fixed smooth real $(1,1)$-forms. Then \[  \bigwedge _{a=1}^ k(\theta _ a+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j^ a) \longrightarrow \bigwedge _{a=1}^ k(\theta _ a+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u^ a) \quad \hbox{as currents}.  \] The current on the right is the product of the almost-everywhere coefficients. No closedness or positivity of the $\theta _ a$ is required. For each compactly supported smooth complementary test form $\eta $, the difference of its pairings is bounded by $C_\eta \max _ a\| u_ j^ a-u^ a\| _\infty $. Proof. Set $D_ j^ a=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j^ a$ and $D^ a=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u^ a$. On a smaller coordinate ball, convolution gives smooth $u_\epsilon ^ a$ whose complex Hessians are uniformly bounded and converge to $H(u^ a)$ in every finite $L^ p$ space. Their coefficient products consequently converge in finite $L^ p$ spaces. In particular the products of the $D^ a$ are closed currents, since their smooth approximants are closed. Expand the smooth background factors and telescope each remaining product. Every difference has the form \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ j^ a-u^ a)\wedge T_ j,  \] where $T_ j$ is a product of $D_ j^ b$ and $D^ b$ with $b\ne a$. It has uniformly bounded coefficients and is closed. Local convolution, followed by strong convergence of its finite coefficient products, justifies integration by parts: \[  \left\langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ j^ a-u^ a)\wedge T_ j,\xi \right\rangle =\int (u_ j^ a-u^ a)\, T_ j\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\xi .  \] Here $\xi $ includes the chosen smooth background factors and the test form, so their derivatives are retained. The right-hand side has the asserted uniform bound. A finite partition of unity proves the claim on $X$. This argument also proves that the coefficient product is the distributional limit; it does not identify a separately defined bounded Hessian operator for all nonsmooth admissible functions. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.5.3
section: 8.5 Bounded complex Hessians and elliptic extensions
text: Lemma 8.5.3 . BAC60298D0F2 For $f_0>0$ and $L>0$, assume the set \[  K=\{ A\in C_{n,m}:\operatorname {tr}A\leq L, \  \sigma _ m(A)\geq f_0^ m\}   \] is nonempty. It is a compact subset of the interior, and there are $\vartheta ,\Theta >0$, depending only on $n,m,f_0,L$, such that \[  \vartheta I\leq DF_ A\leq \Theta I\qquad (A\in K).  \] The function on all Hermitian matrices defined by \[  \widehat F(B)=\inf _{A\in K} \bigl (F(A)+\operatorname {tr}(DF_ A(B-A))\bigr )  \] is concave, agrees with $F$ on $K$, and satisfies, for $P\geq 0$, \[  \vartheta \operatorname {tr}P\leq \widehat F(B+P)-\widehat F(B) \leq \Theta \operatorname {tr}P.  \] Proof. In the closed $2$-cone, \[  \sum _ i\lambda _ i^2=(\operatorname {tr}A)^2-2S_2(A) \leq L^2.  \] Thus $K$ is bounded and closed. Maclaurin gives $\sigma _ j(A)\geq \sigma _ m(A)^{j/m}\geq f_0^ j$ for $j\leq m$, so every matrix in $K$ is in the interior. In a unitary eigenframe, \[  F_ i=\frac{F^{1-m}S_{m-1}(\lambda |i)}{m\binom nm}, \qquad \frac{f_0}{m!L}\leq F_ i\leq \frac{L^{m-1}}{n f_0^{m-1}}.  \] The lower bound is 8.2.5 ; the upper bound uses $|\lambda _ i|\leq L$ in the polynomial numerator and its positivity. These bounds give possible values of $\vartheta $ and $\Theta $. Concavity places each tangent plane above $F$ on the cone; the plane at $B$ gives equality when $B\in K$. An infimum of affine functions is concave. Each plane increases under $P\geq 0$ by a number between the two displayed trace bounds; taking infima preserves these bounds. The same estimates give global Lipschitz continuity of $\widehat F$. $\square$

title: Proposition 8.5.4
section: 8.5 Bounded complex Hessians and elliptic extensions
text: Proposition 8.5.4 . 6FBA7BB8AC94 Suppose $v_ j\to \varphi $ uniformly on $X$, $h(x,t)$ is smooth on a fixed bounded interval containing their values, and smooth admissible $u_ j$ satisfy \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m} =e^{u_ j+h(x,v_ j)}\omega ^ n.  \] Assume $u_ j\to u$ uniformly and the complex Hessians of $u_ j$ are uniformly bounded. title: 8.6 Proper equations and admissible approximation
text: For a smooth potential write $H_ m(w)=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m}$. The positive exponential coefficient controls additive constants by the maximum principle. The resulting smooth equations will also construct admissible approximations of bounded potentials, before any continuous Hessian product is defined. Lemma 8.6.1 . 8B310CC2C1A1 For every $a>0$ and smooth real $H$ on $X$, there is a unique smooth strictly admissible solution of \[  H_ m(w)=e^{aw+H}\omega ^ n.  \] It satisfies \[  -\frac{\max _ X H}{a}\leq w\leq -\frac{\min _ X H}{a}.  \] Proof. At a maximum of $w$, the admissible form $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ is at most $\omega $, hence $e^{aw+H}\leq 1$ there. At a minimum it is at least $\omega $, and the reverse inequality holds. These give the bounds. For two solutions, a positive maximum of their difference would imply $H_ m(w_1)\leq H_ m(w_2)$ there, contradicting the exponential factor. This proves uniqueness. First take $a=1$ and use the path $H_ m(w_ t)=e^{w_ t+tH}\omega ^ n$, starting with $w_0=0$. The trace estimate of 8.4.6 applies with prescribed potential $v=0$, fixed smooth comparison $0$, and $h(x,v)=tH(x)$; its constants are uniform for $t\in [0,1]$. 8.3.3 then gives a uniform gradient and complex-Hessian bound. 8.5.1 gives uniform $W^{2,p}$ and hence $C^{1,\alpha }$ bounds, for any fixed $\alpha <1$. Consequently $r_ t=e^{(w_ t+tH)/m}$ has a uniform Hölder bound. The extension of 8.5.3 is uniformly elliptic and concave on all real Hessians, with coefficient oscillation bounded by $C|x-y|(1+\| R\| )$. The analytic estimate recalled in section 8.5 therefore gives uniform $C^{2,\beta }$ bounds on a finite cover. The original smooth Hessian operator is uniformly elliptic near the attained compact cone set. Differentiating and applying Schauder estimates gives bounds for every higher derivative. The linearization of $\log (H_ m(w)/\omega ^ n)-w-tH$ is $L_ w-1$, where \[  L_ w\xi =\frac{m\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\xi \wedge (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^{m-1} \wedge \omega ^{n-m}}{H_ m(w)}.  \] Its principal coefficients are positive definite. The maximum principle gives zero kernel; smooth elliptic Fredholm theory gives surjectivity and Schauder inversion. The implicit-function theorem proves openness. The uniform estimates prove closedness, so the path reaches $t=1$. For general $a$, use the metric $a\omega $ and potential $\widehat w=aw$. Both sides of its coefficient-one equation acquire the same factor $a^ n$, so it is exactly the stated equation after division by that factor. $\square$ An ordinary smooth approximation need not be admissible. To obtain an admissible one, choose a smooth obstacle above the continuous potential and penalize the solution's distance from that obstacle. Lemma 8.6.2 . B8367971A40D Every continuous admissible $\varphi $ on $X$ is the uniform limit of smooth strictly admissible functions. Proof. Fix a smooth $h\geq \varphi $ and a constant \[  b>\max \left\{ 1,\left\| H_ m(h)/\omega ^ n\right\| _\infty \right\} .  \] For each positive integer $N$ solve, by the preceding lemma, \[  H_ m(w_ N)=b e^{N(w_ N-h)}\omega ^ n.  \] At a positive maximum of $w_ N-h$, the form $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ lies above the strictly admissible form $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ N$, hence is admissible there. Monotonicity would give $b e^{N(w_ N-h)}\leq H_ m(h)/\omega ^ n<b$, a contradiction. Thus $w_ N\leq h$. The preceding zero-order estimate also gives \[  \| w_ N\| _\infty \leq M_ N:=\| h\| _\infty +\frac{\log b}{N}.  \] Let $x_ N$ maximize $\varphi -(1+N^{-1})w_ N$. The smooth positive form $T_ N=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ N)^{m-1}\wedge \omega ^{n-m}$ defines a strictly elliptic linear operator. Admissibility gives $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )\wedge T_ N\geq 0$ in distributions. Its linear maximum principle, applied to the upper test $(1+N^{-1})w_ N$ plus the maximum value, gives at $x_ N$ \[  0\leq \bigl (\omega +(1+N^{-1})\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ N\bigr )\wedge T_ N.  \] This application is to a continuous distributional subsolution of a smooth strictly elliptic operator. It does not assume a second derivative of $\varphi $. Writing $d_ N=H_ m(w_ N)/\omega ^ n$, polarized Gårding positivity yields \[  (N+1)d_ N\geq \omega \wedge T_ N/\omega ^ n \geq d_ N^{(m-1)/m}.  \] Therefore, at this maximum point, \[  w_ N-h\geq -E_ N,\qquad E_ N=\frac{m\log (N+1)+\log b}{N}.  \] Since $\varphi \leq h$, the maximum of $\varphi -(1+N^{-1})w_ N$ is at most $E_ N+M_ N/N$. It follows on all of $X$ that \[  \varphi -E_ N-2M_ N/N\leq w_ N\leq h.  \] Given $\delta >0$, choose an ordinary smooth majorant $\varphi \leq h\leq \varphi +\delta $, and then $N$ so large that $E_ N+2M_ N/N\leq \delta $. The resulting $w_ N$ is strictly admissible and within $\delta $ of $\varphi $. Let $\delta \downarrow 0$. No monotonicity of the chosen approximants is needed. $\square$

title: 8.6.3 Decreasing approximation of bounded potentials
text: Upper semicontinuity supplies smooth obstacles decreasing to a bounded potential. The same penalty equation gives admissible functions between the potential and each obstacle, up to an error tending to zero. Choosing successive obstacles below the preceding smooth approximation makes the admissible approximations decrease as well. Lemma 8.6.4 . EBF9BA687F39 Every bounded upper semicontinuous real function $u$ on $X$ is the pointwise decreasing limit of smooth functions $h_ j>u$. Proof. Fix a Riemannian distance $d$ on $X$ and put \[  c_ j(x)=\sup _{y\in X}\{ u(y)-j d(x,y)\} .  \] Each $c_ j$ is Lipschitz, $c_ j\geq u$, and $c_{j+1}\leq c_ j$. The supremum is attained. If $y_ j$ attains it at a fixed $x$, then $j d(x,y_ j)\leq \sup _ X u-u(x)$, so $y_ j\to x$. Upper semicontinuity gives $\limsup _ j c_ j(x)\leq u(x)$, and hence $c_ j\downarrow u$ pointwise. Set $\delta _ j=4^{-j}$. Smooth approximation of continuous functions on a compact manifold gives $s_ j\in C^\infty (X)$ with $\| s_ j-c_ j\| _\infty \leq \delta _ j/4$. Take $h_ j=s_ j+\delta _ j$. Then \[  u+\tfrac 34\delta _ j\leq h_ j\leq c_ j+\tfrac 54\delta _ j, \qquad h_{j+1}\leq c_ j+\tfrac 5{16}\delta _ j < c_ j+\tfrac 34\delta _ j\leq h_ j.  \] The bounds also imply $h_ j(x)\to u(x)$ at every point. $\square$ Lemma 8.6.5 . DFE78235C5E9 Let $u$ be bounded admissible and $h\geq u$ smooth. Choose \[  b>\max \{ 1,\| H_ m(h)/\omega ^ n\| _\infty \} .  \] For each positive integer $N$, let $w_ N$ be the smooth strictly admissible solution of \[  H_ m(w_ N)=b e^{N(w_ N-h)}\omega ^ n.  \] With \[  M_ N=\| h\| _\infty +\frac{\log b}{N},\qquad E_ N=\frac{m\log (N+1)+\log b}{N},  \] one has $\| w_ N\| _\infty \leq M_ N$ and \[  u-E_ N-2M_ N/N\leq w_ N\leq h.  \] Proof. Existence follows from 8.6.1 . The maximum comparison with $h$ in the proof of 8.6.2 gives $w_ N\leq h$; it involves only the smooth obstacle and solution. The zero-order bound from 8.6.1 gives $\| w_ N\| _\infty \leq M_ N$. The upper semicontinuous function $u-(1+N^{-1})w_ N$ attains its maximum at some $x_ N$. The smooth function $(1+N^{-1})w_ N$ plus this maximum is an upper test for $u$ there. Put \[  T_ N=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ N)^{m-1}\wedge \omega ^{n-m}, \qquad d_ N=H_ m(w_ N)/\omega ^ n>0.  \] Condition ( 8.2.2 ) and polarized positivity yield, at $x_ N$, \[  (N+1)d_ N\geq \omega \wedge T_ N/\omega ^ n \geq d_ N^{(m-1)/m}.  \] Consequently $d_ N\geq (N+1)^{-m}$ and $w_ N-h\geq -E_ N$ there. Using $u\leq h$, the maximum is at most $E_ N+M_ N/N$. On all of $X$ this gives \[  u\leq (1+N^{-1})w_ N+E_ N+M_ N/N \leq w_ N+E_ N+2M_ N/N.  \] $\square$ Theorem 8.6.6 . 68BE4F589DCE Every bounded admissible potential $u$ on $X$ is the pointwise decreasing limit of smooth strictly admissible potentials. The sequence may be chosen uniformly bounded. Proof. Choose smooth $h_ k\downarrow u$ by 8.6.4 and put $\varepsilon _ j=8^{-j}$. We construct smooth strictly admissible $u_ j$ with $u_ j\geq u+\varepsilon _ j$. For $j=1$, take $k_1=1$. At a subsequent step choose $k_ j\geq \max \{ j,k_{j-1}+1\} $ so large that \[  h_{k_ j}<u_{j-1}-\tfrac 12\varepsilon _{j-1}\quad \hbox{on }X.  \] Such an index exists: the open sets $\{ h_ k<u_{j-1}-\varepsilon _{j-1}/2\} $ increase with $k$ and cover $X$, since $h_ k\downarrow u\leq u_{j-1}-\varepsilon _{j-1}$. Compactness gives a single index for all of $X$. For this fixed obstacle $h_{k_ j}$ choose $b_ j$ as in 8.6.5 , and then choose $N_ j$ so large that its error $E_{N_ j}+2M_{N_ j}/N_ j$ is at most $\varepsilon _ j$. The resulting smooth solution $w_ j$ satisfies \[  u-\varepsilon _ j\leq w_ j\leq h_{k_ j}.  \] Put $u_ j=w_ j+2\varepsilon _ j$. Adding a constant preserves strict admissibility, and $u_ j\geq u+\varepsilon _ j$. For $j\geq 2$, \[  u_ j\leq h_{k_ j}+2\varepsilon _ j <u_{j-1}-\tfrac 12\varepsilon _{j-1}+2\varepsilon _ j =u_{j-1}-\tfrac 14\varepsilon _{j-1}.  \] Finally, $u\leq u_ j\leq h_{k_ j}+2\varepsilon _ j$ and $k_ j\geq j$ give pointwise convergence to $u$. The bounds $\inf _ X u\leq u_ j\leq \sup _ X u_1$ give a common uniform bound. $\square$ For continuous $u$, Dini's theorem makes these decreasing approximations converge uniformly on $X$. This is the convergence used for the continuous mixed products in the next section.

title: Lemma 8.6.4
text: Lemma 8.6.4 . EBF9BA687F39 Every bounded upper semicontinuous real function $u$ on $X$ is the pointwise decreasing limit of smooth functions $h_ j>u$. Proof. title: Lemma 8.6.5
text: Lemma 8.6.5 . DFE78235C5E9 Let $u$ be bounded admissible and $h\geq u$ smooth. Choose \[  b>\max \{ 1,\| H_ m(h)/\omega ^ n\| _\infty \} .  \] For each positive integer $N$, let $w_ N$ be the smooth strictly admissible solution of \[  H_ m(w_ N)=b e^{N(w_ N-h)}\omega ^ n.  \] With \[  M_ N=\| h\| _\infty +\frac{\log b}{N},\qquad E_ N=\frac{m\log (N+1)+\log b}{N},  \] one has $\| w_ N\| _\infty \leq M_ N$ and \[  u-E_ N-2M_ N/N\leq w_ N\leq h.  \] Proof. Existence follows from 8.6.1 . The maximum comparison with $h$ in the proof of 8.6.2 gives $w_ N\leq h$; it involves only the smooth obstacle and solution. The zero-order bound from 8.6.1 gives $\| w_ N\| _\infty \leq M_ N$. The upper semicontinuous function $u-(1+N^{-1})w_ N$ attains its maximum at some $x_ N$. The smooth function $(1+N^{-1})w_ N$ plus this maximum is an upper test for $u$ there. Put \[  T_ N=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ N)^{m-1}\wedge \omega ^{n-m}, \qquad d_ N=H_ m(w_ N)/\omega ^ n>0.  \] Condition ( 8.2.2 ) and polarized positivity yield, at $x_ N$, \[  (N+1)d_ N\geq \omega \wedge T_ N/\omega ^ n \geq d_ N^{(m-1)/m}.  \] Consequently $d_ N\geq (N+1)^{-m}$ and $w_ N-h\geq -E_ N$ there. Using $u\leq h$, the maximum is at most $E_ N+M_ N/N$. On all of $X$ this gives \[  u\leq (1+N^{-1})w_ N+E_ N+M_ N/N \leq w_ N+E_ N+2M_ N/N.  \] $\square$

title: Theorem 8.6.6
text: Theorem 8.6.6 . 68BE4F589DCE Every bounded admissible potential $u$ on $X$ is the pointwise decreasing limit of smooth strictly admissible potentials. The sequence may be chosen uniformly bounded. Proof. Choose smooth $h_ k\downarrow u$ by 8.6.4 and put $\varepsilon _ j=8^{-j}$. We construct smooth strictly admissible $u_ j$ with $u_ j\geq u+\varepsilon _ j$. For $j=1$, take $k_1=1$. At a subsequent step choose $k_ j\geq \max \{ j,k_{j-1}+1\} $ so large that \[  h_{k_ j}<u_{j-1}-\tfrac 12\varepsilon _{j-1}\quad \hbox{on }X.  \] Such an index exists: the open sets $\{ h_ k<u_{j-1}-\varepsilon _{j-1}/2\} $ increase with $k$ and cover $X$, since $h_ k\downarrow u\leq u_{j-1}-\varepsilon _{j-1}$. Compactness gives a single index for all of $X$. For this fixed obstacle $h_{k_ j}$ choose $b_ j$ as in 8.6.5 , and then choose $N_ j$ so large that its error $E_{N_ j}+2M_{N_ j}/N_ j$ is at most $\varepsilon _ j$. The resulting smooth solution $w_ j$ satisfies \[  u-\varepsilon _ j\leq w_ j\leq h_{k_ j}.  \] Put $u_ j=w_ j+2\varepsilon _ j$. Adding a constant preserves strict admissibility, and $u_ j\geq u+\varepsilon _ j$. For $j\geq 2$, \[  u_ j\leq h_{k_ j}+2\varepsilon _ j <u_{j-1}-\tfrac 12\varepsilon _{j-1}+2\varepsilon _ j =u_{j-1}-\tfrac 14\varepsilon _{j-1}.  \] Finally, $u\leq u_ j\leq h_{k_ j}+2\varepsilon _ j$ and $k_ j\geq j$ give pointwise convergence to $u$. The bounds $\inf _ X u\leq u_ j\leq \sup _ X u_1$ give a common uniform bound. $\square$

title: 8.7 Continuous products, envelopes and domination
text: Uniform admissible approximation allows us to define the mixed Hessian products. Their local bounds retain the derivatives of the Hermitian background; closedness of the background is not required. Proposition 8.7.1 . D2A0F255F625 For continuous admissible $u_1,\ldots ,u_ k$, $1\leq k\leq m$, the current \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1)\wedge \cdots \wedge (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ k) \wedge \omega ^{n-m}  \] is well defined as the limit of uniform smooth admissible approximations. It is positive, local, and continuous when its potentials converge uniformly. Its local masses are bounded in terms of uniform bounds on the potentials. In particular $H_ m(u)$ is a positive Radon measure. Proof. 8.6.1 , 8.6.2 provide the smooth approximations without using any continuous Hessian product or domination input. For a smooth admissible $u$ put $\sigma =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. Since $\mathrm d\sigma =\mathrm d\omega $, the coefficients of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\chi \sigma ^{r-1}\wedge \omega ^{n-r})$ are sums of smooth test factors paired with powers $\sigma ^ q$, $q\leq r-1$, where $\chi $ is a fixed cutoff. The absolute-form lemma and integration by parts give the Chern–Levine–Nirenberg bound by induction on $r\leq m$: \[  \int _ K\sigma ^ r\wedge \omega ^{n-r} \leq C_{K,U,\omega }(1+\| u\| _{L^\infty (U)})^ r.  \] At the induction step write $\sigma ^ r=\omega \wedge \sigma ^{r-1} +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \sigma ^{r-1}$, integrate the second term against $\chi $, and move $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ to $\chi \sigma ^{r-1}\omega ^{n-r}$. The resulting powers have degrees $r-1,r-2,r-3$, with negative powers absent, and the induction applies on nested slightly larger compact sets. Mixed masses reduce to the single potential average, by positivity of the expansion of its power. Positive mixed currents have total variation controlled by these trace masses. To prove independence, telescope the difference between two smooth mixed products whose potentials have a common uniform bound. Each term paired with a fixed smooth complementary test is \[  \int \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ a-v_ a)\wedge T\wedge \eta =\int (u_ a-v_ a)\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(T\wedge \eta ),  \] where $T$ is a product of the remaining admissible factors and $\omega ^{n-m}$. The identity $\mathrm d(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)=\mathrm d\omega $ and its $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$ analogue show that derivatives of $T$ introduce only fixed metric derivatives; every term has at most $k-1<m$ admissible factors. The absolute mixed-form bound and the mass estimate just proved bound the variation of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(T\wedge \eta )$ uniformly. Consequently the pairing difference is at most $C_\eta \max _ a\| u_ a-v_ a\| _\infty $. The same construction with an arbitrary complementary smooth test also defines the signed products of fewer than $m$ factors without the factor $\omega ^{n-m}$: their variation is bounded by the absolute-form lemma. These products justify the metric-derivative terms above. This proves that all approximations have the same limit and that the products are continuous in the uniform topology. Positivity passes from the smooth mixed products. Using a test supported in an open set on which two limiting potentials coincide proves locality by the same estimate on a smaller neighborhood of its support. $\square$ Write $H_ m(u)$ for the measure with every potential equal to $u$. Locality and uniform continuity of these products give comparison on a contact set. Lemma 8.7.2 . 21F540C3F7D1 If $u\leq v$ are continuous admissible functions and the remaining $m-1$ factors are fixed continuous admissible functions, then on $\{ u=v\} $ the mixed measure with first factor $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is at most the one with first factor $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$. In particular $\mathbf1_{\{ u=v\} }H_ m(u)\leq \mathbf1_{\{ u=v\} }H_ m(v)$. Proof. Write $M(w)$ for the mixed measure with first potential $w$. Positivity and locality give, for $t>0$, \[  M(\max (v,u+t))\geq \mathbf1_{\{ v>u+t\} }M(v)+\mathbf1_{\{ u\geq v\} }M(u).  \] The first indicators increase to $\mathbf1_{\{ v>u\} }$ as $t\downarrow 0$, and the potentials on the left converge uniformly to $v$. Integrate against nonnegative continuous tests and pass to the limit. Subtract the first restricted measure to obtain the claimed contact inequality. Replacing one factor at a time proves the pure-power claim and the analogous contact inequalities for all mixed powers. $\square$ For a continuous real obstacle $h$, define $P(h)$ to be the supremum of continuous admissible functions bounded above by $h$. Constants make the family nonempty. The penalty construction also proves that this supremum is continuous and its Hessian measure lies on the contact set. Lemma 8.7.3 . C39ADEAC74E3 The function $P(h)$ is continuous and admissible, and $H_ m(P(h))$ is supported on $\{ P(h)=h\} $. Moreover $\| P(h_1)-P(h_2)\| _\infty \leq \| h_1-h_2\| _\infty $. Proof. For smooth $h$, use the penalty solutions $w_ N$ in 8.6.2 . Its maximum argument applies to every continuous admissible competitor $v\leq h$, with an error depending on $h$ and $N$, and not on $v$. Taking their supremum gives \[  P(h)-E_ N-2M_ N/N\leq w_ N\leq P(h),  \] where the error tends to zero. Thus $P(h)$ is their uniform limit and is continuous and admissible. On every compact subset of $\{ P(h)<h\} $ the penalty densities $b e^{N(w_ N-h)}$ tend uniformly to zero. Product continuity implies the contact support assertion. Adding constants to competitors gives the stated Lipschitz bound. Approximate a continuous $h$ uniformly by smooth obstacles. Their envelopes converge uniformly to $P(h)$, proving continuity and admissibility. Any compact subset of $\{ P(h)<h\} $ also lies outside the contact sets of all sufficiently close smooth obstacles; product continuity gives the support assertion for $h$. $\square$ The obstacle also bounds discontinuous competitors. Their upper-test admissibility suffices for the penalty estimate, so allowing them does not change the continuous envelope of a smooth obstacle. Proposition 8.7.4 . 26DD802A141E For every smooth real obstacle $h$, the envelope $P(h)$ equals the pointwise supremum of all bounded admissible functions below $h$. Proof. The solutions $w_ N$ of 8.6.5 are continuous admissible competitors, so $w_ N\leq P(h)$. For each bounded admissible $u\leq h$, the same lemma gives \[  u\leq w_ N+E_ N+2M_ N/N\leq P(h)+E_ N+2M_ N/N.  \] Let $N\to \infty $ for this fixed obstacle and fixed $b$. Thus $P(h)$ dominates every bounded competitor. Since $P(h)$ itself is a bounded competitor, it equals their supremum. $\square$ The trace test in ( 8.2.1 ) gives $L_\omega u\geq -n$, where $L_\omega u=n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge \omega ^{n-1}/\omega ^ n$. We use the classical normalized Green estimate 5451B220B0B1 8.7.5 \begin{equation}  \int _ X(\sup _ Xu-u)\omega ^ n\leq C_\omega \end{equation} for continuous admissible $u$. The stationary probability of $L_\omega $ has a smooth positive density equivalent to $\omega ^ n$. The positive measure $L_\omega u+n$ has stationary mass $n$, so the Green-kernel estimate gives this bound. It is a linear elliptic input, and does not assert compactness for a nonlinear Hessian measure. To use envelopes in domination, we must first exclude a potential with zero total Hessian mass. Lemma 8.7.6 . E7EA08EFFDE7 Every continuous admissible $u$ satisfies $\int _ X H_ m(u)>0$. Proof. Suppose this integral is zero. For $s>0$ put $w=\max (u,\min _ Xu+s)$ and $U=\{ u<\min _ Xu+s\} $. The open set $U$ is nonempty, $0\leq w-u\leq s$, and $w=u$ outside it. Set $\sigma _ u=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, $\sigma _ w=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$, and $\mu _ q=\sigma _ u^ q\wedge \sigma _ w^{m-q}\wedge \omega ^{n-m}$. The contact lemma gives $\mathbf1_{X\setminus U}\mu _ q\geq \mathbf1_{X\setminus U}\mu _ m$, for $0\leq q\leq m$. For $q<m$ the telescoping identity is \[  \mu _ q-\mu _ m=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w-u)\wedge T_ q,\qquad T_ q=\sigma _ u^ q\wedge \sum _{r=0}^{m-q-1}\sigma _ w^ r\wedge \sigma _ u^{m-q-1-r} \wedge \omega ^{n-m}.  \] Integration by parts on $X$ therefore gives \[  \int _ U(\mu _ q-\mu _ m)\leq \int _ X(\mu _ q-\mu _ m) =\int _ X(w-u)\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_ q.  \] This identity follows first for smooth approximants and then by uniform product continuity. The derivatives of $T_ q$ contain only fixed metric derivatives and products of at most $m-1$ admissible factors, so the absolute-form lemma makes $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_ q$ a measure of uniformly controlled variation. Uniform convergence also justifies its continuous weight. On $U$, locality gives $\sigma _ w=\omega $ and thus \[  |\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_ q|\leq C\sum _{r=0}^{m-1}\mu _ r.  \] The constant depends only on the metric and $m,n$, and not on $u$ or $s$. Consequently \[  \sum _{q=0}^ m\int _ U\mu _ q \leq (m+1)\int _ U H_ m(u)+Cms\sum _{r=0}^{m-1}\int _ U\mu _ r.  \] For sufficiently small $s$, absorption and $H_ m(u)=0$ force all these nonnegative integrals to vanish. But $\mu _0=\omega ^ n$ on the nonempty open set $U$, a contradiction. $\square$ The envelope of a stretched difference now converts vanishing of a restricted measure into an order relation. The linear bound ( 8.7.5 ) prevents these envelopes from tending to $-\infty $ on an open set. Proposition 8.7.7 . 7E8FF9A60609 If continuous admissible $u,v$ satisfy $\mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }H_ m(u)=0$, then $u\geq v$. Proof. Replace $v$ by $\max (u,v)$, so $u\leq v$. For $b>1$ put $p_ b=P(bu-(b-1)v)$ and $z_ b=b^{-1}p_ b+(1-b^{-1})v\leq u$. On the contact set $C_ b=\{ p_ b=bu-(b-1)v\} $ one has $z_ b=u$; the contact inequality and polarized positivity give \[  \mathbf1_{C_ b}b^{-m}H_ m(p_ b) \leq \mathbf1_{C_ b}H_ m(z_ b) \leq \mathbf1_{C_ b}H_ m(u).  \] The envelope measure is supported on $C_ b$ and has positive mass. It vanishes on $C_ b\cap \{ u<v\} $ by the hypothesis, so some point of $C_ b\cap \{ u=v\} $ exists. Hence $\sup _ Xp_ b\geq \inf _ Xv$, while $p_ b\leq u$. The estimate ( 8.7.5 ) is consequently uniform for $p_ b$. On the open set $E_ a=\{ u<v-a\} $, for $a>0$, one has $p_ b\leq v-ba$, and therefore \[  C_\omega \geq \int _ X(\sup _ Xp_ b-p_ b)\omega ^ n \geq (ba-\operatorname {osc}_ Xv)\int _{E_ a}\omega ^ n.  \] Letting $b\to \infty $ gives zero volume for $E_ a$. Since it is open it is empty, and $a\downarrow 0$ gives $u\geq v$. $\square$ Proposition 8.7.8 . 103D0E7E46B0 If continuous admissible $u,v$ satisfy \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }H_ m(u)\leq c\mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }H_ m(v),\qquad 0\leq c<1,  \] then $u\geq v$. Proof. Choose $b>1$ so that $(1-b^{-1})^ m>c$, and put $p=P(bu-(b-1)v)$ and $z=b^{-1}p+(1-b^{-1})v\leq u$. On $C=\{ p=bu-(b-1)v\} $ the contact comparison gives \[  \mathbf1_ C\bigl (b^{-m}H_ m(p)+(1-b^{-1})^ mH_ m(v)\bigr ) \leq \mathbf1_ C H_ m(u).  \] Restricting to $\{ u<v\} $ and using the hypothesis shows that $H_ m(p)$ vanishes on $C\cap \{ u<v\} $. Its support lies in $C$, where $p<v$ is equivalent to $u<v$. Thus $H_ m(p)$ vanishes on $\{ p<v\} $. The preceding domination proposition gives $p\geq v$. Since $p\leq bu-(b-1)v$, it follows that $u\geq v$. $\square$ Strict domination yields the comparison needed for the proper equations. Lemma 8.7.9 . F28CED8C4FAF For continuous admissible $u,v$ and $a>0$, if \[  e^{-av}H_ m(v)\geq e^{-au}H_ m(u),  \] then $u\geq v$. Proof. Fix $\delta >0$. On $\{ u<v-\delta \} $, the assumed inequality gives \[  H_ m(u)\leq e^{a(u-v)}H_ m(v) \leq e^{-a\delta }H_ m(v-\delta ).  \] The constant $e^{-a\delta }$ is strictly smaller than one, so 8.7.8 applied to $u$ and $v-\delta $ gives $u\geq v-\delta $. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ proves the assertion. $\square$

title: Proposition 8.7.4

title: Equation 8.7.5
text: 5451B220B0B1 8.7.5 \begin{equation}  \int _ X(\sup _ Xu-u)\omega ^ n\leq C_\omega \end{equation}

title: Lemma 8.7.6
text: Lemma 8.7.6 . E7EA08EFFDE7 Every continuous admissible $u$ satisfies $\int _ X H_ m(u)>0$. Proof. Suppose this integral is zero. For $s>0$ put $w=\max (u,\min _ Xu+s)$ and $U=\{ u<\min _ Xu+s\} $. The open set $U$ is nonempty, $0\leq w-u\leq s$, and $w=u$ outside it. Set $\sigma _ u=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, $\sigma _ w=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$, and $\mu _ q=\sigma _ u^ q\wedge \sigma _ w^{m-q}\wedge \omega ^{n-m}$. The contact lemma gives $\mathbf1_{X\setminus U}\mu _ q\geq \mathbf1_{X\setminus U}\mu _ m$, for $0\leq q\leq m$. For $q<m$ the telescoping identity is \[  \mu _ q-\mu _ m=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w-u)\wedge T_ q,\qquad T_ q=\sigma _ u^ q\wedge \sum _{r=0}^{m-q-1}\sigma _ w^ r\wedge \sigma _ u^{m-q-1-r} \wedge \omega ^{n-m}.  \] Integration by parts on $X$ therefore gives \[  \int _ U(\mu _ q-\mu _ m)\leq \int _ X(\mu _ q-\mu _ m) =\int _ X(w-u)\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_ q.  \] This identity follows first for smooth approximants and then by uniform product continuity. The derivatives of $T_ q$ contain only fixed metric derivatives and products of at most $m-1$ admissible factors, so the absolute-form lemma makes $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_ q$ a measure of uniformly controlled variation. Uniform convergence also justifies its continuous weight. On $U$, locality gives $\sigma _ w=\omega $ and thus \[  |\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_ q|\leq C\sum _{r=0}^{m-1}\mu _ r.  \] The constant depends only on the metric and $m,n$, and not on $u$ or $s$. Consequently \[  \sum _{q=0}^ m\int _ U\mu _ q \leq (m+1)\int _ U H_ m(u)+Cms\sum _{r=0}^{m-1}\int _ U\mu _ r.  \] For sufficiently small $s$, absorption and $H_ m(u)=0$ force all these nonnegative integrals to vanish. But $\mu _0=\omega ^ n$ on the nonempty open set $U$, a contradiction. $\square$

title: Proposition 8.7.7
text: Proposition 8.7.7 . 7E8FF9A60609 If continuous admissible $u,v$ satisfy $\mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }H_ m(u)=0$, then $u\geq v$. Proof. Replace $v$ by $\max (u,v)$, so $u\leq v$. For $b>1$ put $p_ b=P(bu-(b-1)v)$ and $z_ b=b^{-1}p_ b+(1-b^{-1})v\leq u$. It vanishes on $C_ b\cap \{ u<v\} $ by the hypothesis, so some point of $C_ b\cap \{ u=v\} $ exists. Hence $\sup _ Xp_ b\geq \inf _ Xv$, while $p_ b\leq u$. On the open set $E_ a=\{ u<v-a\} $, for $a>0$, one has $p_ b\leq v-ba$, and therefore \[  C_\omega \geq \int _ X(\sup _ Xp_ b-p_ b)\omega ^ n \geq (ba-\operatorname {osc}_ Xv)\int _{E_ a}\omega ^ n.  \] Letting $b\to \infty $ gives zero volume for $E_ a$. Since it is open it is empty, and $a\downarrow 0$ gives $u\geq v$. $\square$

title: Proposition 8.7.8

title: Lemma 8.7.9
text: Lemma 8.7.9 . F28CED8C4FAF For continuous admissible $u,v$ and $a>0$, if \[  e^{-av}H_ m(v)\geq e^{-au}H_ m(u),  \] then $u\geq v$. Proof. Fix $\delta >0$. On $\{ u<v-\delta \} $, the assumed inequality gives \[  H_ m(u)\leq e^{a(u-v)}H_ m(v) \leq e^{-a\delta }H_ m(v-\delta ).  \] The constant $e^{-a\delta }$ is strictly smaller than one, so 8.7.8 applied to $u$ and $v-\delta $ gives $u\geq v-\delta $. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ proves the assertion. $\square$

title: 8.8 Continuous equations and regularity
text: The proper equation is stable in the uniform norm, so its smooth solutions extend to continuous data. This also identifies the limit of the auxiliary equations with a prescribed continuous weak solution. Proposition 8.8.1 . 5D1E62F09217 Let $a>0$ and let smooth $H_ j$ converge uniformly to a continuous $H$. The smooth solutions of $H_ m(w_ j)=e^{aw_ j+H_ j}\omega ^ n$ converge uniformly to the unique continuous admissible solution of $H_ m(w)=e^{aw+H}\omega ^ n$. For two continuous data $H_1,H_2$, the corresponding solutions satisfy \[  \| w_1-w_2\| _\infty \leq a^{-1}\| H_1-H_2\| _\infty .  \] They also satisfy $-\max _ XH/a\leq w\leq -\min _ XH/a$. Proof. Smooth solutions exist by 8.6.1 . At a maximum of $w_1-w_2$, monotonicity of the smooth Hessian operator gives $e^{aw_1+H_1}\leq e^{aw_2+H_2}$. Hence $a(w_1-w_2)\leq H_2-H_1$ there. Exchanging the functions gives the stated norm estimate for smooth data. Thus a uniformly convergent sequence of smooth data gives a uniformly Cauchy sequence of solutions. Its limit is admissible by the linear distributional inequalities, and 8.7.1 passes the equation to the limit. The bounds follow from those for the smooth solutions. Taking limits in the smooth norm estimate proves it for continuous data. Finally, 8.7.9 in both directions gives uniqueness among continuous admissible solutions. $\square$ For smooth positive densities depending on the potential, the estimate of section 8.4 gives complex-Hessian bounds independent of derivatives of the prescribed approximation. The elliptic extension then upgrades the continuous solution to a classical one. Theorem 8.8.2 . 3B8FDE2FF95D If $\varphi $ is continuous and admissible on $X$, $f(x,t)$ is smooth on a neighborhood of its bounded range, and \[  H_ m(\varphi )=e^{f(x,\varphi )}\omega ^ n,  \] then $\varphi $ is smooth. Proof. Choose smooth admissible $v_ j\to \varphi $ uniformly, by 8.6.2 . Their values lie in a fixed compact interval on which $f$ is smooth. Put $h(x,t)=-t+f(x,t)$ and solve \[  H_ m(u_ j)=e^{u_ j+h(x,v_ j)}\omega ^ n.  \] The preceding stability proposition shows that $u_ j$ converges uniformly to a continuous admissible $u$ satisfying \[  e^{-u}H_ m(u)=e^{-\varphi +f(x,\varphi )}\omega ^ n =e^{-\varphi }H_ m(\varphi ).  \] 8.7.9 , applied in both directions, gives $u=\varphi $. The zero-order bounds for $u_ j$ are uniform. Fix $M$ bounding them and choose $B>\| \varphi \| _\infty +1$. Extend $h$ smoothly away from a neighborhood of the range of $\varphi $ to $X\times [-B-1,B+1]$; this does not change the equations for large $j$. The tolerance $\varepsilon $ in 8.4.6 depends on these bounds and on $h$, without derivatives of the smooth comparison function. Choose a fixed smooth $\widetilde\varphi $ with $\| \widetilde\varphi -\varphi \| _\infty <\varepsilon /2$ and $\| \widetilde\varphi \| _\infty \leq B$. For large $j$, $\| v_ j-\widetilde\varphi \| _\infty <\varepsilon $. 8.4.7 then gives uniform gradient and complex-Hessian bounds for $u_ j$, independent of derivatives of $v_ j$. 8.5.1 yields $\varphi \in W^{2,p}$ for every finite $p$, and $\varphi \in C^{1,\alpha }$ for every $\alpha <1$. 8.5.4 makes $\varphi $ a continuous viscosity solution of the concave uniformly elliptic extension, with right-hand side $e^{f(x,\varphi )/m}$. This right-hand side is Hölder. The analytic estimate in section 8.5 therefore gives $\varphi \in C^{2,\beta }$, for some $\beta >0$. The operator agrees with the original Hessian root on the attained compact cone set; the now classical equation thus has smooth dependence on $x,\varphi $ and its complex Hessian, and is uniformly elliptic there. Difference quotients and interior Schauder estimates give $C^{3,\beta }$; iteration proves smoothness. The estimate applies directly to the viscosity limit. $\square$ The proper equation can now be solved when its exponent depends smoothly on the unknown potential, provided that constant barriers bound the desired range and the dependence is strictly increasing. Theorem 8.8.3 . 76376AD88152 Let $A<B$ and let $f$ be smooth on a neighborhood of $X\times [A,B]$. Suppose that, for every $x\in X$, \[  f(x,A)\leq 0\leq f(x,B),\qquad 0<\kappa \leq \partial _ t f(x,t)\leq L\quad (A\leq t\leq B).  \] There is a unique continuous admissible solution with values in $[A,B]$ of \[  H_ m(w)=e^{f(x,w)}\omega ^ n.  \] This solution is smooth and strictly admissible. Proof. Choose $a\geq L$ and let $\mathcal C=\{ v\in C(X):A\leq v\leq B\} $, a complete subset of $C(X)$ in the uniform norm. For $v\in \mathcal C$ put $H_ v(x)=f(x,v(x))-av(x)$ and let $T(v)$ be the continuous proper solution with exponent $aT(v)+H_ v$, furnished by 8.8.1 . The function $f(x,t)-at$ is nonincreasing in $t$, so \[  -aB\leq f(x,B)-aB\leq H_ v(x) \leq f(x,A)-aA\leq -aA.  \] The zero-order bounds in that proposition give $A\leq T(v)\leq B$. The mean-value theorem also gives \[  \| H_ v-H_ z\| _\infty \leq (a-\kappa )\| v-z\| _\infty , \qquad \| T(v)-T(z)\| _\infty \leq (1-\kappa /a)\| v-z\| _\infty .  \] Since $0\leq 1-\kappa /a<1$, the contraction theorem gives a unique fixed point $w\in \mathcal C$. It is admissible because it equals $T(w)$, and its equation is exactly the stated equation. Every continuous admissible solution in this interval is a fixed point, by uniqueness of the continuous proper equation with its prescribed $H_ w$. This proves uniqueness in the stated class. 8.8.2 makes $w$ smooth. Its form lies in the closed $m$-cone and has positive $m$th symmetric polynomial; Maclaurin's inequalities then put it in the open cone. Thus it is strictly admissible. $\square$

title: Proposition 8.8.1
text: Proposition 8.8.1 . 5D1E62F09217 Let $a>0$ and let smooth $H_ j$ converge uniformly to a continuous $H$. The smooth solutions of $H_ m(w_ j)=e^{aw_ j+H_ j}\omega ^ n$ converge uniformly to the unique continuous admissible solution of $H_ m(w)=e^{aw+H}\omega ^ n$. For two continuous data $H_1,H_2$, the corresponding solutions satisfy \[  \| w_1-w_2\| _\infty \leq a^{-1}\| H_1-H_2\| _\infty .  \] They also satisfy $-\max _ XH/a\leq w\leq -\min _ XH/a$. Proof. Taking limits in the smooth norm estimate proves it for continuous data. Finally, 8.7.9 in both directions gives uniqueness among continuous admissible solutions. $\square$

title: 8.9 Bounded potentials and recursive Hessian currents
search_title: Bounded potentials and recursive Hessian currents
section: 8.9 Bounded potentials and recursive Hessian currents
text: The decreasing approximation of bounded admissible potentials supplies limits that uniform approximation cannot reach. A bounded potential can multiply a current with measure coefficients, so one can apply $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ to the resulting current. Repeating this operation requires bounds on every coefficient, rather than only on the trace of a positive mixed measure. The absolute-form estimate provides these bounds below degree $m$; at degree $m$, positivity is obtained after wedging with $\omega ^{n-m}$. All bounded potentials have their canonical upper semicontinuous representatives from ( 8.2.2 ). Their pointwise values will be used when multiplying measure coefficients. For a real current $T$ of order zero, write $\| T\| _ K$ for the sum of the total variations of its coefficients on a compact coordinate set $K$. Fix $K\Subset U$ in a coordinate chart. Different fixed coordinate frames give equivalent local bounds. Lemma 8.9.1 . C35233382EB9 If $u$ is bounded admissible, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ has signed Radon measure coefficients. For $K\Subset U$ contained in a coordinate chart, \[  \| \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\| _ K\leq C_{K,U,\omega }(1+\| u\| _{L^\infty (X)}).  \] Proof. Choose smooth strictly admissible $u_ j\downarrow u$ by 8.6.6 , and put $\sigma _ j=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$. After discarding finitely many terms, $\| u_ j\| _\infty \leq \| u\| _\infty +1$. Indeed, the increasing open sets $\{ u_ j<\sup _ Xu+1\} $ cover $X$, and compactness gives a single index whose open set is all of $X$; the lower bound follows from $u_ j\geq u$. The closed $m$-cone lies in the closed $2$-cone. In an $\omega $-unitary frame, its eigenvalues satisfy \[  \sum _ i\lambda _ i^2\leq (\operatorname {tr}\sigma _ j)^2, \qquad \operatorname {tr}\sigma _ j\geq 0.  \] Thus every coefficient of $\sigma _ j$ is bounded by its trace. The degree-one Chern–Levine–Nirenberg estimate in 8.7.1 , applied to these smooth functions, bounds the integral of that trace on $K$ by $C(1+\| u\| _\infty )$. Subtracting the fixed smooth $\omega $ gives the same bound for the coefficient variations of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$. Bounded convergence gives $u_ j\to u$ in local $L^1$, and therefore $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\to \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ in distributions. The uniform coefficient bounds show that this limit has measure coefficients with the asserted bound. $\square$ Set $D_0=1$. For an ordered list $u_1,\ldots ,u_ p$ of bounded admissible potentials, define recursively 66BDC02D9E25 8.9.2 \begin{equation}  D_ p(u_1,\ldots ,u_ p) =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl (u_ pD_{p-1}(u_1,\ldots ,u_{p-1})\bigr ). \end{equation} The next result justifies the bounded multiplication at every step up to $p=m$. Proposition 8.9.3 . EB2FA13CDDE0 For $1\leq p<m$, the recursion defines a real closed current of order zero and bidegree $(p,p)$. If $M=\max _ a\| u_ a\| _{L^\infty (X)}$, then \[  \| D_ p(u_1,\ldots ,u_ p)\| _ K \leq C_{K,U,\omega ,p}(1+M)^ p.  \] For $p=m$, it defines a real closed distributional current. For any smooth admissible sequences $u_ a^{j_ a}\downarrow u_ a$ with a common uniform bound, one has 686912AA777F 8.9.4 \begin{equation}  D_ p(u_1,\ldots ,u_ p) =\lim _{j_ p\to \infty }\cdots \lim _{j_1\to \infty } \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1^{j_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ p^{j_ p} \end{equation} in distributions. The index $j_1$ tends to infinity first. Below degree $m$, all these limits have locally uniformly bounded coefficient variations. Proof. The case $p=1$ is the preceding lemma. Suppose the assertions hold through degree $p-1<m$. Since $u_ p$ is bounded Borel and $D_{p-1}$ has measure coefficients, their product is well defined. Applying $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ gives a real current that is both $\mathrm d$- and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$-closed. For a fixed smooth complementary test form $\eta $, dominated convergence against the fixed signed measures gives \[  \begin{aligned}  \langle D_ p,\eta \rangle & =\langle u_ pD_{p-1},\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta \rangle \\ & =\lim _{j_ p\to \infty } \langle u_ p^{j_ p}D_{p-1},\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta \rangle . \end{aligned}  \] With $j_ p$ fixed, the inductive iterated limit for $D_{p-1}$ can be paired with the smooth form $u_ p^{j_ p}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta $. Integration by parts for the smooth closed factors identifies the resulting pairing with the smooth product on the right of ( 8.9.4 ). This proves that identity also when $p=m$. For $p<m$, expand the smooth product using $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ a^{j_ a}=\sigma _ a^{j_ a}-\omega $. A term with $q$ admissible factors, $0\leq q\leq p$, has the form \[  \sigma _{a_1}^{j_{a_1}}\wedge \cdots \wedge \sigma _{a_ q}^{j_{a_ q}}\wedge \omega ^{p-q}.  \] Every such $q$ is strictly less than $m$. Apply 8.2.7 to each coefficient test, and then the smooth mass estimate from 8.7.1 to the potential sum. The term $q=0$ is the fixed smooth form $\omega ^ p$. For $q\geq 1$, the sum of its admissible forms is $q(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bar u)$, where $\bar u$ is their average and $\| \bar u\| _\infty \leq M+1$. The result is a coefficient variation bound $C(1+M)^ p$, after choosing the approximations with norm at most $M+1$ as in the preceding proof. For arbitrary uniformly bounded approximations the same argument uses their common bound. The bounds survive each distributional limit, proving that $D_ p$ has order zero and the stated estimate. This completes the induction. No coefficient bound for the unwedged degree-$m$ current is used or asserted. $\square$ For a subset $I=\{ i_1<\cdots <i_ q\} \subset \{ 1,\ldots ,p\} $, write $D_ I=D_ q(u_{i_1},\ldots ,u_{i_ q})$, with $D_\varnothing =1$. Define the shifted current and its mixed positive current by 17FA1BFF2491 8.9.5 \begin{equation}  R_ p(u_1,\ldots ,u_ p) =\sum _{I\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,p\} }\omega ^{p-|I|}\wedge D_ I, \qquad Q_ p=R_ p\wedge \omega ^{n-m}. \end{equation} Below degree $m$, $R_ p$ has measure coefficients. At degree $m$ it is initially a distributional current. Its positive wedge $Q_ m$ is nevertheless a measure. Put $M=\max _ a\| u_ a\| _{L^\infty (X)}$. Theorem 8.9.6 . 846671D5582A For $1\leq p\leq m$, $Q_ p$ is a positive current of order zero, and \[  \int _ KQ_ p\wedge \omega ^{m-p} \leq C_{K,U,\omega ,p}(1+M)^ p.  \] It is the iterated limit, in the order of ( 8.9.4 ), of \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1^{j_1})\wedge \cdots \wedge (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ p^{j_ p})\wedge \omega ^{n-m}.  \] In particular $Q_ m$ is a positive Radon measure. These currents are local in the canonical potentials and independent of the chosen approximations for the fixed ordering. When all potentials are continuous, $Q_ p$ equals the continuous mixed product of 8.7.1 . Proof. Expand the smooth shifted product over its subsets. Applying ( 8.9.4 ) to each subset, in its inherited ordering, gives ( 8.9.5 ). The absent indices have no effect on a subset's limit. Each smooth product is positive: pairing with a decomposable strongly positive complementary test appends $m-p$ nonnegative rank-one $(1,1)$-forms, and polarized Gårding positivity applies. The smooth mixed mass bound is uniform in all indices. Distributional limits preserve positivity and the local trace bound at every step. Positive currents have order zero, so this gives the assertions for $Q_ p$, including the top-degree measure. The recursion uses only bounded multiplication of canonical values and local distributional differentiation. It is therefore local. Its definition contains no approximation choices, so the proved limit is independent of those choices while the ordering is fixed. For continuous potentials, the approximations converge uniformly by Dini's theorem. The telescoping estimate in 8.7.1 is uniform in all remaining indices and shows that their iterated limit is the same continuous mixed product. This also proves permutation invariance in the continuous case. $\square$ The shifted currents are not closed. Their derivatives can be stated without multiplying a discontinuous function by a distribution of positive order. This is the torsion identity needed before considering integration by parts with bounded weights. Proposition 8.9.7 . 26EFAEC0B76D Write $R_{p-1}^{\widehat a}$ for the shifted current obtained by omitting $u_ a$, in the inherited order, and use two hats for two omissions. Put $R_0=1$. For $1\leq p\leq m$, \[  \begin{aligned}  \mathrm dR_ p& =\mathrm d\omega \wedge \sum _{a=1}^ pR_{p-1}^{\widehat a},\\  \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}R_ p& =\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \wedge \sum _{a=1}^ pR_{p-1}^{\widehat a},\\  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R_ p& =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge \sum _{a=1}^ pR_{p-1}^{\widehat a} +2\, \mathrm d\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \wedge \sum _{a<b}R_{p-2}^{\widehat a\widehat b}. \end{aligned}  \] The last sum is absent for $p=1$. All currents on the right have order zero. If all but at most one potential are smooth, $R_ p$ is independent of the ordering and is the ordinary product of the smooth factors with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. Proof. Every $D_ I$ is both $\mathrm d$- and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$-closed. Differentiating ( 8.9.5 ) therefore gives \[  \mathrm dR_ p=\mathrm d\omega \wedge \sum _ I(p-|I|)\omega ^{p-|I|-1}\wedge D_ I,  \] with zero terms omitted. The coefficient $p-|I|$ counts the omitted indices outside $I$, which proves the first formula; the second is identical with $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$ in place of $\mathrm d$. Apply $\mathrm d$ to the second formula. Each pair of omitted indices occurs twice, and $-\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \wedge \mathrm d\omega =\mathrm d\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega $ because both forms have odd degree three. This gives the displayed $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ formula, with every background derivative retained. If all but one potential are smooth, applying $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ to the bounded potential times a smooth closed product gives its $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ wedged with that product. At later smooth steps, closedness again makes the recursion ordinary smooth multiplication. This is independent of the position of the bounded potential, and the subset expansion gives the last assertion. $\square$ Local capacity arguments naturally concern functions whose unshifted Hessian lies in the cone. On a coordinate ball $U$, call a bounded canonical function $f$ $m$-subharmonic relative to $\omega $ if \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge \gamma _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \gamma _{m-1} \wedge \omega ^{n-m}\geq 0  \] for all smooth $\gamma _ i\in \Gamma _ m(\omega )$. Equivalently, its local upper tests $q$ satisfy $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\in \overline{\Gamma _ m(\omega )}$. The same Hermitian form $\omega $ is used here and in the chapter's shifted admissibility. Lemma 8.9.8 . A1E60FC7AA88 Let $U$ be a coordinate ball compactly contained in a holomorphic chart. There is a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic $\rho $ on a neighborhood of $\overline U$ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq 2\omega $ and, for every bounded admissible $u$ on $X$, $u+\rho $ is $m$-subharmonic relative to $\omega $ on $U$. Adding $\rho $ to the approximations in 8.6.6 gives uniformly bounded smooth decreasing approximations in this local class. Proof. Take $\rho =C|z|^2$ in the chart. On the fixed compact set $\overline U$, a sufficiently large $C$ gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq 2\omega $. An upper test $q$ for $u+\rho $ at $x$ gives the upper test $q-\rho $ for $u$ there. Hence \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(q-\rho ))+(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho -\omega ) \in \overline{\Gamma _ m(\omega )},  \] since the second summand is positive and the cone is preserved by adding nonnegative forms. Smooth addition preserves the canonical representative. The same identity applies pointwise to every smooth admissible approximation. Adding a fixed smooth function preserves pointwise decrease and convergence, and its bounded norm on $\overline U$ preserves the common local bound. $\square$ The correction is a local inclusion of classes. It leaves the metric in the cone tests unchanged. Although $\tau =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ is closed, $\tau -\omega $ has derivative $-\mathrm d\omega $, so the background terms in the preceding torsion identity remain present. In particular, $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+\rho )+(\omega -\tau )$. Comparison of the unshifted Hessians of the corrected functions must therefore account for this smooth remainder. Example 8.9.9 . 5F56B4D9CC35 On the unit ball in $\mathbb C^3$, put $\beta _ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z_ j|^2$, $\beta =\sum _{j=1}^3\beta _ j$ and \[  u=-\tfrac 12\sum _{j=1}^3|z_ j|^2, \qquad v=-\tfrac 45|z_1|^2.  \] Both $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ are strictly positive, but \[  (\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^2\wedge \beta > (\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^2\wedge \beta , \qquad (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^2\wedge \beta <(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^2\wedge \beta .  \] Thus shifted Hessian order does not imply unshifted Hessian order, even for smooth potentials with positive perturbed forms. Proof. The eigenvalues of the two perturbed forms relative to $\beta $ are $(\tfrac 12,\tfrac 12,\tfrac 12)$ and $(\tfrac 15,1,1)$. For a diagonal form with relative eigenvalues $\lambda _1,\lambda _2, \lambda _3$, its second Hessian is $(\lambda _1\lambda _2+\lambda _1\lambda _3+\lambda _2\lambda _3)\beta ^3/3$. Consequently the shifted measures of $u,v$ are $\tfrac 14\beta ^3$ and $\tfrac 7{15}\beta ^3$, while their unshifted expressions are $\tfrac 14\beta ^3$ and $0$. Their unshifted traces are negative, so neither original function belongs to the local unshifted class. Adding $\sum _ j|z_ j|^2$ gives an exact correction in this constant closed background. An exact correction $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho =\omega $ is impossible where $\mathrm d\omega \ne 0$. $\square$ The iterated limit fixes the order of the potentials. Symmetry and simultaneous convergence require control of discontinuous weights against varying coefficient measures. The next section supplies the first-Hessian estimate for 8.10.5 ; the local Hessian capacities in section 8.11 give the control in the remaining degrees.

Bounded convergence gives $u_ j\to u$ in local $L^1$, and therefore $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\to \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ in distributions. The uniform coefficient bounds show that this limit has measure coefficients with the asserted bound. $\square$

title: Proposition 8.9.3
section: 8.9 Bounded potentials and recursive Hessian currents
text: Proposition 8.9.3 . EB2FA13CDDE0 For $1\leq p<m$, the recursion defines a real closed current of order zero and bidegree $(p,p)$. If $M=\max _ a\| u_ a\| _{L^\infty (X)}$, then \[  \| D_ p(u_1,\ldots ,u_ p)\| _ K \leq C_{K,U,\omega ,p}(1+M)^ p.  \] For $p=m$, it defines a real closed distributional current. For any smooth admissible sequences $u_ a^{j_ a}\downarrow u_ a$ with a common uniform bound, one has 686912AA777F 8.9.4 \begin{equation}  D_ p(u_1,\ldots ,u_ p) =\lim _{j_ p\to \infty }\cdots \lim _{j_1\to \infty } \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1^{j_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ p^{j_ p} \end{equation} in distributions. The index $j_1$ tends to infinity first. Below degree $m$, all these limits have locally uniformly bounded coefficient variations. Proof. The case $p=1$ is the preceding lemma. Suppose the assertions hold through degree $p-1<m$. Since $u_ p$ is bounded Borel and $D_{p-1}$ has measure coefficients, their product is well defined. Applying $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ gives a real current that is both $\mathrm d$- and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$-closed. For a fixed smooth complementary test form $\eta $, dominated convergence against the fixed signed measures gives \[  \begin{aligned}  \langle D_ p,\eta \rangle & =\langle u_ pD_{p-1},\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta \rangle \\ & =\lim _{j_ p\to \infty } \langle u_ p^{j_ p}D_{p-1},\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta \rangle . \end{aligned}  \] With $j_ p$ fixed, the inductive iterated limit for $D_{p-1}$ can be paired with the smooth form $u_ p^{j_ p}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta $. Integration by parts for the smooth closed factors identifies the resulting pairing with the smooth product on the right of ( 8.9.4 ). This proves that identity also when $p=m$. For $p<m$, expand the smooth product using $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ a^{j_ a}=\sigma _ a^{j_ a}-\omega $. A term with $q$ admissible factors, $0\leq q\leq p$, has the form \[  \sigma _{a_1}^{j_{a_1}}\wedge \cdots \wedge \sigma _{a_ q}^{j_{a_ q}}\wedge \omega ^{p-q}.  \] Every such $q$ is strictly less than $m$. Apply 8.2.7 to each coefficient test, and then the smooth mass estimate from 8.7.1 to the potential sum. The term $q=0$ is the fixed smooth form $\omega ^ p$. For $q\geq 1$, the sum of its admissible forms is $q(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bar u)$, where $\bar u$ is their average and $\| \bar u\| _\infty \leq M+1$. The result is a coefficient variation bound $C(1+M)^ p$, after choosing the approximations with norm at most $M+1$ as in the preceding proof. For arbitrary uniformly bounded approximations the same argument uses their common bound. The bounds survive each distributional limit, proving that $D_ p$ has order zero and the stated estimate. This completes the induction. No coefficient bound for the unwedged degree-$m$ current is used or asserted. $\square$
