title: Lemma 8.12.3
section: 8.12 Locality and maxima of bounded potentials
text: Lemma 8.12.3 . 132BB9E1B1F5 For bounded admissible $v$, $0\leq \alpha \leq 1$ and a real constant $b$, the function $v_\alpha =\alpha v+b$ is bounded admissible and \[  H_ m(v_\alpha )\geq \alpha ^ m H_ m(v)+(1-\alpha )^ m\omega ^ n.  \] Proof. Take smooth decreasing uniformly bounded admissible $v_ j\downarrow v$. Cone convexity makes $\alpha v_ j+b$ admissible because \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\alpha v_ j+b) =\alpha (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)+(1-\alpha )\omega .  \] For $\alpha >0$, an upper test $q$ for $\alpha v+b$ gives the upper test $(q-b)/\alpha $ for $v$. The same convex combination of forms therefore proves admissibility of the limit. For $\alpha =0$ the potential is constant. The pointwise decreasing limit has the displayed canonical affine values. Expand the smooth top product. Every mixed term is positive by polarized Gårding positivity. Keeping the two extreme terms gives \[  H_ m(\alpha v_ j+b)\geq \alpha ^ m H_ m(v_ j) +(1-\alpha )^ m\omega ^ n.  \] Joint decreasing convergence from 8.11.12 passes this inequality against each nonnegative continuous test to the asserted inequality of positive Radon measures. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.12.4
section: 8.12 Locality and maxima of bounded potentials
text: Lemma 8.12.4 . 3A8C156268BF Put $k=m-1$ and $\ell =n-m$. For bounded admissible $t_1,\ldots ,t_ k$, let $T=R_ k(t_1,\ldots ,t_ k)\wedge \omega ^\ell $. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T$ is a signed Radon measure. If bounded admissible $t_ i^ j\downarrow t_ i$ have a common bound, these measures converge weakly, also after multiplication by any continuous function of finitely many uniformly bounded decreasing admissible potentials. Proof. The subset definition and the torsion formulas in 8.9.7 give, in distributions, \[  \begin{aligned}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T={}& \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \wedge \left(\sum _{a=1}^ kR_{k-1}^{\widehat a}\omega ^\ell +\ell R_ k\omega ^{\ell -1}\right)\\ & +2\, \mathrm d\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \wedge \sum _{a<b}R_{k-2}^{\widehat a\widehat b}\omega ^\ell \\ & +2\ell \, \mathrm d\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \wedge \sum _{a=1}^ kR_{k-1}^{\widehat a}\omega ^{\ell -1}\\ & +\ell (\ell -1)\, \mathrm d\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega \wedge R_ k\omega ^{\ell -2}. \end{aligned}  \] The sum with two hats is absent when $k=1$, and the last term is absent when $\ell =1$. Every factor $R_ r$ has degree $r\leq k<m$, so its coefficients are signed measures. Expanding each $R_ r$ over subsets expresses the displayed measure as fixed smooth forms wedged with raw currents $D_ p$ of degrees $p\leq m-1$. 8.11.10 therefore bounds its variation locally by $C c_{m-1}^*$, uniformly under common bounds on the potentials. Joint convergence follows from 8.11.12 applied to this expansion. All the canonical weights are quasicontinuous for $c_{m-1}^*$. 8.11.11 , with $s=m-1$, thus proves the weighted assertion coefficientwise on a finite coordinate cover. A partition of unity gives it on $X$. The term involving $R_ k\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^\ell )$ retains degree $m-1$; the argument requires no coefficient estimate in degree $m$. $\square$

title: Proposition 8.12.5
section: 8.12 Locality and maxima of bounded potentials
text: Proposition 8.12.5 . BB9187C844DA Every bounded admissible potential $u$ has \[  \int _ X H_ m(u)>0.  \] No differential identities for powers of $\omega $ are required. Proof. Suppose instead that $H_ m(u)=0$. Fix $s>0$, set $c=\inf _ Xu+s$, and put $w=\max \{ u,c\} $. The upper semicontinuity of $u$ makes $U=\{ u<c\} $ open, and the definition of the infimum makes it nonempty. Moreover $0\leq w-u\leq s$ and this difference is zero outside $U$. The maximum is bounded admissible with its canonical pointwise values by 8.2.9 . For $0\leq q\leq m$, define the positive Radon measures \[  \mu _ q=Q_ m(\underbrace{u,\ldots ,u}_{q}, \underbrace{w,\ldots ,w}_{m-q}).  \] Thus $\mu _ m=H_ m(u)=0$. For $q<m$, let $T_ q$ be the sum of $m-q$ currents with $q+r$ slots equal to $u$ and $m-q-1-r$ slots equal to $w$, for $0\leq r<m-q$, each of degree $m-1$ and wedged with $\omega ^{n-m}$. In smooth notation this is \[  T_ q=\sum _{r=0}^{m-q-1} (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{q+r} (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^{m-q-1-r}\omega ^{n-m}.  \] Here each displayed product denotes the symmetric shifted current $R_{m-1}$ of ( 8.9.5 ), wedged with $\omega ^{n-m}$. Choose smooth bounded admissible $u_ j\downarrow u$ and the regularized maxima $w_ j=M_{\epsilon _ j}(u_ j,c)\downarrow w$, where $\epsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, as in 8.2.9 . Both lists have a common bound. The smooth polynomial identity and Stokes' theorem on the compact manifold give \[  \int _ X(\mu _ q^ j-\mu _ m^ j) =\int _ X(w_ j-u_ j)\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_ q^ j.  \] Joint decreasing convergence passes the left side to its limit. The preceding lemma, with $F(x,y)=y-x$ and the decreasing lists $u_ j,w_ j$, passes the right side to its limit. Hence \[  \int _ X\mu _ q=\int _ X(w-u)\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_ q.  \] The difference of the two decreasing sequences need not itself decrease; the continuous two-variable weight is essential here. On the open set $U$, the potential $w$ is constant. Locality of the raw recursion therefore sets every factor $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ to zero there, so that its shifted factors become $\omega $. The formula in the preceding lemma expresses $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_ q|_ U$ as finitely many smooth metric-derivative forms wedged with powers of $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ of degrees at most $m-1$. Use smooth admissible approximations to $u$ and the constant $c$ in these local expressions; their limits are the same restricted currents. For those smooth approximations, the absolute mixed-form estimate 8.2.7 bounds each such term by a constant times the corresponding positive trace, and therefore by $C\sum _{r=0}^{m-1}\mu _ r$ on $U$ after taking joint limits. More explicitly, a term with $r$ factors is bounded by $C(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ r\omega ^{n-r}$; this is $C\mu _ r$ on $U$. Against compactly supported nonnegative tests in $U$, weak convergence and lower semicontinuity of total variation preserve the estimate. Exhaustion gives the measure inequality \[  \mathbf1_ U|\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_ q| \leq C\sum _{r=0}^{m-1}\mathbf1_ U\mu _ r.  \] Here $C$ depends only on $\omega ,m,n$, not on $u$ or $s$; a fixed finite coordinate cover bounds all the smooth metric coefficients. Since $w-u$ vanishes outside $U$, positivity gives \[  \int _ U\mu _ q\leq \int _ X\mu _ q \leq Cs\sum _{r=0}^{m-1}\int _ U\mu _ r \qquad (0\leq q<m).  \] Summing these $m$ inequalities and choosing $s>0$ with $mCs<1$ forces $\sum _{r=0}^{m-1}\int _ U\mu _ r=0$. But locality gives $\mu _0=\omega ^ n$ on the nonempty open set $U$, whose volume is positive. This contradiction proves the result. $\square$

title: 8.13 Hessian mass and global comparison
text: The maximum inequality compares measures on complementary Borel sets. Integrating it leaves a difference of total masses. The recursive currents express this difference through the complex Hessians of the background powers, extending the mass calculation of section 11.1 to bounded admissible potentials. Their vanishing characterizes the unmodified comparison principle. When they do not vanish, a small sublevel set limits the change made by the maximum; the resulting torsion error can still be absorbed after rescaling the upper potential. For bounded admissible $t_1,\ldots ,t_ m$, put \[  \mathcal M_ m(t_1,\ldots ,t_ m)=\int _ XQ_ m(t_1,\ldots ,t_ m), \qquad H_ m(t)=Q_ m(t,\ldots ,t).  \] Here $H_ m(t)$ is a finite positive Radon measure and $\mathcal M_ m$ is the total mass of a mixed positive measure, by 8.9.6 . For a nonempty subset $I=\{ i_1<\cdots <i_ q\} \subset \{ 1,\ldots ,m\} $, put $i(I)=i_ q$ and $I^-=I\setminus \{ i_ q\} $. Use $D_{I^-}$ for the recursive current with those ordered inputs, with $D_\varnothing =1$. Lemma 8.13.1 . 69692CE9985B For every bounded admissible list, B8626F362B85 8.13.2 \begin{equation}  \mathcal M_ m(t_1,\ldots ,t_ m) =\int _ X\omega ^ n+ \sum _{\varnothing \ne I\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,m\} } \int _ X t_{i(I)}D_{I^-}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-|I|}). \end{equation} Every integral on the right is an integral of bounded canonical values against signed measure coefficients. Proof. Expand $Q_ m$ using ( 8.9.5 ). The term for $I$ pairs $D_ I$ with the smooth form $\omega ^{n-|I|}$. By ( 8.9.2 ), \[  \langle D_ I,\omega ^{n-|I|}\rangle =\langle t_{i(I)}D_{I^-},\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-|I|})\rangle .  \] Since $|I^-|\leq m-1$, 8.9.3 gives measure coefficients for $D_{I^-}$; their bounded product with $t_{i(I)}$ is well defined. Thus the displayed pairing is exactly the integral in the sum, and is finite on compact $X$. The empty subset contributes $\int _ X\omega ^ n$. $\square$ Let $\mu _ r$ be the repeated-slot mixed measure from 8.12.2 , for fixed $r$ and $z_1,\ldots ,z_{m-r}$. The total-mass difference below therefore has the explicit expression ( 8.13.2 ) for the two indicated lists. Proposition 8.13.3 . CCDE5B297235 If $u,v$ are bounded admissible and $w=\max \{ u,v\} $, then \[  \int _{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm d\mu _ r(v) \leq \int _{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm d\mu _ r(u) +\int _ X\mathrm d\mu _ r(w)-\int _ X\mathrm d\mu _ r(u).  \] Proof. Set $E=\{ u<v\} $. The contact-set version of 8.12.2 gives \[  \mu _ r(w)\geq \mathbf1_{X\setminus E}\mu _ r(u) +\mathbf1_ E\mu _ r(v).  \] All these measures are finite and positive. Integrating on $X$ and using $\mu _ r(u)(X\setminus E)=\mu _ r(u)(X)-\mu _ r(u)(E)$ gives exactly the assertion. No boundary or closed-background hypothesis enters this calculation. $\square$ The unmodified global comparison principle holds precisely when the powers occurring in this mass formula are $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed. Only the powers $n-m,\ldots ,n-1$ occur at Hessian degree $m$. Theorem 8.13.4 . 53F870DE5980 The following conditions are equivalent: $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-q})=0$ for every $1\leq q\leq m$; $\int _ XH_ m(u)$ is independent of the smooth admissible potential $u$; $\mathcal M_ m(t_1,\ldots ,t_ m)=\int _ X\omega ^ n$ for every bounded admissible list; every pair of bounded admissible $u,v$ satisfies \[  \int _{\{ u<v\} }H_ m(v)\leq \int _{\{ u<v\} }H_ m(u).  \] Under these conditions, for every $1\leq r\leq m$ and every fixed bounded admissible list $z_1,\ldots ,z_{m-r}$, one also has \[  \int _{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm d\mu _ r(v) \leq \int _{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm d\mu _ r(u).  \] Proof. The first condition implies the third by ( 8.13.2 ). The third implies the second by taking all inputs equal to a smooth potential. To prove that the second implies the first, fix any smooth real $f$. For all sufficiently small real $t$ of either sign, $\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ is positive, so $tf$ is strictly admissible. The polynomial \[  \int _ X(\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m} =\sum _{q=0}^ m\binom mq t^ q \int _ X(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^ q\wedge \omega ^{n-q}  \] is constant on an interval. Consequently every coefficient with $q\geq 1$ vanishes. Polarizing that coefficient by replacing $f$ with $\sum _{a=1}^ q s_ af_ a$ gives \[  \int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ q \wedge \omega ^{n-q}=0  \] for all smooth real $f_ a$. Integration by parts in the first factor, using lemma 11.1.2 , gives \[  \int _ Xf_1\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ q \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-q})=0.  \] Since $f_1$ is arbitrary, the smooth top-degree form paired with it vanishes pointwise. At each point the other complex Hessians can be prescribed by real quadratic functions times a cutoff. Complexifying this multilinear identity gives all coordinate $(q-1,q-1)$-forms, as in the proof of theorem 11.1.7 . They detect every coefficient of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-q})$, so that form vanishes. When $q=1$, there are no other Hessians and the same conclusion follows directly from the arbitrariness of $f_1$. Under the third condition, $\mu _ r(w)$ and $\mu _ r(u)$ have the same total mass. 8.13.3 proves the mixed comparison assertion, and $r=m$ gives the fourth condition. Finally, suppose the fourth condition holds and fix smooth admissible $u,v$. Choose $C$ so large that $u<v+C$ everywhere. Constant invariance gives $H_ m(v+C)=H_ m(v)$, so comparison gives $\int _ XH_ m(v)\leq \int _ XH_ m(u)$. Exchanging $u,v$ gives equality, which is the second condition. $\square$ The same varying background that obstructs Monge–Ampère comparison also obstructs comparison at each intermediate Hessian degree. Example 8.13.5 . 0DB9D80DE230 Let $X=(\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z))^ n$, with $z_ j=x_ j+\mathrm i y_ j$, and put \[  \beta _ j=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\, \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j, \qquad b=2+\cos (2\pi x_1), \qquad \omega =\beta _1+b\beta _2+\sum _{j=3}^ n\beta _ j.  \] For $|t|<\pi ^{-2}$ the potential $u_ t=t\cos (2\pi x_1)$ is smooth strictly admissible, and, with $B_ n=\int _ X\beta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \beta _ n$, \[  \int _ X H_ m(u_ t)=n!\left(2-\frac{m\pi ^2t}{2n}\right)B_ n.  \] Thus every $-\pi ^{-2}<t<0$, together with a constant $C>|t|$, gives a pair $u=0$, $v=u_ t+C$ that violates the unmodified global comparison inequality. Proof. As in example 11.1.12 , $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t=-\pi ^2t\cos (2\pi x_1)\beta _1$. The coefficient of $\beta _1$ in $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t$ is strictly positive in the stated range, and all the other coefficients are positive. Since $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t)^2=0$, expansion gives \[  H_ m(u_ t)=\omega ^ n+m\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t\wedge \omega ^{n-1} =n!b\left(1-\frac mn\pi ^2t\cos (2\pi x_1)\right) \beta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \beta _ n.  \] The period averages of $b$ and $b\cos (2\pi x_1)$ are respectively $2$ and $1/2$, proving the mass formula. For $t<0$ this mass is strictly larger than $\int _ XH_ m(0)=2n!B_ n$. Meanwhile $C>|t|$ gives $\{ 0<u_ t+C\} =X$, so the comparison inequality for this pair would assert the opposite ordering of these masses. $\square$

title: Proposition 8.13.3
text: Proposition 8.13.3 . CCDE5B297235 If $u,v$ are bounded admissible and $w=\max \{ u,v\} $, then \[  \int _{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm d\mu _ r(v) \leq \int _{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm d\mu _ r(u) +\int _ X\mathrm d\mu _ r(w)-\int _ X\mathrm d\mu _ r(u).  \] Proof. title: Theorem 8.13.4
text: Theorem 8.13.4 . 53F870DE5980 The following conditions are equivalent: $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-q})=0$ for every $1\leq q\leq m$; $\int _ XH_ m(u)$ is independent of the smooth admissible potential $u$; $\mathcal M_ m(t_1,\ldots ,t_ m)=\int _ X\omega ^ n$ for every bounded admissible list; every pair of bounded admissible $u,v$ satisfies \[  \int _{\{ u<v\} }H_ m(v)\leq \int _{\{ u<v\} }H_ m(u).  \] Under these conditions, for every $1\leq r\leq m$ and every fixed bounded admissible list $z_1,\ldots ,z_{m-r}$, one also has \[  \int _{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm d\mu _ r(v) \leq \int _{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm d\mu _ r(u).  \] Proof. The first condition implies the third by ( 8.13.2 ). The third implies the second by taking all inputs equal to a smooth potential. To prove that the second implies the first, fix any smooth real $f$. For all sufficiently small real $t$ of either sign, $\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ is positive, so $tf$ is strictly admissible. The polynomial \[  \int _ X(\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^ m\wedge \omega ^{n-m} =\sum _{q=0}^ m\binom mq t^ q \int _ X(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^ q\wedge \omega ^{n-q}  \] is constant on an interval. Consequently every coefficient with $q\geq 1$ vanishes. Polarizing that coefficient by replacing $f$ with $\sum _{a=1}^ q s_ af_ a$ gives \[  \int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ q \wedge \omega ^{n-q}=0  \] for all smooth real $f_ a$. Integration by parts in the first factor, using lemma 11.1.2 , gives \[  \int _ Xf_1\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ q \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-q})=0.  \] Since $f_1$ is arbitrary, the smooth top-degree form paired with it vanishes pointwise. At each point the other complex Hessians can be prescribed by real quadratic functions times a cutoff. Complexifying this multilinear identity gives all coordinate $(q-1,q-1)$-forms, as in the proof of theorem 11.1.7 . They detect every coefficient of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-q})$, so that form vanishes. When $q=1$, there are no other Hessians and the same conclusion follows directly from the arbitrariness of $f_1$. Under the third condition, $\mu _ r(w)$ and $\mu _ r(u)$ have the same total mass. 8.13.3 proves the mixed comparison assertion, and $r=m$ gives the fourth condition. Finally, suppose the fourth condition holds and fix smooth admissible $u,v$. Choose $C$ so large that $u<v+C$ everywhere. Constant invariance gives $H_ m(v+C)=H_ m(v)$, so comparison gives $\int _ XH_ m(v)\leq \int _ XH_ m(u)$. Exchanging $u,v$ gives equality, which is the second condition. $\square$

title: 8.13.6 Modified comparison
text: On a sublevel set just above the infimum of a difference, the maximum changes the lower potential by at most a prescribed small number. Integration by parts then expresses the mass defect through this small difference and a torsion measure. Mixed lower-degree traces control its variation. Rescaling the upper potential adds a positive background term that relates these traces to the top Hessian measure. For bounded admissible $u,V$, use the notation \[  \sigma _ u=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u,\qquad M_{p,q}=\sigma _ u^ p\sigma _ V^ q\omega ^{n-p-q} \quad (0\leq p+q\leq m).  \] These expressions denote the positive mixed measure $Q_ m$ with $p$ slots equal to $u$, $q$ slots equal to $V$ and the remaining slots equal to the constant zero. In particular $M_{0,0}=\omega ^ n$.  For $p+q\leq m-1$, put \[  T_{p,q}=\sigma _ u^ p\sigma _ V^ q\omega ^{n-p-q-1}.  \] This denotes $R_{m-1}$ with the same nonconstant slots and zero in its other slots, wedged with $\omega ^{n-m}$. Lemma 8.13.7 . 0F8C3F6B0122 Let $u,V$ be bounded admissible, $b$ a real constant and $s>0$. Suppose $0\leq \max \{ u,V+b\} -u\leq s$. Set $E=\{ u<V+b\} $ and $b_{p,q}=M_{p,q}(E)$. There is a constant $C$, depending only on $X,\omega ,m,n$, such that \[  b_{p,q+1}\leq b_{p+1,q} +Cs\sum _{a+d\leq p+q}b_{a,d} \qquad (p+q\leq m-1).  \] For $q=0$, the error can instead be bounded by $Cs(b_{p,0}+b_{p-1,0}+b_{p-2,0})$, with negative indices zero. Proof. First estimate the torsion of $T_{p,q}$, writing $r=p+q$. For smooth admissible potentials, the product rule expresses $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_{p,q}$ as a sum of fixed smooth metric forms wedged with products of $\sigma _ u,\sigma _ V$ of degrees $r,r-1,r-2$. The terms of degree $r$ come from differentiating the background power; they cannot be discarded. Indeed, $\mathrm d\sigma _ u=\mathrm d\sigma _ V=\mathrm d\omega $, $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\sigma _ u=\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\sigma _ V=\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega $ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\sigma _ u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\sigma _ V=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $. Every term therefore contains either $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ or $\mathrm d\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega $, with its product-rule multiplicity and the appropriate remaining background power. Terms with negative numbers of factors are absent. All variable degrees are at most $r<m$. Apply 8.2.7 to each term. Expanding the resulting positive power of the sum of its variable factors gives the pointwise bound \[  |\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_{p,q}|\leq C\sum _{a+d\leq r}M_{a,d}.  \] For $q=0$ every variable factor is $\sigma _ u$, so the sharper bound is $C(M_{p,0}+M_{p-1,0}+M_{p-2,0})$. The constant bounds fixed metric coefficients on a finite coordinate cover and the finitely many multiplicities; it is independent of the potentials and their bounds. Choose uniformly bounded smooth decreasing approximations to $u,V$. By 8.12.4 , the torsion measures converge weakly; by 8.11.12 , all positive measures in these bounds also converge weakly. Against nonnegative continuous tests, lower semicontinuity of total variation preserves both bounds. They are consequently inequalities of measures and may be restricted to the Borel set $E$. Put $w=\max \{ u,V+b\} $ and $h=w-u$. The mixed maximum theorem 8.12.2 , with one moving slot and the fixed slots defining $T_{p,q}$, gives \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)T_{p,q} \geq \mathbf1_ E\sigma _ VT_{p,q} +\mathbf1_{X\setminus E}\sigma _ uT_{p,q}.  \] All products here are the corresponding positive mixed measures. After integration, this implies \[  b_{p,q+1}\leq b_{p+1,q} +\int _ X\bigl ((\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)-\sigma _ u\bigr )T_{p,q}.  \] Regularized maxima of the smooth decreasing approximations give a uniformly bounded decreasing smooth list $w_ j\downarrow w$. Stokes' theorem on compact $X$ gives for these lists \[  \int _ X\bigl ((\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)-\sigma _{u_ j}\bigr )T_{p,q}^ j =\int _ X(w_ j-u_ j)\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_{p,q}^ j.  \] Joint decreasing convergence passes the positive mixed measures on the left to their limits. The continuous two-variable weight $F(x,y)=y-x$ in 8.12.4 passes the right side to $\int _ Xh\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_{p,q}$. No monotonicity of $w_ j-u_ j$ is needed. Since $h$ is zero outside $E$ and $0\leq h\leq s$, \[  \int _ Xh\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_{p,q}\leq s|\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_{p,q}|(E).  \] The torsion bounds prove both assertions. The argument never passes a varying measure to a weak limit after restriction to $E$. $\square$ Theorem 8.13.8 . B83D4B8CE619 There is $C\geq 1$, depending only on $X,\omega ,m,n$, with the following property. For bounded admissible $u,v$ and $0<\alpha <1$, put $\eta =1-\alpha $, $V=\alpha v$ and $S=\inf _ X(u-V)$. For $0<s<\eta ^3/C$, let $E_ s=\{ u<V+S+s\} $. Then \[  \int _{E_ s}H_ m(V) \leq \left(1+\frac{Cs}{\eta ^ m}\right) \int _{E_ s}H_ m(u).  \] No differential identity for a power of $\omega $ is assumed. Proof. Use the mixed measures above on $E_ s$, writing $b_{p,q}=M_{p,q}(E_ s)$ and $a_ k=b_{k,0}$. The definition of $S$ gives $0\leq \max \{ u,V+S+s\} -u\leq s$, so 8.13.7 applies. Repeatedly moving a $V$ slot to a $u$ slot gives, for $p+q=r$, \[  b_{p,q}\leq a_ r+C_1s\sum _{d=0}^{r-1}A_ d, \qquad A_ d=\max _{a+b=d}b_{a,b},\qquad 1\leq r\leq m.  \] Here there are at most $m$ moves, and the multiplicity $d+1$ in the lower-degree sum is absorbed in $C_1$. For $0<s\leq 1$, induction on $r$ shows \[  A_ r\leq a_ r+K_ rs\sum _{k<r}a_ k.  \] In fact $A_0=a_0$, and one may take $K_ r=C_1(1+\sum _{1\leq d<r}K_ d)$: insert the earlier bounds in the displayed recurrence and use $s^2\leq s$. Thus, for a constant $C_2$ depending only on the setting, \[  b_{0,m}\leq a_ m+C_2s\sum _{k<m}a_ k.  \] It remains to control the lower diagonal masses by $a_ m$. The identity $\sigma _ V=\alpha \sigma _ v+\eta \omega $ and mixed positivity give $b_{k,1}\geq \eta a_ k$; this identity and inequality pass from smooth approximations by joint convergence. The diagonal assertion of 8.13.7 gives \[  \eta a_ k\leq a_{k+1} +C_3s(a_ k+a_{k-1}+a_{k-2})\qquad (0\leq k<m),  \] with $a_{-1}=a_{-2}=0$. Set $B_ k=\eta ^{m-k}a_ k$ for $0\leq k\leq m$, and set $B_{-1}=B_{-2}=0$. Multiplying by $\eta ^{m-k-1}$ and using $0<\eta <1$ gives \[  B_ k\leq B_{k+1} +\delta (B_ k+B_{k-1}+B_{k-2}), \qquad \delta =C_3s\eta ^{-3}.  \] For $M=\max _{0\leq k<m}B_ k$, summing from any $j<m$ through $m-1$ gives $B_ j\leq B_ m+3m\delta M$. If $s<\eta ^3/(6mC_3)$, it follows that $M\leq 2B_ m$. Consequently \[  a_ k\leq 2\eta ^{-(m-k)}a_ m\quad (k<m),\qquad \sum _{k<m}a_ k\leq 2m\eta ^{-m}a_ m.  \] Choose $C\geq \max \{ 1,6mC_3,2mC_2\} $. Then the asserted range for $s$ supplies every preceding restriction, and substitution in the bound for $b_{0,m}$ proves the theorem. No division by $a_ m$ occurs, so zero top mass on $E_ s$ is included. $\square$

title: Lemma 8.13.7
text: Lemma 8.13.7 . 0F8C3F6B0122 Let $u,V$ be bounded admissible, $b$ a real constant and $s>0$. Suppose $0\leq \max \{ u,V+b\} -u\leq s$. Set $E=\{ u<V+b\} $ and $b_{p,q}=M_{p,q}(E)$. There is a constant $C$, depending only on $X,\omega ,m,n$, such that \[  b_{p,q+1}\leq b_{p+1,q} +Cs\sum _{a+d\leq p+q}b_{a,d} \qquad (p+q\leq m-1).  \] For $q=0$, the error can instead be bounded by $Cs(b_{p,0}+b_{p-1,0}+b_{p-2,0})$, with negative indices zero. Proof. First estimate the torsion of $T_{p,q}$, writing $r=p+q$. For smooth admissible potentials, the product rule expresses $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_{p,q}$ as a sum of fixed smooth metric forms wedged with products of $\sigma _ u,\sigma _ V$ of degrees $r,r-1,r-2$. The terms of degree $r$ come from differentiating the background power; they cannot be discarded. Indeed, $\mathrm d\sigma _ u=\mathrm d\sigma _ V=\mathrm d\omega $, $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\sigma _ u=\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\sigma _ V=\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega $ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\sigma _ u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\sigma _ V=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $. Every term therefore contains either $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ or $\mathrm d\omega \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega $, with its product-rule multiplicity and the appropriate remaining background power. Terms with negative numbers of factors are absent. All variable degrees are at most $r<m$. Apply 8.2.7 to each term. Expanding the resulting positive power of the sum of its variable factors gives the pointwise bound \[  |\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_{p,q}|\leq C\sum _{a+d\leq r}M_{a,d}.  \] For $q=0$ every variable factor is $\sigma _ u$, so the sharper bound is $C(M_{p,0}+M_{p-1,0}+M_{p-2,0})$. The constant bounds fixed metric coefficients on a finite coordinate cover and the finitely many multiplicities; it is independent of the potentials and their bounds. Choose uniformly bounded smooth decreasing approximations to $u,V$. By 8.12.4 , the torsion measures converge weakly; by 8.11.12 , all positive measures in these bounds also converge weakly. Against nonnegative continuous tests, lower semicontinuity of total variation preserves both bounds. They are consequently inequalities of measures and may be restricted to the Borel set $E$. Put $w=\max \{ u,V+b\} $ and $h=w-u$. The mixed maximum theorem 8.12.2 , with one moving slot and the fixed slots defining $T_{p,q}$, gives \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)T_{p,q} \geq \mathbf1_ E\sigma _ VT_{p,q} +\mathbf1_{X\setminus E}\sigma _ uT_{p,q}.  \] All products here are the corresponding positive mixed measures. After integration, this implies \[  b_{p,q+1}\leq b_{p+1,q} +\int _ X\bigl ((\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)-\sigma _ u\bigr )T_{p,q}.  \] Regularized maxima of the smooth decreasing approximations give a uniformly bounded decreasing smooth list $w_ j\downarrow w$. Stokes' theorem on compact $X$ gives for these lists \[  \int _ X\bigl ((\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)-\sigma _{u_ j}\bigr )T_{p,q}^ j =\int _ X(w_ j-u_ j)\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_{p,q}^ j.  \] Joint decreasing convergence passes the positive mixed measures on the left to their limits. The continuous two-variable weight $F(x,y)=y-x$ in 8.12.4 passes the right side to $\int _ Xh\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_{p,q}$. No monotonicity of $w_ j-u_ j$ is needed. Since $h$ is zero outside $E$ and $0\leq h\leq s$, \[  \int _ Xh\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_{p,q}\leq s|\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_{p,q}|(E).  \] The torsion bounds prove both assertions. The argument never passes a varying measure to a weak limit after restriction to $E$. $\square$

title: 8.13.9 Domination and proper equations
text:
The weak modified comparison estimate makes strict domination possible on an arbitrary Hermitian background. A convex rescaling supplies a positive volume term, while choosing a sufficiently small sublevel set absorbs the torsion error. Canonical representatives detect its positive volume even when the set is not open. Theorem 8.13.10 . A532C77D7D0C Let $u,v$ be bounded admissible. If, for some $0\leq c<1$, \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }H_ m(u) \leq c\mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }H_ m(v),  \] then $u\geq v$ everywhere, on an arbitrary Hermitian background. In particular, $H_ m(u)(\{ u<v\} )=0$ implies $u\geq v$. Proof. Add the same constant to $u,v$ so that $v\geq 1$. This preserves the measure hypothesis and the desired conclusion. Choose $0<\alpha <1$ with $\alpha ^ m>c$ and put $V=\alpha v$, $\eta =1-\alpha $. Suppose $S=\inf _ X(u-V)<0$. For $0<s<-S$, the set $E_ s=\{ u<V+S+s\} $ is contained in $\{ u<V\} $ and hence in $\{ u<v\} $. It has positive volume. Indeed, if its volume were zero, then $u\geq V+S+s$ almost everywhere. Both functions are bounded admissible with their canonical representatives, so 8.2.10 would give this order everywhere, contradicting the definition of $S$. The argument does not require $E_ s$ to be open or the infimum to be attained. Choose also $s<\eta ^3/C$, where $C$ is from 8.13.8 . By 8.12.3 and the measure hypothesis, \[   egin{aligned}  \alpha ^ m H_ m(v)(E_ s)+\eta ^ m\int _{E_ s}\omega ^ n & \leq H_ m(V)(E_ s)\ & \leq (1+Cs\eta ^{-m})H_ m(u)(E_ s)\ & \leq c(1+Cs\eta ^{-m})H_ m(v)(E_ s). \end{aligned}  \] If $c>0$, take $s$ still smaller so that $c(1+Cs\eta ^{-m})<\alpha ^ m$. If $c=0$, this strict inequality already holds. All measures are finite and positive, so the display forces the positive-volume term to be zero, a contradiction. Hence $S\geq 0$ and $u\geq \alpha v$. Let $\alpha $ increase to one, with $\alpha ^ m>c$. Since $v$ is bounded, $\alpha v	o v$ uniformly, and therefore $u\geq v$. The final assertion is $c=0$. $\square$ Corollary 8.13.11 . 6BFB2EB67A74 Fix $a>0$. If bounded admissible $u,v$ satisfy \[  e^{-av}H_ m(v)\geq e^{-au}H_ m(u),  \] then $u\geq v$. Consequently, for any fixed finite positive Radon measure $
u $, the equation $H_ m(u)=e^{au}
u $ has at most one bounded admissible solution. Proof. For $\delta >0$, put $E_\delta =\{ u<v-\delta \} $. Multiplying the assumed measure inequality by the positive bounded Borel function $e^{au}$ gives on $E_\delta $ \[  H_ m(u)\leq e^{a(u-v)}H_ m(v) \leq e^{-a\delta }H_ m(v-\delta ).  \] The last identity uses invariance under constants. Since $e^{-a\delta }<1$, 8.13.10 applied to $u,v-\delta $ gives $u\geq v-\delta $ everywhere. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ gives $u\geq v$. Two solutions of the stated equation have equal weighted measures $e^{-au}H_ m(u)=
u $. Applying the order assertion in both directions proves uniqueness. $\square$ A strictly increasing exponent also controls changes in logarithmic data for a fixed Radon right-hand measure. Proposition 8.13.12 . FBE7E9A6BE5E Let $A<B$ and $f$ be smooth near $X	imes [A,B]$, with $\partial _ t f\geq \kappa >0$ there, and let $
u $ be a finite positive Radon measure. Suppose bounded admissible $u,v$ have values in $[A,B]$ and satisfy \[  H_ m(u)=e^{f(x,u)+h_1}
u ,\qquad H_ m(v)=e^{f(x,v)+h_2}
u ,  \] where $h_1,h_2$ are bounded Borel functions. Then \[  \| u-v\| _\infty \leq \kappa ^{-1}\| h_1-h_2\| _{L^\infty (
u )}.  \] Proof. Put $K=\| h_1-h_2\| _{L^\infty (
u )}$ and fix $s>K/\kappa $. On $E_ s=\{ v+s<u\} $, the actual values $u,v$ lie in $[A,B]$, so $f(x,u)-f(x,v)\geq \kappa s$. The equations and the essential bound on $h_2-h_1$ therefore give, as restricted measures, \[  \mathbf1_{E_ s}H_ m(v+s) =\mathbf1_{E_ s}H_ m(v) \leq e^{K-\kappa s}\mathbf1_{E_ s}H_ m(u).  \] The constant is smaller than one. Applying 8.13.10 to $v+s,u$ gives $u\leq v+s$ pointwise. Let $s\downarrow K/\kappa $ and exchange $u,v$ to obtain the norm bound. The exponent is evaluated only at $u,v$; the shifted comparison potential need not take its values in $[A,B]$. $\square$ Corollary 8.13.13 . 5460C4009B01 Under the hypotheses of 8.8.3 , every bounded admissible solution with values in $[A,B]$ is its smooth solution. In particular, for every $a>0$ and smooth real $H$, the equation $H_ m(u)=e^{au+H}\omega ^ n$ has exactly one bounded admissible solution, and that solution is smooth and strictly admissible. Proof. For a continuous admissible potential, smooth decreasing admissible approximations converge uniformly on compact $X$ by Dini's theorem. Thus 8.11.12 , 8.7.1 define the same Hessian measure on the continuous class. The smooth solution of 8.8.3 therefore solves the bounded equation as well. Apply 8.13.12 with $
u =\omega ^ n$ and $h_1=h_2=0$ to identify any other bounded solution in $[A,B]$ with it. For the final assertion, smooth existence is already 8.6.1 , and 8.13.11 with $
u =e^ H\omega ^ n$ gives uniqueness among all bounded solutions. $\square$

title: 16.28 Envelopes and volumes of singularities
text: Throughout this chapter, $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, with an auxiliary Hermitian metric $\omega $ and a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V$, and $\theta $ denotes a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$ whose positivity is specified in each section. In a closed background, the non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère mass of a potential depends only on its singularity type; this is what makes mass a tool for comparing singularities. In a nonclosed background, a bounded change of the potential can change the mass, and a singularity type may contain potentials of different, even infinite, masses. This chapter opens the part of the book on relative singularities and the equations they govern, and introduces two kinds of invariants that take this into account. The first records the variation of mass: the lower and upper volumes $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$ and $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$ of a potential $u$ are the infimum and the supremum of the masses of all potentials of the same singularity type. The second replaces a mass condition by a condition on envelopes. Fix a reference potential $\varphi $. Stretching a potential $u$ away from $\varphi $ by a factor $b\geq 1$ gives the obstacle $bu-(b-1)\varphi $, which is more singular than $u$ where $u$ lies below $\varphi $. The relative envelope class $\mathcal E_\varphi $ consists of the potentials $u$ at least as singular as $\varphi $ for which every such stretched obstacle lies above some $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function. This class is convex and stable under finite rooftops, its members have the same singularity envelope as $\varphi $, and its definition involves no mass. The main tool is the contact property of envelopes: the Monge–Ampère measure of an envelope is carried by the set where it touches its obstacle. Together with ordered contact, it gives the domination principle for bounded potentials in a semipositive background and bounds the measures of rooftop envelopes. For envelopes of logarithmic growth on $\mathbb C^ n$, which correspond to envelopes on $\mathbb P^ n$, we also examine how the contact of the regularized envelope with its obstacle depends on the growth allowance. In a semipositive big background, the contact property also produces positive mass. Let $\varphi $ be a model reference, that is, a fixed point of the singularity envelope that admits a competitor in a smaller background. Every member $u$ of $\mathcal E_\varphi $ then has a competitor in a background $a\theta $ with $0<a<1$, and an envelope in the remaining big background $(1-a)\theta $ has positive mass, which it transfers to $u$ on the contact set. The argument uses only that each bounded potential has positive mass, so it applies even when the infimum of these masses is zero. Conversely, if the Hermitian metric $\omega $ does not have the bounded mass property of definition 13.14.14 , the relative envelope class of the zero potential contains potentials of infinite mass. Envelope conditions and mass bounds are therefore different requirements, and this distinction is essential for the equations with prescribed singularities in the next chapter. We use the following notation from section 5.21 . For quasi-plurisubharmonic functions $u,v$, we write $u\preceq v$ if $u\leq v+C$ for a constant $C$, and $u\sim v$ if $u\preceq v$ and $v\preceq u$; the equivalence class of $u$ is its singularity type (definition 16.7.1 ). For an obstacle $f$, the envelope $P_\theta (f)$ is the upper semicontinuous regularization of the supremum of all $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $v\leq f$ quasi-everywhere; it may be identically $-\infty $, and then it does not belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. For $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, the rooftop envelope is $P_\theta (u,v)=P_\theta (\min (u,v))$, and $V_\theta =P_\theta (0)$ is the potential with minimal singularities; see section 5.40 . The singularity envelope $P_\theta [u]$, its variant $P_{\theta ,F}[u]$ with a smooth obstacle $F$, and envelope fixed points, that is, potentials with $P_\theta [u]=u$, are defined in definition 5.40.4 . We write $\theta _ u=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and $\omega _ u=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$ denotes the extended Monge–Ampère measure $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ of theorem 13.14.3 . It is the Bedford–Taylor measure $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ when $u$ is bounded, it puts no mass on pluripolar sets, and its total mass, the extended mass of $u$, may be infinite.

title: 16.28.1 Contact sets
text: The Monge–Ampère measure of an envelope is concentrated on the contact set, where the envelope meets its obstacle. For a smooth obstacle and a Hermitian background, the envelope is the uniform limit of solutions of exponential equations whose densities tend to zero wherever the envelope stays strictly below the obstacle. Continuity of bounded products then carries this property to quasi-continuous obstacles, first bounded ones, through monotone approximation, and then general ones, through truncation. Proposition 16.28.2 . 295F6C861B41 Let $f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$. For $\beta >0$, denote by $u_\beta $ the smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic solution of \[  \omega _{u_\beta }^ n=\mathrm{e}^{\beta (u_\beta -f)}\omega ^ n.  \] As $\beta \to +\infty $, these solutions converge uniformly to $p=P_\omega (f)$. Moreover, \[  \mathbf1_{\{ p<f\} }\omega _ p^ n=0.  \] Proof. The solutions exist by theorem 14.7.2 . Choose $A\geq 0$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\leq A\omega $. At a maximum point of $u_\beta -f$, the second derivative test gives \[  \omega _{u_\beta }\leq \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\leq (1+A)\omega .  \] Evaluating the equation at this point, we obtain \[  u_\beta \leq f+\frac{C_ f}{\beta },\qquad C_ f=n\log (1+A).  \] Thus $u_\beta -C_ f/\beta $ is a competitor for $P_\omega (f)$, and $u_\beta \leq p+C_ f/\beta $. For the lower bound, note that $p$ is continuous by proposition 5.40.3 , and choose smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $v_ j\downarrow p$ by theorem 5.32.1 ; by Dini's theorem the convergence is uniform. For any $\delta >0$, choose $j$ so that \[  p\leq v_ j\leq p+\delta /2.  \] Then $v_ j-\delta \leq f$, since $p\leq f$. Since $\omega _{v_ j}>0$ and $X$ is compact, there is $c_ j>0$ such that $\omega _{v_ j}^ n\geq c_ j\omega ^ n$. Put $C_ j=\max (0,-\log c_ j)$. The function \[  w_{j,\beta }=v_ j-\delta -C_ j/\beta  \] satisfies \[  \omega _{w_{j,\beta }}^ n=\omega _{v_ j}^ n \geq \mathrm{e}^{-C_ j}\omega ^ n \geq \mathrm{e}^{\beta (w_{j,\beta }-f)}\omega ^ n.  \] Exponential comparison, corollary 14.19.12 with $\lambda =\beta $, gives $w_{j,\beta }\leq u_\beta $. Consequently \[  p-\delta -C_ j/\beta \leq u_\beta \leq p+C_ f/\beta .  \] Letting first $\beta \to \infty $ with $j$ fixed, so that no lower bound for $c_ j$ uniform in $j$ is needed, and then $\delta \downarrow 0$, we obtain uniform convergence. Bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity then gives weak convergence of the measures. On a compact subset of the open set $\{ p<f\} $, uniform convergence gives $u_\beta -f\leq -\epsilon $ for some $\epsilon >0$ and all large $\beta $. There the measures $\omega _{u_\beta }^ n$ have densities at most $\mathrm{e}^{-\beta \epsilon }$ with respect to $\omega ^ n$. Testing against continuous functions with compact support in $\{ p<f\} $ and passing to the limit gives $\omega _ p^ n=0$ on this open set. $\square$ Proposition 16.28.3 . 181D96E0C805 If $f$ is bounded and lower semicontinuous, then $P_\omega (f)$ is bounded, lies below $f$ quasi-everywhere, and its Monge–Ampère measure is concentrated on $\{ P_\omega (f)=f\} $. Proof. Suppose first that $f$ is continuous. Choose smooth functions $f_ j\to f$ uniformly. The Lipschitz bound for envelopes in proposition 5.40.3 gives $p_ j=P_\omega (f_ j)\to p=P_\omega (f)$ uniformly. Every compact subset of the open set $\{ p<f\} $ has a neighborhood on which $p_ j<f_ j$ for all large $j$. The preceding proposition and convergence of bounded products then give $\omega _ p^ n=0$ on $\{ p<f\} $. For lower semicontinuous $f$, choose continuous functions $f_ j\uparrow f$ with common upper and lower bounds. For example, for a fixed distance $d$ inducing the topology of $X$, one may take \[  f_ j(x)=\inf _{y\in X}\bigl (f(y)+j d(x,y)\bigr ).  \] These functions are Lipschitz and increase to $f$: if convergence failed at $x$, approximate minimizers $y$ would approach $x$, contradicting lower semicontinuity of $f$ at $x$. The functions $p_ j=P_\omega (f_ j)$ increase and stay bounded, so the regularized limit $p_\infty =(\lim _ jp_ j)^*$ is a bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function. It agrees with $\lim _ jp_ j$ outside a pluripolar set, and since each $p_ j$ lies below $f_ j\leq f$ outside a pluripolar set, we obtain $p_\infty \leq f$ quasi-everywhere. Thus $p_\infty \leq P_\omega (f)$. For fixed $k$, the set $\{ p_\infty <f_ k\} $ is open, since $p_\infty $ is upper semicontinuous and $f_ k$ is continuous. If $j\geq k$, then $p_ j\leq p_\infty <f_ k\leq f_ j$ there, so the continuous case gives $\omega _{p_ j}^ n=0$ on that open set. Bedford–Taylor continuity along increasing sequences applies after adding a fixed smooth local function whose Hessian dominates $\omega $ and expanding with respect to the resulting smooth form. Together with the lower semicontinuity of the mass of open sets under weak convergence, it yields \[  \omega _{p_\infty }^ n(\{ p_\infty <f_ k\} )=0.  \] Taking the union over $k$ gives zero measure on $\{ p_\infty <f\} $, hence also on $\{ p_\infty <P_\omega (f)\} $ outside a pluripolar set, since $P_\omega (f)\leq f$ quasi-everywhere. Bounded measures of this kind do not charge pluripolar sets, so the domination principle, theorem 14.19.10 , gives $p_\infty \geq P_\omega (f)$. The two functions are therefore equal, and the assertion follows. $\square$ Theorem 16.28.4 . 45D3A8D823A8 Let $\theta \geq 0$ be smooth and let $f$ be bounded and quasi-continuous. Then $p=P_\theta (f)$ is bounded, $p\leq f$ quasi-everywhere, and \[  \mathbf1_{\{ p<f\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)=0.  \] Proof. First suppose that $\theta =\omega $ is Hermitian. Choose bounded lower semicontinuous functions $f_ j\downarrow f$ quasi-everywhere, with common bounds, as in lemma 5.29.15 . The bounded functions $p_ j=P_\omega (f_ j)$ decrease to $p$. Indeed, their limit is a competitor for $p$, since it lies below $f$ quasi-everywhere, and the reverse inequality follows from monotonicity. For fixed $k$, put $H_ k=\min \{ 1,(f-p_ k)_+\} $, a bounded quasi-continuous function. Where $H_ k>0$ and $j\geq k$, we have $p_ j\leq p_ k<f\leq f_ j$ outside a pluripolar set. The lower semicontinuous case therefore gives \[  \int _ X H_ k\, \omega _{p_ j}^ n=0.  \] The convergence of bounded products against quasi-continuous weights in section 5.29 gives $\int _ XH_ k\, \omega _ p^ n=0$. Since the sets $\{ p_ k<f\} $ increase to $\{ p<f\} $, this proves the assertion for Hermitian $\theta $. For general semipositive $\theta $, set $\theta _ j=\theta +j^{-1}\omega $. The functions $p_ j=P_{\theta _ j}(f)$ have the common bounds $\inf _ Xf\leq p_ j\leq \sup _ Xf$ and decrease. Their limit is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic by distributional convergence and lies below $f$ quasi-everywhere, so it is at most $p=P_\theta (f)$; since $p\leq p_ j$ for all $j$, it equals $p$. For each fixed $k$, the same coefficient $H_ k=\min \{ 1,(f-p_ k)_+\} $ gives \[  \int _ XH_ k\, \mathrm{MA}_{\theta _ j}(p_ j)=0\qquad (j\geq k).  \] All $p_ j$ are bounded potentials for the fixed Hermitian form $\theta +\omega $. Expanding the products with background $\theta _ j$ with respect to this fixed background, we may use convergence of bounded products and uniform capacity bounds to pass the last identity to the limit, with the quasi-continuous weight $H_ k$; this gives $\int _ XH_ k\, \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)=0$. Exhausting $\{ p<f\} $ as before completes the proof. $\square$ Theorem 16.28.5 . 69A5902CF8C5 Let $\theta $ be smooth and semipositive, and let $f$ be a quasi-continuous obstacle. If $p=P_\theta (f)$ is not identically $-\infty $, then $p\leq f$ quasi-everywhere and \[  \mathbf1_{\{ p<f\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)=0.  \] Here the total extended mass of $p$ may be infinite. Proof. The local envelope theorem, applied to a countable family realizing the supremum (Choquet's lemma), gives $p\leq f$ outside a pluripolar set. Choose $M>\sup _ Xp$ and replace $f$ by $\min (f,M)$. This does not change the envelope, since $p$ itself is a competitor for the smaller obstacle. Since $p<M$, the contact set is also unchanged, so it suffices to prove the theorem for the smaller obstacle; that is, we may assume that $f$ is bounded above. Set $f_ j=\max (f,-j)$ and $p_ j=P_\theta (f_ j)$. The constants $-j$ are competitors, so $p_ j$ is bounded. Theorem 16.28.4 gives $p_ j\leq f_ j$ quasi-everywhere and \[  \mathbf1_{\{ p_ j<f_ j\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p_ j)=0.  \] The sequence $p_ j$ decreases and stays above $p$. Its limit is therefore $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, it lies below $f$ quasi-everywhere, and so it is a competitor for $p$. Hence $p_ j\downarrow p$. Fix an integer $k\geq 1$ and $C>0$, and define the bounded nonnegative quasi-continuous function \[  H_{k,C}=\min \{ 1,(f-p_ k)_+\} \,  \min \{ 1,(p+C)_+\} .  \] Its values on pluripolar sets are immaterial. Where this coefficient is positive, $p_ k<f$ and $p>-C$. For $j\geq k$, we then have $p_ j\leq p_ k<f\leq f_ j$ and $p_ j\geq p>-C$ there. Plurifine locality and theorem 16.28.4 therefore imply \[  \int _ X H_{k,C}\,  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\max (p_ j,-C))=0.  \] The truncated potentials are uniformly bounded and decrease to $\max (p,-C)$, so their measures converge weakly by bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity. The uniform capacity bounds and the weighted convergence in section 5.29 also allow testing against $H_{k,C}$. Hence the last identity holds with $p$ in place of $p_ j$. By plurifine locality, this says that the extended measure of $p$ vanishes on $\{ p_ k<f\} \cap \{ p>-C\} $. Off the pole set of $p$, these sets increase to $\{ p<f\} $ as first $k$ and then $C$ tend to infinity. Continuity of positive measures along increasing sequences proves the assertion, even if the total extended mass is infinite. $\square$ For a smooth big background, constants need not be competitors, and a strictly $\theta $-plurisubharmonic barrier with poles replaces the constant lower truncations. The same contact property for quasi-continuous obstacles finite almost everywhere is proved in this setting in theorem 15.8.6 . Combined with ordered contact, either contact theorem controls the measures of rooftop envelopes. In the following bound, the strict inequality in the first term assigns the common contact set $\{ p=u=v\} $ to the second term. Proposition 16.28.6 . 107D3E29D21B Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form that is semipositive or big, and let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. If $p=P_\theta (u,v)$ is not identically $-\infty $, then \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p) \leq \mathbf1_{\{ p=u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u) +\mathbf1_{\{ p=v\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v).  \] Proof. The envelope lies below both obstacles quasi-everywhere, hence everywhere, since the obstacles are upper semicontinuous. By the contact theorem (theorem 16.28.5 or theorem 15.8.6 ), its measure is carried by $\{ p=\min (u,v)\} $. Partition this set into $\{ p=u<v\} $ and $\{ p=v\} $, and apply proposition 13.14.6 on each part. All measures vanish on the pluripolar pole sets, which can therefore be discarded throughout. $\square$ Proposition 16.28.7 . F0B070E89AE8 Let $\theta $ be smooth and semipositive. Every envelope fixed point $\varphi $ satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\varphi ) \leq \mathbf1_{\{ \varphi =0\} }\theta ^ n.  \] In particular, its extended mass is finite. Proof. Since $\varphi =P_\theta [\varphi ]\leq 0$, the function $\varphi $ is a competitor for $P_\theta (\varphi +1,0)$. This rooftop is also a competitor for $P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi $, being at most $\varphi +1$ and at most zero, so it equals $\varphi $. Now apply proposition 16.28.6 with $u=\varphi +1$ and $v=0$. The contact set $\{ \varphi =\varphi +1<0\} $ is contained in the pole set of $\varphi $, which the extended measure does not charge. Only contact with zero contributes, and this gives the asserted bound. $\square$

For the lower bound, note that $p$ is continuous by proposition 5.40.3 , and choose smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $v_ j\downarrow p$ by theorem 5.32.1 ; by Dini's theorem the convergence is uniform. The function \[  w_{j,\beta }=v_ j-\delta -C_ j/\beta  \] satisfies \[  \omega _{w_{j,\beta }}^ n=\omega _{v_ j}^ n \geq \mathrm{e}^{-C_ j}\omega ^ n \geq \mathrm{e}^{\beta (w_{j,\beta }-f)}\omega ^ n.  \] Exponential comparison, corollary 14.19.12 with $\lambda =\beta $, gives $w_{j,\beta }\leq u_\beta $. Testing against continuous functions with compact support in $\{ p<f\} $ and passing to the limit gives $\omega _ p^ n=0$ on this open set. $\square$

title: 16.28.8 Affine growth and projective envelopes
text: The contact property concerns the regularized envelope. For the classical weighted extremal functions on $\mathbb C^ n$, the obstacle is imposed at every point of a compact set, and one may ask when the regularized envelope still touches the obstacle there. Compactifying $\mathbb C^ n$ to $\mathbb P^ n$ turns the logarithmic growth allowance into a semipositive background. This correspondence distinguishes contact of the raw supremum with the obstacle from contact of its upper semicontinuous regularization, and it shows how both depend on the growth allowance. In the rest of this section we work on $\mathbb C^ n$ and on $\mathbb P^ n$ rather than on $X$. Write $\chi (z)=\log (1+\lVert z\rVert ^2)$ on $\mathbb C^ n$, and let $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ be the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^ n$ with this local potential, so that $\int _{\mathbb P^ n}\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^ n=1$ with our normalization of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$. For $\delta >0$ put \[  \theta _\delta =\tfrac \delta 2\omega _{\mathrm{FS}},\qquad \mathcal L_\delta = \{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb C^ n): u(z)\leq \delta \log ^+\lVert z\rVert +C_ u\} .  \] Here $\log ^+=\max (\log ,0)$, and $C_ u$ is a constant depending on $u$. Thus $\mathcal L_\delta $ is the class of plurisubharmonic functions of logarithmic growth at most $\delta $. Let $\mathcal L_\delta ^+$ consist of the members of $\mathcal L_\delta $ that are also bounded below by $\delta \log ^+\lVert z\rVert -C$ for some constant $C$. Lemma 16.28.9 . 5C02C050C6B5 The map $u\mapsto u-\delta \chi /2$, followed by the canonical extension across the hyperplane at infinity, is a bijection from $\mathcal L_\delta $ onto $\mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^ n,\theta _\delta )$. Proof. Use homogeneous coordinates $[Z_0:\cdots :Z_ n]$ and the affine chart $Z_0\ne 0$. On a chart $Z_ i\ne 0$ meeting $H=\{ Z_0=0\} $, the local plurisubharmonic representative of $p=u-\delta \chi /2$ is \[  p+\frac\delta 2\log \frac{\sum _{j=0}^ n|Z_ j|^2}{|Z_ i|^2} =u+\delta \log |Z_0/Z_ i|.  \] This function is locally bounded above near $H$, by the growth bound on $u$, because the norm of the affine coordinates is at most a constant, depending on the chart, divided by $|Z_0/Z_ i|$. By lemma 5.24.7 , it therefore extends canonically across $H$. Since the local potentials of $\theta _\delta $ differ by smooth functions on overlaps, the extensions agree there. Conversely, every $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^ n,\theta _\delta )$ is bounded above, since $\mathbb P^ n$ is compact. The function $u=p+\delta \chi /2$ is plurisubharmonic on the affine chart, and \[  0\leq \tfrac 12\chi -\log ^+\lVert z\rVert \leq \tfrac 12\log 2  \] gives the required growth bound. Neither function is identically $-\infty $ on the affine chart. Uniqueness of the canonical extension shows that the two maps are inverse to each other. $\square$ Fix a non-pluripolar compact set $K\subset \mathbb C^ n$ and a bounded real function $\psi $ on $K$. Define the raw and the regularized envelope \[  V_\delta =\sup \{ u\in \mathcal L_\delta :u|_ K\leq \psi \} , \qquad F_\delta =V_\delta ^*,  \] where the obstacle condition is imposed at every point of $K$. On $\mathbb P^ n$ put \[  G_\delta =\sup \{ p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^ n,\theta _\delta ): p|_ K\leq \psi -\delta \chi /2\} .  \] Proposition 16.28.10 . B1F342A8772A The regularized envelope $G_\delta ^*$ on $\mathbb P^ n$ is bounded and $\theta _\delta $-plurisubharmonic. On the affine chart, E8DF064EB371 16.28.11 \begin{equation}  V_\delta =\tfrac \delta 2\chi +G_\delta ,\qquad F_\delta =\tfrac \delta 2\chi +G_\delta ^*\in \mathcal L_\delta ^+. \end{equation} Moreover, $V_\delta =F_\delta $ almost everywhere. Proof. By lemma 16.28.9 , the map $u\mapsto u-\delta \chi /2$ is a bijection between the two families of competitors, which proves the identity for $V_\delta $. Constants below $\inf _ K(\psi -\delta \chi /2)$ are competitors for $G_\delta $. Since all competitors for $G_\delta $ lie below the constant $\sup _ K(\psi -\delta \chi /2)$ on $K$, lemma 5.40.1 gives a common upper bound for them. Together with a constant competitor, the upper-envelope theorem shows that $G_\delta ^*$ is bounded and $\theta _\delta $-plurisubharmonic. Addition of the smooth function $\delta \chi /2$ in ( 16.28.11 ) commutes with regularization, and the two-sided bounds for $G_\delta ^*$ give $F_\delta \in \mathcal L_\delta ^+$. Locally, adding a potential of $\theta _\delta $ makes the competitors plurisubharmonic. The upper-envelope theorem recalled in section 5.21 shows that regularization changes their supremum only on a pluripolar set. Thus $G_\delta =G_\delta ^*$ almost everywhere, and adding $\delta \chi /2$ gives the same assertion for $V_\delta $. $\square$ The regularized envelope does not change if the obstacle is imposed only outside a pluripolar subset of $K$. Within the growth class this can be seen directly: a function in $\mathcal L_\delta $ with poles on the exceptional set repairs each competitor. Lemma 16.28.12 . 7A591F1F87FA For every pluripolar set $E\subseteq \mathbb C^ n$ and every $\delta >0$, there is $b\in \mathcal L_\delta $ with $b=-\infty $ on $E$. Given a non-pluripolar compact set $K$, it can be chosen with $b\leq 0$ on $K$. Proof. Put $E_ j=E\cap \overline B(0,j)$. Each $E_ j$ is pluripolar as a subset of $\mathbb P^ n$: it is locally pluripolar near every affine point, and a neighborhood of the hyperplane at infinity does not meet this bounded set. By Josefson's theorem on compact manifolds, [ Theorem 1.1.5 , SGPT ] , there is a quasi-plurisubharmonic function on $\mathbb P^ n$, not identically $-\infty $, that equals $-\infty $ on $E_ j$. Rescaling it so that it becomes $\theta _1$-plurisubharmonic and subtracting its supremum gives \[  p_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^ n,\theta _1),\qquad p_ j\leq 0,\qquad p_ j|_{E_ j}=-\infty .  \] The $L^1$ norms of these normalized potentials are uniformly bounded by theorem 5.25.2 . The partial sums \[  p_ N=\sum _{j=1}^ N2^{-j}p_ j  \] decrease, have uniformly bounded $L^1$ norms, and remain $\theta _1$-plurisubharmonic because $\theta _1\geq 0$ and the coefficients sum to at most one. By corollary 5.25.3 , their limit $p$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^ n,\theta _1)$. Every point of $E$ is a pole of one of the summands, hence $p=-\infty $ on $E$. By lemma 16.28.9 , \[  b=\delta (p+\chi /2)\in \mathcal L_\delta  \] has the required properties. Its supremum on $K$ is finite, since $b$ is bounded above on the compact set $K$ and is not identically $-\infty $ on $K$, which is non-pluripolar. Subtracting this supremum gives $b\leq 0$ on $K$. $\square$ Corollary 16.28.13 . 0C3E3295B18F The envelope $F_\delta $ is unchanged if $u|_ K\leq \psi $ is imposed only quasi-everywhere, or only on $K\setminus E$ for any pluripolar $E\subseteq K$. Proof. Let $u\in \mathcal L_\delta $ satisfy $u\leq \psi $ on $K\setminus E$, where $E$ is pluripolar. Choose $b$ as in the lemma, with $b=-\infty $ on $E$ and $b\leq 0$ on $K$, and put $m=\inf _ K\psi $. For $\epsilon >0$ define \[  u_\epsilon =\frac{u+\epsilon b+\epsilon m}{1+\epsilon }.  \] This function belongs to $\mathcal L_\delta $. On $K\setminus E$, the inequalities $u\leq \psi $, $b\leq 0$ and $m\leq \psi $ give $u_\epsilon \leq \psi $, and on $E$ the pole of $b$ gives $u_\epsilon =-\infty $. Thus $u_\epsilon $ is a competitor for $V_\delta $, so $u_\epsilon \leq F_\delta $; moreover, $u_\epsilon \to u$ almost everywhere as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. By lemma 5.24.3 , $u\leq F_\delta $ everywhere. Taking the supremum over $u$ and regularizing proves the asserted equalities. Alternatively, apply proposition 5.40.6 on $\mathbb P^ n$ with the big background $\theta _\delta $ and the bounded obstacle $\psi -\delta \chi /2$, and then use ( 16.28.11 ). $\square$ These equalities concern regularized envelopes. The raw envelope $V_\delta $ is still defined with the obstacle imposed at every point of $K$. Changing $\delta $ changes both the background $\theta _\delta $ and the obstacle $\psi -\delta \chi /2$. Nevertheless, the set of parameters for which contact holds has a simple structure. Put \[  \Lambda =\{ \delta >0:V_\delta |_ K=\psi \} ,\qquad \Lambda _{\mathrm{reg}}(a)= \{ \delta \in \Lambda :F_\delta (a)=\psi (a)\} \quad (a\in K).  \] The parameters $\delta \in \Lambda $ are those for which the raw envelope touches the obstacle at every point of $K$; we say that raw contact holds for them. For $a\in K$, the parameters in $\Lambda _{\mathrm{reg}}(a)$ are those for which, in addition, the regularized envelope touches the obstacle at $a$; we say that regular contact holds at $a$. Theorem 16.28.14 . 6D209F2CFC94 The set $\Lambda $ is empty, $(0,\infty )$, or $[\lambda ,\infty )$ for some $\lambda >0$. If $\Lambda =[\lambda ,\infty )$, each $\Lambda _{\mathrm{reg}}(a)$ is empty, $\{ \lambda \} $, or $\Lambda $. If $\Lambda =(0,\infty )$, each $\Lambda _{\mathrm{reg}}(a)$ is empty or $\Lambda $. The same alternatives hold for $\bigcap _{a\in K}\Lambda _{\mathrm{reg}}(a)$. Proof. Let $m=\inf _ K\psi $. Inclusion of the growth classes and scaling of competitors give, for $0<\alpha <\beta $, 5251FBE769B2 16.28.15 \begin{equation}  0\leq V_\beta -V_\alpha \leq \frac{\beta -\alpha }{\alpha }(V_\alpha -m). \end{equation} Indeed, if $u$ is a competitor for $V_\beta $, then $(\alpha /\beta )(u-m)+m$ is a competitor for $V_\alpha $, since $\psi \geq m$. The constant $m$ is also a competitor, so all terms are finite and the right-hand side is nonnegative. The estimate shows that $V_\delta (z)$ depends continuously on $\delta >0$ at every point $z$. Since $V_\delta \leq \psi $ on $K$ and $V_\delta $ increases with $\delta $, the set $\Lambda $ is closed upwards, and by continuity it is relatively closed in $(0,\infty )$. This proves the three possible forms of $\Lambda $. For $0\leq t\leq 1$, convex combinations of competitors give \[  V_{(1-t)\alpha +t\beta }\geq (1-t)V_\alpha +tV_\beta .  \] By the preceding proposition, the same inequality holds for the regularized envelopes almost everywhere, and hence everywhere by lemma 5.24.3 . Thus $F_\delta (z)$ is a concave nondecreasing function of $\delta $ at every point $z$. For $a\in K$ and $\delta \in \Lambda $, the defect $d_\delta =F_\delta (a)-\psi (a)$ is nonnegative, concave and nondecreasing in $\delta $. Suppose $d_\alpha =0$, and that there is $\eta \in \Lambda $ with $\eta <\alpha $. For every $\beta >\alpha $, write $\alpha $ as a convex combination of $\eta $ and $\beta $ with positive weights. Concavity then forces both nonnegative defects $d_\eta $ and $d_\beta $ to vanish, and monotonicity gives $d_\delta =0$ for all $\delta \in \Lambda $ with $\delta <\alpha $. Hence a zero of the defect at a parameter other than the smallest element of $\Lambda $ forces every defect to vanish. This proves the alternatives for each $\Lambda _{\mathrm{reg}}(a)$, and intersecting them gives the alternatives for $\bigcap _{a\in K}\Lambda _{\mathrm{reg}}(a)$. $\square$ Thus raw contact persists as the growth allowance increases, whereas regular contact at a point may hold only at the smallest contact parameter. The correspondence with $\mathbb P^ n$ keeps the background and the obstacle matched throughout this variation.

title: Lemma 16.28.9
text: Lemma 16.28.9 . 5C02C050C6B5 The map $u\mapsto u-\delta \chi /2$, followed by the canonical extension across the hyperplane at infinity, is a bijection from $\mathcal L_\delta $ onto $\mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^ n,\theta _\delta )$. Proof. Use homogeneous coordinates $[Z_0:\cdots :Z_ n]$ and the affine chart $Z_0\ne 0$. On a chart $Z_ i\ne 0$ meeting $H=\{ Z_0=0\} $, the local plurisubharmonic representative of $p=u-\delta \chi /2$ is \[  p+\frac\delta 2\log \frac{\sum _{j=0}^ n|Z_ j|^2}{|Z_ i|^2} =u+\delta \log |Z_0/Z_ i|.  \] This function is locally bounded above near $H$, by the growth bound on $u$, because the norm of the affine coordinates is at most a constant, depending on the chart, divided by $|Z_0/Z_ i|$. By lemma 5.24.7 , it therefore extends canonically across $H$. Since the local potentials of $\theta _\delta $ differ by smooth functions on overlaps, the extensions agree there. Conversely, every $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^ n,\theta _\delta )$ is bounded above, since $\mathbb P^ n$ is compact. The function $u=p+\delta \chi /2$ is plurisubharmonic on the affine chart, and \[  0\leq \tfrac 12\chi -\log ^+\lVert z\rVert \leq \tfrac 12\log 2  \] gives the required growth bound. Neither function is identically $-\infty $ on the affine chart. Uniqueness of the canonical extension shows that the two maps are inverse to each other. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.28.10
text: Proposition 16.28.10 . B1F342A8772A The regularized envelope $G_\delta ^*$ on $\mathbb P^ n$ is bounded and $\theta _\delta $-plurisubharmonic. On the affine chart, E8DF064EB371 16.28.11 \begin{equation}  V_\delta =\tfrac \delta 2\chi +G_\delta ,\qquad F_\delta =\tfrac \delta 2\chi +G_\delta ^*\in \mathcal L_\delta ^+. \end{equation} Moreover, $V_\delta =F_\delta $ almost everywhere. Proof. By lemma 16.28.9 , the map $u\mapsto u-\delta \chi /2$ is a bijection between the two families of competitors, which proves the identity for $V_\delta $. Constants below $\inf _ K(\psi -\delta \chi /2)$ are competitors for $G_\delta $. Since all competitors for $G_\delta $ lie below the constant $\sup _ K(\psi -\delta \chi /2)$ on $K$, lemma 5.40.1 gives a common upper bound for them. Together with a constant competitor, the upper-envelope theorem shows that $G_\delta ^*$ is bounded and $\theta _\delta $-plurisubharmonic. Addition of the smooth function $\delta \chi /2$ in ( 16.28.11 ) commutes with regularization, and the two-sided bounds for $G_\delta ^*$ give $F_\delta \in \mathcal L_\delta ^+$. Locally, adding a potential of $\theta _\delta $ makes the competitors plurisubharmonic. The upper-envelope theorem recalled in section 5.21 shows that regularization changes their supremum only on a pluripolar set. Thus $G_\delta =G_\delta ^*$ almost everywhere, and adding $\delta \chi /2$ gives the same assertion for $V_\delta $. $\square$

title: Corollary 16.28.13
text: Corollary 16.28.13 . 0C3E3295B18F The envelope $F_\delta $ is unchanged if $u|_ K\leq \psi $ is imposed only quasi-everywhere, or only on $K\setminus E$ for any pluripolar $E\subseteq K$. Proof. Let $u\in \mathcal L_\delta $ satisfy $u\leq \psi $ on $K\setminus E$, where $E$ is pluripolar. Choose $b$ as in the lemma, with $b=-\infty $ on $E$ and $b\leq 0$ on $K$, and put $m=\inf _ K\psi $. title: Theorem 16.28.14
text: Theorem 16.28.14 . 6D209F2CFC94 The set $\Lambda $ is empty, $(0,\infty )$, or $[\lambda ,\infty )$ for some $\lambda >0$. If $\Lambda =[\lambda ,\infty )$, each $\Lambda _{\mathrm{reg}}(a)$ is empty, $\{ \lambda \} $, or $\Lambda $. If $\Lambda =(0,\infty )$, each $\Lambda _{\mathrm{reg}}(a)$ is empty or $\Lambda $. The same alternatives hold for $\bigcap _{a\in K}\Lambda _{\mathrm{reg}}(a)$. Proof. Let $m=\inf _ K\psi $. title: 16.28.16 Growth slopes and supporting probabilities
text: By concavity, the rate at which $F_\delta $ grows when the growth allowance $\delta $ is increased is at least its rate of growth for large $\delta $, and the latter is the classical extremal function of $K$, without weight. For continuous weights, supporting probabilities express the initial rate of growth through tests by functions of the fixed class $\mathcal L_1$. When the weight varies, we write $V_{\delta ,q}$ and $F_{\delta ,q}=V_{\delta ,q}^*$ for the raw and regularized envelopes defined as above, with a bounded obstacle $q$ on the fixed compact set $K$ in place of $\psi $. Thus $F_\delta =F_{\delta ,\psi }$. Set \[  V_ K=V_{1,0},\qquad V_ K^*=F_{1,0},\qquad m=\inf _ K\psi ,\qquad M=\sup _ K\psi .  \] Thus $V_ K^*$ is the extremal function of $K$. Since the constant $0$ is a competitor for $V_ K$, and since competitors can be scaled and translated by constants, we have $V_ K^*\geq 0$ and C5CFC7F7F4AE 16.28.17 \begin{equation}  \delta V_ K^*+m\leq F_\delta \leq \delta V_ K^*+M. \end{equation} Lemma 16.28.18 . 50B3044AA630 For $0<\alpha <\beta $, one has on $\mathbb C^ n$ 11BD756B4F41 16.28.19 \begin{equation}  (\beta -\alpha )V_ K^*\leq F_\beta -F_\alpha \leq \frac{\beta -\alpha }{\alpha }(F_\alpha -m). \end{equation} Proof. If $u$ is a competitor for $V_\alpha =V_{\alpha ,\psi }$ and $v$ is a competitor for $V_ K=V_{1,0}$, then $u+(\beta -\alpha )v$ is a competitor for $V_\beta $. Taking the suprema over $u$ and $v$ independently gives \[  V_\beta \geq V_\alpha +(\beta -\alpha )V_ K.  \] By proposition 16.28.10 , the raw envelopes agree almost everywhere with their regularizations, so this inequality holds almost everywhere for the regularizations, and hence everywhere by lemma 5.24.3 . This is the first inequality. The same argument applied to ( 16.28.15 ) gives the second. $\square$ Proposition 16.28.20 . 22685BEFF668 For every $a\in \mathbb C^ n$ and $\tau >0$, the right derivative \[  D_\tau (a)=\lim _{h\downarrow 0}\frac{F_{\tau +h}(a)-F_\tau (a)}{h}  \] exists and is finite. The difference quotients decrease as $h>0$ increases, and 89B57A4461F9 16.28.21 \begin{equation}  V_ K^*(a)\leq \frac{F_{\tau +h}(a)-F_\tau (a)}h \leq D_\tau (a)\leq \frac{F_\tau (a)-m}{\tau }. \end{equation} As $h\to \infty $, they converge to $V_ K^*(a)$, with the error bound A8634DE3239C 16.28.22 \begin{equation}  0\leq \frac{F_{\tau +h}(a)-F_\tau (a)}h-V_ K^*(a) \leq \frac{M-m}h. \end{equation} Moreover, $D_\tau (a)=V_ K^*(a)$ if and only if 29BB5B35B07B 16.28.23 \begin{equation}  F_\delta (a)=F_\tau (a)+(\delta -\tau )V_ K^*(a) \qquad (\delta \geq \tau ). \end{equation} Proof. For $0<h_1<h_2$, concavity of $F_\delta (a)$ gives \[  F_{\tau +h_1}(a)-F_\tau (a) \geq \frac{h_1}{h_2}\bigl (F_{\tau +h_2}(a)-F_\tau (a)\bigr ).  \] Thus the difference quotients decrease with $h$. Lemma 16.28.18 bounds them between $V_ K^*(a)$ and $(F_\tau (a)-m)/\tau $, which proves the existence and finiteness of $D_\tau (a)$ and ( 16.28.21 ). Combining the lower bound for the increments with ( 16.28.17 ) gives ( 16.28.22 ), with a bound independent of $a$. If $D_\tau (a)=V_ K^*(a)$, then by ( 16.28.21 ) every difference quotient equals $V_ K^*(a)$, which gives ( 16.28.23 ). Conversely, that formula gives $D_\tau (a)=V_ K^*(a)$. $\square$ Corollary 16.28.24 . 0D01C895AF55 Let $a\in K$ and $\tau \in \Lambda _{\mathrm{reg}}(a)$. Regular contact at $a$ holds for every $\delta >\tau $ if and only if $D_\tau (a)=0$. If $D_\tau (a)>0$, regular contact at $a$ fails for every $\delta >\tau $, and $\tau $ is the smallest element of $\Lambda $. Proof. At $\tau $ one has $F_\tau (a)=\psi (a)$, and raw contact holds for all $\delta \geq \tau $ by theorem 16.28.14 . If $D_\tau (a)=0$, then by ( 16.28.21 ) every difference quotient at $\tau $ vanishes, so $F_\delta (a)=\psi (a)$ for all $\delta >\tau $. If $D_\tau (a)>0$, then $F_\delta (a)>\psi (a)$ for all $\delta $ slightly larger than $\tau $, and by monotonicity for all $\delta >\tau $. In this case $\Lambda _{\mathrm{reg}}(a)$ contains $\tau $ but no larger parameter, so by theorem 16.28.14 it equals $\{ \lambda \} $, where $\lambda =\tau $ is the smallest element of $\Lambda $. $\square$ Assume now that the weights are continuous. If the obstacle is imposed only quasi-everywhere on $K$, the regularized envelope itself becomes a competitor, so the supremum needs no regularization; a constraint imposed at every point would miss the values created by regularization. Indeed, for $q\in C(K,\mathbb R)$, F611672B3A6D 16.28.25 \begin{equation}  F_{\delta ,q}(z)=\sup \{ u(z):u\in \mathcal L_\delta , \  u\leq q\text{ q.e. on }K\} . \end{equation} The envelope $F_{\delta ,q}$ itself is a competitor on the right, since it agrees with the raw envelope off a pluripolar set by proposition 16.28.10 . Conversely, the argument of corollary 16.28.13 shows that every competitor on the right lies below $F_{\delta ,q}$ everywhere. For $a\in \mathbb C^ n$, let $\mathcal J_ a(K)$ be the set of supporting pairs $(\mu ,c)$, where $\mu $ is a Borel probability measure on $K$ and $c\geq 0$, such that 0E7EEE36B8D9 16.28.26 \begin{equation}  u(a)\leq \int _ K f\, \mathrm{d}\mu +c \end{equation} whenever $u\in \mathcal L_1$, $f\in C(K,\mathbb R)$ and $u\leq f$ quasi-everywhere on $K$. We call $\mu $ a supporting probability at $a$. Theorem 16.28.27 . 865AACD2F96A For every $a\in \mathbb C^ n$, $q\in C(K,\mathbb R)$ and $\delta >0$, 2AF7902848CF 16.28.28 \begin{equation}  F_{\delta ,q}(a)=\min _{(\mu ,c)\in \mathcal J_ a(K)} \left(\int _ K q\, \mathrm{d}\mu +\delta c\right). \end{equation} In particular, $\mathcal J_ a(K)$ is nonempty and \[  \min _{(\mu ,c)\in \mathcal J_ a(K)}c=V_ K^*(a).  \] Proof. On the real Banach space $C(K)$, put $T(f)=F_{1,f}(a)$. By ( 16.28.25 ), $T$ is concave, since convex combinations of competitors are competitors. Comparison of obstacles and translation by constants show that $T$ is nondecreasing and satisfies \[  T(f+t)=T(f)+t,\qquad |T(f)-T(g)|\leq \| f-g\| _\infty .  \] Fix $f_0\in C(K)$. The directional derivative of the convex Lipschitz function $-T$ at $f_0$ is finite and sublinear. By the Hahn–Banach theorem, there is a continuous linear functional dominated by it, and since difference quotients of a convex function are monotone, this functional supports $-T$ at $f_0$. Changing the sign, we obtain a continuous linear functional $\ell $ with \[  T(f)\leq T(f_0)+\ell (f-f_0)\qquad (f\in C(K)).  \] Testing $f=f_0+th$ with $h\geq 0$ and $t>0$, and using monotonicity, gives $\ell (h)\geq 0$. Testing with $f=f_0\pm t$ gives $\ell (1)=1$. By the Riesz representation theorem, $\ell (f)=\int _ K f\, \mathrm{d}\mu $ for a Borel probability measure $\mu $ on $K$. Set $c=T(f_0)-\int _ K f_0\, \mathrm{d}\mu $. The supporting inequality at $f=0$ gives $c\geq T(0)=V_ K^*(a)\geq 0$. Together with ( 16.28.25 ), it shows that $(\mu ,c)\in \mathcal J_ a(K)$ and \[  T(f_0)=\int _ K f_0\, \mathrm{d}\mu +c.  \] Conversely, applying ( 16.28.26 ) to $u=F_{1,f_0}$, which lies below $f_0$ quasi-everywhere on $K$, shows that $T(f_0)\leq \int _ Kf_0\, \mathrm{d}\mu +c$ for every pair in $\mathcal J_ a(K)$. This proves ( 16.28.28 ) for $\delta =1$, with the minimum attained. The identity $F_{\delta ,q}=\delta F_{1,q/\delta }$ gives the general case, and the zero obstacle gives the last assertion. $\square$ Theorem 16.28.29 . 4044625470CC If $\psi \in C(K,\mathbb R)$, then for every $a\in \mathbb C^ n$ and $\tau >0$, 926674359DBA 16.28.30 \begin{equation}  D_\tau (a)=\min \left\{ c:(\mu ,c)\in \mathcal J_ a(K), \  \int _ K\psi \, \mathrm{d}\mu +\tau c=F_\tau (a)\right\} . \end{equation} Consequently, $D_\tau (a)=V_ K^*(a)$ if and only if there is a Borel probability measure $\mu $ on $K$ such that \[  (\mu ,V_ K^*(a))\in \mathcal J_ a(K),\qquad \int _ K\psi \, \mathrm{d}\mu =F_\tau (a)-\tau V_ K^*(a).  \] Proof. Each defining inequality of $\mathcal J_ a(K)$ is preserved under weak convergence of the probability measures and convergence of the constants, because the test function $f$ is continuous. Since the Borel probability measures on the compact metric space $K$ form a weakly compact set, the pairs in $\mathcal J_ a(K)$ with $c\leq C$ form a compact set for each finite $C$. Call a pair in $\mathcal J_ a(K)$ active at $\tau $ if it satisfies the equality in ( 16.28.30 ). Such pairs exist by theorem 16.28.27 , and since $\int _ K\psi \, \mathrm{d}\mu \geq m=\inf _ K\psi $, they satisfy \[  0\leq c\leq \frac{F_\tau (a)-m}{\tau }.  \] The set of active pairs is therefore compact, and the minimum of $c$ over it is attained. By theorem 16.28.27 at $\tau +h$, each active pair gives $F_{\tau +h}(a)\leq F_\tau (a)+hc$, hence $D_\tau (a)\leq c$. Conversely, for $h>0$ choose a pair $(\mu _ h,c_ h)$ attaining the minimum in ( 16.28.28 ) at $\tau +h$, with $q=\psi $. The representation at $\tau $ gives \[  F_\tau (a)\leq \int _ K\psi \, \mathrm{d}\mu _ h+\tau c_ h =F_{\tau +h}(a)-hc_ h.  \] Thus $0\leq c_ h\leq (F_{\tau +h}(a)-F_\tau (a))/h$, and these constants are bounded by ( 16.28.21 ). Along a sequence $h\downarrow 0$, compactness gives a limiting pair $(\mu ,c)\in \mathcal J_ a(K)$. The same bound makes $F_{\tau +h}(a)\to F_\tau (a)$ and $hc_ h\to 0$, and continuity of $\psi $ then gives $\int _ K\psi \, \mathrm{d}\mu +\tau c=F_\tau (a)$. Thus the limit pair is active, and it satisfies $c\leq D_\tau (a)$. This proves ( 16.28.30 ). Finally, every pair has $c\geq V_ K^*(a)$ by theorem 16.28.27 , so the attainment of the minimum gives the stated criterion. $\square$ At a point $a$ of regular contact, $F_\tau (a)=\psi (a)$, so the criterion involves only the original weight and tests by functions in $\mathcal L_1$. If the defining tests instead required $u\leq f$ at every point of $K$, the pair $(\delta _ a,0)$, where $\delta _ a$ is the unit point mass at $a\in K$, would always be allowed; the resulting infimum would be at most $\psi (a)$ and would not detect a defect created by regularization.

title: Equation 16.28.17
text: C5CFC7F7F4AE 16.28.17 \begin{equation}  \delta V_ K^*+m\leq F_\delta \leq \delta V_ K^*+M. \end{equation}

title: Lemma 16.28.18
text: Lemma 16.28.18 . 50B3044AA630 For $0<\alpha <\beta $, one has on $\mathbb C^ n$ 11BD756B4F41 16.28.19 \begin{equation}  (\beta -\alpha )V_ K^*\leq F_\beta -F_\alpha \leq \frac{\beta -\alpha }{\alpha }(F_\alpha -m). \end{equation} Proof. If $u$ is a competitor for $V_\alpha =V_{\alpha ,\psi }$ and $v$ is a competitor for $V_ K=V_{1,0}$, then $u+(\beta -\alpha )v$ is a competitor for $V_\beta $. Taking the suprema over $u$ and $v$ independently gives \[  V_\beta \geq V_\alpha +(\beta -\alpha )V_ K.  \] By proposition 16.28.10 , the raw envelopes agree almost everywhere with their regularizations, so this inequality holds almost everywhere for the regularizations, and hence everywhere by lemma 5.24.3 . This is the first inequality. The same argument applied to ( 16.28.15 ) gives the second. $\square$

title: Equation 16.28.19
text: 11BD756B4F41 16.28.19 \begin{equation}  (\beta -\alpha )V_ K^*\leq F_\beta -F_\alpha \leq \frac{\beta -\alpha }{\alpha }(F_\alpha -m). \end{equation}

title: Proposition 16.28.20
text: Proposition 16.28.20 . 22685BEFF668 For every $a\in \mathbb C^ n$ and $\tau >0$, the right derivative \[  D_\tau (a)=\lim _{h\downarrow 0}\frac{F_{\tau +h}(a)-F_\tau (a)}{h}  \] exists and is finite. The difference quotients decrease as $h>0$ increases, and 89B57A4461F9 16.28.21 \begin{equation}  V_ K^*(a)\leq \frac{F_{\tau +h}(a)-F_\tau (a)}h \leq D_\tau (a)\leq \frac{F_\tau (a)-m}{\tau }. \end{equation} As $h\to \infty $, they converge to $V_ K^*(a)$, with the error bound A8634DE3239C 16.28.22 \begin{equation}  0\leq \frac{F_{\tau +h}(a)-F_\tau (a)}h-V_ K^*(a) \leq \frac{M-m}h. \end{equation} Moreover, $D_\tau (a)=V_ K^*(a)$ if and only if 29BB5B35B07B 16.28.23 \begin{equation}  F_\delta (a)=F_\tau (a)+(\delta -\tau )V_ K^*(a) \qquad (\delta \geq \tau ). \end{equation} Proof. For $0<h_1<h_2$, concavity of $F_\delta (a)$ gives \[  F_{\tau +h_1}(a)-F_\tau (a) \geq \frac{h_1}{h_2}\bigl (F_{\tau +h_2}(a)-F_\tau (a)\bigr ).  \] Thus the difference quotients decrease with $h$. Lemma 16.28.18 bounds them between $V_ K^*(a)$ and $(F_\tau (a)-m)/\tau $, which proves the existence and finiteness of $D_\tau (a)$ and ( 16.28.21 ). Combining the lower bound for the increments with ( 16.28.17 ) gives ( 16.28.22 ), with a bound independent of $a$. If $D_\tau (a)=V_ K^*(a)$, then by ( 16.28.21 ) every difference quotient equals $V_ K^*(a)$, which gives ( 16.28.23 ). Conversely, that formula gives $D_\tau (a)=V_ K^*(a)$. $\square$

title: Corollary 16.28.24
text: Corollary 16.28.24 . 0D01C895AF55 Let $a\in K$ and $\tau \in \Lambda _{\mathrm{reg}}(a)$. Regular contact at $a$ holds for every $\delta >\tau $ if and only if $D_\tau (a)=0$. If $D_\tau (a)>0$, regular contact at $a$ fails for every $\delta >\tau $, and $\tau $ is the smallest element of $\Lambda $. Proof. At $\tau $ one has $F_\tau (a)=\psi (a)$, and raw contact holds for all $\delta \geq \tau $ by theorem 16.28.14 . If $D_\tau (a)=0$, then by ( 16.28.21 ) every difference quotient at $\tau $ vanishes, so $F_\delta (a)=\psi (a)$ for all $\delta >\tau $. If $D_\tau (a)>0$, then $F_\delta (a)>\psi (a)$ for all $\delta $ slightly larger than $\tau $, and by monotonicity for all $\delta >\tau $. In this case $\Lambda _{\mathrm{reg}}(a)$ contains $\tau $ but no larger parameter, so by theorem 16.28.14 it equals $\{ \lambda \} $, where $\lambda =\tau $ is the smallest element of $\Lambda $. $\square$

title: Equation 16.28.25
