title: Equation 16.28.26
text: 0E7EEE36B8D9 16.28.26 \begin{equation}  u(a)\leq \int _ K f\, \mathrm{d}\mu +c \end{equation}

title: Theorem 16.28.27
text: Theorem 16.28.27 . 865AACD2F96A For every $a\in \mathbb C^ n$, $q\in C(K,\mathbb R)$ and $\delta >0$, 2AF7902848CF 16.28.28 \begin{equation}  F_{\delta ,q}(a)=\min _{(\mu ,c)\in \mathcal J_ a(K)} \left(\int _ K q\, \mathrm{d}\mu +\delta c\right). \end{equation} In particular, $\mathcal J_ a(K)$ is nonempty and \[  \min _{(\mu ,c)\in \mathcal J_ a(K)}c=V_ K^*(a).  \] Proof. On the real Banach space $C(K)$, put $T(f)=F_{1,f}(a)$. By ( 16.28.25 ), $T$ is concave, since convex combinations of competitors are competitors. Comparison of obstacles and translation by constants show that $T$ is nondecreasing and satisfies \[  T(f+t)=T(f)+t,\qquad |T(f)-T(g)|\leq \| f-g\| _\infty .  \] Fix $f_0\in C(K)$. The directional derivative of the convex Lipschitz function $-T$ at $f_0$ is finite and sublinear. By the Hahn–Banach theorem, there is a continuous linear functional dominated by it, and since difference quotients of a convex function are monotone, this functional supports $-T$ at $f_0$. Changing the sign, we obtain a continuous linear functional $\ell $ with \[  T(f)\leq T(f_0)+\ell (f-f_0)\qquad (f\in C(K)).  \] Testing $f=f_0+th$ with $h\geq 0$ and $t>0$, and using monotonicity, gives $\ell (h)\geq 0$. Testing with $f=f_0\pm t$ gives $\ell (1)=1$. By the Riesz representation theorem, $\ell (f)=\int _ K f\, \mathrm{d}\mu $ for a Borel probability measure $\mu $ on $K$. Set $c=T(f_0)-\int _ K f_0\, \mathrm{d}\mu $. The supporting inequality at $f=0$ gives $c\geq T(0)=V_ K^*(a)\geq 0$. Together with ( 16.28.25 ), it shows that $(\mu ,c)\in \mathcal J_ a(K)$ and \[  T(f_0)=\int _ K f_0\, \mathrm{d}\mu +c.  \] Conversely, applying ( 16.28.26 ) to $u=F_{1,f_0}$, which lies below $f_0$ quasi-everywhere on $K$, shows that $T(f_0)\leq \int _ Kf_0\, \mathrm{d}\mu +c$ for every pair in $\mathcal J_ a(K)$. This proves ( 16.28.28 ) for $\delta =1$, with the minimum attained. The identity $F_{\delta ,q}=\delta F_{1,q/\delta }$ gives the general case, and the zero obstacle gives the last assertion. $\square$

title: Equation 16.28.28
text: 2AF7902848CF 16.28.28 \begin{equation}  F_{\delta ,q}(a)=\min _{(\mu ,c)\in \mathcal J_ a(K)} \left(\int _ K q\, \mathrm{d}\mu +\delta c\right). \end{equation}

title: Theorem 16.28.29
text: Theorem 16.28.29 . 4044625470CC If $\psi \in C(K,\mathbb R)$, then for every $a\in \mathbb C^ n$ and $\tau >0$, 926674359DBA 16.28.30 \begin{equation}  D_\tau (a)=\min \left\{ c:(\mu ,c)\in \mathcal J_ a(K), \  \int _ K\psi \, \mathrm{d}\mu +\tau c=F_\tau (a)\right\} . \end{equation} Consequently, $D_\tau (a)=V_ K^*(a)$ if and only if there is a Borel probability measure $\mu $ on $K$ such that \[  (\mu ,V_ K^*(a))\in \mathcal J_ a(K),\qquad \int _ K\psi \, \mathrm{d}\mu =F_\tau (a)-\tau V_ K^*(a).  \] Proof. Each defining inequality of $\mathcal J_ a(K)$ is preserved under weak convergence of the probability measures and convergence of the constants, because the test function $f$ is continuous. Since the Borel probability measures on the compact metric space $K$ form a weakly compact set, the pairs in $\mathcal J_ a(K)$ with $c\leq C$ form a compact set for each finite $C$. Call a pair in $\mathcal J_ a(K)$ active at $\tau $ if it satisfies the equality in ( 16.28.30 ). Such pairs exist by theorem 16.28.27 , and since $\int _ K\psi \, \mathrm{d}\mu \geq m=\inf _ K\psi $, they satisfy \[  0\leq c\leq \frac{F_\tau (a)-m}{\tau }.  \] The set of active pairs is therefore compact, and the minimum of $c$ over it is attained. By theorem 16.28.27 at $\tau +h$, each active pair gives $F_{\tau +h}(a)\leq F_\tau (a)+hc$, hence $D_\tau (a)\leq c$. Conversely, for $h>0$ choose a pair $(\mu _ h,c_ h)$ attaining the minimum in ( 16.28.28 ) at $\tau +h$, with $q=\psi $. The representation at $\tau $ gives \[  F_\tau (a)\leq \int _ K\psi \, \mathrm{d}\mu _ h+\tau c_ h =F_{\tau +h}(a)-hc_ h.  \] Thus $0\leq c_ h\leq (F_{\tau +h}(a)-F_\tau (a))/h$, and these constants are bounded by ( 16.28.21 ). Along a sequence $h\downarrow 0$, compactness gives a limiting pair $(\mu ,c)\in \mathcal J_ a(K)$. The same bound makes $F_{\tau +h}(a)\to F_\tau (a)$ and $hc_ h\to 0$, and continuity of $\psi $ then gives $\int _ K\psi \, \mathrm{d}\mu +\tau c=F_\tau (a)$. Thus the limit pair is active, and it satisfies $c\leq D_\tau (a)$. This proves ( 16.28.30 ). Finally, every pair has $c\geq V_ K^*(a)$ by theorem 16.28.27 , so the attainment of the minimum gives the stated criterion. $\square$

title: Equation 16.28.30
text: 926674359DBA 16.28.30 \begin{equation}  D_\tau (a)=\min \left\{ c:(\mu ,c)\in \mathcal J_ a(K), \  \int _ K\psi \, \mathrm{d}\mu +\tau c=F_\tau (a)\right\} . \end{equation}

title: 16.28.31 Variation of continuous weights
text: Supporting probabilities also describe how the envelope responds to changes of the weight, jointly with changes of the growth allowance. Keep the non-pluripolar compact set $K\subset \mathbb C^ n$ fixed. For $a\in \mathbb C^ n$, $\delta >0$ and $q\in C(K,\mathbb R)$, let F40A32D819F9 16.28.32 \begin{equation}  \mathcal J^{\mathrm{act}}_ a(\delta ,q)= \left\{ (\mu ,c)\in \mathcal J_ a(K): \int _ Kq\, \mathrm{d}\mu +\delta c=F_{\delta ,q}(a)\right\} . \end{equation} be the set of pairs that are active at $(\delta ,q)$. We give the weights the uniform norm, the probability measures the weak topology, and the constants the usual topology of $\mathbb R$. Lemma 16.28.33 . A143B4417F78 The set $\mathcal J^{\mathrm{act}}_ a(\delta ,q)$ is nonempty, convex and compact. For $\delta ,\eta \geq \epsilon >0$ and $p,q\in C(K,\mathbb R)$, FB1602967EA5 16.28.34 \begin{equation}  |F_{\eta ,p}(a)-F_{\delta ,q}(a)| \leq \| p-q\| _\infty + |\eta -\delta |\left(V_ K^*(a)+ \frac{\operatorname {osc}_ Kq}{\epsilon }\right). \end{equation} If $\delta _ j\to \delta >0$, $q_ j\to q$ uniformly and $(\mu _ j,c_ j)\in \mathcal J^{\mathrm{act}}_ a(\delta _ j,q_ j)$, then these pairs have a convergent subsequence, and every subsequential limit belongs to $\mathcal J^{\mathrm{act}}_ a(\delta ,q)$. Proof. Nonemptiness follows from theorem 16.28.27 . Since the test functions are continuous, $\mathcal J_ a(K)$ is closed and convex, and the equality defining active pairs is a closed affine condition. For an active pair, ( 16.28.17 ), applied with the weight $q$, gives \[  0\leq c\leq \frac{F_{\delta ,q}(a)-\inf _ Kq}{\delta } \leq V_ K^*(a)+\frac{\operatorname {osc}_ Kq}{\delta }.  \] The pairs in $\mathcal J_ a(K)$ with bounded constants form a compact set, as in the proof of theorem 16.28.29 ; hence the set of active pairs is compact. With $q$ fixed, lemma 16.28.18 and ( 16.28.17 ), applied with the weight $q$, bound $|F_{\eta ,q}(a)-F_{\delta ,q}(a)|$ by $|\eta -\delta |(V_ K^*(a)+\operatorname {osc}_ Kq/\epsilon )$. Comparison of obstacles and translation by constants bound $|F_{\eta ,p}(a)-F_{\eta ,q}(a)|$ by $\| p-q\| _\infty $. Adding these bounds gives ( 16.28.34 ). For the sequence in the statement, the constants $c_ j$ have a common bound, by the estimate above, because the weights $q_ j$ are uniformly bounded and the parameters $\delta _ j$ are bounded below by a positive constant. Weak compactness of probability measures gives a convergent subsequence of pairs, and its limit belongs to $\mathcal J_ a(K)$, which is closed. The estimate ( 16.28.34 ) gives $F_{\delta _ j,q_ j}(a)\to F_{\delta ,q}(a)$, while uniform convergence of the $q_ j$ and weak convergence of the $\mu _ j$ give $\int _ Kq_ j\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ j\to \int _ Kq\, \mathrm{d}\mu $. Passing to the limit in the equality defining active pairs proves the last assertion. $\square$ Proposition 16.28.35 . FDDE0F20FBB2 For $r\in C(K,\mathbb R)$ and $s\in \mathbb R$, one has ED5EC6D9783A 16.28.36 \begin{equation}  \lim _{h\downarrow 0} \frac{F_{\delta +hs,q+hr}(a)-F_{\delta ,q}(a)}h =\min _{(\mu ,c)\in \mathcal J^{\mathrm{act}}_ a(\delta ,q)} \left(\int _ Kr\, \mathrm{d}\mu +sc\right). \end{equation} The same limit holds along any sequence $h_ j\downarrow 0$ if $s,r$ in the difference quotient are replaced by $s_ j,r_ j$, where $s_ j\to s$ and $r_ j\to r$ uniformly. Thus the one-sided directional derivative is stable under convergence of the directions. Proof. By compactness of the set of active pairs, the minimum on the right is attained. For a fixed pair $(\mu ,c)$ active at $(\delta ,q)$, the representation ( 16.28.28 ) at the perturbed parameters gives \[  F_{\delta +hs,q+hr}(a) \leq F_{\delta ,q}(a)+h\left(\int _ Kr\, \mathrm{d}\mu +sc\right).  \] Choosing an active pair that attains the minimum on the right, we see that the upper limit of the difference quotients is at most this minimum. Conversely, choose a pair $(\mu _ h,c_ h)$ active at $(\delta +hs,q+hr)$. The representation at $(\delta ,q)$ gives \[  \frac{F_{\delta +hs,q+hr}(a)-F_{\delta ,q}(a)}h \geq \int _ Kr\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ h+sc_ h.  \] The estimate ( 16.28.34 ) bounds the difference quotients. Along a sequence of values of $h$ realizing their lower limit, lemma 16.28.33 gives a subsequence of pairs converging to a pair active at $(\delta ,q)$. For this pair, $\int _ Kr\, \mathrm{d}\mu +sc$ is at least the minimum on the right. This proves ( 16.28.36 ). For convergent directions, the same two inequalities hold. The fixed active pair attaining the minimum gives an upper bound with the right limit. The active pairs at the perturbed parameters still have uniformly bounded constants, and their subsequential limits are active at $(\delta ,q)$. Uniform convergence of the $r_ j$ controls the integrals $\int _ Kr_ j\, \mathrm{d}\mu _{h_ j}$, and $s_ j\to s$ controls the terms $s_ jc_{h_ j}$. The lower bound therefore has the same limit. Note that all perturbed growth allowances $\delta +h_ js_ j$ are positive for small $h_ j$. $\square$ Corollary 16.28.37 . 7D611867F702 For fixed $a$ and $q$, the function $\delta \mapsto F_{\delta ,q}(a)$ has finite left and right derivatives $D^-_{\delta ,q}(a)$ and $D^+_{\delta ,q}(a)$ at every positive parameter, with 63336B576658 16.28.38 \begin{equation}  D^-_{\delta ,q}(a)=\max _{\mathcal J^{\mathrm{act}}_ a(\delta ,q)}c, \qquad D^+_{\delta ,q}(a)=\min _{\mathcal J^{\mathrm{act}}_ a(\delta ,q)}c. \end{equation} It is differentiable exactly when all active pairs have the same constant $c$. For each fixed $a,q$, the set of positive parameters where it fails to be differentiable is at most countable. Proof. Apply ( 16.28.36 ) with $r=0$ and $s=\pm 1$. The direction $s=-1$ gives minus the left derivative, which proves ( 16.28.38 ). Concavity gives \[  D^+_{\alpha ,q}(a)\geq D^-_{\beta ,q}(a) \qquad (0<\alpha <\beta ).  \] Hence the open intervals $(D^+_{\delta ,q}(a),D^-_{\delta ,q}(a))$, which are nonempty exactly at the parameters where differentiability fails, are pairwise disjoint. Choosing a rational number in each of them proves countability. $\square$ Corollary 16.28.39 . DF0FD081C3EF For fixed $a$ and $\delta >0$, the map $q\mapsto F_{\delta ,q}(a)$ on $C(K,\mathbb R)$ is Gâteaux differentiable at $q$ if and only if all pairs active at $(\delta ,q)$ have the same probability measure $\mu $. In that case its derivative is \[  r\longmapsto \int _ Kr\, \mathrm{d}\mu .  \] Proof. With $s=0$, ( 16.28.36 ) shows that the right derivative in the direction $r$ is the minimum of $\int _ Kr\, \mathrm{d}\mu $ over active pairs, and the direction $-r$ shows that the left derivative is the maximum. If all active pairs have the same probability measure, these values agree and define a continuous linear derivative. Conversely, if the map is Gâteaux differentiable, the minimum and the maximum agree for every continuous $r$. Continuous functions separate Borel probability measures on $K$, so all active pairs have the same probability measure; their constant is then determined by ( 16.28.32 ), since $\delta >0$. $\square$ Example 16.28.40 . 9167A00E8F32 Let $D\subset \mathbb C$ be the open unit disk, let $K=\overline D$, and fix $\delta >0$. For $q_ t(z)=-t|z|^2$, B2CEEE021C0E 16.28.41 \begin{equation}  F_{\delta ,q_ t}(0)= \begin{cases}  -t,& t\geq 0,\\  0,& -\delta /2\leq t\leq 0. \end{cases} \end{equation} Thus the map $q\mapsto F_{\delta ,q}(0)$ is not Gâteaux differentiable at $q=0$, and there are active pairs at $(\delta ,0)$ with different probability measures. Proof. For $t\geq 0$, each competitor is at most $-t$ on the unit circle, so the maximum principle for subharmonic functions bounds it by $-t$ on $D$. This bound persists after regularization on $D$, and the constant $-t$ is a competitor. Hence $F_{\delta ,q_ t}(0)=-t$. For $t=-b$ with $0\leq b\leq \delta /2$, define \[  u_ b(z)= \begin{cases}  b|z|^2,& |z|\leq 1,\\  b+\delta \log |z|,& |z|>1. \end{cases}  \] This function is continuous and subharmonic: its Laplacian has density $4b$ inside the disk, density zero outside, and a nonnegative contribution on the circle coming from the jump $\delta -2b\geq 0$ of the radial derivative. It belongs to $\mathcal L_\delta $ and equals $q_{-b}$ on $K$. Hence $F_{\delta ,q_{-b}}(0)\geq u_ b(0)=0$. On $D$ the raw envelope is at most the continuous function $b|z|^2$, so its regularization at zero is at most zero. This proves ( 16.28.41 ). In particular, the right and left derivatives in $t$ at $t=0$ are $-1$ and $0$, and corollary 16.28.39 , applied in the direction $r=-|z|^2$, gives the final assertion. $\square$

title: Corollary 16.28.39
text: Corollary 16.28.39 . DF0FD081C3EF For fixed $a$ and $\delta >0$, the map $q\mapsto F_{\delta ,q}(a)$ on $C(K,\mathbb R)$ is Gâteaux differentiable at $q$ if and only if all pairs active at $(\delta ,q)$ have the same probability measure $\mu $. In that case its derivative is \[  r\longmapsto \int _ Kr\, \mathrm{d}\mu .  \] Proof. With $s=0$, ( 16.28.36 ) shows that the right derivative in the direction $r$ is the minimum of $\int _ Kr\, \mathrm{d}\mu $ over active pairs, and the direction $-r$ shows that the left derivative is the maximum. If all active pairs have the same probability measure, these values agree and define a continuous linear derivative. Conversely, if the map is Gâteaux differentiable, the minimum and the maximum agree for every continuous $r$. Continuous functions separate Borel probability measures on $K$, so all active pairs have the same probability measure; their constant is then determined by ( 16.28.32 ), since $\delta >0$. $\square$

title: Example 16.28.40
text: Example 16.28.40 . 9167A00E8F32 Let $D\subset \mathbb C$ be the open unit disk, let $K=\overline D$, and fix $\delta >0$. For $q_ t(z)=-t|z|^2$, B2CEEE021C0E 16.28.41 \begin{equation}  F_{\delta ,q_ t}(0)= \begin{cases}  -t,& t\geq 0,\\  0,& -\delta /2\leq t\leq 0. \end{cases} \end{equation} Thus the map $q\mapsto F_{\delta ,q}(0)$ is not Gâteaux differentiable at $q=0$, and there are active pairs at $(\delta ,0)$ with different probability measures. Proof. For $t\geq 0$, each competitor is at most $-t$ on the unit circle, so the maximum principle for subharmonic functions bounds it by $-t$ on $D$. This bound persists after regularization on $D$, and the constant $-t$ is a competitor. Hence $F_{\delta ,q_ t}(0)=-t$. For $t=-b$ with $0\leq b\leq \delta /2$, define \[  u_ b(z)= \begin{cases}  b|z|^2,& |z|\leq 1,\\  b+\delta \log |z|,& |z|>1. \end{cases}  \] This function is continuous and subharmonic: its Laplacian has density $4b$ inside the disk, density zero outside, and a nonnegative contribution on the circle coming from the jump $\delta -2b\geq 0$ of the radial derivative. It belongs to $\mathcal L_\delta $ and equals $q_{-b}$ on $K$. Hence $F_{\delta ,q_{-b}}(0)\geq u_ b(0)=0$. On $D$ the raw envelope is at most the continuous function $b|z|^2$, so its regularization at zero is at most zero. This proves ( 16.28.41 ). In particular, the right and left derivatives in $t$ at $t=0$ are $-1$ and $0$, and corollary 16.28.39 , applied in the direction $r=-|z|^2$, gives the final assertion. $\square$

title: Equation 16.28.41
text: B2CEEE021C0E 16.28.41 \begin{equation}  F_{\delta ,q_ t}(0)= \begin{cases}  -t,& t\geq 0,\\  0,& -\delta /2\leq t\leq 0. \end{cases} \end{equation}

title: 16.28.42 Local regularity and strict weights
text: Whether the regularized envelope touches the obstacle at a point $a\in K$ depends only on the parts of $K$ near $a$. Without weight, this local regularity is detected by the relative extremal function $h_{E,B}$ of definition 5.27.4 , for compact pieces $E$ of $K$ near $a$ and small balls $B$ centered at $a$. If the weight extends to a global function whose complex Hessian has a strict lower bound near $a$, a failure of this regularity produces a quantitative defect of the weighted envelope. For a non-pluripolar compact set $E\subset \mathbb C^ n$, write $V_ E$ and $V_ E^*$ for the raw and regularized envelopes of growth one with zero obstacle on $E$; thus $V_ K=V_{1,0}$ as before. For other weights and growth allowances, write $F_{\delta ,E,q}$ for the regularized envelope with growth allowance $\delta $ and obstacle $q$ imposed at every point of $E$. Lemma 16.28.43 . 2A500AE8E8B3 Let $a\in \mathbb C^ n$, $0<r<R$ and $B=B(a,R)$, and let $E\subseteq \overline B(a,r)$ be compact. If $E$ is pluripolar, then $h_{E,B}^*=0$ on $B$. If $E$ is non-pluripolar, then \[  h_{E,B}^*(a)=-1\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad V_ E^*(a)=0.  \] Proof. In the pluripolar case, choose $b\in \mathcal L_1$ with $b=-\infty $ on $E$ by lemma 16.28.12 , and a finite upper bound $C$ for $b$ on $B$. The functions \[  u_\epsilon =\max \{ -1,\epsilon (b-C)\}   \] are competitors for $h_{E,B}$, and they tend to zero almost everywhere as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. Hence $h_{E,B}^*\geq 0$ almost everywhere, and then everywhere by lemma 5.24.3 . Since $h_{E,B}^*\leq 0$, it vanishes. Now suppose that $E$ is non-pluripolar. Proposition 16.28.10 gives a finite upper bound $M\geq 1$ for $V_ E^*$ on $B$. For each competitor $v$ for $V_ E$, the function $\max (-1,v/M-1)$ is a competitor for $h_{E,B}$. Taking suprema and regularizing gives \[  h_{E,B}^*(a)\geq \max \{ -1,V_ E^*(a)/M-1\} .  \] As $V_ E^*\geq 0$, the equality $h_{E,B}^*(a)=-1$ forces $V_ E^*(a)=0$. For the converse, choose $r<R_0<R$ and $k>0$ with $k\log (R_0/r)>1$. The plurisubharmonic function \[  L(z)=k\log \bigl (\lVert z-a\rVert /r\bigr )  \] belongs to $\mathcal L_ k$ and equals $-\infty $ at $a$. For a competitor $u$ for $h_{E,B}$, define $W=\max (u+1,L)$ on $B$ and $W=L$ outside $B$. On the collar $R_0<\lVert z-a\rVert <R$ we have $L>1\geq u+1$, so the two definitions agree there, and $W$ is plurisubharmonic by lemma 5.24.2 . On $E$ one has $u=-1$ and $L\leq 0$, so $W=0$; on the ball $B(a,r)$ one has $L<0\leq u+1$, so $W=u+1$. Hence $W/k$ is a competitor for $V_ E$, with $k$ independent of $u$. Taking the supremum over $u$ and regularizing at $a$ gives \[  V_ E^*(a)\geq (1+h_{E,B}^*(a))/k.  \] Thus $V_ E^*(a)=0$ forces $h_{E,B}^*(a)=-1$. $\square$ Let $K\subset \mathbb C^ n$ again be a non-pluripolar compact set. For $a\in K$ and $r>0$, put $K_ r=K\cap \overline B(a,r)$. Definition 16.28.44 . 0288BA4D7A38 The compact set $K$ is locally pluriregular at $a\in K$ if every $K_ r$, $r>0$, is non-pluripolar and $V_{K_ r}^*(a)=0$. For $\delta >0$ and a bounded function $q$ on $K$, it is locally $(\delta ,q)$-regular at $a$ if $F_{\delta ,K_ r,q}(a)=q(a)$ for every $r>0$. It suffices to check arbitrarily small radii, since envelopes decrease as the compact set increases. By lemma 16.28.43 , $K$ is locally pluriregular at $a$ if and only if $h_{K_ r,B(a,R)}^*(a)=-1$ for all small $0<r<R$. Lemma 16.28.45 . F64C3174FCDB Let $q$ be bounded and upper semicontinuous on $K$, and suppose that raw contact holds for the parameter $\delta >0$ and the obstacle $q$ on $K$, that is, $V_{\delta ,q}=q$ on $K$. If $K$ is locally pluriregular at $a$, then $F_{\delta ,K,q}(a)=q(a)$ and $K$ is locally $(\delta ,q)$-regular at $a$. These equalities also hold with $\delta $ replaced by any larger parameter. Proof. Put $M_ r=\sup _{K_ r}q$. Raw contact, monotonicity of envelopes with respect to the compact set, and ( 16.28.17 ) for $K_ r$ give \[  q(a)\leq F_{\delta ,K,q}(a) \leq F_{\delta ,K_ r,q}(a) \leq M_ r+\delta V_{K_ r}^*(a)=M_ r.  \] Since $q$ is upper semicontinuous and $a\in K_ r$, we have $M_ r\downarrow q(a)$ as $r\downarrow 0$, which gives $F_{\delta ,K,q}(a)=q(a)$. Every compact subset $E\subseteq K$ inherits raw contact: on $E$, the raw envelope for $E$ is at least the raw envelope for $K$, which equals $q$, and at most the obstacle $q$. For fixed $s>0$, apply the same bounds with $r<s$ and $K_ s$ in place of $K$, and let $r\downarrow 0$. This proves local $(\delta ,q)$-regularity. By theorem 16.28.14 , raw contact also holds for every larger parameter, and applying what has been proved to each of them gives the last assertion. $\square$ Theorem 16.28.46 . 09FE648CAD9A Let $a\in K$, $\tau >0$ and $\Psi \in \mathcal L_\tau \cap C(\mathbb C^ n)$, and put $q=\Psi |_ K$. Suppose that, for some $R,c>0$, \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi \geq c\omega _0\quad \text{on }B(a,R), \qquad \omega _0=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\lVert z\rVert ^2.  \] For $0<r<R$ and $\delta \geq \tau $, 8D81382EAE2C 16.28.47 \begin{equation}  F_{\delta ,K,q}(a)-\Psi (a) \geq cr^2\bigl (1+h_{K_ r,B(a,R)}^*(a)\bigr ). \end{equation} Regular contact at $a$, that is, $F_{\delta ,K,q}(a)=q(a)$, holds for some $\delta \geq \tau $ if and only if $K$ is locally pluriregular at $a$. In that case it holds for every $\delta \geq \tau $. Proof. Set $B=B(a,R)$ and $E=K_ r$. For a competitor $u$ for $h_{E,B}$, the function \[  H_ u(z)=\Psi (z)-c\lVert z-a\rVert ^2+cr^2(u(z)+1)  \] is plurisubharmonic on $B$, because the assumption on $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi $ makes $\Psi -c\lVert z-a\rVert ^2$ plurisubharmonic there. Since $u\leq 0$, we have $H_ u\leq \Psi $ where $\lVert z-a\rVert \geq r$. Define $W=\max (\Psi ,H_ u)$ on $B$ and $W=\Psi $ outside $B$. The two definitions agree near $\partial B$, so $W$ is plurisubharmonic on $\mathbb C^ n$, and it belongs to $\mathcal L_\tau $ because it equals $\Psi $ outside $B$. On $E$, the equality $u=-1$ gives $H_ u\leq \Psi $, and on $K\setminus E$ the distance bound gives the same inequality. Thus $W=q$ on $K$, so $W$ is a competitor for $F_{\delta ,K,q}$ for each $\delta \geq \tau $. Since $W\geq H_ u$ near $a$, taking the supremum over $u$, regularizing, and using the continuity of $\Psi $, we obtain ( 16.28.47 ). The function $\Psi $ itself is a competitor, so raw contact holds for every $\delta \geq \tau $. If regular contact holds for one such $\delta $, the left-hand side of the estimate vanishes, so $h_{K_ r,B(a,R)}^*(a)=-1$ for all $0<r<R$. By lemma 16.28.43 , every $K_ r$ with $r<R$ is then non-pluripolar and satisfies $V_{K_ r}^*(a)=0$; for $r\geq R$ this follows by monotonicity. Conversely, local pluriregularity and lemma 16.28.45 give regular contact at $a$ for every $\delta \geq \tau $. $\square$ In this regular case, $V_ K^*(a)\leq V_{K_ r}^*(a)=0$ by monotonicity, and the right derivative $D_\tau (a)$ with respect to the growth allowance, for the weight $q$, vanishes by corollary 16.28.24 , since regular contact persists. Corollary 16.28.48 . DECDD98C3557 Let $\tau >0$, $\Psi \in \mathcal L_\tau \cap C^2(\mathbb C^ n)$ and $a\in K$. If $F_{\tau ,K,\Psi |_ K}(a)=\Psi (a)$, but $F_{\delta ,K,\Psi |_ K}(a)>\Psi (a)$ for some $\delta >\tau $, then \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi )^ n(a)=0.  \] Proof. The complex Hessian of $\Psi $ is semipositive. If its top power did not vanish at $a$, it would be positive definite at $a$, and by continuity $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi \geq c\omega _0$ on a neighborhood of $a$ for some $c>0$. Theorem 16.28.46 would then give regular contact at $a$ for every $\delta \geq \tau $, a contradiction. $\square$

title: Lemma 16.28.43
text: Lemma 16.28.43 . 2A500AE8E8B3 Let $a\in \mathbb C^ n$, $0<r<R$ and $B=B(a,R)$, and let $E\subseteq \overline B(a,r)$ be compact. If $E$ is pluripolar, then $h_{E,B}^*=0$ on $B$. If $E$ is non-pluripolar, then \[  h_{E,B}^*(a)=-1\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad V_ E^*(a)=0.  \] Proof. In the pluripolar case, choose $b\in \mathcal L_1$ with $b=-\infty $ on $E$ by lemma 16.28.12 , and a finite upper bound $C$ for $b$ on $B$. The functions \[  u_\epsilon =\max \{ -1,\epsilon (b-C)\}   \] are competitors for $h_{E,B}$, and they tend to zero almost everywhere as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. Hence $h_{E,B}^*\geq 0$ almost everywhere, and then everywhere by lemma 5.24.3 . Since $h_{E,B}^*\leq 0$, it vanishes. Now suppose that $E$ is non-pluripolar. Proposition 16.28.10 gives a finite upper bound $M\geq 1$ for $V_ E^*$ on $B$. For each competitor $v$ for $V_ E$, the function $\max (-1,v/M-1)$ is a competitor for $h_{E,B}$. Taking suprema and regularizing gives \[  h_{E,B}^*(a)\geq \max \{ -1,V_ E^*(a)/M-1\} .  \] As $V_ E^*\geq 0$, the equality $h_{E,B}^*(a)=-1$ forces $V_ E^*(a)=0$. For the converse, choose $r<R_0<R$ and $k>0$ with $k\log (R_0/r)>1$. The plurisubharmonic function \[  L(z)=k\log \bigl (\lVert z-a\rVert /r\bigr )  \] belongs to $\mathcal L_ k$ and equals $-\infty $ at $a$. For a competitor $u$ for $h_{E,B}$, define $W=\max (u+1,L)$ on $B$ and $W=L$ outside $B$. On the collar $R_0<\lVert z-a\rVert <R$ we have $L>1\geq u+1$, so the two definitions agree there, and $W$ is plurisubharmonic by lemma 5.24.2 . On $E$ one has $u=-1$ and $L\leq 0$, so $W=0$; on the ball $B(a,r)$ one has $L<0\leq u+1$, so $W=u+1$. Hence $W/k$ is a competitor for $V_ E$, with $k$ independent of $u$. Taking the supremum over $u$ and regularizing at $a$ gives \[  V_ E^*(a)\geq (1+h_{E,B}^*(a))/k.  \] Thus $V_ E^*(a)=0$ forces $h_{E,B}^*(a)=-1$. $\square$

title: Definition 16.28.44
text: Definition 16.28.44 . 0288BA4D7A38 The compact set $K$ is locally pluriregular at $a\in K$ if every $K_ r$, $r>0$, is non-pluripolar and $V_{K_ r}^*(a)=0$. For $\delta >0$ and a bounded function $q$ on $K$, it is locally $(\delta ,q)$-regular at $a$ if $F_{\delta ,K_ r,q}(a)=q(a)$ for every $r>0$.

title: Lemma 16.28.45
text: Lemma 16.28.45 . F64C3174FCDB Let $q$ be bounded and upper semicontinuous on $K$, and suppose that raw contact holds for the parameter $\delta >0$ and the obstacle $q$ on $K$, that is, $V_{\delta ,q}=q$ on $K$. If $K$ is locally pluriregular at $a$, then $F_{\delta ,K,q}(a)=q(a)$ and $K$ is locally $(\delta ,q)$-regular at $a$. These equalities also hold with $\delta $ replaced by any larger parameter. Proof. Put $M_ r=\sup _{K_ r}q$. Raw contact, monotonicity of envelopes with respect to the compact set, and ( 16.28.17 ) for $K_ r$ give \[  q(a)\leq F_{\delta ,K,q}(a) \leq F_{\delta ,K_ r,q}(a) \leq M_ r+\delta V_{K_ r}^*(a)=M_ r.  \] Since $q$ is upper semicontinuous and $a\in K_ r$, we have $M_ r\downarrow q(a)$ as $r\downarrow 0$, which gives $F_{\delta ,K,q}(a)=q(a)$. Every compact subset $E\subseteq K$ inherits raw contact: on $E$, the raw envelope for $E$ is at least the raw envelope for $K$, which equals $q$, and at most the obstacle $q$. For fixed $s>0$, apply the same bounds with $r<s$ and $K_ s$ in place of $K$, and let $r\downarrow 0$. This proves local $(\delta ,q)$-regularity. By theorem 16.28.14 , raw contact also holds for every larger parameter, and applying what has been proved to each of them gives the last assertion. $\square$

title: Theorem 16.28.46
text: Theorem 16.28.46 . 09FE648CAD9A Let $a\in K$, $\tau >0$ and $\Psi \in \mathcal L_\tau \cap C(\mathbb C^ n)$, and put $q=\Psi |_ K$. Suppose that, for some $R,c>0$, \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi \geq c\omega _0\quad \text{on }B(a,R), \qquad \omega _0=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\lVert z\rVert ^2.  \] For $0<r<R$ and $\delta \geq \tau $, 8D81382EAE2C 16.28.47 \begin{equation}  F_{\delta ,K,q}(a)-\Psi (a) \geq cr^2\bigl (1+h_{K_ r,B(a,R)}^*(a)\bigr ). \end{equation} Regular contact at $a$, that is, $F_{\delta ,K,q}(a)=q(a)$, holds for some $\delta \geq \tau $ if and only if $K$ is locally pluriregular at $a$. In that case it holds for every $\delta \geq \tau $. Proof. Set $B=B(a,R)$ and $E=K_ r$. For a competitor $u$ for $h_{E,B}$, the function \[  H_ u(z)=\Psi (z)-c\lVert z-a\rVert ^2+cr^2(u(z)+1)  \] is plurisubharmonic on $B$, because the assumption on $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi $ makes $\Psi -c\lVert z-a\rVert ^2$ plurisubharmonic there. Since $u\leq 0$, we have $H_ u\leq \Psi $ where $\lVert z-a\rVert \geq r$. Define $W=\max (\Psi ,H_ u)$ on $B$ and $W=\Psi $ outside $B$. The two definitions agree near $\partial B$, so $W$ is plurisubharmonic on $\mathbb C^ n$, and it belongs to $\mathcal L_\tau $ because it equals $\Psi $ outside $B$. On $E$, the equality $u=-1$ gives $H_ u\leq \Psi $, and on $K\setminus E$ the distance bound gives the same inequality. Thus $W=q$ on $K$, so $W$ is a competitor for $F_{\delta ,K,q}$ for each $\delta \geq \tau $. Since $W\geq H_ u$ near $a$, taking the supremum over $u$, regularizing, and using the continuity of $\Psi $, we obtain ( 16.28.47 ). The function $\Psi $ itself is a competitor, so raw contact holds for every $\delta \geq \tau $. If regular contact holds for one such $\delta $, the left-hand side of the estimate vanishes, so $h_{K_ r,B(a,R)}^*(a)=-1$ for all $0<r<R$. By lemma 16.28.43 , every $K_ r$ with $r<R$ is then non-pluripolar and satisfies $V_{K_ r}^*(a)=0$; for $r\geq R$ this follows by monotonicity. Conversely, local pluriregularity and lemma 16.28.45 give regular contact at $a$ for every $\delta \geq \tau $. $\square$

text: Corollary 16.28.48 . DECDD98C3557 Let $\tau >0$, $\Psi \in \mathcal L_\tau \cap C^2(\mathbb C^ n)$ and $a\in K$. If $F_{\tau ,K,\Psi |_ K}(a)=\Psi (a)$, but $F_{\delta ,K,\Psi |_ K}(a)>\Psi (a)$ for some $\delta >\tau $, then \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi )^ n(a)=0.  \] Proof. Theorem 16.28.46 would then give regular contact at $a$ for every $\delta \geq \tau $, a contradiction. $\square$

title: 16.28.49 A regularization defect along a complex disk
search_title: A regularization defect along a complex disk
text: Raw contact with a constant obstacle can hold for every positive growth parameter while regularization raises the value of the envelope at a point of the compact set. In the following example, a complex disk through the point, transverse to the planar direction, prevents any local plurisubharmonic function from separating the point from the rest of the compact set, but it does not remove this defect. In the complex plane, let $D$ be the open unit disk and put \[  p_ j=2+2^{-j},\qquad r_ j=\exp (-16\, 2^ j),\qquad E=\overline D\cup \{ 2\} \cup \bigcup _{j\geq 1}\overline D(p_ j,r_ j).  \] Lemma 16.28.50 . C78FAC45EABB The set $E$ is compact, and every neighborhood of each of its points contains an open disk contained in $E$. The series \[  h(\zeta )=\sum _{j\geq 1}2^{-j}\log |\zeta -p_ j|+2\log 2  \] defines a subharmonic function on $\mathbb C$ of logarithmic growth at most one; it satisfies $h(2)=0$ and is at most $-16+2\log 2$ on every small disk $\overline D(p_ j,r_ j)$. The function \[  v(\zeta )=\frac{8\log ^+|\zeta |+h(\zeta )-4\log 2}{9}  \] is subharmonic of logarithmic growth at most one, is nonpositive on $E\setminus \{ 2\} $, and satisfies $v(2)=4\log 2/9$. Proof. Since $r_ j<2^{-j-3}$, the small disks are pairwise disjoint and disjoint from $\overline D$, and they accumulate only at $2$. This proves compactness. Every neighborhood of $2$ contains one of the small disks, and every other point of $E$ lies in the closure of the interior of one of the disks. To show that the series defines a subharmonic function, write $\chi (\zeta )=\log (1+|\zeta |^2)$ on $\mathbb C$ and $\theta =\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}/2$ on $\mathbb P^1$. By lemma 16.28.9 , each \[  q_ j=\log |\zeta -p_ j|-\chi /2  \] extends to a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function on $\mathbb P^1$. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives $q_ j\leq \log 4$, while the value of $q_ j$ at infinity is zero. Thus $0\leq \sup q_ j\leq \log 4$, and theorem 5.25.2 bounds $\| q_ j-\log 4\| _{L^1}$ uniformly. The partial sums \[  w_ N=\sum _{j=1}^ N2^{-j}(q_ j-\log 4)  \] decrease, remain $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and have uniformly bounded $L^1$ norms. By corollary 5.25.3 , their limit $w$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^1,\theta )$. Since $\sum _ j2^{-j}=1$, \[  h=w+\chi /2+\log 4+2\log 2  \] on the affine chart. This proves subharmonicity and the growth bound, and $\sum _ j j2^{-j}=2$ gives $h(2)=0$. On the $j$th small disk, all distances to the other centers are less than one, so the corresponding terms are negative, and \[  h\leq 2^{-j}\log r_ j+2\log 2=-16+2\log 2.  \] On $\overline D$ all distances to the centers are less than four, hence $h\leq 4\log 2$ and $v\leq 0$. On each small disk $|\zeta |<4$, so $9v\leq 14\log 2-16<0$. The growth bound for $v$ and its value at $2$ follow directly from the formula. $\square$ Now let $n\geq 2$ and $K=E\times \overline D^{\, n-1}\subset \mathbb C^ n$. For a non-pluripolar compact set $L\subset \mathbb C^ n$, write $V_{\delta ,L}$ and $F_{\delta ,L}$ for the raw envelope with growth allowance $\delta $ and zero obstacle on $L$, and for its regularization. Proposition 16.28.51 . DDC2E6D4F75F For every point of $K$ and every neighborhood $W$ of it, the set $K\cap W$ is non-pluripolar. For $\delta >0$ and $a=(2,w)$ with $w\in \overline D^{\, n-1}$, 09A6A171E444 16.28.52 \begin{equation}  V_{\delta ,K}|_ K=0,\qquad F_{\delta ,K}(a)\geq \frac{4\delta }{9}\log 2>0. \end{equation} For every $r>0$, the same lower bound holds for $F_{\delta ,K\cap \overline B(a,r)}(a)$. At $a_0=(2,0,\ldots ,0)$, every plurisubharmonic function $f$ defined near $a_0$ satisfies 617AF346ABCF 16.28.53 \begin{equation}  f(a_0)\leq \limsup _{K\setminus \{ a_0\} \ni z\to a_0}f(z). \end{equation} Thus $K$ is not plurithin at $a_0$, although the regularized envelope does not touch the obstacle at $a_0$ for any positive growth parameter. Proof. By the preceding lemma, every neighborhood of a point of $K$ contains a nonempty open subset of $K$, namely a product of open disks. This proves the first assertion, which applies in particular to each $K\cap \overline B(a,r)$, $r>0$. Put $b(\zeta )=\log |\zeta -2|-\log 3$. Since $|\zeta -2|\leq 3$ on $E$, we have $b\leq 0$ there, and $b(2)=-\infty $. For $\varepsilon >0$, the plurisubharmonic function \[  u_\varepsilon (z)=\frac{v(z_1)+\varepsilon b(z_1)}{1+\varepsilon }  \] belongs to $\mathcal L_1$ and satisfies $u_\varepsilon \leq 0$ at every point of $K$, including the points with $z_1=2$, where it equals $-\infty $. Thus $u_\varepsilon \leq F_{1,K}$. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $v(z_1)\leq F_{1,K}(z)$ off the hyperplane $\{ z_1=2\} $, and lemma 5.24.3 extends this inequality everywhere. The value $v(2)=4\log 2/9$ gives the lower bound for $\delta =1$. Since $0$ is a competitor, $V_{\delta ,K}|_ K=0$, and scaling of competitors gives $F_{\delta ,K}=\delta F_{1,K}$. Replacing $K$ by a smaller compact set only increases the envelope, which proves the local assertion. Finally, let $f$ be plurisubharmonic near $a_0$. If $f(a_0)=-\infty $, ( 16.28.53 ) is automatic. Otherwise, restrict $f$ to the complex line through $a_0$ in which only the second coordinate varies. Small circles in this line centered at $a_0$ lie in $K\setminus \{ a_0\} $, and the submean inequality on these circles gives ( 16.28.53 ). $\square$

title: Lemma 16.28.50
text: Lemma 16.28.50 . C78FAC45EABB The set $E$ is compact, and every neighborhood of each of its points contains an open disk contained in $E$. The series \[  h(\zeta )=\sum _{j\geq 1}2^{-j}\log |\zeta -p_ j|+2\log 2  \] defines a subharmonic function on $\mathbb C$ of logarithmic growth at most one; it satisfies $h(2)=0$ and is at most $-16+2\log 2$ on every small disk $\overline D(p_ j,r_ j)$. The function \[  v(\zeta )=\frac{8\log ^+|\zeta |+h(\zeta )-4\log 2}{9}  \] is subharmonic of logarithmic growth at most one, is nonpositive on $E\setminus \{ 2\} $, and satisfies $v(2)=4\log 2/9$. Proof. Since $r_ j<2^{-j-3}$, the small disks are pairwise disjoint and disjoint from $\overline D$, and they accumulate only at $2$. This proves compactness. Every neighborhood of $2$ contains one of the small disks, and every other point of $E$ lies in the closure of the interior of one of the disks. To show that the series defines a subharmonic function, write $\chi (\zeta )=\log (1+|\zeta |^2)$ on $\mathbb C$ and $\theta =\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}/2$ on $\mathbb P^1$. By lemma 16.28.9 , each \[  q_ j=\log |\zeta -p_ j|-\chi /2  \] extends to a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function on $\mathbb P^1$. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives $q_ j\leq \log 4$, while the value of $q_ j$ at infinity is zero. Thus $0\leq \sup q_ j\leq \log 4$, and theorem 5.25.2 bounds $\| q_ j-\log 4\| _{L^1}$ uniformly. The partial sums \[  w_ N=\sum _{j=1}^ N2^{-j}(q_ j-\log 4)  \] decrease, remain $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and have uniformly bounded $L^1$ norms. By corollary 5.25.3 , their limit $w$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^1,\theta )$. Since $\sum _ j2^{-j}=1$, \[  h=w+\chi /2+\log 4+2\log 2  \] on the affine chart. This proves subharmonicity and the growth bound, and $\sum _ j j2^{-j}=2$ gives $h(2)=0$. On the $j$th small disk, all distances to the other centers are less than one, so the corresponding terms are negative, and \[  h\leq 2^{-j}\log r_ j+2\log 2=-16+2\log 2.  \] On $\overline D$ all distances to the centers are less than four, hence $h\leq 4\log 2$ and $v\leq 0$. On each small disk $|\zeta |<4$, so $9v\leq 14\log 2-16<0$. The growth bound for $v$ and its value at $2$ follow directly from the formula. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.28.51
text: Proposition 16.28.51 . DDC2E6D4F75F For every point of $K$ and every neighborhood $W$ of it, the set $K\cap W$ is non-pluripolar. For $\delta >0$ and $a=(2,w)$ with $w\in \overline D^{\, n-1}$, 09A6A171E444 16.28.52 \begin{equation}  V_{\delta ,K}|_ K=0,\qquad F_{\delta ,K}(a)\geq \frac{4\delta }{9}\log 2>0. \end{equation} For every $r>0$, the same lower bound holds for $F_{\delta ,K\cap \overline B(a,r)}(a)$. At $a_0=(2,0,\ldots ,0)$, every plurisubharmonic function $f$ defined near $a_0$ satisfies 617AF346ABCF 16.28.53 \begin{equation}  f(a_0)\leq \limsup _{K\setminus \{ a_0\} \ni z\to a_0}f(z). \end{equation} Thus $K$ is not plurithin at $a_0$, although the regularized envelope does not touch the obstacle at $a_0$ for any positive growth parameter. Proof. By the preceding lemma, every neighborhood of a point of $K$ contains a nonempty open subset of $K$, namely a product of open disks. This proves the first assertion, which applies in particular to each $K\cap \overline B(a,r)$, $r>0$. Put $b(\zeta )=\log |\zeta -2|-\log 3$. Since $|\zeta -2|\leq 3$ on $E$, we have $b\leq 0$ there, and $b(2)=-\infty $. For $\varepsilon >0$, the plurisubharmonic function \[  u_\varepsilon (z)=\frac{v(z_1)+\varepsilon b(z_1)}{1+\varepsilon }  \] belongs to $\mathcal L_1$ and satisfies $u_\varepsilon \leq 0$ at every point of $K$, including the points with $z_1=2$, where it equals $-\infty $. Thus $u_\varepsilon \leq F_{1,K}$. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $v(z_1)\leq F_{1,K}(z)$ off the hyperplane $\{ z_1=2\} $, and lemma 5.24.3 extends this inequality everywhere. The value $v(2)=4\log 2/9$ gives the lower bound for $\delta =1$. Since $0$ is a competitor, $V_{\delta ,K}|_ K=0$, and scaling of competitors gives $F_{\delta ,K}=\delta F_{1,K}$. Replacing $K$ by a smaller compact set only increases the envelope, which proves the local assertion. Finally, let $f$ be plurisubharmonic near $a_0$. If $f(a_0)=-\infty $, ( 16.28.53 ) is automatic. Otherwise, restrict $f$ to the complex line through $a_0$ in which only the second coordinate varies. Small circles in this line centered at $a_0$ lie in $K\setminus \{ a_0\} $, and the submean inequality on these circles gives ( 16.28.53 ). $\square$

title: 16.28.54 Bounded domination in a semipositive background
search_title: Bounded domination in a semipositive background
text: We return to the compact manifold $X$. The domination principle for Hermitian backgrounds, theorem 14.19.10 , extends to a smooth semipositive background $\theta $ provided every bounded $\theta $-plurisubharmonic potential has positive mass. For bounded potentials $u,v$ satisfying the measure inequality below, contact support bounds $\sup _ XP_\theta (bu-(b-1)v)$ from below as the stretching parameter $b>1$ increases. A fixed gap between $u$ and $v$ would then force the $L^1$ norms of these envelopes, normalized by their suprema, to diverge, contradicting compactness. We call a smooth semipositive form $\theta $ non-collapsing on bounded potentials if \[  \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w)>0 \quad \hbox{for every }w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\cap L^\infty (X).  \] Every Hermitian form has this property by corollary 14.19.11 . Bigness also implies it, by the following envelope argument. Proposition 16.28.55 . 9BBE1DE257CB If a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ is big, every bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has strictly positive Monge–Ampère mass. Proof. Choose $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $a>0$ with $\theta _\rho \geq a\omega $, normalize $\rho \leq 0$, and put \[  p=P_{a\omega }(u-\rho ).  \] The obstacle is finite almost everywhere and bounded below, so lemma 5.40.2 shows that $p$ is bounded. The obstacle is quasi-continuous off the pluripolar pole set of $\rho $. The contact theorem, theorem 16.28.5 , applied in the Hermitian background $a\omega $, shows that $\mathrm{MA}_{a\omega }(p)$ is carried by $D=\{ p+\rho =u\} $, outside the pole set of $\rho $. By lemma 5.24.3 , $p+\rho \leq u$ everywhere, and \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(p+\rho ) =(a\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p)+(\theta _\rho -a\omega ) \geq a\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p\geq 0.  \] On common finite truncation levels, positivity of the mixed products and ordered contact give \[  \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_{a\omega }(p) \leq \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p+\rho ) \leq \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u).  \] Exhausting by these levels proves the same inequalities for the extended measures. Since $p$ is bounded, its Monge–Ampère mass with respect to the Hermitian form $a\omega $ is positive by corollary 14.19.11 . Integrating the inequalities proves the assertion. $\square$ Theorem 16.28.56 (Guedj–Lu) . C67CEBABC968 Let $\theta \geq 0$ be non-collapsing on bounded potentials. Suppose that $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\cap L^\infty (X)$ and $0\leq c<1$. If \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u) \leq c\, \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v),  \] then $u\geq v$. Proof. If the conclusion failed, we could choose $a>0$ such that $E=\{ u<v-a\} $ is nonempty. This set has positive volume by lemma 5.24.4 . Fix $C$ with $|u|,|v|\leq C$. For $b>1$ define the bounded envelope \[  w_ b=P_\theta \bigl (bu-(b-1)v\bigr ),\qquad D_ b=\{ w_ b=bu-(b-1)v\} .  \] Since $\theta \geq 0$, constants below the obstacle are competitors. By the bounded contact theorem, theorem 16.28.4 , the measure $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w_ b)$ is concentrated on $D_ b$. The potential $b^{-1}w_ b+(1-b^{-1})v$ lies below $u$ quasi-everywhere, hence everywhere by lemma 5.24.3 , and it equals $u$ on $D_ b$ outside a pluripolar set. Ordered contact and positivity of the mixed terms give \[  \mathbf1_{D_ b}\left[b^{-n}\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w_ b) +(1-b^{-1})^ n\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)\right] \leq \mathbf1_{D_ b}\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u).  \] Choose $b$ so large that $(1-b^{-1})^ n>c$. Then the hypothesis forces $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w_ b)=0$ on $D_ b\cap \{ u<v\} $. Since $\theta $ is non-collapsing, $w_ b$ has positive total mass, so some of this mass is carried by $D_ b\cap \{ u\geq v\} $. At a point of this set outside the exceptional pluripolar set, \[  w_ b=bu-(b-1)v=u+(b-1)(u-v)\geq -C.  \] Consequently $\sup _ Xw_ b\geq -C$ for all large $b$. On the other hand, on the fixed set $E$ the obstacle bound gives $w_ b\leq C-(b-1)a$ quasi-everywhere. Hence \[  \int _ X|w_ b-\sup _ Xw_ b|\, \mathrm{d}V \geq \bigl ((b-1)a-2C\bigr )\operatorname {vol}_{\mathrm{d}V}(E)  \] for all sufficiently large $b$. This contradicts the uniform $L^1$ bound for normalized potentials in theorem 5.25.2 . $\square$ The exponential comparison principle follows as in corollary 14.19.12 . For unbounded potentials, the stretched envelopes must also be kept in the required singularity class; this is the role of the relative classes introduced below.

title: 16.28.57 Upper and lower volumes
text: Let $\theta $ be any smooth real $(1,1)$-form. Taking the infimum and the supremum of the mass over a singularity type gives two invariants with values in $[0,+\infty ]$. They can differ, because a bounded change of potential need not preserve the mass. Definition 16.28.58 . 52560A3D59BD For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, define \[  \begin{split}  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) & =\inf _{v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ),\  v\sim u} \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v),\\  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u) & =\sup _{v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ),\  v\sim u} \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v). \end{split}  \] These are the lower and upper volumes of the singularity type of $u$ in the background $\theta $. When $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is nonempty, we write $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}(\theta )$ and $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}(\theta )$ for their values at the potential $V_\theta $ with minimal singularities. For semipositive $\theta $, the singularity type of the zero potential consists of the bounded potentials. Extending the lower mass of definition 13.14.14 to this background, we put \[  v_-(\theta )=\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (0) =\inf _{v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\cap L^\infty (X)} \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v).  \] The condition $v_-(\theta )>0$ is stronger than the non-collapsing property used in bounded domination: it requires a single positive lower bound for the masses of all bounded potentials. Singularity volumes under a bounded mass hypothesis are compared in section 13.16 . Both volumes are invariant under bounded changes of $u$, by definition. They are also invariant under the smooth change of decomposition $(\theta ,u)\mapsto (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f,u-f)$, for $f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$: the map $v\mapsto v-f$ identifies the competitors, their currents and their measures. Scaling gives \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{t\theta }(tu) =t^ n\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u),\qquad \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{t\theta }(tu) =t^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)\quad (t>0).  \] Pullback by a modification also identifies the entire ordinary singularity type. The measure identity below gives preservation of both volumes in the exact pulled background. Proposition 16.28.59 . A8ED96D18B4A Let $\mu :Y\to X$ be a modification of connected compact complex manifolds, let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then \[  \mu _*\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{\mu ^*\theta }(u\circ \mu ) =\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u).  \] Both singularity volumes satisfy \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\mu ^*\theta }(u\circ \mu ) =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u),\qquad \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\mu ^*\theta }(u\circ \mu ) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u),  \] including infinite values. Proof. Choose a proper analytic set $S\subset X$ such that $\mu $ is an isomorphism outside $D=\mu ^{-1}(S)$. On these complements, bounded truncations commute with composition by $\mu $, and their products commute with the biholomorphic change of coordinates. Passing to the increasing limits gives the measure identity there. By theorem 13.14.3 , the two measures give no mass to $S$ and $D$, which proves the global identity and equality of total masses. Pullback is a bijection between the potentials in the two backgrounds by proposition 5.43.18 . Surjectivity of $\mu $ preserves and reflects bounded differences, so this bijection identifies the ordinary-type competitor families. Their masses agree by the first assertion. Taking their infima and suprema proves the volume identities. $\square$ The background upstairs is the exact pullback $\mu ^*\theta $, which may be degenerate even when $\theta >0$. These identities do not compare volumes for an independently chosen Hermitian form on $Y$.
