section: 15.8 Contact support in a big background
text: Throughout this section, $\theta $ is an arbitrary smooth big background, not necessarily semipositive. For a continuous obstacle, regularization shows that the envelope is continuous off the poles of a strict analytic barrier. On a small ball where the envelope stays below the obstacle, a homogeneous replacement then shows that the envelope already solves the homogeneous equation, so its Monge–Ampère measure vanishes away from the contact set. By theorem 5.36.5 , applied to a strict barrier with a sufficiently small curvature error, we may fix $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with analytic singularities and a smooth remainder after resolution such that \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \kappa \omega ,\qquad \kappa >0.  \] Its pole set $Z=\{ \rho =-\infty \} $ is an analytic, hence pluripolar, subset of $X$. Theorem 15.8.1 . F6FD255985FF Let $h\in C(X)$. Then $p=P_\theta (h)$ is a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function, continuous on $X\setminus Z$, whose Monge–Ampère measure satisfies \[  \mathbf1_{\{ p<h\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)=0.  \] Here $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)$ is allowed to have infinite total mass. Proof. Subtract a constant from $\rho $ so that $\rho +2\leq h$. Then $\rho +2$ is a competitor, and since the obstacle is continuous, the envelope lies below it everywhere; thus \[  \rho +2\leq p\leq h.  \] In particular, $p$ is locally bounded off $Z$. We first prove that $p$ is continuous there; this part does not use the contact assertion. Apply lemma 5.42.10 to $p-\sup _ Xp$ and add back the constant. The transforms $\Phi _{c,\delta }$ of that lemma are defined on $X$ and, with fixed constants $A,K,C>0$ and $\epsilon (\delta )=C\delta $, satisfy EE69BB255211 15.8.2 \begin{equation}  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _{c,\delta }\geq -(Ac+\epsilon (\delta ))\omega . \end{equation} Off $Z$ the infimum defining $\Phi _{c,\delta }$ is attained at a positive radius, and \[  p-K(\delta ^2+\delta )\leq \Phi _{c,\delta } \leq R_\delta p\leq R_\delta h.  \] For small $\delta $ the first inequality gives $\Phi _{c,\delta }\geq \rho +1$, hence $\rho \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }$ on $X$. Set \[  m(\delta )=\sup _{0<t\leq \delta }\| R_ th-h\| _\infty , \qquad c=m(\delta )+\epsilon (\delta )+\delta , \qquad s=\frac{Ac+\epsilon (\delta )}{\kappa }.  \] The averaging kernels are positive, have integral one and are supported in balls of radius comparable to $t$, so uniform continuity of $h$ gives $m(\delta )\to 0$. Define \[  v_\delta =\frac{\Phi _{c,\delta }+s\rho }{1+s}.  \] By the choice of $s$, the strict barrier and ( 15.8.2 ) show that $v_\delta $ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. Since $\rho \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }$, \[  v_\delta \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }\leq R_\delta h\leq h+m(\delta ).  \] Thus $v_\delta -m(\delta )$ is a competitor for the envelope, and $v_\delta \leq p+m(\delta )$. Let $L\Subset X\setminus Z$ be compact. On $L$ the difference $p-\rho $ is bounded above. Since $s\leq Cc$, the identity \[  \Phi _{c,\delta }-p=(1+s)(v_\delta -p)+s(p-\rho )  \] therefore gives $\Phi _{c,\delta }-p\leq C_ Lc$ on $L$. At a radius $t$ where the infimum is attained, \[  -c\log (t/\delta ) \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }-p+K(\delta ^2+\delta )\leq C_ Lc.  \] Since $c\geq \delta $, this yields $t\geq a_ L\delta $ with a fixed $a_ L>0$. Because $R_ tp+Kt^2$ is increasing in $t$, it follows that \[  p-K(a_ L\delta )^2\leq R_{a_ L\delta }p \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }+K\delta ^2+K\delta .  \] Consequently $R_{a_ L\delta }p\to p$ uniformly on $L$. These averages are smooth for positive radius, even though $p$ is unbounded on $X$. Applying this to compact neighborhoods of the points of $X\setminus Z$ proves that $p$ is continuous on $X\setminus Z$. We turn to the contact assertion. By the continuity just proved, the set $\{ p<h\} \setminus Z$ is open. Let $x$ be one of its points, and choose a small coordinate ball $B_ r$ centered at $x$ whose closure lies in this set. Let $H$ be the homogeneous replacement of theorem 15.7.2 with boundary values $p|_{\partial B_ r}$. Its domination property gives $H\geq p$ on the ball. We claim that $H\leq h$ on $B_ r$ if $r$ is small enough. Indeed, in the chosen Euclidean coordinates $z$, with Laplacian $\Delta $, the inequality $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H\geq 0$ implies a fixed bound $\Delta H\geq -C$. Comparison with the function $\sup _{\partial B_ r}p+C'(r^2-|z-x|^2)$, with $C'$ fixed large enough, gives \[  H\leq \sup _{\partial B_ r}p+C'r^2.  \] As $r\to 0$, the right-hand side tends to $p(x)$, whereas $\inf _{B_ r}h\to h(x)>p(x)$. This proves the claim for sufficiently small $r$. Now replace $p$ by $H$ on the ball. The resulting function is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. To see this, fix $a>0$ and take $\max \{ p,H-a\} $ inside the ball and $p$ outside. Since $H$ and $p$ are continuous with equal boundary values, $H-a<p$ on a collar of $\partial B_ r$, so this is an ordinary local maximum construction. Letting $a\downarrow 0$ gives the function equal to $H$ on $B_ r$ and to $p$ outside, with locally uniform convergence near the boundary of the ball. This function is bounded above by $h$ on all of $X$, so the definition of the envelope forces it to be at most $p$. Thus $p=H$ on $B_ r$, and $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)$ vanishes there. These balls cover $\{ p<h\} \setminus Z$. There the extended measure agrees with the local bounded product, and it does not charge the pluripolar set $Z$. This proves the contact assertion on $X$; no bound on the total mass of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)$ was needed. $\square$

We now extend the contact property to discontinuous obstacles. Continuous approximations of an obstacle need not preserve every competitor of its envelope pointwise. For lower semicontinuous obstacles, the approximation of lemma 5.40.5 repairs this, and quasi-continuity then allows us to pass to limits of weighted measures. An unbounded obstacle is truncated at finite levels; in an arbitrary smooth background this produces signed products, whose limits are controlled by lemma 5.29.17 before we restrict to the region where the product is positive. The strict analytic barrier $ho $ and its pole set $Z$ are those fixed above. Proposition 15.8.4 . 29A74E6E8A18 If $f$ is bounded and lower semicontinuous, then $p=P_	heta (f)$ is locally bounded on $X\setminus Z$, and \[  \mathbf1_{\{ p<f\} }\mathrm{MA}_	heta (p)=0.  \] Proof. Using the infimum construction in the proof of proposition 16.28.3 , take continuous $f_ j\uparrow f$ with common bounds $m\leq f_ j\leq M$, and shift $ho $ below $m$. The envelopes $p_ j=P_	heta (f_ j)$ increase and satisfy \[  ho \leq p_ j\leq M.  \] Their regularized limit $q=(\lim _ jp_ j)^*$ is therefore $	heta $-plurisubharmonic. Outside a pluripolar set it equals the pointwise limit, which is at most $f$; hence $q\leq p=P_	heta (f)$. We prove the reverse inequality without using a domination theorem. Let $u$ be any competitor for $P_	heta (f)$, and let $u_ t\leq f$ be the potentials given by lemma 5.40.5 , which satisfy this inequality everywhere. For fixed $t,\eta >0$, the sets \[  \{ u_ t<f_ j+\eta \} ,\qquad j\geq 1,  \] are open, increase with $j$, and cover $X$. By compactness, $u_ t\leq f_ j+\eta $ everywhere for all large $j$. Thus $u_ t-\eta $ is a competitor for $p_ j$, and $q\geq u_ t-\eta $. Letting first $\eta \downarrow 0$ and then $t\downarrow 0$, we obtain $q\geq u$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere by lemma 5.24.3 . Taking the supremum over all competitors $u$ gives $q\geq p$, so $q=p$. For fixed $k$, the set $U_ k=\{ p<f_ k\} $ is open. If $j\geq k$, then $p_ j\leq p<f_ k\leq f_ j$ on $U_ k$, so theorem 15.8.1 gives $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (p_ j)=0$ there. On every relatively compact open subset of $X\setminus Z$ the functions $p_ j$ have common bounds. After a common smooth correction and a finite expansion, the local Bedford–Taylor continuity along increasing sequences shows that their measures converge to $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (p)$ there. Since the measure of an open set is at most the lower limit of the measures of the approximating sequence, $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (p)$ vanishes on $U_ k\setminus Z$. The sequence decreases to $p$: its limit is not identically $-\infty $ because it dominates $p$, and it lies below $f$ quasi-everywhere, so it is itself a competitor for $P_	heta (f)$. u _{j,C}=(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{j,C})^ n$ therefore agrees there with $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (p_ j)$, and ( 15.8.7 ) gives \[  H_{k,C}
u _{j,C}=0.  \] For fixed $C$, the potentials $v_{j,C}$ have common global bounds and decrease to $v_ C$, so lemma 5.29.17 yields \[  \int _ X H_{k,C}(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ C)^ n=0.  \] On the set where $H_{k,C}$ is positive we have $p>-C$, so the restricted product in theorem 13.14.3 identifies $H_{k,C}(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ C)^ n$ with the positive measure $H_{k,C}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (p)$; on the complement the coefficient is zero. title: Proposition 15.8.4
section: 15.8 Contact support in a big background
text: Proposition 15.8.4 . 29A74E6E8A18 If $f$ is bounded and lower semicontinuous, then $p=P_\theta (f)$ is locally bounded on $X\setminus Z$, and \[  \mathbf1_{\{ p<f\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)=0.  \] Proof. Using the infimum construction in the proof of proposition 16.28.3 , take continuous $f_ j\uparrow f$ with common bounds $m\leq f_ j\leq M$, and shift $\rho $ below $m$. The envelopes $p_ j=P_\theta (f_ j)$ increase and satisfy \[  \rho \leq p_ j\leq M.  \] Their regularized limit $q=(\lim _ jp_ j)^*$ is therefore $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. Outside a pluripolar set it equals the pointwise limit, which is at most $f$; hence $q\leq p=P_\theta (f)$. We prove the reverse inequality without using a domination theorem. Let $u$ be any competitor for $P_\theta (f)$, and let $u_ t\leq f$ be the potentials given by lemma 5.40.5 , which satisfy this inequality everywhere. For fixed $t,\eta >0$, the sets \[  \{ u_ t<f_ j+\eta \} ,\qquad j\geq 1,  \] are open, increase with $j$, and cover $X$. By compactness, $u_ t\leq f_ j+\eta $ everywhere for all large $j$. Thus $u_ t-\eta $ is a competitor for $p_ j$, and $q\geq u_ t-\eta $. Letting first $\eta \downarrow 0$ and then $t\downarrow 0$, we obtain $q\geq u$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere by lemma 5.24.3 . Taking the supremum over all competitors $u$ gives $q\geq p$, so $q=p$. For fixed $k$, the set $U_ k=\{ p<f_ k\} $ is open. If $j\geq k$, then $p_ j\leq p<f_ k\leq f_ j$ on $U_ k$, so theorem 15.8.1 gives $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p_ j)=0$ there. On every relatively compact open subset of $X\setminus Z$ the functions $p_ j$ have common bounds. After a common smooth correction and a finite expansion, the local Bedford–Taylor continuity along increasing sequences shows that their measures converge to $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)$ there. Since the measure of an open set is at most the lower limit of the measures of the approximating sequence, $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)$ vanishes on $U_ k\setminus Z$. The union of these sets is $\{ p<f\} \setminus Z$, and the extended measure does not charge the pluripolar set $Z$. $\square$

title: Proposition 15.8.5
section: 15.8 Contact support in a big background
text: Proposition 15.8.5 . BDE06B833BC8 The conclusion of proposition 15.8.4 holds for every bounded quasi-continuous obstacle $f$. Proof. By lemma 5.29.15 , there are bounded lower semicontinuous $f_ j$ with common bounds and $f_ j\downarrow f$ quasi-everywhere. The envelopes $p_ j=P_\theta (f_ j)$ decrease to $p=P_\theta (f)$. title: 15.9 Compactness with a common lower barrier

section: 15.9 Compactness with a common lower barrier
text:
We return to a semipositive big background $	heta $. Convergence of potentials in $L^1$ does not by itself imply convergence of their Monge–Ampère measures. We give a criterion for convergence in capacity when the potentials stay within a bounded distance of a reference admitting a smaller-background envelope. This common lower barrier ensures that all finite and infinite rooftop envelopes of the sequence are $	heta $-plurisubharmonic. A small error integral of each potential against its own Monge–Ampère measure bounds the corresponding error of the rooftops by a summable tail. Weighted lower semicontinuity passes this bound to the limit, and singular domination identifies the limit of the lower envelopes with the $L^1$ limit. Squeezing the sequence between lower and upper envelopes then gives convergence in capacity, and a domination of the measures also controls their mass on deep sublevels. Theorem 15.9.1 . A15C1A7CB4F8 Let $	heta \geq 0$ be big. Suppose $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfies $P_{\delta 	heta }(\varphi )
ot\equiv -\infty $ for some $0<\delta <1$. Let $u_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfy, for a fixed $C$, \[  \varphi -C\leq u_ j\leq \varphi +C,\qquad u_ j\longrightarrow u	ext{ in }L^1(X).  \] If B172EB5C34CB 15.9.2  egin{equation}  I_ j:=\int _ X|\mathrm{e}^{u_ j}-\mathrm{e}^ u|\,  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (u_ j)\longrightarrow 0, \end{equation} then $u_ j	o u$ in capacity. Proof. The canonical representative of the limit also lies between $\varphi -C$ and $\varphi +C$. It suffices to show that every subsequence has a further subsequence converging in capacity. We may therefore assume that $I_ j\leq 2^{-j}$ and that $u_ j	o u$ almost everywhere. For $N\geq j$ define \[  p_{j,N}=P_	heta (\min \{ u_ j,\ldots ,u_ N\} ),\qquad p_ j=P_	heta \left(\inf _{\ell \geq j}u_\ell ight).  \] All these envelopes lie between $\varphi -C$ and $\varphi +C$. The contact theorem and ordered contact give an inequality for the finite rooftops. Partition the contact set of $p_{j,N}$ according to the first index $\ell $ for which $p_{j,N}=u_\ell $. On the corresponding piece, the measure of $p_{j,N}$ is bounded by that of $u_\ell $, and $\mathrm{e}^{p_{j,N}}=\mathrm{e}^{u_\ell }$. Therefore \[  \int _ X|\mathrm{e}^{p_{j,N}}-\mathrm{e}^ u|\,  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (p_{j,N}) \leq \sum _{\ell =j}^ N I_\ell \leq 2^{1-j}.  \] Only positive measures enter this argument, so it applies also when their total masses are infinite. As $N	o \infty $, $p_{j,N}$ decreases to $p_ j$; the limit is the envelope of the infimum because every competitor lies below every finite rooftop. The sequence $p_ j$ increases, and its canonical limit $p$ is $	heta $-plurisubharmonic. By lemma 5.29.19 , both monotone limits hold in capacity. Applying lemma 13.14.8 to the bounded nonnegative weights $|\mathrm{e}^{p_{j,N}}-\mathrm{e}^ u|$, first in $N$ and then in $j$, we obtain \[  \int _ X|\mathrm{e}^ p-\mathrm{e}^ u|\, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (p)=0.  \] The inequalities $p_ j\leq u_\ell $ for all $\ell \geq j$ imply $p\leq u$, first almost everywhere and then for the canonical representatives. Also $p\sim u\sim \varphi $. Off the pole sets, $\mathrm{e}^ p<\mathrm{e}^ u$ exactly on $\{ p<u\} $, so $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (p)(\{ p<u\} )=0$. Since $P_{\delta 	heta }(\varphi )-C$ is a competitor for $P_{\delta 	heta }(p)$, the latter is not identically $-\infty $. Theorem 15.2.2 , applied with coefficient zero, gives $p\geq u$, and hence $p=u$. Finally, by Hartogs' lemma and the almost-everywhere convergence, $U_ j=(\sup _{\ell \geq j}u_\ell )^*$ decreases to $u$. The inequalities $p_ j\leq u_ j\leq U_ j$, together with the convergence in capacity of both monotone sequences, prove the claim. $\square$ Proposition 15.9.3 . EFAF50966FDF In theorem 15.9.1 , the two bounds on $u_ j$ may be replaced by \[  \varphi -C\leq u_ j\leq C,  \] provided that the $L^1$ limit satisfies $u\preceq \varphi $. In particular, the approximants may be bounded while $\varphi $ is unbounded. Proof. The $L^1$ limit satisfies $u\geq \varphi -C$, so the additional hypothesis gives $u\sim \varphi $. We repeat the construction of the finite rooftops in the theorem. Every $p_{j,N}$ is still $	heta $-plurisubharmonic and lies between $\varphi -C$ and $C$, which is enough for contact support and for the boundedness of the exponential weights. The resulting inequality is again \[  \int _ X|\mathrm{e}^{p_{j,N}}-\mathrm{e}^ u|\,  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (p_{j,N})\leq 2^{1-j}.  \] The limits $p_ j$ exist because of the common lower bound, and $p_ j\leq u$ follows from $p_ j\leq u_\ell $ for every $\ell \geq j$ and almost-everywhere convergence. Thus $\varphi -C\leq p_ j\leq u$, so all $p_ j$ and their increasing limit $p$ have the same ordinary singularity type as $\varphi $. Monotone convergence in capacity and weighted lower semicontinuity give $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (p)(\{ p<u\} )=0$, and singular domination applies to $(p,u)$ exactly as before, so $p=u$. The upper envelopes of the tails decrease to $u$, and the same squeezing argument gives convergence in capacity. Neither the finite rooftops nor the individual approximants needed to have the singularity type of $\varphi $. $\square$ Corollary 15.9.4 . F856D22ADF4C In the setting of theorem 15.9.1 , with the bounds $\varphi -C\leq u_ j\leq \varphi +C$, suppose either $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (u_ j)\leq 
u $ for a fixed finite non-pluripolar measure $
u $; or $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (u_ j)\leq A\omega _{w_ j}^ n$, where $A$ is fixed and $w_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ are uniformly bounded and converge in capacity to a bounded $w$. Then $u_ j	o u$ in capacity, all the measures $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (u_ j)$ and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (u)$ have finite mass, and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (u_ j) ightharpoonup \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (u).  \] Proof. In the first case, lemma 5.44.2 , applied to the exponentials $\mathrm{e}^{u_ j}$, proves ( 15.9.2 ). In the second case we use lemma 5.44.7 instead, since these exponentials are bounded and have a common lower bound for their curvature. In both cases the criterion gives convergence in capacity. The masses are uniformly bounded by those of the dominating measures. For the deep sublevels we use $u_ j\geq \varphi -C$, which gives $\{ u_ j<-T\} \subset \{ \varphi <C-T\} $. In the first case the masses of these sublevels are at most $
u (\{ \varphi <C-T\} )$, which tends to zero as $T	o \infty $ because $
u $ does not charge the pole set of $\varphi $. In the second case lemma 5.29.16 bounds them by $C'\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (\{ \varphi <C-T\} )$, which also tends to zero. The tail criterion theorem 13.15.13 , in the general-background form of theorem 13.15.23 , now gives finiteness of the limiting measure and weak convergence. $\square$ The reference $\varphi $ in these results need not be an envelope fixed point; the smaller-background condition suffices. Envelope fixed points enter when the two barriers must be derived from an a priori estimate, as in theorem 15.12.3 . When no common lower barrier is available, one has to be constructed in a relative envelope class; this problem is treated in subsection 15.37.30 .

title: 15.11 Adding weighted Monge–Ampère measures
text:
Let $u$ and $v$ be potentials of the same ordinary singularity type. We show that the sum of their weighted measures $\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda u}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (u)+\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda v}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (v)$ is again of the form $\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda a}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (a)$ for a potential $a$ of that type. Truncating $u$ and $v$ gives bounded equations, solved by the bounded subsolution theorem, whose solutions have a common lower barrier. Their exponential error tends to zero even though the approximating masses may grow, so the lower-barrier criterion identifies the limit. This addition step will remove a deficit of mass in the existence proof of section 15.12 . Theorem 15.11.1 . 7A54D08FEB18 Let $	heta \geq 0$ be big, and suppose $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfies $P_{\delta 	heta }(\varphi )
ot\equiv -\infty $ for some $0<\delta <1$. Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ satisfy $u,v\sim \varphi $, and let $\lambda >0$. If \[  \mu =\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda u}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (u) +\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda v}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (v)  \] is a finite measure, then there exists $a\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, with $a\sim \varphi $, such that \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (a)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda a}\mu .  \] Here the weights are evaluated off the pole sets. section: 15.12 Equations in a prescribed ordinary type
text: We return to a semipositive big background $\theta $ and now require the solution to have the ordinary singularity type of a fixed reference $\varphi $. Throughout this section, $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is an envelope fixed point admitting a smaller-background envelope; that is, ( 16.28.67 ) holds: \[  P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi ,\qquad P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )\not\equiv -\infty \quad \text{for some }0<\varepsilon <1.  \] We fix such an $\varepsilon $. Note that $\varphi \leq 0$, since every competitor for $P_\theta [\varphi ]$ is nonpositive. For a normalized solution $u$, the fixed-point property gives the upper bound $u\leq \varphi $, while the smaller-background envelope $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )$ yields a uniform lower bound $u\geq \varphi -C$. A supersolution and the addition theorem then prove existence in this type. Theorem 15.12.1 . 7AFA75E73767 Let $\theta $ and $\varphi $ be as above, and let $\mu =f\, \mathrm{d}V$, where $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, and $\mu (X)>0$. Then: For every $\lambda >0$ there is a unique $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\sim \varphi $ such that \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}\mu .  \] There are $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\sim \varphi $ and a uniquely determined constant $c>0$ such that \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=c\mu .  \] The potential in part (2) need not be unique up to an additive constant, even for a Hermitian background and the reference $\varphi =0$; see the counterexample in theorem 14.26.1 . The proof uses two estimates in the prescribed type. The first is a lower bound for the norm of a Monge–Ampère density. Lemma 15.12.2 . D0B5A6CE28E9 Fix $q>1$. There is $b_ q>0$ such that every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\sim \varphi $ and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)=F\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad 0\leq F\in L^ q(\mathrm{d}V),  \] satisfies $\| F\| _ q\geq b_ q$. For fixed $\theta $ and $\varepsilon $, the constant $b_ q$ is independent of $\varphi $. Proof. Since $u\sim \varphi $, the smaller-background envelope $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(u)$ is not identically $-\infty $. If $F=0$, then theorem 15.2.2 , applied to $u$ and $u+1$ with coefficient zero, would give $u\geq u+1$; hence $N=\| F\| _ q>0$. Apply lemma 15.3.1 in the semipositive big background $(1-\varepsilon )\theta $ to $F/N$, whose $L^ q$ norm is one. It gives a bounded $s$ with $-1\leq s\leq 0$ and a constant $b_ q>0$, depending only on this fixed background and on $q$, such that \[  \mathrm{MA}_{(1-\varepsilon )\theta }(s)\geq (b_ q/N)F\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Put $h=P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )+s$. This is a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function with $h\preceq u$. Since $\theta _ h$ is the sum of the positive currents $\varepsilon \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )$ and $(1-\varepsilon )\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s$, the same density bound holds for $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (h)$. To justify this, we truncate $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )$ at finite levels, use positivity of bounded mixed products, and exhaust the set where $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )$ is finite; its pole set has zero volume. If $N<b_ q$, we would have \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u) \leq (N/b_ q)\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (h+t) \quad \text{for every }t\in \mathbb R.  \] Since $N/b_ q<1$, theorem 15.2.2 would then imply $u\geq h+t$ for every $t$, which is impossible at a point where both potentials are finite. Thus $N\geq b_ q$. The construction of $s$ used no property of $\varphi $, which proves the last assertion. $\square$ The lemma bounds the $L^ q$ norm of the density from below; it gives no positive lower bound for the total mass $\int _ XF\, \mathrm{d}V$. The second estimate bounds a normalized solution from below by $\varphi $ minus a uniform constant. It is what keeps limits of solutions in the ordinary singularity type of $\varphi $. Theorem 15.12.3 . 413B92CD2B72 Let $\theta $ and $\varphi $ be as above. Suppose $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $u\sim \varphi $, $\sup _ Xu=0$, and \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\leq f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad 0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V),\quad p>1.  \] There is a constant $C$, depending only on the fixed geometry, $\varphi $, $p$, and an upper bound for $\| f\| _{L^ p}$, such that \[  \varphi -C\leq u\leq \varphi .  \] Proof. The upper bound follows directly from the fixed-point property: since $u\leq 0$ and $u\preceq \varphi $, the function $u$ is a competitor for $P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi $. For the lower bound we construct a subsolution $\psi $ of the type of $\varphi $ whose measure dominates a multiple of $\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma u}\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$, and then apply singular domination. Put $\varphi _\varepsilon =P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )$, so that $\varphi _\varepsilon \leq \varphi \leq 0$. Uniform exponential integrability (lemma 5.26.2 ) for the normalized potentials $u$ and exponential integrability for the fixed function $\varphi _\varepsilon $ allow us to choose $\gamma >0$ and $1<q<p$ such that \[  g=\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma (\varphi _\varepsilon +u)}f  \] has a uniform $L^ q$ bound. Explicitly, we first choose $q<p$ and apply Hölder's inequality with exponents $p/q$ and $p/(p-q)$; then we choose $\gamma $ so small that the exponential factor is controlled by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and the two exponential integrability estimates. Theorem 15.3.5 , applied in the semipositive big background $(1-\varepsilon )\theta $ to the density $1+g$, gives a bounded $v$ with $\sup _ Xv=0$ and a constant $c>0$ such that \[  ((1-\varepsilon )\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n=c(1+g)\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Both $\| v\| _\infty $ and $c^{-1}$ are uniformly bounded. Adding the constant one to $g$ makes the root integral of the density at least one, so no lower bound for the integral of $f$ is needed. Put $h=\varphi _\varepsilon +v\leq \varphi $, which is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, and define \[  \chi (t)=\frac1{1-t}\quad (t\leq 0),\qquad \psi =\varphi +\chi (h-\varphi ),  \] where the formula for $\psi $ is evaluated off the pole sets. Then $0\leq \chi \leq 1$, $0<\chi '\leq 1$, and $\chi ''>0$. For bounded potentials with $h\leq \varphi $, lemma 5.28.13 , applied with $G(x,y)=x+\chi (y-x)$, gives \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G(\varphi ,h) \geq (1-\chi '(h-\varphi ))\theta _\varphi +\chi '(h-\varphi )\theta _ h\geq 0.  \] For unbounded potentials we apply this bounded assertion to $\varphi _ k=\max (\varphi ,-k)$ and $h_ k=\max (h,-k)\leq \varphi _ k$. Since $G$ is nondecreasing in both variables, $G(\varphi _ k,h_ k)$ decreases as $k$ increases. Its limit is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and lies between $\varphi $ and $\varphi +1$; hence it is not identically $-\infty $, and it equals $\psi $. Locality on common finite levels and positivity of bounded products give \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\psi ) \geq (\varphi -h+1)^{-2n}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (h) \geq c(\varphi -h+1)^{-2n}\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma \varphi _\varepsilon } \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma u}f\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] where the second inequality uses $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (h)\geq ((1-\varepsilon )\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\geq cg\, \mathrm{d}V$. These inequalities are first obtained off the pole sets; since pole sets have zero volume, they extend by exhaustion to all Borel sets. Write $T=-\varphi _\varepsilon \geq 0$. If $C_1\geq 1+\| v\| _\infty $, then $\varphi -h+1\leq T+C_1$. Since \[  A:=\inf _{T\geq 0}\frac{\mathrm{e}^{\gamma T}}{(T+C_1)^{2n}}>0,  \] we obtain, with a uniform $d>0$, \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\psi ) \geq d \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma u}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u).  \] Choose $K=2+\gamma ^{-1}|\log d|$. On $\{ u<\psi -K\} $ we have $u<1-K$, because $\psi \leq \varphi +1\leq 1$; hence \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u) \leq d^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{\gamma (1-K)} \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\psi -K) \leq \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\psi -K).  \] The potentials $u$ and $\psi -K$ have the same ordinary singularity type. Moreover, $u\geq \varphi -C_ u$ for some constant $C_ u$, so $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(u)\geq \varphi _\varepsilon -C_ u$ is not identically $-\infty $. Theorem 15.2.2 therefore yields $u\geq \psi -K\geq \varphi -K$. All constants used to choose $K$ are uniform over the family in the theorem; the possibly nonuniform constant $C_ u$ serves only to show that the smaller-background envelope of $u$ is not identically $-\infty $, and it enters no estimate. $\square$ The existence proof starts from a supersolution in the prescribed type. It is obtained from a bounded solution by a rooftop envelope with $\varphi $. Lemma 15.12.4 . 5A797D7301BB For nonzero $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, and $\lambda >0$, there exists $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $w\sim \varphi $ such that \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (w)\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda w}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Proof. Let $v$ be the bounded solution of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ given by theorem 15.3.3 , and write $M=\sup _ Xv$ and $a=v-M\leq 0$. The rooftop envelope $p=P_\theta (a,\varphi )$ satisfies $\varphi -\| a\| _\infty \leq p\leq \varphi $, so $p\sim \varphi $. By the rooftop inequality of proposition 16.28.6 , \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (p) \leq \mathbf1_{\{ p=a\leq \varphi \} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (a) +\mathbf1_{\{ p=\varphi <a\} }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\varphi ).  \] The second term vanishes: by proposition 16.28.7 , the measure of $\varphi $ is carried by $\{ \varphi =0\} $, whereas $\varphi <a\leq 0$ on the set in question. On the first contact set, $a=p$ and $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (a)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda (a+M)}f\, \mathrm{d}V$. Thus $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (p)\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda (p+M)}f\, \mathrm{d}V$, and $w=p+M$ has the required properties. $\square$

title: Lemma 15.12.2
section: 15.12 Equations in a prescribed ordinary type
text: Lemma 15.12.2 . D0B5A6CE28E9 Fix $q>1$. There is $b_ q>0$ such that every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\sim \varphi $ and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)=F\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad 0\leq F\in L^ q(\mathrm{d}V),  \] satisfies $\| F\| _ q\geq b_ q$. For fixed $\theta $ and $\varepsilon $, the constant $b_ q$ is independent of $\varphi $. Proof. Since $u\sim \varphi $, the smaller-background envelope $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(u)$ is not identically $-\infty $. If $F=0$, then theorem 15.2.2 , applied to $u$ and $u+1$ with coefficient zero, would give $u\geq u+1$; hence $N=\| F\| _ q>0$. Apply lemma 15.3.1 in the semipositive big background $(1-\varepsilon )\theta $ to $F/N$, whose $L^ q$ norm is one. It gives a bounded $s$ with $-1\leq s\leq 0$ and a constant $b_ q>0$, depending only on this fixed background and on $q$, such that \[  \mathrm{MA}_{(1-\varepsilon )\theta }(s)\geq (b_ q/N)F\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Put $h=P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )+s$. This is a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function with $h\preceq u$. Since $\theta _ h$ is the sum of the positive currents $\varepsilon \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )$ and $(1-\varepsilon )\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s$, the same density bound holds for $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (h)$. To justify this, we truncate $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )$ at finite levels, use positivity of bounded mixed products, and exhaust the set where $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )$ is finite; its pole set has zero volume. If $N<b_ q$, we would have \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u) \leq (N/b_ q)\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (h+t) \quad \text{for every }t\in \mathbb R.  \] Since $N/b_ q<1$, theorem 15.2.2 would then imply $u\geq h+t$ for every $t$, which is impossible at a point where both potentials are finite. Thus $N\geq b_ q$. The construction of $s$ used no property of $\varphi $, which proves the last assertion. $\square$

title: Theorem 15.12.3
section: 15.12 Equations in a prescribed ordinary type
text: Theorem 15.12.3 . 413B92CD2B72 Let $\theta $ and $\varphi $ be as above. Suppose $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $u\sim \varphi $, $\sup _ Xu=0$, and \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\leq f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad 0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V),\quad p>1.  \] There is a constant $C$, depending only on the fixed geometry, $\varphi $, $p$, and an upper bound for $\| f\| _{L^ p}$, such that \[  \varphi -C\leq u\leq \varphi .  \] Proof. The upper bound follows directly from the fixed-point property: since $u\leq 0$ and $u\preceq \varphi $, the function $u$ is a competitor for $P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi $. For the lower bound we construct a subsolution $\psi $ of the type of $\varphi $ whose measure dominates a multiple of $\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma u}\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$, and then apply singular domination. Put $\varphi _\varepsilon =P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )$, so that $\varphi _\varepsilon \leq \varphi \leq 0$. Uniform exponential integrability (lemma 5.26.2 ) for the normalized potentials $u$ and exponential integrability for the fixed function $\varphi _\varepsilon $ allow us to choose $\gamma >0$ and $1<q<p$ such that \[  g=\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma (\varphi _\varepsilon +u)}f  \] has a uniform $L^ q$ bound. Explicitly, we first choose $q<p$ and apply Hölder's inequality with exponents $p/q$ and $p/(p-q)$; then we choose $\gamma $ so small that the exponential factor is controlled by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and the two exponential integrability estimates. Theorem 15.3.5 , applied in the semipositive big background $(1-\varepsilon )\theta $ to the density $1+g$, gives a bounded $v$ with $\sup _ Xv=0$ and a constant $c>0$ such that \[  ((1-\varepsilon )\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n=c(1+g)\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Both $\| v\| _\infty $ and $c^{-1}$ are uniformly bounded. Adding the constant one to $g$ makes the root integral of the density at least one, so no lower bound for the integral of $f$ is needed. Put $h=\varphi _\varepsilon +v\leq \varphi $, which is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, and define \[  \chi (t)=\frac1{1-t}\quad (t\leq 0),\qquad \psi =\varphi +\chi (h-\varphi ),  \] where the formula for $\psi $ is evaluated off the pole sets. Then $0\leq \chi \leq 1$, $0<\chi '\leq 1$, and $\chi ''>0$. For bounded potentials with $h\leq \varphi $, lemma 5.28.13 , applied with $G(x,y)=x+\chi (y-x)$, gives \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G(\varphi ,h) \geq (1-\chi '(h-\varphi ))\theta _\varphi +\chi '(h-\varphi )\theta _ h\geq 0.  \] For unbounded potentials we apply this bounded assertion to $\varphi _ k=\max (\varphi ,-k)$ and $h_ k=\max (h,-k)\leq \varphi _ k$. Since $G$ is nondecreasing in both variables, $G(\varphi _ k,h_ k)$ decreases as $k$ increases. Its limit is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and lies between $\varphi $ and $\varphi +1$; hence it is not identically $-\infty $, and it equals $\psi $. Locality on common finite levels and positivity of bounded products give \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\psi ) \geq (\varphi -h+1)^{-2n}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (h) \geq c(\varphi -h+1)^{-2n}\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma \varphi _\varepsilon } \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma u}f\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] where the second inequality uses $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (h)\geq ((1-\varepsilon )\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\geq cg\, \mathrm{d}V$. These inequalities are first obtained off the pole sets; since pole sets have zero volume, they extend by exhaustion to all Borel sets. Write $T=-\varphi _\varepsilon \geq 0$. If $C_1\geq 1+\| v\| _\infty $, then $\varphi -h+1\leq T+C_1$. Since \[  A:=\inf _{T\geq 0}\frac{\mathrm{e}^{\gamma T}}{(T+C_1)^{2n}}>0,  \] we obtain, with a uniform $d>0$, \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\psi ) \geq d \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma u}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u).  \] Choose $K=2+\gamma ^{-1}|\log d|$. On $\{ u<\psi -K\} $ we have $u<1-K$, because $\psi \leq \varphi +1\leq 1$; hence \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u) \leq d^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{\gamma (1-K)} \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\psi -K) \leq \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\psi -K).  \] The potentials $u$ and $\psi -K$ have the same ordinary singularity type. Moreover, $u\geq \varphi -C_ u$ for some constant $C_ u$, so $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(u)\geq \varphi _\varepsilon -C_ u$ is not identically $-\infty $. Theorem 15.2.2 therefore yields $u\geq \psi -K\geq \varphi -K$. All constants used to choose $K$ are uniform over the family in the theorem; the possibly nonuniform constant $C_ u$ serves only to show that the smaller-background envelope of $u$ is not identically $-\infty $, and it enters no estimate. $\square$

title: Lemma 15.12.4
section: 15.12 Equations in a prescribed ordinary type
text: Lemma 15.12.4 . 5A797D7301BB For nonzero $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, and $\lambda >0$, there exists $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $w\sim \varphi $ such that \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (w)\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda w}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Proof. Let $v$ be the bounded solution of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ given by theorem 15.3.3 , and write $M=\sup _ Xv$ and $a=v-M\leq 0$. The rooftop envelope $p=P_\theta (a,\varphi )$ satisfies $\varphi -\| a\| _\infty \leq p\leq \varphi $, so $p\sim \varphi $. By the rooftop inequality of proposition 16.28.6 , \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (p) \leq \mathbf1_{\{ p=a\leq \varphi \} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (a) +\mathbf1_{\{ p=\varphi <a\} }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\varphi ).  \] The second term vanishes: by proposition 16.28.7 , the measure of $\varphi $ is carried by $\{ \varphi =0\} $, whereas $\varphi <a\leq 0$ on the set in question. On the first contact set, $a=p$ and $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (a)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda (a+M)}f\, \mathrm{d}V$. Thus $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (p)\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda (p+M)}f\, \mathrm{d}V$, and $w=p+M$ has the required properties. $\square$

title: 15.12.6 The normalized equation
section: 15.12 Equations in a prescribed ordinary type
text: For the normalized equation we let the positive exponent tend to zero. Bounded comparison controls the normalizing constants from above, while the lower density estimate of lemma 15.12.2 keeps them away from zero. The common barriers then give convergence of the Monge–Ampère measures and keep the limit in the prescribed type. of theorem 15.12.1 , part (2). For each $j\geq 1$, part (1) gives $u_ j\sim \varphi $ with \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j)=\mathrm{e}^{u_ j/j}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Write $M_ j=\sup _ Xu_ j$, $v_ j=u_ j-M_ j$ and $c_ j=\mathrm{e}^{M_ j/j}$. Let $h$ be a bounded normalized solution of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (h)=\alpha f\, \mathrm{d}V$, with $\alpha >0$, given by theorem 15.3.5 . For $H_ j=h+\| h\| _\infty +j\log \alpha $ we have \[  \mathrm{e}^{-H_ j/j}\mathrm{MA}_\theta (H_ j) =\mathrm{e}^{-(h+\| h\| _\infty )/j}f\, \mathrm{d}V \leq f\, \mathrm{d}V =\mathrm{e}^{-u_ j/j}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j).  \] The bounded function $H_ j$ admits a smaller-background envelope, and $u_ j\preceq H_ j$, so corollary 15.2.3 gives $u_ j\leq H_ j$. In particular, \[  0<c_ j\leq \alpha \exp (2\| h\| _\infty /j).  \] The lower density bound of lemma 15.12.2 , applied to $v_ j$ with $q=p$, gives \[  b_ p\leq \| c_ j\mathrm{e}^{v_ j/j}f\| _ p\leq c_ j\| f\| _ p,  \] so the $c_ j$ are also bounded away from zero. Since $\sup _ Xv_ j=0$ and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (v_ j)=c_ j\mathrm{e}^{v_ j/j}f\, \mathrm{d}V\leq C f\, \mathrm{d}V$, theorem 15.12.3 gives $\varphi -C'\leq v_ j\leq \varphi $. Extract a subsequence with $v_ j\to v$ in $L^1(X)$ and $c_ j\to c>0$. By corollary 15.9.4 , the convergence holds in capacity, $v\sim \varphi $, and the Monge–Ampère measures converge weakly. Meanwhile, lemma 5.44.5 gives \[  \int _ X|\mathrm{e}^{v_ j/j}-1|f\, \mathrm{d}V\longrightarrow 0.  \] Thus the right-hand sides converge in total variation to $cf\, \mathrm{d}V$, and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (v)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$. For the uniqueness of the constant, suppose that $a,b\sim \varphi $ solve the normalized equation with constants $c_ a<c_ b$. For every real $t$, \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (a) =\frac{c_ a}{c_ b}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (b+t),  \] so theorem 15.2.2 gives $a\geq b+t$. title: 15.13 Comparison above a strict singular barrier
search_title: Comparison above a strict singular barrier
section: 15.13 Comparison above a strict singular barrier
text: From now on, $\theta $ is an arbitrary smooth big real $(1,1)$-form. Then $V_\theta $ may be unbounded, and the smaller-background construction used above is no longer available. Its role is taken by a strict analytic barrier. When two potentials bounded below by the barrier are compared, adding a small multiple of the barrier forces a negative infimum of their difference to be attained away from its pole set, and there a local comparison principle rules it out. Since $\theta $ is big, theorem 5.36.5 provides $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with analytic singularities and a smooth remainder after resolution such that $\theta _\rho \geq \kappa \omega $ for some $\kappa >0$. Replacing $\omega $ by a small positive multiple and subtracting a constant from $\rho $, we fix such a $\rho $ with $\rho \leq 0$ and $\theta _\rho \geq \omega $. Put $Z=\{ \rho =-\infty \} $ and $\Omega =X\setminus Z$. From now on until the end of section 15.18 , these data remain fixed, and $\Omega $ always denotes this open set rather than an auxiliary Hermitian form. A potential bounded below by $\rho -C$ is locally bounded on $\Omega $, and there its extended Monge–Ampère measure agrees with the local bounded product. Lemma 15.13.1 . E6E5D71344DD Let $B\Subset \Omega $ be a coordinate ball, and let $u,v$ be bounded $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions on $B$. Assume \[  \liminf _{x\to \partial B}(u-v)(x)\geq 0, \qquad \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\leq \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v).  \] Then $u\geq v$ on $B$. Proof. Fix $\varepsilon >0$ and set $v_\varepsilon =\max (u,v-\varepsilon )$, which equals $u$ near the boundary. We claim that \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\leq \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\varepsilon )  \] throughout $B$. On $\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} $ this follows from locality, since $v_\varepsilon =u$ there. On $\{ u\leq v-\varepsilon \} $ it follows from ordered contact and from the assumed inequality, which applies because this set is contained in $\{ u<v\} $. Let $q$ be the plurisubharmonic envelope on $B$ of the obstacle $u-v_\varepsilon $, in the sense of ( 5.27.8 ). This obstacle is bounded, quasi-continuous and zero near the boundary. Hence it lies between $Ah$ and zero for a sufficiently large $A$, where $h<0$ is a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic defining function for the ball. Thus $q$ tends to zero at the boundary, and ( 5.27.8 ) shows that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n$ is carried by $D=\{ q=u-v_\varepsilon \} $. Since $q\leq u-v_\varepsilon $ quasi-everywhere, the canonical representatives satisfy $q+v_\varepsilon \leq u$. Ordered contact, followed by the measure inequality above, yields \[  \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_\theta (q+v_\varepsilon ) \leq \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u) \leq \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\varepsilon ).  \] The positive expansion of $(\theta _{v_\varepsilon }+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n$ contains both $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\varepsilon )$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n$. Thus $\mathbf1_ D(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n=0$, and since $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n$ is carried by $D$, we get $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n=0$. The classical Bedford–Taylor comparison principle for bounded plurisubharmonic functions with zero boundary values implies $q=0$. Consequently $u\geq v_\varepsilon $, first quasi-everywhere and then everywhere. Finally let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. $\square$ Theorem 15.13.2 . F71978C42841 Suppose $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy, for constants $C_0,C_1\geq 0$, \[  \min (u,v)\geq \rho -C_0,\qquad v\leq u+C_1.  \] If, for some $0\leq c<1$, \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\leq c\, \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v),  \] then $u\geq v$. The measures in the theorem need not have finite total mass. Proof. We first modify the barrier. Let $r=a\rho -A$, where $a>1$ is sufficiently close to one and $A$ is sufficiently large. Since \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a\rho )=a\theta _\rho +(1-a)\theta ,  \] we can arrange $\theta _ r\geq \omega /2$ and $r-v\leq -1$, and moreover $u-r\to +\infty $ at $Z$, because $u-r\geq (a-1)(-\rho )+A-C_0$. When $Z$ is empty, the last property is not needed. Choose $0<\delta <1$ with $(1-\delta )^ n>c$, and put $v_\delta =(1-\delta )v+\delta r$. Then \[  u-v_\delta \geq \delta (u-r)-(1-\delta )C_1.  \] Suppose that the infimum $m$ of $u-v_\delta $ on $\Omega $ were negative. Since $u-v_\delta \to +\infty $ at $Z$, a sequence $x_ j$ along which $u-v_\delta $ tends to $m$ has a subsequence converging to a point $x_0\in \Omega $. Choose a coordinate ball $B\Subset \Omega $ centered at $x_0$, identify it with $\{ |z|<1\} $, and take \[  \eta (z)=b(1-|z|^2),\qquad 0<b<1, \qquad \omega /2+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta \geq 0.  \] The function $w=v_\delta +\delta \eta +m$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic on $B$, and $\liminf _{\partial B}(u-w)\geq 0$ because $\eta $ vanishes on $\partial B$. Also \[  w-v=\delta (r-v+\eta )+m<0.  \] Thus $\{ u<w\} \subset \{ u<v\} $, and positivity of mixed products gives on this set \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\leq c\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)\leq (1-\delta )^ n\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)\leq \mathrm{MA}_\theta (w).  \] By lemma 15.13.1 , $u\geq w$ on $B$. Evaluating at $x_ j$ gives $u(x_ j)-v_\delta (x_ j)\geq m+\delta \eta (x_ j)$, which contradicts $\eta (x_0)>0$ in the limit. Hence $u\geq v_\delta $ on $\Omega $. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ along values with $(1-\delta )^ n>c$, we obtain $u\geq v$ on $\Omega $, and lemma 5.24.3 extends this inequality to $X$. $\square$ Corollary 15.13.3 . 24CD508AEB8D Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $u,v\geq \rho -C$ for some $C\geq 0$ and $u\sim v$. If $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\leq c\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)$ for some $c\geq 0$, then $c\geq 1$. If $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda (u-v)}\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)$ for some $\lambda >0$, then $u\geq v$. In particular, let $\mu $ be a positive measure. Among potentials bounded below by $\rho $ minus a constant, each ordinary singularity type contains at most one solution of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}\mu $, and the constant $c>0$ in $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=c\mu $ is uniquely determined within each type. Proof. If $c<1$, apply the theorem to $u$ and $v+A$ for every constant $A>0$; the constants in its hypotheses may depend on $A$. The resulting inequality $u\geq v+A$ for all $A$ is impossible. For the second assertion, fix $a>0$ and restrict the measure inequality to $\{ u<v-a\} $. title: Lemma 15.13.1
section: 15.13 Comparison above a strict singular barrier
text: Lemma 15.13.1 . E6E5D71344DD Let $B\Subset \Omega $ be a coordinate ball, and let $u,v$ be bounded $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions on $B$. Assume \[  \liminf _{x\to \partial B}(u-v)(x)\geq 0, \qquad \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\leq \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v).  \] Then $u\geq v$ on $B$. Proof. Fix $\varepsilon >0$ and set $v_\varepsilon =\max (u,v-\varepsilon )$, which equals $u$ near the boundary. We claim that \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\leq \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\varepsilon )  \] throughout $B$. On $\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} $ this follows from locality, since $v_\varepsilon =u$ there. On $\{ u\leq v-\varepsilon \} $ it follows from ordered contact and from the assumed inequality, which applies because this set is contained in $\{ u<v\} $. Let $q$ be the plurisubharmonic envelope on $B$ of the obstacle $u-v_\varepsilon $, in the sense of ( 5.27.8 ). This obstacle is bounded, quasi-continuous and zero near the boundary. Hence it lies between $Ah$ and zero for a sufficiently large $A$, where $h<0$ is a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic defining function for the ball. Thus $q$ tends to zero at the boundary, and ( 5.27.8 ) shows that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n$ is carried by $D=\{ q=u-v_\varepsilon \} $. Since $q\leq u-v_\varepsilon $ quasi-everywhere, the canonical representatives satisfy $q+v_\varepsilon \leq u$. Ordered contact, followed by the measure inequality above, yields \[  \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_\theta (q+v_\varepsilon ) \leq \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u) \leq \mathbf1_ D\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\varepsilon ).  \] The positive expansion of $(\theta _{v_\varepsilon }+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n$ contains both $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\varepsilon )$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n$. Thus $\mathbf1_ D(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n=0$, and since $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n$ is carried by $D$, we get $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n=0$. The classical Bedford–Taylor comparison principle for bounded plurisubharmonic functions with zero boundary values implies $q=0$. Consequently $u\geq v_\varepsilon $, first quasi-everywhere and then everywhere. Finally let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. $\square$

title: Theorem 15.13.2
section: 15.13 Comparison above a strict singular barrier
text: Theorem 15.13.2 . F71978C42841 Suppose $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy, for constants $C_0,C_1\geq 0$, \[  \min (u,v)\geq \rho -C_0,\qquad v\leq u+C_1.  \] If, for some $0\leq c<1$, \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\leq c\, \mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v),  \] then $u\geq v$. Proof. We first modify the barrier. Let $r=a\rho -A$, where $a>1$ is sufficiently close to one and $A$ is sufficiently large. Since \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a\rho )=a\theta _\rho +(1-a)\theta ,  \] we can arrange $\theta _ r\geq \omega /2$ and $r-v\leq -1$, and moreover $u-r\to +\infty $ at $Z$, because $u-r\geq (a-1)(-\rho )+A-C_0$. When $Z$ is empty, the last property is not needed. Choose $0<\delta <1$ with $(1-\delta )^ n>c$, and put $v_\delta =(1-\delta )v+\delta r$. Then \[  u-v_\delta \geq \delta (u-r)-(1-\delta )C_1.  \] Suppose that the infimum $m$ of $u-v_\delta $ on $\Omega $ were negative. Since $u-v_\delta \to +\infty $ at $Z$, a sequence $x_ j$ along which $u-v_\delta $ tends to $m$ has a subsequence converging to a point $x_0\in \Omega $. Choose a coordinate ball $B\Subset \Omega $ centered at $x_0$, identify it with $\{ |z|<1\} $, and take \[  \eta (z)=b(1-|z|^2),\qquad 0<b<1, \qquad \omega /2+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta \geq 0.  \] The function $w=v_\delta +\delta \eta +m$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic on $B$, and $\liminf _{\partial B}(u-w)\geq 0$ because $\eta $ vanishes on $\partial B$. Also \[  w-v=\delta (r-v+\eta )+m<0.  \] Thus $\{ u<w\} \subset \{ u<v\} $, and positivity of mixed products gives on this set \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\leq c\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)\leq (1-\delta )^ n\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)\leq \mathrm{MA}_\theta (w).  \] By lemma 15.13.1 , $u\geq w$ on $B$. Evaluating at $x_ j$ gives $u(x_ j)-v_\delta (x_ j)\geq m+\delta \eta (x_ j)$, which contradicts $\eta (x_0)>0$ in the limit. Hence $u\geq v_\delta $ on $\Omega $. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ along values with $(1-\delta )^ n>c$, we obtain $u\geq v$ on $\Omega $, and lemma 5.24.3 extends this inequality to $X$. $\square$

title: 15.14 Subsolutions and the Gauduchon trace
text: The strict barrier also yields subsolutions within a bounded distance of any reference between $\rho $ and zero. The curvature estimate comes from composing a convex function with the difference between the reference and a barrier-based subsolution, which produces a convex combination of positive currents. Pairing the equation with a Gauduchon metric then bounds the normalizing constants through a linear trace. Lemma 15.14.1 . 869D3138741D Fix $p>1$ and $L>0$. There is $m>0$ such that, whenever \[  \rho \leq \eta \leq 0,\quad \eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ), \qquad g\geq 0,\quad \| g\| _{L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)}\leq L,  \] there exists $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with \[  \eta \leq v\leq \eta +1,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)\geq m g\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The constant $m$ depends only on the fixed geometry and on $\rho ,p,L$. Proof. Choose $1<q<p$. By Hölder's inequality and the finiteness of all polynomial moments of the fixed quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\rho $, the functions $h=g(2-\rho )^{2n}$ have uniformly bounded $L^ q$ norms. Lemma 15.3.1 , applied in the Hermitian background $\omega $, gives $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $-1\leq s\leq 0$ and \[  \omega _ s^ n\geq m h\, \mathrm{d}V  \] for a fixed $m>0$. Put $u_1=\rho +s$. Then $\theta _{u_1}\geq \omega _ s$ and $u_1\leq \rho \leq \eta $. On $\Omega $ define \[  t=1+\eta -u_1,\qquad v=\eta +t^{-1},  \] so that $1\leq t\leq 2-\rho $. Lemma 5.28.13 , applied on relatively compact subsets of $\Omega $ with $a=\eta $, $h=u_1$ and $\chi (x)=(1-x)^{-1}$, gives \[  \theta _ v=(1-t^{-2})\theta _\eta +t^{-2}\theta _{u_1} +2t^{-3}\, \mathrm{d}(\eta -u_1)\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(\eta -u_1) \geq t^{-2}\theta _{u_1}.  \] Since $\eta \leq v\leq \eta +1$, lemma 5.24.7 extends $v$ across $Z$, and the bounds extend by lemma 5.24.3 . On $\Omega $, positivity of the local products gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)\geq t^{-2n}\theta _{u_1}^ n \geq (2-\rho )^{-2n}\omega _ s^ n \geq m g\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Neither side charges $Z$, so the inequality holds on $X$. $\square$ Proposition 15.14.2 . 0A5580561320 Let $\gamma $ be a Gauduchon metric on $X$, write $\gamma ^ n=G\, \mathrm{d}V$, and put \[  T_\gamma =\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] Then $T_\gamma >0$. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies $u\geq \rho -C$ and $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\geq F\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $F\geq 0$, then B100E71E56DE 15.14.3 \begin{equation}  \int _ X F^{1/n}G^{1-1/n}\, \mathrm{d}V\leq T_\gamma . \end{equation} Consequently, let $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, be nonzero, and let $\lambda >0$. Every solution of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ that is bounded below by $\rho $ minus a constant satisfies $\sup _ Xu\leq C'$, where $C'$ depends only on $\theta $, $\gamma $, $f$ and $\lambda $. Moreover, if $v_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $j\geq 1$, and constants $C_ j\geq 0$ and $c_ j>0$ satisfy \[  \sup _ Xv_ j=0,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_ j)=c_ j \mathrm{e}^{v_ j/j}f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad v_ j\geq \rho -C_ j,  \] then the constants $c_ j$ are uniformly bounded above. Proof. The current $\theta _ u\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ is linear in $\theta _ u$, so it is a globally defined positive current, even at $Z$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\gamma ^{n-1}=0$, Stokes' theorem in the sense of currents gives \[  \int _ X\theta _ u\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] Applied to $\rho $, this identity proves $T_\gamma \geq \int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}>0$. On $\Omega $, lemma 5.28.7 , applied to $\theta _ u$ and $\gamma $, gives \[  \theta _ u\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}\geq F^{1/n}G^{1-1/n}\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Exhausting $\Omega $ and using positivity of the global trace measure, we obtain ( 15.14.3 ), since the complement $Z$ has zero volume. For the exponential equation, write $a=\sup _ Xu$ and $w=u-a$. The estimate becomes \[  \mathrm{e}^{\lambda a/n}\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{\lambda w/n}f^{1/n}G^{1-1/n}\, \mathrm{d}V \leq T_\gamma .  \] The integral has a positive lower bound over all normalized $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Otherwise, normalized compactness would give a sequence of such $w$ with integrals tending to zero and converging almost everywhere to a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function; since $w\leq 0$ and $f^{1/n}G^{1-1/n}$ is integrable, dominated convergence would give a strictly positive limit integral, a contradiction. This bounds $a$ from above. For the last assertion, the same estimate contains the factors $c_ j^{1/n}$ and $\mathrm{e}^{v_ j/(jn)}$. If the integrals $\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{v_ j/(jn)}f^{1/n}G^{1-1/n}\, \mathrm{d}V$ tended to zero along a subsequence with $j\to \infty $, normalized compactness and almost-everywhere convergence would give $v_ j/j\to 0$ almost everywhere along a further subsequence. Dominated convergence would then give the positive limit $\int _ Xf^{1/n}G^{1-1/n}\, \mathrm{d}V$. This contradiction bounds $c_ j$ for all large $j$, and each of the finitely many remaining constants is finite. Neither argument uses the total Monge–Ampère mass. $\square$

title: 15.15 Stability above a strict barrier
text: The subsolutions of lemma 15.14.1 stay within a bounded distance of a given reference. With them, the proof of theorem 15.4.1 extends to unbounded potentials lying above $\rho $, and the resulting estimate is uniform over all references between $\rho $ and zero. For a fixed reference, it upgrades $L^1$ compactness of solutions to uniform convergence of their differences on $\Omega $. Theorem 15.15.1 . 668D07ADFF44 Fix $C_0,L>0$, $p>1$, and \[  0<\gamma <\frac{p-1}{np+p-1}.  \] Let $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $\rho \leq \eta \leq 0$, and suppose that $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies \[  \eta -C_0\leq u\leq \eta ,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=f\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad 0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V), \quad \| f\| _ p\leq L.  \] There is a constant $C$, depending only on the fixed geometry and on $\rho ,C_0,L,p,\gamma $, such that every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $v\leq \eta $ satisfies 6B6C204B9D9E 15.15.2 \begin{equation}  \sup _\Omega (v-u)_+ \leq C\left(\int _\Omega (v-u)_+\, \mathrm{d}V\right)^\gamma . \end{equation} In particular, the constant does not depend on the reference $\eta $, and the comparison potential $v$ need not have the ordinary singularity type of $\eta $. The difference $v-u$ is evaluated on $\Omega $, where $u$ and $\eta $ are locally bounded; since $Z$ has zero volume, the integral is the same as over $X$. Since $Z$ is pluripolar, the resulting inequality $v\leq u+C\bigl (\int _\Omega (v-u)_+\, \mathrm{d}V\bigr )^\gamma $ on $\Omega $ extends to the canonical representatives on all of $X$. Proof. Replacing $v$ by $\max (v,u)$, we may assume $\eta -C_0\leq u\leq v\leq \eta $, so that $0\leq v-u\leq C_0$ on $\Omega $.  Fix $q\in (1,p)$ and $\delta >0$, and put \[  E_\delta =\{ u<v-\delta \} \cap \Omega ,\qquad g_\delta =\mathbf1_{E_\delta }f,\qquad m_\delta =\| g_\delta \| _ q.  \] When $m_\delta >0$, lemma 15.14.1 , followed by subtracting one from its potential, gives $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and a fixed $b>0$ such that \[  \eta -1\leq h\leq \eta ,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (h)\geq b\, g_\delta /m_\delta \, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The constant $b$ is uniform in $\eta $, because the auxiliary density has $L^ q$ norm one and the strict barrier is fixed. If $0<m_\delta <b/2$, set \[  t=(2m_\delta /b)^{1/n},\qquad w=(1-t)v+th-\delta -C_0t.  \] Since $h-v\leq C_0$, we have $w\leq v-\delta $, so the set $\{ u<w\} \cap \Omega $ is contained in $E_\delta $. On this set the local expansion into positive mixed products gives $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w)\geq t^ n\mathrm{MA}_\theta (h)\geq 2\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$. Both potentials are bounded below by $\rho $ minus a constant, and $w\leq u+C_0$, so theorem 15.13.2 applies and gives $u\geq w$. It follows that \[  v-u\leq \delta +C_0t+t(v-h)\leq \delta +(C_0+1)t.  \] If $m_\delta =0$, we apply the same domination theorem with coefficient zero to $u$ and $v-\delta $. If $m_\delta \geq b/2$, we use $v-u\leq C_0$. In all cases, \[  \sup _\Omega (v-u)\leq \delta +C_1m_\delta ^{1/n}.  \] Write $I=\int _\Omega (v-u)\, \mathrm{d}V$. If $I=0$, the canonical potentials agree. Otherwise Hölder's and Chebyshev's inequalities give \[  m_\delta \leq L(I/\delta )^{(p-q)/(pq)}.  \] For $0<I\leq 1$, the choice $\delta =I^{(p-q)/(npq+p-q)}$ yields the exponent $\gamma _ q=(p-q)/(npq+p-q)$. We choose $q>1$ so close to one that $\gamma _ q>\gamma $. The case $I>1$ follows from the bound $v-u\leq C_0$. This proves ( 15.15.2 ). $\square$ Corollary 15.15.3 . 131F17206F6A Fix $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\rho \leq \eta \leq 0$, constants $C_0,L>0$, and $p>1$. Consider the family of potentials $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfying \[  \eta -C_0\leq u\leq \eta ,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=f_ u\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad 0\leq f_ u\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V), \quad \| f_ u\| _ p\leq L.  \] This family is compact for uniform convergence of differences on $\Omega $. If $u_ j$ belong to the family and $u_ j\to u$ in $L^1$, then $u$ belongs to the family and \[  \sup _\Omega |u_ j-u|\leq C\| u_ j-u\| _{L^1(\mathrm{d}V)}^\gamma \longrightarrow 0  \] for every exponent $\gamma $ as in theorem 15.15.1 . Moreover, $f_{u_ j}$ converges weakly to $f_ u$ in $L^ p$. Proof. Applying the theorem in both orders to $u_ j$ and $u_ k$, with the common reference $\eta $, we see that an $L^1$-Cauchy sequence in the family is uniformly Cauchy in differences on $\Omega $. Its uniform limit on $\Omega $ is locally $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and agrees almost everywhere, hence everywhere for the canonical representatives, with the $L^1$ limit $u$. The bounds $\eta -C_0\leq u\leq \eta $ hold on all of $X$. Letting $k\to \infty $ in the pairwise estimate proves the quantitative bound, before any equation for $u$ is used. The densities form a bounded set in the reflexive space $L^ p$. Let $f$ be the weak limit of a subsequence $f_{u_{j_ k}}$. Since the potentials are locally bounded and converge locally uniformly on $\Omega $, Bedford–Taylor continuity, which holds also for the smooth nonclosed background, gives $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=f\, \mathrm{d}V$ on $\Omega $. Neither measure charges the analytic set $Z$, so this equality holds on $X$. Positivity and weak lower semicontinuity of the norm give $f\geq 0$ and $\| f\| _ p\leq L$. Thus every weak cluster point equals the density $f_ u$ of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$, which proves weak convergence of the whole sequence. Finally, the common bounds by $\eta $ and $\eta -C_0$ give $L^1$ compactness of the family, by the compactness of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions, and the preceding argument upgrades each convergent subsequence to uniform convergence of differences on $\Omega $. $\square$ For solutions with minimal singularities, normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$, we take $\eta =V_\theta $. Then $\rho \leq V_\theta \leq 0$, and every normalized comparison potential $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies $v\leq V_\theta $, as the theorem requires.

title: Theorem 15.15.1
text: Theorem 15.15.1 . 668D07ADFF44 Fix $C_0,L>0$, $p>1$, and \[  0<\gamma <\frac{p-1}{np+p-1}.  \] Let $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $\rho \leq \eta \leq 0$, and suppose that $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies \[  \eta -C_0\leq u\leq \eta ,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=f\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad 0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V), \quad \| f\| _ p\leq L.  \] There is a constant $C$, depending only on the fixed geometry and on $\rho ,C_0,L,p,\gamma $, such that every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $v\leq \eta $ satisfies 6B6C204B9D9E 15.15.2 \begin{equation}  \sup _\Omega (v-u)_+ \leq C\left(\int _\Omega (v-u)_+\, \mathrm{d}V\right)^\gamma . \end{equation} Proof. Replacing $v$ by $\max (v,u)$, we may assume $\eta -C_0\leq u\leq v\leq \eta $, so that $0\leq v-u\leq C_0$ on $\Omega $.  Fix $q\in (1,p)$ and $\delta >0$, and put \[  E_\delta =\{ u<v-\delta \} \cap \Omega ,\qquad g_\delta =\mathbf1_{E_\delta }f,\qquad m_\delta =\| g_\delta \| _ q.  \] When $m_\delta >0$, lemma 15.14.1 , followed by subtracting one from its potential, gives $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and a fixed $b>0$ such that \[  \eta -1\leq h\leq \eta ,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (h)\geq b\, g_\delta /m_\delta \, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The constant $b$ is uniform in $\eta $, because the auxiliary density has $L^ q$ norm one and the strict barrier is fixed. If $0<m_\delta <b/2$, set \[  t=(2m_\delta /b)^{1/n},\qquad w=(1-t)v+th-\delta -C_0t.  \] Since $h-v\leq C_0$, we have $w\leq v-\delta $, so the set $\{ u<w\} \cap \Omega $ is contained in $E_\delta $. On this set the local expansion into positive mixed products gives $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (w)\geq t^ n\mathrm{MA}_\theta (h)\geq 2\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$. Both potentials are bounded below by $\rho $ minus a constant, and $w\leq u+C_0$, so theorem 15.13.2 applies and gives $u\geq w$. It follows that \[  v-u\leq \delta +C_0t+t(v-h)\leq \delta +(C_0+1)t.  \] If $m_\delta =0$, we apply the same domination theorem with coefficient zero to $u$ and $v-\delta $. If $m_\delta \geq b/2$, we use $v-u\leq C_0$. In all cases, \[  \sup _\Omega (v-u)\leq \delta +C_1m_\delta ^{1/n}.  \] Write $I=\int _\Omega (v-u)\, \mathrm{d}V$. If $I=0$, the canonical potentials agree. Otherwise Hölder's and Chebyshev's inequalities give \[  m_\delta \leq L(I/\delta )^{(p-q)/(pq)}.  \] For $0<I\leq 1$, the choice $\delta =I^{(p-q)/(npq+p-q)}$ yields the exponent $\gamma _ q=(p-q)/(npq+p-q)$. We choose $q>1$ so close to one that $\gamma _ q>\gamma $. The case $I>1$ follows from the bound $v-u\leq C_0$. This proves ( 15.15.2 ). $\square$
