title: Corollary 15.15.3
text: Corollary 15.15.3 . 131F17206F6A Fix $\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\rho \leq \eta \leq 0$, constants $C_0,L>0$, and $p>1$. Consider the family of potentials $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfying \[  \eta -C_0\leq u\leq \eta ,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=f_ u\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad 0\leq f_ u\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V), \quad \| f_ u\| _ p\leq L.  \] This family is compact for uniform convergence of differences on $\Omega $. If $u_ j$ belong to the family and $u_ j\to u$ in $L^1$, then $u$ belongs to the family and \[  \sup _\Omega |u_ j-u|\leq C\| u_ j-u\| _{L^1(\mathrm{d}V)}^\gamma \longrightarrow 0  \] for every exponent $\gamma $ as in theorem 15.15.1 . Moreover, $f_{u_ j}$ converges weakly to $f_ u$ in $L^ p$. Proof. Applying the theorem in both orders to $u_ j$ and $u_ k$, with the common reference $\eta $, we see that an $L^1$-Cauchy sequence in the family is uniformly Cauchy in differences on $\Omega $. Its uniform limit on $\Omega $ is locally $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and agrees almost everywhere, hence everywhere for the canonical representatives, with the $L^1$ limit $u$. The bounds $\eta -C_0\leq u\leq \eta $ hold on all of $X$. Letting $k\to \infty $ in the pairwise estimate proves the quantitative bound, before any equation for $u$ is used. The densities form a bounded set in the reflexive space $L^ p$. Let $f$ be the weak limit of a subsequence $f_{u_{j_ k}}$. Since the potentials are locally bounded and converge locally uniformly on $\Omega $, Bedford–Taylor continuity, which holds also for the smooth nonclosed background, gives $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=f\, \mathrm{d}V$ on $\Omega $. Neither measure charges the analytic set $Z$, so this equality holds on $X$. Positivity and weak lower semicontinuity of the norm give $f\geq 0$ and $\| f\| _ p\leq L$. Thus every weak cluster point equals the density $f_ u$ of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$, which proves weak convergence of the whole sequence. Finally, the common bounds by $\eta $ and $\eta -C_0$ give $L^1$ compactness of the family, by the compactness of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions, and the preceding argument upgrades each convergent subsequence to uniform convergence of differences on $\Omega $. $\square$

title: 15.16 Minimal singularities in an arbitrary big background
search_title: Minimal singularities in an arbitrary big background
section: 15.16 Minimal singularities in an arbitrary big background
text: We now solve the equations in the ordinary singularity type of $V_\theta $. Demailly's regularization approximates $V_\theta $ by strict potentials with analytic singularities. On a resolution of these singularities, the corresponding equations become equations in a semipositive big background, which we have already solved. The solutions satisfy bounds relative to the approximating singularities that are uniform in the approximation, and upper and lower envelopes then produce a solution with minimal singularities. For the normalized equation, the normalized exponential solutions lie in a common interval below $V_\theta $, so the compactness theorem of the preceding section applies directly. Since $\rho \leq 0$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, it is a competitor for $V_\theta $, and hence $\rho \leq V_\theta \leq 0$. We use the analytic regularization of theorem 5.36.5 in its resolved form. Lemma 15.16.1 . 154DE11154EE Let $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $\theta _\psi \geq a\omega $ for some $a>0$, and suppose that $\psi $ has a smooth remainder after resolution, as in theorem 5.36.5 . For every nonzero $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, and every $\lambda >0$, there exists $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\sim \psi $ such that \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Proof. Let $\pi :Y\to X$ be a modification resolving the singularities of $\psi $. The pulled-back current has the form \[  \pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\pi ^*\psi =\beta +[D],  \] where $D$ is an effective real divisor, $[D]$ is its current of integration, and $\beta $ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $Y$. Off $D$ we have $\beta \geq a\pi ^*\omega $, and by continuity this inequality holds everywhere. In particular, $\beta $ is semipositive. We check that $\beta $ is big. For a blowup with smooth center and exceptional divisor $E$, choose a metric on $\mathcal O(-E)$ whose curvature is positive in the directions tangent to the projective fibers. Along $E$, the pullback of a Hermitian metric is positive in the complementary directions. Consequently, its sum with a sufficiently small positive multiple of this curvature form is a Hermitian metric: positivity holds first along $E$, then on a neighborhood of $E$, and finally on the compact complement, where the pullback is already positive. Iterating over the blowups, we obtain an effective real exceptional divisor $F$, with logarithmic potential $\zeta $, and a smooth Hermitian form $\kappa $ such that \[  \pi ^*\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\zeta =\kappa +[F].  \] At each step of the iteration, we pull back the smooth positive form obtained so far, apply the construction for one blowup, and add the pullback of the previous divisor to the new positive multiple of $E$. Hence $\beta +a\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\zeta \geq a\kappa $, so $\beta $ is big. This argument only involves Hermitian metrics and never requires a closed positive form on $Y$. Fix a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V_ Y$ on $Y$, and write $\pi ^*\mathrm{d}V=J\, \mathrm{d}V_ Y$. The function $J$ is smooth, nonnegative and bounded, and it is positive off the exceptional locus. Define \[  H=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda \pi ^*\psi }(f\circ \pi )J.  \] This function is nonzero and belongs to $L^ p(\mathrm{d}V_ Y)$. Indeed, $\psi $ is bounded above, and the change of variables formula gives \[  \int _ Y|(f\circ \pi )J|^ p\, \mathrm{d}V_ Y \leq \| J\| _\infty ^{p-1}\int _ X|f|^ p\, \mathrm{d}V;  \] the analytic exceptional sets do not affect these integrals. Theorem 15.3.3 , applied on $Y$ in the semipositive big background $\beta $, gives a bounded $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\beta )$ with \[  \mathrm{MA}_\beta (s)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda s}H\, \mathrm{d}V_ Y.  \] The function $\pi ^*\psi +s$ is $\pi ^*\theta $-plurisubharmonic, because the corresponding current is $\beta _ s+[D]\geq 0$, where $\beta _ s=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s$. By theorem 9.11.5 it descends to some $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and $u\sim \psi $ because $s$ is bounded. Off the exceptional set and the pole set of $\psi $, the change of variables formula gives the required equation. Neither the extended measure on the left nor the measure $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ on the right charges these analytic sets, so the equation holds on all of $X$. $\square$ Theorem 15.16.2 . 352C3567BAAD Let $\theta $ be any smooth big real $(1,1)$-form and let $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, be nonzero. For every $\lambda >0$ there is a unique $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ such that \[  u\sim V_\theta ,\qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Proof. Step 1: approximating singularity types. Apply theorem 5.36.5 to $V_\theta $. Set $\delta _ j=2^{-j}$ and pass to a subsequence whose curvature errors are at most $\delta _ j$. Denote its potentials by $\widetilde\psi _ j$; thus $\widetilde\psi _ j\downarrow V_\theta $ and $\theta _{\widetilde\psi _ j}\geq -\delta _ j\omega $. Set \[  a_ j=(1-\delta _ j)\sup _ X\widetilde\psi _ j\geq 0, \qquad \psi _ j=(1-\delta _ j)\widetilde\psi _ j+\delta _ j\rho -a_ j.  \] By Hartogs' lemma, $\sup _ X\widetilde\psi _ j\to \sup _ XV_\theta =0$, so $a_ j\to 0$. A common resolution of the singularities of $\widetilde\psi _ j$ and $\rho $ shows that $\psi _ j$ has a smooth remainder after resolution. Moreover, A8E86D90F114 15.16.3 \begin{equation}  \theta _{\psi _ j}\geq \delta _ j^2\omega , \qquad (1-\delta _ j)V_\theta +\delta _ j\rho -a_ j \leq \psi _ j\leq V_\theta . \end{equation} The upper inequality holds because $\psi _ j$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and nonpositive. Subtracting $a_ j$ explicitly keeps the normalization separate from the fixed barrier $\rho $. Step 2: uniform bounds. By lemma 15.16.1 there are $u_ j\sim \psi _ j$ satisfying \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_ j)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Each $u_ j$ is bounded below by $\rho $ minus a constant depending on $j$, so proposition 15.14.2 gives a uniform upper bound for $\sup _ Xu_ j$. There is also a uniform lower bound. We apply lemma 15.14.1 with the barrier $\rho $ replaced by $\rho -1-\sup _ ja_ j$ and with the reference $\psi _ j-1$, which lies between this barrier and zero. The lemma gives $v_ j$ with $\psi _ j-1\leq v_ j\leq \psi _ j\leq 0$ and $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_ j)\geq mf\, \mathrm{d}V$, where $m>0$ is independent of $j$. Put $w_ j=v_ j+\lambda ^{-1}\log m$. Then \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (w_ j)\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda w_ j}f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad u_ j\sim w_ j\sim \psi _ j,  \] and the exponential order in corollary 15.13.3 gives $u_ j\geq w_ j$. Thus, for a uniform constant $C$, B66C3AA2C051 15.16.4 \begin{equation}  \psi _ j-C\leq u_ j\leq V_\theta +C. \end{equation} After extraction, $u_ j$ converges in $L^1$ and almost everywhere to a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function $u$, and the preceding bounds give $V_\theta -C\leq u\leq V_\theta +C$. Step 3: the equation for the limit. We identify the equation using envelopes. Put $A_ j=\sup _{k\geq j}a_ k$ and, for $N\geq j$, define \[  p_{j,N}=P_\theta (\min \{ u_ j,\ldots ,u_ N\} ),\qquad t_{j,N}=\max _{j\leq k\leq N}u_ k.  \] Both functions lie above the $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function \[  b_ j=(1-\delta _ j)V_\theta +\delta _ j\rho -C-A_ j,  \] which is a competitor for every $p_{j,N}$; in particular, no envelope is identically $-\infty $. All these functions are locally bounded on $\Omega $, uniformly in $j$ and $N$. Contact support (theorem 15.8.6 ), together with a partition of the contact set according to the first index of contact, gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p_{j,N})\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda p_{j,N}}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] No factor $N$ appears here: on each piece the envelope equals a single $u_ k$, and ordered contact bounds its measure by the measure of that $u_ k$. Similarly, locality and ordered contact for a finite maximum give \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (t_{j,N})\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda t_{j,N}}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Now let $N\to \infty $, and set $p_ j=\lim _ Np_{j,N}$ and $t_ j=(\lim _ Nt_{j,N})^*$. Continuity of local bounded products along monotone sequences passes both inequalities to these limits. Next, $p_ j$ increases to a regularized limit $p$, while $t_ j$ decreases to $u$ by Hartogs' lemma. The bound by $b_ j$ gives $p\sim V_\theta $, and $p\leq u$. A second application of the monotone continuity gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda p}f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] These inequalities hold on $\Omega $, and they extend across $Z$ because no measure involved charges $Z$. Thus $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda (p-u)}\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$, and the exponential order in corollary 15.13.3 gives $p\geq u$. Hence $p=u$, and the equation follows. Applying the same order in both directions proves uniqueness. Note that the Monge–Ampère operator was only ever applied along monotone sequences that are locally bounded on $\Omega $. $\square$ Lemma 15.16.5 . DA20F7BB0188 Under the hypotheses of theorem 15.16.2 , let $u_\lambda $ be the solution given there, and put \[  v_\lambda =u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda , \qquad c_\lambda =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda \sup _ Xu_\lambda }.  \] There are constants $B,C,m>0$, independent of $0<\lambda \leq 1$, such that 27B45CD3E8B0 15.16.6 \begin{equation}  V_\theta -B\leq v_\lambda \leq V_\theta , \qquad m\leq c_\lambda \leq C. \end{equation} Proof. The normalized potential satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\lambda )=c_\lambda \mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda } f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Fix a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ and write $\gamma ^ n=G\, \mathrm{d}V$. Since $v_\lambda \leq 0$ and $0<\lambda \leq 1$, ( 15.14.3 ) gives \[  c_\lambda ^{1/n} \int _ X\mathrm{e}^{v_\lambda /n}f^{1/n}G^{1-1/n}\, \mathrm{d}V \leq \int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] The integrals on the left have a positive lower bound independent of $\lambda $. Otherwise, the compactness of normalized quasi-plurisubharmonic functions would give an almost everywhere convergent sequence of the normalized $v_\lambda $ whose integrals tend to zero, with a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic limit; since $f$ is nonzero, dominated convergence would give a positive limit integral. Thus $c_\lambda \leq C$. To control the singularity type, we use uniform exponential integrability (lemma 5.26.2 ) and Hölder's inequality to choose $\varepsilon >0$ and $1<q<p$ such that $\| \mathrm{e}^{-\varepsilon v_\lambda }f\| _ q$ is uniformly bounded. Lemma 15.14.1 , applied with the reference $V_\theta -1$ and the barrier $\rho -1$, gives $\eta _\lambda \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with \[  V_\theta -1\leq \eta _\lambda \leq V_\theta , \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\eta _\lambda )\geq m\mathrm{e}^{-\varepsilon v_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V \geq mf\, \mathrm{d}V  \] for a fixed $m>0$. The scalar order in corollary 15.13.3 , together with $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\lambda )\leq c_\lambda f\, \mathrm{d}V$, gives $c_\lambda \geq m$. Set $D=\varepsilon ^{-1}\max \{ 0,\log (C/m)\} $ and $w_\lambda =\eta _\lambda -D$. Then \[  \mathrm{e}^{\varepsilon (w_\lambda -v_\lambda )}\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\lambda ) \leq m\mathrm{e}^{-\varepsilon v_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V \leq \mathrm{MA}_\theta (w_\lambda ),  \] since $\lambda v_\lambda \leq 0$ and $\eta _\lambda \leq 0$. The exponential order in corollary 15.13.3 gives $v_\lambda \geq w_\lambda $, which proves the uniform bounds with $B=1+D$. $\square$ Theorem 15.16.7 . B7C31259154B Under the assumptions of theorem 15.16.2 , there are $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, a constant $C>0$ and a uniquely determined $c>0$ such that \[  \sup _ Xv=0, \qquad V_\theta -C\leq v\leq V_\theta , \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] As in the semipositive case, only the constant $c$ is asserted to be unique, not the normalized potential. Proof. Apply lemma 15.16.5 with $\lambda =1/j$, and write $v_ j=v_{1/j}$ and $c_ j=c_{1/j}$. Extract a subsequence with $v_ j\to v$ in $L^1$ and almost everywhere, and with $c_ j\to c\in [m,C]$. The limit is normalized, $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, and has minimal singularities. The densities $c_ j\mathrm{e}^{v_ j/j}f$ have a common $L^ p$ bound. Hence corollary 15.15.3 , applied with the reference $V_\theta $, upgrades the convergence to uniform convergence of differences on $\Omega $ and identifies the weak $L^ p$ limit of these densities with the density of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)$. At almost every point, $v_ j$ converges to a finite value, so $v_ j/j\to 0$. Since $v_ j\leq 0$ and $c_ j\leq C$, dominated convergence gives $c_ j\mathrm{e}^{v_ j/j}f\to cf$ in $L^ p$. Therefore $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$. The uniqueness of the constant follows from corollary 15.13.3 . $\square$

All these functions are locally bounded on $\Omega $, uniformly in $j$ and $N$. Contact support (theorem 15.8.6 ), together with a partition of the contact set according to the first index of contact, gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p_{j,N})\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda p_{j,N}}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] No factor $N$ appears here: on each piece the envelope equals a single $u_ k$, and ordered contact bounds its measure by the measure of that $u_ k$. Similarly, locality and ordered contact for a finite maximum give \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (t_{j,N})\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda t_{j,N}}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Now let $N\to \infty $, and set $p_ j=\lim _ Np_{j,N}$ and $t_ j=(\lim _ Nt_{j,N})^*$. Continuity of local bounded products along monotone sequences passes both inequalities to these limits. Next, $p_ j$ increases to a regularized limit $p$, while $t_ j$ decreases to $u$ by Hartogs' lemma. The bound by $b_ j$ gives $p\sim V_\theta $, and $p\leq u$. A second application of the monotone continuity gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda p}f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] These inequalities hold on $\Omega $, and they extend across $Z$ because no measure involved charges $Z$. Thus $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (p)\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda (p-u)}\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$, and the exponential order in corollary 15.13.3 gives $p\geq u$. Hence $p=u$, and the equation follows. Applying the same order in both directions proves uniqueness. Note that the Monge–Ampère operator was only ever applied along monotone sequences that are locally bounded on $\Omega $. $\square$

title: Lemma 15.16.5
section: 15.16 Minimal singularities in an arbitrary big background
text: Lemma 15.16.5 . DA20F7BB0188 Under the hypotheses of theorem 15.16.2 , let $u_\lambda $ be the solution given there, and put \[  v_\lambda =u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda , \qquad c_\lambda =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda \sup _ Xu_\lambda }.  \] There are constants $B,C,m>0$, independent of $0<\lambda \leq 1$, such that 27B45CD3E8B0 15.16.6 \begin{equation}  V_\theta -B\leq v_\lambda \leq V_\theta , \qquad m\leq c_\lambda \leq C. \end{equation} Proof. The normalized potential satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\lambda )=c_\lambda \mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda } f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Fix a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ and write $\gamma ^ n=G\, \mathrm{d}V$. Since $v_\lambda \leq 0$ and $0<\lambda \leq 1$, ( 15.14.3 ) gives \[  c_\lambda ^{1/n} \int _ X\mathrm{e}^{v_\lambda /n}f^{1/n}G^{1-1/n}\, \mathrm{d}V \leq \int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] The integrals on the left have a positive lower bound independent of $\lambda $. Otherwise, the compactness of normalized quasi-plurisubharmonic functions would give an almost everywhere convergent sequence of the normalized $v_\lambda $ whose integrals tend to zero, with a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic limit; since $f$ is nonzero, dominated convergence would give a positive limit integral. Thus $c_\lambda \leq C$. To control the singularity type, we use uniform exponential integrability (lemma 5.26.2 ) and Hölder's inequality to choose $\varepsilon >0$ and $1<q<p$ such that $\| \mathrm{e}^{-\varepsilon v_\lambda }f\| _ q$ is uniformly bounded. Lemma 15.14.1 , applied with the reference $V_\theta -1$ and the barrier $\rho -1$, gives $\eta _\lambda \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with \[  V_\theta -1\leq \eta _\lambda \leq V_\theta , \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\eta _\lambda )\geq m\mathrm{e}^{-\varepsilon v_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V \geq mf\, \mathrm{d}V  \] for a fixed $m>0$. The scalar order in corollary 15.13.3 , together with $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\lambda )\leq c_\lambda f\, \mathrm{d}V$, gives $c_\lambda \geq m$. Set $D=\varepsilon ^{-1}\max \{ 0,\log (C/m)\} $ and $w_\lambda =\eta _\lambda -D$. Then \[  \mathrm{e}^{\varepsilon (w_\lambda -v_\lambda )}\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\lambda ) \leq m\mathrm{e}^{-\varepsilon v_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V \leq \mathrm{MA}_\theta (w_\lambda ),  \] since $\lambda v_\lambda \leq 0$ and $\eta _\lambda \leq 0$. The exponential order in corollary 15.13.3 gives $v_\lambda \geq w_\lambda $, which proves the uniform bounds with $B=1+D$. $\square$

title: Theorem 15.16.7
section: 15.16 Minimal singularities in an arbitrary big background
text: Theorem 15.16.7 . B7C31259154B Under the assumptions of theorem 15.16.2 , there are $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, a constant $C>0$ and a uniquely determined $c>0$ such that \[  \sup _ Xv=0, \qquad V_\theta -C\leq v\leq V_\theta , \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Proof. Apply lemma 15.16.5 with $\lambda =1/j$, and write $v_ j=v_{1/j}$ and $c_ j=c_{1/j}$. Extract a subsequence with $v_ j\to v$ in $L^1$ and almost everywhere, and with $c_ j\to c\in [m,C]$. The limit is normalized, $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, and has minimal singularities. The densities $c_ j\mathrm{e}^{v_ j/j}f$ have a common $L^ p$ bound. Hence corollary 15.15.3 , applied with the reference $V_\theta $, upgrades the convergence to uniform convergence of differences on $\Omega $ and identifies the weak $L^ p$ limit of these densities with the density of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)$. At almost every point, $v_ j$ converges to a finite value, so $v_ j/j\to 0$. Since $v_ j\leq 0$ and $c_ j\leq C$, dominated convergence gives $c_ j\mathrm{e}^{v_ j/j}f\to cf$ in $L^ p$. Therefore $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$. The uniqueness of the constant follows from corollary 15.13.3 . $\square$

text: We now combine the stability estimate above $\rho $ with the regularization of lemma 5.42.10 , whose curvature error is linear in the regularization parameter. As in the proof of theorem 15.5.1 , a small multiple of the strict barrier absorbs the curvature error of the transforms, and a lower bound for the minimizing radius converts the estimate for the transforms into an estimate for the smoothing on compact subsets of $\Omega $. This gives a local Hölder modulus for solutions with minimal singularities. Theorem 15.17.1 . D662421F3436 Fix $C_0>0$. Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy \[  \sup _ Xu=0,\qquad V_\theta -C_0\leq u\leq V_\theta , \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=f\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] where $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ and $p>1$. Then $u$ is locally Hölder continuous on $\Omega $, with every exponent \[  0<\beta <\frac{2(p-1)}{np+3(p-1)}.  \] For fixed bounds on $C_0$ and $\| f\| _ p$, the Hölder constants are uniform on each fixed compact subset of $\Omega $. Proof. Since $u\geq V_\theta -C_0\geq \rho -C_0$, we may subtract a constant from the strict barrier so that $\rho \leq u-1$; it still satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \kappa \omega $ for a fixed $\kappa >0$. Choose $0<\gamma <(p-1)/(np+p-1)$ and set $\alpha =2\gamma <1$. Apply lemma 5.42.10 with $a=u$, and let $A,K,C$ and $\Phi _{c,\delta }$ be the constants and transforms given there. For small $\delta >0$ set \[  c=\delta ^\alpha ,\qquad e=Ac+C\delta ,\qquad s=e/\kappa , \qquad v_\delta =\frac{\Phi _{c,\delta }+s\rho }{1+s}.  \] By the curvature bound of lemma 5.42.10 , $v_\delta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. The lower bound for $\Phi _{c,\delta }$ in that lemma implies $\rho \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }$ when $\delta $ is small. Thus \[  v_\delta \leq \Phi _{c,\delta }\leq R_\delta u\leq 0.  \] In particular $v_\delta \leq V_\theta $, so theorem 15.15.1 applies with the reference $V_\theta $ and the comparison potential $v_\delta $. Together with the $L^1$ smoothing estimate, it gives \[  \sup _\Omega (v_\delta -u)_+ \leq C\| (R_\delta u-u)_+\| _1^\gamma \leq C\delta ^\alpha .  \] Fix a compact subset of $\Omega $ on which $\rho \geq -M$. Since $s\leq C\delta ^\alpha $ and $u\leq 0$, the identity \[  \Phi _{c,\delta }-u=(1+s)(v_\delta -u)+s(u-\rho )  \] gives $\Phi _{c,\delta }-u\leq C_ M\delta ^\alpha $ there. At a radius $t$ where the infimum defining $\Phi _{c,\delta }$ is attained, the monotone lower bound yields \[  -c\log (t/\delta )\leq \Phi _{c,\delta }-u+K(\delta ^2+\delta ) \leq C_ Mc.  \] Hence $t\geq a_ M\delta $ for a fixed $a_ M>0$. As in the proof of theorem 15.5.1 , monotonicity of the smoothing now gives \[  R_{a_ M\delta }u-u\leq C_ M\delta ^\alpha , \qquad R_{a_ M\delta }u-u\geq -K(a_ M\delta )^2  \] on the chosen compact set. Since every small radius has the form $a_ M\delta $, we obtain $|R_ tu-u|\leq C_ Mt^\alpha $ there for all small $t>0$, with constants uniform on that compact set.  We apply this to a slightly larger compact neighborhood, on which also $\| \nabla R_ tu\| \leq C_ M/t$. For nearby points $x,y$ at distance $d>0$, the smooth function $R_ tu$ and a short path in that neighborhood give \[  |u(x)-u(y)|\leq C_ M(t^\alpha +d/t).  \] The choice $t=d^{1/(1+\alpha )}$ gives the exponent $\alpha /(1+\alpha )$, and letting $\gamma $ approach its upper endpoint gives the asserted range. Pairs of points farther apart are handled by the boundedness of $u$ on the compact neighborhood. $\square$ It suffices that the equation hold on $\Omega $. Suppose that $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$ on $\Omega $, where $c>0$ and $0\leq f\in L^ p(X,\mathrm{d}V)$, and that $u$ satisfies the same bounds as in the theorem. The lower bound $u\geq V_\theta -C_0\geq \rho -C_0$ shows that $u$ is locally bounded on $\Omega $, so there $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$ is the local bounded product. Since $Z$ has zero volume and is not charged by $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$, the equation holds on $X$, and the theorem applies with $cf$ in place of $f$. The uniform estimates then depend on a bound for $\| cf\| _ p$, which includes the constant $c$.

title: 15.17.2 Limits of normalized exponential solutions
section: 15.17 Local Hölder continuity in a big background
text: For the normalized exponential family $(v_\lambda ,c_\lambda )$ of lemma 15.16.5 , the reference interval $[V_\theta -B,V_\theta ]$ is uniform in $0<\lambda \leq 1$. Stability therefore controls differences on all of $\Omega $, and the local Hölder estimates strengthen the convergence on compact subsets. We fix the nonzero density $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, and use the constants $B,C,m$ of that lemma. Proposition 15.17.3 . D11439C1393F For the family $(v_\lambda ,c_\lambda )$ of lemma 15.16.5 , the normalized potentials are relatively compact for uniform convergence of differences on $\Omega $. As $\lambda \downarrow 0$, every cluster limit $v$ is normalized, has minimal singularities, and satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] where $c>0$ is the unique constant of theorem 15.16.7 . Moreover, \[  c_\lambda \longrightarrow c, \qquad c_\lambda \mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda }f \longrightarrow cf\quad \text{in }L^ p(\mathrm{d}V).  \] Every sequence of parameters in $(0,1]$ has a subsequence for which the potentials converge in $C^\beta $ on each compact subset of $\Omega $, for all \[  0<\beta <\frac{2(p-1)}{np+3(p-1)}.  \] Proof. By lemma 15.16.5 , all $v_\lambda $ lie in a common reference interval, and their densities are bounded in $L^ p$ by $C\| f\| _ p$. We may therefore apply corollary 15.15.3 with $\eta =V_\theta $. Given any sequence $\lambda _ j\downarrow 0$, we pass to a subsequence with $v_{\lambda _ j}\to v$ uniformly in differences on $\Omega $ and in $L^1(X)$, and with $c_{\lambda _ j}\to c_*\in [m,C]$. The limit satisfies the same reference bounds and is normalized. Off the pole set, \[  0\leq 1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda } \leq 1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda (V_\theta -B)}\longrightarrow 0  \] as $\lambda \downarrow 0$. Multiplying by $f$ and using dominated convergence, we obtain $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda }f\to f$ in $L^ p$ for the whole family. The compactness corollary therefore identifies the limit equation as $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)=c_*f\, \mathrm{d}V$, and the uniqueness of the constant gives $c_*=c$. Since every subsequential limit of $c_\lambda $ as $\lambda \downarrow 0$ equals $c$, we conclude that $c_\lambda \to c$, and the stated convergence of the densities follows. Finally, theorem 15.17.1 gives uniform local $C^\alpha $ bounds for every $\alpha $ below its endpoint, and the uniform limit inherits these bounds by pointwise convergence. For $0<\beta <\alpha $, uniform convergence and the elementary interpolation inequality on smaller coordinate balls give \[  [v_{\lambda _ j}-v]_{C^\beta } \leq C\| v_{\lambda _ j}-v\| _\infty ^{1-\beta /\alpha } [v_{\lambda _ j}-v]_{C^\alpha }^{\beta /\alpha } \longrightarrow 0,  \] where the Hölder bounds are taken on slightly larger compact neighborhoods. The uniformly convergent subsequence given by compactness thus converges in $C^\beta $ on every compact subset of $\Omega $ and for every exponent below the endpoint; no further extraction depending on the exponent is needed. $\square$ Corollary 15.17.4 . 64893D9DABFE Suppose a group $G$ of biholomorphisms of $X$ preserves $\theta $ and the measure $f\, \mathrm{d}V$. Then every $v_\lambda $ and every cluster limit as $\lambda \downarrow 0$ is $G$-invariant. If the normalized zero-exponent equation has only one $G$-invariant solution with minimal singularities, then the whole family $v_\lambda $ converges to it as $\lambda \downarrow 0$, uniformly in differences on $\Omega $ and in each local $C^\beta $ topology of the proposition. Proof. For $g\in G$, pullback by $g$ preserves $\theta $-plurisubharmonicity, and $V_\theta \circ g=V_\theta $ by the definition of the envelope. Pullback also preserves the positive-exponent equation, so its uniqueness gives $u_\lambda \circ g=u_\lambda $, and the normalization preserves this equality. Pullback by a fixed smooth biholomorphism is continuous on $L^1(X)$, since its Jacobian relative to the fixed smooth volume is bounded. Hence every cluster limit is invariant almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere for the canonical representatives. This argument does not require $g$ to preserve the barrier $\rho $ or the set $\Omega $. If the invariant solution is unique, every cluster limit is the same potential. Relative compactness then implies convergence of the whole family for uniform convergence of differences on $\Omega $: a sequence staying at a fixed positive distance from that potential would have a convergent subsequence, a contradiction. The interpolation argument above upgrades this to the asserted local $C^\beta $ convergence. $\square$ The proposition gives compactness and identifies the equation of every cluster limit, and the symmetry criterion is one way to identify the limit itself. In general, theorem 11.44.2 shows that the whole family converges, and it describes the limit through the greatest subsolution of the zero-exponent equation that satisfies a family of integral normalizations determined by how the constant $c$ depends on the density. This holds even when the zero-exponent equation has several normalized solutions.

title: 15.18 Interior smoothness on the regular locus
search_title: Interior smoothness on the regular locus
section: 15.18 Interior smoothness on the regular locus
text: Throughout this section, $\theta $ is a smooth big real $(1,1)$-form, and $\rho $, $Z=\{ \rho =-\infty \} $ and $\Omega =X\setminus Z$ are the strict analytic barrier and its regular locus fixed in section 15.13 . Thus $\rho \leq 0$ has analytic singularities with smooth remainder, and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \omega $. If $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has minimal singularities, then $\varphi \geq V_\theta -C\geq \rho -C$ for a constant $C$. Hence $\varphi $ is locally bounded on $\Omega $, and its Monge–Ampère measure there is the bounded-potential product. For such a potential, theorem 15.17.1 gives local Hölder continuity on $\Omega $ when the density belongs to $L^ p$ for some $p>1$. We show that a smooth strictly positive density on the whole of $\Omega $ then makes the potential smooth on $\Omega $. Local information alone cannot give this: example 15.21.15 below is a locally Lipschitz plurisubharmonic function with constant Monge–Ampère density that is not $C^1$. The argument therefore uses the barrier globally. By the proper gap of lemma 5.40.7 , the difference between the solution and the barrier attains a minimum on the closed set where smoothness fails, and strict positivity of $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $ turns this minimum into a quadratic separation. Near the minimum, smooth Dirichlet approximants have traces of polynomial growth; the separation improves this growth until a uniform trace bound yields elliptic regularity. Theorem 15.18.1 . 43AC522E5ED8 Suppose $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has minimal singularities and is locally Hölder continuous on $\Omega $. Let $c>0$ and let $f$ be smooth and strictly positive on $\Omega $. Assume \[  (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n=cf\, \omega ^ n\quad \text{on }\Omega .  \] Then $\varphi \in C^\infty (\Omega )$ and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi >0$ there. The Hölder hypothesis holds when, in addition, $f\in L^ p(X,\omega ^ n)$ for some $p>1$, by theorem 15.17.1 ; see corollary 15.18.50 . The theorem also applies when local Hölder continuity is obtained by another argument. The proof is by contradiction and occupies the rest of the section. Let $\mathcal S\subset \Omega $ be the closed set of points near which $\varphi $ is not smooth, suppose that $\mathcal S\neq \varnothing $, and let $p\in \mathcal S$ minimize $\varphi -\rho $ on $\mathcal S$. On a small ball centered at $p$ the argument has four steps. A comparison principle for continuous solutions (subsection 15.18.2 ) and the smooth Dirichlet problem give smooth solutions $u_ j$ of the equation that converge uniformly to $\varphi $ at a polynomial rate in $j$, while the traces of $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$, measured in Euclidean coordinates, grow at most polynomially in $j$ (subsection 15.18.7 ). Near $p$, the quadratic separation along $\mathcal S$, together with uniform trace bounds on compact sets where $\varphi $ is already smooth, improves the trace growth to $O(j^\gamma )$ for every $\gamma >0$. Interpolation with the convergence rate then gives uniform $C^{1,\alpha }$ bounds for every $\alpha <1$ (subsection 15.18.24 ). A third-order estimate whose constants depend polynomially on the ellipticity turns uniform $C^{1,\alpha }$ bounds, for $\alpha $ close to one, into a uniform trace bound (subsection 15.18.34 ). A continuous solution with bounded trace is smooth (subsection 15.18.4 ). Hence $\varphi $ is smooth near $p$, contradicting $p\in \mathcal S$ (subsection 15.18.49 ).

title: Theorem 15.18.1
section: 15.18 Interior smoothness on the regular locus
text: Theorem 15.18.1 . 43AC522E5ED8 Suppose $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has minimal singularities and is locally Hölder continuous on $\Omega $. Let $c>0$ and let $f$ be smooth and strictly positive on $\Omega $. Assume \[  (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n=cf\, \omega ^ n\quad \text{on }\Omega .  \] Then $\varphi \in C^\infty (\Omega )$ and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi >0$ there. of theorem 15.18.1 . If $n=1$, the equation is the linear identity \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi =cf\, \omega -\theta \quad \text{on }\Omega .  \] Its right-hand side is smooth, so interior elliptic regularity gives $\varphi \in C^\infty (\Omega )$, and the original equation gives $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi =cf\, \omega >0$. We henceforth assume $n\geq 2$. Let \[  \mathcal S=\{ p\in \Omega :\varphi \text{ is not smooth on any neighborhood of }p\} .  \] This is closed in $\Omega $. Suppose $\mathcal S\neq \varnothing $. By lemma 5.40.7 , the restriction of $\varphi -\rho $ to $\mathcal S$ attains its minimum $m$ at some $p\in \mathcal S$. Choose nested coordinate balls \[  B\Subset B_0\Subset \Omega  \] centered at $p$. On $B_0$, proposition 15.18.21 gives smooth exact Dirichlet solutions $u_ j$ converging uniformly to $\varphi $ at a polynomial rate and having polynomial global trace growth. On the open set $\Omega \setminus \mathcal S$ the function $\varphi $ is smooth, and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is semipositive with positive determinant, hence positive definite. Proposition 15.18.31 therefore gives a uniform trace bound for the $u_ j$ on every compact subset of $B_0\setminus \mathcal S$. In coordinates centered at $p$, take $\kappa >0$ small and set \[  q(z)=\rho (z)-\kappa |z|^2.  \] After shrinking $B$, the lower bound $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \omega $ gives $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q>0$ on $\overline B$. If $v=\varphi -q$, then the minimizing property of $p$ gives \[  v(p)=m, \qquad v(z)=(\varphi -\rho )(z)+\kappa |z|^2 \geq m+\kappa |z|^2 \quad (z\in \mathcal S\cap \overline B).  \] Thus proposition 15.18.25 applies on $B$ with the closed set $\mathcal S\cap \overline B$: the approximation rate and global polynomial trace bound come from proposition 15.18.21 , and the bound away from $\mathcal S$ comes from proposition 15.18.31 . Its second assertion gives, for every $0<\alpha <1$, a neighborhood of $p$ on which the approximants have a uniform $C^{1,\alpha }$ bound. Choose $\alpha >\alpha _*$ as in proposition 15.18.46 , and apply that proposition on a ball centered at $p$ inside this neighborhood. It yields \[  \sup _ j\operatorname {tr}_\beta (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)<\infty  \] on a still smaller neighborhood of $p$. Since $u_ j\to \varphi $ uniformly, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\to \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ as currents. The trace bound passes to the limit, so $\operatorname {tr}_\beta (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )$ has a bounded density near $p$. Proposition 15.18.5 now implies that $\varphi $ is smooth near $p$, contradicting $p\in \mathcal S$. Hence $\mathcal S=\varnothing $ and $\varphi \in C^\infty (\Omega )$. The form $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is smooth and semipositive there, while \[  (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n=cf\, \omega ^ n>0.  \] Its nonnegative eigenvalues have positive product, so every eigenvalue is positive. Therefore $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi >0$ on $\Omega $. $\square$

title: 15.18.2 Local comparison
section: 15.18 Interior smoothness on the regular locus
text: The comparison principle below, for continuous sub- and supersolutions on a bounded domain, identifies the given continuous potential with limits of smooth Dirichlet solutions. Since the background need not be closed, the classical Bedford–Taylor comparison does not apply directly. We freeze the background at a point, apply the closed-current comparison formula ( 5.27.7 ) to quadratic modifications, and control the error by the mixed inequalities of lemma 5.28.7 , lemma 5.28.10 . The local arguments of this section take place in coordinate balls, always with compact closure in a larger coordinate chart. There we put $\beta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$, write $\partial _ i=\partial /\partial z_ i$ and $\partial _{\bar i}=\partial /\partial \bar z_ i$, and take coefficient matrices of real $(1,1)$-forms relative to $\beta $. For such a form $A$, $\operatorname {tr}_\beta A$ and $\det _\beta A$ denote the trace and the determinant of its coefficient matrix, so that $A^ n=(\det _\beta A)\beta ^ n$, and $\Delta _\beta =\operatorname {tr}_\beta \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$. For a positive form $T$, $\operatorname {tr}_ T$ is the trace computed with the inverse of the coefficient matrix of $T$. Indices run from $1$ to $n$, repeated indices in tensor expressions are summed, and $I$ denotes the identity matrix. In local statements, $\vartheta $ denotes a smooth real $(1,1)$-form, not necessarily closed, which plays the role of $\theta $. Proposition 15.18.3 . D2F8F8FD5A17 Let $D\Subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a bounded domain and let $\vartheta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form near $\overline D$. Suppose $u,v\in C(\overline D)$ are $\vartheta $-plurisubharmonic, \[  (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\geq F\beta ^ n, \qquad (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\leq F\beta ^ n,  \] where $F>0$ is continuous on $D$. If $u\leq v$ on $\partial D$, then $u\leq v$ in $D$. Proof. Step 1: $v$ admits no strict smooth lower test. Suppose, to the contrary, that a $C^2$ function $q$ touches $v$ from below at a point $p\in D$ and that, at $p$, \[  \vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q>0, \qquad \det _\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)>F.  \] Choose a sufficiently small $a>0$. After replacing $q$ by $q-a|z-p|^2$, which makes the contact strict, and restricting to a small ball $B_ r(p)$, there are fixed $\lambda ,\eta >0$ such that \[  A:=\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq \lambda \beta , \qquad A^ n\geq (F+\eta )\beta ^ n.  \] To compare with closed currents, freeze the background at $p$: put $\kappa =\sup _{B_ r}\lVert \vartheta -\vartheta (p)\rVert _\beta $ and $B_0=\vartheta (p)+\kappa \beta $. Then $S=B_0-\vartheta $ satisfies $0\leq S\leq 2\kappa \beta $. For small $s>0$ the set $E=\{ v<q+s\} $ is nonempty and relatively compact in $B_ r$. If $Q_0$ is a quadratic potential for the constant form $B_0$, then \[  P=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v+Q_0)=\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v+S, \qquad Q=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(q+s+Q_0)=A+S\geq \lambda \beta  \] are closed positive Hessians. Applying ( 5.27.7 ), expanding $P$, and using $S\leq 2\kappa \beta \leq 2\kappa \lambda ^{-1}Q$, we obtain \[  \int _ E P^ n\leq \int _ E F\beta ^ n+e_\kappa \int _ E P^ n, \qquad e_\kappa =\left(1+\frac{2\kappa }{\lambda }\right)^ n-1.  \] On the other hand, ( 5.27.7 ) with $j=n$ gives \[  \int _ E P^ n\geq \int _ E Q^ n\geq \int _ E(F+\eta )\beta ^ n.  \] If $M$ bounds $F$ on the ball, the two estimates give $(1-e_\kappa )\eta \leq e_\kappa M$. Since $\kappa \to 0$, and hence $e_\kappa \to 0$, as $r\downarrow 0$, this is impossible for small $r$. Thus no such lower test exists. Step 2: comparison. Suppose that $\max _ D(u-v)>0$. We regularize $u$ to produce a forbidden lower test for $v$. Let $\chi _\delta $ be a nonnegative smooth mollifier of mass one and radius $\delta >0$. For small $t>0$ and $C\geq \sup _ D|z|^2$, set \[  u_ t=u+t(|z|^2-C).  \] Then $u_ t\leq v$ on $\partial D$, the positive maximum persists, and $T_ t=\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t\geq t\beta $. Lemma 5.28.7 gives \[  T_ t^ n\geq (F^{1/n}+t)^ n\beta ^ n.  \] Choose a relatively compact neighborhood $W$ of the positive maximum set. By lemma 5.28.10 , \[  (T_ t*\chi _\delta )^ n \geq \bigl ((F^{1/n}+t)*\chi _\delta \bigr )^ n\beta ^ n.  \] Since \[  \vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ t*\chi _\delta ) =T_ t*\chi _\delta +(\vartheta -\vartheta *\chi _\delta ),  \] the convolution satisfies $T_ t*\chi _\delta \geq t\beta $. If $\epsilon _\delta =\| \vartheta -\vartheta *\chi _\delta \| _{C^0(W)}$, then \[  \vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ t*\chi _\delta ) \geq (1-\epsilon _\delta /t)(T_ t*\chi _\delta ).  \] For fixed $t>0$, uniform convergence of the convolved density and $\epsilon _\delta \to 0$ show that the left-hand side is positive and has determinant strictly larger than $F$ on $W$ for small $\delta $. Since $u_ t*\chi _\delta \to u_ t$ uniformly on $W$, the difference $u_ t*\chi _\delta -v$ still attains its maximum over $\overline W$ at an interior point of $W$ for small $\delta $. Subtracting this maximum from $u_ t*\chi _\delta $ produces a smooth function touching $v$ from below with the properties excluded in Step 1, a contradiction. $\square$

title: 15.18.4 Bounded traces and smoothness
section: 15.18 Interior smoothness on the regular locus
text: We begin with the criterion used in the last step of the proof. A bounded trace of a positive current bounds all its coefficient measures, so a continuous solution with bounded trace is a strong solution with $W^{2,q}$ regularity for every finite $q$. The equation then bounds the eigenvalues from below, so it becomes uniformly elliptic. Since the solution is not yet known to be $C^2$, the Evans–Krylov theory is applied to it as a viscosity solution of a concave extension of the operator. Proposition 15.18.5 . 7DF8FE8A18D7 Let $B\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a coordinate ball, let $\vartheta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form there and let $F\in C^\infty (B)$ be strictly positive. Suppose $u$ is continuous, $T=\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$, and 7A41D9785A7C 15.18.6 \begin{equation}  T^ n=F\beta ^ n. \end{equation} For a point $p\in B$, the following conditions, each required on some neighborhood of $p$, are equivalent: $u$ is smooth; $T\geq \delta \beta $ for some $\delta >0$; $\operatorname {tr}_\beta T$ has a locally bounded measure density. Proof. Choose $C$ so that $v=u+C|z|^2$ is plurisubharmonic, and use nonnegative radial mollifiers for which $v_\eta \downarrow v$. The smooth matrix convolutions $T_\eta =T*\chi _\eta $ can be written as \[  T_\eta =(\vartheta *\chi _\eta -C\beta )+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\eta .  \] Bedford–Taylor monotone continuity and smooth convergence of the background imply $T_\eta ^ k\to T^ k$ for every $k$. (2)$\Rightarrow $(3). Assume (2). For every Hermitian matrix $M\geq \delta I$, \[  \det M\geq \delta ^{n-1}\bigl (\operatorname {tr} M-(n-1)\delta \bigr ).  \] Apply this to the regularizations and pass to currents. Equation ( 15.18.6 ) gives \[  \operatorname {tr}_\beta T\leq \delta ^{1-n}F+(n-1)\delta ,  \] which is (3). (3)$\Rightarrow $(1). Assume (3), say $\operatorname {tr}_\beta T\leq L$. Positivity makes every coefficient of the matrix-valued current $T$ a bounded density. Hence the Euclidean Laplacian of $u$ is locally bounded, and interior Poisson estimates give $u\in W^{2,q}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for every finite $q$. Mollification converges in $W^{2,q}$; taking $q>2n$ identifies the bounded-potential determinant with the ordinary almost-everywhere determinant. Thus $\det _\beta T=F$ almost everywhere. On a smaller ball with $F\geq m>0$, all eigenvalues of $T$ are at most $L$ and their product is at least $m$, so \[  \frac{m}{L^{n-1}}I\leq T\leq LI  \] almost everywhere. It remains to show that this strong solution is smooth. Let $P$ be the real linear map from real symmetric $2n\times 2n$ Hessian matrices to Hermitian $n\times n$ matrices, sending $D^2u$ to the coefficient matrix of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ relative to $\beta $, and let $\Theta (x)$ be the matrix of $\vartheta $. With $\delta =mL^{1-n}$, define the concave extension \[  G(x,M)=\inf _{\delta I\leq A\leq LI} \left\{ \log \det A+\operatorname {tr}\! \left[A^{-1}\bigl (\Theta (x)+P(M)-A\bigr )\right]\right\} -\log F(x).  \] For fixed $A$, write $\mathcal E_ A(x,M)$ for the expression in braces minus $\log F(x)$. The tangent-plane formula for $\log \det $ gives \[  G(x,D^2u)=0\quad \text{almost everywhere}.  \] The operator $G$ is concave and uniformly elliptic on real symmetric matrices. The affine operators $\mathcal E_ A$ have constant principal matrices with eigenvalues bounded above and below in terms of $\delta $ and $L$. Their $x$-dependence is smooth uniformly in $A$, so $G$ has a uniform local Lipschitz modulus in $x$. We claim that $u$ is a viscosity solution of $G(x,D^2u)=0$. Suppose that a smooth function $\psi $ touches $u$ from above at $x_0$ and that $G(x_0,D^2\psi )<0$. Some fixed matrix $A$ then satisfies $\mathcal E_ A(x,D^2\psi )<-\eta $ on a small ball. Since $G(x,D^2u)=0$ almost everywhere, $\mathcal E_ A(x,D^2u)\geq 0$ there. Thus $u-\psi $ has an interior maximum and satisfies \[  \operatorname {tr}\! \left(A^{-1}P(D^2(u-\psi ))\right)\geq \eta \quad \text{almost everywhere}.  \] After a small quadratic perturbation makes the contact strict, this contradicts the Aleksandrov maximum principle [ Chapter 9, Theorem 9.1 , GT01 ] . If instead $\psi $ touches $u$ from below and $G(x_0,D^2\psi )>0$, then $\mathcal E_ A(x,D^2\psi )>\eta $ for every admissible $A$ on a small ball. At almost every point choose an admissible $A(x)$ with $\mathcal E_{A(x)}(x,D^2u)<\eta /2$. A measurable choice is obtained by taking the first qualifying element of a countable dense family. The function $\psi -u$ then violates the same maximum principle for the measurable uniformly elliptic coefficients $A(x)^{-1}$. This proves the claim. The classical variable-coefficient Evans–Krylov theorem gives $u\in C^{2,\alpha }_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for some $0<\alpha <1$. The original equation is now uniformly elliptic with smooth data. Difference quotients satisfy linear equations whose principal coefficients are averages of inverse matrices along positive definite segments. Interior Schauder estimates first give $u\in C^{3,\alpha }_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and then, by iteration, $u\in C^\infty $. This proves (3)$\Rightarrow $(1). (1)$\Rightarrow $(2). If $u$ is smooth, then $T$ is a smooth semipositive form with determinant $F>0$, so it is positive definite; on a smaller neighborhood this gives (2). $\square$

title: 15.18.7 Smooth exact approximants
section: 15.18 Interior smoothness on the regular locus
text:
We now construct the approximants of the first step. The smooth Dirichlet theorem, lemma 15.7.1 , applies to every smooth positive density $F$. Approximating the Hölder boundary values of $\varphi $ by smooth functions therefore gives smooth solutions, and the point is to control them quantitatively. The estimates below bound the trace of a smooth solution by a power of the $C^4$ norm of its boundary value. The $C^4$ norms of the boundary approximations grow polynomially while their uniform errors decay polynomially, so both the convergence and the trace growth have polynomial rates. In this subsection balls are centered at the origin. On the boundary sphere, $
u $ is the outward Euclidean unit normal and $
abla _{	an }$ denotes tangential differentiation. For a positive form $T$, inner products $\langle \cdot ,\cdot angle _ T$ and norms $|\cdot |_ T$ of $(1,0)$-covectors are computed with the inverse of the coefficient matrix of $T$. Lemma 15.18.8 . 3EBB652C42D7 Let $B$ be a coordinate ball, let $\vartheta $ and $F>0$ be smooth near $\overline B$, and let $q$ be smooth with $R=\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq \varepsilon  eta $ for a fixed $\varepsilon >0$. Fix a finite $L\geq 0$. If $u\in C^\infty (B)$ satisfies \[  T=\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0, \qquad T^ n=F eta ^ n, \qquad |u-q|\leq L,  \] put $S=\operatorname {tr}_ eta T$ and $v=u-q$. For $A>0$, define \[  Q_ A=\log S-Av+\mathrm{e}^{-v}.  \] There are $A_0,C$, depending only on the fixed data and $L$, such that at every interior local maximum of $Q_ A$, with $A\geq A_0$, 59253C0B8B5A 15.18.9  egin{equation}  S\leq C\sqrt A. \end{equation} The constants do not depend on any bound for the gradient of $u$. Proof. This is the maximum-principle computation behind the classical second-order estimate. The non-closedness of $\vartheta $ produces a first-order error term, which is absorbed by the convex term $\mathrm{e}^{-v}$. title: 15.18.20 Exact approximation

text: We apply these estimates to smooth approximations of the boundary values of $\varphi $ on a ball in $\Omega $. Recall that $\theta $, $\omega $, $c$ and $f$ are the data of theorem 15.18.1 . Proposition 15.18.21 . 59A5B60FAB74 Let $B\Subset \Omega $ be a coordinate ball, identified with $\{ |z|<r_0\} $, with closure in a larger coordinate chart, and put \[  F=\frac{cf\, \omega ^ n}{\beta ^ n}.  \] There are $a>0$, $b,C<\infty $, and $u_ j\in C^\infty (\overline B)$ such that 9F54A2578D16 15.18.22 \begin{equation}  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j>0, \qquad (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ n=F\beta ^ n, \end{equation} and 082B0A6218F2 15.18.23 \begin{equation}  \lVert u_ j-\varphi \rVert _{L^\infty (B)}\leq Cj^{-a}, \qquad \sup _{\overline B}\operatorname {tr}_\beta (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)\leq Cj^ b. \end{equation} Proof. Since $\varphi $ is Hölder continuous near $\overline B$, mollification at scale $1/j$ gives smooth boundary approximations $g_ j$ with \[  \lVert g_ j-\varphi \rVert _{L^\infty (\partial B)}\leq Cj^{-a}, \qquad \lVert g_ j\rVert _{C^4(\partial B)}\leq Cj^4.  \] Choose a fixed quadratic $q$ with $\eta =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q>0$ near $\overline B$. Extend $g_ j$ smoothly to $G_ j$. For a sufficiently large, polynomially bounded $A_ j$, the function \[  \underline w_ j=G_ j-q+A_ j(|z|^2-r_0^2)  \] has boundary value $g_ j-q$ and satisfies \[  \eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\underline w_ j =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ j+A_ j\beta >0, \qquad (\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\underline w_ j)^ n\geq F\beta ^ n.  \] Apply the smooth Dirichlet theorem recalled at the beginning of this subsection, with density $H=F\beta ^ n/\eta ^ n$ to obtain a solution $w_ j$ for the Hermitian background $\eta $; put $u_ j=w_ j+q$. Comparing $u_ j$ with $\varphi \pm \lVert g_ j-\varphi \rVert _\infty $ by proposition 15.18.3 proves the first bound in ( 15.18.23 ). The functions $u_ j$ are therefore uniformly bounded. Proposition 15.18.14 and the polynomial $C^4$ boundary norm give the second bound. $\square$

title: 15.18.24 Localization near the nonregular set
section: 15.18 Interior smoothness on the regular locus
text: In the auxiliary function of lemma 15.18.8 , the term $-A(u_ j-q)$ penalizes points where $u_ j-q$ is large. A quadratic gap of $u-q$ along the nonregular set therefore suppresses the contribution of the boundary of a neighborhood of that set. Taking $A$ proportional to $\log j$ makes this suppression beat the polynomial growth of the boundary trace, and near the point of minimal $u-q$ the trace then grows more slowly than every positive power of $j$. Interpolation with the polynomial approximation rate gives uniform $C^{1,\alpha }$ bounds. Distances and norms below are Euclidean. By a smooth exact solution for $(\vartheta ,F)$ we mean a smooth function $u_ j$ with $\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j>0$ and $(\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ n=F\beta ^ n$. Proposition 15.18.25 . F9CDEC120FA0 For $R>0$, let $B=B_ R(0)$, let $\vartheta $ and $F>0$ be smooth near $\overline B$, and let $u\in C(\overline B)$. Suppose $q$ is smooth and $\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq \varepsilon \beta $ for some $\varepsilon >0$. Put $v=u-q$ and $m=v(0)$, and fix $\kappa >0$. Let $\mathcal S\subset \overline B$ be closed, contain $0$, and satisfy 87542664E1D7 15.18.26 \begin{equation}  v(0)=m, \qquad v(z)\geq m+\kappa |z|^2\quad (z\in \mathcal S). \end{equation} Assume that smooth exact solutions $u_ j$, $j\geq 2$, satisfy, for fixed constants $a>0$, $b\geq 0$ and $C>0$, E603AE0642F8 15.18.27 \begin{align}  \lVert u_ j-u\rVert _\infty & \leq Cj^{-a}, \\  \sup _{\overline B}\operatorname {tr}_\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)& \leq Cj^ b, \tag{15.18.28}\\  \sup _ j\sup _ K\operatorname {tr}_\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)& <\infty \quad \text{for every }K\Subset \overline B\setminus \mathcal S. \tag{15.18.29} \end{align} Then for every $\gamma >0$ there are a neighborhood $U_\gamma $ of $0$ and $C_\gamma $ such that EBBDF08FE74B 15.18.30 \begin{equation}  \operatorname {tr}_\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)\leq C_\gamma j^\gamma \quad \text{on }U_\gamma . \end{equation} For every $0<\alpha <1$, there is also a neighborhood $U$ of $0$ on which $u_ j\to u$ in $C^{1,\alpha }$. In particular the approximants are uniformly bounded in that norm and $u\in C^{1,\alpha }(U)$. Proof. Step 1: the trace bound ( 15.18.30 ). Write $e_ j=Cj^{-a}$, fix $d=\kappa R^2/2$, and choose $D>(b+1)/d$. Choose $\eta >0$ so that $2D\eta <\gamma /2$. For small $\delta >0$, the neighborhood \[  W_\delta =\{ z\in B:\operatorname {dist}(z,\mathcal S)<\delta \}   \] contains $0$, has $v\geq m-\eta $ on its closure, and satisfies $v\geq m+d$ on $\partial B\cap \overline W_\delta $ with the fixed $d$ above. These properties follow from ( 15.18.26 ), continuity, and compactness. The remaining part of the boundary of $W_\delta $ is a compact subset of $\overline B\setminus \mathcal S$, where ( 15.18.29 ) applies. Set $A_ j=D\log j$. Apply the maximum principle on $\overline W_\delta $ to \[  Q_ j=\log \operatorname {tr}_\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)-A_ j(u_ j-q)+\mathrm{e}^{-(u_ j-q)}.  \] At an interior maximum, lemma 15.18.8 gives $\log \operatorname {tr}_\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)\leq C+\frac12\log A_ j$. On the part of $\partial W_\delta $ inside $B$, which stays away from $\mathcal S$, the trace has a bound independent of $j$. On the outer part $\partial B\cap \overline W_\delta $, ( 15.18.28 ) and the gap $d$ give \[  Q_ j\leq C+b\log j-A_ j(m+d-e_ j),  \] and the choice $Dd>b+1$ makes this smaller than the bound below for large $j$. Hence throughout $W_\delta $, \[  Q_ j\leq C_\delta +\tfrac 12\log A_ j-A_ j(m-\eta -e_ j).  \] On a small ball about $0$ where $v\leq m+\eta $, this implies \[  \log \operatorname {tr}_\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j) \leq C_\delta +\tfrac 12\log A_ j+A_ j(2\eta +2e_ j).  \] By the choice of $\eta $, the logarithmic factor and $A_ je_ j$ are absorbed into the remaining power. This proves ( 15.18.30 ). Step 2: $C^{1,\alpha }$ convergence. On a smaller ball, the real Laplacian of $u_ j$ is bounded by $Cj^\gamma $. Interior Poisson estimates give a $W^{2,q_0}$ bound for every finite $q_0$, and Sobolev embedding with $q_0$ large then gives, for every $\sigma <1$, \[  \lVert u_ j\rVert _{W^{2,q_0}}+\lVert u_ j\rVert _{C^{1,\sigma }} \leq Cj^\gamma .  \] For $d_ k=u_{2^{k+1}}-u_{2^ k}$, \[  \lVert d_ k\rVert _\infty \leq C2^{-ka}, \qquad \lVert d_ k\rVert _{C^{1,\sigma }}\leq C2^{k\gamma }.  \] If $\alpha <\sigma $ and $t=(1+\alpha )/(1+\sigma )$, Hölder interpolation gives \[  \lVert d_ k\rVert _{C^{1,\alpha }} \leq C2^{k[-a(1-t)+\gamma t]}.  \] Since $\gamma $ may be arbitrarily small, the exponent can be made negative. The dyadic series converges in $C^{1,\alpha }$ to its uniform limit $u$. If $2^ k\leq j<2^{k+1}$, interpolation applied to $u_ j-u_{2^ k}$ gives the same decaying bound. Hence the full sequence converges to $u$ in $C^{1,\alpha }$ on a smaller ball. $\square$ Proposition 15.18.31 . 45A010B2A5AF Suppose $u_ j$ solve the same smooth equation as in proposition 15.18.25 , satisfy ( 15.18.27 )–( 15.18.28 ), and $u$ is smooth with $\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$ on an open set $O\subset B$. Then, for every $K\Subset O$, D534513E3EFA 15.18.32 \begin{equation}  \sup _ j\sup _ K\operatorname {tr}_\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)<\infty . \end{equation} Proof. Where $u$ is smooth and strictly $\vartheta $-plurisubharmonic, it provides its own quadratic separation, so the argument of proposition 15.18.25 applies around every point of $O$. A first application gives trace growth of order $\sqrt{\log j}$; the resulting gradient convergence then allows the variant of lemma 15.18.8 with a gradient bound, which removes this growth. For $p$ in a fixed compact subset of $O$, take a uniformly sized ball $B_ r(p)\Subset O$ and set \[  q_ p(z)=u(z)-\kappa |z-p|^2  \] with $\kappa >0$ small, so $\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_ p\geq \varepsilon \beta $. If $e_ j=Cj^{-a}$ and $v_{j,p}=u_ j-q_ p$, then \[  v_{j,p}\geq -e_ j, \quad v_{j,p}(p)\leq e_ j, \quad v_{j,p}\geq \kappa r^2-e_ j\text{ on }\partial B_ r(p).  \] With $A_ j=D\log j$ and $D\kappa r^2>b+1$, the same maximum argument as above gives 4E46369984C7 15.18.33 \begin{equation}  \operatorname {tr}_\beta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)(p)\leq C\sqrt{\log j}. \end{equation} The constants are uniform on compact subsets of $O$. Put $T_ j=\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$ and $w_ j=u_ j-u$. On slightly larger compact sets, ( 15.18.33 ) bounds $|\Delta w_ j|$ by $C\sqrt{\log j}$. Poisson estimates and Sobolev embedding give \[  \lVert w_ j\rVert _{C^{1,\sigma }}\leq C_\sigma \sqrt{\log j}, \qquad \sigma <1.  \] Interpolating with $\lVert w_ j\rVert _\infty \leq Cj^{-a}$ shows $\nabla w_ j\to 0$ uniformly on smaller compact sets. The gradients of $v_{j,p}$ are therefore uniformly bounded. Repeat the maximum argument with $\log \operatorname {tr}_\beta T_ j-A_ jv_{j,p}$, now using the variant of lemma 15.18.8 with a gradient bound. Its interior trace bound is now independent of $A_ j$, while the boundary term is suppressed as before. Evaluation at $p$ gives \[  \operatorname {tr}_\beta T_ j(p)\leq C\exp (2A_ je_ j)\leq C,  \] proving ( 15.18.32 ). $\square$

section: 15.18 Interior smoothness on the regular locus
text:
Uniform $C^{1,\alpha }$ bounds control averages of the trace $\operatorname {tr}_ eta (\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)=\operatorname {tr}_ eta \vartheta +\Delta _ eta u_ j$ over small balls. To pass from averages to pointwise values we need a bound for the gradient of the trace, that is, a third-order estimate, whose dependence on the ellipticity constants is polynomial. We prove it by Calabi's maximum-principle argument, computed with the Chern connection of the solution so that the torsion of the nonclosed background appears explicitly. The resulting averaging inequality is nonlinear in the trace, and it closes under iteration when $\alpha $ is sufficiently close to one. In this subsection $B$ is the unit ball and $B_ r(p)$ is the Euclidean ball of radius $r$ centered at $p$. For a Hermitian metric $g$, $\partial g$ denotes the ordinary coordinate derivatives of its coefficient matrix, while tensor derivatives in the proofs are taken with respect to the Chern connection of $g$. There are $C,N<\infty $, depending only on finitely many derivatives of the fixed data, such that any smooth solution \[  g=\vartheta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u, \qquad g^ n=F eta ^ n, \qquad M^{-1} eta \leq g\leq M eta , \qquad M\geq 1,  \] satisfies E4388ADCCF56 15.18.36  egin{equation}  \sup _{B_{1/2}}|\partial g|_ eta \leq CM^ N. \end{equation} If only $\sup _ B\operatorname {tr}_ eta g\leq L$ is given, the same bound holds with a fixed power of $1+L$. On a ball of radius $r\leq 1$, 3DC50D5C4903 15.18.37  egin{equation}  \sup _{B_{r/2}}|
abla \operatorname {tr}_ eta g|_ eta \leq Cr^{-1}(1+L)^ N. \end{equation} Proof. title: 15.18.49 Proof of the main theorem
section: 15.18 Interior smoothness on the regular locus
text: We now assemble the four steps outlined after theorem 15.18.1 . The barrier enters only once, but globally: it locates a point of the nonsmooth set at which the quadratic separation required in proposition 15.18.25 holds. of theorem 15.18.1 . If $n=1$, the equation is the linear identity \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi =cf\, \omega -\theta \quad \text{on }\Omega .  \] Its right-hand side is smooth, so interior elliptic regularity gives $\varphi \in C^\infty (\Omega )$, and the original equation gives $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi =cf\, \omega >0$. We henceforth assume $n\geq 2$. Let \[  \mathcal S=\{ p\in \Omega :\varphi \text{ is not smooth on any neighborhood of }p\} .  \] This is closed in $\Omega $. Suppose $\mathcal S\neq \varnothing $. By lemma 5.40.7 , the restriction of $\varphi -\rho $ to $\mathcal S$ attains its minimum $m$ at some $p\in \mathcal S$. Choose nested coordinate balls \[  B\Subset B_0\Subset \Omega  \] centered at $p$. On $B_0$, proposition 15.18.21 gives smooth exact Dirichlet solutions $u_ j$ converging uniformly to $\varphi $ at a polynomial rate and having polynomial global trace growth. On the open set $\Omega \setminus \mathcal S$ the function $\varphi $ is smooth, and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is semipositive with positive determinant, hence positive definite. Proposition 15.18.31 therefore gives a uniform trace bound for the $u_ j$ on every compact subset of $B_0\setminus \mathcal S$. In coordinates centered at $p$, take $\kappa >0$ small and set \[  q(z)=\rho (z)-\kappa |z|^2.  \] After shrinking $B$, the lower bound $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \omega $ gives $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q>0$ on $\overline B$. If $v=\varphi -q$, then the minimizing property of $p$ gives \[  v(p)=m, \qquad v(z)=(\varphi -\rho )(z)+\kappa |z|^2 \geq m+\kappa |z|^2 \quad (z\in \mathcal S\cap \overline B).  \] Thus proposition 15.18.25 applies on $B$ with the closed set $\mathcal S\cap \overline B$: the approximation rate and global polynomial trace bound come from proposition 15.18.21 , and the bound away from $\mathcal S$ comes from proposition 15.18.31 . Its second assertion gives, for every $0<\alpha <1$, a neighborhood of $p$ on which the approximants have a uniform $C^{1,\alpha }$ bound. Choose $\alpha >\alpha _*$ as in proposition 15.18.46 , and apply that proposition on a ball centered at $p$ inside this neighborhood. It yields \[  \sup _ j\operatorname {tr}_\beta (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)<\infty  \] on a still smaller neighborhood of $p$. Since $u_ j\to \varphi $ uniformly, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\to \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ as currents. The trace bound passes to the limit, so $\operatorname {tr}_\beta (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )$ has a bounded density near $p$. Proposition 15.18.5 now implies that $\varphi $ is smooth near $p$, contradicting $p\in \mathcal S$. Hence $\mathcal S=\varnothing $ and $\varphi \in C^\infty (\Omega )$. The form $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is smooth and semipositive there, while \[  (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n=cf\, \omega ^ n>0.  \] Its nonnegative eigenvalues have positive product, so every eigenvalue is positive. Therefore $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi >0$ on $\Omega $. $\square$ Corollary 15.18.50 . AD8A02A6088D Let $0\leq f\in L^ p(X,\omega ^ n)$, $p>1$, be smooth and strictly positive on $\Omega $. Every minimal-singularity solution of $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n=cf\, \omega ^ n$, $c>0$, is smooth and strictly $\theta $-plurisubharmonic on $\Omega $. Proof. The analytic complement of $\Omega $ has zero mass for both measures, so it suffices to know the equation in the bounded-potential sense on $\Omega $. Apply theorem 15.17.1 with density $cf$ to obtain local Hölder continuity. All hypotheses of theorem 15.18.1 are now satisfied. $\square$ By theorem 15.16.7 , such a solution exists, with a uniquely determined $c>0$. For a smooth closed big representative on a compact Kähler manifold, theorem 10.20.1 applies this conclusion to the classical full-mass solution and identifies the regular open set with the ample locus.

title: 15.19 Degenerating semipositive backgrounds
text: Adding a small multiple of a Hermitian form makes a semipositive background strictly positive, and the smooth theory then solves the normalized equation with a smooth positive density. We study these smooth solutions as the added multiple tends to zero. Bounded subsolutions give uniform bounds for the potentials and the normalizing constants, and a strict analytic barrier gives uniform bounds for the trace on compact sets away from its poles. Smooth local convergence then identifies the limiting equation, without any global continuity property of the Monge–Ampère operator. The main example is a small resolution of a threefold with nodes ( 15.19.8 ). There the background is the pullback of a positive form from the singular threefold, and it degenerates exactly along the exceptional curves. When this background is closed, the limit is unique and the whole family converges smoothly away from the exceptional curves. Convergence of the associated metric spaces then reduces to controlling the diameters of neighborhoods of these curves, in the limiting metric and in the approximating metrics ( 15.19.18 ). Throughout this section $n\geq 2$. The background $\theta $, the barrier $\rho $ and its pole set $Z$ are new data, independent of those fixed in section 15.13 . Let $\theta \geq 0$ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form, and fix a Hermitian form $\eta $ and a smooth positive probability volume form $\mu $ on $X$. Suppose that there are $\delta >0$ and $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with analytic singularities such that C397B905A723 15.19.1 \begin{equation}  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \delta \eta , \qquad \sup _ X\rho =0. \end{equation} Write $Z=\{ \rho =-\infty \} $ and assume that $\rho $ is smooth on $X\setminus Z$. For $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$, the form $\theta +\varepsilon \eta $ is Hermitian, and theorem 14.2.1 gives $u_\varepsilon \in C^\infty (X)$ and $c_\varepsilon >0$ with 8C6C5AF468B2 15.19.2 \begin{equation}  \omega _\varepsilon :=\theta +\varepsilon \eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon >0, \qquad \omega _\varepsilon ^ n=c_\varepsilon \mu , \qquad \sup _ Xu_\varepsilon =0. \end{equation} Lemma 15.19.3 . 4A0FCD6D9FCD There are constants $b,B,C>0$, independent of $\varepsilon $, such that \[  b\leq c_\varepsilon \leq B, \qquad -C\leq u_\varepsilon \leq 0.  \] Proof. Write $\mu =f\, \mathrm{d}V$, where $f$ is smooth and positive. The strict barrier makes $\theta $ big. By lemma 15.3.1 , there is a bounded $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $-1\leq s\leq 0$ and $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (s)\geq b\mu $ for some fixed $b>0$. If $c_\varepsilon <b$, positivity gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\varepsilon \eta }(u_\varepsilon ) \leq (c_\varepsilon /b)\mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\varepsilon \eta }(s+A)  \] for every constant $A$. Strict bounded domination would imply $u_\varepsilon \geq s+A$ for every $A$, which is absurd. Hence $c_\varepsilon \geq b$. For an upper bound, choose a fixed Gauduchon form $\gamma $. The arithmetic–geometric mean inequality and Stokes give \[  c_\varepsilon ^{1/n} \int _ X\left(\frac{\mu }{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n \leq \int _ X\omega _\varepsilon \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\int _ X(\theta +\varepsilon \eta )\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \leq \int _ X(\theta +\eta )\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] The first integral is fixed and positive, giving $c_\varepsilon \leq B$. For the lower bound on $u_\varepsilon $, note that all $u_\varepsilon $ are normalized $(\theta +\eta )$-plurisubharmonic functions. Uniform exponential integrability, lemma 5.26.2 , gives $a>0$ such that $g_\varepsilon =\mathrm{e}^{-a u_\varepsilon }f$ has a common $L^2$ bound. Also $g_\varepsilon \geq f$. By theorem 15.3.3 , the solutions \[  w_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ), \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (w_\varepsilon ) =\mathrm{e}^{a w_\varepsilon }g_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{d}V  \] are uniformly bounded. Put $B_0=\max \{ 1,B\} $ and $z_\varepsilon =w_\varepsilon -a^{-1}\log B_0$. Then \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\varepsilon \eta }(z_\varepsilon ) \geq \mathrm{e}^{a z_\varepsilon }c_\varepsilon g_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\varepsilon \eta }(u_\varepsilon ) =\mathrm{e}^{a u_\varepsilon }c_\varepsilon g_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The comparison principle for the exponential equation in the background $\theta +\varepsilon \eta $ gives $z_\varepsilon \leq u_\varepsilon \leq 0$, and $z_\varepsilon $ is bounded below uniformly in $\varepsilon $. $\square$ Since $\theta $ may degenerate along $Z$, we do not estimate the trace by local arguments. Instead we apply the maximum principle on all of $X\setminus Z$ to the logarithm of the trace minus a multiple of $u_\varepsilon -\rho $. This function tends to $-\infty $ at $Z$, so its maximum is attained off $Z$, where $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \delta \eta $ provides positivity. An additional logarithmic term in the weight absorbs the torsion term without a gradient bound for $\rho $. Lemma 15.19.4 . C390030D09AE For every compact $K\Subset X\setminus Z$, there is $C_ K>1$, independent of $\varepsilon $, such that \[  C_ K^{-1}\eta \leq \omega _\varepsilon \leq C_ K\eta \quad \hbox{on }K.  \] Proof. For the differentiated calculation write $U=u_\varepsilon /(2\pi )$ and $P=\rho /(2\pi )$, so that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon =\mathrm{i}\partial \bar\partial U$. Put \[  S=\operatorname {tr}_\eta \omega _\varepsilon , \quad R=\operatorname {tr}_{\omega _\varepsilon }\eta , \quad D=\omega _\varepsilon ^ n/\eta ^ n.  \] The previous lemma and the smooth positive density give $0<d_1\leq D\leq d_2$. Choose a fixed $C_0$ so that $v=U-P+C_0>1$, and set \[  H=\log S-\gamma (v),\qquad \gamma (v)=Av+\log v,  \] where $A$ will be fixed below. For each $\varepsilon $, $S$ is smooth on $X$ and $v$ tends to infinity at $Z$. Thus $H\to -\infty $ there, and $H$ attains its maximum on $X\setminus Z$. We bound this maximum independently of $\varepsilon $. In local holomorphic coordinates, $h$ and $g$ denote the coefficient matrices of $\eta $ and $\omega _\varepsilon $ with respect to $\mathrm{i}\, \mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ k$, and commas denote coordinate derivatives, as in $h_{i\bar j,k}=\partial _ kh_{i\bar j}$ and $h_{i\bar j,\bar k}=\partial _{\bar k}h_{i\bar j}$. At a maximum point choose holomorphic coordinates in which \[  h_{i\bar j}=\delta _{ij},\qquad h_{i\bar i,k}=0, \qquad g_{i\bar j}=\lambda _ i\delta _{ij}.  \] A linear change first normalizes $h$ and diagonalizes $g$. In these coordinates, the quadratic change $z_ i=w_ i+\frac12\sum _{j,k}a^ i_{jk}w_ jw_ k$, with symmetric coefficients chosen so that $a^ i_{ik}=-h_{i\bar i,k}$, then kills $h_{i\bar i,k}$. Its coefficients are uniformly bounded on a fixed finite cover. Write \[  \Delta _ g=\sum _ i\lambda _ i^{-1}\partial _ i\partial _{\bar i}, \quad T_{ij\bar k}=g_{j\bar k,i}-g_{i\bar k,j}, \quad E_ i=\sum _ jT_{ij\bar j}.  \] The lowered torsion coefficients $T_{ij\bar k}$ and their first derivatives are uniformly bounded: the potential Hessian cancels, leaving only derivatives of $\theta +\varepsilon \eta $. Let $\mu _{\mathrm{loc}}$ be the density of $\mu $ with respect to the coordinate volume form. Differentiating $S=h^{k\bar\ell }g_{k\bar\ell }$ and the equation $\log \det g=\log c_\varepsilon +\log \mu _{\mathrm{loc}}$ gives 279BD7D5BB42 15.19.5 \begin{equation}  \Delta _ g S\geq Q-CRS-CR, \qquad Q=\sum _{i,j}\frac{|g_{i\bar j,j}|^2}{\lambda _ i\lambda _ j}. \end{equation} The second derivatives of $g$ contribute $\sum _{i,j,k}|g_{i\bar j,k}|^2/(\lambda _ i\lambda _ j)$, up to $-CR-C$, by commuting the potential derivatives. The first derivatives of $h$ contribute $-2\operatorname {Re}\sum _{i,j,k}\lambda _ i^{-1}h_{j\bar k,\bar i}g_{k\bar j,i}$. Its terms with $j=k$ vanish. Replace $g_{k\bar j,i}$ by $g_{i\bar j,k}+T_{ik\bar j}$ and apply weighted Cauchy–Schwarz. This consumes exactly the terms of the preceding square with $j\ne k$ and costs at most $CRS+CR$. The second derivatives of $h^{-1}$ cost $CRS$. Finally the fixed density term $-C$ is absorbed using $SR\geq n^2$. Since $\partial _ iS=\sum _ jg_{i\bar j,j}+E_ i$ at the maximum point, weighted Cauchy–Schwarz also gives \[  |\partial S|_ g^2 \leq SQ+2\operatorname {Re}\langle E,\partial S\rangle _ g.  \] Indeed expand around $\partial S-E$ and discard the resulting term $-|E|_ g^2$. Combining with ( 15.19.5 ) yields \[  \Delta _ g\log S\geq -CR-CR/S -\frac2S\operatorname {Re}\langle E,\partial \log S\rangle _ g.  \] At the maximum, $\partial \log S=\gamma '\partial v$. Moreover ( 15.19.1 ) gives $\Delta _ gv\leq n-\delta R$, and $|E|_ g^2\leq CR$. Young's inequality with the positive coefficient $-\gamma ''=v^{-2}$ therefore gives \[  0\geq \Delta _ g H \geq (\delta \gamma '-C)R-n\gamma '-CR/S -\frac{CR}{S^2}\frac{\gamma '^2}{-\gamma ''}.  \] Since $\gamma '=A+v^{-1}$, choose $A$ with $\delta A-C\geq 1$. The resulting inequality is 2D587C24F80B 15.19.6 \begin{equation}  0\geq R-C\left(1+\frac RS+\frac{R(1+v^2)}{S^2}\right). \end{equation} All constants are independent of $\varepsilon $. If the maxima of $H$ were unbounded, then at a sequence of maximizing points \[  \log (S/v)=H+Av\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] Thus $S/v\to \infty $ and $S\to \infty $. Inequality ( 15.19.6 ) would imply $R\leq 2C$ along this sequence. But \[  S=D\sum _ i\prod _{j\ne i}\lambda _ j^{-1} \leq nDR^{n-1}\leq nd_2(2C)^{n-1},  \] a contradiction. Hence $H$ is uniformly bounded. On $K$, both $U$ and $P$ are bounded, so $S\leq C_ K$. The determinant lower bound then gives $\lambda _ i\geq d_1/C_ K^{n-1}$, completing the proof. $\square$ Theorem 15.19.7 . E00C93820852 In the preceding setting, $c_\varepsilon $ decreases to a positive number $c_0$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. This number is independent of the perturbing Hermitian form $\eta $. For every sequence $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, a subsequence satisfies \[  u_{\varepsilon _ j}\longrightarrow u_0 \quad \hbox{in }L^1(X)\cap C^\infty _{\mathrm{loc}}(X\setminus Z),  \] where $u_0\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\cap L^\infty (X)$, $\sup _ Xu_0=0$, and \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_0)=c_0\mu .  \] If $\theta $ is closed, then $c_0=\int _ X\theta ^ n$. Proof. Monotonicity of the constants. Let $\alpha \leq \beta $ be Hermitian forms, and let $(u_\alpha ,c_\alpha )$ and $(u_\beta ,c_\beta )$ be the normalized smooth solutions of $(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\alpha )^ n=c_\alpha \mu $ and $(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\beta )^ n=c_\beta \mu $. At a maximum point of $u_\alpha -u_\beta $, \[  \alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\alpha \leq \beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\beta ,  \] so $c_\alpha \leq c_\beta $. Hence $c_\varepsilon $ decreases as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, and lemma 15.19.3 gives $c_0\geq b>0$. Write $c_\eta (\varepsilon )$ for the constant $c_\varepsilon $ defined with the perturbation $\eta $. For two perturbations with $M^{-1}\eta _1\leq \eta _2\leq M\eta _1$, the same comparison gives \[  c_{\eta _1}(\varepsilon /M) \leq c_{\eta _2}(\varepsilon ) \leq c_{\eta _1}(M\varepsilon ).  \] Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ shows that $c_0$ does not depend on $\eta $. Local estimates. The trace bound of lemma 15.19.4 gives uniform ellipticity on compact subsets of $X\setminus Z$. The smooth coefficients of $\theta +\varepsilon \eta $ and all derivatives of $\log \mu _{\mathrm{loc}}$ have common bounds there. Interior complex Evans–Krylov and Schauder estimates, as in the ellipticity argument of proposition 15.18.5 , give uniform $C^ k$ bounds on smaller compact subsets for every $k$. Convergence and the limiting equation. Normalized compactness in the fixed background $\theta +\eta $, followed by a diagonal extraction over an exhaustion of $X\setminus Z$, gives the stated convergence. The uniform bound $-C\leq u_\varepsilon \leq 0$ passes to the canonical limit, and normalized compactness preserves the supremum zero. Current convergence gives $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0\geq 0$, and smooth convergence identifies the equation on $X\setminus Z$. The bounded non-pluripolar measure $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_0)$ and the smooth measure $\mu $ both vanish on the analytic set $Z$. This proves the equation on all of $X$. For closed $\theta $, bounded closed-background Stokes gives $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_0)=\int _ X\theta ^ n$, proving the last assertion. $\square$ Since $\theta \geq 0$ is nef, theorem 12.11.1 identifies $c_0$ with the Gauduchon variational volume $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )$. The proof uses no bound on Monge–Ampère masses: all estimates concern the solutions for the fixed smooth density $\mu $. If the bounded normalized limiting equation has a unique solution, all cluster limits coincide, and the whole family converges in $L^1(X)\cap C^\infty _{\mathrm{loc}}(X\setminus Z)$.
