title: Lemma 15.19.3
text: Lemma 15.19.3 . 4A0FCD6D9FCD There are constants $b,B,C>0$, independent of $\varepsilon $, such that \[  b\leq c_\varepsilon \leq B, \qquad -C\leq u_\varepsilon \leq 0.  \] Proof. Write $\mu =f\, \mathrm{d}V$, where $f$ is smooth and positive. The strict barrier makes $\theta $ big. By lemma 15.3.1 , there is a bounded $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $-1\leq s\leq 0$ and $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (s)\geq b\mu $ for some fixed $b>0$. If $c_\varepsilon <b$, positivity gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\varepsilon \eta }(u_\varepsilon ) \leq (c_\varepsilon /b)\mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\varepsilon \eta }(s+A)  \] for every constant $A$. Strict bounded domination would imply $u_\varepsilon \geq s+A$ for every $A$, which is absurd. Hence $c_\varepsilon \geq b$. For an upper bound, choose a fixed Gauduchon form $\gamma $. The arithmetic–geometric mean inequality and Stokes give \[  c_\varepsilon ^{1/n} \int _ X\left(\frac{\mu }{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n \leq \int _ X\omega _\varepsilon \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\int _ X(\theta +\varepsilon \eta )\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \leq \int _ X(\theta +\eta )\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] The first integral is fixed and positive, giving $c_\varepsilon \leq B$. For the lower bound on $u_\varepsilon $, note that all $u_\varepsilon $ are normalized $(\theta +\eta )$-plurisubharmonic functions. Uniform exponential integrability, lemma 5.26.2 , gives $a>0$ such that $g_\varepsilon =\mathrm{e}^{-a u_\varepsilon }f$ has a common $L^2$ bound. Also $g_\varepsilon \geq f$. By theorem 15.3.3 , the solutions \[  w_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ), \qquad \mathrm{MA}_\theta (w_\varepsilon ) =\mathrm{e}^{a w_\varepsilon }g_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{d}V  \] are uniformly bounded. Put $B_0=\max \{ 1,B\} $ and $z_\varepsilon =w_\varepsilon -a^{-1}\log B_0$. Then \[  \mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\varepsilon \eta }(z_\varepsilon ) \geq \mathrm{e}^{a z_\varepsilon }c_\varepsilon g_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \mathrm{MA}_{\theta +\varepsilon \eta }(u_\varepsilon ) =\mathrm{e}^{a u_\varepsilon }c_\varepsilon g_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The comparison principle for the exponential equation in the background $\theta +\varepsilon \eta $ gives $z_\varepsilon \leq u_\varepsilon \leq 0$, and $z_\varepsilon $ is bounded below uniformly in $\varepsilon $. $\square$

title: Lemma 15.19.4
text: Lemma 15.19.4 . C390030D09AE For every compact $K\Subset X\setminus Z$, there is $C_ K>1$, independent of $\varepsilon $, such that \[  C_ K^{-1}\eta \leq \omega _\varepsilon \leq C_ K\eta \quad \hbox{on }K.  \] Proof. For the differentiated calculation write $U=u_\varepsilon /(2\pi )$ and $P=\rho /(2\pi )$, so that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon =\mathrm{i}\partial \bar\partial U$. Put \[  S=\operatorname {tr}_\eta \omega _\varepsilon , \quad R=\operatorname {tr}_{\omega _\varepsilon }\eta , \quad D=\omega _\varepsilon ^ n/\eta ^ n.  \] The previous lemma and the smooth positive density give $0<d_1\leq D\leq d_2$. Choose a fixed $C_0$ so that $v=U-P+C_0>1$, and set \[  H=\log S-\gamma (v),\qquad \gamma (v)=Av+\log v,  \] where $A$ will be fixed below. For each $\varepsilon $, $S$ is smooth on $X$ and $v$ tends to infinity at $Z$. Thus $H\to -\infty $ there, and $H$ attains its maximum on $X\setminus Z$. We bound this maximum independently of $\varepsilon $. In local holomorphic coordinates, $h$ and $g$ denote the coefficient matrices of $\eta $ and $\omega _\varepsilon $ with respect to $\mathrm{i}\, \mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ k$, and commas denote coordinate derivatives, as in $h_{i\bar j,k}=\partial _ kh_{i\bar j}$ and $h_{i\bar j,\bar k}=\partial _{\bar k}h_{i\bar j}$. At a maximum point choose holomorphic coordinates in which \[  h_{i\bar j}=\delta _{ij},\qquad h_{i\bar i,k}=0, \qquad g_{i\bar j}=\lambda _ i\delta _{ij}.  \] A linear change first normalizes $h$ and diagonalizes $g$. In these coordinates, the quadratic change $z_ i=w_ i+\frac12\sum _{j,k}a^ i_{jk}w_ jw_ k$, with symmetric coefficients chosen so that $a^ i_{ik}=-h_{i\bar i,k}$, then kills $h_{i\bar i,k}$. Its coefficients are uniformly bounded on a fixed finite cover. Write \[  \Delta _ g=\sum _ i\lambda _ i^{-1}\partial _ i\partial _{\bar i}, \quad T_{ij\bar k}=g_{j\bar k,i}-g_{i\bar k,j}, \quad E_ i=\sum _ jT_{ij\bar j}.  \] The lowered torsion coefficients $T_{ij\bar k}$ and their first derivatives are uniformly bounded: the potential Hessian cancels, leaving only derivatives of $\theta +\varepsilon \eta $. Let $\mu _{\mathrm{loc}}$ be the density of $\mu $ with respect to the coordinate volume form. Differentiating $S=h^{k\bar\ell }g_{k\bar\ell }$ and the equation $\log \det g=\log c_\varepsilon +\log \mu _{\mathrm{loc}}$ gives 279BD7D5BB42 15.19.5 \begin{equation}  \Delta _ g S\geq Q-CRS-CR, \qquad Q=\sum _{i,j}\frac{|g_{i\bar j,j}|^2}{\lambda _ i\lambda _ j}. \end{equation} The second derivatives of $g$ contribute $\sum _{i,j,k}|g_{i\bar j,k}|^2/(\lambda _ i\lambda _ j)$, up to $-CR-C$, by commuting the potential derivatives. The first derivatives of $h$ contribute $-2\operatorname {Re}\sum _{i,j,k}\lambda _ i^{-1}h_{j\bar k,\bar i}g_{k\bar j,i}$. Its terms with $j=k$ vanish. Replace $g_{k\bar j,i}$ by $g_{i\bar j,k}+T_{ik\bar j}$ and apply weighted Cauchy–Schwarz. This consumes exactly the terms of the preceding square with $j\ne k$ and costs at most $CRS+CR$. The second derivatives of $h^{-1}$ cost $CRS$. Finally the fixed density term $-C$ is absorbed using $SR\geq n^2$. Since $\partial _ iS=\sum _ jg_{i\bar j,j}+E_ i$ at the maximum point, weighted Cauchy–Schwarz also gives \[  |\partial S|_ g^2 \leq SQ+2\operatorname {Re}\langle E,\partial S\rangle _ g.  \] Indeed expand around $\partial S-E$ and discard the resulting term $-|E|_ g^2$. Combining with ( 15.19.5 ) yields \[  \Delta _ g\log S\geq -CR-CR/S -\frac2S\operatorname {Re}\langle E,\partial \log S\rangle _ g.  \] At the maximum, $\partial \log S=\gamma '\partial v$. Moreover ( 15.19.1 ) gives $\Delta _ gv\leq n-\delta R$, and $|E|_ g^2\leq CR$. Young's inequality with the positive coefficient $-\gamma ''=v^{-2}$ therefore gives \[  0\geq \Delta _ g H \geq (\delta \gamma '-C)R-n\gamma '-CR/S -\frac{CR}{S^2}\frac{\gamma '^2}{-\gamma ''}.  \] Since $\gamma '=A+v^{-1}$, choose $A$ with $\delta A-C\geq 1$. The resulting inequality is 2D587C24F80B 15.19.6 \begin{equation}  0\geq R-C\left(1+\frac RS+\frac{R(1+v^2)}{S^2}\right). \end{equation} All constants are independent of $\varepsilon $. If the maxima of $H$ were unbounded, then at a sequence of maximizing points \[  \log (S/v)=H+Av\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] Thus $S/v\to \infty $ and $S\to \infty $. Inequality ( 15.19.6 ) would imply $R\leq 2C$ along this sequence. But \[  S=D\sum _ i\prod _{j\ne i}\lambda _ j^{-1} \leq nDR^{n-1}\leq nd_2(2C)^{n-1},  \] a contradiction. Hence $H$ is uniformly bounded. On $K$, both $U$ and $P$ are bounded, so $S\leq C_ K$. The determinant lower bound then gives $\lambda _ i\geq d_1/C_ K^{n-1}$, completing the proof. $\square$

title: Equation 15.19.5

title: Theorem 15.19.7
text: Theorem 15.19.7 . E00C93820852 In the preceding setting, $c_\varepsilon $ decreases to a positive number $c_0$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. This number is independent of the perturbing Hermitian form $\eta $. For every sequence $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, a subsequence satisfies \[  u_{\varepsilon _ j}\longrightarrow u_0 \quad \hbox{in }L^1(X)\cap C^\infty _{\mathrm{loc}}(X\setminus Z),  \] where $u_0\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\cap L^\infty (X)$, $\sup _ Xu_0=0$, and \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_0)=c_0\mu .  \] If $\theta $ is closed, then $c_0=\int _ X\theta ^ n$. Proof. Monotonicity of the constants. Let $\alpha \leq \beta $ be Hermitian forms, and let $(u_\alpha ,c_\alpha )$ and $(u_\beta ,c_\beta )$ be the normalized smooth solutions of $(\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\alpha )^ n=c_\alpha \mu $ and $(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\beta )^ n=c_\beta \mu $. At a maximum point of $u_\alpha -u_\beta $, \[  \alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\alpha \leq \beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\beta ,  \] so $c_\alpha \leq c_\beta $. Hence $c_\varepsilon $ decreases as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, and lemma 15.19.3 gives $c_0\geq b>0$. Write $c_\eta (\varepsilon )$ for the constant $c_\varepsilon $ defined with the perturbation $\eta $. For two perturbations with $M^{-1}\eta _1\leq \eta _2\leq M\eta _1$, the same comparison gives \[  c_{\eta _1}(\varepsilon /M) \leq c_{\eta _2}(\varepsilon ) \leq c_{\eta _1}(M\varepsilon ).  \] Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ shows that $c_0$ does not depend on $\eta $. Local estimates. The trace bound of lemma 15.19.4 gives uniform ellipticity on compact subsets of $X\setminus Z$. The smooth coefficients of $\theta +\varepsilon \eta $ and all derivatives of $\log \mu _{\mathrm{loc}}$ have common bounds there. Interior complex Evans–Krylov and Schauder estimates, as in the ellipticity argument of proposition 15.18.5 , give uniform $C^ k$ bounds on smaller compact subsets for every $k$. Convergence and the limiting equation. Normalized compactness in the fixed background $\theta +\eta $, followed by a diagonal extraction over an exhaustion of $X\setminus Z$, gives the stated convergence. The uniform bound $-C\leq u_\varepsilon \leq 0$ passes to the canonical limit, and normalized compactness preserves the supremum zero. Current convergence gives $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0\geq 0$, and smooth convergence identifies the equation on $X\setminus Z$. The bounded non-pluripolar measure $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_0)$ and the smooth measure $\mu $ both vanish on the analytic set $Z$. This proves the equation on all of $X$. For closed $\theta $, bounded closed-background Stokes gives $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_0)=\int _ X\theta ^ n$, proving the last assertion. $\square$

title: 15.19.8 Small resolutions of nodes
text: The pullback of a positive form from a singular space loses positivity along the contracted curves. In the standard small resolution of a node, the logarithm of the norm in the normal bundle of the exceptional curve provides the missing curvature along the curve. Cutting this logarithm off where the pullback is already positive gives a global strict barrier, so the results above apply. Assume now $n=3$. Let $Y$ be a connected compact normal complex threefold, smooth outside a finite set $\Sigma $ of nodes. A node is locally the hypersurface \[  \{ x_1x_4-x_2x_3=0\} \subset \mathbb C^4.  \] Let $\pi :X\to Y$ be a proper holomorphic map that is biholomorphic over $Y\setminus \Sigma $. Assume each local resolution is the standard small resolution: a neighborhood of its exceptional curve is identified with a neighborhood of the zero section of \[  \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1)\oplus \mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1),  \] and the contraction, in bundle coordinates $(z,y_1,y_2)$, is 5C6AB7F124F9 15.19.9 \begin{equation}  \pi (z,y_1,y_2)=(y_1,zy_1,y_2,zy_2). \end{equation} Interchanging the two rulings gives the other standard model. Write $E=\pi ^{-1}(\Sigma )$; its components $E_ j$ are disjoint copies of $\mathbb P^1$. Fix a positive form $\omega _ Y$ on $Y$ in the local embedding sense: in each ambient chart it is induced by a smooth strictly positive real $(1,1)$-form. Set $\theta =\pi ^*\omega _ Y$, and let $\eta $ be an arbitrary Hermitian form on $X$. Lemma 15.19.10 . C6428C798D5F The form $\theta $ is smooth and semipositive, positive on $X\setminus E$. There are $\delta >0$ and $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with analytic poles precisely on $E$, smooth on $X\setminus E$, such that \[  \sup _ X\rho =0,\qquad \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \delta \eta .  \] Proof. Smoothness and positivity off $E$ follow from the pullback and the biholomorphism. In one standard model put \[  r^2=(1+|z|^2)(|y_1|^2+|y_2|^2),\qquad b=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2).  \] The function $r^2$ is the sum of the squared absolute values of the four contracted coordinates. It is therefore globally defined on the bundle; $b$ is the pullback of the Fubini–Study form from its base. In the chart ( 15.19.9 ), AC4599B20814 15.19.11 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log r^2 =b+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (|y_1|^2+|y_2|^2)\geq b. \end{equation} This is an inequality of currents across the zero section as well as a smooth inequality off it. Ambient positivity gives $\theta \geq c\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r^2$ on a sufficiently small tube, for some $c>0$. The smooth form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r^2+b$ is positive definite there. Indeed the contraction is an immersion off the zero section, and on that section $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r^2$ is positive in both fiber directions while $b$ is positive along the base. Compactness of the zero section and a smaller closed tube give a uniform lower bound by a positive multiple of $\eta $. Thus, for every fixed $a>0$, \[  \theta +a\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log r^2 \geq c\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r^2+ab \geq \delta _ a\eta  \] near the zero section, with $\delta _ a>0$. Choose disjoint model tubes with nonempty complement and numbers $0<t_1<t_2<1$ in each. Let $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ be a smooth cutoff of $r^2$, equal to one for $r^2\leq t_1$ and zero for $r^2\geq t_2$. Extend $\chi (r^2)\log r^2$ by zero outside its tube. On the compact transition annuli, the pullback $\theta $ is uniformly positive and the second derivatives of this cutoff potential are bounded. A sufficiently small positive rational $a$ therefore makes \[  \rho =a\sum _ j\chi _ j(r_ j^2)\log r_ j^2  \] satisfy $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \delta \eta $ there and near every $E_ j$. On the remaining compact set, $\rho =0$ and $\theta $ is positive, so decreasing $\delta $ proves the global inequality. Near $E_ j$ the function is $a\log (|y_1|^2+|y_2|^2)+a\log (1+|z|^2)$, hence has analytic singularities with rational coefficient and pole set exactly $E_ j$. It is smooth elsewhere and nonpositive; its zero extension gives supremum zero. If $E$ is empty, take $\rho =0$ and use the positivity of $\theta $ on compact $X$. $\square$ Corollary 15.19.12 . A1536B3C6F39 For the preceding geometric data and every smooth positive probability volume form $\mu $ on $X$, the solutions of ( 15.19.2 ) have the bounds and subsequential convergence of theorem 15.19.7 , with $Z=E$. Moreover, for each exceptional curve, \[  \int _{E_ j}\omega _\varepsilon =\varepsilon \int _{E_ j}\eta \longrightarrow 0.  \] Proof. Apply the theorem using lemma 15.19.10 . Since $\pi $ contracts $E_ j$, the restriction of $\theta $ to it is zero. Stokes on the compact smooth curve gives $\int _{E_ j}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon =0$, proving the area identity. $\square$ When $K_ X$ is torsion, the density can be chosen so that these metrics are Chern–Ricci flat. Recall that the Chern–Ricci form $\operatorname {Ric}^{\mathrm{Ch}}(\omega )$ of a Hermitian metric $\omega $ is $-\mathrm{i}\partial \bar\partial $ of the logarithm of the density of $\omega ^ n$ with respect to a coordinate volume form. Choose a nowhere vanishing holomorphic section of $K_ X^{\otimes m}$ for some $m\geq 1$. If its local expression is $f(\mathrm{d}z_1\wedge \mathrm{d}z_2\wedge \mathrm{d}z_3)^{\otimes m}$, use $|f|^{2/m}$ as the density relative to the standard coordinate volume form. The coordinate Jacobians cancel, so this defines a smooth positive volume form on $X$; normalize it to total mass one and take it as $\mu $. Its logarithmic density is pluriharmonic. Applying $-\mathrm{i}\partial \bar\partial \log $ to $\omega _\varepsilon ^3=c_\varepsilon \mu $ therefore gives $\operatorname {Ric}^{\mathrm{Ch}}(\omega _\varepsilon )=0$, and the same holds for the smooth limiting metric on $X\setminus E$.

title: 15.19.18 Distances across finitely many contracting regions

text: On the small resolutions above, the potential limit for a closed background gives smooth convergence of the metrics away from the exceptional curves. Global distances, however, are also affected by paths through neighborhoods of these curves, so their convergence requires control of the diameters of such neighborhoods. The criterion of proposition 15.19.22 separates the two controls: uniform convergence on compact subsets of the regular part, and small diameters of neighborhoods of the contracted sets, in the limiting metric and uniformly in the approximating metrics. We first recall the Gromov–Hausdorff distance. Definition 15.19.19 . 0EB9DF723176 For nonempty subsets $E,F$ of a metric space $(W,d_ W)$, their Hausdorff distance is \[  d_{\mathrm H}^ W(E,F)=\max \left\{  \sup _{x\in E}\inf _{y\in F}d_ W(x,y), \sup _{y\in F}\inf _{x\in E}d_ W(x,y)\right\} .  \] For nonempty bounded metric spaces $E,F$, put \[  d_{\mathrm{GH}}(E,F) =\inf _{W,\iota ,\jmath }d_{\mathrm H}^ W(\iota (E),\jmath (F)),  \] where $\iota ,\jmath $ are isometric embeddings into a common metric space $W$. A correspondence is a subset $R\subset E\times F$ whose two coordinate projections are surjective. Its distortion is \[  \operatorname {dis}R =\sup _{(x,y),(x',y')\in R} |d_ E(x,x')-d_ F(y,y')|.  \] Lemma 15.19.20 . 022849340F28 For any correspondence $R$ between nonempty bounded metric spaces, \[  \frac12|\operatorname {diam}E-\operatorname {diam}F| \leq d_{\mathrm{GH}}(E,F) \leq \frac12\operatorname {dis}R.  \] Proof. Choose $\varepsilon >0$ with $2\varepsilon \geq \operatorname {dis}R$. Give the disjoint union $E\sqcup F$ its original distances within each space, and use the symmetric cross distance \[  D(x,y)=\inf _{(x_0,y_0)\in R} \bigl (d_ E(x,x_0)+\varepsilon +d_ F(y_0,y)\bigr ), \qquad x\in E,\  y\in F.  \] It is finite and at least $\varepsilon $. The triangle inequalities involving one cross distance follow from the triangle inequality within the corresponding space and the infimum. For two cross distances, take $(x_0,y_0),(x_1,y_1)\in R$. The distortion bound gives \[  \begin{split}  d_ E(x,x') & \leq d_ E(x,x_0)+d_ F(y_0,y_1) +2\varepsilon +d_ E(x_1,x')\\ & \leq d_ E(x,x_0)+d_ F(y_0,y)+\varepsilon +\varepsilon +d_ F(y,y_1)+d_ E(x_1,x'). \end{split}  \] Taking the two infima gives $d_ E(x,x')\leq D(x,y)+D(y,x')$. The same argument with $E,F$ exchanged treats the other case. Hence $D$ is a metric extending both metrics. Each point has a correspondent at cross distance $\varepsilon $, so the Hausdorff distance between $E$ and $F$ in $(E\sqcup F,D)$ is at most $\varepsilon $. Letting $\varepsilon $ decrease to half the distortion proves the upper bound, including zero distortion. For the lower bound, suppose two isometric images have Hausdorff distance $h$. For every $\delta >0$, two points in the first image have points in the second within $h+\delta $. Their distance is at most $\operatorname {diam}F+2h+2\delta $. Taking the supremum and then $\delta \downarrow 0$ gives $\operatorname {diam}E\leq \operatorname {diam}F+2h$. Exchanging the images and taking the infimum over embeddings proves the lower bound. $\square$ We now work in a purely metric setting, which contains the nodal one. Let $Y$ be a compact metrizable space and let $S=\{ s_1,\ldots ,s_ N\} \subset Y$ be finite. Assume $Y^\circ =Y\setminus S$ is a dense connected smooth manifold. Let $g_0$ be a smooth Riemannian metric on $Y^\circ $, and denote its intrinsic length distance by $d_0$. Lemma 15.19.21 . E3C9C96E314E Suppose every $s_ a$ has a neighborhood basis of open sets $V_{a,r}$ such that \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\operatorname {diam}_{d_0}(V_{a,r}\setminus S)=0.  \] Then the metric completion $(\widehat Y,\widehat d_0)$ of $(Y^\circ ,d_0)$ is compact, and the identity on $Y^\circ $ extends to a homeomorphism $\iota :Y\to \widehat Y$. Proof. The neighborhoods can be chosen nested, with closures avoiding the other points of $S$. Every sequence of regular points converging to $s_ a$ is $d_0$-Cauchy: its tail lies in each prescribed neighborhood, whose punctured diameter tends to zero. Interleaving two such sequences shows that they define the same completion point, denoted by $\widehat s_ a$. Density of $Y^\circ $ guarantees the existence of these sequences. For each prescribed positive diameter, remove sufficiently small neighborhoods of all the points of $S$. Their complement is a compact subset of $Y^\circ $ and hence is totally bounded for $d_0$. The removed punctured neighborhoods each have the prescribed small diameter. Thus $Y^\circ $ is totally bounded, and its completion is compact. The points $\widehat s_ a$ are distinct from one another and from the regular points. To see this, fix $s_ a$ and a different point $y\in Y$. Choose an open neighborhood $V$ of $s_ a$ whose closure avoids $y$ and $S\setminus \{ s_ a\} $, and choose $W\Subset V$ containing $s_ a$. There is a smooth function $\chi $ on $Y^\circ $, equal to one on $W\setminus S$ and zero outside $V$, whose derivative has compact support in $Y^\circ $. Indeed the transition takes place in the compact regular set $\overline V\setminus W$, where smooth cutoffs exist. Therefore $|\mathrm{d}\chi |_{g_0}\leq C$ for some finite $C$. Integration along curves gives \[  |\chi (p)-\chi (q)|\leq C d_0(p,q),\qquad p,q\in Y^\circ .  \] The Lipschitz extension of $\chi $ to the completion has value one at $\widehat s_ a$ and zero at the regular point $y$, or at $\widehat s_ b$ if $y=s_ b$. This proves the assertion. Define $\iota $ by the identity on the regular locus and by $\iota (s_ a)=\widehat s_ a$. The intrinsic distance induces the smooth topology at each regular point. At $s_ a$, adjoining $\widehat s_ a$ to a punctured neighborhood does not increase its diameter, so the diameter hypothesis proves continuity of $\iota $. Every completion point is represented by a Cauchy sequence in $Y^\circ $. Compact metrizability of $Y$ gives a subsequence converging topologically either to a regular point or to some $s_ a$; the preceding arguments give its metric limit. Hence $\iota $ is surjective as well as injective. A continuous bijection from compact $Y$ to Hausdorff $\widehat Y$ is a homeomorphism. $\square$ Let $X$ be a compact connected smooth manifold and let $\pi :X\to Y$ be a continuous surjection, with $E=\pi ^{-1}(S)$ and with $\pi :X\setminus E\to Y^\circ $ a diffeomorphism. Assume that the identity of $Y^\circ $ extends to a homeomorphism $\iota :Y\to \widehat Y$, for instance under the hypothesis of lemma 15.19.21 , and write $G=\iota \circ \pi $. For a smooth Riemannian metric $g$ on $X$ and an open subset $U$, let $\operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U,g)$ denote the intrinsic diameter of $U$, computed with the lengths of piecewise smooth curves contained in $U$. Proposition 15.19.22 . 65049DB7855E Let $g_ j$ be smooth Riemannian metrics on $X$ such that $g_ j\to \pi ^*g_0$ uniformly on every compact subset of $X\setminus E$. Suppose each $s_ a$ has a nested neighborhood basis $V_{a,r}$, with $U_{a,r}=\pi ^{-1}(V_{a,r})$, satisfying \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\operatorname {diam}_{\widehat d_0}(\iota (V_{a,r}))=0, \qquad \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\limsup _{j\to \infty } \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U_{a,r},g_ j)=0.  \] Then, for the global length distances $d_ j$ of $g_ j$, \[  \lim _{j\to \infty }\sup _{x,x'\in X} |d_ j(x,x')-\widehat d_0(G(x),G(x'))|=0.  \] Consequently $(X,d_ j)$ converges to $(\widehat Y,\widehat d_0)$ in Gromov–Hausdorff distance. Proof. If $S$ is empty, uniform metric comparison on compact $X$ proves the distance convergence. Assume $N\geq 1$. Fix $\tau >0$. Choose pairwise disjoint neighborhoods $V_ a$ from the specified bases with \[  \operatorname {diam}_{\widehat d_0}(\iota (V_ a))<\tau , \qquad \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U_ a,g_ j)<\tau  \] for all sufficiently large $j$, where $U_ a=\pi ^{-1}(V_ a)$. Pick $q_ a\in V_ a\setminus S$, and then choose open neighborhoods $W_ a$ of $s_ a$ with $\overline W_ a\subset V_ a$ and $q_ a\notin \overline W_ a$. The regular cores \[  K_ Y=Y\setminus \bigcup _ a W_ a, \qquad K_ X=\pi ^{-1}(K_ Y)  \] are compact and identified by $\pi $. Uniform convergence and positivity of $g_0$ on this core give numbers $A_ j\geq 1$, with $A_ j\to 1$, such that lengths of curves contained in the cores compare in both directions by the factor $A_ j$. Consider a piecewise smooth path in $Y^\circ $ joining two points of $K_ Y$. The preimages of the closed sets $\overline W_ a$ are compact subsets of its parameter interval. At its first visit to any such set, delete the portion from that visit through its last visit to the same set. Resume with the remaining tail. That set is never visited again; thus there are at most $N$ deleted portions. Each retained segment lies in $K_ Y$, and each deleted portion has endpoints in a single $\overline W_ a\subset V_ a$. The lifts of those endpoints can be joined in $U_ a$ with $g_ j$-length less than $\tau $, up to an arbitrarily small error. Applying this procedure to almost minimizing paths, comparing retained lengths, and letting the errors tend to zero gives, for $x,x'\in K_ X$, \[  d_ j(x,x')\leq A_ j\widehat d_0(G(x),G(x'))+N\tau .  \] Conversely start with an almost minimizing $g_ j$-path in $X$ and apply the same deletion procedure to the closed sets $\pi ^{-1}(\overline W_ a)$. Project its retained segments, which avoid $E$, to $K_ Y$. The two images of each deleted portion have completion distance less than $\tau $. The triangle inequality in $\widehat Y$ therefore gives \[  \widehat d_0(G(x),G(x'))\leq A_ j d_ j(x,x')+N\tau , \qquad x,x'\in K_ X.  \] For any $x\notin K_ X$ with $\pi (x)\in W_ a$, replace $x$ by $p=\pi ^{-1}(q_ a)\in U_ a\cap K_ X$. Then $d_ j(x,p)<\tau $ and $\widehat d_0(G(x),G(p))<\tau $. Leave points of $K_ X$ fixed. Replacing both endpoints extends the two inequalities to all $x,x'\in X$, with the same error \[  C_ j=(N+2+2A_ j)\tau .  \] If $D=\operatorname {diam}(\widehat Y,\widehat d_0)$, the first inequality gives $\operatorname {diam}(X,d_ j)\leq A_ jD+C_ j$. The positive and negative distance errors are consequently bounded by \[  (A_ j-1)D+C_ j, \qquad (A_ j-1)(A_ jD+C_ j)+C_ j,  \] respectively. Their upper limits are at most $(N+4)\tau $. Letting $\tau \downarrow 0$ proves uniform convergence. The graph of $G$ is a correspondence between $X$ and $\widehat Y$, and its distortion $b_ j$ for the distances $d_ j$ and $\widehat d_0$ is the supremum in the statement. By lemma 15.19.20 , \[  d_{\mathrm{GH}}((X,d_ j),(\widehat Y,\widehat d_0))\leq b_ j/2\longrightarrow 0.  \] $\square$ For the standard nodal small resolutions of 15.19.8 with closed $\theta $, the smooth convergence of the whole family off $E$ in theorem 15.19.17 gives the uniform convergence on compact subsets of $X\setminus E$ required in proposition 15.19.22 . What remains are the two conditions on the diameters of neighborhoods. The next estimates control the approximating neighborhoods by metric bounds along and normal to the exceptional curves.

title: Definition 15.19.19
text: Definition 15.19.19 . 0EB9DF723176 For nonempty subsets $E,F$ of a metric space $(W,d_ W)$, their Hausdorff distance is \[  d_{\mathrm H}^ W(E,F)=\max \left\{  \sup _{x\in E}\inf _{y\in F}d_ W(x,y), \sup _{y\in F}\inf _{x\in E}d_ W(x,y)\right\} .  \] For nonempty bounded metric spaces $E,F$, put \[  d_{\mathrm{GH}}(E,F) =\inf _{W,\iota ,\jmath }d_{\mathrm H}^ W(\iota (E),\jmath (F)),  \] where $\iota ,\jmath $ are isometric embeddings into a common metric space $W$. A correspondence is a subset $R\subset E\times F$ whose two coordinate projections are surjective. Its distortion is \[  \operatorname {dis}R =\sup _{(x,y),(x',y')\in R} |d_ E(x,x')-d_ F(y,y')|.  \]

title: 15.19.23 Curve areas and radial tube lengths
search_title: Curve areas and radial tube lengths
text: The approximating metrics give each exceptional curve an area tending to zero, by corollary 15.19.12 . Along the curve, small area forces small diameter as long as the metrics are bounded above; in the normal directions, an integrable bound for the speed of radial rays has the same effect. Let $C$ be a connected compact Riemann surface. Fix a smooth Hermitian metric $h$ of area one on $C$, and use the associated Riemannian metrics for lengths and areas. Lemma 15.19.24 . 240B8EBF50C3 There is $K_ h>0$ such that every smooth Hermitian metric $g\leq M h$, with $M>0$ and $A=\operatorname {Area}_ g(C)$, satisfies \[  \operatorname {diam}(C,g) \leq K_ h\sqrt{A\bigl (1+\log (M/A)\bigr )}.  \] Here $0<A\leq M$. In particular, for a fixed upper bound $M$, area tending to zero implies diameter tending to zero. Proof. Replace $g$ by $g/M$. Its area is $a=A/M\leq 1$, and it is bounded above by $h$. We prove the estimate for this normalized metric. Choose a finite cover by holomorphic coordinate disks $U_ i$ represented by $\{ |z|<1\} $, with each coordinate defined on the larger disk $\{ |z|<2\} $. Write $g=\rho _ i|\mathrm{d}z|^2$ there. There is a common $L>0$ such that $0<\rho _ i\leq L$ on all the closed unit disks, and \[  \int _{U_ i}\rho _ i\, \mathrm{d}\lambda _2\leq a,  \] where $\lambda _2$ is Euclidean area. For $p,z\in U_ i$, let $\ell _ p(z)$ be the $g$-length of their straight coordinate segment, which stays in $U_ i$. Polar coordinates about $p$ and Fubini give \[  \int _{U_ i}\ell _ p(z)\, \mathrm{d}\lambda _2(z) \leq 2\int _{U_ i}\frac{\sqrt{\rho _ i(w)}}{|w-p|} \, \mathrm{d}\lambda _2(w).  \] Indeed each ray meets the convex unit disk in an interval of length $R\leq 2$. Interchanging the radial integrals multiplies the length integrand at radius $s$ by $(R^2-s^2)/2\leq 2$. For $0<a\leq 1/4$, put $t=\sqrt a$. The integral on the right, without its factor two, is bounded by \[  \begin{split}  \sqrt L\int _{\{ |w-p|<t\} }\frac{\mathrm{d}\lambda _2(w)}{|w-p|} & +\left(\int _{U_ i}\rho _ i\, \mathrm{d}\lambda _2\right)^{1/2} \left(\int _{\{ t<|w-p|<2\} }\frac{\mathrm{d}\lambda _2(w)}{|w-p|^2}\right)^{1/2}\\ & \leq 2\pi \sqrt L\, t+\sqrt{2\pi a\log (2/t)} \leq K\sqrt{a\bigl (1+\log (1/a)\bigr )}. \end{split}  \] Thus for any $p,q\in U_ i$, averaging $\ell _ p(z)+\ell _ q(z)$ over $z\in U_ i$ gives a two-segment path of length at most $K\sqrt{a(1+\log (1/a))}$. The constant is common to the finite cover. The overlap graph of this cover is connected because $C$ is connected. Choose points in consecutive overlaps along a simple path in this finite graph. The local estimates join any two points of $C$ through at most the number of covering disks, proving the global bound for $a\leq 1/4$. For $1/4\leq a\leq 1$, the comparison $g\leq h$ gives $\operatorname {diam}(C,g)\leq \operatorname {diam}(C,h)$, and increasing $K_ h$ gives the same estimate. Restoring the factor $M$ scales lengths by $\sqrt M$ and proves the assertion. $\square$ Example 15.19.25 . F7F939140E90 On every such $(C,h)$ there are smooth Hermitian metrics $g_\varepsilon \leq h$, for $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, such that \[  \begin{aligned}  A_\varepsilon :=\operatorname {Area}_{g_\varepsilon }(C) & \asymp \varepsilon ^2\log (1/\varepsilon ),\\  \operatorname {diam}(C,g_\varepsilon ) & \asymp \varepsilon \log (1/\varepsilon ). \end{aligned}  \] Consequently the preceding diameter bound has sharp order under its uniform upper bound. Without that bound, area can tend to zero while diameter stays bounded below by a positive constant. Proof. Choose a coordinate disk $\{ |z|<R\} $ with $0<R<1$, on whose closure $h=\lambda (z)|\mathrm{d}z|^2$ with $\lambda >0$ smooth. Choose a smooth cutoff $0\leq \chi \leq 1$, supported in this disk and equal to one for $|z|\leq R/2$, and a constant $c>0$ with $c\leq \min \lambda $. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$, set \[  g_\varepsilon = \left(\chi \frac{c\varepsilon ^2}{\lambda (z)(\varepsilon ^2+|z|^2)} +(1-\chi )\varepsilon ^2\right)h  \] in the disk, and set $g_\varepsilon =\varepsilon ^2h$ outside it. The cutoff makes this a smooth positive metric, and both coefficients in its convex combination are at most one. On $|z|\leq R/2$ its metric density is $c\varepsilon ^2/(\varepsilon ^2+|z|^2)$, whose area is \[  \pi c\varepsilon ^2 \log \left(1+\frac{R^2}{4\varepsilon ^2}\right).  \] The remaining area is $O(\varepsilon ^2)$, proving the asserted area comparison. Any path from the origin to a point outside this smaller disk must first cross its boundary. Radial variation is bounded by Euclidean speed, so that initial portion has length at least \[  \sqrt c\, \varepsilon \int _0^{R/2} \frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\sqrt{\varepsilon ^2+r^2}} =\sqrt c\, \varepsilon \operatorname {arsinh}(R/(2\varepsilon )) \asymp \varepsilon \log (1/\varepsilon ).  \] This gives the diameter lower bound. The upper bound follows from lemma 15.19.24 , since $A_\varepsilon (1+\log (1/A_\varepsilon ))\asymp \varepsilon ^2\log ^2(1/\varepsilon )$. Finally rescale by \[  \widetilde g_\varepsilon =\frac{g_\varepsilon }{\varepsilon ^2\log ^2(1/\varepsilon )}.  \] Its area is comparable to $1/\log (1/\varepsilon )$ and tends to zero, whereas its diameter is comparable to one. At the origin its ratio to $h$ tends to infinity, so it has no uniform upper bound. $\square$ Let $V\to C$ be a holomorphic vector bundle of positive rank with a fixed smooth Hermitian fiber norm. Write $U_\delta =\{ v\in V:|v|<\delta \} $ and identify its zero section with $C$. Proposition 15.19.26 . 4A271B6E1DDB Let $g_ j$ be smooth Hermitian metrics on $U_{\delta _0}$. Suppose their restrictions to $C$ satisfy \[  g_ j|_ C\leq M h,\qquad A_ j=\operatorname {Area}_{g_ j|_ C}(C)\longrightarrow 0  \] for a fixed $M>0$. Suppose also that there are $B>0$ and $0<\alpha \leq 1$ such that, for every unit fiber vector $v$ over any $x\in C$, the ray $\gamma _{x,v}(s)=sv$ satisfies \[  g_ j(\gamma _{x,v}'(s),\gamma _{x,v}'(s)) \leq B s^{2\alpha -2}, \qquad 0<s<\delta _0,  \] uniformly in $j,x,v$. Then \[  \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U_\delta ,g_ j) \leq \frac{2\sqrt B}{\alpha }\delta ^\alpha +K_ h\sqrt{A_ j\bigl (1+\log (M/A_ j)\bigr )}, \qquad 0<\delta <\delta _0.  \] In particular, \[  \lim _{\delta \downarrow 0}\limsup _{j\to \infty } \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U_\delta ,g_ j)=0.  \] Proof. A point of fiber radius $r<\delta $ joins its base point on the zero section along the radial segment, entirely inside $U_\delta $. Its length is at most \[  \sqrt B\int _0^ r s^{\alpha -1}\, \mathrm{d}s =\frac{\sqrt B}{\alpha }r^\alpha .  \] The metric is smooth at the zero section for each $j$; the integrable uniform bound controls the whole segment. Join the two base points by an almost minimizing path in $(C,g_ j|_ C)$. This path also lies in $U_\delta $, and up to an arbitrarily small excess its length is bounded by lemma 15.19.24 . Together with the two radial segments, this gives the asserted bound for the intrinsic diameter. Since $A_ j(1+\log (M/A_ j))\to 0$, taking $j\to \infty $ and then $\delta \downarrow 0$ proves the final assertion. $\square$ Return to the standard nodal small resolutions of 15.19.8 . On a nodal tube put $r^2=\sum _{k=1}^4|x_ k\circ \pi |^2$, the squared bundle norm used in lemma 15.19.10 . Let $V_\delta \subset Y$ be the nodal coordinate ball $\sum _ k|x_ k|^2<\delta ^2$. For sufficiently small $\delta $, properness gives $\pi ^{-1}(V_\delta )=\{ r<\delta \} $. Write $g_\varepsilon $ for the Riemannian metric associated to $\omega _\varepsilon $. Its area on $E_ a$ is $\varepsilon \int _{E_ a}\eta $ by corollary 15.19.12 . Fix an area-one Hermitian metric $h_ a$ on $E_ a$. If $g_\varepsilon |_{E_ a}\leq M h_ a$ uniformly and the radial bound of proposition 15.19.26 holds with $\alpha =1/2$, substitution in that proposition gives \[  \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(\{ r<\delta \} ,g_\varepsilon ) \leq K\delta ^{1/2} +K\sqrt{\varepsilon \bigl (1+\log (1/\varepsilon )\bigr )}  \] for sufficiently small $\varepsilon $ and $\delta $, with $K$ independent of both. Under these two pointwise metric bounds, the condition on approximating neighborhoods in proposition 15.19.22 therefore holds. The condition on punctured neighborhoods in the limiting metric does not follow from it, as the next example shows. In the following surface example the volume form is fixed and the approximating tubes shrink, but the punctured neighborhoods of the contracted point keep a positive diameter in the limiting metric. Example 15.19.27 . 11425F03EC01 There are a compact complex surface $X$, a holomorphic map $\pi :X\to Y=\mathbb P^2$ contracting a curve $E$ to a point $p$, and smooth Hermitian metrics $g_ j,g_*$ on $X$ with the following properties. The map is biholomorphic from $X\setminus E$ to $Y\setminus \{ p\} $, and $g_ j=g_*$ eventually on each compact subset of $X\setminus E$. Their associated Hermitian forms satisfy \[  \omega _ j^2=\omega _*^2.  \] The curve areas tend to zero, and the metrics have a uniform integrable radial bound near $E$. For a neighborhood basis $V_\delta $ of $p$, with $U_\delta =\pi ^{-1}(V_\delta )$, \[  \lim _{\delta \downarrow 0}\limsup _{j\to \infty } \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U_\delta ,g_ j)=0.  \] Nevertheless, for the intrinsic distance $d_0$ of $g_0=(\pi ^{-1})^*g_*$ on $Y\setminus \{ p\} $, there is $c>0$ such that \[  \operatorname {diam}_{d_0}(V_\delta \setminus \{ p\} )\geq c  \] for every sufficiently small $\delta $. Proof. Put $p=[1:0:0]$ and take the incidence surface \[  \begin{gathered} X=\bigl \{ ([z_0:z_1:z_2],[u:v])\in \mathbb P^2\times \mathbb P^1: z_1v=z_2u\bigr \} ,\\ \pi ([z],[u:v])=[z]. \end{gathered}  \] Off $p$, the second coordinate is $[z_1:z_2]$, so $\pi $ is biholomorphic there. Its exceptional curve is $E=\{ p\} \times \mathbb P^1$. In the affine chart $z_0=1$, a chart of $X$ is \[  (t,w)\longmapsto ([1:w:tw],[1:t]).  \] The other chart is $([1:t'w':w'],[t':1])$, with $t'=1/t$ and $w'=tw$ on their overlap. These are the charts of the tautological line bundle $L=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1)$. They also show smoothness along $E$; smoothness elsewhere follows from the biholomorphism. Thus $X$ is a compact smooth complex surface. Its connected dense complement $X\setminus E$ makes it connected. Let $q:L\to \mathbb P^1$ be the bundle projection. Give $L$ the norm induced by its tautological inclusion into $\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb C^2$. In the first chart its squared norm is \[  r^2=(1+|t|^2)|w|^2=|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2.  \] Fix an area-one Hermitian metric $h$ on $\mathbb P^1$. The Chern connection of the fiber norm defines a smooth semipositive Hermitian tensor $k$ on $L$ by the squared norm of the covariant fiber differential. Explicitly, with $\lambda =1+|t|^2$, \[  k=\lambda \left|\mathrm{d}w+w\partial \log \lambda \right|^2.  \] Under $t'=1/t$, $w'=tw$, the differential in this formula multiplies by $t$ and $\lambda $ divides by $|t|^2$, so the tensor is globally defined. It has complex rank one, is positive on nonzero vertical tangent vectors, and restricts to zero on $TE$. Consequently $q^*h+k$ is a smooth positive Hermitian metric on $L$. Choose $0<\delta _0<1$ and extend this metric from $U_{\delta _0}=\{ r<\delta _0\} $ to a smooth Hermitian metric $g_*$ on $X$. Such an extension follows by a smooth cutoff supported in a slightly larger bundle tube and a convex combination with any global Hermitian metric. It agrees exactly with $q^*h+k$ on $U_{\delta _0}$. Choose $0<\varepsilon _ j<1$ tending to zero, with $2\varepsilon _ j^2<\delta _0$, and a smooth function $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ on $[0,\infty )$, equal to zero on $[0,1]$ and to one on $[4,\infty )$. Set \[  \begin{aligned}  f_ j(r)& =\varepsilon _ j^2+(1-\varepsilon _ j^2) \chi (r^2/\varepsilon _ j^4),\\  g_ j& =f_ jq^*h+f_ j^{-1}k, \end{aligned}  \] on $U_{\delta _0}$, and set $g_ j=g_*$ elsewhere. The function $f_ j$ is smooth at $E$, is at least $\varepsilon _ j^2$, and equals one for $r\geq 2\varepsilon _ j^2$. Hence the metrics glue smoothly and are positive. They equal $g_*$ eventually on every compact subset of $X\setminus E$. Let $\beta ,\kappa $ be the Hermitian forms of $q^*h,k$. Their complex rank one gives $\beta ^2=\kappa ^2=0$. On the tube, \[  (f_ j\beta +f_ j^{-1}\kappa )^2 =2\beta \wedge \kappa =(\beta +\kappa )^2.  \] Outside it the metrics coincide. This proves the global volume identity. On $E$, the restriction is $g_ j|_ E=\varepsilon _ j^2h$, so its area is $\varepsilon _ j^2$. For any unit fiber vector $a$, a radial ray $\gamma (s)=sa$ has $k$-squared speed one and zero base component. Thus its $g_ j$-squared speed is $f_ j(s)^{-1}$. If $s<2\varepsilon _ j^2$, this is at most $\varepsilon _ j^{-2}\leq 2/s$; otherwise it is one, still at most $2/s$ for $s<\delta _0$. This is the uniform integrable radial bound with exponent $1/2$. A radial segment of radius $r<\delta $ has length at most $r+2\varepsilon _ j$: its portion below $2\varepsilon _ j^2$ has speed at most $\varepsilon _ j^{-1}$ and length at most $2\varepsilon _ j$, and its remaining speed is one. Connect two points by their radial segments and an almost minimizing path on $E$. All three segments stay inside $U_\delta $, giving \[  \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U_\delta ,g_ j) \leq 2\delta +\varepsilon _ j\bigl (4+\operatorname {diam}(\mathbb P^1,h)\bigr ).  \] Taking $j\to \infty $ before $\delta \downarrow 0$ proves the asserted shrinking condition. The affine balls \[  V_\delta =\{ [1:z_1:z_2]:|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2<\delta ^2\}   \] have precisely these tubes as their preimages. Let $d_*$ be the global distance of the fixed smooth metric $g_*$. Choose distinct points $a,b\in E$, and put $c=d_*(a,b)>0$. Choose points $a_ r,b_ r$ of fiber norm $r>0$ over these base points. They tend to $a,b$ as $r\downarrow 0$. Every path in $Y\setminus \{ p\} $ lifts to a path in $X\setminus E$ with the same $g_0$-length as its $g_*$-length. Therefore \[  d_0(\pi (a_ r),\pi (b_ r))\geq d_*(a_ r,b_ r)\longrightarrow c.  \] For any fixed $\delta >0$, these two images lie in $V_\delta $ when $r<\delta $. Taking the supremum and then $r\downarrow 0$ gives its punctured diameter at least $c$. $\square$

title: Lemma 15.19.24
text: Lemma 15.19.24 . 240B8EBF50C3 There is $K_ h>0$ such that every smooth Hermitian metric $g\leq M h$, with $M>0$ and $A=\operatorname {Area}_ g(C)$, satisfies \[  \operatorname {diam}(C,g) \leq K_ h\sqrt{A\bigl (1+\log (M/A)\bigr )}.  \] Here $0<A\leq M$. In particular, for a fixed upper bound $M$, area tending to zero implies diameter tending to zero. Proof. Replace $g$ by $g/M$. Its area is $a=A/M\leq 1$, and it is bounded above by $h$. We prove the estimate for this normalized metric. Choose a finite cover by holomorphic coordinate disks $U_ i$ represented by $\{ |z|<1\} $, with each coordinate defined on the larger disk $\{ |z|<2\} $. Write $g=\rho _ i|\mathrm{d}z|^2$ there. There is a common $L>0$ such that $0<\rho _ i\leq L$ on all the closed unit disks, and \[  \int _{U_ i}\rho _ i\, \mathrm{d}\lambda _2\leq a,  \] where $\lambda _2$ is Euclidean area. For $p,z\in U_ i$, let $\ell _ p(z)$ be the $g$-length of their straight coordinate segment, which stays in $U_ i$. Polar coordinates about $p$ and Fubini give \[  \int _{U_ i}\ell _ p(z)\, \mathrm{d}\lambda _2(z) \leq 2\int _{U_ i}\frac{\sqrt{\rho _ i(w)}}{|w-p|} \, \mathrm{d}\lambda _2(w).  \] Indeed each ray meets the convex unit disk in an interval of length $R\leq 2$. Interchanging the radial integrals multiplies the length integrand at radius $s$ by $(R^2-s^2)/2\leq 2$. For $0<a\leq 1/4$, put $t=\sqrt a$. The integral on the right, without its factor two, is bounded by \[  \begin{split}  \sqrt L\int _{\{ |w-p|<t\} }\frac{\mathrm{d}\lambda _2(w)}{|w-p|} & +\left(\int _{U_ i}\rho _ i\, \mathrm{d}\lambda _2\right)^{1/2} \left(\int _{\{ t<|w-p|<2\} }\frac{\mathrm{d}\lambda _2(w)}{|w-p|^2}\right)^{1/2}\\ & \leq 2\pi \sqrt L\, t+\sqrt{2\pi a\log (2/t)} \leq K\sqrt{a\bigl (1+\log (1/a)\bigr )}. \end{split}  \] Thus for any $p,q\in U_ i$, averaging $\ell _ p(z)+\ell _ q(z)$ over $z\in U_ i$ gives a two-segment path of length at most $K\sqrt{a(1+\log (1/a))}$. The constant is common to the finite cover. The overlap graph of this cover is connected because $C$ is connected. Choose points in consecutive overlaps along a simple path in this finite graph. The local estimates join any two points of $C$ through at most the number of covering disks, proving the global bound for $a\leq 1/4$. For $1/4\leq a\leq 1$, the comparison $g\leq h$ gives $\operatorname {diam}(C,g)\leq \operatorname {diam}(C,h)$, and increasing $K_ h$ gives the same estimate. Restoring the factor $M$ scales lengths by $\sqrt M$ and proves the assertion. $\square$

title: Example 15.19.25
text: Example 15.19.25 . F7F939140E90 On every such $(C,h)$ there are smooth Hermitian metrics $g_\varepsilon \leq h$, for $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, such that \[  \begin{aligned}  A_\varepsilon :=\operatorname {Area}_{g_\varepsilon }(C) & \asymp \varepsilon ^2\log (1/\varepsilon ),\\  \operatorname {diam}(C,g_\varepsilon ) & \asymp \varepsilon \log (1/\varepsilon ). \end{aligned}  \] Consequently the preceding diameter bound has sharp order under its uniform upper bound. Without that bound, area can tend to zero while diameter stays bounded below by a positive constant. Proof. Choose a coordinate disk $\{ |z|<R\} $ with $0<R<1$, on whose closure $h=\lambda (z)|\mathrm{d}z|^2$ with $\lambda >0$ smooth. Choose a smooth cutoff $0\leq \chi \leq 1$, supported in this disk and equal to one for $|z|\leq R/2$, and a constant $c>0$ with $c\leq \min \lambda $. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$, set \[  g_\varepsilon = \left(\chi \frac{c\varepsilon ^2}{\lambda (z)(\varepsilon ^2+|z|^2)} +(1-\chi )\varepsilon ^2\right)h  \] in the disk, and set $g_\varepsilon =\varepsilon ^2h$ outside it. The cutoff makes this a smooth positive metric, and both coefficients in its convex combination are at most one. On $|z|\leq R/2$ its metric density is $c\varepsilon ^2/(\varepsilon ^2+|z|^2)$, whose area is \[  \pi c\varepsilon ^2 \log \left(1+\frac{R^2}{4\varepsilon ^2}\right).  \] The remaining area is $O(\varepsilon ^2)$, proving the asserted area comparison. Any path from the origin to a point outside this smaller disk must first cross its boundary. Radial variation is bounded by Euclidean speed, so that initial portion has length at least \[  \sqrt c\, \varepsilon \int _0^{R/2} \frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\sqrt{\varepsilon ^2+r^2}} =\sqrt c\, \varepsilon \operatorname {arsinh}(R/(2\varepsilon )) \asymp \varepsilon \log (1/\varepsilon ).  \] This gives the diameter lower bound. The upper bound follows from lemma 15.19.24 , since $A_\varepsilon (1+\log (1/A_\varepsilon ))\asymp \varepsilon ^2\log ^2(1/\varepsilon )$. Finally rescale by \[  \widetilde g_\varepsilon =\frac{g_\varepsilon }{\varepsilon ^2\log ^2(1/\varepsilon )}.  \] Its area is comparable to $1/\log (1/\varepsilon )$ and tends to zero, whereas its diameter is comparable to one. At the origin its ratio to $h$ tends to infinity, so it has no uniform upper bound. $\square$

title: Proposition 15.19.26
text: Proposition 15.19.26 . 4A271B6E1DDB Let $g_ j$ be smooth Hermitian metrics on $U_{\delta _0}$. Suppose their restrictions to $C$ satisfy \[  g_ j|_ C\leq M h,\qquad A_ j=\operatorname {Area}_{g_ j|_ C}(C)\longrightarrow 0  \] for a fixed $M>0$. Suppose also that there are $B>0$ and $0<\alpha \leq 1$ such that, for every unit fiber vector $v$ over any $x\in C$, the ray $\gamma _{x,v}(s)=sv$ satisfies \[  g_ j(\gamma _{x,v}'(s),\gamma _{x,v}'(s)) \leq B s^{2\alpha -2}, \qquad 0<s<\delta _0,  \] uniformly in $j,x,v$. Then \[  \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U_\delta ,g_ j) \leq \frac{2\sqrt B}{\alpha }\delta ^\alpha +K_ h\sqrt{A_ j\bigl (1+\log (M/A_ j)\bigr )}, \qquad 0<\delta <\delta _0.  \] In particular, \[  \lim _{\delta \downarrow 0}\limsup _{j\to \infty } \operatorname {diam}^{\mathrm{int}}(U_\delta ,g_ j)=0.  \] Proof. A point of fiber radius $r<\delta $ joins its base point on the zero section along the radial segment, entirely inside $U_\delta $. Join the two base points by an almost minimizing path in $(C,g_ j|_ C)$. This path also lies in $U_\delta $, and up to an arbitrarily small excess its length is bounded by lemma 15.19.24 . Together with the two radial segments, this gives the asserted bound for the intrinsic diameter. Since $A_ j(1+\log (M/A_ j))\to 0$, taking $j\to \infty $ and then $\delta \downarrow 0$ proves the final assertion. $\square$

title: 15.20 Symmetry and the selected projective limit
search_title: Symmetry and the selected projective limit
section: 15.20 Symmetry and the selected projective limit
text: Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form and $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, a nonzero density. When the normalized equation $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$ has several solutions, the positive-exponent equations $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ still have unique solutions, and their normalized limits as $\lambda \downarrow 0$ single out particular solutions of the normalized equation. We study this selection in the projective example of theorem 14.26.1 , whose density vanishes on an open band. The starting point is a general observation: uniqueness at positive exponent preserves the symmetries of the data, and uniform compactness carries them to every normalized cluster limit. For the projective data this already gives a solution distinct from the two smooth solutions exchanged by the involution. The radial form of the equation then identifies the selected limit (theorem 15.20.4 ) and shows that the positive-exponent solutions fail to be $C^2$ along the same hypersurfaces (proposition 15.20.8 ). Proposition 15.20.1 . 1750C7E75315 Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form on $X$, let $\mathrm{d}V$ be a smooth positive volume form, and let $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, be nonzero. Let $c>0$ be the unique scalar for the bounded equation $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$ (theorem 14.19.2 ). For $\lambda >0$ denote by $u_\lambda $ the unique bounded solution of \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u_\lambda )=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad a_\lambda =u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda .  \] The family $\{ a_\lambda :0<\lambda \leq 1\} $ is relatively compact in $C(X)$. Every cluster limit as $\lambda \downarrow 0$ is a normalized bounded solution of $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (a)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$. Suppose a group $G$ of biholomorphisms of $X$ preserves $\omega $ and the measure $f\, \mathrm{d}V$. Then every $a_\lambda $ and every such cluster limit is $G$-invariant. In particular, the zero-exponent equation has a $G$-invariant normalized solution. Proof. The barriers of proposition 14.19.34 give a uniform oscillation bound for $u_\lambda $ and uniform convergence $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }\to c$. Thus the equation densities are uniformly bounded in $L^ p$ for $0<\lambda \leq 1$ and tend to $cf$ in $L^ p$ as $\lambda \downarrow 0$. Apply theorem 14.19.21 to obtain relative compactness of $a_\lambda $ in $C(X)$ and the asserted equation for every cluster limit. For each $g\in G$, pullback of the positive-exponent equation shows that $u_\lambda \circ g$ solves the same equation. Its uniqueness gives $u_\lambda \circ g=u_\lambda $. Surjectivity of $g$ preserves the supremum, so $a_\lambda \circ g=a_\lambda $. Uniform convergence preserves these equalities for every $g$. Compactness gives at least one cluster limit as $\lambda \downarrow 0$, yielding the invariant solution. $\square$ Corollary 15.20.2 . D0124640DBA7 On $\mathbb P(\mathbb C^2\oplus \mathbb C^2)$, with block homogeneous coordinates $[A:B]$, the data in theorem 14.26.1 can be chosen so that the same zero-exponent equation has at least three distinct normalized bounded solutions. Two are smooth, and a third is Hölder continuous and fixed by the involution $\iota [A:B]=[B:A]$. Proof. Use the radial coordinate $r$, rank-one forms $P,Q,R$, Fubini–Study form $\omega _ X$, and scalar functions $F,x,y,z$ from 14.26.2 , 14.26.7 . Set $w=F(r)$, $\omega _0=xP+yQ+zR$, $H=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w/2$, $A_0=\omega _0-H$ and $B_0=\omega _0+H$ as in 14.26.9 . The Hermitian form is $\omega =\omega _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $, with $\rho =\varepsilon (r^2-1)\kappa (r)$ from 14.26.10 . Choose the cutoff $\kappa $ even; all its required support and plateau properties are preserved by this choice. Then $\rho $ is even, while $w=F(r)$ is odd. The involution sends $r$ to $-r$, interchanges $P,Q$, and fixes $R$. The coefficient identities $x(-r)=y(r)$ and $z(-r)=z(r)$ show that $\iota ^*\omega _0=\omega _0$. Thus $\iota ^*\omega =\omega $, and $\iota ^*\omega _ X=\omega _ X$. Since $\iota ^*H=-H$, the involution interchanges $A_0$ and $B_0$. Their cubes are equal, so $f\omega _ X^3$ is invariant. It also interchanges $\widetilde u=-w/2-\rho $ and $\widetilde v=w/2-\rho $. These functions therefore have the same supremum, and the normalized solutions $u,v$ are interchanged. They are distinct, so neither is invariant. Apply proposition 15.20.1 to the group generated by $\iota $. Here $c=1$, as the two constructed solutions already have that scalar. An invariant cluster solution $a$ cannot equal either $u$ or $v$. Its bounded equation with smooth density gives Hölder regularity by theorem 15.5.1 . This gives a third solution. Its regularity is determined in subsection 15.20.3 , subsection 15.20.7 : it is $C^{1,1}$ but not $C^2$. $\square$ To identify the whole normalized limit for these symmetric data, we now use the radial form of the equation. It determines the invariant solution even among bounded potentials whose differentiability is not known in advance.

title: Proposition 15.20.1
section: 15.20 Symmetry and the selected projective limit
text: Proposition 15.20.1 . 1750C7E75315 Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form on $X$, let $\mathrm{d}V$ be a smooth positive volume form, and let $0\leq f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, be nonzero. For $\lambda >0$ denote by $u_\lambda $ the unique bounded solution of \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u_\lambda )=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad a_\lambda =u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda .  \] The family $\{ a_\lambda :0<\lambda \leq 1\} $ is relatively compact in $C(X)$. title: Corollary 15.20.2
section: 15.20 Symmetry and the selected projective limit
text: Corollary 15.20.2 . D0124640DBA7 On $\mathbb P(\mathbb C^2\oplus \mathbb C^2)$, with block homogeneous coordinates $[A:B]$, the data in theorem 14.26.1 can be chosen so that the same zero-exponent equation has at least three distinct normalized bounded solutions. Two are smooth, and a third is Hölder continuous and fixed by the involution $\iota [A:B]=[B:A]$. Proof. Use the radial coordinate $r$, rank-one forms $P,Q,R$, Fubini–Study form $\omega _ X$, and scalar functions $F,x,y,z$ from 14.26.2 , 14.26.7 . Set $w=F(r)$, $\omega _0=xP+yQ+zR$, $H=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w/2$, $A_0=\omega _0-H$ and $B_0=\omega _0+H$ as in 14.26.9 . The Hermitian form is $\omega =\omega _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho $, with $\rho =\varepsilon (r^2-1)\kappa (r)$ from 14.26.10 . Choose the cutoff $\kappa $ even; all its required support and plateau properties are preserved by this choice. Then $\rho $ is even, while $w=F(r)$ is odd. The involution sends $r$ to $-r$, interchanges $P,Q$, and fixes $R$. The coefficient identities $x(-r)=y(r)$ and $z(-r)=z(r)$ show that $\iota ^*\omega _0=\omega _0$. Thus $\iota ^*\omega =\omega $, and $\iota ^*\omega _ X=\omega _ X$. Since $\iota ^*H=-H$, the involution interchanges $A_0$ and $B_0$. Their cubes are equal, so $f\omega _ X^3$ is invariant. It also interchanges $\widetilde u=-w/2-\rho $ and $\widetilde v=w/2-\rho $. These functions therefore have the same supremum, and the normalized solutions $u,v$ are interchanged. They are distinct, so neither is invariant. Apply proposition 15.20.1 to the group generated by $\iota $. Here $c=1$, as the two constructed solutions already have that scalar. An invariant cluster solution $a$ cannot equal either $u$ or $v$. Its bounded equation with smooth density gives Hölder regularity by theorem 15.5.1 . This gives a third solution. Its regularity is determined in subsection 15.20.3 , subsection 15.20.7 : it is $C^{1,1}$ but not $C^2$. $\square$

The limit is therefore one. Integrating the equation gives \[   rac{a^2}{2}- rac{a^3}{3} = rac{\sigma ^2}{2}- rac{\sigma ^3}{3}+C.  \] Taking the limit at infinity gives $C=0$. The scalar function $s^2/2-s^3/3$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1)$, so $a=\sigma $ and $h=0$ for $r\geq 2$. If convergence of the whole family failed, a sequence staying a fixed positive uniform distance from $u_*$ would have a convergent subsequence, contradicting that identification. This proves uniform convergence and the asserted $C^{1,1}$ regularity of the limit. $\square$

title: 15.20.7 Second derivatives at positive exponent
section: 15.20 Symmetry and the selected projective limit
text: On the band where the density vanishes, the exponential factor plays no role, and the radial equation determines the slope of the solution independently of the exponent. Consequently the positive-exponent solutions have the same failure of second differentiability as the selected limit $u_*$. We keep the notation $A$, $\Phi $, $k$ and the transition radius $t_*$ of subsection 15.20.3 . Proposition 15.20.8 . 517F0BB04B80 For the symmetric projective data of theorem 15.20.4 , let $u_\lambda $ solve \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u_\lambda ) =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\omega _ X^3, \qquad \lambda >0.  \] On the open band $\{ -1<r<1\} $, $u_\lambda -u_*$ is constant. Both potentials are $C^{1,1}$ there and fail to be $C^2$ at every point of the two hypersurfaces $r=\pm t_*$. In particular, none of these positive-exponent solutions is a globally $C^2$ potential. Proof. Uniqueness and invariance of the data imply that $u_\lambda $ is $K$-invariant. Write $u_\lambda +\rho =G_\lambda (r)$ on $U$. The positivity argument in lemma 15.20.5 uses only boundedness and invariance, so $G_\lambda $ is locally Lipschitz and $h_\lambda =G_\lambda '$ is locally of bounded variation, with \[  -x\leq h_\lambda (r\pm )\leq y, \qquad \mathrm{d}h_\lambda +z\, \mathrm{d}r\geq 0.  \] Its weak flux equation is the same one, with the prescribed coefficient replaced by \[  k_\lambda (r)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda (G_\lambda (r)-\rho (r))}k(r).  \] Indeed, the scalar convolution and signed-product argument of that lemma is unchanged, and $k_\lambda $ is exactly the radial coefficient of the right-hand measure. Since $G_\lambda $ is bounded on compact $r$-intervals, $k_\lambda $ is locally bounded. Hence the right side of the flux equation has no atoms. The same strictly positive jump integral eliminates every jump of $h_\lambda $. Thus $h_\lambda $ is continuous and $G_\lambda $ is $C^1$. The coefficient $k_\lambda $ is consequently continuous. Where $A(r,h_\lambda )>0$, inversion of the $C^1$ flux gives \[  h_\lambda '=\frac{k_\lambda (r)}{A(r,h_\lambda )}-z.  \] On $-1<r<1$ the coefficient $k_\lambda $ is identically zero. Exchange invariance gives $h_\lambda (0)=0$ and oddness. On the positive half-band, the first-contact and no-departure arguments in the proof of theorem 15.20.4 apply verbatim: the first branch solves $h'=-z_0$, reaches $-p$ at $t_*$, and cannot leave that lower boundary to its right because $(h+p)'=p'-z_0<0$ on every proposed departure interval. Therefore \[  h_\lambda (r)= \begin{cases}  p(r),& -1<r\leq -t_*,\\  -\displaystyle \int _0^ r z_0(s)\, \mathrm{d}s,& -t_*\leq r\leq t_*,\\  -p(r),& t_*\leq r<1. \end{cases}  \] This is the derivative of $u_*+\rho $. Its primitive differs from $G_\lambda $ by one constant on the connected band. The claimed local $C^{1,1}$ regularity follows from the explicit slope. At $t_*\in (0,1)$ the two one-sided derivatives of this slope are \[  h_\lambda '(t_*-)=-z_0(t_*)<0, \qquad h_\lambda '(t_*+)=-p'(t_*)>0.  \] These unequal derivatives prevent the scalar primitive from having a second derivative at $t_*$. Through every point of that level set, the submersion $r$ provides a smooth curve parametrized by $r$, transferring the failure to $u_\lambda $. Smooth $\rho $ cannot cancel the jump. Oddness gives the conclusion at $-t_*$, and the identical slope proves it for $u_*$. $\square$ The zero set of $f$ contains the whole band. This example therefore does not concern the smooth strictly positive densities in the Hermitian Calabi–Yau theorem. It does show why smoothness of a nonnegative density alone is insufficient for second-order regularity, even when the equation includes a strictly increasing exponential factor.

title: 15.21 Local density and boundary control
text: Theorem 15.18.1 requires a smooth positive density on the whole regular locus of a global strict barrier, and the global minimum of the difference between the solution and the barrier drives its proof. If the density is smooth and positive only on a smaller open set, smoothness can fail there. A bounded solution with minimal singularities can be discontinuous on a ball where its density is constant (theorem 15.21.12 ), and a locally Lipschitz plurisubharmonic function with constant density need not be $C^1$ (example 15.21.15 ). Boundary data give a different route to regularity: if the solution has smooth boundary values on small balls, uniqueness for the bounded Dirichlet problem identifies it with the smooth Dirichlet solution. In this section $\theta $ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \varepsilon \omega $ for some $\varepsilon >0$; in particular $\theta $ is big. We fix an open set $\Omega \subset X$ on which $\rho $ is smooth and $\mathrm{d}\theta =0$.

title: 15.21.1 Smooth boundary traces
text: Let $B\Subset \Omega $ be a coordinate ball. A function $u$ on $B$ has boundary trace $g$, a function on $\partial B$, if $u(z)\to g(\xi )$ as $B\ni z\to \xi $, for every $\xi \in \partial B$. Theorem 15.21.2 . 9826C9FA5510 Suppose that $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has minimal ordinary singularities and \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=f\, \mathrm{d}V\quad \text{on }\Omega , \qquad f\in C^\infty (\Omega ),\quad f>0.  \] Assume that $\Omega $ is covered by coordinate Euclidean balls $B_ j\Subset \Omega $ such that $\theta $ has a smooth local potential near $\overline{B_ j}$ and $u$ has a smooth boundary trace on $\partial B_ j$. Then $u\in C^\infty (\Omega )$ and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$ there. Proof. Since $\rho -\sup _ X\rho \leq V_\theta $, minimal singularities give $u\geq \rho -C$ for a constant $C$. Thus $u$ is locally bounded on $\Omega $. Fix one of the balls, write it as $B=B_ R(z_0)$, let $g$ be the boundary trace of $u$ on $\partial B$, and choose a smooth function $h$ near $\overline B$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=\theta $. By proposition 5.28.2 , the bounded plurisubharmonic function $v=u+h$ has Bedford–Taylor measure $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ and smooth boundary trace $\varphi =g+h|_{\partial B}$. For a smooth function $V$ and the Euclidean volume $\mathrm{d}\Lambda $, 80E9773F7495 15.21.3 \begin{equation}  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V)^ n=\frac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\det (V_{j\bar k})\, \mathrm{d}\Lambda . \end{equation} The smooth Dirichlet theorem recalled in subsection 15.18.7 , with zero background and density $f\, \mathrm{d}V$, gives a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic $V$ on $\overline B$ with $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V)^ n=f\, \mathrm{d}V$ and boundary value $\varphi $; a smooth extension $\Phi $ of $\varphi $ gives the required strict subsolution $\Phi +A(|z-z_0|^2-R^2)$ for large $A$. In dimension one this is the Dirichlet problem for the Poisson equation. The difference $v-V$ tends to zero at every boundary point. Compactness of $\partial B$ makes this convergence uniform near the boundary: otherwise a sequence approaching the boundary with difference bounded away from zero would have a subsequence approaching one fixed boundary point. Uniqueness for the bounded Dirichlet problem, that is, the Bedford–Taylor comparison principle, gives $v=V$. Therefore $u=V-h$ is smooth on $B$, and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V>0$ there. Since the balls cover $\Omega $, the theorem follows. $\square$ The proof uses minimal singularities only to obtain the local lower bound by $\rho $. Consequently the same conclusion holds for any solution already known to be locally bounded on $\Omega $ and satisfying the same trace condition. Closedness of $\theta $ on $\Omega $ provides the local potentials $h$ once the coordinate balls are small enough; the background may be nonclosed elsewhere. Example 15.21.4 . DF2D43B90C47 For every $n\geq 1$, the trace criterion applies to a bounded continuous solution whose global density belongs to $L^1$ but to no $L^ p$ with $p>1$, and which is not Hölder continuous at the points of $X\setminus \Omega $. Let $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm{i}\mathbb Z)$, $X=E^ n$, and \[  \omega _ j=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\, \mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ j, \qquad \theta =\sum _{j=1}^ n\omega _ j, \qquad D=\{ 0\} \times E^{n-1}.  \] Take $\mathrm{d}V=\theta ^ n$ and $\rho =0$. Choose a nonnegative smooth cutoff $\chi $ supported in a coordinate disk $|z|<r_0<1$ of $E$ and equal to one near zero. For $\beta >0$, define \[  \psi (z)=\chi (z)(-\log |z|^2)^{-\beta }\quad (z\ne 0), \qquad \psi (0)=0,  \] and extend by zero. On the smaller punctured disk put $t=|z|^2$ and $L=-\log t$. Differentiation gives 334EFF96259F 15.21.5 \begin{equation}  \psi _{z\bar z}=\frac{\beta (\beta +1)}{tL^{\beta +2}}, \qquad t\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}L^{-\beta } =\beta L^{-\beta -1}\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} The first expression is integrable and the second is the radial flux. Integration by parts on punctured disks, using also $\psi \to 0$, shows that the distributional Hessian has no atom at zero. On the cutoff annulus its negative part is bounded. Hence, for a sufficiently small fixed $\eta >0$, $u=\eta \psi (z_1)$ satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \theta /2$. Only one coordinate contributes to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. Locally approximate the bounded subharmonic potential in that coordinate from above and use theorem 5.27.1 ; the smooth diagonal determinant identity passes to the limit and yields \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=f\theta ^ n, \qquad f=1+\eta \psi _{z\bar z}(z_1).  \] Give $f$ any positive value on the null set $D$. It is smooth and positive on $\Omega =X\setminus D$, where $u$ is smooth and has smooth traces on all relatively compact coordinate balls. Near $D$ its singular term is comparable to $|z_1|^{-2}(-\log |z_1|^2)^{-\beta -2}$. Its radial $L^1$ integral converges, whereas \[  \int _0^{r_0}s^{1-2p}(-\log s^2)^{-p(\beta +2)}\, \mathrm{d}s=+\infty \qquad (p>1).  \] Also $(-\log |z|^2)^{-\beta }/|z|^\alpha \to +\infty $ for every $\alpha >0$, so $u$ is not Hölder at $D$. Finally, boundedness gives minimal ordinary singularities, since every global $\theta $-plurisubharmonic competitor is bounded above.

title: 15.21.6 A bounded discontinuous potential
text: We construct a bounded plurisubharmonic function on a bidisk whose Monge–Ampère measure is a constant multiple of Lebesgue measure, but which is discontinuous. The construction places logarithmic poles with summable weights at points accumulating at the origin; the resulting weight $b$ vanishes at the poles but not at their limit. It is the local model for theorem 15.21.12 . Let $U=W=\{ |z|<1/4\} \subset \mathbb C$, with coordinates $z$ and $w$ on the two factors. Write $\mathrm{d}A$ for planar Lebesgue measure and set \[  a_ k=\alpha _ k=2^{-k-4},\qquad A=\sum _{k\geq 1}\alpha _ k=\frac1{16},\qquad S=\{ 0\} \cup \{ a_ k:k\geq 1\} .  \] Define on $U$ 6321AD313CED 15.21.7 \begin{equation}  h(z)=\sum _{k\geq 1}\alpha _ k\log |z-a_ k|^2, \qquad b(z)=\mathrm{e}^{h(z)}, \end{equation} with $b=0$ where $h=-\infty $. Lemma 15.21.8 . 5E22269BEE55 The function \[  a(z)=\frac1\pi \int _ U\log |z-\zeta |^2\, b(\zeta )^{-1}\, \mathrm{d}A(\zeta )  \] is bounded and continuous on $U$. The bounded function \[  P(z,w)=a(z)+b(z)|w|^2  \] is plurisubharmonic on $U\times W$, is smooth off $S\times W$, and satisfies 69692418B3EE 15.21.9 \begin{equation}  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}P)^2=\frac2{\pi ^2}\, \mathrm{d}A(z)\, \mathrm{d}A(w). \end{equation} It is discontinuous at every $(0,w_0)$ with $w_0\ne 0$. Proof. The summands defining $h$ are negative on $U$, so their partial sums decrease. Since $h(0)=2\sum _ k\alpha _ k\log a_ k> -\infty $, the limit is subharmonic. On compact subsets of $U\setminus S$, the series and its derivatives converge uniformly, making $h$ harmonic there. Moreover $0\leq b\leq 1$, $b(a_ k)=0$, and $b(0)>0$. Weighted arithmetic–geometric mean gives, almost everywhere, 331160A2E4B5 15.21.10 \begin{equation}  b(z)^{-2}\leq \sum _{k\geq 1}\frac{\alpha _ k}{A}|z-a_ k|^{-4A}. \end{equation} For the countable inequality, first use the first $N$ weights and assign the remaining weight to the factor $1$; then let $N$ increase. Since $4A=1/4<2$, the integrals of the terms $|z-a_ k|^{-4A}$ on $U$ are bounded uniformly in $k$. Thus $b^{-1}\in L^2(U)$. The logarithmic kernel has uniformly bounded $L^2$ norm on the translates of $U$ that occur in the definition of $a$. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds $a$ uniformly. Choose a compactly supported $L^2(\mathbb C)$ kernel agreeing with $\log |z|^2$ on $U-U$. Translation continuity in $L^2$, paired with $b^{-1}\mathbf1_ U\in L^2$, proves continuity of $a$. The distribution identity $\partial _ z\partial _{\bar z}\log |z|^2=\pi \delta _0$ gives $a_{z\bar z}=b^{-1}$. In particular $a$ is subharmonic and, by local elliptic regularity, smooth off $S$. The second summand of $P$ is $\exp (h(z)+\log |w|^2)$, a convex increasing composition of a plurisubharmonic function, extended by zero at its poles. Thus $P$ is bounded and plurisubharmonic. At smooth points the harmonicity of $h=\log b$ gives $bb_{z\bar z}=|b_ z|^2$, and hence \[  \det (P_{j\bar k}) =ba_{z\bar z}+|w|^2\bigl (bb_{z\bar z}-|b_ z|^2\bigr )=1.  \] The set $S\times W$ is contained in the pole set of $h(z)+\log |z|$, a plurisubharmonic function not identically $-\infty $. It is also Lebesgue-null. Pluripolar nullity in theorem 5.27.1 and ( 15.21.3 ) prove ( 15.21.9 ) throughout the bidisk. Finally, \[  P(a_ k,w_0)=a(a_ k)\longrightarrow a(0) <a(0)+b(0)|w_0|^2=P(0,w_0)  \] when $w_0\ne 0$. $\square$

title: 15.21.11 Compact gluing
text:
We now glue the local example into a compact torus by a regularized maximum with a quadratic function. The result is a bounded solution with minimal singularities whose density is constant on a ball, where the solution is discontinuous; in the transition region the density acquires singularities that destroy every $L^ p$ bound with $p>1$. We work on the flat complex torus $X=(\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm{i}\mathbb Z))^2$, identifying a small coordinate ball with a ball in $U	imes W$. For a smooth function $v$ on the ball write $H_ v=(v_{j ar k})$ for its complex Hessian and $I$ for the two-dimensional identity matrix. Theorem 15.21.12 . 5FC2412C22E9 There are a positive flat Kähler form $	heta $ on $X$, a bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with minimal ordinary singularities, and a density $F>0$ almost everywhere such that \[  \mathrm{MA}_	heta (u)=F	heta ^2,\qquad F\in L^1(X,	heta ^2),\qquad F
otin L^ p(X,	heta ^2)\quad (p>1).  \] On an open coordinate ball $\Omega $, $F$ is a positive constant and $u$ is discontinuous. The constant function $ho =0$ is a smooth strict barrier on $X$. Proof. Set $R=1/8$ and choose $M$ so that $P_0=P+M$ satisfies $0\leq P_0\leq L$ on $B_ R\Subset U	imes W$ for some finite $L$. Choose $C>0$ with 477A59B42B24 15.21.13  egin{equation}   rac{3CR^2}{16}\geq 2,\qquad  rac{5CR^2}{16}>L+2, \end{equation} and put $Q(Z)=C(|Z|^2-R^2/4)$ for $Z=(z,w)$. Let $\chi $ be the convolution of $|t|$ with an even nonnegative smooth probability kernel supported in $(-1,1)$. title: 15.22 Equations with resolved logarithmic poles
text: We now prescribe a singularity type with logarithmic poles. If the poles become a divisor on a modification, the singular part can be removed there, and what remains is a smooth residual form. When this residual form is strictly positive, the bounded Hermitian theory on the modification provides the remaining bounded potential, and pushing forward solves the equation in the prescribed type. In this section $n\geq 2$, and the background is a Hermitian form $h$ on $X$. Let $\psi \leq 0$ be a quasi-plurisubharmonic function that is smooth outside a nonempty analytic set $A$, its pole set. Assume that there is a modification $\pi :Y\to X$, biholomorphic over $X\setminus A$, such that $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ is the support $|D|$ of a simple normal crossing divisor $D=\sum _ jD_ j$ and 1B942D170060 15.22.1 \begin{equation}  \psi \circ \pi =\sum _ j c_ j\log |s_ j|^2+b, \qquad \beta =\pi ^*h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b-\sum _ jc_ j\Theta _ j>0, \end{equation} where $c_ j>0$, $b$ is smooth on $Y$, $s_ j$ is a holomorphic section of $\mathcal O(D_ j)$ defining $D_ j$, and $\Theta _ j$ is the curvature form of a smooth Hermitian metric on $\mathcal O(D_ j)$, so that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s_ j|^2=[D_ j]-\Theta _ j$. Thus $\beta $ is the smooth part of the current $\pi ^*h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi \circ \pi )$, which we call the residual form . Theorem 15.22.2 . 3B5397268E44 For every nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^ p(X,h^ n)$, $p>1$, there are $\kappa >0$ and a normalized $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ such that 4669708E978C 15.22.3 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=\kappa f h^ n, \qquad u=\psi +O(1). \end{equation} The lifted remainder $v=(u-\psi )\circ \pi $ extends Hölder continuously over $Y$, so $u$ is locally Hölder on $X\setminus A$. Its current is 91C08F2AC112 15.22.4 \begin{equation}  \pi ^*h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi ) =\sum _ jc_ j[D_ j]+\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v. \end{equation} The positive residual current $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ has zero Lelong numbers. If $h$ is Kähler, then $\kappa =\int _ Y\beta ^ n/\int _ X f h^ n$, and the normalized solution is unique among all normalized solutions $u'$ of ( 15.22.3 ) with $u'=\psi +O(1)$, continuous or not. If the density $g=(f\circ \pi )\, \pi ^*h^ n/\beta ^ n$ is smooth and strictly positive on $Y$, the residual current $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ may be chosen smooth and strictly positive. Proof. Define $J=\pi ^*h^ n/\beta ^ n$ and $g=(f\circ \pi )J$ off the exceptional set, assigning any value to $g$ on that volume-zero set. The smooth nonnegative $J$ is bounded. Change of variables on the biholomorphic locus gives BBA63F88F7F7 15.22.5 \begin{equation}  \int _ Yg\beta ^ n=\int _ Xfh^ n, \qquad \int _ Yg^ p\beta ^ n\leq \| J\| _\infty ^{p-1}\int _ Xf^ ph^ n. \end{equation} Thus $g$ is a nonzero $L^ p$ density. Theorem 14.19.2 , Theorem 15.5.1 give a bounded Hölder $\beta $-plurisubharmonic $v$ and $\kappa >0$ with $(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n=\kappa g\beta ^ n$. If $h$ is Kähler, then $\beta $ is Kähler and the mass identity fixes the stated scalar. For smooth positive $g$, theorem 14.2.1 gives a smooth solution instead. Set $u=\psi +v\circ \pi ^{-1}$ on $X\setminus A$ and $u=-\infty $ on $A$. Push forward the positive current $\sum c_ j[D_ j]+\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$. Pushforward commutes with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$, $\pi _*\pi ^*h=h$, and the pushed locally integrable potential is $u$ almost everywhere. Its quasi-plurisubharmonic representative equals $\psi +v\circ \pi ^{-1}$ off $A$ and tends to $-\infty $ at $A$ because $v$ is bounded. Hence $h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ and $u=\psi +O(1)$ in the two-sided ordinary sense. The pulled-back identity is ( 15.22.4 ); bounded residuals have zero Lelong number. The equation holds off $A$ by ( 15.22.5 ), and theorem 13.14.3 extends it as ( 15.22.3 ). Subtracting $\sup _ Xu$ changes neither the equation nor the ordinary type. For uniqueness when $h$ is Kähler, let $u'$ be a normalized solution with $u'=\psi +O(1)$. On $Y\setminus D$, $w=(u'-\psi )\circ \pi $ is bounded and $\beta $-plurisubharmonic. Since $w$ is bounded, lemma 5.24.7 extends it across $D$ to a bounded $\beta $-plurisubharmonic function on $Y$. On each relatively compact subset of $Y\setminus D$, sufficiently deep truncations of $u'$ equal $u'$. Thus locality in theorem 13.14.3 gives the bounded equation $\kappa g\beta ^ n$ there; both sides give $D$ zero mass. The global equation follows, its mass fixes $\kappa $, and closed full-mass uniqueness gives $w=v+$constant as recalled in section 25.21 . Normalization fixes that constant. $\square$ The Hölder constants depend on the fixed geometry and divisor metrics, the $c_ j$, a lower bound for the positivity of $\beta $, $p$, and the $L^ p$ norm of the density $\kappa g$ itself. In particular, the argument gives no estimate that is uniform as $\beta $ degenerates or as $\kappa $ becomes unbounded. In simple normal crossing coordinates a density comparable to $\prod _ j|z_ j|^{-2a_ j}$ belongs locally to $L^ p$ exactly when 7DF899E20ABD 15.22.6 \begin{equation}  pa_ j<1\quad \hbox{for every }j, \end{equation} by the factors $\int _0^\epsilon r_ j^{1-2pa_ j}\, \mathrm{d} r_ j$. A smooth positive density $f$ on $X$ need not give a strictly positive $g$ on $Y$, since the Jacobian factor $J=\pi ^*h^ n/\beta ^ n$ of the proof can vanish on the exceptional set. Example 15.22.7 . 0362BBF11A0B Take $X=\mathbb P^ n$, $h=\lambda \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$, $\int _ X\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^ n=1$, and $0<c<\lambda $. Put \[  \psi _ c=c\log \frac{\sum _{j=1}^ n|Z_ j|^2}{\sum _{j=0}^ n|Z_ j|^2}.  \] Its pole is $P=[1:0:\cdots :0]$. On the point blowup $\pi :Y\to X$, let $q:Y\to \mathbb P^{n-1}$ be the direction map. In affine blowup coordinates $x=(z,zw)$, Poincaré–Lelong gives \[  \pi ^*h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi _ c\circ \pi ) =c[E]+(\lambda -c)\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+cq^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}.  \] The residual form $\beta =(\lambda -c)\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+cq^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ is positive: $\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ is positive in the directions normal to $E$, and $q^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ in the directions tangent to $E$. Write $H=\pi ^*[\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}]$. Since $H|_ E=0$ and $E^ n=(-1)^{n-1}$, its mass is 853BE83A0787 15.22.8 \begin{equation}  \int _ Y\bigl ((\lambda -c)\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+cq^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}\bigr )^ n=\lambda ^ n-c^ n. \end{equation} Hence, for every nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^ p$ with $\int _ Xfh^ n=\lambda ^ n-c^ n$, theorem 15.22.2 gives $\kappa =1$ and a solution of $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=fh^ n$ with the nonminimal type $u=\psi _ c+O(1)$. For an explicit solution, choose a smooth function $v$ on $Y$ with $v|_ E$ nonconstant, small enough that $S=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is still positive, and put $u=\psi _ c+v\circ \pi ^{-1}$ off $P$. The density $f$ of its measure, given by $f\circ \pi =S^ n/\pi ^*h^ n$ off $E$, lies in every $L^ p$ with $1<p<n/(n-1)$: $\pi ^*h^ n$ vanishes to order $|z|^{2(n-1)}$ along $E$, so the local integral of $f^ p$ is finite precisely when $(n-1)(p-1)<1$. Different directions of approach to $P$ give different limits of $u-\psi _ c$. The divisor $c[E]$ of the current upstairs leaves no divisor downstairs, since $E$ is contracted to a point. On $X\setminus \{ P\} $, where $u$ is smooth and strictly $h$-plurisubharmonic, the Hermitian metric $h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is isometric to $(Y\setminus E,S)$. Its metric completion is $Y$ with the metric $S$, so the whole divisor $E$ is restored: removing the smooth real codimension-two submanifold $E$ does not change the infimum of path lengths in $Y$. Finally, if $h$ is replaced by a sufficiently small nonclosed perturbation, both $h$ and the residual form remain positive, so the existence part of theorem 15.22.2 still applies.

Put \[  \psi _ c=c\log \frac{\sum _{j=1}^ n|Z_ j|^2}{\sum _{j=0}^ n|Z_ j|^2}.  \] Its pole is $P=[1:0:\cdots :0]$.
