In affine blowup coordinates $x=(z,zw)$, Poincaré–Lelong gives \[  \pi ^*h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi _ c\circ \pi ) =c[E]+(\lambda -c)\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+cq^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}.  \] The residual form $\beta =(\lambda -c)\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+cq^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ is positive: $\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ is positive in the directions normal to $E$, and $q^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ in the directions tangent to $E$. Write $H=\pi ^*[\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}]$. Since $H|_ E=0$ and $E^ n=(-1)^{n-1}$, its mass is 853BE83A0787 15.22.8 \begin{equation}  \int _ Y\bigl ((\lambda -c)\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+cq^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}\bigr )^ n=\lambda ^ n-c^ n. \end{equation} Hence, for every nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^ p$ with $\int _ Xfh^ n=\lambda ^ n-c^ n$, theorem 15.22.2 gives $\kappa =1$ and a solution of $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=fh^ n$ with the nonminimal type $u=\psi _ c+O(1)$. For an explicit solution, choose a smooth function $v$ on $Y$ with $v|_ E$ nonconstant, small enough that $S=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is still positive, and put $u=\psi _ c+v\circ \pi ^{-1}$ off $P$. The density $f$ of its measure, given by $f\circ \pi =S^ n/\pi ^*h^ n$ off $E$, lies in every $L^ p$ with $1<p<n/(n-1)$: $\pi ^*h^ n$ vanishes to order $|z|^{2(n-1)}$ along $E$, so the local integral of $f^ p$ is finite precisely when $(n-1)(p-1)<1$. Different directions of approach to $P$ give different limits of $u-\psi _ c$. The divisor $c[E]$ of the current upstairs leaves no divisor downstairs, since $E$ is contracted to a point. On $X\setminus \{ P\} $, where $u$ is smooth and strictly $h$-plurisubharmonic, the Hermitian metric $h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is isometric to $(Y\setminus E,S)$. Its metric completion is $Y$ with the metric $S$, so the whole divisor $E$ is restored: removing the smooth real codimension-two submanifold $E$ does not change the infimum of path lengths in $Y$. Finally, if $h$ is replaced by a sufficiently small nonclosed perturbation, both $h$ and the residual form remain positive, so the existence part of theorem 15.22.2 still applies.

title: 15.22.9 Residual mass
text: When $h$ is not Kähler, the scalar in theorem 15.22.2 is still determined by masses if $h$ satisfies the power condition $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h^ k)=0$, $1\leq k\leq n-1$, of theorem 11.1.7 , which fixes the mass of every bounded solution. The condition persists under pullback and under addition of a smooth closed form: expand each power and apply the original identities to its terms. For $n=2$ the condition is simply $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=0$, so it includes the nonclosed Hopf metric of proposition 19.8.13 . The residual form then has strictly smaller mass than $h$, the difference being carried by the divisor. Proposition 15.22.10 . D1ADF0EFDD30 Under ( 15.22.1 ), assume $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h^ k)=0$ for $1\leq k\leq n-1$, and put $H=\pi ^*h$. Then 00D02AC76853 15.22.11 \begin{equation}  \int _ Xh^ n-\int _ Y\beta ^ n =\sum _ jc_ j\sum _{i=0}^{n-1} \int _{D_ j}H^ i\wedge \beta ^{n-1-i}>0. \end{equation} Thus the constructed solution of theorem 15.22.2 has $\kappa =\int _ Y\beta ^ n/\int _ Xfh^ n$. If $\int _ Xfh^ n=\int _ Xh^ n$, its scalar is strictly less than one. Proof. Let $C=\sum _ jc_ j\Theta _ j-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b$, so $\beta =H-C$ with $C$ closed. The mixed forms $Q_ i=H^ i\wedge \beta ^{n-1-i}$ satisfy $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Q_ i=0$: expand $\beta =H-C$ and apply the power condition to each $H^ k$. With $\Psi =\psi \circ \pi $, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi =\sum _ jc_ j[D_ j]-C$. Distributional integration by parts against the smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed $Q_ i$ gives \[  \int _ Y(H^ n-\beta ^ n)=\sum _ i\int _ Y C\wedge Q_ i =\sum _ jc_ j\sum _ i\int _{D_ j}Q_ i.  \] Change of variables gives $\int _ YH^ n=\int _ Xh^ n$. Every integrand on the right is nonnegative, since $H$ is semipositive and $\beta $ positive; the $i=0$ term on each nonempty $D_ j$ is strictly positive. This includes exceptional divisors. By theorem 11.1.7 , the residual solution has mass $\int _ Y\beta ^ n$, giving the scalar. $\square$

title: 15.23 Minimal singularities on blowups
text: On a blowup, the background itself can force an exceptional divisor into every positive current. The coefficient of this divisor is then part of the minimal ordinary type, while the rest of the potential descends to the target of the blowup, so the equation reduces to one on the target. The density changes by the Jacobian of the blowup, which determines the loss of integrability. In this section the roles of the letters differ from those in section 15.22 : $X$ is a blowup and $Y$ its target. Let $(Y,h)$ be a connected compact Hermitian $n$-fold, $n\geq 2$, let $Z\subset Y$ be a connected smooth center of codimension $r\geq 2$, and write $\pi :X=\operatorname {Bl}_ ZY\to Y$ for the blowup, with exceptional divisor $E$. Let $s_ E$ be the canonical section of $\mathcal O(E)$, choose a smooth Hermitian metric on $\mathcal O(E)$ with curvature form $\Theta _ E$, so that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s_ E|^2=[E]-\Theta _ E$, put $L=\log |s_ E|^2$, and fix $c>0$. The smooth background 04B0CB069F1C 15.23.1 \begin{equation}  \theta =\pi ^*h+c\Theta _ E \end{equation} can be indefinite, and it is nonclosed when $h$ is nonclosed. Positivity is imposed on $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, not on $\theta $. Proposition 15.23.2 . E42F32DA29D8 Every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has, up to an additive constant, a unique $h$-plurisubharmonic target potential $q$ such that C7554C964203 15.23.3 \begin{equation}  u=cL+q\circ \pi +C, \qquad \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\pi ^*(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)+c[E]. \end{equation} The potentials with minimal ordinary singularities are exactly those of the form $cL+O(1)$, and $u$ is one of them if and only if $q$ is bounded. There is a strict $\theta $-plurisubharmonic barrier with logarithmic coefficient $c+\delta $ for some $\delta >0$. Proof. Put $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ and $q=\pi _*(u-cL)$ as a scalar distribution. The latter is locally integrable: off $Z$ it is the inverse-coordinate function, and a smooth target volume pulls back with bounded Jacobian, so its absolute integral is controlled by that of $u-cL$ on $X$. Since $\pi _*[E]=0$, \[  S=\pi _*T=h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq 0.  \] A smooth local strictly plurisubharmonic shift gives a quasi-plurisubharmonic representative of $q$. Its pullback $q\circ \pi $ is not identically $-\infty $ and satisfies $\pi ^*(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)\geq 0$, by lemma 5.43.2 : since $\pi $ is dominant, the composition of a local plurisubharmonic function with $\pi $ is again plurisubharmonic and not identically $-\infty $. Off $E$, $T=\pi ^*S$. The difference is an order-zero current supported on $E$, and it is closed: both derivatives equal $\pi ^*\mathrm{d} h$. To identify it, write $R=T-\pi ^*S$. In a chart where $E=\{ z=0\} $, order zero gives $zR=\bar zR=0$. Closedness then gives $\mathrm{d}z\wedge R=\mathrm{d}\bar z\wedge R=0$. Thus only its normal $(1,1)$ coefficient remains, a measure on $E$; the tangential equations in $\mathrm{d}R=0$ make that measure a constant multiple of integration on $E$. Connectedness of $E$ identifies one constant $a$ globally, so $R=a[E]$. Its cohomology class is $c[E]$. On a line in an exceptional fiber, $\mathcal O(E)$ has degree $-1$, so $[E]$ is nonzero and $a=c$. The difference between the two scalar potentials in ( 15.23.3 ) has $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ zero. Local elliptic regularity makes it pluriharmonic; compactness and connectedness make it constant. Since $h>0$, $q=0$ is admissible, and every $h$-plurisubharmonic $q$ is bounded above on compact $Y$. Hence $cL$ is minimal and two-sided bounded comparison with it is exactly boundedness of $q$. For the barrier choose another divisor metric, with logarithmic norm $L'=L+\sigma $ and curvature $\Theta '_ E=\Theta _ E-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\sigma $ for a smooth real function $\sigma $, so that $-\Theta '_ E$ is positive on the vertical tangent bundle of $E\to Z$, using the tautological $\mathcal O(-1)$. In adapted coordinates 282A5F737F88 15.23.4 \begin{equation}  \pi (y,z,w)=(y,z,zw), \end{equation} $\pi ^*h$ controls the nonvertical directions and $|z|^2|\mathrm{d} w|^2$. For small $\delta >0$, the vertical positivity of $-\delta \Theta '_ E$ dominates its mixed errors by completing the square; away from $E$, compactness allows the same $\delta $. Thus $\pi ^*h-\delta \Theta '_ E>0$. For the fixed background $\theta $ in ( 15.23.1 ), take \[  w=(c+\delta )L'-c\sigma =(c+\delta )L+\delta \sigma .  \] Then $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=(c+\delta )[E]+\pi ^*h-\delta \Theta '_ E$ dominates a positive Hermitian form. The smooth correction $\delta \sigma $ preserves the stated logarithmic coefficient. $\square$ Theorem 15.23.5 . 66FFA0C36433 Fix a smooth positive volume form $\mu $ on $X$ and a nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^ p(X,\mu )$, $p>1$. There exist $\kappa >0$ and a normalized minimal-type solution of 70493856D26C 15.23.6 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)=\kappa f\mu , \qquad u=cL+q\circ \pi +C, \end{equation} where $q$ is Hölder on $Y$. The divisor coefficient is exactly $c$. In ( 15.23.4 ), $u-cL=q(y,0)+C+O(|z|^\alpha )$ on smaller charts for some $\alpha >0$, so its limit is constant along each exceptional fiber. If $\pi _*(f\mu )=Fh^ n$, then $F\in L^ s(Y,h^ n)$ for every 7E7FF8A6A54E 15.23.7 \begin{equation}  1<s<\frac{rp}{(r-1)p+1}. \end{equation} For a point center, data bounded above and below by positive constants near $E$ attain the strict threshold $s<n/(n-1)$, and for finite $p$ no strictly larger universal exponent than $np/((n-1)p+1)$ can be guaranteed. If $h$ is Kähler, the class $[\theta ]$ is big and non-nef, has volume $\int _ Yh^ n$, and $\kappa =\int _ Yh^ n/\int _ Xf\mu $; the normalized solution is unique among all normalized solutions of ( 15.23.6 ) with minimal ordinary singularities. Under $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(h^ j)=0$, $1\leq j\leq n-1$, the scalar of the constructed solution has the same integral formula. Proof. Integrability and existence. In ( 15.23.4 ) the complex Jacobian is $z^{r-1}$. Put $J=\pi ^*h^ n/\mu $, so $J\asymp |z|^{2(r-1)}$ on nested charts and $F\circ \pi =f/J$ off $E$. For $1<s<p$, change of variables and Hölder's inequality give 2BE1216FD9F5 15.23.8 \begin{align}  \int _ YF^ s h^ n & =\int _ X f^ sJ^{1-s}\mu \\ & \leq \| f\| _{L^ p(\mu )}^ s \left(\int _ XJ^{-(s-1)p/(p-s)}\mu \right)^{(p-s)/p}. \end{align} The normal complex integral is finite precisely if $(r-1)(s-1)p/(p-s)<1$, which is ( 15.23.7 ). Theorem 14.19.2 , Theorem 15.5.1 on $(Y,h)$ supply $q$ and $\kappa $ with $(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)^ n=\kappa Fh^ n$. Use ( 15.23.3 ) off $E$ and theorem 13.14.3 across it. Hölder continuity gives $q(\pi (y,z,w))=q(y,0)+O(|z|^\alpha )$ uniformly on smaller charts. Sharpness of the exponent. For $f$ bounded above and below by positive constants near the exceptional divisor of a point center, $F$ is comparable to $\operatorname {dist}_ h(\cdot ,Z)^{-2(n-1)}$ near $Z$, giving the strict threshold. More generally, $f\asymp |s_ E|^{-2a}$ with $0\leq a<1/p$ belongs to $L^ p$ upstairs, while its pushforward has threshold $s<n/(n-1+a)$. Letting $a\uparrow 1/p$ proves the stated limitation; it makes no finite-$p$ endpoint assertion. The Kähler case. When $h$ is Kähler, the strict barrier current $(c+\delta )[E]+\pi ^*h-\delta \Theta '_ E$ constructed in proposition 15.23.2 makes $[\theta ]$ big. Its degree on an exceptional-fiber line is $-c$, so it is not nef. The minimal current $c[E]+\pi ^*h$ has non-pluripolar top mass $\int _ Yh^ n$, and the minimal mass theorem identifies this with $\operatorname {vol}([\theta ])$ as recalled in section 25.18 . Full-mass uniqueness and mass integration fix the scalar and normalized current as recalled in section 25.21 . A normalized solution of minimal ordinary type, possibly discontinuous, still has bounded $q$ by proposition 15.23.2 ; on every relatively compact set off $E$, deep truncations equal that competitor, so locality in theorem 13.14.3 gives the bounded target equation off $Z$. Both target measures give $Z$ zero mass, so closed uniqueness applies globally. If only the power conditions hold, theorem 11.1.7 fixes the scalar of the constructed solution. Quantitative Hölder bounds depend on $\kappa F$, not on an unnormalized $F$ alone. $\square$ For the prescribed pullback measure $\pi ^*(h^ n)$, choose $q=0$ and $\kappa =1$. The current is $c[E]+\pi ^*h$. Its smooth part $\pi ^*h$ is degenerate on $E$ exactly in the directions tangent to the exceptional fibers, and its density relative to a smooth volume form is $|z|^{2(r-1)}$ times a smooth positive factor. On $X\setminus E$, where the solution $u=cL$ is smooth and strictly $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, the metric $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\pi ^*h$ is isometric to $(Y\setminus Z,h)$; its metric completion is $Y$, so each exceptional fiber collapses to a point of $Z$. The distance to $E$ is comparable to $|z|$ on bounded adapted charts. Neither the density order nor this distance exponent depends on $c$. Example 15.23.9 . 6C568E91A192 If $n=2$ and $Z$ is a point on a compact Kähler surface, $[\theta ]=\pi ^*[h]+c[E]$ has Zariski positive part $\pi ^*[h]$ and negative part $cE$: $E^2=-1$ and $\pi ^*[h]\cdot E=0$. Its volume is $\int _ Yh^2$, although it is non-nef. The solution with $\kappa =1$ for the measure $\pi ^*(h^2)$ has logarithmic coefficient exactly $c$, its density vanishes to order $|z|^2$ along $E$, and the completion of its metric on $X\setminus E$ collapses $E$ to the point $Z$. The stronger barrier from proposition 15.23.2 has coefficient $c+\delta $. Theorem 15.23.10 . 37D35D78F0C6 Let $\pi :Y_ m\to Y_0$ be a finite nonempty sequence of blowups of connected smooth centers of codimensions $r_ j\geq 2$ over a compact Hermitian $(Y_0,h_0)$. Let $E_ j$ be the exceptional divisor at stage $j$, let $\pi _{>j}$ denote the subsequent map, choose $a_ j>0$, and set \[  \Delta =\sum _ j a_ j\pi _{>j}^*E_ j, \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}L_\Delta =[\Delta ]-\Theta _\Delta , \qquad \theta =\pi ^*h_0+\Theta _\Delta ,  \] where $L_\Delta =\sum _ ja_ j\log |s_ j|^2$, with $s_ j$ the canonical section of $\pi _{>j}^*\mathcal O(E_ j)$ for a smooth Hermitian metric, and $\Theta _\Delta $ is the corresponding combination of curvature forms. Every $\theta $-positive current is $\pi ^*(h_0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)+[\Delta ]$ and every potential is $L_\Delta +q\circ \pi +C$, with $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y_0,h_0)$. Minimal ordinary type is exactly $L_\Delta +O(1)$, equivalent to bounded $q$. For potentials of this type, every prime exceptional coefficient is the one prescribed by the effective total transform $\Delta $. There is a strict barrier with divisor $\Delta +B$ for an effective exceptional $B$ positive on every exceptional component. For nonzero nonnegative upstairs $L^ p$ data, $p>1$, a minimal solution has Hölder $q$, with pushed density in every $L^ s$ satisfying 749BE96956FE 15.23.11 \begin{equation}  1<s<\frac{Rp}{(R-1)p+1},\qquad R=\prod _ jr_ j. \end{equation} For Kähler $h_0$ the mass, scalar, and closed full-mass uniqueness are those of the target; the power conditions on $h_0$ fix the scalar for the constructed nonclosed solution. For the pullback measure $\pi ^*(h_0^ n)$, the metric $\pi ^*h_0$ on the complement of the exceptional set has metric completion $Y_0$, each fiber collapsing to a point, and the zero divisor of the density is that of the squared modulus of the holomorphic Jacobian, independently of the $a_ j$. Proof. Apply proposition 15.23.2 successively, allowing an intermediate smooth background to be indefinite. The difference between each current and the pullback of its pushforward is closed of order zero, and exceptional-fiber degree fixes its coefficient. Pullback of earlier divisor currents produces the total transforms, proving the representation without an SNC requirement. The initial $q=0$ is admissible; upper bounds on compact targets prove minimality and the bounded-$q$ criterion. At SNC charts this is the usual sum of logarithms. At each stage choose an auxiliary divisor metric as in proposition 15.23.2 , with curvature $\Theta '_{E_ j}$, so that $h_ j=\pi _ j^*h_{j-1}-\delta _ j\Theta '_{E_ j}>0$ for a sufficiently small $\delta _ j>0$. Expanding yields $h_ m=\pi ^*h_0-\Theta _ B$ for $B=\sum _ j\delta _ j\pi _{>j}^*E_ j$, effective with a positive coefficient on every exceptional component. If $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}L_ B=[B]-\Theta _ B$ uses these auxiliary metrics, then the fixed background satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(L_\Delta +L_ B)=h_ m+[\Delta +B]$, which is the strict barrier current. The Jacobian calculation and Hölder estimate apply stagewise. If $s=rp/((r-1)p+1)$, then $1-1/s=(1-1/p)/r$; iteration over the stages gives ( 15.23.11 ), with strict inequality. The target Hölder equation, mass and uniqueness are obtained as in theorem 15.23.5 . For the pullback measure take $q=0$ and use the target path comparison away from the exceptional set. The Jacobian fixes the density, while $[\Delta ]$ fixes the divisor current; these are independent pieces of the equation. $\square$

text: Example 15.23.9 . 6C568E91A192 If $n=2$ and $Z$ is a point on a compact Kähler surface, $[\theta ]=\pi ^*[h]+c[E]$ has Zariski positive part $\pi ^*[h]$ and negative part $cE$: $E^2=-1$ and $\pi ^*[h]\cdot E=0$. The solution with $\kappa =1$ for the measure $\pi ^*(h^2)$ has logarithmic coefficient exactly $c$, its density vanishes to order $|z|^2$ along $E$, and the completion of its metric on $X\setminus E$ collapses $E$ to the point $Z$. title: Theorem 15.23.10
text: Theorem 15.23.10 . 37D35D78F0C6 Let $\pi :Y_ m\to Y_0$ be a finite nonempty sequence of blowups of connected smooth centers of codimensions $r_ j\geq 2$ over a compact Hermitian $(Y_0,h_0)$. Let $E_ j$ be the exceptional divisor at stage $j$, let $\pi _{>j}$ denote the subsequent map, choose $a_ j>0$, and set \[  \Delta =\sum _ j a_ j\pi _{>j}^*E_ j, \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}L_\Delta =[\Delta ]-\Theta _\Delta , \qquad \theta =\pi ^*h_0+\Theta _\Delta ,  \] where $L_\Delta =\sum _ ja_ j\log |s_ j|^2$, with $s_ j$ the canonical section of $\pi _{>j}^*\mathcal O(E_ j)$ for a smooth Hermitian metric, and $\Theta _\Delta $ is the corresponding combination of curvature forms. Every $\theta $-positive current is $\pi ^*(h_0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q)+[\Delta ]$ and every potential is $L_\Delta +q\circ \pi +C$, with $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y_0,h_0)$. Minimal ordinary type is exactly $L_\Delta +O(1)$, equivalent to bounded $q$. For potentials of this type, every prime exceptional coefficient is the one prescribed by the effective total transform $\Delta $. There is a strict barrier with divisor $\Delta +B$ for an effective exceptional $B$ positive on every exceptional component. For nonzero nonnegative upstairs $L^ p$ data, $p>1$, a minimal solution has Hölder $q$, with pushed density in every $L^ s$ satisfying 749BE96956FE 15.23.11 \begin{equation}  1<s<\frac{Rp}{(R-1)p+1},\qquad R=\prod _ jr_ j. \end{equation} For Kähler $h_0$ the mass, scalar, and closed full-mass uniqueness are those of the target; the power conditions on $h_0$ fix the scalar for the constructed nonclosed solution. For the pullback measure $\pi ^*(h_0^ n)$, the metric $\pi ^*h_0$ on the complement of the exceptional set has metric completion $Y_0$, each fiber collapsing to a point, and the zero divisor of the density is that of the squared modulus of the holomorphic Jacobian, independently of the $a_ j$. Proof. Apply proposition 15.23.2 successively, allowing an intermediate smooth background to be indefinite. The difference between each current and the pullback of its pushforward is closed of order zero, and exceptional-fiber degree fixes its coefficient. Pullback of earlier divisor currents produces the total transforms, proving the representation without an SNC requirement. The initial $q=0$ is admissible; upper bounds on compact targets prove minimality and the bounded-$q$ criterion. At SNC charts this is the usual sum of logarithms. At each stage choose an auxiliary divisor metric as in proposition 15.23.2 , with curvature $\Theta '_{E_ j}$, so that $h_ j=\pi _ j^*h_{j-1}-\delta _ j\Theta '_{E_ j}>0$ for a sufficiently small $\delta _ j>0$. Expanding yields $h_ m=\pi ^*h_0-\Theta _ B$ for $B=\sum _ j\delta _ j\pi _{>j}^*E_ j$, effective with a positive coefficient on every exceptional component. If $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}L_ B=[B]-\Theta _ B$ uses these auxiliary metrics, then the fixed background satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(L_\Delta +L_ B)=h_ m+[\Delta +B]$, which is the strict barrier current. The Jacobian calculation and Hölder estimate apply stagewise. If $s=rp/((r-1)p+1)$, then $1-1/s=(1-1/p)/r$; iteration over the stages gives ( 15.23.11 ), with strict inequality. The target Hölder equation, mass and uniqueness are obtained as in theorem 15.23.5 . For the pullback measure take $q=0$ and use the target path comparison away from the exceptional set. The Jacobian fixes the density, while $[\Delta ]$ fixes the divisor current; these are independent pieces of the equation. $\square$

text:
We return to the general setting of the chapter, with the Hermitian form $\omega $ fixed at its beginning. Locally, every finite non-pluripolar measure is absolutely continuous with respect to the Monge–Ampère measure of a bounded plurisubharmonic function (lemma 5.27.10 ). We globalize this statement in a prescribed ordinary type. The local potentials are glued to a strictly $	heta $-plurisubharmonic potential lying below the reference and are then truncated relative to the reference. A decreasing convex sum of the resulting countable family has a Monge–Ampère measure that dominates every local piece in the sense of absolute continuity. Its potential has the prescribed ordinary type, and the given measure has an integrable density with respect to its Monge–Ampère measure. Proposition 15.24.1 . A46357C92C12 Let $	heta \geq 0$ be a smooth big real $(1,1)$-form, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ be such that the envelope $P_{\epsilon 	heta }(\varphi )$ of section 5.40 is not identically $-\infty $ for some $0<\epsilon <1$. For every finite non-pluripolar measure $\mu $ there are \[  \psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ),\qquad \psi \sim \varphi , \qquad 0\leq f\in L^1 igl (\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (\psi ) igr )  \] such that \[  \mu =f\, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (\psi ).  \] The measure $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (\psi )$ may have infinite mass, but the density $f$ is integrable with respect to it. Proof. Translate $\varphi $ below zero. Put $q=P_{\epsilon 	heta }(\varphi )\leq \varphi $, and choose a strict big potential $ho \leq 0$ with $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho \geq a\omega $, where $a>0$. Then \[  s=q+(1-\epsilon )ho \leq \varphi ,\qquad 	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s\geq (1-\epsilon )a\omega .  \] In particular $s$ is $	heta $-plurisubharmonic and not identically $-\infty $. Its pole set is pluripolar, as is that of $\varphi $, so both are negligible for $\mu $. Cover $X$ by finitely many closed coordinate balls $K_ i$, each contained in a larger coordinate ball $B_ i$. Apply lemma 5.27.10 to $\mu _ i=\mathbf1_{K_ i}\mu $. This gives bounded local plurisubharmonic $v_ i$, normalized by $1\leq v_ i\leq 2$, with \[  \mu _ i\ll 
u _ i:=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ i)^ n.  \] Take a smooth cutoff $\chi _ i$ which is zero near $K_ i$ and $-3$ on a boundary collar of $B_ i$. Choose $\delta _ i>0$ so small that \[  	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}} igl (s+\delta _ i(v_ i+\chi _ i) igr ) \geq 	frac 12(1-\epsilon )a\omega +\delta _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ i.  \] Let $S_ i$ equal $\max (s,s+\delta _ i(v_ i+\chi _ i))$ on $B_ i$ and $s$ elsewhere. The boundary collar makes this a global $	heta $-plurisubharmonic function. Since $\chi _ i\leq 0$ may be arranged, \[  s\leq S_ i\leq s+2\delta _ i\leq \varphi +2\delta _ i.  \] For every positive integer $m$, set \[  q_{i,m}=\max (\varphi -m,S_ i)-2\delta _ i.  \] These potentials have the same ordinary type as $\varphi $, and 036B1477ABB4 15.24.2  egin{equation}  \varphi -m-2\delta _ i\leq q_{i,m}\leq \varphi . \end{equation} On a neighborhood of $K_ i$, $S_ i=s+\delta _ i v_ i$ away from the pole set of $s$. Let \[  D_{i,m}=\{ s+\delta _ i v_ i>\varphi -m\}   \] in that neighborhood, restricting to points where the potentials are finite. This is a plurifinely open set there. Locality and positive mixed products give 3F73A2DB6267 15.24.3  egin{equation}  \mathbf1_{D_{i,m}}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (q_{i,m}) \geq \delta _ i^ n\mathbf1_{D_{i,m}}
u _ i. \end{equation} Here $s$ need not be bounded. After a local smooth correction, the positive product inequality holds at every common finite truncation level of $s$ and the bounded potential $v_ i$. Exhaust the complement of the pole set of $s$. The measure $
u _ i$ is non-pluripolar, so it loses no mass in that exhaustion. Then restrict the resulting inequality by plurifine locality. This proves ( 15.24.3 ) for the extended measures. For $\mu _ i$-almost every point of $K_ i$, both $s$ and $\varphi $ are finite, and hence that point belongs to $D_{i,m}$ for some $m$. Consequently, a Borel set which is null for every $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (q_{i,m})$ is null for every $\mu _ i$, and therefore for $\mu $. Enumerate the countable family $q_{i,m}$ as $q_ k$, and write its bounds as $\varphi -C_ k\leq q_ k\leq \varphi $ with $C_ k<\infty $. Choose positive $t_ k$ such that \[  \sum _ k t_ k<1,\qquad B:=\sum _ k t_ kC_ k<\infty .  \] The finite convex combinations \[  \psi _ N=\sum _{k=1}^ N t_ kq_ k +\left(1-\sum _{k=1}^ N t_ kight)\varphi  \] decrease and lie between $\varphi -B$ and $\varphi $. Their limit $\psi $ is $	heta $-plurisubharmonic, satisfies $\psi \geq \varphi -B$, and hence $\psi \sim \varphi $. For any fixed $k$, separate its summand to write \[  \psi =t_ kq_ k+(1-t_ k)w_ k, \qquad w_ k\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ),\qquad w_ k\sim \varphi .  \] The remainder is obtained by the same decreasing convex-sum construction. All measures ignore that pole set. The preceding null-set conclusion now gives $\mu \ll \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (\psi )$. By theorem 13.14.3 , the measure $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (\psi )$ is $\sigma $-finite. The Radon–Nikodym theorem applies to this $\sigma $-finite measure and the finite $\mu $. It gives a nonnegative density $f$ with \[  \int _ X f\, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (\psi )=\mu (X)<\infty ,  \] as claimed. If $\mu =0$, one may simply take $\psi =\varphi $ and $f=0$. $\square$ Lemma 15.24.4 . F9088D3DDEBB Let $	heta \geq 0$ be a smooth big real $(1,1)$-form, and let $\mu $ be a finite non-pluripolar measure on $X$. There are a bounded $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and a nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathrm{MA}_	heta (\psi ))$ such that \[  \mu =f\, \mathrm{MA}_	heta (\psi ).  \] Proof. Apply proposition 15.24.1 with $\varphi =0$. Semipositivity of $	heta $ gives $P_{\epsilon 	heta }(0)=0$ for every $0<\epsilon <1$, and $\psi \sim 0$ means that $\psi $ is bounded. $\square$ These representations give only an $L^1$ density, whereas theorem 15.10.1 requires a bounded density with respect to the measure of a bounded potential; for an unbounded prescribed type, moreover, the representing potential is itself unbounded. The existence argument for general measures in subsection 15.37.30 therefore uses a bounded Hermitian reference and relative compactness instead.

On the transition region of $\chi $, $R$ is bounded away from zero and exceeds all $r_ j$. Hence all $\psi _ j$ agree there with the same smooth function. Where $\chi =1$ they are plurisubharmonic, and outside its support they are constant. One fixed $K\geq 1$ therefore satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ j\geq -Kh$ for every $j$. Put \[  Z=2K\sum _{j\geq 1}\sqrt{r_ j},\qquad d_ j= rac{\sqrt{r_ j}}Z,\qquad u_0=\sum _{j\geq 1}d_ j\psi _ j.  \] The estimate $\| \psi _ j\| _\infty \leq C(1+|\log r_ j|)$ gives uniform convergence, and $\sum d_ j=1/(2K)$ yields $h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0\geq h/2$. For two points of the inner ball at Euclidean distance $t$, the reverse triangle inequality gives \[  |\log \max \{ |z|^2,r_ j^2\} -\log \max \{ |z'|^2,r_ j^2\} | \leq 2\log (1+t/r_ j).  \] The contribution of $r_ j\geq t$ is at most $Ct\sum _{r_ j\geq t}r_ j^{-1/2}\leq C\sqrt t$. section: 15.27 Lower mass and solvability for all measures
text:
Throughout the rest of the chapter, $h$ denotes a Hermitian form on $X$, used as the background, and densities are taken with respect to the fixed smooth positive probability volume form $\mathrm{d}V$; the sections that use another background say so explicitly. No singularity type is prescribed: the unknown potentials range over all of $\mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$. Constants belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$, and every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ is bounded above, so $u\preceq v$ for every bounded $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$. The masses of bounded potentials are measured by the lower and upper masses of definition 13.14.14 , \[  v_-(h)=\inf _ v\int _ X(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n,\qquad v_+(h)=\sup _ v\int _ X(h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n,  \] where $v$ ranges over the bounded functions in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$. The form $h$ has positive lower mass if $v_-(h)>0$. If $h$ is Kähler, Stokes' theorem gives $v_-(h)=v_+(h)=\int _ Xh^ n$; on a non-Kähler manifold the lower mass can vanish (theorem 12.19.1 ). For a nonzero nonnegative $q\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ with $p>1$, theorem 14.19.2 gives a constant $c>0$ and a continuous $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\mathrm{MA}_ h(u)=cq\, \mathrm{d}V$, and proposition 14.19.34 shows that $c$ is determined by $q$. We call $c_ h(q)=c$ the normalization scalar of $q$, and for the measure $
u =q\, \mathrm{d}V$ we also write $c_ h(
u )=c_ h(q)$. We say that a finite measure $
u $ admits a positive scaled subsolution if there are $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ and a constant $a>0$ such that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq a
u $. If $
u $ admits a solution of $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=c
u $ with $c>0$, then it admits in particular a positive scaled subsolution. We show that every nonzero finite non-pluripolar measure admits such a solution if and only if $h$ has positive lower mass. The key estimate is a consequence of strict domination: if $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq aq\, \mathrm{d}V$, then $a\leq c_ h(q)$. When $v_-(h)=0$, there are smooth probability densities with arbitrarily small normalization scalars, and a weighted sum of such densities, with scalars decreasing fast enough, is a single probability density admitting no positive scaled subsolution. Lemma 15.27.1 . CE5CA1071A3C Let $0\leq q\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, be nonzero. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ and $a>0$ satisfy \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq aq\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] then $a\leq c_ h(q)$. Consequently, for nonzero nonnegative bounded densities $q,r$, \[  q\leq r\  \Longrightarrow \  c_ h(q)\geq c_ h(r), \qquad c_ h(tq)=t^{-1}c_ h(q)\quad (t>0).  \] Proof. Let $v$ be a continuous solution of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(v)=c_ h(q)q\, \mathrm{d}V$, and suppose, to reach a contradiction, that $a>c_ h(q)$. Then $	au =c_ h(q)/a<1$ and, for every real $A$, \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(v+A)=c_ h(q)q\, \mathrm{d}V \leq 	au \, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u).  \] The translate $v+A$ is bounded, so $P_{h/2}(v+A)\geq \inf _ Xv+A$ is not identically $-\infty $, and $u\preceq v+A$. Theorem 15.2.2 , with $\delta =1/2$ and $c=	au $, therefore gives $v+A\geq u$ for every real $A$. Letting $A	o -\infty $ at a point where $u$ is finite gives a contradiction. Hence $a\leq c_ h(q)$. If $q\leq r$, a continuous solution of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(w)=c_ h(r)r\, \mathrm{d}V$ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}_ h(w)\geq c_ h(r)q\, \mathrm{d}V$, so the first assertion gives $c_ h(r)\leq c_ h(q)$. Finally, the equation $\mathrm{MA}_ h(v)=c_ h(q)q\, \mathrm{d}V$ can be written as $\mathrm{MA}_ h(v)=t^{-1}c_ h(q)\, (tq)\, \mathrm{d}V$, and uniqueness of the scalar gives $c_ h(tq)=t^{-1}c_ h(q)$. $\square$ The proof uses only that $v$ is bounded. Hence, more generally, if a nonnegative density $g$ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}_ h(v)=c\, g\, \mathrm{d}V$ for some bounded $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ and some $c>0$, then every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ and $a>0$ with $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq ag\, \mathrm{d}V$ satisfy $a\leq c$. Lemma 15.27.2 . 366F6832AB46 Fix $p>1$. If nonzero nonnegative densities $q_ j,q\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ satisfy $q_ j	o q$ in $L^ p$, then $c_ h(q_ j)	o c_ h(q)$. Proof. We first show that the scalars $c_ h(q_ j)$ lie in a compact subset of $(0,+\infty )$. Fix a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ on $X$ (definition 11.4.1 ; in dimension one, any Hermitian metric). Pairing the equation for $q_ j$ with $\gamma ^{n-1}$, as in proposition 15.14.2 with $	heta =h$ and barrier $ho =0$, gives \[  c_ h(q_ j)^{1/n}\int _ X\left( rac{q_ j\, \mathrm{d}V}{\gamma ^ n}ight)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n \leq \int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] Since $q_ j^{1/n}	o q^{1/n}$ in $L^ n$, the integrals on the left converge to the corresponding integral for $q$, which is positive. Hence the scalars are bounded above. The lower-density estimate of theorem 14.19.19 gives $c_ h(q_ j)\| q_ j\| _{L^ p}\geq c_ p>0$, so they are also bounded away from zero. Consequently, the normalized continuous solutions $u_ j$ of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(u_ j)=c_ h(q_ j)q_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$ have uniformly bounded $L^ p$ densities. By theorem 14.19.21 , every subsequence has a further subsequence along which $u_ j$ converges uniformly to some $u$ and $c_ h(q_ j)$ converges to some $c>0$. Continuity of bounded Monge–Ampère products under uniform convergence gives $\mathrm{MA}_ h(u)=cq\, \mathrm{d}V$, and uniqueness of the scalar gives $c=c_ h(q)$. Since every subsequence of $(c_ h(q_ j))$ has a further subsequence converging to $c_ h(q)$, the whole sequence converges to $c_ h(q)$. $\square$ Theorem 15.27.3 . C7AA7377C144 Suppose $v_-(h)=0$. There is a probability measure $\mu =f\, \mathrm{d}V$, with $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ and $f\geq m$ almost everywhere for a constant $m>0$, such that no $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ and $a>0$ satisfy 8D5EB0B8CCD7 15.27.4  egin{equation}  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq a\mu . \end{equation} In particular, the equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=c\mu $ has no solution $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ for any $c>0$; neither a singularity type nor finiteness of the mass of $u$ is imposed. Proof. By theorem 12.15.4 , theorem 12.2.3 , $v_-(h)$ is the infimum of the normalization scalars $c_ h(
u )$ over smooth strictly positive probability measures $
u $. Since $v_-(h)=0$, we can choose such measures $
u _ j=f_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$ with \[  c_ h(
u _ j)\leq 2^{-2j}\qquad (j\geq 1).  \] Set \[  \mu =\sum _{j=1}^{\infty }2^{-j}
u _ j, \qquad f=\sum _{j=1}^{\infty }2^{-j}f_ j.  \] By monotone convergence, $\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V=1$, so $f\in L^1$. Moreover $f\geq 	frac 12\min _ X f_1=:m>0$, and $\mu $ is non-pluripolar, being absolutely continuous with respect to $\mathrm{d}V$. Suppose that ( 15.27.4 ) held for some $u$ and $a>0$. Since $\mu \geq 2^{-j}
u _ j$, we would have \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq a2^{-j}
u _ j  \] for every $j$, and lemma 15.27.1 would give $a2^{-j}\leq c_ h(
u _ j)\leq 2^{-2j}$. Thus $a\leq 2^{-j}$ for every $j$, contradicting $a>0$. $\square$ For the reference $0$, definition 16.28.61 says that $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ belongs to the relative envelope class $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,h,0)$ if, for every $b\geq 1$, some $g\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ satisfies $g\leq bu$. Corollary 15.27.5 . 810CC86832BF The following conditions are equivalent: $v_-(h)>0$. For every nonzero finite non-pluripolar measure $\mu $ there are $c>0$ and $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,h,0)$ such that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=c\mu $. For every probability density $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ bounded below by a positive constant, there are $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ and $a>0$ such that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq af\, \mathrm{d}V$. Proof. The Hermitian form $h$ is semipositive and big, and the reference $0$ satisfies ( 16.28.67 ), since $P_ h[0]=0$ and $P_{\varepsilon h}(0)=0$ for every $0<\varepsilon <1$. Hence, if $v_-(h)>0$, theorem 15.37.4 , applied with $	heta =h$ and $\varphi =0$, gives (2). Condition (2) implies (3), because a finite measure that is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mathrm{d}V$ is non-pluripolar. Finally, if $v_-(h)=0$, the density of theorem 15.27.3 violates (3); thus (3) implies (1). $\square$ Corollary 15.27.6 . 05B92E5A4684 Assume $v_-(h)=0$, and let $\mu =f\, \mathrm{d}V$ be the measure of theorem 15.27.3 . Then $f
otin L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ for every $p>1$. Moreover, for every probability density $g\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ and every $0<t<1$, the probability density \[  g_ t=(1-t)g+tf  \] admits no positive scaled subsolution, although $\| g_ t-g\| _{L^1}\leq 2t$. In particular, the probability densities admitting no positive scaled subsolution are dense among all probability densities in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$. Proof. If $f\in L^ p$ for some $p>1$, theorem 14.19.2 would give a continuous solution of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(u)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $c>0$, contradicting the theorem. Since $g_ t\, \mathrm{d}V\geq t\mu $, a positive scaled subsolution for $g_ t\, \mathrm{d}V$ would also give one for $\mu $. Finally, $\| g_ t-g\| _{L^1}=t\| f-g\| _{L^1}\leq 2t$. $\square$ Smooth strictly positive probability densities are also dense in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, and each of them admits a smooth solution of the normalized equation. Thus, when the lower mass vanishes, solvability is not preserved under $L^1$ approximation. The obstruction comes from the way the density concentrates, not from its size: the density in theorem 15.27.3 is bounded below by a positive constant. It occurs, for instance, on the compact threefold of theorem 12.19.1 , where every Hermitian form has zero lower mass. Theorem 15.27.3 does not exclude unbounded solutions of the exponential equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}\mu $ with $\lambda >0$, because the factor $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}$ need not have a positive lower bound. It does exclude bounded solutions, since a bounded solution would satisfy $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda \inf _ Xu}\mu $. On suitable products, theorem 15.35.10 chooses the concentrating components of such a density so that its exponential equation has a solution for every positive exponent. We do not know whether this holds for every density admitting no positive scaled subsolution, nor which individual measures admit a solution of the normalized equation when $v_-(h)=0$.

title: Lemma 15.27.1
section: 15.27 Lower mass and solvability for all measures
text: Lemma 15.27.1 . CE5CA1071A3C Let $0\leq q\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$, $p>1$, be nonzero. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ and $a>0$ satisfy \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq aq\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] then $a\leq c_ h(q)$. Consequently, for nonzero nonnegative bounded densities $q,r$, \[  q\leq r\  \Longrightarrow \  c_ h(q)\geq c_ h(r), \qquad c_ h(tq)=t^{-1}c_ h(q)\quad (t>0).  \] Proof. Let $v$ be a continuous solution of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(v)=c_ h(q)q\, \mathrm{d}V$, and suppose, to reach a contradiction, that $a>c_ h(q)$. Then $\tau =c_ h(q)/a<1$ and, for every real $A$, \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(v+A)=c_ h(q)q\, \mathrm{d}V \leq \tau \, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u).  \] The translate $v+A$ is bounded, so $P_{h/2}(v+A)\geq \inf _ Xv+A$ is not identically $-\infty $, and $u\preceq v+A$. Theorem 15.2.2 , with $\delta =1/2$ and $c=\tau $, therefore gives $v+A\geq u$ for every real $A$. Letting $A\to -\infty $ at a point where $u$ is finite gives a contradiction. Hence $a\leq c_ h(q)$. If $q\leq r$, a continuous solution of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(w)=c_ h(r)r\, \mathrm{d}V$ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}_ h(w)\geq c_ h(r)q\, \mathrm{d}V$, so the first assertion gives $c_ h(r)\leq c_ h(q)$. Finally, the equation $\mathrm{MA}_ h(v)=c_ h(q)q\, \mathrm{d}V$ can be written as $\mathrm{MA}_ h(v)=t^{-1}c_ h(q)\, (tq)\, \mathrm{d}V$, and uniqueness of the scalar gives $c_ h(tq)=t^{-1}c_ h(q)$. $\square$

title: Lemma 15.27.2
section: 15.27 Lower mass and solvability for all measures
text: Lemma 15.27.2 . 366F6832AB46 Fix $p>1$. If nonzero nonnegative densities $q_ j,q\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ satisfy $q_ j\to q$ in $L^ p$, then $c_ h(q_ j)\to c_ h(q)$. Proof. We first show that the scalars $c_ h(q_ j)$ lie in a compact subset of $(0,+\infty )$. Fix a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ on $X$ (definition 11.4.1 ; in dimension one, any Hermitian metric). Pairing the equation for $q_ j$ with $\gamma ^{n-1}$, as in proposition 15.14.2 with $\theta =h$ and barrier $\rho =0$, gives \[  c_ h(q_ j)^{1/n}\int _ X\left(\frac{q_ j\, \mathrm{d}V}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n \leq \int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] Since $q_ j^{1/n}\to q^{1/n}$ in $L^ n$, the integrals on the left converge to the corresponding integral for $q$, which is positive. Hence the scalars are bounded above. The lower-density estimate of theorem 14.19.19 gives $c_ h(q_ j)\| q_ j\| _{L^ p}\geq c_ p>0$, so they are also bounded away from zero. Consequently, the normalized continuous solutions $u_ j$ of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(u_ j)=c_ h(q_ j)q_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$ have uniformly bounded $L^ p$ densities. By theorem 14.19.21 , every subsequence has a further subsequence along which $u_ j$ converges uniformly to some $u$ and $c_ h(q_ j)$ converges to some $c>0$. Continuity of bounded Monge–Ampère products under uniform convergence gives $\mathrm{MA}_ h(u)=cq\, \mathrm{d}V$, and uniqueness of the scalar gives $c=c_ h(q)$. Since every subsequence of $(c_ h(q_ j))$ has a further subsequence converging to $c_ h(q)$, the whole sequence converges to $c_ h(q)$. $\square$

title: Corollary 15.27.5
section: 15.27 Lower mass and solvability for all measures
text: Corollary 15.27.5 . 810CC86832BF The following conditions are equivalent: $v_-(h)>0$. For every nonzero finite non-pluripolar measure $\mu $ there are $c>0$ and $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,h,0)$ such that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=c\mu $. For every probability density $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ bounded below by a positive constant, there are $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ and $a>0$ such that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq af\, \mathrm{d}V$. Proof. The Hermitian form $h$ is semipositive and big, and the reference $0$ satisfies ( 16.28.67 ), since $P_ h[0]=0$ and $P_{\varepsilon h}(0)=0$ for every $0<\varepsilon <1$. Hence, if $v_-(h)>0$, theorem 15.37.4 , applied with $\theta =h$ and $\varphi =0$, gives (2). Condition (2) implies (3), because a finite measure that is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mathrm{d}V$ is non-pluripolar. Finally, if $v_-(h)=0$, the density of theorem 15.27.3 violates (3); thus (3) implies (1). $\square$

title: Corollary 15.27.6
section: 15.27 Lower mass and solvability for all measures
text: Corollary 15.27.6 . 05B92E5A4684 Assume $v_-(h)=0$, and let $\mu =f\, \mathrm{d}V$ be the measure of theorem 15.27.3 . Then $f\notin L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ for every $p>1$. Moreover, for every probability density $g\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ and every $0<t<1$, the probability density \[  g_ t=(1-t)g+tf  \] admits no positive scaled subsolution, although $\| g_ t-g\| _{L^1}\leq 2t$. In particular, the probability densities admitting no positive scaled subsolution are dense among all probability densities in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$. Proof. If $f\in L^ p$ for some $p>1$, theorem 14.19.2 would give a continuous solution of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(u)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $c>0$, contradicting the theorem. Since $g_ t\, \mathrm{d}V\geq t\mu $, a positive scaled subsolution for $g_ t\, \mathrm{d}V$ would also give one for $\mu $. Finally, $\| g_ t-g\| _{L^1}=t\| f-g\| _{L^1}\leq 2t$. $\square$

title: 15.28 Subsolutions for an individual density
text: When $v_-(h)=0$, some densities admit no positive scaled subsolution. For one fixed density $f$, we now determine the largest coefficient $a$ for which $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq af\, \mathrm{d}V$ has a solution. The bounded truncations of $f$ have normalization scalars, and their limit is the answer. Moreover, the largest coefficient is attained: the normalized continuous solutions for the truncations have an $L^1$ cluster limit, and a lower bound for Monge–Ampère densities passes to $L^1$ limits of potentials by means of monotone upper envelopes. Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ have positive integral. Its truncations are bounded and nonzero, and we put E3AA9E3C0D2D 15.28.1 \begin{equation}  f_ k=\min (f,k),\qquad b_ h(f)=\lim _{k\to \infty }c_ h(f_ k). \end{equation} By lemma 15.27.1 , the scalars $c_ h(f_ k)$ decrease as $k$ increases, so the limit exists in $[0,c_ h(f_1)]$. We call $b_ h(f)$ the subsolution threshold of $f$; theorem 15.28.4 below justifies the name. The same lemma gives 4A9175A29709 15.28.2 \begin{equation}  b_ h(f)=\inf \{ c_ h(q):0\leq q\leq f,\  q\in L^\infty , \  \textstyle \int _ Xq\, \mathrm{d}V>0\} . \end{equation} Indeed, every such $q$ satisfies $q\leq f_ k$ for $k\geq \| q\| _{L^\infty }$, hence $c_ h(q)\geq c_ h(f_ k)\geq b_ h(f)$, while the truncations $f_ k$ are themselves admissible. The Monge–Ampère operator is not continuous under $L^1$ convergence of potentials, but a lower bound for a Monge–Ampère density survives such convergence. The proof replaces the sequence by monotone upper envelopes, which converge in capacity, and uses the continuity of damped measures, theorem 13.15.9 , applied with the Hermitian form $h$ and the weight $t\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{-t}$. For nonpositive $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$, the corresponding damped measure is $\mathrm{e}^{v}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v)$, with weight zero on the pole set; it has finite mass and depends weakly continuously on $v$ under convergence in capacity. Lemma 15.28.3 . 8298FD96E154 Let $s_ j,s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ be bounded above by a common constant and satisfy $s_ j\to s$ in $L^1(X)$. Suppose $g_ j,g\geq 0$, $g_ j\to g$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s_ j)\geq g_ j\, \mathrm{d}V \quad \text{for every }j.  \] Then $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)\geq g\, \mathrm{d}V$. Proof. Subtracting a common constant, which does not change the extended measures, we may assume that all potentials are nonpositive. Pass to a subsequence along which $s_ j\to s$ and $g_ j\to g$ almost everywhere, and set \[  a_ j=\inf _{\ell \geq j}g_\ell ,\qquad w_ j=\left(\sup _{\ell \geq j}s_\ell \right)^*.  \] Then $0\leq a_ j\uparrow g$ almost everywhere, and $w_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ decreases to $s$. Step 1: $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w_ j)\geq a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$. Fix $j$. For $N\geq j$, the finite maximum $m_ N=\max _{j\leq \ell \leq N}s_\ell $ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(m_ N)\geq a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$: on the set $\{ m_ N=s_\ell \} $, proposition 13.14.6 gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(m_ N)\geq \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s_\ell )\geq g_\ell \, \mathrm{d}V\geq a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$, and these sets cover $X$. As $N\to \infty $, the functions $m_ N$ increase, are bounded above by zero, and have regularized limit $w_ j$. By lemma 5.29.19 , $m_ N\to w_ j$ in capacity, so the damped measures $\mathrm{e}^{m_ N}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(m_ N)$ converge weakly to $\mathrm{e}^{w_ j}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w_ j)$. Since $m_ N\to w_ j$ almost everywhere and $a_ j\leq g$, dominated convergence gives $\mathrm{e}^{m_ N}a_ j\to \mathrm{e}^{w_ j}a_ j$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$. Passing to the limit in $\mathrm{e}^{m_ N}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(m_ N)\geq \mathrm{e}^{m_ N}a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$ gives \[  \mathrm{e}^{w_ j}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w_ j) \geq \mathrm{e}^{w_ j}a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The pole set of $w_ j$ has zero volume and is not charged by $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w_ j)$. Dividing by the positive weight off this set gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w_ j)\geq a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$. Step 2: passage to $s$. Since $w_ j$ decreases to $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$, lemma 5.29.19 gives $w_ j\to s$ in capacity, and the damped measures of $w_ j$ converge weakly to $\mathrm{e}^ s\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)$. Moreover $0\leq \mathrm{e}^{w_ j}a_ j\leq g$ and $\mathrm{e}^{w_ j}a_ j\to \mathrm{e}^ sg$ almost everywhere, so dominated convergence and Step 1 give \[  \mathrm{e}^ s\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s) \geq \mathrm{e}^ s g\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Dividing by $\mathrm{e}^ s$ on $\{ s>-N\} $ and letting $N\to \infty $ gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)\geq g\, \mathrm{d}V$ off the pole set of $s$. Both measures give zero mass to the pole set, which proves the lemma. $\square$ Theorem 15.28.4 . CC13A9B1D927 For every nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ with positive integral, \[  b_ h(f)=\max \{ a\geq 0:\text{there exists }u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h) \text{ with }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u) \geq af\, \mathrm{d}V\} .  \] In particular, $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ admits a positive scaled subsolution if and only if $b_ h(f)>0$. Proof. If $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq af\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $a>0$, then also $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq af_ k\, \mathrm{d}V$ for every $k$, and lemma 15.27.1 gives $a\leq c_ h(f_ k)$. Letting $k\to \infty $ gives $a\leq b_ h(f)$. If $b_ h(f)=0$, the coefficient zero is attained by the zero potential. Suppose now that $b=b_ h(f)>0$, and let $u_ k$ be continuous solutions of \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(u_ k)=c_ h(f_ k)f_ k\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \sup _ Xu_ k=0.  \] By theorem 5.25.2 , a subsequence $u_{k_ j}$ converges in $L^1$ to some $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$. The densities $c_ h(f_{k_ j})f_{k_ j}$ are dominated by $c_ h(f_1)f$ and converge to $bf$ almost everywhere, hence in $L^1$. Lemma 15.28.3 now gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V$, so the maximum is attained at $a=b$. $\square$ When $b_ h(f)>0$, a function $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq b_ h(f)f\, \mathrm{d}V$ is called a threshold subsolution for $f$, and a threshold subsolution with $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=b_ h(f)f\, \mathrm{d}V$ is called a threshold solution ; the theorem shows that threshold subsolutions exist. Its proof preserves only a lower bound for the density. It shows neither that the normalized solutions $u_ k$ converge in capacity, nor that their limit has finite mass, nor that equality holds in the limit; these are the additional difficulties of the exact equation for an individual density. The threshold does not depend on the choice of truncations. If $(q_ k)$ is any increasing sequence of nonzero bounded densities converging to $f$ almost everywhere, then $c_ h(q_ k)\geq b_ h(f)$ by ( 15.28.2 ); conversely, the second half of the proof, applied to normalized solutions for $q_ k$, gives a subsolution with coefficient $\lim _ kc_ h(q_ k)$, which is therefore at most $b_ h(f)$. Hence $\lim _ kc_ h(q_ k)=b_ h(f)$.

title: Lemma 15.28.3
text: Lemma 15.28.3 . 8298FD96E154 Let $s_ j,s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ be bounded above by a common constant and satisfy $s_ j\to s$ in $L^1(X)$. Suppose $g_ j,g\geq 0$, $g_ j\to g$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s_ j)\geq g_ j\, \mathrm{d}V \quad \text{for every }j.  \] Then $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)\geq g\, \mathrm{d}V$. Step 1: $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w_ j)\geq a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$. Fix $j$. For $N\geq j$, the finite maximum $m_ N=\max _{j\leq \ell \leq N}s_\ell $ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(m_ N)\geq a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$: on the set $\{ m_ N=s_\ell \} $, proposition 13.14.6 gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(m_ N)\geq \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s_\ell )\geq g_\ell \, \mathrm{d}V\geq a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$, and these sets cover $X$. Since $m_ N\to w_ j$ almost everywhere and $a_ j\leq g$, dominated convergence gives $\mathrm{e}^{m_ N}a_ j\to \mathrm{e}^{w_ j}a_ j$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$. Passing to the limit in $\mathrm{e}^{m_ N}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(m_ N)\geq \mathrm{e}^{m_ N}a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$ gives \[  \mathrm{e}^{w_ j}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w_ j) \geq \mathrm{e}^{w_ j}a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The pole set of $w_ j$ has zero volume and is not charged by $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w_ j)$. Dividing by the positive weight off this set gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(w_ j)\geq a_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$. Step 2: passage to $s$. Since $w_ j$ decreases to $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$, lemma 5.29.19 gives $w_ j\to s$ in capacity, and the damped measures of $w_ j$ converge weakly to $\mathrm{e}^ s\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)$. Moreover $0\leq \mathrm{e}^{w_ j}a_ j\leq g$ and $\mathrm{e}^{w_ j}a_ j\to \mathrm{e}^ sg$ almost everywhere, so dominated convergence and Step 1 give \[  \mathrm{e}^ s\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s) \geq \mathrm{e}^ s g\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Dividing by $\mathrm{e}^ s$ on $\{ s>-N\} $ and letting $N\to \infty $ gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)\geq g\, \mathrm{d}V$ off the pole set of $s$. Both measures give zero mass to the pole set, which proves the lemma. $\square$

title: Theorem 15.28.4
text: Theorem 15.28.4 . CC13A9B1D927 For every nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ with positive integral, \[  b_ h(f)=\max \{ a\geq 0:\text{there exists }u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h) \text{ with }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u) \geq af\, \mathrm{d}V\} .  \] In particular, $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ admits a positive scaled subsolution if and only if $b_ h(f)>0$. Proof. If $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq af\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $a>0$, then also $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq af_ k\, \mathrm{d}V$ for every $k$, and lemma 15.27.1 gives $a\leq c_ h(f_ k)$. Letting $k\to \infty $ gives $a\leq b_ h(f)$. If $b_ h(f)=0$, the coefficient zero is attained by the zero potential. Suppose now that $b=b_ h(f)>0$, and let $u_ k$ be continuous solutions of \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(u_ k)=c_ h(f_ k)f_ k\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \sup _ Xu_ k=0.  \] By theorem 5.25.2 , a subsequence $u_{k_ j}$ converges in $L^1$ to some $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\sup _ Xu=0$. The densities $c_ h(f_{k_ j})f_{k_ j}$ are dominated by $c_ h(f_1)f$ and converge to $bf$ almost everywhere, hence in $L^1$. Lemma 15.28.3 now gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V$, so the maximum is attained at $a=b$. $\square$

title: 15.28.5 The greatest normalized threshold subsolution
text: Suppose $b_ h(f)>0$. The threshold subsolutions with supremum zero form a family that is stable under finite maxima and under $L^1$ limits. Its upper envelope is therefore again a normalized threshold subsolution, and it dominates all the others. Proposition 15.28.6 . D42D2088B421 Suppose $b=b_ h(f)>0$. The family \[  \mathcal S_ f=\{ s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h):\sup _ Xs=0, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V\}   \] is nonempty and compact in $L^1(X)$. Its upper envelope \[  \Phi _ f=\left(\sup _{s\in \mathcal S_ f}s\right)^*  \] belongs to $\mathcal S_ f$ and is therefore its greatest member. Moreover, let $u_\lambda $ be the greatest exponential solutions of corollary 15.35.3 and $v_\lambda =u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda $. Every $L^1$ limit of a sequence $v_{\lambda _ j}$ with $\lambda _ j\downarrow 0$ belongs to $\mathcal S_ f$, and hence lies below $\Phi _ f$. Proof. The family is nonempty by theorem 15.28.4 . By theorem 5.25.2 , an $L^1$ limit of members of $\mathcal S_ f$ is $h$-plurisubharmonic with supremum zero, and lemma 15.28.3 , with $g_ j=g=bf$, shows that it satisfies the measure inequality. Thus $\mathcal S_ f$ is a closed subset of the compact set of normalized $h$-plurisubharmonic functions, hence compact. It is also stable under finite maxima: if $s_1,s_2\in \mathcal S_ f$, then $\max (s_1,s_2)$ has supremum zero, and proposition 13.14.6 , applied on the sets where the maximum equals $s_1$ or $s_2$, gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(\max (s_1,s_2))\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V$. By Choquet's lemma there is a sequence $(s_ i)_{i\geq 1}$ in $\mathcal S_ f$ with $(\sup _ is_ i)^*=\Phi _ f$. Fix $s_0\in \mathcal S_ f$. The finite maxima $t_ N=\max (s_0,s_1,\ldots ,s_ N)$ belong to $\mathcal S_ f$, increase with $N$, and satisfy $s_0\leq t_ N\leq 0$; their regularized limit is $\Phi _ f$. Hence $t_ N\to \Phi _ f$ almost everywhere and, by dominated convergence, in $L^1$. Lemma 15.28.3 gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(\Phi _ f)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V$, and $s_0\leq \Phi _ f\leq 0$ forces $\sup _ X\Phi _ f=0$. Thus $\Phi _ f\in \mathcal S_ f$, and by construction it dominates every member of $\mathcal S_ f$. Finally, suppose $v_{\lambda _ j}\to v$ in $L^1$ with $\lambda _ j\downarrow 0$. The measures $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v_{\lambda _ j})=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ ju_{\lambda _ j}}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ have densities converging in $L^1$ to $bf$, by corollary 15.35.3 . Applying lemma 15.28.3 to these densities and potentials shows that $v\in \mathcal S_ f$. $\square$ The proposition gives a greatest normalized threshold subsolution, but not the equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(\Phi _ f)=bf\, \mathrm{d}V$; in particular, it does not show that $\Phi _ f$ has finite mass. Proposition 15.28.7 . 69BB1D568698 Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ have positive integral. If $f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ for some $p>1$, then $b_ h(f)=c_ h(f)$. In general, \[  b_ h(f)\geq \frac{v_-(h)}{\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V}.  \] If $h$ is Kähler, then $b_ h(f)=\int _ Xh^ n/\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V$. Proof. Suppose that $f\in L^ p$ with $p>1$, and let $v$ be a continuous solution of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(v)=c_ h(f)f\, \mathrm{d}V$. It is a subsolution with coefficient $c_ h(f)$, so theorem 15.28.4 gives $c_ h(f)\leq b_ h(f)$. Conversely, lemma 15.27.1 , applied to a threshold subsolution, gives $b_ h(f)\leq c_ h(f)$. For general $f$, the continuous solution for $f_ k$ has total mass $c_ h(f_ k)\int _ Xf_ k\, \mathrm{d}V$, which is at least $v_-(h)$ by the definition of the lower mass. Letting $k\to \infty $ and using monotone convergence gives the lower bound for $b_ h(f)$. If $h$ is Kähler, Stokes' theorem for bounded potentials gives instead the identity $c_ h(f_ k)\int _ Xf_ k\, \mathrm{d}V=\int _ Xh^ n$, and the same limit proves the last assertion. $\square$

title: Proposition 15.28.6
text: Proposition 15.28.6 . D42D2088B421 Suppose $b=b_ h(f)>0$. The family \[  \mathcal S_ f=\{ s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h):\sup _ Xs=0, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V\}   \] is nonempty and compact in $L^1(X)$. Its upper envelope \[  \Phi _ f=\left(\sup _{s\in \mathcal S_ f}s\right)^*  \] belongs to $\mathcal S_ f$ and is therefore its greatest member. Moreover, let $u_\lambda $ be the greatest exponential solutions of corollary 15.35.3 and $v_\lambda =u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda $. Every $L^1$ limit of a sequence $v_{\lambda _ j}$ with $\lambda _ j\downarrow 0$ belongs to $\mathcal S_ f$, and hence lies below $\Phi _ f$. Proof. The family is nonempty by theorem 15.28.4 . By theorem 5.25.2 , an $L^1$ limit of members of $\mathcal S_ f$ is $h$-plurisubharmonic with supremum zero, and lemma 15.28.3 , with $g_ j=g=bf$, shows that it satisfies the measure inequality. Thus $\mathcal S_ f$ is a closed subset of the compact set of normalized $h$-plurisubharmonic functions, hence compact. It is also stable under finite maxima: if $s_1,s_2\in \mathcal S_ f$, then $\max (s_1,s_2)$ has supremum zero, and proposition 13.14.6 , applied on the sets where the maximum equals $s_1$ or $s_2$, gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(\max (s_1,s_2))\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V$. By Choquet's lemma there is a sequence $(s_ i)_{i\geq 1}$ in $\mathcal S_ f$ with $(\sup _ is_ i)^*=\Phi _ f$. Fix $s_0\in \mathcal S_ f$. The finite maxima $t_ N=\max (s_0,s_1,\ldots ,s_ N)$ belong to $\mathcal S_ f$, increase with $N$, and satisfy $s_0\leq t_ N\leq 0$; their regularized limit is $\Phi _ f$. Hence $t_ N\to \Phi _ f$ almost everywhere and, by dominated convergence, in $L^1$. Lemma 15.28.3 gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(\Phi _ f)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V$, and $s_0\leq \Phi _ f\leq 0$ forces $\sup _ X\Phi _ f=0$. Thus $\Phi _ f\in \mathcal S_ f$, and by construction it dominates every member of $\mathcal S_ f$. Finally, suppose $v_{\lambda _ j}\to v$ in $L^1$ with $\lambda _ j\downarrow 0$. The measures $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v_{\lambda _ j})=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ ju_{\lambda _ j}}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ have densities converging in $L^1$ to $bf$, by corollary 15.35.3 . Applying lemma 15.28.3 to these densities and potentials shows that $v\in \mathcal S_ f$. $\square$

title: Proposition 15.28.7
text: Proposition 15.28.7 . 69BB1D568698 Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ have positive integral. If $f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ for some $p>1$, then $b_ h(f)=c_ h(f)$. In general, \[  b_ h(f)\geq \frac{v_-(h)}{\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V}.  \] If $h$ is Kähler, then $b_ h(f)=\int _ Xh^ n/\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V$. Proof. Suppose that $f\in L^ p$ with $p>1$, and let $v$ be a continuous solution of $\mathrm{MA}_ h(v)=c_ h(f)f\, \mathrm{d}V$. It is a subsolution with coefficient $c_ h(f)$, so theorem 15.28.4 gives $c_ h(f)\leq b_ h(f)$. Conversely, lemma 15.27.1 , applied to a threshold subsolution, gives $b_ h(f)\leq c_ h(f)$. For general $f$, the continuous solution for $f_ k$ has total mass $c_ h(f_ k)\int _ Xf_ k\, \mathrm{d}V$, which is at least $v_-(h)$ by the definition of the lower mass. Letting $k\to \infty $ and using monotone convergence gives the lower bound for $b_ h(f)$. If $h$ is Kähler, Stokes' theorem for bounded potentials gives instead the identity $c_ h(f_ k)\int _ Xf_ k\, \mathrm{d}V=\int _ Xh^ n$, and the same limit proves the last assertion. $\square$

title: 15.28.8 Smooth comparison tests
text: The infimum ( 15.28.2 ) runs over bounded measurable densities below $f$. One may ask whether smooth densities suffice to compute the threshold. A smooth test $g$ is in general not below $f$, so we compare it with $f$ through the ratio $\| g/f\| _{L^\infty }$. Thus let $f$ be a probability density bounded below by a positive constant, and define \[  C_ h^{\mathrm{sm}}(f)=\inf _ g c_ h(g)\| g/f\| _{L^\infty },  \] where $g$ ranges over smooth strictly positive probability densities. For each such $g$, with $R=\| g/f\| _{L^\infty }$, a subsolution with coefficient $a$ for $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ is a subsolution with coefficient $a/R$ for $g\, \mathrm{d}V$, so $a\leq Rc_ h(g)$ by lemma 15.27.1 . Hence $b_ h(f)\leq C_ h^{\mathrm{sm}}(f)$, with equality if $f$ is smooth (take $g=f$). When the lower mass vanishes, the two quantities can differ even in their positivity. Theorem 15.28.9 . 4AC87EC7D266 If $v_-(h)=0$, there is a probability density $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ bounded below by a positive constant such that \[  b_ h(f)=0<C_ h^{\mathrm{sm}}(f).  \] Thus $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ admits no positive scaled subsolution, although $c_ h(g)\| g/f\| _{L^\infty }$ is bounded below by a positive constant for all smooth strictly positive probability densities $g$. Proof. We construct $f=(1+Q)/M$, where $Q\geq 0$ concentrates on closed nowhere dense sets in such a way that it has essential infimum zero on every nonempty open set. Step 1: the pieces. Let $(U_ i)_{i\geq 1}$ be a countable basis of nonempty open subsets of $X$. We construct inductively numbers $\alpha _ j>0$, nonzero bounded densities $q_ j$, and closed nowhere dense sets $K_ j\subset X$ such that \[  \int _ Xq_ j\, \mathrm{d}V\leq 1,\qquad q_ j=0\text{ outside }K_ j,\qquad c_ h(q_ j)\leq \alpha _ j2^{-j}.  \] Start with $\alpha _1=1/4$. Once $\alpha _ j$ has been chosen, theorem 12.15.4 , theorem 12.2.3 and $v_-(h)=0$ give a smooth strictly positive probability density $g_ j$ with $c_ h(g_ j)<\alpha _ j2^{-j}$. Removing from $X$ an open dense set of small volume, we obtain a closed nowhere dense set $K_ j$ for which $q_ j=g_ j\mathbf1_{K_ j}$ is nonzero and, since $g_ j$ is bounded, arbitrarily close to $g_ j$ in $L^2$. By lemma 15.27.2 with $p=2$, we can therefore choose $K_ j$ so that $c_ h(q_ j)\leq \alpha _ j2^{-j}$. After $K_1,\ldots ,K_ N$ have been chosen, put \[  m_ N=\min _{1\leq i\leq N} \mathrm{d}V\left(U_ i\setminus \bigcup _{j=1}^ NK_ j\right)>0;  \] each set inside the minimum is open and nonempty, since a finite union of closed nowhere dense sets is closed and nowhere dense. Choose \[  0<\alpha _{N+1}\leq \min \{ \alpha _ N/2,\  2^{-N-2}m_ N\} ,  \] and continue. In particular, \[  \sum _{j>N}\alpha _ j\leq 2\alpha _{N+1} \leq 2^{-N-1}m_ N.  \] Step 2: the concentrating part. The function $Q=\sum _ j\alpha _ jq_ j$ is nonnegative and integrable. We claim that its essential infimum on every nonempty open set is zero. Since every nonempty open set contains some $U_ i$, it suffices to consider $U_ i$. Take $N\geq i$ and remove $K_1,\ldots ,K_ N$ from $U_ i$. On the remaining set, whose volume is at least $m_ N$, the first $N$ summands of $Q$ vanish. By Markov's inequality, the set where the tail $\sum _{j>N}\alpha _ jq_ j$ exceeds $2^{-N}$ has volume at most \[  2^ N\sum _{j>N}\alpha _ j\int _ Xq_ j\, \mathrm{d}V \leq m_ N/2.  \] Hence $Q\leq 2^{-N}$ on a subset of $U_ i$ of positive volume. Letting $N\to \infty $ proves the claim. Step 3: $b_ h(f)=0$. Set $M=\int _ X(1+Q)\, \mathrm{d}V$ and $f=(1+Q)/M$, a probability density with $f\geq 1/M$. If $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq af\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $a>0$, then $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)\geq (a\alpha _ j/M)q_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$, and lemma 15.27.1 gives \[  \frac{a\alpha _ j}{M}\leq c_ h(q_ j)\leq \alpha _ j2^{-j} \quad \text{for every }j.  \] This is impossible. Hence $b_ h(f)=0$ by theorem 15.28.4 . Step 4: $C_ h^{\mathrm{sm}}(f)>0$. Let $g$ be a smooth strictly positive probability density and put $R=\| g/f\| _{L^\infty }$. Then $g\leq R(1+Q)/M$ almost everywhere, and this forces $g\leq R/M$ everywhere. Otherwise, by continuity, $g>R(1+\varepsilon )/M$ on a nonempty open set for some $\varepsilon >0$, while $Q<\varepsilon $ on a subset of positive volume of this set by Step 2, a contradiction. The order and homogeneity of the scalar in lemma 15.27.1 now give $c_ h(g)\geq c_ h(R/M)=(M/R)c_ h(1)$, that is, \[  R c_ h(g)\geq M c_ h(1).  \] The constant density $g=1$ attains this value, since $\operatorname *{ess\, inf}_ XQ=0$ gives $\| 1/f\| _{L^\infty }=M$. Thus $C_ h^{\mathrm{sm}}(f)=M c_ h(1)>0$, as required. $\square$ The point is that a smooth test $g$ with $\| g/f\| _{L^\infty }\leq R$ is controlled by the essential infimum of $f$ on open sets. It therefore cannot detect an increase of $f$ that leaves this essential infimum unchanged on every open set, whereas bounded measurable tests below $f$ do detect it. The theorem concerns only the existence of subsolutions. Exact solutions of $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=b_ h(f)f\, \mathrm{d}V$, the singularity class in which they should be sought, and compactness of their normalized solutions are further problems; see 24.2.2 .

title: 15.29 Gauduchon tests for integrable densities
text: For a smooth strictly positive probability density, the normalization scalar is an infimum of Gauduchon quotients by theorem 12.2.3 . We extend this dual formula to the threshold of an arbitrary integrable density. A uniform bound for all Gauduchon tests in a single $L^ r$ norm allows the passage from smooth to bounded densities, and monotone truncation then reaches all integrable densities, including those with zero threshold. The formula is most naturally written for the $n$th root of the density. Recall that a Hermitian form $\gamma $ is Gauduchon if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})=0$ (definition 11.4.1 ); in dimension one every Hermitian form is Gauduchon. For a Gauduchon form $\gamma $ and a nonnegative measurable function $p$, put \[  L_{h,\gamma }(p)= \frac{\displaystyle \int _ Xp(\mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n}{\displaystyle \int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}} =\int _ Xp\, a_\gamma \, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad a_\gamma =\frac{(\gamma ^ n/\mathrm{d}V)^{(n-1)/n}}{\int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}.  \] Since the coefficient $a_\gamma $ is smooth and strictly positive, each individual test $L_{h,\gamma }$ is finite on $L^ n$; the supremum over $\gamma $ may be infinite. In dimension one the test is $\int _ Xp\, \mathrm{d}V/\int _ Xh$. For real or complex $p\in L^ n(\mathrm{d}V)$, define the root functional \[  \rho _ h(p)=b_ h(|p|^ n)^{-1/n}\quad (p\ne 0),\qquad \rho _ h(0)=0,  \] with the convention $0^{-1/n}=+\infty $. Theorem 15.29.1 . 346B39C3F0B6 For every real or complex $p\in L^ n(\mathrm{d}V)$, 77553DB34B46 15.29.2 \begin{equation}  \rho _ h(p)=\sup _{\gamma \text{ Gauduchon}}L_{h,\gamma }(|p|). \end{equation} Equivalently, for every nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, 3FECA4E31049 15.29.3 \begin{equation}  b_ h(f)^{1/n}= \inf _{\gamma \text{ Gauduchon}} \frac{\displaystyle \int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{\displaystyle \int _ X(f\, \mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n}. \end{equation} Both sides of ( 15.29.2 ) may be $+\infty $, and both sides of ( 15.29.3 ) may vanish. Proof. It suffices to prove ( 15.29.2 ) for $p\geq 0$, since both sides depend only on $|p|$; the case $p=0$ is immediate. Step 1: smooth strictly positive $p$. Apply theorem 12.2.3 , with background $h$, to the probability measure $\mu =p^ n\mathrm{d}V/Z$, where $Z=\int _ Xp^ n\, \mathrm{d}V$. By homogeneity (lemma 15.27.1 ) its scalar is $c_ h(\mu )=Zc_ h(p^ n)$, while the denominator of each Gauduchon quotient is $Z^{-1/n}\int _ Xp(\mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n$. The factors of $Z$ cancel, and the dual formula becomes \[  c_ h(p^ n)^{-1/n}=\sup _\gamma L_{h,\gamma }(p).  \] Since $b_ h(p^ n)=c_ h(p^ n)$ by proposition 15.28.7 , this proves ( 15.29.2 ) for such $p$. Step 2: a uniform bound for the tests. The lower-density estimate of theorem 14.19.19 , with exponent two, gives a constant $m_ h>0$ such that \[  c_ h(p^ n)\| p^ n\| _{L^2}\geq m_ h  \] for smooth strictly positive $p$. By Step 1, therefore, C6012A389791 15.29.4 \begin{equation}  L_{h,\gamma }(p)\leq m_ h^{-1/n}\| p\| _{L^{2n}} \quad \text{for every }\gamma . \end{equation} Approximating nonnegative functions in $L^{2n}$ by smooth strictly positive ones extends this bound to all nonnegative $p\in L^{2n}$. Since $a_\gamma >0$, duality gives $\| a_\gamma \| _{L^{2n/(2n-1)}}\leq m_ h^{-1/n}$ for every $\gamma $. In particular, $p\mapsto \sup _\gamma L_{h,\gamma }(p)$ is Lipschitz on the cone of nonnegative functions in $L^{2n}$, with the same constant. Step 3: bounded $p$. Let $p\geq 0$ be bounded and nonzero, and approximate it in $L^{2n}$ by smooth strictly positive functions $p_ j$. By Hölder's inequality, $p_ j^ n\to p^ n$ in $L^2$, so lemma 15.27.2 gives \[  c_ h(p_ j^ n)\longrightarrow c_ h(p^ n)>0.  \] By the Lipschitz bound derived from ( 15.29.4 ), \[  \sup _\gamma L_{h,\gamma }(p_ j) \longrightarrow \sup _\gamma L_{h,\gamma }(p).  \] Passing to the limit in the identity of Step 1 for $p_ j$, and using $b_ h(p^ n)=c_ h(p^ n)$ (proposition 15.28.7 ), we obtain ( 15.29.2 ) for bounded $p$. Step 4: general $p$. For nonnegative $p\in L^ n$, put $p_ k=\min (p,k)$. Then $p_ k^ n=\min (p^ n,k^ n)$ are truncations of $p^ n$, so the definition of $b_ h$ and Step 3 give \[  \rho _ h(p)=\lim _{k\to \infty }c_ h(p_ k^ n)^{-1/n} =\sup _ k\sup _\gamma L_{h,\gamma }(p_ k).  \] For each fixed $\gamma $, monotone convergence gives $\sup _ kL_{h,\gamma }(p_ k)=L_{h,\gamma }(p)$. Interchanging the two suprema proves ( 15.29.2 ). Finally, every denominator in ( 15.29.3 ) is positive; taking reciprocals in ( 15.29.2 ) with $p=f^{1/n}$ proves ( 15.29.3 ), including the case $b_ h(f)=0$. $\square$ For a nonsmooth density we do not claim that the infimum in ( 15.29.3 ) is attained by a Gauduchon form; attainment by Gauduchon currents is studied in section 12.10 . For $n\geq 2$, the coefficient of the test has norm \[  \| a_\gamma \| _{L^{n/(n-1)}} =\frac{(\int _ X\gamma ^ n)^{(n-1)/n}}{\int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}  \] in the exponent dual to $n$. By ( 12.15.5 ) in theorem 12.15.4 , positive lower mass is therefore equivalent to a uniform bound for these norms, that is, for all tests on $L^ n$ simultaneously. Without positive lower mass, Step 2 of the proof still bounds the coefficients uniformly in the weaker norm of $L^{2n/(2n-1)}$, on every compact Hermitian manifold. This suffices to pass from smooth to bounded densities, and monotone truncation then treats all integrable densities. Proposition 15.29.5 . 429BB0FF98A9 Let $f$ be a nonzero nonnegative function in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ and let $p\in L^ n(\mathrm{d}V)$ be real or complex. If $h_1,h_2$ are Hermitian forms on $X$ and $m h_1\leq h_2\leq M h_1$ for positive constants $m,M$, then \[  m^ n b_{h_1}(f)\leq b_{h_2}(f)\leq M^ n b_{h_1}(f), \qquad M^{-1}\rho _{h_1}(p)\leq \rho _{h_2}(p)\leq m^{-1}\rho _{h_1}(p).  \] If $h_2-h_1=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$ for a smooth real function $a$, then $b_{h_1}(f)=b_{h_2}(f)$ and $\rho _{h_1}(p)=\rho _{h_2}(p)$. Proof. For every Gauduchon form $\gamma $, the numerators in ( 15.29.3 ) satisfy \[  m\int _ Xh_1\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}\leq \int _ Xh_2\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \leq M\int _ Xh_1\wedge \gamma ^{n-1},  \] while the denominators do not depend on the background. Taking the infimum over $\gamma $ and then $n$th powers proves the bounds for the thresholds; taking reciprocal $n$th roots gives the bounds for $\rho $, with the stated conventions at zero and infinity. If $h_2-h_1=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$, the numerators agree by Stokes' theorem, since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})=0$. $\square$ Any two Hermitian metrics on the compact manifold $X$ are comparable. Hence the positivity of $b_ h(f)$, and the set of real or complex $p\in L^ n$ with $\rho _ h(p)<+\infty $, do not depend on the choice of $h$. The dependence on the reference volume is equally simple. If $\mathrm{d}V$ is replaced by $\mathrm{d}V'=\sigma \, \mathrm{d}V$ with a smooth function $\sigma >0$, the measure $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ has density $f'=f/\sigma $ with respect to $\mathrm{d}V'$, and theorem 15.28.4 shows that the threshold of $f'$ relative to $\mathrm{d}V'$ equals $b_ h(f)$. Correspondingly, the map $p\mapsto \sigma ^{-1/n}p$ from $L^ n(\mathrm{d}V)$ to $L^ n(\mathrm{d}V')$ preserves both the $L^ n$ norm and the root functional.

title: Proposition 15.29.5
text: Proposition 15.29.5 . 429BB0FF98A9 Let $f$ be a nonzero nonnegative function in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ and let $p\in L^ n(\mathrm{d}V)$ be real or complex. If $h_1,h_2$ are Hermitian forms on $X$ and $m h_1\leq h_2\leq M h_1$ for positive constants $m,M$, then \[  m^ n b_{h_1}(f)\leq b_{h_2}(f)\leq M^ n b_{h_1}(f), \qquad M^{-1}\rho _{h_1}(p)\leq \rho _{h_2}(p)\leq m^{-1}\rho _{h_1}(p).  \] If $h_2-h_1=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$ for a smooth real function $a$, then $b_{h_1}(f)=b_{h_2}(f)$ and $\rho _{h_1}(p)=\rho _{h_2}(p)$. Proof. For every Gauduchon form $\gamma $, the numerators in ( 15.29.3 ) satisfy \[  m\int _ Xh_1\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}\leq \int _ Xh_2\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \leq M\int _ Xh_1\wedge \gamma ^{n-1},  \] while the denominators do not depend on the background.
