title: 15.30 Exact equations on products with zero lower mass
search_title: Exact equations on products with zero lower mass
section: 15.30 Exact equations on products with zero lower mass
text: Positive lower mass guarantees solvability for all measures, but an individual density can have a positive threshold and an exact equation even when the lower mass vanishes. We construct explicit examples on products. Let $(X_0,h_0)$ be a connected compact Hermitian manifold of dimension $m\geq 1$ with $v_-(h_0)=0$. On its product with a projective space, a singular potential pulled back from the projective factor solves an explicit equation whose density has a sublogarithmic singularity. The coefficient is computed from the normalization scalars of bounded truncations, the equation itself follows from the product structure of the Monge–Ampère measure, and the product background again has zero lower mass. Throughout this section, $Y=\mathbb P^ k$ with $k\geq 1$, $\kappa $ is the Fubini–Study form normalized by $\int _ Y\kappa ^ k=1$, and $X=X_0\times Y$, a compact complex manifold of dimension $N=m+k$ with the Hermitian background $H=h_0+\kappa $. Forms and functions on the factors are identified with their pullbacks to $X$. Put \[  V_0=\int _{X_0}h_0^ m,\qquad C=\binom Nm,\qquad \mu =V_0^{-1}h_0^ m\wedge \kappa ^ k,\qquad R=\frac{\mu }{\mathrm{d}V},  \] where $\mathrm{d}V$ is any smooth positive probability volume form on $X$. Then $\mu $ is a smooth positive probability volume form, and $R$ is smooth and bounded above and below by positive constants. The normalization scalar $c_ H$ and the threshold $b_ H$ are those of section 15.27 , section 15.28 , now on the $N$-dimensional manifold $X$ with background $H$. For $0<\alpha <1$ define, on $Y$, \[  \psi ([z_0:\cdots :z_ k])=\log \frac{\sum _{i=1}^ k|z_ i|^2}{\sum _{i=0}^ k|z_ i|^2}, \qquad u_\alpha =1-(1-\psi )^\alpha .  \] The function $\psi $ is smooth on $Y\setminus \{ o\} $, where $o=[1:0:\cdots :0]$, and tends to $-\infty $ at $o$; moreover $\psi \leq 0$, with equality exactly on the hyperplane $\{ z_0=0\} $. Thus $u_\alpha \leq 0$, and $u_\alpha $ has a single pole at $o$, where $u_\alpha (o)=-\infty $. Lemma 15.30.1 . B30B4EF45772 The function $u_\alpha $ is $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic with supremum zero, and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (u_\alpha )=q_\alpha \kappa ^ k, \qquad \int _ Yq_\alpha \kappa ^ k=1.  \] The density $q_\alpha $ is smooth and strictly positive on $Y\setminus \{ o\} $, belongs to $L^1(\kappa ^ k)$, and belongs to no $L^ p(\kappa ^ k)$ with $p>1$. If we set $q_\alpha (o)=+\infty $, then every truncation $\min (q_\alpha ,s)$, $s>0$, is strictly positive and continuous on $Y$. Proof. In homogeneous coordinates, $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \sum _{i=1}^ k|z_ i|^2\geq 0$ on $Y\setminus \{ o\} $. The function $\chi (t)=1-(1-t)^\alpha $, $t\leq 0$, is increasing and convex, with $0<\chi '\leq \alpha $. Hence, off $o$, \[  \kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\alpha \geq (1-\chi '(\psi ))\kappa +\chi '(\psi )(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi ) \geq (1-\alpha )\kappa .  \] Since $u_\alpha $ is bounded above, it extends across $o$ as a $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic function, with value $-\infty $ at $o$. On the hyperplane $\{ z_0=0\} $ we have $\psi =0$, hence $u_\alpha =0$, so $\sup _ Yu_\alpha =0$. To compute the measure, work in the affine chart $z_0=1$ and put $r=\sum _{i=1}^ k|z_ i|^2$. On this chart $\kappa =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+r)$ and $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F$, where $s(r)=1-\log (r/(1+r))$ and \[  F(r)=\log (1+r)+1-s(r)^\alpha ,\qquad Q(r)=rF'(r)=\frac{r+\alpha s(r)^{\alpha -1}}{1+r}.  \] For a radial function, the Levi form has the tangential eigenvalue $F'(r)=Q(r)/r$, with multiplicity $k-1$, and the radial eigenvalue \[  Q'(r)=\frac{1-\alpha s(r)^{\alpha -1}+\alpha (1-\alpha )r^{-1}s(r)^{\alpha -2}}{(1+r)^2}>0.  \] Integrating in the radial variable gives $\int _{\{ a<r<b\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^ k=Q(b)^ k-Q(a)^ k$; the constant of proportionality is fixed by the case $F=\log (1+r)$, for which $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^ k=\kappa ^ k$ has mass one on the chart and $Q(r)=r/(1+r)$. Since again $Q(0)=0$ and $Q(\infty )=1$, the punctured chart has mass one. The complement of the chart is a hyperplane, which has zero volume, and the non-pluripolar measure does not charge $o$. Hence $\int _ Yq_\alpha \kappa ^ k=1$. Relative to $\kappa ^ k$, whose tangential and radial eigenvalues are $1/(1+r)$ and $1/(1+r)^2$, the density on this chart is \[  q_\alpha (r)=(1+r)^{k+1}(Q(r)/r)^{k-1}Q'(r) \asymp r^{-k}(1-\log r)^{-1-k(1-\alpha )}\quad (r\downarrow 0).  \] Near $r=0$ the smooth volume is comparable to $r^{k-1}\mathrm{d}r$ in the radial variable, so $q_\alpha $ is integrable. For $p>1$, the substitution $L=1-\log r$ turns the integral of $q_\alpha ^ p$ into the integral of $\mathrm{e}^{k(p-1)L}$ times a power of $L$, which diverges. The same asymptotics show that $q_\alpha (r)\to +\infty $ uniformly as $r\downarrow 0$, so every truncation $\min (q_\alpha ,s)$ is continuous at $o$. Finally, $q_\alpha \geq (1-\alpha )^ k>0$ by the lower bound $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\alpha \geq (1-\alpha )\kappa $. $\square$ Lemma 15.30.2 . 40B884870886 Let $g$ be a strictly positive continuous function on $Y$, and put $M_ g=\int _ Yg\kappa ^ k$. Then \[  c_ H(Rg)=\frac{CV_0}{M_ g}.  \] Proof. Suppose first that $g$ is smooth. Since $\kappa $ is Kähler, theorem 14.2.1 on $Y$ gives a smooth $\phi _ g$ with $A_ g=\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ g>0$ and $A_ g^ k=(g/M_ g)\kappa ^ k$; the scalar is determined by integration, since both sides have mass one. On $X$, since $h_0^{m+1}=0$ and $A_ g^{k+1}=0$ for dimensional reasons, \[  (H+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ g)^ N=C h_0^ m\wedge A_ g^ k =(CV_0/M_ g)Rg\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Uniqueness of the scalar gives $c_ H(Rg)=CV_0/M_ g$. For continuous $g>0$, choose smooth $g_ l>0$ converging uniformly to $g$. Since $g$ has a positive minimum, $(1-\varepsilon _ l)g\leq g_ l\leq (1+\varepsilon _ l)g$ for some $\varepsilon _ l\in (0,1)$ tending to zero. The order and homogeneity of the scalar in lemma 15.27.1 give \[  (1-\varepsilon _ l)c_ H(Rg_ l)\leq c_ H(Rg) \leq (1+\varepsilon _ l)c_ H(Rg_ l).  \] Since $M_{g_ l}\to M_ g$, the smooth case proves the formula. $\square$ Theorem 15.30.3 . B36BAA6B4AA0 The Hermitian form $H$ is not closed and satisfies $v_-(H)=0$. For every $0<\alpha <1$, the function $f=Rq_\alpha $ is a probability density in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, belonging to no $L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ with $p>1$, and \[  b_ H(f)=CV_0>0,\qquad \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u_\alpha )=b_ H(f)f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The potential $u_\alpha $, pulled back to $X$, has supremum zero and finite mass $CV_0$. It belongs to $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,H,0)$, and $P_{\delta H}(u_\alpha )\not\equiv -\infty $ for every $0<\delta <1$. Proof. Step 1: the threshold. Write $a=\min _ XR>0$, $A=\max _ XR$, and $M_ s=\int _ Y\min (q_\alpha ,s)\kappa ^ k$ for $s>0$. By lemma 15.30.1 , the truncations $\min (q_\alpha ,s)$ are continuous and strictly positive, and $M_ s\uparrow 1$ as $s\to \infty $. The truncations of $f$ satisfy \[  R\min (q_\alpha ,j/A)\leq \min (Rq_\alpha ,j) \leq R\min (q_\alpha ,j/a).  \] Hence lemma 15.30.2 and the monotonicity of the scalar give \[  \frac{CV_0}{M_{j/a}}\leq c_ H(\min (f,j)) \leq \frac{CV_0}{M_{j/A}}.  \] Both bounds tend to $CV_0$ as $j\to \infty $, so $b_ H(f)=CV_0$, whatever the reference volume $\mathrm{d}V$. Step 2: the equation. For $u_{\alpha ,j}=\max (u_\alpha ,-j)$, the binomial expansion of bounded local products, with factor forms of degrees $m$ and $k$, gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_ H(u_{\alpha ,j}) =C h_0^ m\wedge \mathrm{MA}_\kappa (u_{\alpha ,j}).  \] Multiplying by $\mathbf1_{\{ u_\alpha >-j\} }$ and letting $j\to \infty $, as in the definition ( 13.14.4 ) of the extended measure, we obtain \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u_\alpha )=Ch_0^ m\wedge q_\alpha \kappa ^ k =CV_0\, q_\alpha \mu =CV_0f\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] a measure of mass $CV_0$. The bounds $a\leq R\leq A$ transfer the integrability properties of $q_\alpha $ to $f$. Step 3: lower mass and nonclosedness. Pull back bounded $h_0$-plurisubharmonic functions whose masses on $X_0$ tend to zero. The same expansion shows that their $H$-masses are $C$ times their masses on $X_0$, so $v_-(H)=0$. If $h_0$ were closed, Stokes' theorem would give every bounded $h_0$-plurisubharmonic function the mass $V_0>0$, contradicting $v_-(h_0)=0$. Hence $h_0$, and therefore $H$, is not closed. Step 4: the envelopes. Choose $\alpha <\beta <1$. For $b\geq 1$ and $\varepsilon >0$ with $\varepsilon \beta \leq 1$, the number \[  K_ b=\sup _{s\geq 1}\{ b s^\alpha -\varepsilon s^\beta \} -b  \] is finite, since $\beta >\alpha $. The function $g_ b=-\varepsilon (1-\psi )^\beta -K_ b$ on $Y$ satisfies $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_ b\geq (1-\varepsilon \beta )\kappa \geq 0$, by the chain-rule computation in the proof of lemma 15.30.1 , applied to the increasing convex function $t\mapsto -\varepsilon (1-t)^\beta $, whose derivative is at most $\varepsilon \beta $ for $t\leq 0$. With $L=1-\psi \geq 1$, the inequality $g_ b\leq bu_\alpha $ reads $bL^\alpha -\varepsilon L^\beta -b\leq K_ b$, so it holds on $Y\setminus \{ o\} $, and also at $o$, where both sides are $-\infty $. Thus the pullback of $g_ b$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,H)$ and lies below $bu_\alpha $. Since $b\geq 1$ is arbitrary, $u_\alpha \in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,H,0)$ by definition 16.28.61 . For $0<\delta <1$, take $b=1$ and $\varepsilon \beta \leq \delta $. Then $g_1$ is $\delta H$-plurisubharmonic and lies below $u_\alpha $, so $P_{\delta H}(u_\alpha )\geq g_1$ is not identically $-\infty $. $\square$ Corollary 15.30.4 . 8C4A9CEF04C8 Let $X_0$ be the elliptic threefold of theorem 12.19.1 , with the balanced metric $\omega $ of proposition 12.19.18 . On $X_0\times \mathbb P^2$, with background $H=\omega +\kappa $, the densities $f=Rq_\alpha $ of the preceding theorem satisfy \[  v_-(H)=0,\qquad b_ H(f)=240\pi , \qquad \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u_\alpha )=240\pi f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Proof. Theorem 12.19.1 gives $v_-(\omega )=0$, and proposition 12.19.18 gives $V_0=24\pi $. The product theorem applies with $m=3$, $k=2$ and $C=\binom 53=10$. $\square$ These examples show that an individual density can have a positive threshold and an exact equation even though the background has zero lower mass. The exactness comes from the product structure. For $k\geq 2$, the radial flux also identifies the normalized exponential limit in theorem 15.36.5 ; the first moment determines whether scalar centering has a finite limit. 24.2.2 asks for an exact equation for every integrable density with positive threshold.

title: 15.30.5 Closed factors and arbitrary integrable densities

section: 15.30 Exact equations on products with zero lower mass
text: The preceding examples use an explicit potential on projective space. On a closed factor, the mass bound from Stokes' theorem instead makes every threshold subsolution exact. This gives equations for arbitrary integrable densities on that factor, with no assumption that they are bounded below. For this subsection let $(X_0,h_0)$ be any connected compact Hermitian manifold of dimension $m\geq 1$, and let $(Y,\kappa )$ be connected compact Kähler of dimension $k\geq 2$, normalized by $\int _ Y\kappa ^ k=1$. On $X=X_0\times Y$ put \[  N=m+k,\qquad H=h_0+\kappa ,\qquad C=\binom Nm,\qquad V_0=\int _{X_0}h_0^ m,\qquad c_0=CV_0.  \] Forms and functions on the factors are pulled back when used on $X$. For any smooth positive probability volume form $\mathrm dV$ on $X$, put \[  \mu =V_0^{-1}h_0^ m\wedge \kappa ^ k,\qquad R=\frac\mu {\mathrm dV},\qquad a=\min _ XR>0,\qquad A=\max _ XR.  \] Theorem 15.30.6 . AB3D52EC73EF For every nonzero nonnegative $g\in L^1(Y,\kappa ^ k)$, with $M_ g=\int _ Yg\kappa ^ k$, one has \[  b_ H(Rg)=\frac{c_0}{M_ g}.  \] There is $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\kappa )$ with $\sup _ Yv=0$ and $\int _ Y\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (v)=1$ whose pullback $u$ satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u) =\frac{c_0}{M_ g}Rg\, \mathrm dV,\qquad \int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)=c_0.  \] If $v_-(h_0)=0$, then $v_-(H)=0$ and $H$ is not closed. Proof. We first compute the scalars of bounded densities, then use the closed factor's mass bound to identify the equation for an unbounded density. Step 1: bounded densities. If $g$ is bounded and nonzero, theorem 14.19.2 on $Y$ gives a bounded continuous $v$ with $\mathrm{MA}_\kappa (v)=c_\kappa (g)g\kappa ^ k$. Closed Stokes gives $c_\kappa (g)=1/M_ g$. The bounded product expansion gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_ H(v)=C h_0^ m\wedge \mathrm{MA}_\kappa (v) =\frac{c_0}{M_ g}Rg\, \mathrm dV.  \] Uniqueness of the bounded normalization scalar therefore gives $c_ H(Rg)=c_0/M_ g$, including densities with zeros. Step 2: the threshold. section: 15.31 Singular measures on products with a curve
text: The closed-factor equations above concern integrable densities. A curve factor also allows a direct test on a measure: its logarithmic potential determines an exact equation, and continuity of that potential supplies the energy control needed for every positive exponent. The resulting product measure may be singular with respect to smooth volume, even when the solution is continuous. Let $Y=\mathbb P^1$ and let $\kappa $ be the Fubini–Study form of mass one. For the chordal distance $d_{\mathrm{ch}}$, put \[  G(x,y)=\log d_{\mathrm{ch}}(x,y)^2+1,\qquad K(x,y)=1-G(x,y)\geq 0.  \] For a Borel probability $\mu $ on $Y$, define 55B17A6945D4 15.31.1 \begin{equation}  Q_\mu (x)=\int _ YG(x,y)\, \mathrm d\mu (y). \end{equation} We say that $\mu $ is non-polar if it gives every polar Borel set mass zero.

text: Lemma 15.31.3 . 2CA6CA22B712 For every probability $\mu $, the function $Q_\mu $ is $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic, has $\kappa $-mean zero, and satisfies \[  \kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Q_\mu =\mu ,\qquad Q_\mu \leq 1.  \] If $\mu $ is non-polar, then $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (Q_\mu )=\mu $. Every $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\kappa )$ with $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (p)\geq \mu $ is of the form $Q_\mu +C$. Proof. The Poincaré–Lelong formula gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ xG(x,y)=\delta _ y-\kappa $. After a rotation sending $y$ to $[1:0]$, the variable $t=d_{\mathrm{ch}}(x,y)^2$ is uniformly distributed on $[0,1]$ for the measure $\kappa $. Thus \[  \int _ YG(x,y)\kappa (x)=\int _0^1(\log t+1)\, \mathrm dt=0, \qquad \sup _ y\int _ Y|G(x,y)|\kappa (x)<\infty .  \] The continuous potentials $\int \max (G(x,y),-L)\, \mathrm d\mu (y)$ are $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic by lemma 5.24.1 and averaging, and decrease to $Q_\mu $. Tonelli's theorem gives its integrability and mean zero; the decreasing-limit property gives its canonical values. Distributional Fubini proves the curvature identity. In degree one the extended measure of $p$ is \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (p) =\mathbf1_{\{ p>-\infty \} }(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p).  \] The pole set of $Q_\mu $ is polar, so non-polarity gives its asserted measure. For any $p$, distributional Stokes gives the full current $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p$ mass one, and its extended measure has mass at most one. Domination of the probability $\mu $ therefore forces both measures to equal $\mu $. The distribution $p-Q_\mu $ is harmonic on the compact connected curve, hence constant, and canonical equality gives the assertion everywhere. $\square$ For real Sobolev functions on $Y$ use the Dirichlet form \[  E(p,q)=\int _ Y\mathrm dp\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}q.  \] It is symmetric and nonnegative on the diagonal. The space $H^1(Y)$ and its norm are taken for the Fubini–Study Riemannian metric. Lemma 15.31.4 . F5E3175FA178 Suppose $Q=Q_\mu $ is finite and continuous. Then $\mu $ is non-polar, $Q\in H^1(Y)$, and smooth restriction extends to a continuous linear map \[  \operatorname {Tr}_\mu :H^1(Y)\longrightarrow L^1(\mu ).  \] For every $h\in H^1(Y)$, DB0D4C618F78 15.31.5 \begin{equation}  \int _ Y\operatorname {Tr}_\mu h\, \mathrm d\mu =\int _ Yh\kappa -E(h,Q). \end{equation} For $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\kappa )\cap H^1(Y)$ this trace agrees $\mu $-almost everywhere with its canonical values. The trace commutes with Lipschitz real compositions. Proof. Continuity gives the uniform kernel bound 79703FA8B5E7 15.31.6 \begin{equation}  A_\mu :=\sup _ x\int _ YK(x,y)\, \mathrm d\mu (y) =1-\inf _ YQ<\infty . \end{equation} To prove non-polarity, take a nontrivial subharmonic function on a coordinate disk. Cut off its positive Hessian measure on a slightly larger disk. The logarithmic potential of this finite measure has the same Hessian on the smaller disk, so their difference is harmonic there. This is the local Riesz decomposition: it also follows directly from the distributional fundamental solution and harmonic regularity. On compact subdisks the kernel $-\log |z-a|^2$ differs from $K(z,a)$ by a bounded smooth term. Symmetry of $K$, Tonelli's theorem and ( 15.31.6 ) make the logarithmic potential integrable against $\mu $; its harmonic remainder is bounded. The pole set consequently has $\mu $-mass zero. A countable disk cover proves the claim for polar Borel sets. The group $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ acts on $Y$ by Fubini–Study isometries. Average with smooth nonnegative conjugation-invariant kernels of mass one supported near the identity. This gives smooth $Q_\epsilon $, probability measures $\mu _\epsilon $, and \[  Q_\epsilon \longrightarrow Q\  \text{uniformly},\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Q_\epsilon =\mu _\epsilon -\kappa ,\qquad \int _ YQ_\epsilon \kappa =0.  \] Smooth Stokes gives $E(Q_\epsilon ,Q_\epsilon )=-\int Q_\epsilon \, \mathrm d\mu _\epsilon \leq \| Q\| _\infty $. Poincaré's inequality and weak Hilbert compactness show that $Q\in H^1$. Its distributional curvature identity gives ( 15.31.5 ) first for smooth $h$. Apply this identity to $\sqrt{h^2+\epsilon ^2}$, whose gradient has magnitude at most $|\mathrm dh|$. Letting $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ yields \[  \int _ Y|h|\, \mathrm d\mu \leq \| h\| _{L^1(\kappa )}+E(h,h)^{1/2}E(Q,Q)^{1/2} \leq C_\mu \| h\| _{H^1}.  \] Completion defines the trace and extends the identity. These group averages converge strongly in $H^1$: rotations act continuously and isometrically on that space, and the averaging kernels approach the identity. They also converge pointwise to every canonical quasi-subharmonic function. Indeed their induced averages about a point are radial by conjugation invariance. In a coordinate centered at that point they are positive averages of circular means; after a smooth quadratic correction, the submean inequality and upper semicontinuity give the required limit. The correction error tends to zero, and upper semicontinuity gives the limit also at a pole. For a $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic $H^1$ function, strong convergence and the trace bound give $L^1(\mu )$ convergence, while a subsequence converges $\mu $-almost everywhere to the trace. Non-polarity makes the canonical value finite there and identifies the two. Finally, the Sobolev chain rule and smooth approximation show that Lipschitz compositions are continuous in $H^1$; the corresponding $L^1(\mu )$ limits prove the composition assertion. $\square$

text: Theorem 15.31.8 . 346FA2C8C90A Suppose $Q=Q_\mu $ is finite and continuous. For every $\lambda >0$ there is a unique bounded $w_\lambda \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\kappa )$ satisfying C82032A970D1 15.31.9 \begin{equation}  \kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_\lambda =\mathrm e^{\lambda w_\lambda }\mu , \qquad \int _ Y\mathrm e^{\lambda w_\lambda }\, \mathrm d\mu =1. \end{equation} It is continuous and obeys C8BB18387ED9 15.31.10 \begin{equation}  Q-\sup _ YQ\leq w_\lambda \leq Q-\inf _ YQ. \end{equation} The entire family satisfies, as $\lambda \downarrow 0$, \[  \left\| w_\lambda -Q+\int _ YQ\, \mathrm d\mu \right\| _\infty =O(\lambda ).  \] The limit is the greatest $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\kappa )$ with $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (p)\geq \mu $ and $\int _ Yp\, \mathrm d\mu \leq 0$. Proof. Variational existence. On the real Hilbert space \[  \mathcal H=\{ q\in H^1(Y):\int _ Yq\kappa =0\}   \] consider the extended functional \[  J_\lambda (q)=\tfrac 12E(q,q) +\lambda ^{-1}\log \int _ Y\mathrm e^{\lambda \operatorname {Tr}_\mu q}\, \mathrm d\mu .  \] It is finite at zero. Jensen's inequality and ( 15.31.5 ) give \[  J_\lambda (q)\geq \tfrac 12E(q,q)-E(q,Q),  \] so it is coercive and bounded below. Strong $H^1$ convergence gives $L^1(\mu )$ convergence of traces. A subsequence realizing the lower limit converges almost everywhere for $\mu $, and Fatou's lemma proves strong lower semicontinuity of the exponential term. Jensen excludes a zero integral or a logarithm tending to $-\infty $. Hölder's inequality makes the logarithmic term convex, while the Dirichlet term is strictly convex on $\mathcal H$. Separation of a closed convex epigraph makes $J_\lambda $ weakly lower semicontinuous. Weak compactness therefore gives a unique minimizer $q_\lambda $, with \[  0<Z_\lambda :=\int _ Y\mathrm e^{\lambda \operatorname {Tr}_\mu q_\lambda }\, \mathrm d\mu <\infty .  \] Variation in a smooth mean-zero direction $h$ is justified by its boundedness, which dominates the differentiated integrand by a constant times the integrable exponential. Put $\rho _\lambda =\mathrm e^{\lambda \operatorname {Tr}_\mu q_\lambda }/Z_\lambda $. The Euler equation is \[  E(q_\lambda ,h)+\int _ Yh\rho _\lambda \, \mathrm d\mu =0, \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_\lambda =\rho _\lambda \mu -\kappa .  \] The second identity follows for arbitrary smooth tests by subtracting their $\kappa $-mean; $\int \rho _\lambda \, \mathrm d\mu =1$ fixes the constant term. The minimizer has a canonical $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic representative. Its mean-zero Green representation and lemma 15.31.4 give \[  q_\lambda (x)=\int _ YG(x,y)\rho _\lambda (y)\, \mathrm d\mu (y)\leq 1, \qquad \rho _\lambda \leq \mathrm e^\lambda /Z_\lambda \quad \mu \text{-a.e.}  \] The kernel bound then gives $q_\lambda \geq 1-(\mathrm e^\lambda /Z_\lambda )A_\mu $. To obtain continuity, the continuous functions $\int \min (K(x,y),L)\, \mathrm d\mu (y)$ increase to the continuous function $1-Q(x)$. Dini's theorem gives 91D68636194F 15.31.11 \begin{equation}  \sup _ x\int _ Y(K(x,y)-L)_+\, \mathrm d\mu (y)\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} Multiplication by the bounded density $\rho _\lambda $ preserves this estimate. Its truncated Green potentials converge uniformly, so $q_\lambda $ is continuous. Now \[  w_\lambda =q_\lambda -\lambda ^{-1}\log Z_\lambda  \] solves ( 15.31.9 ) with precisely the displayed constant. Uniqueness and the barriers. Every bounded $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic function is in $H^1$, by the same smoothing and energy bound used above after subtracting its $\kappa $-mean. For two bounded solutions $w_1,w_2$, their right-hand sides have bounded densities relative to $\mu $. The trace inequality extends distributional Stokes to their difference, giving \[  E(w_1-w_2,w_1-w_2) =-\int _ Y(w_1-w_2)(\mathrm e^{\lambda w_1}-\mathrm e^{\lambda w_2})\, \mathrm d\mu \leq 0.  \] The difference is constant; the unit exponential integrals force that constant to be zero. Set $L_0=Q-\sup Q\leq 0$, $R_0=Q-\inf Q\geq 0$, and $z=(L_0-w_\lambda )_+$. The $H^1$ chain rule, canonical trace and extended Stokes give \[  E(z,z)=-\int _ Yz(1-\mathrm e^{\lambda w_\lambda })\, \mathrm d\mu \leq 0.  \] Indeed $z>0$ implies $w_\lambda <L_0\leq 0$. Thus $z$ is constant. If it were a positive constant, continuity would give $w_\lambda =L_0-z\leq -z$ everywhere, contradicting its unit exponential integral. This proves the lower barrier. Testing $(w_\lambda -R_0)_+$ gives the upper barrier with the same argument and the reversed exponential difference. In particular $\| w_\lambda \| _\infty \leq \operatorname {osc}Q$. Selection. Write $q_\lambda =w_\lambda -\int _ Yw_\lambda \kappa $, consistent with the variational normalization. The barriers give $\mathrm e^{\lambda w_\lambda }=1+O(\lambda )$ uniformly, and the Green identity gives \[  \| q_\lambda -Q\| _\infty \leq \| \mathrm e^{\lambda w_\lambda }-1\| _\infty \sup _ x\int _ Y|G(x,y)|\, \mathrm d\mu (y)=O(\lambda ).  \] The last kernel integral is bounded by $1+A_\mu $. The $q_\lambda $ are uniformly bounded, so Taylor's formula gives \[  \lambda ^{-1}\log Z_\lambda =\int _ Yq_\lambda \, \mathrm d\mu +O(\lambda ) =\int _ YQ\, \mathrm d\mu +O(\lambda ).  \] This proves the whole-family estimate. Finally, lemma 15.31.3 identifies every critical subsolution as $Q+C$. Its $\mu $-mean is at most zero exactly when $C\leq -\int Q\, \mathrm d\mu $, proving the order characterization. $\square$

Dini's theorem gives 91D68636194F 15.31.11 \begin{equation}  \sup _ x\int _ Y(K(x,y)-L)_+\, \mathrm d\mu (y)\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} Multiplication by the bounded density $\rho _\lambda $ preserves this estimate. Its truncated Green potentials converge uniformly, so $q_\lambda $ is continuous. Now \[  w_\lambda =q_\lambda -\lambda ^{-1}\log Z_\lambda  \] solves ( 15.31.9 ) with precisely the displayed constant. Uniqueness and the barriers. Every bounded $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic function is in $H^1$, by the same smoothing and energy bound used above after subtracting its $\kappa $-mean. For two bounded solutions $w_1,w_2$, their right-hand sides have bounded densities relative to $\mu $. The trace inequality extends distributional Stokes to their difference, giving \[  E(w_1-w_2,w_1-w_2) =-\int _ Y(w_1-w_2)(\mathrm e^{\lambda w_1}-\mathrm e^{\lambda w_2})\, \mathrm d\mu \leq 0.  \] The difference is constant; the unit exponential integrals force that constant to be zero. Set $L_0=Q-\sup Q\leq 0$, $R_0=Q-\inf Q\geq 0$, and $z=(L_0-w_\lambda )_+$. The $H^1$ chain rule, canonical trace and extended Stokes give \[  E(z,z)=-\int _ Yz(1-\mathrm e^{\lambda w_\lambda })\, \mathrm d\mu \leq 0.  \] Indeed $z>0$ implies $w_\lambda <L_0\leq 0$. Thus $z$ is constant. If it were a positive constant, continuity would give $w_\lambda =L_0-z\leq -z$ everywhere, contradicting its unit exponential integral. This proves the lower barrier. Testing $(w_\lambda -R_0)_+$ gives the upper barrier with the same argument and the reversed exponential difference. In particular $\| w_\lambda \| _\infty \leq \operatorname {osc}Q$. Selection. Write $q_\lambda =w_\lambda -\int _ Yw_\lambda \kappa $, consistent with the variational normalization. The barriers give $\mathrm e^{\lambda w_\lambda }=1+O(\lambda )$ uniformly, and the Green identity gives \[  \| q_\lambda -Q\| _\infty \leq \| \mathrm e^{\lambda w_\lambda }-1\| _\infty \sup _ x\int _ Y|G(x,y)|\, \mathrm d\mu (y)=O(\lambda ).  \] The last kernel integral is bounded by $1+A_\mu $. The $q_\lambda $ are uniformly bounded, so Taylor's formula gives \[  \lambda ^{-1}\log Z_\lambda =\int _ Yq_\lambda \, \mathrm d\mu +O(\lambda ) =\int _ YQ\, \mathrm d\mu +O(\lambda ).  \] This proves the whole-family estimate. Finally, lemma 15.31.3 identifies every critical subsolution as $Q+C$. Its $\mu $-mean is at most zero exactly when $C\leq -\int Q\, \mathrm d\mu $, proving the order characterization. $\square$

title: 15.32 Stability of the subsolution threshold
text: We now study how the threshold $b_ h(f)$ depends on $f$. By ( 15.29.3 ), $b_ h^{1/n}$ is an infimum of functions that are continuous on $L^1$, and is therefore upper semicontinuous. It is not continuous in general: when $v_-(h)=0$, every density with positive threshold is an $L^1$ limit of densities with zero threshold. For density roots, ( 15.29.2 ) expresses $\rho _ h$ as a supremum of positive linear functionals. Hence $\rho _ h$ is a norm on the space where it is finite, this space is complete for a suitable norm, and the threshold depends continuously on the root in that norm. Theorem 15.32.1 . D988D47D5E0E Suppose $f_ j,f$ are nonzero nonnegative $L^1$ densities and $f_ j\to f$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$. Then \[  \limsup _{j\to \infty }b_ h(f_ j)\leq b_ h(f).  \] Moreover, ACC15559958B 15.32.2 \begin{equation}  b_ h(f)=\lim _{\delta \downarrow 0}\sup \{ c_ h(q):q\in L^\infty ,\  q\geq 0,\  q\not\equiv 0, \  \| q-f\| _{L^1}<\delta \} , \end{equation} and the suprema are finite for sufficiently small $\delta $. Proof. For a Gauduchon form $\gamma $ on $X$, write $A_\gamma (f)=\int _ X(f\, \mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n$. Since $|s^{1/n}-t^{1/n}|\leq |s-t|^{1/n}$ for $s,t\geq 0$, Hölder's inequality shows that $A_\gamma $ is continuous on $L^1$; it is positive at every nonzero nonnegative density. By theorem 15.29.1 , $b_ h^{1/n}$ is the infimum over $\gamma $ of the continuous positive functions $f\mapsto \int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}/A_\gamma (f)$. It is therefore upper semicontinuous, and testing a single $\gamma $ bounds it above on an $L^1$ neighborhood of $f$. For the second assertion, recall that $b_ h(q)=c_ h(q)$ for bounded $q$ (proposition 15.28.7 ). By the first assertion, $\limsup _ jc_ h(q_ j)\leq b_ h(f)$ for every sequence of nonzero nonnegative bounded densities $q_ j\to f$ in $L^1$. Hence the limit in ( 15.32.2 ) is at most $b_ h(f)$, and the local upper bound makes the suprema finite for small $\delta $. Conversely, the truncations $f_ k$ converge to $f$ in $L^1$ and satisfy $c_ h(f_ k)\geq b_ h(f)$, so every supremum in ( 15.32.2 ) is at least $b_ h(f)$. $\square$ Since $b_ h\geq 0$, upper semicontinuity makes $b_ h$ continuous at every density where it vanishes. If $v_-(h)=0$, these are its only points of continuity. Indeed, let $b_ h(f)>0$ and $g=f/\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V$. By corollary 15.27.6 and theorem 15.28.4 , the densities $(1-t)g+tf_0$, where $f_0$ is the density of theorem 15.27.3 , have zero threshold and converge to $g$ in $L^1$ as $t\downarrow 0$; multiplying them by $\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V$ gives densities with zero threshold converging to $f$. These statements concern only the scalar $b_ h$; they say nothing about capacity convergence of the corresponding potentials or about the limits of their Monge–Ampère measures.

Since ( 15.29.2 ) expresses $ho _ h(p)$ as a supremum of positive linear functionals evaluated at $|p|$, the root functional is homogeneous, monotone and subadditive. Subadditivity shows that the sum of two densities with positive threshold again has positive threshold. In the statements below, $f$ and $g$ are nonzero nonnegative $L^1$ densities, and $p$ and $q$ are real or complex functions in $L^ n$. Proposition 15.32.4 . D697A55DE07C The functional $ho _ h$ satisfies $ho _ h(tp)=|t|ho _ h(p)$ for scalars $t
e 0$, $ho _ h(p)\leq ho _ h(q)$ whenever $|p|\leq |q|$, and \[  ho _ h(p+q)\leq ho _ h(p)+ho _ h(q).  \] In particular, if $b_ h(f),b_ h(g)>0$, then \[  b_ h(f+g)\geq  igl (b_ h(f)^{-1/n}+b_ h(g)^{-1/n} igr )^{-n}>0.  \] Proof. By ( 15.29.2 ), $ho _ h(p)=\sup _\gamma L_{h,\gamma }(|p|)$ is a supremum of positive linear functionals evaluated at $|p|$. This gives homogeneity and monotonicity, and, together with $|p+q|\leq |p|+|q|$, the triangle inequality. Finally, $(f+g)^{1/n}\leq f^{1/n}+g^{1/n}$ gives \[  b_ h(f+g)^{-1/n}=ho _ h igl ((f+g)^{1/n} igr )\leq ho _ h(f^{1/n})+ho _ h(g^{1/n}) =b_ h(f)^{-1/n}+b_ h(g)^{-1/n},  \] which is equivalent to the asserted lower bound for $b_ h(f+g)$. $\square$ Proposition 15.32.5 . 4C06D1B94BD1 The real or complex vector space \[  \mathcal D_ h=\{ p\in L^ n(\mathrm{d}V):ho _ h(p)<+\infty \}   \] is complete for the norm $\| p\| _{\mathcal D_ h}=\| p\| _{L^ n}+ho _ h(p)$. It is an order ideal in $L^ n$: if $q\in \mathcal D_ h$ and $|p|\leq |q|$, then $p\in \mathcal D_ h$. It contains $L^\infty $ and is therefore dense in $L^ n$ for the $L^ n$ norm. Moreover, $\mathcal D_ h=L^ n$ if and only if $v_-(h)>0$, and in that case the norm $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ is equivalent to the $L^ n$ norm. If $h$ is Kähler, then \[  ho _ h(p)=\left(\int _ Xh^ night)^{-1/n}\| p\| _{L^ n}.  \] Proof. By proposition 15.32.4 , $\mathcal D_ h$ is a vector space and an order ideal, and $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ is a norm on it. Bounded functions belong to $\mathcal D_ h$, because $b_ h(|p|^ n)=c_ h(|p|^ n)>0$ for bounded nonzero $p$. We next show that $ho _ h$ is lower semicontinuous on $L^ n$. If $p_ j	o p$ in $L^ n$, then $|p_ j|^ n	o |p|^ n$ in $L^1$, and the upper semicontinuity of $b_ h$ in theorem 15.32.1 gives \[  ho _ h(p)\leq \liminf _ jho _ h(p_ j).  \] This includes the case $b_ h(|p|^ n)=0$, in which the right side must be infinite; for $p=0$ the inequality is trivial. Now let $(p_ j)$ be a Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal D_ h$. It converges in $L^ n$ to some $p$, and lower semicontinuity gives $ho _ h(p)\leq \liminf _ jho _ h(p_ j)<+\infty $, so $p\in \mathcal D_ h$. Applied to $p_ j-p_ k$ as $k	o \infty $, lower semicontinuity also gives \[  ho _ h(p_ j-p)\leq \liminf _{k	o \infty }ho _ h(p_ j-p_ k),  \] which tends to zero as $j	o \infty $. Together with $L^ n$ convergence, this proves completeness. If $v_-(h)>0$, proposition 15.28.7 gives $ho _ h(p)\leq v_-(h)^{-1/n}\| p\| _{L^ n}$, so $\mathcal D_ h=L^ n$ with an equivalent norm. If $v_-(h)=0$, the density $f$ of theorem 15.27.3 has $b_ h(f)=0$ by theorem 15.28.4 ; thus $f^{1/n}$ belongs to $L^ n$ but not to $\mathcal D_ h$. The Kähler formula follows from the same proposition. $\square$ Thus, when the lower mass vanishes, $\mathcal D_ h$ is a proper dense subspace of $L^ n$, complete for the stronger norm $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$; its nonnegative elements are the $n$th roots of the densities admitting a positive scaled subsolution. A finite sum of such densities again admits a positive scaled subsolution, but a convergent infinite sum need not: the smooth summands in theorem 15.27.3 give an example. By proposition 15.29.5 , the space $\mathcal D_ h$ does not depend on the Hermitian form $h$, and the norms $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ for different Hermitian forms are equivalent. The closure of the bounded functions for this norm is studied in 15.32.7 . The restriction of $ho _ h$ to $\mathcal D_ h$ is itself a norm: if $p
e 0$, then $ho _ h(p)\geq L_{h,\gamma }(|p|)>0$ for any Gauduchon form $\gamma $. Whether this weaker norm is complete depends on the upper mass. Proposition 15.32.6 . C926F63790E3 The norm $ho _ h$ is complete on $\mathcal D_ h$ if and only if $v_+(h)<+\infty $. When the upper mass is finite, \[  \| p\| _{L^ n}\leq v_+(h)^{1/n}ho _ h(p)\qquad (p\in \mathcal D_ h),  \] so $ho _ h$ and $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ are equivalent norms. Proof. Suppose $v_+(h)<+\infty $. A continuous solution for a bounded density $q$ has mass $c_ h(q)\int _ Xq\, \mathrm{d}V\leq v_+(h)$. Applying this to the truncations of $|p|^ n$ and letting the truncation level increase gives $b_ h(|p|^ n)\| p\| _{L^ n}^ n\leq v_+(h)$, which is the asserted inequality. Hence $ho _ h$ and $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ are equivalent, and completeness follows from proposition 15.32.5 . Suppose instead that $v_+(h)=+\infty $. By theorem 12.15.4 , theorem 12.2.3 , the normalization scalars of smooth strictly positive probability densities are unbounded above. For each $j$, choose such a density $f_ j$ with \[  c_ h(f_ j)\geq (j2^ j)^ n, \qquad 	ext{and put}\qquad p_ j=jf_ j^{1/n}.  \] Then $\| p_ j\| _{L^ n}=j$ and $ho _ h(p_ j)=jc_ h(f_ j)^{-1/n}\leq 2^{-j}$, so the partial sums $P_ N=\sum _{j\leq N}p_ j$ form a Cauchy sequence for $ho _ h$. Fix a Gauduchon form $\gamma $. Its coefficient $a_\gamma $ is bounded below by a positive constant, so ( 15.29.2 ) gives $ho _ h(p)\geq c\| p\| _{L^1}$ with a constant $c>0$. Hence $\sum _ jp_ j$ converges in $L^1$ to a nonnegative function $P$. If $P_ N$ converged for $ho _ h$ to an element of $\mathcal D_ h$, that element would also be the $L^1$ limit, hence equal to $P$ almost everywhere. But $P\geq p_ j$ gives $\| P\| _{L^ n}\geq j$ for every $j$, so $P
otin L^ n$. Therefore $ho _ h$ is not complete. $\square$ The two mass properties play separate roles: positive lower mass makes every $L^ n$ function admissible, whereas finite upper mass makes the root norm control the $L^ n$ norm. The norm $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ is complete without either assumption. All four combinations occur. On a compact Kähler manifold both mass properties hold. The Hopf threefold has positive lower mass and infinite upper mass (corollary 23.1.40 ). The elliptic threefold of theorem 12.19.1 has zero lower mass, and finite upper mass for its balanced metric (proposition 12.19.18 ). The product manifolds of corollary 12.19.16 have zero lower mass and infinite upper mass. Since neither $\mathcal D_ h$ nor the completeness of $ho _ h$ depends on the choice of $h$ (proposition 15.29.5 , proposition 13.14.15 ), we obtain the following table. title: Proposition 15.32.4
text: Proposition 15.32.4 . D697A55DE07C The functional $\rho _ h$ satisfies $\rho _ h(tp)=|t|\rho _ h(p)$ for scalars $t\ne 0$, $\rho _ h(p)\leq \rho _ h(q)$ whenever $|p|\leq |q|$, and \[  \rho _ h(p+q)\leq \rho _ h(p)+\rho _ h(q).  \] In particular, if $b_ h(f),b_ h(g)>0$, then \[  b_ h(f+g)\geq \bigl (b_ h(f)^{-1/n}+b_ h(g)^{-1/n}\bigr )^{-n}>0.  \] Proof. By ( 15.29.2 ), $\rho _ h(p)=\sup _\gamma L_{h,\gamma }(|p|)$ is a supremum of positive linear functionals evaluated at $|p|$. This gives homogeneity and monotonicity, and, together with $|p+q|\leq |p|+|q|$, the triangle inequality. Finally, $(f+g)^{1/n}\leq f^{1/n}+g^{1/n}$ gives \[  b_ h(f+g)^{-1/n}=\rho _ h\bigl ((f+g)^{1/n}\bigr )\leq \rho _ h(f^{1/n})+\rho _ h(g^{1/n}) =b_ h(f)^{-1/n}+b_ h(g)^{-1/n},  \] which is equivalent to the asserted lower bound for $b_ h(f+g)$. $\square$

title: Proposition 15.32.5
text: Proposition 15.32.5 . 4C06D1B94BD1 The real or complex vector space \[  \mathcal D_ h=\{ p\in L^ n(\mathrm{d}V):\rho _ h(p)<+\infty \}   \] is complete for the norm $\| p\| _{\mathcal D_ h}=\| p\| _{L^ n}+\rho _ h(p)$. It is an order ideal in $L^ n$: if $q\in \mathcal D_ h$ and $|p|\leq |q|$, then $p\in \mathcal D_ h$. It contains $L^\infty $ and is therefore dense in $L^ n$ for the $L^ n$ norm. Moreover, $\mathcal D_ h=L^ n$ if and only if $v_-(h)>0$, and in that case the norm $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ is equivalent to the $L^ n$ norm. If $h$ is Kähler, then \[  \rho _ h(p)=\left(\int _ Xh^ n\right)^{-1/n}\| p\| _{L^ n}.  \] Proof. By proposition 15.32.4 , $\mathcal D_ h$ is a vector space and an order ideal, and $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ is a norm on it. Bounded functions belong to $\mathcal D_ h$, because $b_ h(|p|^ n)=c_ h(|p|^ n)>0$ for bounded nonzero $p$. We next show that $\rho _ h$ is lower semicontinuous on $L^ n$. If $p_ j\to p$ in $L^ n$, then $|p_ j|^ n\to |p|^ n$ in $L^1$, and the upper semicontinuity of $b_ h$ in theorem 15.32.1 gives \[  \rho _ h(p)\leq \liminf _ j\rho _ h(p_ j).  \] This includes the case $b_ h(|p|^ n)=0$, in which the right side must be infinite; for $p=0$ the inequality is trivial. Now let $(p_ j)$ be a Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal D_ h$. It converges in $L^ n$ to some $p$, and lower semicontinuity gives $\rho _ h(p)\leq \liminf _ j\rho _ h(p_ j)<+\infty $, so $p\in \mathcal D_ h$. Applied to $p_ j-p_ k$ as $k\to \infty $, lower semicontinuity also gives \[  \rho _ h(p_ j-p)\leq \liminf _{k\to \infty }\rho _ h(p_ j-p_ k),  \] which tends to zero as $j\to \infty $. Together with $L^ n$ convergence, this proves completeness. If $v_-(h)>0$, proposition 15.28.7 gives $\rho _ h(p)\leq v_-(h)^{-1/n}\| p\| _{L^ n}$, so $\mathcal D_ h=L^ n$ with an equivalent norm. If $v_-(h)=0$, the density $f$ of theorem 15.27.3 has $b_ h(f)=0$ by theorem 15.28.4 ; thus $f^{1/n}$ belongs to $L^ n$ but not to $\mathcal D_ h$. The Kähler formula follows from the same proposition. $\square$

title: 15.32.7 Approximation by bounded density roots
text: Bounded functions are dense in $\mathcal D_ h$ for the $L^ n$ norm, but not obviously for the norm $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$. Let $\mathcal D_ h^0$ denote the closure of $L^\infty $ in $\mathcal D_ h$ for this norm. We show that a function belongs to $\mathcal D_ h^0$ exactly when its tails are small uniformly over all Gauduchon tests. The basic tool is a subcritical estimate. For every $r>n$, CA92BD48A42D 15.32.8 \begin{equation}  \rho _ h(p)\leq C_ r\| p\| _{L^ r}\qquad (p\in L^ r), \end{equation} where the constant $C_ r$ depends on $h$, the reference volume and $r$, but not on $p$. Indeed, for nonzero $p\in L^ r$ the density $|p|^ n$ belongs to $L^{r/n}$, so $b_ h(|p|^ n)=c_ h(|p|^ n)$ by proposition 15.28.7 , and the lower-density estimate of theorem 14.19.19 , with exponent $r/n$, gives $c_ h(|p|^ n)\| |p|^ n\| _{L^{r/n}}\geq c_{r/n}>0$. Proposition 15.32.9 . 2210D4123A64 For $p\in \mathcal D_ h$, the following conditions are equivalent: $p\in \mathcal D_ h^0$; $\rho _ h(|p|\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>K\} })\to 0$ as $K\to \infty $; whenever $|q_ j|\leq |p|$ and $q_ j\to 0$ in measure, one has $\| q_ j\| _{\mathcal D_ h}\to 0$. By ( 15.29.2 ), the second condition can be written as \[  \sup _{\gamma \text{ Gauduchon}} L_{h,\gamma }(|p|\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>K\} })\longrightarrow 0 \qquad (K\to \infty ).  \] The space $\mathcal D_ h^0$ is a closed order ideal in $\mathcal D_ h$. It contains $L^ r$ for every $r>n$, and smooth functions are dense in it. If $v_-(h)>0$, then $\mathcal D_ h^0=\mathcal D_ h=L^ n$. Proof. For $K>0$, set $p_ K=p\min (1,K/|p|)$ where $p\ne 0$, and $p_ K=0$ where $p=0$. Then $|p-p_ K|=(|p|-K)_+$ and \[  (|p|-K)_+\leq |p|\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>K\} },\qquad |p|\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>2K\} }\leq 2(|p|-K)_+.  \] Since the $L^ n$ norms of the tails tend to zero, these inequalities and the monotonicity of $\rho _ h$ show that the second condition is equivalent to $p_ K\to p$ in $\mathcal D_ h$; in particular, it implies the first. Conversely, if $a$ is bounded and $K\geq \| a\| _{L^\infty }$, then $(|p|-K)_+\leq |p-a|$, so $\| p-p_ K\| _{\mathcal D_ h}\leq \| p-a\| _{\mathcal D_ h}$. Approximating $p$ by bounded functions $a$ shows that the first condition implies $p_ K\to p$, hence the second. Assume the second condition, and let $q_ j$ be as in the third. Fix $K$. On $\{ |p|\leq K\} $, the functions $q_ j$ are bounded by $K$ and tend to zero in measure, hence in $L^{2n}$; by ( 15.32.8 ) with $r=2n$, the root functional of $q_ j\mathbf1_{\{ |p|\leq K\} }$ tends to zero. On the complementary set, $\rho _ h(q_ j\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>K\} })\leq \rho _ h(|p|\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>K\} })$. Letting first $j$ and then $K$ tend to infinity gives $\rho _ h(q_ j)\to 0$, and dominated convergence gives $\| q_ j\| _{L^ n}\to 0$. Conversely, the third condition applied to $q_ j=|p|\mathbf1_{\{ |p|>j\} }$ gives the second. Since the second condition passes from $p$ to every function dominated by $|p|$, the space $\mathcal D_ h^0$ is an order ideal; it is closed by definition. For $p\in L^ r$ with $r>n$, the truncations $p_ K$ converge to $p$ in $L^ r$, hence in $\mathcal D_ h$ by ( 15.32.8 ). Bounded functions can be approximated in $L^{2n}$ by smooth functions, which then converge in $\mathcal D_ h$ by the same estimate; hence smooth functions are dense in $\mathcal D_ h^0$. Under positive lower mass, proposition 15.32.5 shows that $\mathcal D_ h=L^ n$ with an equivalent norm, and bounded functions are dense in $L^ n$; hence $\mathcal D_ h^0=\mathcal D_ h=L^ n$. $\square$ By proposition 15.29.5 , the space $\mathcal D_ h^0$ does not depend on the choice of the Hermitian form $h$. Convergence in $\mathcal D_ h$ controls the threshold: if $p_ j\to p\ne 0$ in $\mathcal D_ h$, then \[  |\rho _ h(p_ j)-\rho _ h(p)|\leq \rho _ h(p_ j-p)\longrightarrow 0, \qquad b_ h(|p_ j|^ n)\longrightarrow b_ h(|p|^ n)>0.  \] For $p\in \mathcal D_ h^0$, the uniform tail condition also gives a uniform modulus for exponential damping and error bounds for the scalars of the exponential equations; see proposition 15.35.5 . It does not by itself give capacity convergence of the solutions. We do not know whether $\mathcal D_ h^0=\mathcal D_ h$ when $v_-(h)=0$.

title: 15.32.10 Density roots from a closed factor
search_title: Density roots from a closed factor
text: The product formula of theorem 15.30.6 identifies a complete subspace of density roots with uniformly vanishing tails even when the ambient lower mass is zero. Use the product data $X_0,Y,N,H,c_0,\mu ,R$ of 15.30.5 . The spaces $\mathcal D_ H$ and $\mathcal D_ H^0$ are now taken on the $N$-dimensional product with reference volume $\mathrm dV$. Proposition 15.32.11 . 7A2CC1A3258E For real or complex $\xi \in L^ N(Y,\kappa ^ k)$, put $J\xi =R^{1/N}\pi _ Y^*\xi $. Then \[  \| J\xi \| _{L^ N(\mathrm dV)}=\| \xi \| _{L^ N(\kappa ^ k)},\qquad \rho _ H(J\xi )=c_0^{-1/N}\| \xi \| _{L^ N(\kappa ^ k)}.  \] The image of $J$ is a closed linear subspace of $\mathcal D_ H^0$. If $g=|\xi |^ N$ and $A=\max _ XR$, then \[  \rho _ H\bigl (J\xi \mathbf1_{\{ |J\xi |>K\} }\bigr ) \leq \left(\frac1{c_0}\int _{\{ g>K^ N/A\} }g\kappa ^ k\right)^{1/N} \longrightarrow 0.  \] For $\mathrm dV=\mu $, so that $R=1$, the exact tail formula is \[  \rho _ H\bigl (\pi _ Y^*\xi \mathbf1_{\{ |\xi |>K\} }\bigr ) =\left(\frac1{c_0}\int _{\{ |\xi |>K\} }|\xi |^ N\kappa ^ k\right)^{1/N}.  \] Proof. Since $|J\xi |^ N=R|\xi |^ N$, integration against $\mathrm dV$ gives the first norm identity. For nonzero $\xi $, theorem 15.30.6 applied to $g=|\xi |^ N$ gives the root-functional identity; for $\xi =0$ it holds by definition. Applying the two identities to differences yields \[  \| J\xi -J\eta \| _{\mathcal D_ H} =(1+c_0^{-1/N})\| \xi -\eta \| _{L^ N(\kappa ^ k)}.  \] Bounded approximations of $\xi $ in $L^ N$ have bounded images because $R$ is bounded, so $J\xi \in \mathcal D_ H^0$. Completeness of $L^ N(Y,\kappa ^ k)$ and the displayed identity make the image closed. On $\{ |J\xi |>K\} $ one has $g>K^ N/A$, and hence \[  |J\xi |\mathbf1_{\{ |J\xi |>K\} } \leq \bigl (Rg\mathbf1_{\{ g>K^ N/A\} }\bigr )^{1/N}.  \] Monotonicity of the root functional and its identity for factor roots give the estimate, with the value zero when the tail vanishes. Integrability of $g$ makes the bound tend to zero; the $L^ N$ tails also vanish. When $R=1$, the amplitude cutoff itself is pulled back from $Y$, so the same norm identity gives equality. $\square$ For $Y=\mathbb P^ k$ and $\mathrm dV=\mu $, take $p_\alpha =\pi _ Y^*(q_\alpha ^{1/N})$ with $q_\alpha $ from lemma 15.30.1 . Then $p_\alpha \in \mathcal D_ H^0$ but $p_\alpha \notin L^ r(\mathrm dV)$ for every $r>N$. Moreover, \[  \rho _ H\bigl (p_\alpha \mathbf1_{\{ p_\alpha >K\} }\bigr ) \asymp (\log K)^{-k(1-\alpha )/N}\qquad (K\to +\infty ).  \] Indeed, the radial estimate of that lemma gives $q_\alpha \asymp r^{-k}(1-\log r)^{-1-k(1-\alpha )}$. With $L=1-\log r$, the density level set $\{ q_\alpha >K^ N\} $ lies between two sets $\{ L>c\log K\} $ for fixed positive constants $c$, once $K$ is large. Integrating the radial density $L^{-1-k(1-\alpha )}\, \mathrm dL$ and taking its $N$th root gives the claimed tail. The integrability exclusion follows from $q_\alpha \notin L^ s$ for $s>1$. These roots enlarge the examples in $\mathcal D_ H^0$ beyond the subcritical $L^ r$ classes. They give neither $\mathcal D_ H^0=\mathcal D_ H$ nor a general criterion for an exact equation at zero lower mass.

title: 15.33 Power capacity bounds and threshold equations

section: 15.33 Power capacity bounds and threshold equations
text: In this section, $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 3$, with a Hermitian form $h$ and a smooth positive probability volume $\mathrm dV$. The root-tail condition of proposition 15.32.9 controls the scalar threshold. A power bound for one density's measure supplies the missing control of its approximating potentials: the capacity estimates give a common bound, and stability against the solution measure gives uniform convergence. Theorem 15.33.1 . 35816840F731 Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm dV)$ have positive integral. Suppose that $A,\alpha >0$ satisfy 7DAF690D3482 15.33.2 \begin{equation}  \int _ Ef\, \mathrm dV\leq A\operatorname {Cap}_ h(E)^{1+\alpha } \qquad (E\subset X\text{ Borel}). \end{equation} There is $C>0$, depending only on $(X,h),A,\alpha $, such that every measurable $0\leq g\leq f$ with positive integral satisfies E5CF15D0251A 15.33.3 \begin{equation}  b_ h(g)\geq C\left(\int _ Xg\, \mathrm dV\right)^{-\alpha /(1+\alpha )}, \qquad \rho _ h(g^{1/n})\leq C^{-1/n} \left(\int _ Xg\, \mathrm dV\right)^{\alpha /(n(1+\alpha ))}. \end{equation} In particular, $f^{1/n}\in \mathcal D_ h^0$. There is $\phi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)\cap C(X)$, with $\sup _ X\phi =0$, such that 1A3F6C7B811B 15.33.4 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{MA}_ h(\phi )=b_ h(f)f\, \mathrm dV. \end{equation} The coefficient $b_ h(f)$ and the mass of this measure are finite and strictly positive. Proof. Step 1: the coefficient and root tails. Put $g_ j=\min (g,j)$ and let $\phi _ j$ be normalized continuous solutions of \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(\phi _ j)=c_ jg_ j\, \mathrm dV, \qquad c_ j=c_ h(g_ j),\qquad \sup _ X\phi _ j=0,  \] given by theorem 14.19.2 . The definition ( 15.28.1 ) gives $c_ j\downarrow b_ h(g)$. Their measures satisfy a power capacity bound with constant $c_ jA$. Take competitor zero, $H=1$ and $\varepsilon =1/2$ in lemma 14.19.16 , lemma 14.19.14 . Choose $D>0$ fixed with $2D<\delta _{1/2}$ and put $U_ D=\{ \phi _ j<\inf _ X\phi _ j+D\} $. These estimates give \[  D\leq C_\alpha (C_1c_ jA)^{1/n} \operatorname {Cap}_ h(U_ D)^{\alpha /n}, \qquad D^ n\operatorname {Cap}_ h(U_ D) \leq C_1c_ j\int _ Xg_ j\, \mathrm dV.  \] Combining them yields \[  c_ j^{1+\alpha }\left(\int _ Xg_ j\, \mathrm dV\right)^\alpha \geq c>0.  \] Taking the limit proves the lower bound for $b_ h(g)$. The identity ( 15.29.2 ), with its full family of Gauduchon tests, gives the root estimate. Apply it to $g=f\mathbf1_{\{ f>K^ n\} }$ whenever this density is nonzero. Its mass tends to zero; the zero density has root norm zero. Thus the tails of $f^{1/n}$ tend to zero in both $L^ n$ and $\rho _ h$, and proposition 15.32.9 gives $f^{1/n}\in \mathcal D_ h^0$. Step 2: uniform convergence of a subsequence. Now use $f_ j=\min (f,j)$, $c_ j=c_ h(f_ j)$ and normalized continuous solutions $\phi _ j$. Step 1 gives $b_ h(f)>0$, while $c_ j\leq c_1<\infty $. Hence \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(\phi _ j)(E) \leq Ac_1\operatorname {Cap}_ h(E)^{1+\alpha }.  \] The first part of the proof of proposition 14.19.23 , using the capacity tail estimate, gives one $M\geq 1$ with $-M\leq \phi _ j\leq 0$ for all $j$. By theorem 5.25.2 , extract a subsequence converging in $L^1(\mathrm dV)$ and almost everywhere. section: 15.33 Power capacity bounds and threshold equations
text: The power capacity condition can hold for a density outside every $L^ p$ class with $p>1$. A bounded continuous potential with logarithmic modulus at one point gives such a datum on each fixed Hermitian background. Theorem 15.33.6 . B37DD22EFF75 In the setting of theorem 15.33.1 , fix $\alpha >0$. There is $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)\cap C(X)$ with $h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq h/2$ whose measure $\mathrm{MA}_ h(u)=f\, \mathrm dV$ satisfies \[  f\in L^1(\mathrm dV),\qquad f\notin L^ p(\mathrm dV)\quad \text{for every }p>1.  \] For some $A>0$ it satisfies ( 15.33.2 ), and $b_ h(f)=1$. For all sufficiently large $K$, E4AFA559F42C 15.33.7 \begin{equation}  \rho _ h\bigl (f^{1/n}\mathbf1_{\{ f>K\} }\bigr ) \leq C(\log K)^{-\alpha }. \end{equation} Proof. Choose a holomorphic ball with coordinates centred at $x_0$ and $R=|z|<1$, and a smooth cutoff $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ supported in it and equal to one on a smaller ball. Put \[  q(s)=(1-s)^{-\alpha },\qquad s=\log R^2, \qquad \psi =\chi q(\log R^2)+1-\chi .  \] Set $\psi (x_0)=0$ and extend $\psi =1$ outside the ball. In the smaller ball, $q'=\alpha (1-s)^{-\alpha -1}>0$ and $q''=\alpha (\alpha +1)(1-s)^{-\alpha -2}>0$, so $\psi $ is plurisubharmonic there, including its continuous extension at $x_0$. The transition is smooth and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi \geq -K_0h$ globally for a fixed $K_0$. For sufficiently small $\delta >0$, the normalized potential $u=\delta \psi -\sup _ X\delta \psi $ satisfies $h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq h/2$. The bounded product gives zero mass to $x_0$. Indeed, after a smooth local correction, its expansion is dominated in total variation by a constant times the top product of a bounded plurisubharmonic function plus a strictly plurisubharmonic quadratic function. Rescaling this sum into $[0,1]$ bounds that top product by local capacity, and a pluripolar point has capacity zero. Off $x_0$ the potential is smooth. Thus the measure is absolutely continuous; write it as $f\, \mathrm dV$. The strict lower bound implies $f\geq c>0$ almost everywhere. In the smaller ball the tangential and radial eigenvalues of the Hessian of $q(\log R^2)$ are $q'/R^2$ and $q''/R^2$. In the operator convention of the book this gives F1C776CF9796 15.33.8 \begin{equation}  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n =\frac{\delta ^ nn!\alpha ^ n(\alpha +1)}{\pi ^ n} R^{-2n}(1-\log R^2)^{-n(\alpha +1)-1}\, \mathrm d\lambda , \end{equation} where $\mathrm d\lambda $ is Euclidean volume. Integration over the ball gives \[  \int _{B_ r}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n =\delta ^ n\alpha ^ n(1-\log r^2)^{-n(\alpha +1)}.  \] For $k<n$, the degree-$k$ mixed terms with the smooth positive form $h$ have density bounded by $CR^{-2k}(1-\log R^2)^{-k(\alpha +1)}$ and mass $O(r^2)$ on $B_ r$. The expansion has positive terms in this ball. Hence $f\in L^1$. For $p>1$, the pure top term gives a positive multiple of the divergent integral \[  \int _0^ r R^{2n(1-p)-1} (1-\log R^2)^{-p(n(\alpha +1)+1)}\, \mathrm dR  \] as a lower bound for $\int _{B_ r}f^ p\, \mathrm dV$, since smooth volume densities are comparable. Thus $f\notin L^ p$. For all sufficiently small $r$, F69DF10A862E 15.33.9 \begin{equation}  \int _{B_ r}f\, \mathrm dV \leq C\bigl [(1-\log r^2)^{-n(\alpha +1)}+r^2\bigr ], \qquad \mathop{\rm ess\, sup}_{X\setminus B_ r}f\leq Cr^{-2n}. \end{equation} By ( 5.29.3 ), \[  \mathrm dV(E)\leq C\exp \bigl (-a\operatorname {Cap}_ h(E)^{-1/n}\bigr ).  \] Let $s=\operatorname {Cap}_ h(E)>0$ be small and choose $r=\exp [-as^{-1/n}/(4n)]$. Splitting $E$ inside and outside $B_ r$ and applying ( 15.33.9 ), we obtain \[  \int _ Ef\, \mathrm dV \leq Cs^{1+\alpha } +C\exp [-as^{-1/n}/(2n)] +C\exp [-as^{-1/n}/2] \leq C's^{1+\alpha }.  \] For larger $s$ use the finite total mass; for $s=0$ the volume estimate gives $\mathrm dV(E)=0$. This proves ( 15.33.2 ) for every Borel set. By theorem 15.33.1 , there is a normalized continuous $\phi $ with $\mathrm{MA}_ h(\phi )=b_ h(f)f\, \mathrm dV$. The explicit potential $u$ is a subsolution with coefficient one, so theorem 15.28.4 gives $b_ h(f)\geq 1$. Suppose $b_ h(f)>1$, and choose $0<\varepsilon <1$ with $(1-\varepsilon )^ nb_ h(f)>1$. The set $U_ s$ is open and nonempty, and $f\geq c>0$ almost everywhere, so its $f\, \mathrm dV$ measure is positive. This contradiction proves $b_ h(f)=1$. Finally take $r_ K=K^{-1/(4n)}$. The outside bound in ( 15.33.9 ) gives $f\leq CK^{1/2}<K$ almost everywhere on $X\setminus B_{r_ K}$ for large $K$. Its root-tail estimate follows from the capacity bound despite the failure of higher $L^ p$ integrability. The construction applies to each fixed background, including one with $v_-(h)=0$.

title: 15.34 Limits of exponential equations
text: In this section $\theta $ is an arbitrary smooth real $(1,1)$-form and $\mu $ a finite non-pluripolar measure. We consider solutions $u_\lambda \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ of \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (u_\lambda )=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }\mu \qquad (\lambda >0).  \] As $\lambda \downarrow 0$, one expects suitably normalized solutions to converge to a solution of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)=c\mu $ with a scalar $c>0$. For an $L^ p$ density with $p>1$ and a Hermitian background, the continuous solutions satisfy $\lambda u_\lambda \to \log c$ uniformly (proposition 14.19.34 ). For solutions in a fixed unbounded ordinary type, no such uniform convergence is possible: by proposition 5.44.4 , the $L^\infty $ distance from $\lambda u_\lambda $ to every finite constant is infinite for each $\lambda >0$. The limit must instead be formulated through normalized potentials and their measures. Write \[  v_\lambda =u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda ,\qquad c_\lambda =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda \sup _ Xu_\lambda },  \] so that $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_\lambda )=c_\lambda \mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda }\mu $. By lemma 5.44.5 , $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda }\to 1$ in $L^1(\mu )$ as $\lambda \downarrow 0$; hence, if $c_\lambda \to c<+\infty $, the right-hand sides converge in total variation to $c\mu $. If $\mu =f\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $f\in L^ p$ for some $p>1$, lemma 5.44.5 gives an error linear in $\lambda $. To identify the Monge–Ampère measure of an $L^1$ limit of the $v_\lambda $, one needs in addition a continuity theorem for the Monge–Ampère operator. For potentials of a fixed ordinary type, corollary 15.9.4 identifies the limiting measure under a common barrier and a domination hypothesis. In a relative envelope class, theorem 15.37.19 instead constructs a common lower envelope under positive lower mass: for a semipositive big $\theta $ and a reference satisfying ( 16.28.67 ), an $L^1$-convergent sequence in the class whose measures are dominated by one finite non-pluripolar measure converges in capacity, and its measures converge weakly. That argument, with its mass hypothesis, is developed in section 15.37 .

title: 15.34.1 A positive limiting exponent
text: When the exponents converge to a positive limit, the factor $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}$ makes the Monge–Ampère mass of deep sublevels uniformly small. If the potentials converge in capacity, the tail criterion of theorem 13.15.13 then identifies the limit of their Monge–Ampère measures, and convergence of the right-hand sides identifies the equation. Theorem 15.34.2 . 9F0AB366D34B Let $\theta $ be any smooth real $(1,1)$-form and $\mu $ a finite non-pluripolar measure. Suppose $f_ j\geq 0$, $f_ j\to f$ in $L^1(\mu )$, and $\lambda _ j>0$ with $\lambda _ j\to \lambda >0$. Let $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ be nonpositive, suppose $u_ j\to u$ in capacity, and assume \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j) =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ j u_ j}f_ j\, \mu .  \] Then $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ is finite and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mu .  \] Moreover, $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j)\rightharpoonup \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ weakly, and the right-hand sides converge in total variation. Proof. Discarding finitely many indices, we may assume that $\lambda _ j\geq \lambda /2$. The measures $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j)$ have masses at most $\| f_ j\| _{L^1(\mu )}$, which are uniformly bounded, and since $u_ j\leq 0$, their deep sublevels satisfy \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j)(\{ u_ j<-T\} ) \leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda T/2}\| f_ j\| _{L^1(\mu )}.  \] The tail criterion theorem 13.15.13 , which holds for an arbitrary smooth background by theorem 13.15.23 , therefore shows that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ is finite and that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j)\rightharpoonup \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$. It remains to identify this limit with $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mu $. By lemma 5.29.18 , $u_ j\to u$ in $\mu $-measure. Since $t\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}$ is $\lambda $-Lipschitz for $t\leq 0$, the functions $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}$, which are bounded by one, converge in $\mu $-measure to $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}$. The change of exponent is uniform for nonpositive arguments, because the mean value theorem gives \[  \sup _{t\leq 0}|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ jt}-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}| \leq |\lambda _ j-\lambda | \sup _{s\geq 0}s \mathrm{e}^{-(\lambda /2)s}\longrightarrow 0.  \] Thus $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ j u_ j}\to \mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}$ in $\mu $-measure, and hence in $f\mu $-measure, since the finite measure $f\mu $ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu $. As these functions are bounded by one, the convergence also holds in $L^1(f\mu )$. Therefore \[  \begin{split}  \int _ X|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ j u_ j}f_ j-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f|\, \mathrm{d}\mu & \leq \| f_ j-f\| _{L^1(\mu )}\\ & \quad +\int _ X|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ j u_ j}-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}|f\, \mathrm{d}\mu \longrightarrow 0. \end{split}  \] This proves the total-variation convergence of the right-hand sides, and comparing the two limits gives the equation for $u$. $\square$ Additive normalizations of the potentials can be absorbed into the densities: translating each $u_ j$ by a constant multiplies $f_ j$ by an exponential factor, and the theorem applies as long as the modified densities still converge in $L^1(\mu )$. Convergence in capacity is a hypothesis; the theorem says nothing about sequences that converge only in $L^1$, and it does not keep the limit in a prescribed envelope class. The proof also shows where the difficulty lies as $\lambda _ j\downarrow 0$: the tail bound $\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda _ jT}\| f_ j\| _{L^1(\mu )}$ no longer tends to zero uniformly in $j$ as $T\to \infty $. A zero-exponent limit therefore needs another source of uniform tail control, such as the integrability condition of corollary 13.15.14 ; a uniform bound on the total masses does not by itself control these tails.

title: Theorem 15.34.2
text: Theorem 15.34.2 . 9F0AB366D34B Let $\theta $ be any smooth real $(1,1)$-form and $\mu $ a finite non-pluripolar measure. Suppose $f_ j\geq 0$, $f_ j\to f$ in $L^1(\mu )$, and $\lambda _ j>0$ with $\lambda _ j\to \lambda >0$. Let $u_ j,u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ be nonpositive, suppose $u_ j\to u$ in capacity, and assume \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j) =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ j u_ j}f_ j\, \mu .  \] Then $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ is finite and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mu .  \] Moreover, $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j)\rightharpoonup \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ weakly, and the right-hand sides converge in total variation. Proof. Discarding finitely many indices, we may assume that $\lambda _ j\geq \lambda /2$. The measures $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j)$ have masses at most $\| f_ j\| _{L^1(\mu )}$, which are uniformly bounded, and since $u_ j\leq 0$, their deep sublevels satisfy \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j)(\{ u_ j<-T\} ) \leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda T/2}\| f_ j\| _{L^1(\mu )}.  \] The tail criterion theorem 13.15.13 , which holds for an arbitrary smooth background by theorem 13.15.23 , therefore shows that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ is finite and that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u_ j)\rightharpoonup \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$. It remains to identify this limit with $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mu $. By lemma 5.29.18 , $u_ j\to u$ in $\mu $-measure. Since $t\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}$ is $\lambda $-Lipschitz for $t\leq 0$, the functions $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ j}$, which are bounded by one, converge in $\mu $-measure to $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}$. The change of exponent is uniform for nonpositive arguments, because the mean value theorem gives \[  \sup _{t\leq 0}|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ jt}-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}| \leq |\lambda _ j-\lambda | \sup _{s\geq 0}s \mathrm{e}^{-(\lambda /2)s}\longrightarrow 0.  \] Thus $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ j u_ j}\to \mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}$ in $\mu $-measure, and hence in $f\mu $-measure, since the finite measure $f\mu $ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu $. As these functions are bounded by one, the convergence also holds in $L^1(f\mu )$. Therefore \[  \begin{split}  \int _ X|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ j u_ j}f_ j-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f|\, \mathrm{d}\mu & \leq \| f_ j-f\| _{L^1(\mu )}\\ & \quad +\int _ X|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ j u_ j}-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}|f\, \mathrm{d}\mu \longrightarrow 0. \end{split}  \] This proves the total-variation convergence of the right-hand sides, and comparing the two limits gives the equation for $u$. $\square$

section: 15.35 Exponential equations for an individual density
text: We return to the Hermitian background $h$ and a fixed nonzero density $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, and consider, for $\lambda >0$, the exponential equation A708922257FB 15.35.1 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h). \end{equation} A solution is a function $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ satisfying ( 15.35.1 ), and an exponential subsolution at exponent $\lambda $ is a function $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda s}f\, \mathrm{d}V$. For the truncations $f_ k=\min (f,k)$, theorem 14.19.3 gives continuous solutions $u_ k$ of the truncated equations, and these decrease as $k$ increases. Strict domination shows that every exponential subsolution is a common lower bound for the $u_ k$. Hence, as soon as one subsolution exists, the decreasing limit is not identically $-\infty $, and theorem 15.34.2 shows that it solves ( 15.35.1 ); it is the greatest subsolution. A positive threshold $b_ h(f)$ provides exponential subsolutions for every exponent, and the normalized greatest solutions then recover $b_ h(f)$ as $\lambda \downarrow 0$. Theorem 15.35.2 . 9016C2906071 Fix $\lambda >0$, and suppose that ( 15.35.1 ) has an exponential subsolution $s\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$. For $k\geq 1$, let $u_ k$ be the continuous solution of \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(u_ k)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ k}f_ k\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad f_ k=\min (f,k),  \] given by theorem 14.19.3 . Then $u_ k$ decreases to a solution $u_\lambda $ of ( 15.35.1 ), and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u_\lambda )$ has finite mass. Moreover, $u_\lambda $ is the greatest exponential subsolution: every exponential subsolution $v$ at exponent $\lambda $ satisfies $v\leq u_\lambda $. In particular, $u_\lambda $ is the greatest solution of ( 15.35.1 ). Proof. Since $f_ k\leq f_{k+1}$, lemma 14.19.28 gives $u_{k+1}\leq u_ k$. We first show that every exponential subsolution $v$ lies below each $u_ k$. Let $t>0$. On the set $\{ u_ k<v-t\} $, \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(u_ k)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_ k}f_ k\, \mathrm{d}V \leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v}f\, \mathrm{d}V \leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v-t).  \] Since $u_ k$ is bounded, $P_{h/2}(u_ k)\geq \inf _ Xu_ k$ is not identically $-\infty $, and $v-t\preceq u_ k$. Strict domination, theorem 15.2.2 , therefore gives $u_ k\geq v-t$. Letting $t\downarrow 0$ gives $u_ k\geq v$. In particular $s\leq u_ k\leq u_1$ for every $k$, so the decreasing limit $u_\lambda \geq s$ is not identically $-\infty $ and belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$. By lemma 5.29.19 , $u_ k\to u_\lambda $ in capacity. Choose a constant $A\geq \sup _ Xu_1$. The nonpositive functions $u_ k-A$ satisfy \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u_ k-A)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda (u_ k-A)}\, \mathrm{e}^{\lambda A}f_ k\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] and $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda A}f_ k\to \mathrm{e}^{\lambda A}f$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$. Theorem 15.34.2 , applied with $\mu =\mathrm{d}V$ and constant exponents, shows that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u_\lambda )$ is finite and that $u_\lambda $ solves ( 15.35.1 ). Finally, every exponential subsolution lies below all $u_ k$, hence below $u_\lambda $, which is itself a subsolution. $\square$ Being the greatest subsolution, $u_\lambda $ does not depend on the approximation used to construct it. The equation may have other, smaller solutions with different singularities. If $f\in L^ p$ for some $p>1$, the continuous solution of theorem 14.19.3 is a subsolution and therefore lies below $u_\lambda $. Thus $u_\lambda $ is bounded, and bounded exponential comparison (corollary 14.19.12 ) shows that it coincides with the continuous solution. Corollary 15.35.3 . B2672237F244 Suppose $b=b_ h(f)>0$. Then ( 15.35.1 ) has a greatest solution $u_\lambda $ for every $\lambda >0$. If $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ satisfies $\sup _ Xv=0$ and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V$, then \[  u_\lambda \geq v+\lambda ^{-1}\log b.  \] Put \[  M_\lambda =\sup _ Xu_\lambda ,\qquad v_\lambda =u_\lambda -M_\lambda ,\qquad c_\lambda =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda M_\lambda }.  \] Then, as $\lambda \downarrow 0$, \[  c_\lambda \longrightarrow b_ h(f),\qquad \mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\longrightarrow b_ h(f)f \quad \text{in }L^1(\mathrm{d}V).  \] Proof. By theorem 15.28.4 , a function $v$ as in the statement exists. Since $v\leq 0$, the function $s=v+\lambda ^{-1}\log b$ satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V \geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda s}f\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] so it is an exponential subsolution. Theorem 15.35.2 gives the greatest solution $u_\lambda $ and the bound $u_\lambda \geq s$; in particular, $c_\lambda \geq b$. Set $g_\lambda =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda }f$. By lemma 5.44.5 , applied to the finite measure $f\, \mathrm{d}V$, we have $g_\lambda \to f$ in $L^1$ as $\lambda \downarrow 0$. Each $g_\lambda $ is nonzero, since $v_\lambda $ is finite almost everywhere. The equation for $u_\lambda $ reads $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v_\lambda )=c_\lambda g_\lambda \, \mathrm{d}V$, so theorem 15.28.4 , applied to the density $g_\lambda $, gives \[  c_\lambda \leq b_ h(g_\lambda ).  \] The upper semicontinuity of the threshold (theorem 15.32.1 ) therefore gives \[  b\leq \liminf _{\lambda \downarrow 0}c_\lambda \leq \limsup _{\lambda \downarrow 0}c_\lambda \leq b_ h(f)=b.  \] This proves $c_\lambda \to b$. Since $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f=c_\lambda g_\lambda $ and $g_\lambda \to f$ in $L^1$, it also proves $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\to bf$ in $L^1$. $\square$ Since $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v_\lambda )=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V$, the Monge–Ampère measures of the normalized greatest solutions converge in total variation to $b_ h(f)f\, \mathrm{d}V$. This answers the questions about the scalar and the measure raised in section 15.34 ; the potentials $v_\lambda $ themselves are harder to control. Under positive lower mass, corollary 15.37.32 shows that every $L^1$-convergent sequence $v_{\lambda _ j}$ with $\lambda _ j\downarrow 0$ converges in capacity to a solution of $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v)=b_ h(f)f\, \mathrm{d}V$. For $L^ p$ data with $p>1$, proposition 15.20.1 gives uniform precompactness. In both cases, convergence of the whole family $(v_\lambda )$ requires that all its cluster limits coincide. This holds when the dual problem for $f^{1/n}$ over Gauduchon currents, studied in section 12.10 , has a smooth strictly positive maximizer: the whole family then converges uniformly (corollary 12.10.13 ). If the maximizer is smooth and semipositive, and strictly positive outside a proper analytic set, proposition 12.10.20 gives $L^1$ convergence of the whole family and a fixed lower barrier, and corollary 12.10.31 strengthens this to uniform convergence for $L^ p$ data with $p>1$. For a general positive threshold, the corollary gives the lower bound \[  v_\lambda \geq v-\lambda ^{-1}\log (c_\lambda /b_ h(f))  \] for every normalized threshold subsolution $v$. The next subsection estimates the scalar error $\log (c_\lambda /b_ h(f))$ when $f^{1/n}$ can be approximated by bounded functions in the norm of $\mathcal D_ h$. When $b_ h(f)=0$, theorem 15.35.2 still applies whenever an exponential subsolution exists; examples are constructed in 15.35.7 .

text: Suppose that $f^{1/n}$ belongs to the space $\mathcal D_ h^0$ of 15.32.7 . The uniform tail condition of proposition 15.32.9 then gives a rate for the convergence $c_\lambda \to b_ h(f)$ in corollary 15.35.3 . Split the root $p=f^{1/n}$ at a height $K$. On $\{ p\leq K\} $, the error $p(1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v/n})$ of the damped root has norm $O(K\lambda )$ in $\mathcal D_ h$, uniformly over normalized potentials $v$, while on $\{ p>K\} $ it is bounded by the tail of $p$, which is small in that norm. Optimizing over $K$ gives a modulus valid for every normalized potential. Proposition 15.35.5 . AC5E6031A12C Let $0\leq p\in \mathcal D_ h^0$ be nonzero, and put $f=p^ n$, $R=\rho _ h(p)$ and $b=R^{-n}=b_ h(f)$. There is a constant $C_ h$, depending only on $h$ and $\mathrm{d}V$, such that the function \[  \eta _ p(\lambda )=\inf _{K>0} \left(\| p\mathbf1_{\{ p>K\} }\| _{\mathcal D_ h}+C_ hK\lambda \right)  \] tends to zero as $\lambda \downarrow 0$ and satisfies 747F5A0D1221 15.35.6 \begin{equation}  \big \| p(1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v/n})\big \| _{\mathcal D_ h} \leq \eta _ p(\lambda ) \qquad \bigl (v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h),\  \sup _ Xv=0\bigr ). \end{equation} Let $u_\lambda $, $v_\lambda $ and $c_\lambda $ be the greatest exponential solutions and their normalizations from corollary 15.35.3 . If $\eta _ p(\lambda )<R$, then \[  b\leq c_\lambda \leq \bigl (R-\eta _ p(\lambda )\bigr )^{-n}  \] and \begin{align*}  \big \| \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v_\lambda ) -bf\, \mathrm{d}V\big \| _{\mathrm{TV}} & \leq (c_\lambda -b)\| p\| _{L^ n}^{n} +nb\| p\| _{L^ n}^{n-1}\eta _ p(\lambda ). \end{align*} If $p\in L^ r$ for some finite $r>n$, the same bounds hold with $\eta _ p(\lambda )$ replaced by $C_{h,r}\| p\| _{L^ r}\lambda $, where $C_{h,r}$ depends only on $h$, $\mathrm{d}V$ and $r$. In particular, for each such $p$ the scalar and total-variation errors are $O(\lambda )$. Proof. By lemma 5.26.2 , normalized $h$-plurisubharmonic functions are uniformly bounded in every $L^ s$ with $s<+\infty $. By ( 15.32.8 ) with $r=2n$, their norms $\| v\| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ are therefore uniformly bounded; let $C_ h$ be $1/n$ times this bound. Let $v$ be normalized and $K>0$. On $\{ p\leq K\} $ we have \[  0\leq p(1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v/n}) \leq K\lambda (-v)/n,  \] since $1-\mathrm{e}^{-x}\leq x$ for $x\geq 0$, while on $\{ p>K\} $ we use the bound $p(1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v/n})\leq p$. The monotonicity of $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ and the triangle inequality give \[  \big \| p(1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v/n})\big \| _{\mathcal D_ h} \leq \| p\mathbf1_{\{ p>K\} }\| _{\mathcal D_ h}+C_ hK\lambda ,  \] and taking the infimum over $K$ proves ( 15.35.6 ). By proposition 15.32.9 , and since the $L^ n$ tails of $p$ tend to zero, $\| p\mathbf1_{\{ p>K\} }\| _{\mathcal D_ h}\to 0$ as $K\to \infty $. Choosing $K$ first and then letting $\lambda \downarrow 0$ shows that $\eta _ p(\lambda )\to 0$. Now set $q_\lambda =p\, \mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda /n}$, so that $q_\lambda ^ n=g_\lambda =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda }f$, with $g_\lambda $ as in the proof of corollary 15.35.3 . Since $0\leq q_\lambda \leq p$ and $\rho _ h(p-q_\lambda )\leq \eta _ p(\lambda )$ by ( 15.35.6 ), the triangle inequality and monotonicity give \[  R-\eta _ p(\lambda )\leq \rho _ h(q_\lambda )\leq R.  \] The same proof gives $b\leq c_\lambda \leq b_ h(g_\lambda )=\rho _ h(q_\lambda )^{-n}$, which yields the scalar bound. For the measures, the factorization of $p^ n-q_\lambda ^ n$ gives $0\leq p^ n-q_\lambda ^ n\leq np^{n-1}(p-q_\lambda )$, and Hölder's inequality implies \[  \| f-g_\lambda \| _{L^1} \leq n\| p\| _{L^ n}^{n-1}\| p-q_\lambda \| _{L^ n} \leq n\| p\| _{L^ n}^{n-1}\eta _ p(\lambda ).  \] Since $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v_\lambda )=c_\lambda g_\lambda \, \mathrm{d}V$, the identity $c_\lambda g_\lambda -bf=(c_\lambda -b)g_\lambda -b(f-g_\lambda )$, together with $\| g_\lambda \| _{L^1}\leq \| f\| _{L^1}=\| p\| _{L^ n}^ n$, proves the total-variation bound. Finally, suppose $p\in L^ r$ with $n<r<+\infty $, and choose $n<s<r$. By ( 15.32.8 ) with exponent $s$, and since $\| \cdot \| _{L^ n}\leq \| \cdot \| _{L^ s}$, we have $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}\leq (1+C_ s)\| \cdot \| _{L^ s}$. Hölder's inequality and lemma 5.26.2 then give, for every normalized $v$, \[  \| p(-v)\| _{\mathcal D_ h} \leq (1+C_ s)\| p(-v)\| _{L^ s} \leq (1+C_ s)\| p\| _{L^ r}\| v\| _{L^{rs/(r-s)}} \leq nC_{h,r}\| p\| _{L^ r}.  \] Since $0\leq 1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v/n}\leq \lambda (-v)/n$, the left side of ( 15.35.6 ) is therefore at most $C_{h,r}\| p\| _{L^ r}\lambda $, and the two estimates above can be repeated with this bound in place of $\eta _ p(\lambda )$. For $\lambda $ so small that $C_{h,r}\| p\| _{L^ r}\lambda \leq R/2$, the function $t\mapsto (R-t)^{-n}$ has bounded derivative on $[0,R/2]$, so the scalar error $c_\lambda -b$, and hence the total-variation error, is $O(\lambda )$. $\square$ For a general $p\in \mathcal D_ h^0$ the modulus $\eta _ p(\lambda )$ tends to zero, but we do not know whether it is $O(\lambda )$. Combined with the lower bound $v_\lambda \geq v-\lambda ^{-1}\log (c_\lambda /b)$ for normalized threshold subsolutions $v$, the proposition gives \[  0\leq \lambda ^{-1}\log (c_\lambda /b) \leq -\frac n\lambda \log \bigl (1-\eta _ p(\lambda )/R\bigr ),  \] which stays bounded as $\lambda \downarrow 0$ when $\eta _ p(\lambda )=O(\lambda )$, in particular for $p\in L^ r$ with $r>n$; root tails alone do not give such a bound. Even when a uniform lower barrier for $v_\lambda $ is available, passing to the limit in capacity requires the singularity-type or lower-mass hypotheses of a continuity theorem. The proposition estimates only scalars and measures; when the lower mass vanishes, it does not give an exact equation at the threshold.
