By lemma 5.26.2 , normalized $h$-plurisubharmonic functions are uniformly bounded in every $L^ s$ with $s<+\infty $. By ( 15.32.8 ) with $r=2n$, their norms $\| v\| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ are therefore uniformly bounded; let $C_ h$ be $1/n$ times this bound. Let $v$ be normalized and $K>0$. On $\{ p\leq K\} $ we have \[  0\leq p(1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v/n}) \leq K\lambda (-v)/n,  \] since $1-\mathrm{e}^{-x}\leq x$ for $x\geq 0$, while on $\{ p>K\} $ we use the bound $p(1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v/n})\leq p$. The monotonicity of $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}$ and the triangle inequality give \[  \big \| p(1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v/n})\big \| _{\mathcal D_ h} \leq \| p\mathbf1_{\{ p>K\} }\| _{\mathcal D_ h}+C_ hK\lambda ,  \] and taking the infimum over $K$ proves ( 15.35.6 ). By proposition 15.32.9 , and since the $L^ n$ tails of $p$ tend to zero, $\| p\mathbf1_{\{ p>K\} }\| _{\mathcal D_ h}\to 0$ as $K\to \infty $. Choosing $K$ first and then letting $\lambda \downarrow 0$ shows that $\eta _ p(\lambda )\to 0$. Now set $q_\lambda =p\, \mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda /n}$, so that $q_\lambda ^ n=g_\lambda =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda }f$, with $g_\lambda $ as in the proof of corollary 15.35.3 . Since $0\leq q_\lambda \leq p$ and $\rho _ h(p-q_\lambda )\leq \eta _ p(\lambda )$ by ( 15.35.6 ), the triangle inequality and monotonicity give \[  R-\eta _ p(\lambda )\leq \rho _ h(q_\lambda )\leq R.  \] The same proof gives $b\leq c_\lambda \leq b_ h(g_\lambda )=\rho _ h(q_\lambda )^{-n}$, which yields the scalar bound. For the measures, the factorization of $p^ n-q_\lambda ^ n$ gives $0\leq p^ n-q_\lambda ^ n\leq np^{n-1}(p-q_\lambda )$, and Hölder's inequality implies \[  \| f-g_\lambda \| _{L^1} \leq n\| p\| _{L^ n}^{n-1}\| p-q_\lambda \| _{L^ n} \leq n\| p\| _{L^ n}^{n-1}\eta _ p(\lambda ).  \] Since $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v_\lambda )=c_\lambda g_\lambda \, \mathrm{d}V$, the identity $c_\lambda g_\lambda -bf=(c_\lambda -b)g_\lambda -b(f-g_\lambda )$, together with $\| g_\lambda \| _{L^1}\leq \| f\| _{L^1}=\| p\| _{L^ n}^ n$, proves the total-variation bound. Finally, suppose $p\in L^ r$ with $n<r<+\infty $, and choose $n<s<r$. By ( 15.32.8 ) with exponent $s$, and since $\| \cdot \| _{L^ n}\leq \| \cdot \| _{L^ s}$, we have $\| \cdot \| _{\mathcal D_ h}\leq (1+C_ s)\| \cdot \| _{L^ s}$. Hölder's inequality and lemma 5.26.2 then give, for every normalized $v$, \[  \| p(-v)\| _{\mathcal D_ h} \leq (1+C_ s)\| p(-v)\| _{L^ s} \leq (1+C_ s)\| p\| _{L^ r}\| v\| _{L^{rs/(r-s)}} \leq nC_{h,r}\| p\| _{L^ r}.  \] Since $0\leq 1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v/n}\leq \lambda (-v)/n$, the left side of ( 15.35.6 ) is therefore at most $C_{h,r}\| p\| _{L^ r}\lambda $, and the two estimates above can be repeated with this bound in place of $\eta _ p(\lambda )$. For $\lambda $ so small that $C_{h,r}\| p\| _{L^ r}\lambda \leq R/2$, the function $t\mapsto (R-t)^{-n}$ has bounded derivative on $[0,R/2]$, so the scalar error $c_\lambda -b$, and hence the total-variation error, is $O(\lambda )$. $\square$

title: 15.35.7 Exponential equations at zero threshold
section: 15.35 Exponential equations for an individual density
text: When $b_ h(f)=0$, no positive multiple of $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ is dominated by a Monge–Ampère measure. An exponential subsolution $s$ only needs $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s)\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda s}f\, \mathrm{d}V$, however, and the factor $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda s}$ is small where $s$ is very negative. A density concentrating near the pole of a singular potential can therefore admit exponential subsolutions although its threshold vanishes. We construct such densities on the products of section 15.30 . We keep the notation of that section: $X=X_0\times Y$ with $Y=\mathbb P^ k$, the background $H=h_0+\kappa $, the constants $N$, $C$ and $V_0$, the probability volume form $\mu =V_0^{-1}h_0^ m\wedge \kappa ^ k$ with density $R=\mu /\mathrm{d}V$, and the potential $u_\alpha $ with density $q_\alpha $ from lemma 15.30.1 , for a fixed $0<\alpha <1$. On $Y\setminus \{ o\} $ put $L=1-\psi \geq 1$, so that $u_\alpha =1-L^\alpha $, and $t=\mathrm e^{1-L}$. As functions of $L$, define \[  a=\alpha L^{\alpha -1},\qquad Q=t+(1-t)a,\qquad D=t(1-a)+(1-t)\alpha (1-\alpha )L^{\alpha -2},  \] \[  W=kQ^{k-1}D,\qquad B_\tau =q_\alpha \mathrm e^{\tau (L^\alpha -1)}\quad (\tau >0),\qquad b_0=(1-\alpha )^ k.  \] Here $Q$ is the function $Q(r)$ of lemma 15.30.1 , written in terms of $L$, and $D=-\mathrm{d}Q/\mathrm{d}L$. The weight $B_\tau $ is chosen so that $\mathrm e^{\tau u_\alpha }B_\tau =q_\alpha $ off $o$. Lemma 15.35.8 . C9E4D8D9901A As functions of $L$, \[  q_\alpha =Q^{k-1}D\, \mathrm e^{k(L-1)},\qquad q_\alpha \geq b_0,  \] and $W(L)\sim k\alpha ^ k(1-\alpha )L^{-1-k(1-\alpha )}$ as $L\to +\infty $. For every $\tau >0$, $\mathrm e^{\tau (L^\alpha -1)}W(L)\to +\infty $ as $L\to +\infty $. In particular, $B_\tau \kappa ^ k$ has infinite mass on every punctured neighborhood of $o$. Proof. In the notation of the proof of lemma 15.30.1 , $t=r/(1+r)$ and $s(r)=L$. Since the mass of $q_\alpha \kappa ^ k$ on $\{ r_1<r<r_2\} $ is $Q(r_2)^ k-Q(r_1)^ k$, this measure has radial distribution $-\mathrm{d}(Q^ k)/\mathrm{d}L=W(L)\, \mathrm{d}L$. The Fubini–Study measure $\kappa ^ k$ corresponds to $Q=t$, so its radial distribution is $k\mathrm e^{-k(L-1)}\mathrm{d}L$. Both measures are invariant under the unitary group of the chart, so $q_\alpha $ is the ratio of the two distributions, which is the stated formula. The lower bound $q_\alpha \geq b_0$ follows from $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\alpha \geq (1-\alpha )\kappa $ off $o$. As $L\to +\infty $, $t$ tends to zero exponentially, so $Q\sim \alpha L^{\alpha -1}$ and $D\sim \alpha (1-\alpha )L^{\alpha -2}$; this gives the asymptotics of $W$. Consequently, \[  \log \bigl (\mathrm e^{\tau (L^\alpha -1)}W(L)\bigr )=\tau L^\alpha -[1+k(1-\alpha )]\log L+O(1)\longrightarrow +\infty ,  \] and the mass of $B_\tau \kappa ^ k$ on $\{ L>T\} $, which equals $\int _ T^\infty \mathrm e^{\tau (L^\alpha -1)}W(L)\, \mathrm{d}L$, is infinite for every $T$. $\square$ Theorem 15.35.9 . 8FF7FBD67552 Let $f\geq 0$ be a nonzero integrable function on $X$, and put $F=f/R$. If $\lambda >0$ and $F\leq AB_\lambda $ almost everywhere for a constant $A>0$, then \[  s_\lambda =u_\alpha +\lambda ^{-1}\log (CV_0/A)  \] is an exponential subsolution at exponent $\lambda $, of mass $CV_0$, and the equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ has a greatest solution, whose mass is finite and positive. Suppose that $F$ is locally essentially bounded on $X\setminus (X_0\times \{ o\} )$ and \[  \lim _{T\to +\infty }\operatorname *{ess\, sup}_{x\in X_0,\  L(y)>T} \frac{\log ^+(F(x,y)/q_\alpha (y))}{L(y)^\alpha }=0,  \] where $\log ^+r=\log \max (1,r)$ for $r\geq 0$. Then the hypothesis of (1), and hence its conclusion, holds for every $\lambda >0$. Proof. (1) By theorem 15.30.3 , $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u_\alpha )=CV_0q_\alpha \mu $. Off the pole fiber $X_0\times \{ o\} $ we have $\mathrm e^{\lambda u_\alpha }B_\lambda =q_\alpha $ and $f\, \mathrm{d}V=F\mu \leq AB_\lambda \mu $, hence \[  \mathrm e^{\lambda s_\lambda }f\, \mathrm dV \leq (CV_0/A)\mathrm e^{\lambda u_\alpha }AB_\lambda \mu =CV_0q_\alpha \mu =\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(s_\lambda ),  \] and both measures vanish on the pole fiber. Thus $s_\lambda $ is an exponential subsolution, and its mass is $CV_0$, since adding a constant does not change the Monge–Ampère measure. Theorem 15.35.2 now gives the greatest solution $u$ and the finiteness of its mass. The mass $\int _ X\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ is positive because $u$ is finite almost everywhere and $f$ has positive integral. (2) Fix $\lambda >0$. By hypothesis, there is $T$ such that $F/q_\alpha \leq \mathrm e^{(\lambda /2)L^\alpha }$ almost everywhere on $\{ L>T\} $. Since $\mathrm e^{(\lambda /2)L^\alpha }\leq \mathrm e^{\lambda }\mathrm e^{\lambda (L^\alpha -1)}$ for $L\geq 1$, we have $F\leq \mathrm e^{\lambda }B_\lambda $ there. On the complement $\{ L\leq T\} $, which is compact and disjoint from the pole fiber, $F$ is essentially bounded, while $B_\lambda \geq q_\alpha \geq b_0>0$. Increasing the constant, we obtain $F\leq AB_\lambda $ almost everywhere on $X$. $\square$ Theorem 15.35.10 . 092A98EE953D Let $F_ j$, $j\geq 1$, be smooth strictly positive probability densities on $X_0$ with respect to $\mathrm dV_0=V_0^{-1}h_0^ m$, whose normalization scalars on $X_0$, relative to $h_0$ and $\mathrm dV_0$, satisfy $c_{h_0}(F_ j)\leq 2^{-2j}/C$. There are smooth strictly positive probability densities $g_ j$ on $Y$ with respect to $\kappa ^ k$ such that the probability densities \[  f_ j=RF_ jg_ j,\qquad f=\sum _{j\geq 1}2^{-j}f_ j  \] on $X$ satisfy $c_ H(f_ j)\leq 2^{-2j}$ and $b_ H(f)=0$. The function $f$ is finite everywhere, smooth off the pole fiber $X_0\times \{ o\} $, has integral one and is bounded below by a positive constant. For every $\lambda >0$, the equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\, \mathrm{d}V$ has an exponential subsolution and a greatest solution, of finite mass, and every solution is unbounded. Proof. Put $w_ j=2^{-j}$ and $M_ j=\max _{X_0}F_ j$. Step 1: a smooth baseline. Fix $C^ j$ norms $\| \cdot \| _{C^ j}$ on $X_0$, computed in a fixed finite atlas, so that they increase with $j$. Choose $0<\varepsilon _ j\leq 1/2$ with \[  w_ j\varepsilon _ jM_ j\leq b_0 2^{-j-2},\qquad w_ j\varepsilon _ j\| F_ j\| _{C^ j}\leq 2^{-j}.  \] Then $E=\sum _ jw_ j\varepsilon _ jF_ j$ converges in every $C^ l$ norm, so $E$ is smooth on $X_0$, and $0<E\leq b_0/4$. Step 2: bumps escaping to the pole. Choose a smooth function $\chi :\mathbb R\to [0,1]$, supported in $[0,1]$, positive on $(0,1)$ and flat at $0$ and $1$. Starting with $T_0=0$, choose inductively $T_ j\geq 2$ with $T_ j>T_{j-1}+2$ and \[  Z_ j=\int _{T_ j}^{T_ j+1}\chi (L-T_ j) \mathrm e^{(L^\alpha -1)/j}W(L)\, \mathrm dL \geq 2w_ jM_ j.  \] This is possible because, by lemma 15.35.8 with $\tau =1/j$, the factor $\mathrm e^{(L^\alpha -1)/j}W(L)$ is uniformly large on sufficiently distant intervals. On the annulus $\{ T_ j\leq L\leq T_ j+1\} $ put $\beta _ j=\chi (L-T_ j)B_{1/j}/Z_ j$, extend $\beta _ j$ by zero, and set $g_ j=\varepsilon _ j+(1-\varepsilon _ j)\beta _ j$. Since $\chi $ is flat at the endpoints, $\beta _ j$ is smooth; it vanishes near $o$ and near the hyperplane $\{ L=1\} $. Its integral against $\kappa ^ k$ is one, so $g_ j$ is a smooth strictly positive probability density with respect to $\kappa ^ k$. Moreover, \[  w_ jM_ j(1-\varepsilon _ j)\beta _ j\leq B_{1/j}/2.  \] Step 3: the scalars $c_ H(f_ j)$. By theorem 14.2.1 on $Y$, there is a smooth $\phi _ j$ with $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ j>0$ and $(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ j)^ k=g_ j\kappa ^ k$; the scalar is one because both sides have mass one. On $X_0$, the same theorem gives a smooth $v_ j$ with $h_0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j>0$ and $(h_0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ m=c_{h_0}(F_ j)F_ j\, \mathrm dV_0$. Since only one term of the binomial expansion survives for dimensional reasons, \[  (H+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ j+\phi _ j))^ N =C c_{h_0}(F_ j)F_ jg_ j\mu =C c_{h_0}(F_ j)f_ j\, \mathrm dV.  \] Uniqueness of the scalar gives $c_ H(f_ j)=C c_{h_0}(F_ j)\leq 2^{-2j}$. Step 4: properties of $f$. By Tonelli's theorem, $\int _ Xf\, \mathrm dV=\sum _ jw_ j=1$. The density of $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ with respect to $\mu $ is \[  F=f/R=\sum _ jw_ jF_ jg_ j=E+\sum _ jw_ j(1-\varepsilon _ j)F_ j\beta _ j.  \] The annuli are disjoint and escape to the pole, so only finitely many bumps meet any compact subset of $Y\setminus \{ o\} $; hence $F$, and therefore $f$, is smooth off the pole fiber. On the pole fiber all bumps vanish and $F=E$, so $f$ is finite everywhere. Also $f\geq w_1f_1\geq \frac12\min _ Xf_1>0$. If $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)\geq af\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $a>0$, then $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)\geq aw_ jf_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$, and lemma 15.27.1 gives \[  aw_ j\leq c_ H(f_ j)\leq 2^{-2j},\quad \text{that is,}\quad a\leq 2^{-j}, \quad \text{for every }j.  \] This is impossible, so $b_ H(f)=0$ by theorem 15.28.4 . Step 5: exponential subsolutions. Fix $\lambda >0$, and choose $J$ with $1/j\leq \lambda $ for $j\geq J$. Since $L^\alpha -1\geq 0$, we have $B_{1/j}\leq B_\lambda $ for these $j$. As the bumps have disjoint supports, Step 2 bounds their total contribution $\sum _{j\geq J}w_ j(1-\varepsilon _ j)F_ j\beta _ j$ by $B_\lambda /2$. The baseline satisfies $E\leq b_0/4\leq B_\lambda /4$, because $B_\lambda \geq q_\alpha \geq b_0$. The remaining finitely many bumps are bounded by the constant \[  K_\lambda =\max _ Y\sum _{j<J}w_ j(1-\varepsilon _ j)M_ j\beta _ j,  \] and $K_\lambda \leq (K_\lambda /b_0)B_\lambda $. Hence $F\leq A_\lambda B_\lambda $ with $A_\lambda =3/4+K_\lambda /b_0$, and theorem 15.35.9 gives the exponential subsolution $u_\alpha +\lambda ^{-1}\log (CV_0/A_\lambda )$ and the greatest solution. Finally, a bounded solution $u$ would satisfy $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda \inf _ Xu}f\, \mathrm{d}V$, a positive scaled subsolution, contradicting $b_ H(f)=0$. Hence every solution is unbounded. $\square$ The density just constructed also satisfies the criterion in part (2) of theorem 15.35.9 : on the $j$th annulus, $F/q_\alpha \leq 1/4+\frac12\mathrm e^{(L^\alpha -1)/j}$, and away from all annuli the ratio is at most $1/4$. Approaching the pole through the annuli forces $j\to \infty $, so the required limit is zero. Since $b_ H(f)=0$, proposition 15.28.7 also shows that $f$ belongs to no $L^ p$ with $p>1$. Densities $F_ j$ as in the theorem exist whenever $v_-(h_0)=0$, by theorem 12.15.4 , theorem 12.2.3 . For instance, on the elliptic threefold, theorem 12.19.1 gives smooth functions $v_\ell $ with $h_0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\ell >0$ and masses $\delta _\ell =\int _{X_0}(h_0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\ell )^3\to 0$. The probability densities $F_\ell =(h_0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\ell )^3/(\delta _\ell \, \mathrm dV_0)$ satisfy $c_{h_0}(F_\ell )=\delta _\ell $ by uniqueness of the scalar, and a subsequence with $\delta _{\ell _ j}\leq 2^{-2j}/C$ gives the required densities. Thus the construction applies to this threefold times $\mathbb P^ k$ for every $k\geq 1$. With the balanced metric of proposition 12.19.18 , $V_0=24\pi $, so the explicit subsolutions have mass $CV_0$, equal to $96\pi $ on the fourfold ($k=1$) and $240\pi $ on the fivefold ($k=2$). These values concern the subsolutions; the greatest solutions have their own finite positive masses. In this construction the projective components $g_ j$ are chosen after the densities $F_ j$, to fit them. We do not know whether the exponential equation is solvable for every prescribed concentration family of this kind, and we have no necessary criterion for solvability at zero threshold.

text: Theorem 15.35.10 . 092A98EE953D Let $F_ j$, $j\geq 1$, be smooth strictly positive probability densities on $X_0$ with respect to $\mathrm dV_0=V_0^{-1}h_0^ m$, whose normalization scalars on $X_0$, relative to $h_0$ and $\mathrm dV_0$, satisfy $c_{h_0}(F_ j)\leq 2^{-2j}/C$. Step 4: properties of $f$. By Tonelli's theorem, $\int _ Xf\, \mathrm dV=\sum _ jw_ j=1$. The density of $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ with respect to $\mu $ is \[  F=f/R=\sum _ jw_ jF_ jg_ j=E+\sum _ jw_ j(1-\varepsilon _ j)F_ j\beta _ j.  \] The annuli are disjoint and escape to the pole, so only finitely many bumps meet any compact subset of $Y\setminus \{ o\} $; hence $F$, and therefore $f$, is smooth off the pole fiber. On the pole fiber all bumps vanish and $F=E$, so $f$ is finite everywhere. Also $f\geq w_1f_1\geq \frac12\min _ Xf_1>0$. If $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)\geq af\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $a>0$, then $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)\geq aw_ jf_ j\, \mathrm{d}V$, and lemma 15.27.1 gives \[  aw_ j\leq c_ H(f_ j)\leq 2^{-2j},\quad \text{that is,}\quad a\leq 2^{-j}, \quad \text{for every }j.  \] This is impossible, so $b_ H(f)=0$ by theorem 15.28.4 . Step 5: exponential subsolutions. Fix $\lambda >0$, and choose $J$ with $1/j\leq \lambda $ for $j\geq J$. Since $L^\alpha -1\geq 0$, we have $B_{1/j}\leq B_\lambda $ for these $j$. As the bumps have disjoint supports, Step 2 bounds their total contribution $\sum _{j\geq J}w_ j(1-\varepsilon _ j)F_ j\beta _ j$ by $B_\lambda /2$. The baseline satisfies $E\leq b_0/4\leq B_\lambda /4$, because $B_\lambda \geq q_\alpha \geq b_0$. The remaining finitely many bumps are bounded by the constant \[  K_\lambda =\max _ Y\sum _{j<J}w_ j(1-\varepsilon _ j)M_ j\beta _ j,  \] and $K_\lambda \leq (K_\lambda /b_0)B_\lambda $. Hence $F\leq A_\lambda B_\lambda $ with $A_\lambda =3/4+K_\lambda /b_0$, and theorem 15.35.9 gives the exponential subsolution $u_\alpha +\lambda ^{-1}\log (CV_0/A_\lambda )$ and the greatest solution. Finally, a bounded solution $u$ would satisfy $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(u)\geq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda \inf _ Xu}f\, \mathrm{d}V$, a positive scaled subsolution, contradicting $b_ H(f)=0$. Hence every solution is unbounded. $\square$

title: 15.35.11 Solvable exponents and collapse at zero threshold

section: 15.35 Exponential equations for an individual density
text: We return to a general Hermitian form $h$ on $X$ and a nonzero density $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm dV)$. Let $\Lambda _ h(f)$ be the set of exponents $\lambda >0$ for which ( 15.35.1 ) has a solution. By theorem 15.35.2 , $\lambda \in \Lambda _ h(f)$ if and only if the equation has an exponential subsolution at exponent $\lambda $. Proposition 15.35.12 . B2DB6BD3AC4D If $\lambda _0\in \Lambda _ h(f)$, then $[\lambda _0,+\infty )\subset \Lambda _ h(f)$. Consequently, $\Lambda _ h(f)$ is empty, or equals $(a,+\infty )$ for some $a\geq 0$, or equals $[a,+\infty )$ for some $a>0$. If $b_ h(f)>0$, then $\Lambda _ h(f)=(0,+\infty )$. Proof. Let $u$ be a solution at $\lambda _0$, and put $s=u-\max (0,\sup _ Xu)$. Then $s\leq \min (u,0)$, so for $\lambda \geq \lambda _0$, \begin{align*}  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(s) & =\mathrm e^{\lambda _0u}f\, \mathrm dV\\ & \geq \mathrm e^{\lambda _0s}f\, \mathrm dV \geq \mathrm e^{\lambda s}f\, \mathrm dV. \end{align*} Thus $s$ is an exponential subsolution at every $\lambda \geq \lambda _0$, and theorem 15.35.2 gives a solution. Hence $\Lambda _ h(f)$ contains $[\lambda _0,+\infty )$ together with each of its points $\lambda _0$. A nonempty subset of $(0,+\infty )$ with this property is determined by its infimum $a$ and by whether $a$ belongs to it, which gives the stated forms. If $b_ h(f)>0$, corollary 15.35.3 gives $\Lambda _ h(f)=(0,+\infty )$. $\square$ Proposition 15.35.13 . C791D4F48DEC Suppose $b_ h(f)=0$. Let $\lambda _ j>0$ decrease to zero, and let $u_ j$ be any solution of ( 15.35.1 ) at exponent $\lambda _ j$. Put \[  M_ j=\sup _ Xu_ j,\qquad v_ j=u_ j-M_ j,\qquad c_ j=\mathrm e^{\lambda _ jM_ j}.  \] Then \begin{gather*}  c_ j\longrightarrow 0,\qquad \lambda _ jM_ j\longrightarrow -\infty ,\\  \| \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u_ j)\| _{\mathrm{TV}} =\| \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v_ j)\| _{\mathrm{TV}} \longrightarrow 0. \end{gather*} Moreover, $\mathrm e^{\lambda _ ju_ j}\to 0$ uniformly on $X$, where the exponential is zero on the pole set, and $u_ j\to -\infty $ uniformly, that is, $\sup _ Xu_ j\to -\infty $. Proof. Set $g_ j=\mathrm e^{\lambda _ jv_ j}f$. By lemma 5.44.5 , applied to the finite non-pluripolar measure $f\, \mathrm dV$, $g_ j\to f$ in $L^1$; each $g_ j$ is nonzero, since $v_ j$ is finite almost everywhere. Since the Monge–Ampère measure is unchanged by adding constants, \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(v_ j)=c_ jg_ j\, \mathrm dV, \qquad \text{hence}\qquad 0<c_ j\leq b_ h(g_ j)  \] by theorem 15.28.4 . The upper semicontinuity of the threshold, theorem 15.32.1 , gives $\limsup _ jc_ j\leq b_ h(f)=0$. Since $0\leq g_ j\leq f$, the total masses are at most $c_ j\| f\| _{L^1}$ and tend to zero. Moreover $\lambda _ jM_ j=\log c_ j\to -\infty $, and $0\leq \mathrm e^{\lambda _ ju_ j}\leq \mathrm e^{\lambda _ jM_ j}=c_ j$. Finally, once $\lambda _ j<1$ and $\log c_ j<0$, we have $M_ j=\lambda _ j^{-1}\log c_ j\leq \log c_ j$, so $M_ j\to -\infty $. $\square$ For the density of theorem 15.35.10 , solutions exist for every positive exponent, so the collapse applies as $\lambda \downarrow 0$ to every choice of solutions, in particular to the greatest ones. By contrast, the subsolutions of theorem 15.35.9 keep the mass $CV_0$ for every exponent, while the masses of the solutions above them tend to zero: on a nonclosed background, the order of two potentials does not give an order of their total Monge–Ampère masses. Whether the normalized potentials converge in capacity, and which equation a normalized cluster limit satisfies at exponent zero, are not decided by this argument. Positive endpoints of $\Lambda _ h(f)$ are governed instead by the compactness criterion below.

text: Lemma 15.35.15 . A9F34BD594E1 For every $\tau >0$, there is a nonnegative $t_\tau \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)\cap C(X)$ such that every exponential subsolution at an exponent $\lambda \geq \tau $ lies below $t_\tau $. Put $K_\tau =\sup _ Xt_\tau $. If $\tau \leq \lambda _1\leq \lambda _2$ belong to $\Lambda _ h(f)$, then \[  U_{\lambda _2}\geq U_{\lambda _1} -K_\tau \frac{\lambda _2-\lambda _1}{\lambda _2}.  \] Consequently, $\lambda \mapsto U_\lambda +K_\tau \log (\lambda /\tau )$ is nondecreasing on $\Lambda _ h(f)\cap [\tau ,+\infty )$. Proof. Set $q=\min (f,1)$, a nonzero bounded density. By theorem 14.19.3 , there is a continuous $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with $\mathrm{MA}_ h(w)=\mathrm e^{\tau w}q\, \mathrm dV$. Put $t_\tau =w+\max (0,-\inf _ Xw)$. Then $t_\tau \geq 0$ and $t_\tau \geq w$, so for $\lambda \geq \tau $, \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(t_\tau )=\mathrm e^{\tau w}q\, \mathrm dV \leq \mathrm e^{\lambda t_\tau }f\, \mathrm dV.  \] Let $u$ be an exponential subsolution at an exponent $\lambda \geq \tau $, and let $\epsilon >0$. On $\{ t_\tau <u-\epsilon \} $, \[  \mathrm{MA}_ h(t_\tau ) \leq \mathrm e^{\lambda (u-\epsilon )}f\, \mathrm dV \leq \mathrm e^{-\lambda \epsilon } \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(u-\epsilon ).  \] The bounded function $t_\tau $ satisfies $P_{h/2}(t_\tau )\not\equiv -\infty $, and $u-\epsilon \preceq t_\tau $. Thus theorem 15.2.2 gives $t_\tau \geq u-\epsilon $, and letting $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $t_\tau \geq u$. For the order estimate, put $\delta =K_\tau (\lambda _2-\lambda _1)/\lambda _2$. By the first part, $U_{\lambda _1}\leq t_\tau \leq K_\tau $, so $(\lambda _2-\lambda _1)U_{\lambda _1}\leq \lambda _2\delta $, that is, $\lambda _1U_{\lambda _1}\geq \lambda _2(U_{\lambda _1}-\delta )$. Since the Monge–Ampère measure is unchanged by adding constants, \begin{align*}  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(U_{\lambda _1}-\delta ) & =\mathrm e^{\lambda _1U_{\lambda _1}}f\, \mathrm dV\\ & \geq \mathrm e^{\lambda _2(U_{\lambda _1}-\delta )}f\, \mathrm dV. \end{align*} Thus $U_{\lambda _1}-\delta $ is an exponential subsolution at $\lambda _2$, and the maximality of $U_{\lambda _2}$ gives $U_{\lambda _2}\geq U_{\lambda _1}-\delta $. Finally, $1-x^{-1}\leq \log x$ for $x\geq 1$; with $x=\lambda _2/\lambda _1$ this gives $\delta \leq K_\tau \log (\lambda _2/\lambda _1)$, which proves the monotonicity. $\square$

title: Proposition 15.35.17
section: 15.35 Exponential equations for an individual density
text: Proposition 15.35.17 . B1974D837A1A For every $a\in \Lambda _ h(f)$, the greatest solutions satisfy \[  U_\lambda \longrightarrow U_ a \quad \text{in }L^1\text{ and in capacity}\quad (\lambda \downarrow a),  \] and their Monge–Ampère measures converge in total variation to $\mathrm e^{aU_ a}f\, \mathrm dV$. Proof. Let $K=K_ a$ be the constant of the lemma with $\tau =a$, and let $\lambda _ j>a$ decrease to $a$. By the lemma, the functions \[  V_ j=U_{\lambda _ j}+K\log (\lambda _ j/a)  \] decrease and satisfy $V_ j\geq U_ a$. Their limit $V$ therefore belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ and satisfies $V\geq U_ a$. Dominated convergence between the integrable bounds $U_ a$ and $V_1$ gives $V_ j\to V$ in $L^1$, and lemma 5.29.19 gives convergence in capacity. Since the added constants tend to zero, $U_{\lambda _ j}\to V$ in both senses. The nonpositive functions $U_{\lambda _ j}-K$ satisfy \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(U_{\lambda _ j}-K)=\mathrm e^{\lambda _ j(U_{\lambda _ j}-K)}\, \mathrm e^{\lambda _ jK}f\, \mathrm dV,  \] and $\mathrm e^{\lambda _ jK}f\to \mathrm e^{aK}f$ in $L^1$. Theorem 15.34.2 therefore gives $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(V)=\mathrm e^{aV}f\, \mathrm dV$, together with total-variation convergence of the measures $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(U_{\lambda _ j})$. Hence $V$ is a solution at $a$, so $V\leq U_ a$ by maximality, while $V\geq U_ a$ by construction. Thus $V=U_ a$. Since every sequence of exponents converging to $a$ from above has a decreasing subsequence, this proves the assertions. $\square$

title: Proposition 15.35.18
section: 15.35 Exponential equations for an individual density
text: Proposition 15.35.18 . 0535F55900CB Suppose $\Lambda _ h(f)\ne \varnothing $, and put $a_0=\inf \Lambda _ h(f)$. For every $a>a_0$, there is $L_ a\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ such that \[  U_\lambda \longrightarrow L_ a \quad \text{in }L^1\text{ and in capacity}\quad (\lambda \uparrow a).  \] It satisfies \[  L_ a\leq U_ a,\qquad \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ h(L_ a)=\mathrm e^{aL_ a}f\, \mathrm dV.  \] The equation measures converge in total variation to this finite measure. The left limit is independent of the auxiliary exponent and of the cofinal sequence used to construct it. Proof. Choose $\tau \in \Lambda _ h(f)$ with $0<\tau <a$; the upper-interval property gives such a choice. Put $K=K_\tau $ from lemma 15.35.15 and \[  V_\lambda =U_\lambda +K\log (\lambda /\tau ) \qquad (\lambda \in \Lambda _ h(f),\  \lambda \geq \tau ).  \] This family is increasing. For a sequence $\lambda _ j\uparrow a$ with $\tau \leq \lambda _ j<a$, its members lie between the integrable potentials $V_\tau $ and $V_ a$. The upper-envelope construction in section 5.40 gives \[  V^-_ a=\left(\sup _{\tau \leq \lambda <a}V_\lambda \right)^* =\left(\lim _ jV_{\lambda _ j}\right)^*\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h).  \] Indeed cofinality and the order give the same pointwise supremum for every such sequence. Regularization changes it only on a pluripolar set. Dominated convergence between the integrable bounds gives $L^1$ convergence to $V^-_ a$, and lemma 5.29.19 gives convergence in capacity. Since the added constants converge, set \[  L_ a=V^-_ a-K\log (a/\tau ).  \] Then $U_{\lambda _ j}\to L_ a$ in both topologies and $L_ a\leq U_ a$; the latter inequality survives regularization because $V_ a$ is upper semicontinuous. The potentials $U_{\lambda _ j}-K$ and their limit $L_ a-K$ are nonpositive. Apply theorem 15.34.2 with exponents tending to $a>0$ and densities $\mathrm e^{\lambda _ jK}f\to \mathrm e^{aK}f$ in $L^1$. It proves the exact equation and total-variation convergence. Every sequence approaching $a$ from the left has a cofinal increasing subsequence. If potential convergence in either topology, or total-variation convergence of the equation measures, failed, a sequence staying outside a fixed neighbourhood of the proposed limit would therefore have an increasing subsequence, contrary to the preceding argument. This proves the full left limit and measure convergence. Repeating the construction with another $\tau $ gives the same $L^1$ limit; canonical quasi-plurisubharmonic representatives that agree almost everywhere agree everywhere. Thus the auxiliary choice does not change $L_ a$. $\square$

title: 15.36 Radial selection for integrable densities
text: The scalar and measure limits in corollary 15.35.3 do not by themselves determine a limit potential. For the sublogarithmic densities of lemma 15.30.1 , the radial flux supplies the missing information. It also distinguishes convergence after subtracting the supremum from convergence after subtracting $\lambda ^{-1}\log b$, where $b$ is the critical scalar: the latter depends on a first moment of the limiting measure. Use the product $X=X_0\times Y$, $Y=\mathbb P^ k$, $H=h_0+\kappa $, and the probability volume $\mu =V_0^{-1}h_0^ m\wedge \kappa ^ k$ of section 15.30 , with $\dim X_0=m$, $v_-(h_0)=0$ and $k\geq 2$. Put $b=\binom NmV_0$, where $N=m+k$. For $0<\alpha <1$, let $U_{\lambda ,\alpha }$ be the greatest solution of \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(U_{\lambda ,\alpha }) =\mathrm e^{\lambda U_{\lambda ,\alpha }}q_\alpha \mu , \qquad \lambda >0.  \] The threshold of this forcing measure is $b>0$, by theorem 15.30.3 , so the solutions exist by corollary 15.35.3 .

title: 15.36.1 Separation and the radial flux
text: Lemma 15.36.2 . 91B8E02B5759 There is a $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic function $w_{\lambda ,\alpha }$ on $Y$ such that \[  U_{\lambda ,\alpha }=\lambda ^{-1}\log b+w_{\lambda ,\alpha },\qquad w_{\lambda ,\alpha }\geq u_\alpha , \qquad \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (w_{\lambda ,\alpha }) =\mathrm e^{\lambda w_{\lambda ,\alpha }}q_\alpha \kappa ^ k.  \] The last measure has mass one. On the affine chart centered at $o$, set $s=\log |z|^2$, $\rho (s)=\log (1+\mathrm e^ s)$ and $m(s)=\rho '(s)$. The function $w=w_{\lambda ,\alpha }$ is radial and satisfies C1A1056DFED6 15.36.3 \begin{equation}  \begin{aligned}  Q_{\lambda ,\alpha }(s) & =\int _{-\infty }^ s\mathrm e^{\lambda w(r)}q_\alpha (r)\,  \mathrm d(m(r)^ k),\\  w'(s)& =Q_{\lambda ,\alpha }(s)^{1/k}-m(s), \qquad Q_{\lambda ,\alpha }(-\infty )=0, \quad Q_{\lambda ,\alpha }(+\infty )=1. \end{aligned} \end{equation} Proof. Choose a smooth nondecreasing concave function $\chi $ on $[0,+\infty )$, equal to the identity on $[0,1]$ and constant on $[2,+\infty )$, and put $q_ j=j\chi (q_\alpha /j)$. Concavity gives $q_ j\uparrow q_\alpha $ and \[  \min (q_\alpha ,j)\leq q_ j\leq \min (q_\alpha ,2j).  \] The functions $q_ j$ are smooth and positive on $Y$: near $o$ they are constant, and elsewhere the density is smooth. Let $w_ j$ be the continuous solution of $\mathrm{MA}_\kappa (w_ j)=\mathrm e^{\lambda w_ j}q_ j\kappa ^ k$ from theorem 14.19.3 . It is the greatest subsolution by theorem 15.35.2 and bounded uniqueness. Since $u_\alpha \leq 0$ and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (u_\alpha )=q_\alpha \kappa ^ k$, it is a subsolution for every $q_ j$, whence $u_\alpha \leq w_ j$. Density comparison gives $w_ j\downarrow w$. The pullback $W_ j=\lambda ^{-1}\log b+w_ j$ is a bounded solution on $X$, by the product expansion in theorem 15.30.3 . For the smooth density $q_ j\mu $ it is therefore also the greatest subsolution. Every subsolution for $q_\alpha \mu $ is a subsolution for $q_ j\mu $, so $U_{\lambda ,\alpha }\leq W_ j$. Monotone convergence in capacity and theorem 15.34.2 on $Y$ identify the equation for $w\geq u_\alpha $. Moreover, Stokes gives $\int _ Y\mathrm e^{\lambda w_ j}q_ j\kappa ^ k=1$. The integrands are dominated by $\mathrm e^{\lambda \sup _ Yw_1}q_\alpha $, so dominated convergence gives the same identity for $w$. Its pullback is a product solution, hence lies below the greatest solution on $X$. Together with $U_{\lambda ,\alpha }\leq \lim _ jW_ j$, this proves separation and all measure assertions. Uniqueness makes each $w_ j$ invariant under the unitary action on the affine coordinates $z\in \mathbb C^ k$, and the limit has the same invariance. A radial $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic function has a convex nondecreasing profile $\rho +w$. Symmetric convolution of this convex profile on compact $s$ intervals, decreasing as the scale decreases, and bounded-product continuity give its radial measure $\mathrm d((\rho +w)'^ k)$, as in lemma 15.30.1 . The bound $w\geq u_\alpha $, whose growth is $o(|s|)$ at $-\infty $, forces the initial derivative to vanish. The positive density makes the flux continuous and positive at finite $s$, yielding ( 15.36.3 ). Its final value is the mass one already proved. The profile is consequently smooth on finite $s$ intervals. $\square$

title: 15.36.4 The normalized limit
text: Set \[  a_{\lambda ,\alpha }=\sup _ Yw_{\lambda ,\alpha },\qquad v_{\lambda ,\alpha }=w_{\lambda ,\alpha }-a_{\lambda ,\alpha },\qquad c_{\lambda ,\alpha }=\mathrm e^{\lambda \sup _ XU_{\lambda ,\alpha }} =b\mathrm e^{\lambda a_{\lambda ,\alpha }}.  \] In particular $a_{\lambda ,\alpha }\geq 0$. Theorem 15.36.5 . AACA90B5B52B Let $\alpha _ j\to \alpha \in (0,1)$ and $\lambda _ j\to 0$ with $\lambda _ j>0$, at arbitrary relative rates. Then \[  v_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}\longrightarrow u_\alpha \quad \text{in }L^1(Y),\text{ in capacity, and locally uniformly on }Y\setminus \{ o\} .  \] Their pullbacks converge in $L^1(X)$, in capacity on $X$, and locally uniformly off $X_0\times \{ o\} $. Furthermore $q_{\alpha _ j}\to q_\alpha $ in $L^1(\kappa ^ k)$, $c_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}\to b$, and the equation measures converge in total variation to $bq_\alpha \mu $. The limiting pullback has finite mass $b$ and belongs to $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,H,0)$. Proof. Choose $[\alpha _-,\alpha _+]\Subset (0,1)$ containing all late parameters. The density formula in lemma 15.30.1 gives, uniformly for $\delta $ in this interval and $t=-s$ large, \[  q_\delta (s)\leq C\mathrm e^{kt}(1+t)^{-1-k(1-\alpha _+)}.  \] Away from $o$ the densities are jointly smooth, including on the hyperplane at infinity. Thus one integrable density $g$ dominates all $q_\delta $, and dominated convergence gives $q_{\alpha _ j}\to q_\alpha $ in $L^1$. For every normalized $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic $v$, theorem 5.25.2 gives $\int _ Y(-v)\kappa ^ k\leq C_ k$. Absolute continuity of the integral of $g$ therefore implies \[  \sup _{\sup _ Yv=0}\int _{\{ v<-T\} }g\kappa ^ k\longrightarrow 0 \quad (T\to \infty ).  \] Taking $T=\lambda ^{-1/2}$ shows that \[  \int _ Y(1-\mathrm e^{\lambda v})q_\delta \kappa ^ k \leq \lambda T+\int _{\{ v<-T\} }g\kappa ^ k\longrightarrow 0  \] uniformly in $\delta $ and $v$. Write $v_ j=v_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}$ and $a_ j=a_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}$. The exact mass identity of the lemma is FF104C305C42 15.36.6 \begin{equation}  1=\mathrm e^{\lambda _ ja_ j} \int _ Y\mathrm e^{\lambda _ jv_ j}q_{\alpha _ j}\kappa ^ k. \end{equation} It gives $\mathrm e^{\lambda _ ja_ j}\to 1$, hence $\lambda _ ja_ j\to 0$. The actual densities $\mathrm e^{\lambda _ ja_ j}\mathrm e^{\lambda _ jv_ j}q_{\alpha _ j}$ converge in $L^1$ to $q_\alpha $ and are bounded by $2g$ for all late $j$. Their cumulative radial fluxes $Q_ j$ consequently converge uniformly to the flux $Q_\alpha $ of $u_\alpha $. By ( 15.36.3 ), $v_ j'\to u_\alpha '$ uniformly on compact $s$ intervals. The normalized $L^1$ bound controls one value of each profile on a fixed annulus; thus every sequence has a subsequence converging uniformly on compact $s$ intervals to $u_\alpha +d$ for some finite constant $d$. Near infinity the common bound for the densities is smooth and bounded. Hence $1-Q_ j(s)\leq C\mathrm e^{-s}$ and $|v_ j'(s)|\leq C\mathrm e^{-s}$ for large $s$. Integrating gives uniform convergence up to the hyperplane at infinity. At the other end, monotonicity of $\rho +v_ j$ gives, for $s<s_0$, \[  v_ j(s)\leq v_ j(s_0)+\rho (s_0).  \] Choose $s_0$ so negative that the right side is negative for all late members of the subsequence. The supremum zero is then attained outside this inner ball. Uniform convergence on its compact complement gives $\sup _ Y(u_\alpha +d)=0$, so $d=0$. Normalized compactness identifies every $L^1$ cluster limit with $u_\alpha $; this proves convergence of the entire family and its local uniform convergence off $o$. For capacity convergence, fix $T>0$. The sublevel $\{ u_\alpha <-T\} $ is a neighborhood of $o$, and its complement is a compact set on which convergence is uniform. Its capacity is at most $C/T$ by ( 5.29.4 ). Let $j\to \infty $ and then $T\to \infty $. The same argument on $X$ uses the normalized pullback of $u_\alpha $ and proves convergence in Hermitian capacity there; comparison sets omit pole sets. Pullback also preserves the $L^1$ and local uniform limits. The product expansion proves total-variation convergence of the measures, and theorem 15.30.3 supplies the exact limiting mass and envelope class. $\square$

title: 15.36.7 Scalar centering and its moment boundary
search_title: Scalar centering and its moment boundary
text: Proposition 15.36.8 . 704167C1A830 The first moment \[  M_\alpha =\int _ Yu_\alpha q_\alpha \kappa ^ k  \] is finite exactly when $\alpha <k/(k+1)$. In this range, 24634670B4B5 15.36.9 \begin{equation}  -M_\alpha =\alpha \int _1^\infty x^{\alpha -1} \left[\alpha x^{\alpha -1}+(1-\alpha x^{\alpha -1})\mathrm e^{1-x}\right]^ k\, \mathrm dx. \end{equation} For the joint limits of theorem 15.36.5 , if $\alpha <k/(k+1)$, then \[  a_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}\to -M_\alpha ,\qquad U_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}-\lambda _ j^{-1}\log b \to u_\alpha -M_\alpha  \] in $L^1$, in capacity, and locally uniformly away from the pole fiber. If $\alpha \geq k/(k+1)$, then $a_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}\to +\infty $ and the latter translated potentials tend to $+\infty $ locally uniformly off the pole fiber, although $\lambda _ ja_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}\to 0$. In both cases the exact scalar error is \[  \lambda _ j^{-1}\log (c_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}/b) =a_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}.  \] Proof. As $t=-s\to \infty $, the radial profile of lemma 15.30.1 satisfies \[  u_\alpha \sim -t^\alpha ,\qquad Q_\alpha '(s)\sim k(1-\alpha )\alpha ^ k t^{-1-k(1-\alpha )}.  \] Thus the first moment is finite precisely when $(k+1)\alpha <k$. In that case, write $x=1-\psi $. Its cumulative flux is \[  Q_\alpha =\left[\alpha x^{\alpha -1} +(1-\alpha x^{\alpha -1})\mathrm e^{1-x}\right]^ k.  \] Integration by parts gives ( 15.36.9 ); the pole boundary term vanishes since $(k+1)\alpha -k<0$. Suppose $\alpha <k/(k+1)$ and choose the parameter interval in the preceding proof with $\alpha _+<k/(k+1)$. Its dominating density $g$ satisfies $(-u_{\alpha _+})g\in L^1$. Write $w_ j=w_{\lambda _ j,\alpha _ j}=v_ j+a_ j$. Since $w_ j\geq u_{\alpha _ j}\geq u_{\alpha _+}$, the mass identity and $\mathrm e^ r\geq 1+r$ give $\int _ Yw_ jq_{\alpha _ j}\kappa ^ k\leq 0$. title: 15.36.10 Order in the separated class
text: We use here the closed-class uniqueness theorem: on a compact connected Kähler manifold, two potentials whose non-pluripolar measures have full mass and are equal differ by a constant. This is an external input; its source is identified in 25.13 . Corollary 15.36.11 . E75339160354 Every separated threshold subsolution $r=r(y)$ with $r\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\kappa )$ and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ H(r)\geq bq_\alpha \mu $ equals $u_\alpha +d$ for some constant $d$. In particular $u_\alpha $ is its unique supremum-zero member. If $\alpha <k/(k+1)$, then $u_\alpha -M_\alpha $ is the greatest such subsolution whose $q_\alpha $-mean on $Y$ is nonpositive. Proof. The product formula reduces the inequality to $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\kappa (r)\geq q_\alpha \kappa ^ k$. Closed Stokes gives each bounded truncation mass one, so the extended measure of $r$ has mass at most one. The inequality therefore gives equality and full mass. Closed-class uniqueness yields $r=u_\alpha +d$. In the finite-moment range its mean is $M_\alpha +d$, which is nonpositive exactly when $d\leq -M_\alpha $. $\square$ At and beyond the moment boundary every constant translate has mean $-\infty $, so that mean condition no longer chooses a greatest translate. The order assertion concerns separated potentials. Selection for arbitrary integrable densities and uniqueness of arbitrary critical potentials on the nonclosed product remain the questions of 24.2.2 and section 15.34 .

title: 11.32 Normalization and weak adjoint measures
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$ with a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V$. Function spaces are real, and Lebesgue norms are taken with respect to $\mathrm{d}V$. Until section 11.40 , $\theta $ is a smooth semipositive big real $(1,1)$-form and $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is a model reference in the sense of ( 16.28.67 ): it is a fixed point of the ordinary singularity envelope $P_\theta [\cdot ]$ of definition 5.40.4 , and its envelope $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )$ in a smaller background is not identically $-\infty $ for some $0<\varepsilon <1$. We write $u\sim \varphi $ when $u$ has the ordinary singularity type of $\varphi $ (definition 16.7.1 ), and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta $ for the extended non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of theorem 13.14.3 ; when its total mass is finite, it is the usual non-pluripolar measure, which we also denote by $\mathrm{MA}_\theta $. In the ordinary type of $\varphi $, the equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)=c\, \mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V$ determines the constant $c>0$ uniquely, even when it has several normalized solutions. As a function of the logarithmic density $F$, the logarithm of this constant is concave. Its supporting functionals are probability measures that describe the first-order response of the constant to a change of density; for smooth Hermitian equations they are the Gauduchon adjoint probabilities of the linearized operator. The convex dual of the functional controls the concentration of these measures through entropy, and this gives compactness when the density, the reference or the positive background varies. The same measures provide the integral normalizations that single out the limit of the exponential equations as the exponent tends to zero. The scalar functional does not, however, determine the singularities of the solutions: examples with moving divisors have identical functionals but different limiting potentials. On closed projective backgrounds, convex geometry gives quantitative criteria for varying references, including references with nonanalytic poles or degenerate residuals.

title: 11.33 The scalar functional
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: The domination principle makes the constant decrease as the density increases, and mixed Monge–Ampère products strengthen this monotonicity to concavity in the logarithmic density. Compactness of the solutions then gives continuity under uniformly bounded $L^1$ perturbations. For a bounded real measurable function $F$, part (2) of theorem 15.12.1 , applied to the bounded density $\mathrm{e}^ F$, gives $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\sim \varphi $ and a unique constant $c_\varphi (F)>0$ such that 9D47DB96B6E3 11.33.1 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u) =c_\varphi (F)\mathrm{e}^ F\, \mathrm{d}V. \end{equation} The normalization scalar is \[  B_\varphi (F)=\log c_\varphi (F).  \] Since the constant is unique, $B_\varphi $ is well defined; it depends on $\varphi $ only through its ordinary singularity type. Proposition 11.33.2 . 2770AB03C0D2 Let $F,G\in L^\infty (\mathrm{d}V)$ be real. The functional $B_\varphi $ is decreasing, and for every constant $a\in \mathbb R$, \[  B_\varphi (F+a)=B_\varphi (F)-a.  \] Consequently 7BAFE60C3D66 11.33.3 \begin{equation}  -\mathop{\rm ess\, sup}_ X(G-F) \leq B_\varphi (G)-B_\varphi (F) \leq -\mathop{\rm ess\, inf}_ X(G-F), \end{equation} and $|B_\varphi (G)-B_\varphi (F)|\leq \| G-F\| _\infty $. Proof. Suppose that $F\leq G$ almost everywhere and, to reach a contradiction, that $c_\varphi (F)<c_\varphi (G)$. Let $u,v\sim \varphi $ solve the two equations. Since $F\leq G$ and the extended measure is unchanged by adding constants, for every constant $a$, \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u) \leq \frac{c_\varphi (F)}{c_\varphi (G)} \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (v+a),  \] and the ratio is strictly less than one. As $u\sim \varphi $, the envelope $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(u)$ dominates a translate of $P_{\varepsilon \theta }(\varphi )$ and is therefore not identically $-\infty $; moreover $v+a\preceq u$. The singular strict domination principle, theorem 15.2.2 , gives $u\geq v+a$ for every $a$, which is impossible at any point where both potentials are finite. Thus $B_\varphi (F)\geq B_\varphi (G)$. Replacing $F$ by $F+a$ and the constant by $\mathrm{e}^{-a}c_\varphi (F)$ leaves the right-hand side of ( 11.33.1 ) unchanged, so uniqueness of the constant proves the translation rule. Finally, $G$ lies between the constant translates $F+\mathop{\rm ess\, inf}_ X(G-F)$ and $F+\mathop{\rm ess\, sup}_ X(G-F)$; monotonicity and the translation rule give ( 11.33.3 ). $\square$ The scalar does not depend on the smooth representative of the background: for a smooth real $h$, replacing $\theta $ by $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ and each potential $u$, including $\varphi $, by $u-h$ preserves the currents and the prescribed ordinary type, and hence leaves the equation and its constant unchanged. Concavity comes from mixed products. A convex combination of two solutions stays in the prescribed ordinary type, and lemma 13.14.10 bounds its measure below by the corresponding mixed density. Theorem 11.33.4 . 8810E18F852C The functional $B_\varphi $ is concave on the real space $L^\infty (\mathrm{d}V)$: for $F,G$ in that space, \[  B_\varphi (tF+(1-t)G) \geq tB_\varphi (F)+(1-t)B_\varphi (G),\qquad 0\leq t\leq 1.  \] Proof. Let $u,v\sim \varphi $ solve the equations for $F$ and $G$, and set $H=tF+(1-t)G$ and $D=c_\varphi (F)^ t c_\varphi (G)^{1-t}$. Lemma 13.14.10 and the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality give \[  \begin{split}  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (tu+(1-t)v) & \geq \bigl (t(c_\varphi (F)\mathrm{e}^ F)^{1/n} +(1-t)(c_\varphi (G)\mathrm{e}^ G)^{1/n}\bigr )^ n\, \mathrm{d}V\\ & \geq D \mathrm{e}^ H\, \mathrm{d}V. \end{split}  \] The averaged potential $tu+(1-t)v$ has the ordinary type of $\varphi $. If $c_\varphi (H)<D$, its measure dominates the measure of a solution $w\sim \varphi $ for $H$ by the factor $D/c_\varphi (H)>1$. Applying the singular strict domination principle to $w$ and to every constant translate of the averaged potential, as in the proof of proposition 11.33.2 , leads to the same contradiction. Hence $c_\varphi (H)\geq D$, and taking logarithms proves concavity. $\square$ For smooth Hermitian data, this concavity agrees with the second-variation formula of theorem 14.8.1 . Uniformly bounded logarithmic densities give the solutions a common lower barrier, and compactness of the solutions identifies the limiting scalar even when the densities converge only in $L^1$. Theorem 11.33.5 . 5E3583383688 If $F_ j,F$ are uniformly bounded real measurable functions and $F_ j\to F$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, then \[  B_\varphi (F_ j)\longrightarrow B_\varphi (F).  \] Proof. Choose solutions $u_ j\sim \varphi $ normalized by $\sup _ Xu_ j=0$, and write $c_ j=c_\varphi (F_ j)$. If $|F_ j|\leq M$, monotonicity and the translation rule of proposition 11.33.2 give \[  \mathrm{e}^{-M}c_\varphi (0)\leq c_ j\leq \mathrm{e}^ M c_\varphi (0).  \] In particular, the Monge–Ampère measures of the $u_ j$ are dominated by a fixed multiple of $\mathrm{d}V$, and theorem 15.12.3 gives a constant $C$ such that \[  \varphi -C\leq u_ j\leq \varphi .  \] From any subsequence, extract a further subsequence with $c_ j\to c>0$ and $u_ j\to u$ in $L^1(X)$. By corollary 15.9.4 , the convergence also holds in capacity, $u\sim \varphi $, and the measures converge weakly. On the other hand, the exponential function is Lipschitz on the common range of the $F_ j$, so $c_ j\mathrm{e}^{F_ j}\to c\mathrm{e}^ F$ in $L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$. Therefore \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)=c\mathrm{e}^ F\, \mathrm{d}V,  \] and uniqueness of the constant gives $c=c_\varphi (F)$. Since every subsequence has a further subsequence along which $c_ j\to c_\varphi (F)$, the whole sequence converges, and so do the logarithms. $\square$

For a smooth Hermitian equation, differentiating the scalar identifies the supporting probability with the adjoint probability of the linearized operator. Theorem 11.34.9 . 7E60599DA339 Let $	heta =\omega $ be a Hermitian form, let $\varphi =0$, and let $F$ be a smooth real function. Let $u$ be the smooth solution of ( 11.33.1 ), unique up to an additive constant by corollary 14.24.17 , and let $\mu _ u$ be its Gauduchon adjoint probability from proposition 11.23.2 ; for $n=1$, this is $\mu _ u=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)/\int _ X\omega $. Then \[  \mathcal A_0(F)=\{ \mu _ u\} .  \] Proof. Suppose first that $n\geq 2$. By uniqueness of the constant, the normalization scalar of the smooth equation in theorem 14.8.1 is $B_0$, and that theorem gives, for every smooth real $G$, \[  \left. rac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}ight|_{t=0}B_0(F+tG) =-\int _ XG\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ u.  \] Let $
u \in \mathcal A_0(F)$. Testing the supporting inequality at $F+tG$ for both signs of $t$ and letting $t	o 0$ shows that $G$ has the same integral against $
u $ and $\mu _ u$. Since smooth functions are uniformly dense in $C(X)$, it follows that $
u =\mu _ u$, and the assertion follows from nonemptiness of $\mathcal A_0(F)$. In dimension one, Stokes' theorem gives $c_0(F)=\int _ X\omega /\int _ X\mathrm{e}^ F \mathrm{d}V$; differentiating its logarithm in the same way yields the stated measure, since $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=c_0(F)\mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V$. $\square$ Consequently, in the Hermitian case the supporting probabilities at a continuous $F$ can be approached through smooth data. A weak linearized operator requires more than a supporting probability. Identifying that current with a scalar multiple of a weak power $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{n-1}$ would require a well-defined product and its compatibility with approximation. A similar representation holds for a functional defined by subsolutions rather than by an equation in a prescribed singularity type. Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ be nonzero with $f^{1/n}\in \mathcal D_\omega ^0$, the space of densities with uniformly vanishing Gauduchon tails from 15.32.7 . Then proposition 12.10.9 describes the supporting probabilities of $F\mapsto \log b_\omega (\mathrm{e}^ Ff)$, where $b_\omega (\cdot )$ is the density threshold of theorem 15.28.4 .

title: 11.34.10 Continuous positive complex Hessians
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text:
The smooth recovery theorem extends to a bounded solution whose complex Hessian is continuous and everywhere positive. In this case one can vary the potential in both directions, and the resulting densities force every supporting probability to annihilate the same elliptic operator. The Sobolev range theorem then gives uniqueness. Theorem 11.34.11 . F4FDB7BC8A03 Let $n\geq 2$, let $	heta =\omega $ be a Hermitian form, and let $\varphi =0$. Suppose $F\in C(X)$ and a bounded solution $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ of ( 11.33.1 ) has distributional complex Hessian represented by a continuous form \[  \sigma =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0  \] everywhere on $X$. Then $\mathcal A_0(F)$ consists of one probability $
u _ F$. It satisfies  egin{align*}  \int _ X L_\sigma h\, \mathrm d
u _ F& =0\quad (h\in C^\infty (X)),\  DB_0(F)[H]& =-\int _ XH\, \mathrm d
u _ F\quad (H\in C(X)). \end{align*} The derivative is taken in the Gâteaux sense. Proof. The continuous trace of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is the Euclidean Laplacian of $u$, up to the fixed normalization. Local constant-coefficient elliptic regularity gives $u\in W^{2,p}$ for every finite $p$. Indeed, subtract the Newtonian potential of a cutoff of this trace. Its second high-frequency derivatives are order-zero multipliers, and the low-frequency kernels are locally bounded; the remaining distribution is harmonic. Sobolev embedding gives a $C^{1,\alpha }$ representative for every $\alpha <1$, which agrees with the quasi-psh representative. On a coordinate ball choose smooth $ho $ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho \geq \omega $. The radial regularizations of the bounded psh function $u+ho $ decrease to it, and their complex Hessians converge uniformly on smaller balls. Continuity of bounded products and the finite smooth-background expansion identify $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ with $\sigma ^ n$. For smooth real $h$, the same argument applies to $u+th$, which is admissible for all sufficiently small signed $t$ by uniform positivity. Define \[  F_ t=F+\log  rac{(\sigma +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n}{\sigma ^ n}.  \] Its equation has the same normalization scalar as the equation for $u$, so $B_0(F_ t)=B_0(F)$. The supporting inequality gives $\int _ X(F_ t-F)\, \mathrm d
u \leq 0$ for each $
u \in \mathcal A_0(F)$. Since $F_ t-F=tL_\sigma h+O(t^2)$ uniformly, using both signs yields stationarity. Choose $p=4n+1$ and $q=p/(p-1)=1+1/(4n)$. By corollary 12.9.3 , every supporting probability has an $L^ q$ density, since $q<n/(n-1)$. Smooth density in $W^{2,p}$ extends its stationarity to every $W^{2,p}$ test. By lemma 11.24.1 , all these densities lie in a one-dimensional space. Their integrals equal one, so they coincide. Nonemptiness is theorem 11.34.2 , and the derivative formula follows from proposition 11.34.5 . $\square$

title: 11.34.12 Products with a Hermitian factor
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text:
An explicit product construction exhibits the criterion for densities with an arbitrary continuous modulus. Let $(Y,\kappa )$ be a connected compact Hermitian $k$-fold, $k\geq 1$, with $\int _ Y\kappa ^ k=1$. Denote by $
u _\kappa $ the smooth stationary probability of $L_\kappa =\operatorname {tr}_\kappa \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$, given by the Gauduchon multiplier when $k\geq 2$; for $k=1$ it is $\kappa $. Write $w$ for the Fubini–Study area of mass one on $\mathbb P^1$. All factor forms and functions below are pulled back to $X=\mathbb P^1	imes Y$. Proposition 11.34.13 . D2CCD76890C8 Let $a>0$, let $b$ be smooth and positive on $\mathbb P^1$, and let $A$ be continuous and positive there, with $\int _{\mathbb P^1}Aw=a$. For \[  \omega =aw+b\kappa ,\qquad \mathrm dV=w\wedge \kappa ^ k, \qquad F=\log ((k+1)Ab^ k),  \] one has \[  c_0(F)=1,\qquad \mathcal A_0(F)=\left\{  rac Aa\, w\otimes 
u _\kappa ight\} .  \] Proof. The Green solution of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=(A-a)w$ on $\mathbb P^1$ has continuous complex Hessian and is bounded. Its pullback yields $\sigma =Aw+b\kappa >0$, and $\sigma ^{k+1}=(k+1)Ab^ kw\wedge \kappa ^ k$. Thus scalar uniqueness gives $c_0(F)=1$, and theorem 11.34.11 gives a unique support. For every smooth $h$ depending on all variables, the block decomposition \[  L_\sigma h=A^{-1}L_ wh+b^{-1}L_\kappa h  \] shows that $(A/a)w\otimes 
u _\kappa $ is stationary: the first term integrates to zero by Stokes on $\mathbb P^1$, and the second by stationarity on $Y$ and Fubini. This candidate has a bounded density with respect to $\mathrm dV$. The one-dimensional annihilator of lemma 11.24.1 and probability normalization therefore identify it with the supporting probability. $\square$ Example 11.34.14 . 1B8C3827F8D7 There is a non-Kähler threefold with a nonclosed Hermitian background and a positive continuous density whose logarithm is neither Dini continuous nor Hölder continuous of any positive order, but whose supporting probability is explicit and unique. Proof. Take the Hopf surface $Y=(\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} )/\langle z\mapsto 2zangle $ and its unit-volume metric $\kappa =c|z|^{-2}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$, where $c>0$ is chosen so that $\int _ Y\kappa ^2=1$. Put $s=\log |z|^2$, $\alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s$ and $ eta =\mathrm ds\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s$, so that $\kappa =c(\alpha + eta )$. The differentiation in ( 23.1.3 ) applies in this dimension. Here $\alpha $ has rank one, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\kappa =-c\alpha ^2=0$ and $
u _\kappa =\kappa ^2$. Polar coordinates identify $Y$ with $S^3	imes S^1$, hence $H^2(Y,\mathbb R)=0$. A closed positive form would be exact and have positive square integral, contradicting Stokes. Thus $Y$ is non-Kähler, and so is $\mathbb P^1	imes Y$, by restriction. Let $	au \in [-1,1]$ be the height on $\mathbb P^1$, set $b=2+	au $, and put \[  f(t)= egin{cases}  1/\log (e/|t|),& 0<|t|\leq 1,\  0,& t=0, \end{cases}  \] \[  A=a+\varepsilon \left(f(	au )-\int _{\mathbb P^1}f(	au )wight), \quad 0<\varepsilon <a.  \] Since $0\leq f\leq 1$, this is a positive continuous function of mean $a$. Along a normal segment to the equator, $|	au |$ is comparable to the distance $r$. The oscillation of $A$ is therefore bounded below by a positive multiple of $1/\log (e/r)$. Its Dini integral $\int _0^{r_0}\mathrm dr/(r\log (e/r))$ diverges, and this modulus is larger than every $r^\gamma $, $\gamma >0$, as $r\downarrow 0$. The logarithm of $A$ has the same lower bound, because $A$ is uniformly positive and bounded. The smooth term $2\log b$ contributes only $O(r)$, so $F=\log (3Ab^2)$ has neither regularity. The mixed component $\mathrm db\wedge \kappa $ shows that $\omega =aw+b\kappa $ is nonclosed. By proposition 11.34.13 , its supporting probability is $(A/a)w\wedge \kappa ^2$. $\square$ The theorem assumes a continuous positive complex Hessian for a bounded solution. It does not establish that hypothesis for every continuous $F$; the uniqueness question for arbitrary continuous data remains open.

title: 11.34.15 Divisorial smoothing
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text:
For a singular reference, the supporting probability can be unique while smoothings of the solution have different limiting adjoint probabilities. The reason is that the non-pluripolar product discards the mass on a divisor that the smoothings keep. On a product of two projective lines, explicit formulas exhibit both the lost mass and its dependence on the smoothing. In this subsection, $X=\mathbb P^1	imes \mathbb P^1$. Let $\omega _1$ and $\omega _2$ be the pullbacks of the Fubini–Study forms of the two factors, normalized to have integral one on their factors, and put \[  	heta =2\omega _1+2\omega _2,\qquad  eta =\omega _1+2\omega _2,\qquad \omega =\omega _1+\omega _2,\qquad \mathrm dV=\omega _1\wedge \omega _2.  \] Thus $\mathrm dV$ is a probability volume form, $	heta ^2=8\mathrm dV$ and $ eta ^2=4\mathrm dV$. Let $z$ be the affine coordinate on the first factor, and put \[  r= rac{|z|^2}{1+|z|^2},\qquad \psi =\log r,\qquad D=\{ 0\} 	imes \mathbb P^1.  \] The function $r$ extends smoothly to the first factor, with value one at infinity, and $\psi $ is quasi-plurisubharmonic with value $-\infty $ exactly on $D$. The Poincaré–Lelong formula gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =[D]-\omega _1$, so $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi = eta +[D]$. For a smooth positive $(1,1)$-form $\Omega $ on the surface $X$, the linearization $v\mapsto 2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Omega /\Omega ^2$ of the logarithmic Monge–Ampère operator has the adjoint probability $ho \Omega ^2$, where the Gauduchon multiplier $ho >0$ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(ho \Omega )=0$ and $\int _ Xho \Omega ^2=1$ (proposition 11.23.2 ). We call $Q=ho \Omega $ the adjoint cofactor of $\Omega $: it is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed, and $\Omega \wedge Q$ is the adjoint probability. Lemma 11.34.16 . FADB0C708F54 Write $x=\log |z|^2$ and $\chi (x)=\log (1+\mathrm e^ x)$. The envelope $\varphi =P_	heta [\psi ]$ is 69FAA61D9E93 11.34.17  egin{equation}  \varphi =W(x)-2\chi (x),\qquad W(x)= egin{cases} x+2\log 2,& x\leq 0,\ 2\chi (x),& x\geq 0.\end{cases} \end{equation} It satisfies $\psi \leq \varphi \leq 0$, $0\leq \varphi -\psi \leq 2\log 2$, and the model condition ( 16.28.67 ) with $\varepsilon =3/4$. Proof. The function $W$ is convex: both one-sided derivatives at zero equal one, and the derivative of $2\chi $ increases from one to two on $[0,\infty )$. Since $\omega _1=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi (x)$ on the affine chart, $W-2\chi $ is $2\omega _1$-plurisubharmonic there. Since $W$ has slope one for $x\leq 0$ and agrees with $2\chi $ for $x\geq 0$, the function $W-2\chi $ extends to a global $2\omega _1$-plurisubharmonic function, with a logarithmic pole along $D$ and equal to zero where $|z|\geq 1$. The asserted bounds follow from $\psi =x-\chi $: the difference $\varphi -\psi $ equals $2\log 2-\chi $ for $x\leq 0$ and $\chi -x$ for $x\geq 0$. For $C>0$ write $v_ C=P_	heta (\min \{ \psi +C,0\} )$. Rotations of the first factor and the transitive unitary action on the second preserve the whole competitor class, so the envelope is radial and independent of the second factor. The function $V_ C=2\chi +v_ C$ is then convex in $x$ and satisfies $V_ C\leq \chi +x+C$. This upper bound as $x	o -\infty $ forces the slope of $V_ C$ at $-\infty $ to be at least one, and by convexity all its slopes are at least one. For $x<0$, \[  V_ C(x)\leq V_ C(0)+x\leq 2\log 2+x=W(x).  \] For $x\geq 0$, the zero obstacle gives $V_ C\leq 2\chi =W$. Consequently $v_ C\leq \varphi $. If $C\geq 2\log 2$, the bounds already proved make $\varphi $ a competitor, so $v_ C=\varphi $. Letting $C	o \infty $ proves $P_	heta [\psi ]=\varphi $. Since $\varphi \sim \psi $ and the ordinary envelope depends only on the singularity type, also $P_	heta [\varphi ]=\varphi $. Finally \[  	frac 34	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =	frac 12\omega _1+	frac 32\omega _2+[D]\geq 0.  \] Since $\psi \leq \varphi $, the function $\psi $ is a competitor for $P_{(3/4)	heta }(\varphi )$, which is therefore not identically $-\infty $. $\square$ Proposition 11.34.18 . 3A41CC697C2A Every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $v\sim \varphi $ is uniquely of the form $v=\psi +w$, where $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X, eta )$ is bounded. Its non-pluripolar measure is E178383CB355 11.34.19  egin{equation}  \mathrm{MA}_	heta (v)=( eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^2,\qquad \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_	heta (v)=4. \end{equation} For every real continuous $F$, \[  B_\varphi (F)=\log 4-\log \int _ X\mathrm e^ F\mathrm dV, \qquad \mathcal A_\varphi (F)= \left\{  rac{\mathrm e^ F\mathrm dV}{\int _ X\mathrm e^ F\mathrm dV}ight\} .  \] At $v=\psi $, the non-pluripolar part of $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi $ is $ eta $, whose adjoint cofactor is $Q= eta /4$, with adjoint probability $ eta \wedge Q=\mathrm dV$. Proof. On $X\setminus D$, the function $w=v-\psi $ is bounded, because $v\sim \varphi \sim \psi $, and satisfies $ eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq 0$. After adding local potentials of the closed form $ eta $, lemma 5.24.7 extends $w$ across $D$; the extensions agree on overlaps and give a bounded $ eta $-plurisubharmonic function on $X$. Conversely, for every bounded $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X, eta )$, the function $\psi +w$ is $	heta $-plurisubharmonic with current $ eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w+[D]$, and it has the ordinary type of $\varphi $. The decomposition is unique, since two such functions $w$ agree off $D$ and hence everywhere. Put $T= eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$. The bounded-product construction gives \[  T^2- eta ^2=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}} igl (w(T+ eta ) igr ),  \] and Stokes' theorem against the constant function yields $\int _ XT^2=4$. The product gives no mass to $D$ by proposition 5.28.2 ; we also give a direct cutoff estimate, which will be used again below. Shift $w$ so that $0\leq w\leq M$, and set $f_ t=\max \{ \psi /t,-1\} $ for $t>0$. Choose smooth convex functions $\sigma _\epsilon $ with derivative in $[0,1]$, equal to $-1$ below $-1-\epsilon $ and to the identity above $-1+\epsilon $, converging uniformly to $\max \{ \cdot ,-1\} $. Then $f_{t,\epsilon }=\sigma _\epsilon (\psi /t)$ is globally smooth, constant near $D$, and \[  f_{t,\epsilon }\longrightarrow f_ t\  	ext{uniformly},\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_{t,\epsilon }\geq -\omega _1/t.  \] Testing the distributional identity against $f_{t,\epsilon }$, using positivity of $T+ eta $, and letting $\epsilon 	o 0$, we obtain 4D939EBD023F 11.34.20  egin{equation}  \int _ X(-f_ t)T^2 \leq \int _ X(-f_ t) eta ^2 + rac Mt\int _ X\omega _1\wedge (T+ eta ) =\int _ X(-f_ t) eta ^2+ rac{4M}{t}. \end{equation} Here the last integral equals four by Stokes' theorem. The right-hand side tends to zero as $t	o \infty $, since $f_ t	o 0$ off $D$ and $ eta ^2(D)=0$; as $-f_ t=1$ on $D$, this gives $T^2(D)=0$. Off $D$ the currents $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ and $T$ agree, so locality and the fact that the extended measure puts no mass on the pole set prove ( 11.34.19 ). For the Hermitian background $ eta $, theorem 14.19.2 with density $\mathrm e^ F$ gives a bounded solution $w$ and a constant $c>0$, and the correspondence above turns it into a solution $\psi +w$ in the ordinary type of $\varphi $. Every potential of that type has mass four, so integration forces $c=4/\int _ X\mathrm e^ F\mathrm dV$, which is the formula for $B_\varphi $. Jensen's inequality for the probability $
u _ F=\mathrm e^ F\mathrm dV/\int _ X\mathrm e^ F\mathrm dV$ gives \[  B_\varphi (G)\leq B_\varphi (F)-\int _ X(G-F)\, \mathrm d
u _ F.  \] Thus $

title: Lemma 11.34.16

text: Lemma 11.34.16 . FADB0C708F54 Write $x=\log |z|^2$ and $\chi (x)=\log (1+\mathrm e^ x)$. The envelope $\varphi =P_\theta [\psi ]$ is 69FAA61D9E93 11.34.17 \begin{equation}  \varphi =W(x)-2\chi (x),\qquad W(x)=\begin{cases} x+2\log 2,& x\leq 0,\\ 2\chi (x),& x\geq 0.\end{cases} \end{equation} It satisfies $\psi \leq \varphi \leq 0$, $0\leq \varphi -\psi \leq 2\log 2$, and the model condition ( 16.28.67 ) with $\varepsilon =3/4$. Proof. The function $W$ is convex: both one-sided derivatives at zero equal one, and the derivative of $2\chi $ increases from one to two on $[0,\infty )$. Since $\omega _1=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi (x)$ on the affine chart, $W-2\chi $ is $2\omega _1$-plurisubharmonic there. Since $W$ has slope one for $x\leq 0$ and agrees with $2\chi $ for $x\geq 0$, the function $W-2\chi $ extends to a global $2\omega _1$-plurisubharmonic function, with a logarithmic pole along $D$ and equal to zero where $|z|\geq 1$. The asserted bounds follow from $\psi =x-\chi $: the difference $\varphi -\psi $ equals $2\log 2-\chi $ for $x\leq 0$ and $\chi -x$ for $x\geq 0$. For $C>0$ write $v_ C=P_\theta (\min \{ \psi +C,0\} )$. Rotations of the first factor and the transitive unitary action on the second preserve the whole competitor class, so the envelope is radial and independent of the second factor. The function $V_ C=2\chi +v_ C$ is then convex in $x$ and satisfies $V_ C\leq \chi +x+C$. This upper bound as $x\to -\infty $ forces the slope of $V_ C$ at $-\infty $ to be at least one, and by convexity all its slopes are at least one. For $x<0$, \[  V_ C(x)\leq V_ C(0)+x\leq 2\log 2+x=W(x).  \] For $x\geq 0$, the zero obstacle gives $V_ C\leq 2\chi =W$. Consequently $v_ C\leq \varphi $. If $C\geq 2\log 2$, the bounds already proved make $\varphi $ a competitor, so $v_ C=\varphi $. Letting $C\to \infty $ proves $P_\theta [\psi ]=\varphi $. Since $\varphi \sim \psi $ and the ordinary envelope depends only on the singularity type, also $P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi $. Finally \[  \tfrac 34\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\tfrac 12\omega _1+\tfrac 32\omega _2+[D]\geq 0.  \] Since $\psi \leq \varphi $, the function $\psi $ is a competitor for $P_{(3/4)\theta }(\varphi )$, which is therefore not identically $-\infty $. $\square$

u _ F=\mathrm e^ F\mathrm dV/\int _ X\mathrm e^ F\mathrm dV$ gives \[  B_\varphi (G)\leq B_\varphi (F)-\int _ X(G-F)\, \mathrm d
u _ F.  \] Thus $

u _ F$. This normalization uses the residual mass: since $\int _ X	heta \wedge Q=3/2$, the cofactor $Q$ is not a normalized Gauduchon current for $	heta $ in the sense of section 11.7 . $\square$

The right-hand side tends to zero and is dominated by an integrable logarithmic pole, which proves $L^1$ convergence. Continuity of distributional differentiation then gives the limit of the cofactors. A locally integrable function times the smooth form $\beta $ has absolutely continuous coefficients, so it cannot produce the singular coefficients of $[D]$. For convergence in capacity, use the capacity $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega $ of section 5.29 ; after subtracting one, its test potentials range over $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $-1\leq v\leq 0$. For such $v$, apply the cutoff argument of ( 11.34.20 ) with $\beta $ replaced by $\omega $ and $w=v+1$. Stokes' theorem gives $\int _ X\omega _1\wedge (2\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)=2$, so \[  \operatorname {Cap}_\omega \{ \psi <-t\}  \leq \int _ X(-f_ t)\omega ^2+2/t\longrightarrow 0.  \] The same bound shows that $D$ has capacity zero. For $\eta >0$, the set of points off $D$ where $u_{\delta ,g}-\psi >\eta $ is contained in \[  \left\{ r<\frac{\delta \mathrm e^{\max g}}{\mathrm e^\eta -1}\right\} .  \] This is a sublevel set of $\psi $ whose level tends to $-\infty $ as $\delta \downarrow 0$. The capacity bound for such sublevel sets, together with $\operatorname {Cap}_\omega (D)=0$, proves convergence in capacity. Finally, $\Omega _{\delta ,g}\geq \omega $ gives $F_{\delta ,g}\geq -\log 2$. In the affine chart $|\mathrm d\psi |_\omega ^2\leq C/r$, while $g$ and its first two derivatives are bounded. The decomposition above yields $\Omega _{\delta ,g}\leq C_ g(1+r^{-1})\omega $, hence \[  |F_{\delta ,g}|\leq C_ g+2|\log r|.  \] Every finite power of this logarithmic bound is integrable. Smooth convergence off $D$ gives $F_{\delta ,g}\to 0$ there, and dominated convergence proves convergence in $L^ p$. $\square$

Proposition 11.38.1 . 170451FB65CB Let $	heta =\omega $ be a Hermitian form, and let $\varphi =0$. There are real constants $A$ and, for every $q>1$, $a_ q$ such that every Borel probability measure $

By proposition 11.38.1 , the difference $H_0(
u )-\operatorname {Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}(
u )$ is a finite real number for every $

u \in \mathcal P_{\mathrm{ent}}(X)}  igl (H_0(

u \in \mathcal P_{\mathrm{ent}}(X)}  igl (H_0(
u )-\operatorname {Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}(
u ) igr ) & =\log v_+(\omega ). \end{split}  \] The same extrema are obtained over smooth strictly positive probability measures. Here $\log 0=-\infty $ and $\log (+\infty )=+\infty $. u _ G=Z_ G^{-1}\mathrm{e}^ G\, \mathrm{d}V$, which has finite entropy. Testing the supremum defining $H_0$ with $G$ gives \[  H_0(
u _ G)-\operatorname {Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}(
u _ G) \geq B_0(G)+\log Z_ G.  \] In the other direction, let $\sigma _ G$ be the smooth strictly positive Gauduchon adjoint probability of theorem 11.34.9 . u _ G$ and $\sigma _ G$ are smooth and strictly positive, the last two inequalities prove sharpness on this smaller domain, including the cases $v_-(\omega )=0$ and $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $. u )$ by $-\int _ Xa\, \mathrm{d}

text: Theorem 11.40.1 . 133439CA2DC1 Suppose $0<\varepsilon <1$ and $(1-\varepsilon )\beta \leq \beta '\leq (1+\varepsilon )\beta $. For every bounded measurable $F$, 2E9A16E3BAFF 11.40.2 \begin{equation}  n\log (1-\varepsilon )\leq B_{\beta '}(F)-B_\beta (F)\leq n\log (1+\varepsilon ). \end{equation} In particular, $d(B_\beta ,B_{\beta '})\leq -n\log (1-\varepsilon )$. The same conclusion holds if the two inequalities between forms are satisfied by positive representatives $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ and $\beta '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h'$, with $h,h'$ smooth real functions. Proof. First let $F$ be smooth, and let $v,v'$ be smooth solutions in the two backgrounds. At a maximum point of $v'-(1+\varepsilon )v$, \[  0<\beta '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v'\leq (1+\varepsilon )(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v).  \] Taking determinants and canceling $\mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V$ gives the upper bound. At a minimum point of $v'-(1-\varepsilon )v$, the reverse inequality between forms gives the lower bound. For bounded measurable $F$, choose smooth uniformly bounded approximations converging in $L^1$ and apply theorem 11.33.5 in each of the two backgrounds. Finally, the correspondence $v\mapsto v-h$ preserves both boundedness and the current, so $B_{\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h}=B_\beta $ whenever both backgrounds are positive. text: Proposition 11.40.4 . 1A47D2E8B6D5 Let $\beta _ j,\beta $ be Hermitian forms and $F_ j,F$ smooth real functions with $\beta _ j\to \beta $ and $F_ j\to F$ in $C^\infty $. Then the solutions $v_ j$ for $(\beta _ j,F_ j)$ normalized by $\int _ Xv_ j\, \mathrm{d}V=0$ converge in $C^\infty $ to the similarly normalized solution $v$ for $(\beta ,F)$, and their scalars converge as well. Proof. Fix $k\geq 0$ and $0<\alpha <1$. On the open set where $\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w>0$, consider the smooth map \[  (\eta ,G,w,a)\longmapsto \log \frac{(\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n}{\mathrm{d}V}-a-G  \] defined for $C^{k,\alpha }$ forms $\eta $ and functions $G$, mean-zero $C^{k+2,\alpha }$ potentials $w$ and $a\in \mathbb R$, with values in $C^{k,\alpha }$. At the limiting solution its derivative in $(w,a)$ is $(h,q)\mapsto \Delta _\Omega h-q$, where $\Omega =\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ and $\Delta _\Omega h=n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\wedge \Omega ^{n-1}/\Omega ^ n$. Given a target $g$, choose $q=-\int _ Xg\, \mathrm{d}\mu _ v$, where $\mu _ v$ is the adjoint probability of proposition 11.23.2 . The Fredholm alternative then gives a unique mean-zero $h$ with $\Delta _\Omega h=g+q$, and the inverse is bounded as in proposition 14.4.1 . In dimension one this is the Fredholm alternative for the Poisson equation. The implicit function theorem gives a local branch of solutions depending continuously on the parameters in these spaces. For smooth parameters, uniqueness of bounded solutions modulo constants, corollary 14.24.17 , identifies this branch with the global smooth solution. Thus $v_ j\to v$ in $C^{k+2,\alpha }$ for every $k$, which proves the assertion. $\square$
