title: 11.41 Divisorial types and moving sections
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: For a reference given by logarithms of holomorphic sections, removing its divisorial part identifies its ordinary singularity type with the bounded potentials of the residual background. The normalization scalar therefore depends only on the residual form, whereas convergence of the full potentials also requires control of the sections defining the divisors. In this section, $\theta $ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Fix finitely many holomorphic line bundles $L_ r$ on $X$ with smooth Hermitian metrics $h_ r$, nonzero holomorphic sections $s_ r$, and weights $t_ r>0$. Put \[  \varphi =\sum _ r t_ r\log |s_ r|_{h_ r}^2,\qquad \Gamma =\sum _ r t_ r\operatorname {div}(s_ r),\qquad \beta =\theta -\sum _ r t_ rc_1(L_ r,h_ r),  \] where $c_1(L_ r,h_ r)$ is the Chern curvature form, and assume that the residual form $\beta $ is positive. The empty family is allowed, with $\varphi =0$ and $\beta =\theta $. Theorem 11.41.1 . 7281EDB812F1 The ordinary singularity type of $\varphi $ is described by \[  \{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):u\sim \varphi \}  =\{ \varphi +w:w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\beta )\cap L^\infty (X)\} ,  \] and for each such $w$, 345F0935B009 11.41.2 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\varphi +w)=(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n. \end{equation} For every bounded measurable $F$, the equation ( 11.33.1 ) in this ordinary type has a unique constant and a solution unique modulo constants. Its normalization scalar $B_{\theta ,[\varphi ]}$ satisfies \[  B_{\theta ,[\varphi ]}(F)=B_\beta (F),  \] so its dual functional and supporting sets coincide with $H_\beta $ and $\mathcal A_\beta $. Proof. The Poincaré–Lelong formula gives $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi =[\Gamma ]+\beta $, so every function on the right is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic and has the type of $\varphi $. Conversely, let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\sim \varphi $. Then $u$ has the same generic Lelong numbers as $\varphi $ along the components of $\Gamma $, namely the coefficients of $\Gamma $, and lemma 5.38.1 gives \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-[\Gamma ]\geq 0.  \] The locally integrable difference $w=u-\varphi $ therefore has a $\beta $-plurisubharmonic representative. It is bounded off the divisor because $u\sim \varphi $, and the local submean property preserves both bounds across the divisor. Since $u$ and $\varphi +w$ agree almost everywhere, they are equal as quasi-plurisubharmonic functions. Off the divisor, the currents $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi +w)$ and $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ agree, and locality identifies their Monge–Ampère products there. The extended measure on the left gives the divisor zero mass, and so does the bounded product on the right, which is finite and charges no analytic set by section 5.28 . This proves ( 11.41.2 ). In the background $\beta $, the equation with bounded density has a continuous solution and a unique constant by theorem 14.19.2 , proposition 14.19.34 . The density $\mathrm{e}^ F$ is bounded above and below by positive constants, so corollary 14.24.17 gives uniqueness modulo constants. The correspondence transfers these assertions to the whole ordinary type and identifies the functionals. $\square$ In particular, the comparison of backgrounds and the stability of supporting probabilities in theorem 11.40.1 , corollary 11.40.3 apply whenever the positive residual forms satisfy the two-sided inequalities there; the location of the divisors does not enter these estimates. This statement concerns ordinary types. To interpret it in terms of model references, one also needs the envelope $P_\theta [\varphi ]$ to differ from $\varphi $ by a bounded function. For a Hermitian $\theta $, lemma 11.41.5 below proves this bounded difference and the smaller-background model condition. For a fixed positive residual $\beta $, uniformly bounded $F_ j\to F$ in $L^1$ give uniform convergence of the residual solutions normalized by $\sup _ Xv_ j=0$. Indeed, continuity of the scalar gives uniformly bounded densities $\mathrm{e}^{B_\beta (F_ j)+F_ j}$ converging in every $L^ p$, $p<\infty $. The compactness theorem theorem 14.19.21 gives uniform convergence of subsequences, continuity of bounded products identifies the limiting equation, and corollary 14.24.17 identifies every limit. Subtracting the means gives the same conclusion for solutions normalized to have mean zero. Theorem 11.41.3 . BF6A67E9A40E Keep the line bundles and metrics fixed. Let nonzero sections $s_{jr}$ converge to $s_ r\ne 0$ in the finite-dimensional spaces of global sections, and let positive weights satisfy $t_{jr}\to t_ r>0$. Given Hermitian forms $\beta _ j$, define $\varphi _ j$ and $\theta _ j=\beta _ j+\sum _ rt_{jr}c_1(L_ r,h_ r)$ by the preceding formulas. Suppose either that $\beta _ j\to \beta $ in $C^\infty $ for a Hermitian form $\beta >0$ and $F_ j\to F$ in $C^\infty $, or that $\beta _ j=\beta $ for all $j$ and the tests $F_ j$ converge to $F$ in $L^1$ with a common $L^\infty $ bound. Then $\varphi _ j\to \varphi $ in $L^1$, and the solutions $u_ j\sim \varphi _ j$ for $(\theta _ j,F_ j)$, normalized by $\sup _ Xu_ j=0$, converge in $L^1$ to the similarly normalized solution $u\sim \varphi $. For the residual solutions $v_ j$ normalized to have mean zero, one also has \[  \sup _ X(\varphi _ j+v_ j)\longrightarrow \sup _ X(\varphi +v).  \] The residuals converge smoothly in the first regime and uniformly in the second. Proof. The convergence of the residual solutions follows from proposition 11.40.4 in the first case and from the preceding compactness argument in the second. The fixed metrics and bounded weights give a common smooth lower bound for $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j$. The convergent sections give a common upper bound for $\varphi _ j$ and convergence at a point outside all limiting divisors, so the suprema of the $\varphi _ j$ are bounded above and below. By theorem 5.25.2 , every subsequence has a further subsequence converging in $L^1$. Off the limiting divisors, convergence of the sections and weights gives local uniform convergence to $\varphi $; since those divisors have zero volume, every $L^1$ cluster point equals $\varphi $. Thus $\varphi _ j\to \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$. Put $C_ j=\sup _ X(\varphi _ j+v_ j)$ and $C=\sup _ X(\varphi +v)$. The sums converge in $L^1$ and have a common smooth lower bound for their complex Hessians, since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j\geq -\beta _ j$ and the residual forms are uniformly bounded. Applying lemma 5.25.1 at maximum points gives $\limsup _ jC_ j\leq C$. A maximum point of $\varphi +v$ lies off the poles of $\varphi $, and evaluation there, using local uniform convergence, gives $\liminf _ jC_ j\geq C$. It follows that $u_ j=\varphi _ j+v_ j-C_ j\to \varphi +v-C=u$ in $L^1$. For an empty family of divisors, the assertion reduces to the convergence of the residual solutions and of their suprema. $\square$

text:
The ordinary-type correspondence extends to potentials with additional poles. It then identifies the largest subsolution coefficient in the whole one-sided class, even for merely integrable data. For smooth positive data, the prescribed divisor causes a strict loss relative to the global coefficient. Keep the divisorial setting above, assume also that $	heta $ is a Hermitian form and $n\ge 2$, and subtract a constant from $\varphi $ so that $\sup _ X\varphi =0$. Write $S=\operatorname {Supp}\Gamma $ and $\psi =P_	heta [\varphi ]$. For a nonempty class $\mathcal A\subset \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and nonzero $0\le f\in L^1(\mathrm dV)$, define \[  b_{	heta ,\mathcal A}(f)=\sup \{ c\ge 0:	ext{some }u\in \mathcal A 	ext{ satisfies }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (u) \ge cf\, \mathrm dV\} .  \] The three classes considered here are \[   egin{aligned}  \mathcal A_{\preceq }& =\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):u\preceq \varphi \} ,\  \mathcal A_{\sim }& =\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):u\sim \varphi \} ,\  \mathcal A_{\mathrm{env}}& =\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,	heta ,\psi ). \end{aligned}  \] The following lemma supplies the genuine reference $\psi $ used in the last definition. Lemma 11.41.5 . CC6718D255AC The map $w\mapsto \varphi +w$ is a bijection from $\mathrm{PSH}(X, eta )$ onto $\mathcal A_{\preceq }$, and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_	heta (\varphi +w) =\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_ eta (w).  \] Its bounded members correspond to $\mathcal A_{\sim }$. The envelope $\psi $ is genuine, satisfies $\varphi \le \psi \le \varphi +K$ for some finite $K$, meets the model condition ( 16.28.67 ), and \[  \mathcal A_{\sim }\subset \mathcal A_{\mathrm{env}} \subset \mathcal A_{\preceq }.  \] Proof. If $u\preceq \varphi $, its generic Lelong numbers dominate the coefficients of $\Gamma $. By lemma 5.38.1 , $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-[\Gamma ]\ge 0$. The locally integrable distribution $w=u-\varphi $ therefore has a canonical $ eta $-psh representative. Off $S$ it equals the difference and is bounded above. The identity $u=\varphi +w$ holds almost everywhere, hence everywhere for the canonical quasi-psh functions. Conversely, $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X, eta )$ has finite supremum, and \[  	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi +w)= eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w+[\Gamma ]\ge 0, \qquad \varphi +w\preceq \varphi .  \] These maps are inverse. The bounded correspondence is theorem 11.41.1 . Off $S$ the currents agree; locality of the extended products identifies their measures there. Both measures give the analytic set $S$ zero mass by theorem 13.14.3 , even when $w$ has additional poles or infinite mass. This proves the measure identity on $X$ without subtracting infinite pointwise values. For an envelope competitor $v\le 0$ with $v\preceq \varphi $, the corresponding $w=v-\varphi $ satisfies $w\le -\varphi $ off $S$. Hence \[  \int _ Xw^+\, \mathrm dV\le \int _ X(-\varphi )\, \mathrm dV<\infty ,  \] uniformly in $v$. On a fixed finite cover by inner and outer coordinate balls, add smooth quadratic corrections making $w$ locally psh. Submean at a point attaining $\sup _ Xw$, with uniform correction and volume-ratio bounds, gives $\sup _ Xw\le C_1\int _ Xw^+\, \mathrm dV+C_2\le K$. Thus $v\le \varphi +K$ canonically. The function $\varphi $ itself is a competitor, so the ordinary envelope construction gives a genuine $	heta $-psh function between $\varphi $ and $\varphi +K$. The upper bound survives upper regularization because $\varphi +K$ is upper semicontinuous. Ordinary equivalence gives $P_	heta [\psi ]=P_	heta [\varphi ]=\psi $. For $\varepsilon <1$ sufficiently close to one, $ eta -(1-\varepsilon )	heta >0$, so $\varphi $ is an $\varepsilon 	heta $-psh competitor below $\psi $. Hence $P_{\varepsilon 	heta }(\psi )$ is not identically $-\infty $, as required in ( 16.28.67 ). If $u\sim \varphi \sim \psi $, choose $K_ u\ge 0$ with $\psi -K_ u\le u$. For each $t\ge 1$, the $	heta $-psh function $a_ t=\psi -tK_ u$ obeys \[  t^{-1}a_ t+(1-t^{-1})\psi =\psi -K_ u\le u.  \] This proves relative envelope-class membership in definition 16.28.61 , including the convention at $t=1$ and common poles. The other containment follows from its defining order $u\preceq \psi \sim \varphi $. $\square$ Theorem 11.41.6 . C87E852ED386 For every nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathrm dV)$, \[  b_{	heta ,\mathcal A_{\preceq }}(f)=b_ eta (f),  \] and this coefficient is attained. If $f$ is smooth and strictly positive, then \[  b_{	heta ,\mathcal A_{\sim }}(f) =b_{	heta ,\mathcal A_{\mathrm{env}}}(f) =b_{	heta ,\mathcal A_{\preceq }}(f)=c_ eta (f),  \] with an exact finite equation attained in the ordinary type of $\varphi $. title: Lemma 11.41.5
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Lemma 11.41.5 . CC6718D255AC The map $w\mapsto \varphi +w$ is a bijection from $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\beta )$ onto $\mathcal A_{\preceq }$, and \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\varphi +w) =\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\beta (w).  \] Its bounded members correspond to $\mathcal A_{\sim }$. The envelope $\psi $ is genuine, satisfies $\varphi \le \psi \le \varphi +K$ for some finite $K$, meets the model condition ( 16.28.67 ), and \[  \mathcal A_{\sim }\subset \mathcal A_{\mathrm{env}} \subset \mathcal A_{\preceq }.  \] Proof. If $u\preceq \varphi $, its generic Lelong numbers dominate the coefficients of $\Gamma $. By lemma 5.38.1 , $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-[\Gamma ]\ge 0$. The locally integrable distribution $w=u-\varphi $ therefore has a canonical $\beta $-psh representative. Off $S$ it equals the difference and is bounded above. The identity $u=\varphi +w$ holds almost everywhere, hence everywhere for the canonical quasi-psh functions. Conversely, $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\beta )$ has finite supremum, and \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi +w)=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w+[\Gamma ]\ge 0, \qquad \varphi +w\preceq \varphi .  \] These maps are inverse. The bounded correspondence is theorem 11.41.1 . Off $S$ the currents agree; locality of the extended products identifies their measures there. Both measures give the analytic set $S$ zero mass by theorem 13.14.3 , even when $w$ has additional poles or infinite mass. This proves the measure identity on $X$ without subtracting infinite pointwise values. For an envelope competitor $v\le 0$ with $v\preceq \varphi $, the corresponding $w=v-\varphi $ satisfies $w\le -\varphi $ off $S$. The other containment follows from its defining order $u\preceq \psi \sim \varphi $. $\square$

title: 11.42 The mass determined by the functional
search_title: The mass determined by the functional
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
section: 11.42 The mass determined by the functional
text: In a closed background, the information lost by the scalar functional can be described exactly: for the model references below, two functionals agree precisely when the masses agree. This also gives examples in which the supporting probabilities stay fixed while the potentials have different limits. In this section $X$ is a compact Kähler manifold and $\theta $ is any smooth closed big real $(1,1)$-form. Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi $, have small unbounded locus in the sense of section 5.33 , and have positive mass \[  m_\varphi =\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (\varphi )>0.  \] Write $B_{\theta ,\varphi }$ and $\mathcal A_{\theta ,\varphi }$ for the normalization scalar and the supporting sets of the equation ( 11.33.1 ) in the ordinary type of $\varphi $, and put $Z_ F=\int _ X\mathrm{e}^ F\, \mathrm{d}V$. Theorem 11.42.1 . 1DCF668EBCCF For every such pair $(\theta ,\varphi )$ and every bounded measurable $F$, the equation in the ordinary type of $\varphi $ has a unique constant and a solution unique modulo constants. Its normalization scalar is \[  B_{\theta ,\varphi }(F)=\log m_\varphi -\log Z_ F.  \] For continuous real $F$, its supporting set is \[  \mathcal A_{\theta ,\varphi }(F)=\{ \mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V/Z_ F\} .  \] For two such pairs on the same $X$, with the same $\mathrm{d}V$ and possibly in different classes, B169C3B4AD17 11.42.2 \begin{equation}  \sup _{F\in L^\infty }|B_{\theta ,\varphi }(F)-B_{\theta ',\psi }(F)| =|\log m_\varphi -\log m_\psi |. \end{equation} Thus an invariant of these pairs is determined by the whole functional if and only if it is constant on every fiber of the map $(\theta ,\varphi )\mapsto m_\varphi $. Proof. Existence follows from corollary 10.31.56 . Indeed, a Kähler manifold has the bounded mass property by lemma 19.9.12 , and since in a closed background all potentials of the ordinary type of $\varphi $ have the same mass $m_\varphi >0$, the reference satisfies the positive-volume model condition ( 13.20.5 ). Uniqueness modulo constants is the classical theorem on equations with prescribed singularities in closed big classes, which applies under the model and small-unbounded-locus hypotheses; see the notes in section 25.13 . Every potential of the ordinary type of $\varphi $ has mass $m_\varphi $, so integrating the equation forces $cZ_ F=m_\varphi $, which is the scalar formula. For continuous $F$, Jensen's inequality shows, as for ( 11.37.2 ), that the normalized exponential measure is a supporting probability, and differentiating at zero in both signs of every continuous direction shows that it is the only one. Subtracting the scalar formulas gives ( 11.42.2 ). Finally, $m_\varphi =\mathrm{d}V(X)\exp B_{\theta ,\varphi }(0)$, so the functional and the mass determine each other, and an invariant factors through either one exactly when it is constant on the fibers of the mass map. $\square$ For an ordinary divisorial type whose residual form $\beta $ is positive and closed, theorem 11.41.1 gives the same formula with mass $\int _ X\beta ^ n$, since Stokes' theorem for bounded products in a closed background fixes the mass of every bounded $\beta $-plurisubharmonic function. This computation does not require the real weighted sum of divisors to have a model representative. If $\beta _ j\to \beta $ uniformly, the masses converge by continuity of $\beta \mapsto \int _ X\beta ^ n$; under the two-sided bounds $(1-\varepsilon _ j)\beta \leq \beta _ j\leq (1+\varepsilon _ j)\beta $ one has the sharper inequalities $(1-\varepsilon _ j)^ n\int \beta ^ n\leq \int \beta _ j^ n\leq (1+\varepsilon _ j)^ n\int \beta ^ n$. Example 11.42.3 . C6588E30CFF6 Let $X=\mathbb P^ n$ with $n\geq 1$, let $\theta $ be the Fubini–Study form, normalized by $\int _ X\theta ^ n=1$, and let $D$ be a hyperplane. Let $s_ D$ be a section of $\mathcal O(1)$ defining $D$, measured with the Fubini–Study metric and rescaled so that $a_ D=\log |s_ D|^2\leq 0$, and choose $t\in (0,1)$. Then \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ D=[D]-\theta ,\qquad \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(ta_ D)=(1-t)\theta +t[D].  \] Put $\varphi _{t,D}=P_\theta [ta_ D]$. By proposition 18.4.8 , this envelope fixed point has the ordinary type of $ta_ D$. Moreover $ta_ D\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,t\theta )$ and $ta_ D\leq \varphi _{t,D}$, so $\varphi _{t,D}$ satisfies ( 16.28.67 ) with $\varepsilon =t$. Off $D$, the potential $ta_ D$ has Monge–Ampère measure $(1-t)^ n\theta ^ n$, and its non-pluripolar measure puts no mass on $D$. Since mass is invariant under bounded changes of the potential in a closed background, \[  m_{\varphi _{t,D}}=(1-t)^ n,\qquad B_{\varphi _{t,D}}(G)-B_0(G)=n\log (1-t)\quad (G\in C(X,\mathbb R)).  \] Thus the constant in proposition 11.39.1 is sharp. Now let $n=1$, and take for $D$ two distinct points $p,q\in \mathbb P^1$. The corresponding references have distance zero, although $\varphi _{t,p}$ is unbounded near $p$ and bounded near $q$, while $\varphi _{t,q}$ behaves in the opposite way; in particular they are not ordinarily equivalent. For every positive integer $m$, \[  \mathcal I(m\varphi _{t,p})=\mathcal O(-\lfloor mt\rfloor p),\qquad \mathcal I(m\varphi _{t,q})=\mathcal O(-\lfloor mt\rfloor q),  \] by lemma 5.37.1 , and for $mt\geq 1$ these ideals differ. Thus the distance $\Delta $ of ( 11.39.3 ) does not even separate multiplier-ideal types, and it determines neither the ordinary nor the ideal singularity type. Fix a smooth real function $F$ on $\mathbb P^1$, and let $w_ F$ be the solution of $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ F=\mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V/Z_ F$ with $\int _ Xw_ F\, \mathrm{d}V=0$. The normalized solutions for $D=p$ and $D=q$ are \[  u_{t,D}=ta_ D+(1-t)w_ F-\sup _ X\bigl (ta_ D+(1-t)w_ F\bigr ).  \] Their difference satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_{t,p}-u_{t,q})=t([p]-[q])\ne 0$. Hence the sequence of solutions obtained by alternating between $D=p$ and $D=q$ has two different $L^1$ cluster points, although the scalar functional and all its supporting sets are the same at every step. Within this one-parameter family, the functional does recover $t$, since $t\mapsto (1-t)^ n$ is injective. Example 11.42.4 . 0B7F3ACBCCC4 On $\mathbb P^ n$, $n\geq 2$, let $\omega $ be the Fubini–Study form, normalized as in example 11.42.3 , and let $f$ be a nonconstant smooth real function. Fix $0<t<1$ and put \[  \beta =\mathrm{e}^ f\omega ,\qquad \theta =\beta +t\omega ,\qquad \varphi _ D=t\log |s_ D|^2.  \] Here $s_ D$ defines a hyperplane $D$ as in example 11.42.3 , and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ D=\beta +t[D]$, so every hyperplane has the same positive residual form $\beta $. This form is not closed: $\mathrm{d}\beta =\mathrm{e}^ f\mathrm{d}f\wedge \omega \not\equiv 0$, since $\mathrm{d}f$ is nonzero somewhere and wedging a one-form with $\omega ^{n-1}$ is injective. By theorem 11.41.1 , the ordinary types of all $\varphi _ D$ have the same functional $B_\beta $ on bounded tests, hence the same supporting sets. At a smooth test, the common supporting probability is the Gauduchon adjoint probability of theorem 11.34.9 . If $v_ F$ is the common smooth residual solution, the normalized solutions are the functions $\varphi _ D+v_ F-\sup _ X(\varphi _ D+v_ F)$. Two distinct hyperplanes $D_1,D_2$ give different poles, different divisorial coefficients and, for sufficiently large $k$, different multiplier ideals $\mathcal O(-\lfloor kt\rfloor D_ i)$, by the calculation in normal coordinates of lemma 5.37.1 . The potentials differ by more than a constant, since the difference of their complex Hessians is $t([D_1]-[D_2])$, and alternating between the two hyperplanes again produces two distinct $L^1$ limits. These conclusions come from the common residual form; for general nonclosed backgrounds we do not claim that the functional is determined by a mass.

The normalized solutions for $D=p$ and $D=q$ are \[  u_{t,D}=ta_ D+(1-t)w_ F-\sup _ X\bigl (ta_ D+(1-t)w_ F\bigr ).  \] Their difference satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_{t,p}-u_{t,q})=t([p]-[q])\ne 0$. Hence the sequence of solutions obtained by alternating between $D=p$ and $D=q$ has two different $L^1$ cluster points, although the scalar functional and all its supporting sets are the same at every step. Within this one-parameter family, the functional does recover $t$, since $t\mapsto (1-t)^ n$ is injective.

text: Example 11.42.4 . 0B7F3ACBCCC4 On $\mathbb P^ n$, $n\geq 2$, let $\omega $ be the Fubini–Study form, normalized as in example 11.42.3 , and let $f$ be a nonconstant smooth real function. Fix $0<t<1$ and put \[  \beta =\mathrm{e}^ f\omega ,\qquad \theta =\beta +t\omega ,\qquad \varphi _ D=t\log |s_ D|^2.  \] Here $s_ D$ defines a hyperplane $D$ as in example 11.42.3 , and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ D=\beta +t[D]$, so every hyperplane has the same positive residual form $\beta $. This form is not closed: $\mathrm{d}\beta =\mathrm{e}^ f\mathrm{d}f\wedge \omega \not\equiv 0$, since $\mathrm{d}f$ is nonzero somewhere and wedging a one-form with $\omega ^{n-1}$ is injective. By theorem 11.41.1 , the ordinary types of all $\varphi _ D$ have the same functional $B_\beta $ on bounded tests, hence the same supporting sets. At a smooth test, the common supporting probability is the Gauduchon adjoint probability of theorem 11.34.9 . If $v_ F$ is the common smooth residual solution, the normalized solutions are the functions $\varphi _ D+v_ F-\sup _ X(\varphi _ D+v_ F)$. Two distinct hyperplanes $D_1,D_2$ give different poles, different divisorial coefficients and, for sufficiently large $k$, different multiplier ideals $\mathcal O(-\lfloor kt\rfloor D_ i)$, by the calculation in normal coordinates of lemma 5.37.1 . The potentials differ by more than a constant, since the difference of their complex Hessians is $t([D_1]-[D_2])$, and alternating between the two hyperplanes again produces two distinct $L^1$ limits. title: 11.43 Convex-body criteria for varying references
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: When the singularities of a torus-invariant reference are described by a convex body, the closed mass formula of theorem 11.42.1 turns convergence of the convex bodies into convergence of the functionals. A translated simplex contained in all the bodies keeps the limiting reference solvable, and the Hausdorff distance then controls the functionals uniformly over all continuous tests, even though the ordinary types vary. Let $n\geq 2$, and let $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ be the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^ n$, normalized by $\int _{\mathbb P^ n}\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}^ n=1$. In homogeneous coordinates $[Z_0:\cdots :Z_ n]$, consider the torus $T=\{ Z_0\cdots Z_ n\ne 0\} $, and put \[  x_ i=\log |Z_ i/Z_0|^2,\qquad L(x)=\log \bigl (1+\textstyle \sum _ i\mathrm{e}^{x_ i}\bigr ),\qquad \Sigma =\{ p_ i\geq 0:\textstyle \sum _ i p_ i\leq 1\} ,  \] where $1\leq i\leq n$ and $\Sigma \subset \mathbb R^ n$ is the standard simplex. Functions of $x=(x_1,\ldots ,x_ n)$ are regarded as functions on $T$; thus $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}L$ on $T$. Define the continuous function $\ell $ on $\Sigma $ by \[  \ell (p)=\sum _ i p_ i\log p_ i+ (1-\textstyle \sum _ i p_ i)\log (1-\textstyle \sum _ i p_ i), \qquad 0\log 0=0.  \] For a convex body $K\subset \Sigma $, that is, a compact convex set with nonempty interior, set \[  h_ K(x)=\sup _{p\in K}p\cdot x,\qquad g_ K(x)=\sup _{p\in K}\{ p\cdot x-\ell (p)\} .  \]

ot\equiv -\infty $. Proof. The Legendre transform of $L$ is $L^*=\ell $ on $\Sigma $ and $+\infty $ outside it. Since $-\log (n+1)\leq \ell \leq 0$, \[  h_ K\leq g_ K\leq h_ K+\log (n+1),\qquad g_ K\leq L,\qquad h_ K\leq h_\Sigma \leq L.  \] A finite convex function of the logarithmic moduli is plurisubharmonic: for a smooth convex function the complex Hessian is positive, and convolution gives the general case. On $T\cap \{ Z_ j
e 0\} $, add the local Fubini–Study potential $\log \sum _ i|Z_ i/Z_ j|^2$; the resulting functions are again convex functions of the logarithmic moduli of the affine coordinates, and they are bounded above by that smooth potential because $h_ K,g_ K\leq L$. If $p\in \operatorname {int}K$, then $p\in \operatorname {int}\Sigma $, and at $x_ i=\log (p_ i/(1-\sum _ k p_ k))$ the supremum defining $L=\ell ^*$ is attained at $p\in K$, so $g_ K(x)=L(x)$. For $r>0$, the reference $r\pi ^*\Phi _ K$ satisfies $P_{r\Theta }[r\pi ^*\Phi _ K]=r\pi ^*\Phi _ K$, has small unbounded locus, and satisfies C1218CE2B784 11.43.4  egin{equation}  \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_{r\Theta }(r\pi ^*\Phi _ K) =r^ n n!\operatorname {Vol}_ n(K). \end{equation} If $p_*+\delta \Sigma \subset K$ with $0<\delta <1$, then $P_{(1-\delta )r\Theta }(r\pi ^*\Phi _ K)
ot\equiv -\infty $. Proof. On $\mathbb P^ n$, the envelope identity is lemma 11.43.2 . In the blowup case, every $\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$-plurisubharmonic function descends to $\mathbb P^ n$. The hypothesis of a common simplex allows ordinary singularity types that contain no potential with analytic singularities. Let $o=[1:0:\cdots :0]$ be the origin of the affine chart $Z_0
e 0$, with affine coordinates $z_ i=Z_ i/Z_0$. For $0<a\leq 1$, define \[  P_ a=\{ p\in \Sigma :	extstyle \sum _ i\sqrt{p_ i}\geq \sqrt a\} , \qquad \kappa _ n= rac{2^ n n!}{(2n)!}= rac1{(2n-1)!!}.  \] Proposition 11.43.10 . 70BE47F32080 The function $\Phi _{P_ a}$ is locally bounded outside the single point $o$, where it has a pole, and it does not have the ordinary singularity type of any function with analytic singularities. Its generic Lelong number along every prime divisor of $\mathbb P^ n$ is zero, and 47DDB1E89607 11.43.11  egin{equation}  \int _{\mathbb P^ n}\mathrm{MA}_{\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}}(\Phi _{P_ a}) =1-\kappa _ n a^ n>0. \end{equation} The same assertions about the pole, nonanalyticity and generic Lelong numbers hold for $\pi ^*\Phi _{P_ a}$ on the blowup $\operatorname {Bl}_ q\mathbb P^ n$ at a fixed point $q
e o$. Proof. The function $p\mapsto \sum _ i\sqrt{p_ i}$ is concave, so $P_ a$ is convex. Set \[  b= rac{n+1}{2n},\qquad p_{*,i}= rac bn, \qquad \delta = rac{n-1}{4n}.  \] Then $b+\delta <1$ and $\sum _ i\sqrt{p_{*,i}}=\sqrt{(n+1)/2}>1$. Adding a point of $\delta \Sigma $ preserves the last inequality and keeps the sum of the coordinates below one, so $p_*+\delta \Sigma $ lies in every $P_ a$. All the standard basis vectors $e_ i$ belong to $P_ a$, and therefore \[  \psi _{P_ a}\geq \log  rac{\max _{1\leq i\leq n}|Z_ i|^2}{\sum _{i=0}^ n|Z_ i|^2}.  \] Hence the reference is locally bounded away from $o$. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives $\sum _ ip_ i\geq a/n$ on $P_ a$. When all $x_ i<0$, this yields $h_{P_ a}(x)\leq (a/n)\max _ i x_ i$, which tends to $-\infty $ as $z	o o$, and lemma 11.43.2 gives the pole at $o$. Local boundedness outside one point implies that all generic Lelong numbers along prime divisors vanish, and pulling back to the blowup at a different point introduces no pole. To test analyticity, fix positive $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ n$ and approach $o$ along $|z_ i|^2=\mathrm{e}^{-R\lambda _ i}$, $R	o \infty $. Writing $y_ i=\sqrt{p_ i}$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives 6654DDDC658F 11.43.12  egin{equation}  \min _{p\in P_ a}\sum _ i\lambda _ i p_ i = rac a{\sum _ i\lambda _ i^{-1}}=:d_ a(\lambda ),\qquad y_ i= rac{\sqrt a}{\lambda _ i\sum _ k\lambda _ k^{-1}}, \end{equation} where the minimizer satisfies $\sum _ ip_ i\leq a\leq 1$, so that it lies in $P_ a$. Since $L(-R\lambda )	o 0$ and $\Phi _{P_ a}-\psi _{P_ a}$ is bounded, $-\Phi _{P_ a}/R	o d_ a(\lambda )$ along these curves. Suppose that the type were that of $c\log \sum _ k|f_ k|^2$ near $o$, with $c>0$ and holomorphic germs $f_ k=\sum _\alpha c_{k,\alpha }z^\alpha $. Exponentiating the two inequalities expressing this equivalence and averaging over the arguments of the $z_ i$ gives the positive series \[  \sum _{k,\alpha }|c_{k,\alpha }|^2\mathrm{e}^{-R\alpha \cdot \lambda },  \] whose exponential decay rate in $R$ must be $d_ a(\lambda )/c$. That rate is the minimum of $\alpha \cdot \lambda $ over the monomials with nonzero coefficients: a minimizing term gives one bound, and convergence at a fixed $R_0$ bounds the series above by a constant times $\mathrm{e}^{-(R-R_0)\min \alpha \cdot \lambda }$. Near any $\lambda $ with positive coordinates, only finitely many monomials can attain the minimum, because these coordinates have a common positive lower bound and any one nonzero coefficient bounds the degree of the minimizing monomials. The rate is therefore locally piecewise linear in $\lambda $. But \[  d_ a(s,1,\ldots ,1)= rac{as}{1+(n-1)s},\qquad  rac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}s^2}d_ a(s,1,\ldots ,1) =- rac{2a(n-1)}{(1+(n-1)s)^3}<0.  \] This contradiction proves nonanalyticity. The assertion persists on a blowup at a point different from $o$, which does not change a neighborhood of the pole. The removed corner $C_ a=\{ p\in \mathbb R^ n:p_ i\geq 0,\  \sum _ i\sqrt{p_ i}<\sqrt a\} =aC_1$ lies in $\Sigma $. The substitution $p_ i=y_ i^2$ gives \[  \operatorname {Vol}_ n(C_1) =2^ n\int _{y_ i\geq 0,\, \sum y_ i<1}\prod _ i y_ i\, \mathrm{d}y = rac{2^ n}{(2n)!}.  \] The last equality follows by iterated integration of monomials over a simplex. Removing the corner from $\Sigma $, whose volume is $1/n!$, and applying ( 11.43.4 ) gives ( 11.43.11 ). Since $n\geq 2$, one has $\kappa _ n<1$. $\square$ Corollary 11.43.13 . F57433433789 Put $a_ j=1-1/(j+2)$ and $r_ j=1+1/(j+2)$ for $j\geq 1$. On $\mathbb P^ n$, or on its blowup at a fixed point $q
e o$, the references $r_ j\pi ^*\Phi _{P_{a_ j}}$ satisfy the hypotheses of theorem 11.43.6 , with limit $\pi ^*\Phi _{P_1}$. Their ordinary types and masses vary with $j$, and \[  \sup _ G|B_ j(G)-B(G)| \leq n|\log r_ j|+ rac{n\kappa _ n}{1-\kappa _ n}|1-a_ j|\longrightarrow 0.  \] The equation is solvable in the limiting ordinary type, whose mass is $1-\kappa _ n$; for $n=2$ this mass is $2/3$. title: Proposition 11.43.10
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Proposition 11.43.10 . 70BE47F32080 The function $\Phi _{P_ a}$ is locally bounded outside the single point $o$, where it has a pole, and it does not have the ordinary singularity type of any function with analytic singularities. Its generic Lelong number along every prime divisor of $\mathbb P^ n$ is zero, and 47DDB1E89607 11.43.11 \begin{equation}  \int _{\mathbb P^ n}\mathrm{MA}_{\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}}(\Phi _{P_ a}) =1-\kappa _ n a^ n>0. \end{equation} The same assertions about the pole, nonanalyticity and generic Lelong numbers hold for $\pi ^*\Phi _{P_ a}$ on the blowup $\operatorname {Bl}_ q\mathbb P^ n$ at a fixed point $q\ne o$. Proof. The function $p\mapsto \sum _ i\sqrt{p_ i}$ is concave, so $P_ a$ is convex. Set \[  b=\frac{n+1}{2n},\qquad p_{*,i}=\frac bn, \qquad \delta =\frac{n-1}{4n}.  \] Then $b+\delta <1$ and $\sum _ i\sqrt{p_{*,i}}=\sqrt{(n+1)/2}>1$. Adding a point of $\delta \Sigma $ preserves the last inequality and keeps the sum of the coordinates below one, so $p_*+\delta \Sigma $ lies in every $P_ a$. All the standard basis vectors $e_ i$ belong to $P_ a$, and therefore \[  \psi _{P_ a}\geq \log \frac{\max _{1\leq i\leq n}|Z_ i|^2}{\sum _{i=0}^ n|Z_ i|^2}.  \] Hence the reference is locally bounded away from $o$. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives $\sum _ ip_ i\geq a/n$ on $P_ a$. When all $x_ i<0$, this yields $h_{P_ a}(x)\leq (a/n)\max _ i x_ i$, which tends to $-\infty $ as $z\to o$, and lemma 11.43.2 gives the pole at $o$. Local boundedness outside one point implies that all generic Lelong numbers along prime divisors vanish, and pulling back to the blowup at a different point introduces no pole. To test analyticity, fix positive $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ n$ and approach $o$ along $|z_ i|^2=\mathrm{e}^{-R\lambda _ i}$, $R\to \infty $. Writing $y_ i=\sqrt{p_ i}$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives 6654DDDC658F 11.43.12 \begin{equation}  \min _{p\in P_ a}\sum _ i\lambda _ i p_ i =\frac a{\sum _ i\lambda _ i^{-1}}=:d_ a(\lambda ),\qquad y_ i=\frac{\sqrt a}{\lambda _ i\sum _ k\lambda _ k^{-1}}, \end{equation} where the minimizer satisfies $\sum _ ip_ i\leq a\leq 1$, so that it lies in $P_ a$. Since $L(-R\lambda )\to 0$ and $\Phi _{P_ a}-\psi _{P_ a}$ is bounded, $-\Phi _{P_ a}/R\to d_ a(\lambda )$ along these curves. Suppose that the type were that of $c\log \sum _ k|f_ k|^2$ near $o$, with $c>0$ and holomorphic germs $f_ k=\sum _\alpha c_{k,\alpha }z^\alpha $. Exponentiating the two inequalities expressing this equivalence and averaging over the arguments of the $z_ i$ gives the positive series \[  \sum _{k,\alpha }|c_{k,\alpha }|^2\mathrm{e}^{-R\alpha \cdot \lambda },  \] whose exponential decay rate in $R$ must be $d_ a(\lambda )/c$. That rate is the minimum of $\alpha \cdot \lambda $ over the monomials with nonzero coefficients: a minimizing term gives one bound, and convergence at a fixed $R_0$ bounds the series above by a constant times $\mathrm{e}^{-(R-R_0)\min \alpha \cdot \lambda }$. Near any $\lambda $ with positive coordinates, only finitely many monomials can attain the minimum, because these coordinates have a common positive lower bound and any one nonzero coefficient bounds the degree of the minimizing monomials. The rate is therefore locally piecewise linear in $\lambda $. But \[  d_ a(s,1,\ldots ,1)=\frac{as}{1+(n-1)s},\qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}s^2}d_ a(s,1,\ldots ,1) =-\frac{2a(n-1)}{(1+(n-1)s)^3}<0.  \] This contradiction proves nonanalyticity. The assertion persists on a blowup at a point different from $o$, which does not change a neighborhood of the pole. The removed corner $C_ a=\{ p\in \mathbb R^ n:p_ i\geq 0,\  \sum _ i\sqrt{p_ i}<\sqrt a\} =aC_1$ lies in $\Sigma $. The substitution $p_ i=y_ i^2$ gives \[  \operatorname {Vol}_ n(C_1) =2^ n\int _{y_ i\geq 0,\, \sum y_ i<1}\prod _ i y_ i\, \mathrm{d}y =\frac{2^ n}{(2n)!}.  \] The last equality follows by iterated integration of monomials over a simplex. Removing the corner from $\Sigma $, whose volume is $1/n!$, and applying ( 11.43.4 ) gives ( 11.43.11 ). Since $n\geq 2$, one has $\kappa _ n<1$. $\square$

title: 11.43.14 Positive mass with a degenerate smooth residual
search_title: Positive mass with a degenerate smooth residual
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: A second family has a logarithmic pole whose resolution leaves a smooth residual form degenerating along a different exceptional divisor. Let $o=[1:0:\cdots :0]$ as in subsection 11.43.9 , and fix $q\ne o$ in $\mathbb P^ n$. On $X=\operatorname {Bl}_ q\mathbb P^ n$, keep $\Theta =\pi ^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$. For $0<t<1$, put \[  \psi _ t=t\log \frac{\sum _{i=1}^ n|Z_ i|^2}{\sum _{i=0}^ n|Z_ i|^2}, \qquad K_ t=\{ p\in \Sigma :\textstyle \sum _ i p_ i\geq t\} .  \] On $T$, the function $\psi _ t+L$, a potential of $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ t$, equals $(1-t)L+t\log \sum _ i\mathrm{e}^{x_ i}$. It differs by a bounded function from \[  (1-t)h_\Sigma +t\max _ i x_ i=h_{K_ t},\qquad K_ t=(1-t)\Sigma +t\operatorname {conv}(e_1,\ldots ,e_ n).  \] Thus $\psi _ t\sim \psi _{K_ t}\sim \Phi _{K_ t}$, and $n!\operatorname {Vol}_ n(K_ t)=1-t^ n$. We call $\psi _ t$ the prototype of this ordinary type. Proposition 11.43.15 . C9CD848ECB1A Let $\tau :Z\to X$ be the blowup of the point of $X$ above $o$, with exceptional divisor $E_ o$, and denote the inverse image of $E_ q$ in $Z$ again by $E_ q$. There is a smooth semipositive closed form $\alpha _ t$ on $Z$ such that B2ABC5CB86A3 11.43.16 \begin{equation}  (\pi \circ \tau )^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}} +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi _ t\circ \pi \circ \tau )=\alpha _ t+t[E_ o]. \end{equation} It is positive away from $E_ q$, has rank exactly one at every point of $E_ q$, and satisfies $\int _ Z\alpha _ t^ n=1-t^ n>0$. Moreover, for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\Theta )$ with the ordinary type of $\pi ^*\Phi _{K_ t}$, in particular for every solution of the equation in this type, the function $u\circ \tau -\psi _ t\circ \pi \circ \tau $ extends from $Z\setminus E_ o$ to a bounded $\alpha _ t$-plurisubharmonic function on $Z$. Proof. On $Y=\operatorname {Bl}_ o\mathbb P^ n$, let $\pi _ o$ be the blowdown map and $Q_ o:Y\to \mathbb P^{n-1}$ the map induced by the linear projection from $o$. As in the proof of lemma 11.43.3 , the incidence graph embedding shows that \[  \beta _ t=(1-t)\pi _ o^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}} +tQ_ o^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS},n-1}  \] is a Kähler form, where $\omega _{\mathrm{FS},n-1}$ is the Fubini–Study form of $\mathbb P^{n-1}$. Since the two centers are distinct, $Z$ is also the blowup $\sigma :Z\to Y$ of the point above $q$. Put $\alpha _ t=\sigma ^*\beta _ t$. The Poincaré–Lelong formula gives ( 11.43.16 ); there is no term along $E_ q$, since $\psi _ t$ is locally bounded near $q$. In a blowup chart, $\sigma $ is $(s,w_2,\ldots ,w_ n)\mapsto (s,sw_2,\ldots ,sw_ n)$. At $s=0$ its differential has rank one and kills the $n-1$ tangent directions of $E_ q$. Positivity of $\beta _ t$ therefore gives the assertion about the rank; off $E_ q$ the map is biholomorphic. Write $H=\pi _ o^*[\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}]$ and $E=[E_ o]$ for the cohomology classes on $Y$. The current identity gives $[\beta _ t]=H-tE$. Since $H|_{E_ o}=0$, all mixed top intersections vanish. The normal bundle of $E_ o\cong \mathbb P^{n-1}$ is $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{n-1}}(-1)$, so $\int _ YE^ n=(-1)^{n-1}$. Therefore \[  \int _ Z\alpha _ t^ n=\int _ Y(H-tE)^ n=1-t^ n.  \] The first equality holds because $\sigma $ has degree one. Finally, if $u\sim \pi ^*\Phi _{K_ t}\sim \pi ^*\psi _ t$, then $u\circ \tau $ differs from the pulled-back prototype $\psi _ t\circ \pi \circ \tau $ by a bounded function off $E_ o$. By ( 11.43.16 ), after adding a local potential of $\alpha _ t$ this bounded difference becomes plurisubharmonic off $E_ o$, and it extends across $E_ o$ by lemma 5.24.7 . No Monge–Ampère product of unbounded potentials is involved. $\square$ Corollary 11.43.17 . FB3A15C67170 Let $t_ j,t\in [t_{\min },t_{\max }]\subset (0,1)$ with $t_ j\to t$, and let $r_ j>0$ tend to $r>0$. The references $r_ j\pi ^*\Phi _{K_{t_ j}}$ satisfy the hypotheses of theorem 11.43.6 , so in particular the equation is solvable in the limiting ordinary type, and \[  \sup _ G|B_ j(G)-B(G)| \leq n|\log (r_ j/r)|+ \frac{nt_{\max }^{n-1}}{1-t_{\max }^ n}|t_ j-t|.  \] At continuous tests, all supporting sets consist of the normalized exponential probabilities of that theorem. At the endpoint $t=1$, where the mass vanishes, no equation with a positive bounded density is solvable in the ordinary type of the prototype $\pi ^*\psi _1$. Proof. Choose $p_{*,i}=t_{\max }/n$ and $\delta =(1-t_{\max })/2$; then $p_*+\delta \Sigma $ lies in every $K_ t$ with $t\leq t_{\max }$. For $s\geq t$, moving a point of $K_ t$ toward a vertex $e_ i$ until its coordinate sum reaches $s$ gives \[  d_ H(K_ s,K_ t)\leq \frac{\sqrt2}{1-t_{\max }}|s-t|.  \] Hence the stability theorem applies. Instead of its general bound, the derivative bound for $\log (1-t^ n)$ on $[t_{\min },t_{\max }]$ and the mass formula give the sharper estimate for the functionals. At $t=1$, the resolved residual form $\alpha _1$ is pulled back from $\mathbb P^{n-1}$, so $\int _ Z\alpha _1^ n=0$. The argument of proposition 11.43.15 shows that every potential of the ordinary type of $\pi ^*\psi _1$ has a bounded $\alpha _1$-plurisubharmonic remainder. Stokes' theorem for bounded products in a closed background gives this remainder mass zero, and positivity forces its Monge–Ampère measure to vanish. Thus no such potential can solve the equation with density $c\mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V$ for bounded $F$ and $c>0$. In contrast, the endpoint $a=1$ in corollary 11.43.13 has positive mass and remains solvable. $\square$ Scaling by $r>0$ multiplies both the resolved residual form and the divisor coefficient by $r$. Solvability is obtained on $X$ through the criterion of theorem 11.42.1 , without requiring the resolved residual form to be strictly positive. These criteria use closed projective backgrounds and fixed modifications; we do not know analogous convergence criteria for general nonclosed Hermitian backgrounds, for moving modifications, or for unrestricted degenerations of the singularities. Moreover, the supporting probabilities here only identify the limiting functional: we make no claim about convergence of the solutions or of weighted adjoint products.

title: 11.44.4 A norm defined by the critical scalar
search_title: A norm defined by the critical scalar
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality

text: Mixed products turn the comparison of critical scalars into a triangle inequality for $n$th roots of densities, and the subsolution estimate associated with the strict barrier gives continuity in the corresponding Lebesgue norm. Fix $1<q<p$ and set $\ell =nq$. On real $L^\ell (\mathrm{d}V)$ define \[  N(a)= \begin{cases}  c(|a|^ n)^{-1/n},& a\ne 0,\\  0,& a=0. \end{cases}  \] Proposition 11.44.5 . 91FDE4AB5C22 The function $N$ is a lattice norm on $L^\ell (\mathrm{d}V)$, that is, a norm satisfying $N(a)\leq N(b)$ whenever $|a|\leq |b|$. There is $C_ q<\infty $, depending only on $X,\theta ,\mathrm{d}V$ and $q$, such that 8267EBDA38A9 11.44.6 \begin{equation}  N(a)\leq C_ q\| a\| _\ell ,\qquad |N(a)-N(b)|\leq C_ q\| a-b\| _\ell . \end{equation} Consequently, for nonzero $g,h\geq 0$ in $L^ q$, \[  |c(g)^{-1/n}-c(h)^{-1/n}| \leq C_ q\| g-h\| _ q^{1/n}.  \] Proof. If a potential $v$ of minimal type satisfies $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (v)\geq d g\, \mathrm{d}V$, then $d\leq c(g)$, since otherwise comparison with a critical potential for $g$ contradicts part (1) of corollary 15.13.3 . Hence $g\leq h$ implies $c(g)\geq c(h)$. Uniqueness of the critical scalar also gives $c(tg)=c(g)/t$ for $t>0$. These facts prove that $N$ is monotone and absolutely homogeneous, and positivity follows from $0<c(g)<\infty $. For the triangle inequality, let $a,b\geq 0$ be nonzero, put $A=N(a)$ and $B=N(b)$, and choose critical potentials $v_ a,v_ b$ with measures $(a/A)^ n\mathrm{d}V$ and $(b/B)^ n\mathrm{d}V$. On every relatively compact subset of $\Omega $, ( 5.28.9 ) gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta \left(\frac{A v_ a+B v_ b}{A+B}\right) \geq \left(\frac{a+b}{A+B}\right)^ n\mathrm{d}V,  \] where both potentials are locally bounded. Exhausting $\Omega $ gives the inequality on $X$, since $X\setminus \Omega $ has zero smooth volume. The averaged potential has minimal type, so the first paragraph gives $N(a+b)\leq A+B$. The cases where $a$ or $b$ vanishes are trivial, and for real functions we use $|a+b|\leq |a|+|b|$ and monotonicity. Next, apply lemma 15.14.1 with $\eta =V_\theta $ to nonnegative densities of $L^ q$ norm at most one. It gives a uniform $m>0$ and subsolutions of minimal type, hence $c(g)\geq m$ for each such nonzero density. For $a\ne 0$, take $g=|a|^ n/\| a\| _\ell ^ n$, which has $L^ q$ norm one. Homogeneity gives $N(a)\leq m^{-1/n}\| a\| _\ell $, which is the first bound in ( 11.44.6 ), and the reverse triangle inequality gives the second. Applying the second bound to $g^{1/n},h^{1/n}$ and using $|g^{1/n}-h^{1/n}|^ n\leq |g-h|$ proves the last assertion. $\square$

Hence $g\leq h$ implies $c(g)\geq c(h)$. Uniqueness of the critical scalar also gives $c(tg)=c(g)/t$ for $t>0$. These facts prove that $N$ is monotone and absolutely homogeneous, and positivity follows from $0<c(g)<\infty $. For the triangle inequality, let $a,b\geq 0$ be nonzero, put $A=N(a)$ and $B=N(b)$, and choose critical potentials $v_ a,v_ b$ with measures $(a/A)^ n\mathrm{d}V$ and $(b/B)^ n\mathrm{d}V$. On every relatively compact subset of $\Omega $, ( 5.28.9 ) gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta \left(\frac{A v_ a+B v_ b}{A+B}\right) \geq \left(\frac{a+b}{A+B}\right)^ n\mathrm{d}V,  \] where both potentials are locally bounded. Exhausting $\Omega $ gives the inequality on $X$, since $X\setminus \Omega $ has zero smooth volume. The averaged potential has minimal type, so the first paragraph gives $N(a+b)\leq A+B$. The cases where $a$ or $b$ vanishes are trivial, and for real functions we use $|a+b|\leq |a|+|b|$ and monotonicity. Next, apply lemma 15.14.1 with $\eta =V_\theta $ to nonnegative densities of $L^ q$ norm at most one. It gives a uniform $m>0$ and subsolutions of minimal type, hence $c(g)\geq m$ for each such nonzero density. For $a\ne 0$, take $g=|a|^ n/\| a\| _\ell ^ n$, which has $L^ q$ norm one. Homogeneity gives $N(a)\leq m^{-1/n}\| a\| _\ell $, which is the first bound in ( 11.44.6 ), and the reverse triangle inequality gives the second. Applying the second bound to $g^{1/n},h^{1/n}$ and using $|g^{1/n}-h^{1/n}|^ n\leq |g-h|$ proves the last assertion. $\square$

Lemma 11.44.19 . 0E0F3A0EC129 The functional $\mathcal F_{\lambda ,x}$ is finite, concave, decreasing and $\lambda ^{-1}$-Lipschitz for the uniform norm on $C(X)$. It satisfies \[  \mathcal F_{\lambda ,x}(0)=w_\lambda (x),\qquad \mathcal F_{\lambda ,x}(r+b) =\mathcal F_{\lambda ,x}(r)-b/\lambda .  \] There is a probability measure $
u _{\lambda ,x}$ such that, for every $r\in C(X)$ and every $s$ admissible for $r$ in ( 11.44.18 ), D8630F60DEBD 11.44.20  egin{equation}  \lambda s(x)+\int _ Xr\, \mathrm{d}
u _{\lambda ,x} \leq \lambda w_\lambda (x). \end{equation} Proof. By part (2) of corollary 15.13.3 , $w_\lambda $ is the greatest admissible potential for $r=0$. If $m=\min _ Xr$ and $M=\max _ Xr$, then $w_\lambda -M/\lambda $ is admissible for $r$, and translating any potential admissible for $r$ by $m/\lambda $ makes it admissible for $r=0$. Hence \[  w_\lambda (x)-M/\lambda \leq \mathcal F_{\lambda ,x}(r) \leq w_\lambda (x)-m/\lambda .  \] The mixed density inequality on $\Omega $ and the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality show that a convex combination of potentials admissible for $r_0$ and $r_1$ is admissible for the same convex combination of the forcing terms. Approximating the two suprema at $x$ proves concavity. Inclusion of the admissible classes proves monotonicity, and translation by constants proves the translation rule and the Lipschitz bound. Now apply the Hahn–Banach construction in the proof of theorem 11.34.2 to $-\lambda \mathcal F_{\lambda ,x}$ at zero. This functional is finite, continuous, convex and increasing, and it satisfies $-\lambda \mathcal F_{\lambda ,x}(r+b)=-\lambda \mathcal F_{\lambda ,x}(r)+b$ for constants $b$. The same tests with nonnegative functions and constants show that its subgradient is a probability measure $
u _{\lambda ,x}$. The resulting supporting inequality, combined with $s(x)\leq \mathcal F_{\lambda ,x}(r)$, gives ( 11.44.20 ); it is not necessary that the supremum be attained. $\square$

section: 11.45 Selection for logarithmic models on products
text: For a logarithmic reference with a positive residual background, removing the divisor turns the singular exponential equation into a bounded equation. On a product with a curve, the selected residual can then be determined by the Green operator. This also controls simultaneous changes of the reference, background and density, for which the centering constant must follow the changing data. Let $(Y,\kappa )$ be a connected compact Hermitian manifold of dimension $k\geq 1$, with $\int _ Y\kappa ^ k=1$, and put $X=\mathbb P^1\times Y$, $N=k+1$. Write $\omega _1$ for the mass-one Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^1$ and $\mathrm{d}W=\omega _1\wedge \kappa ^ k$; pullbacks to $X$ are implicit. Fix $a,d>0$, a smooth positive nonconstant function $b$ on $\mathbb P^1$, and a continuous positive function $H$ on $\mathbb P^1$. Set \[  \begin{aligned}  \theta & =(a+d)\omega _1+b\kappa ,& \eta & =a\omega _1+b\kappa ,\\  f& =N b^ kH,& m& =\int _{\mathbb P^1}H\omega _1,\qquad c_0=\frac am. \end{aligned}  \] Both forms are positive and nonclosed: the component $\mathrm{d}b\wedge \kappa $ of horizontal degree one cannot cancel the vertical component $b\, \mathrm{d}\kappa $. For homogeneous coordinates $[Z_0:Z_1]$, put \[  \ell =\frac{|Z_0|^2}{|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2},\qquad D=\{ Z_0=0\} \times Y,\qquad \psi =d\log \ell .  \] The Poincaré–Lelong formula gives $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\eta +d[D]$.

text: Put $K=a+d$, $R=a/d$ and $C_*=K\log (K/d)-a\log (a/d)$. In the coordinate $z=Z_1/Z_0$ define 254FB5175831 11.45.2 \begin{equation}  \phi _{a,d}=\begin{cases}  0,& |z|^2\leq R,\\  a\log |z|^2+C_*-K\log (1+|z|^2),& |z|^2>R, \end{cases} \qquad \phi _{a,d}|_ D=-\infty . \end{equation} Proposition 11.45.3 . DA11AEC1C7C7 The function $\phi _{a,d}$ is an ordinary model reference for $\theta $, with \[  P_\theta [\psi ]=P_\theta [\phi _{a,d}]=\phi _{a,d},\qquad \psi \leq \phi _{a,d}\leq \psi +C_*,\qquad \sup _ X\phi _{a,d}=0.  \] For $d/(a+d)<\delta <1$, the envelope $P_{\delta \theta }(\phi _{a,d})$ is not identically $-\infty $. The model has finite positive Monge–Ampère measure \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (\phi _{a,d}) =N b^ kK\mathbf1_{\{ |z|^2<R\} }\, \mathrm{d}W.  \] The difference $\phi _{a,d}-\psi $ extends continuously across $D$. If $(a_ j,d_ j)\to (a,d)$ in $(0,+\infty )^2$, these residual extensions converge uniformly. Proof. First take the ordinary envelope on the curve with background $K\omega _1$ and obstacle $\min (\psi +C,0)$. Rotation of $z$ preserves both the obstacle and the admissible family, so the envelope is rotation invariant. With $s=\log |z|^2$ and $F(s)=K\log (1+\mathrm{e}^ s)$, its profile plus $F$ is convex and lies below $F$. The comparison with $\psi +C$ bounds its final slope by $a$. At $s_*=\log R$, one has $F'(s_*)=a$. Above $s_*$, convexity and the final slope bound give \[  u(s)+F(s)\leq F(s_*)+a(s-s_*),  \] and below $s_*$ the obstacle gives $u\leq 0$. The function in ( 11.45.2 ) attains both bounds. Its convex profile, including its logarithmic value at infinity, gives a curve potential, and direct calculation gives $\psi \leq \phi _{a,d}\leq \psi +C_*$. It is therefore a competitor for every $C\geq C_*$, so the curve envelope is exactly $\phi _{a,d}$. A product competitor restricts to each curve $\mathbb P^1\times \{ y\} $ as either the constant $-\infty $ or a curve competitor. It is thus bounded above by $\phi _{a,d}$. Conversely, the curve model is a product competitor because the vertical form $b\kappa $ is positive. Hence the product envelope is the same function. Ordinary-type invariance of the singularity envelope gives its model property. Moreover, \[  \delta \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =(\delta K-d)\omega _1+\delta b\kappa +d[D]\geq 0,  \] which proves the smaller-background assertion. Off $D$, the horizontal curvature of $\phi _{a,d}$ is $K\mathbf1_{\{ |z|^2<R\} }\omega _1$. The first derivatives of its convex profile agree at $R$, so there is no boundary-circle atom. Expanding the product off $D$ gives the displayed measure, and the non-pluripolar product assigns $D$ zero mass. Finally, in terms of $\ell $ the residual extension is \[  \phi _{a,d}-\psi =\begin{cases}  -d\log \ell ,& \ell \geq d/K,\\  a\log (1-\ell )+C_*,& \ell <d/K. \end{cases}  \] The formulas agree at the moving interface and extend to both endpoints. On compact positive parameter ranges each logarithm is used away from its singular endpoint. Joint continuity on the resulting compact set proves uniform variation. $\square$ Lemma 11.45.4 . 688DA0FB893F For every $\sigma >0$, the equation D9B5F3712AAE 11.45.5 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (s_\sigma )=\mathrm{e}^{\sigma s_\sigma }f\, \mathrm{d}W \end{equation} has a solution of ordinary type $\phi _{a,d}$, unique in that type. It is the greatest exponential subsolution among all $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\preceq \phi _{a,d}$, and its measure has finite mass. Proof. The one-sided ordinary class has the description 37E96D4A1D80 11.45.6 \begin{equation}  u\preceq \psi \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad u=\psi +r,\quad r\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta ),\qquad \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (\psi +r) =\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\eta (r). \end{equation} Indeed, $u\preceq \psi $ gives $\nu (u,D)\geq d$. Divisorial removal, lemma 5.38.1 , shows that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-d[D]\geq 0$. Thus the locally integrable difference $u-\psi $ has an $\eta $-plurisubharmonic representative $r$. The equality $u=\psi +r$ holds off $D$ by canonical equality and on $D$ because both sides equal $-\infty $. Conversely, adding $\psi $ to $r$ adds the positive current $d[D]$; since $r$ has a finite compact upper bound, the one-sided comparison follows. Off $D$ the currents agree, so finite-level locality identifies their extended products, including at any additional poles of $r$. Both measures give $D$ zero mass, proving the global equality. The bounded ordinary type corresponds exactly to bounded $r$, as in theorem 11.41.1 . The function $g_\sigma =\mathrm{e}^{\sigma \psi }f$ extends continuously by zero on $D$ and is positive elsewhere. Since $\eta >0$, theorem 14.19.3 gives a continuous solution $R_\sigma $ of \[  \mathrm{MA}_\eta (R_\sigma )=\mathrm{e}^{\sigma R_\sigma }g_\sigma \, \mathrm{d}W.  \] For this bounded density, the greatest solution of theorem 15.35.2 is bounded and coincides with $R_\sigma $ by corollary 14.19.12 . Thus it dominates every $\eta $-plurisubharmonic exponential subsolution. The correspondence ( 11.45.6 ) transfers this order to the entire one-sided ordinary class and gives $s_\sigma =\psi +R_\sigma $. Bounded residual uniqueness gives uniqueness in the ordinary type. The bounded residual equation has finite mass, so the singular equation does too. $\square$
